docs.title: Odoo Developer Handbook
docs.text:
A handbook for people who write Odoo modules. It starts with the Python, SQL and web basics that Odoo code relies on, then covers the ORM, security, views, the frontend, backend logic, testing and migration, and ends with complete modules.

Read online: GitBook or GitHub Pages.

Odoo 18 is the reference version. Differences in 16, 17 and 20 are marked in version notes. Odoo 20 ships OWL 3, so the frontend differs a lot from 18; the chapter OWL 3 and Odoo 20 covers the port.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text: Part What it covers Python for Odoo The language, limited to what Odoo code uses PostgreSQL for Odoo SQL, indexes, transactions, locks, the Odoo schema Web basics HTML, CSS, JavaScript, HTTP, XML Odoo architecture Installation, module layout, the registry, the request lifecycle, Odoo.sh Shell and debugging odoo shell, scripts, logging, debuggers, profiling, common errors The ORM Fields, recordsets, search, inheritance, overrides Security Access rights, record rules, field access, multi-company, secure coding Data and views XML data, views, XPath inheritance, wizards, reports, cron Frontend and JavaScript OWL, assets, patching, widgets, portal pages, tours, tests Backend logic Controllers, state machines, concurrency, APIs, synchronisation Testing and quality Tests, coding standards, git workflow Migration and versions What changed between versions, upgrading modules and databases Blueprints Complete example modules Reference Cheat sheets and catalogues

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• New to programming: Python for Odoo, in order.
  • Know Python, new to Odoo: Odoo architecture, then the ORM.
  • Debugging something now: Shell and debugging, then the common errors chapter.
  • Upgrading a module: Migration and versions.

Examples use a small teaching module called library (library.book, library.loan). The conventions chapter lists its models and naming.

docs.title: Conventions and version notes
docs.text: This chapter lists the notation used in the book: how code, commands and placeholders are written, what each hint colour means, how version differences between Odoo 16 and 20 are marked, and what the teaching module library is.

docs.title: Code and commands
docs.text:
Code blocks carry a language tag (python, xml, js, bash, sql, text, json). A block is one of three kinds, and the text around it says which:

  • Runnable: complete enough to run as written. Python snippets run in a plain interpreter or the Odoo shell; JavaScript snippets run in Node as .mjs files (or the browser console when marked // browser); SQL runs in psql.
  • Fragment: a piece of a larger file, marked with a comment such as # fragment or <!-- fragment -->. It shows the lines that matter and omits imports, surrounding classes, or manifest entries.
  • Output: plain text blocks, or trailing # ... comments that show what a statement prints.

Shell commands are written for Bash. A line beginning with $ is not used: commands are shown without a prompt so they can be copied. Long commands break with a trailing backslash:

odoo-bin -d <db> -i library \
  --stop-after-init \
  --log-level=info

On Windows PowerShell, the line continuation is the backtick, environment variables are set with $env:NAME = "value", and paths use backslashes. Where a Windows variation matters, the text gives it. In SQL examples, psql meta-commands (\d table) are used where they are shorter than the catalogue query.

Inline names use code font: library.book, partner_id, res.partner, action_library_book, odoo-bin. File paths use forward slashes: library/models/book.py.

Ellipsis (...) inside code means "omitted here", never valid syntax to copy. In Python, a literal Ellipsis is never used in the book's examples.

Python style follows the project coding standards covered in the testing part: four-space indentation, double or single quotes consistently within a file, and Odoo naming conventions (_name = "library.book", method names action_*, _compute_*, _onchange_*, _check_*). JavaScript style uses ES modules, const/let, double quotes, semicolons, and four spaces in Odoo-facing code but two in short generic snippets for width.

Command safety. Commands that change data are always preceded by their read-only counterpart. If the book shows UPDATE, you will see the SELECT with the same WHERE first. If it shows -u library, it first shows how to check what the update would touch. Copy the habit.

docs.title: Placeholders
docs.text:
Angle brackets mark a value you replace. They are never typed literally.

Placeholder Means Example value <db> Name of a PostgreSQL database library_dev <model> Technical model name library.book <module> Technical module name (directory name) library <field> A field name on a model year <xml_id> Full external identifier module.name library.book_dune <login>, <password> Credentials; never commit real ones <uid> Numeric user id 2 <host>, <port> Network address of a server localhost, 8069 <path> A filesystem path you choose <version> An Odoo version number 18.0 <ids> A list of record ids [1, 2, 3]

All names, people, and numbers in examples are invented. Example people are "Ann" and "Bob"; example books are well-known public-domain titles. Hosts are localhost or example.com-style reserved names. No example contains a real client, a real company, or real data, and neither should yours when you copy it into a ticket or a forum post.

docs.title: Hints
docs.text:
Hint boxes have fixed meanings:

Info. Background, a version note, or a pointer to another chapter. Safe to skip on a first read.

Warning. A pitfall that costs time: a behaviour that looks like it works and does not, or that works only in certain conditions.

Danger. Data loss, a security hole, or a breaking change. If you ignore a danger hint, the damage may not be reversible.

Success. The recommended practice when several options exist.

Tabs, where used, separate per-version or per-operating-system variants of the same step. They are never used for content that every reader needs.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text: A "Try it" section ends most chapters. Solutions sit inside <details markdown="1"><summary>Solution</summary> ... </details> blocks, which render as folds in GitBook and in any Markdown viewer that supports HTML.

docs.title: Version notes
docs.text: The book covers Odoo 16 through 20 (the number is the major version; each release is <number>.0). Text is written for Odoo 18 unless it says otherwise, and differences in other versions are marked.

docs.title: How differences are marked
docs.text:
1. An info hint headed "Versions" for a difference that changes how you write code but does not break old code:

!!! info "" Versions: the view root <tree> was replaced by <list> in 18. Version 17 and earlier require <tree>.

  1. A danger hint for a breaking change: code written for one version fails or silently misbehaves on another.

!!! danger "" Versions: view attributes attrs and states were removed in 17. Code that uses them loads in 16 and fails in 17 and later.

  1. A "Versions" section at the end of a chapter when the differences are several and belong together. The chapter "Version differences, 16 to 20" in the migration part collects them across the whole book, and "Deprecations and replacements" lists the old name next to the new one.

  2. Tabs for side-by-side code that differs between versions, so you can read your own version and ignore the other.

A statement without a version mark holds for every version in scope. If a hint says "Odoo 17 and later", it holds from 17 to the newest verified release unless a later hint says otherwise. Where a behaviour is the same but a name changed, the text gives both names.

The details are in the chapters where they occur.

docs.title: What was checked, and where
docs.text:
Standard Odoo names (models, fields, XML ids, methods, templates) were checked in the Odoo source before they were used. Odoo 18 is the main reference; chapters for the security and frontend parts also checked the Odoo 20 source, and version notes for 16 and 17 come from the 16.0 and 17.0 branches. Where a detail varies between releases and could not be confirmed, the text says "check the source for your version".

Behaviour is claimed for a version only if it was checked in that version.

Odoo 20 changed several things that matter to module authors:

Odoo 20 ships OWL 3: static props becomes useProps, useState becomes proxy, refs are signals and templates address members with this.. On the server side, groups move from category_id to a privilege, and @route(type='json') is a deprecated alias of type='jsonrpc'. The chapters of the frontend and security parts mark each case. Chapters not yet revised against Odoo 20 say nothing specific about it, so check your own installation.

docs.title: Checking your version
docs.text:
# From the installation directory
python odoo-bin --version

# From the Odoo shell
env["ir.module.module"].search([("name", "=", "base")]).latest_version

# From the source
grep version_info odoo/release.py

The first prints the series (for example Odoo Server 18.0). The shell command reads the installed version of the base module in the current database, which can lag the source after a code upgrade until you run -u base. Odoo.sh exposes the version in the branch settings. Learn which of these your team trusts and use it.

docs.title: Editions and platforms
docs.text: Odoo exists as Community and Enterprise, and as Odoo Online and Odoo.sh. The book covers what a module developer meets in Community and notes where behaviour needs Enterprise or depends on the platform (Odoo.sh restrictions are in their own chapter). Enterprise modules are not available for inspection in every setup; when the text refers to an Enterprise-only feature it says so.

docs.title: The neutral teaching module: library
docs.text:
Almost every example in the book uses a small module called library. It exists only to teach, so that no example drags in a real business's rules.

Models:

Model Purpose Notable fields library.book A title in the catalogue name, isbn, year, author_id, tag_ids, copies, state library.loan A book lent to a member name, book_id, member_id, date_out, date_due, date_back, state, line_ids library.loan.line One line of a loan loan_id, book_id, copies library.tag A label for books name, color

Members are standard partners (res.partner), authors too. Using real standard models next to the invented ones lets examples show relationships to things that exist in every installation.

External IDs follow a fixed pattern so they can be recognised: library.book_dune is a demo book, library.library_book_view_form is a form view (<module>_<model>_view_<type>), library.action_library_book is a window action, library.menu_library_books is a menu, library.group_library_manager is a security group. Example people: Ann and Bob. Example books: Dune, Emma, Ulysses.

The library module is not an installable package you must obtain; the Blueprints part builds it from scratch, and every chapter's snippets are self-explanatory without it. When a snippet uses a field of library.book, the field is shown or its type is evident from use.

When a standard Odoo model is the better teacher (a sale order for extending a workflow, a partner for relationships), the chapter uses it and says so.

docs.title: Terms used consistently
docs.text:
A few words are used in one sense only, to avoid confusion:

  • Module and addon: an Odoo module is a directory with a manifest; "addon" refers to the same thing in the context of the addons path. The book uses "module" for the thing you write and "addons path" for where Odoo finds them.
  • Record is one database row of a model; recordset is an ordered collection of records of one model (possibly empty, possibly one).
  • Model is the Python class and its database table; table is only the database side.
  • XML ID (also external ID) is the module.name identifier stored in ir.model.data.
  • Backend is the web client used by internal users, website the public pages, portal the logged-in customer area.
  • Staging and production are environments; "production" is never changed without a copy-first plan.

The glossary in the reference part defines the rest.

docs.title: When you find a mistake
docs.text: If a name does not exist in your version, an example does not run, or the source contradicts a statement, reproduce it on a scratch database, note your version and the exact error, compare with the source of your installation, and open an issue.

docs.title: How to read this book
docs.text: The book takes someone who has written some code in any language to the point of building, extending, debugging and deploying Odoo modules: business logic, security, views, reports, a frontend component and integrations. Nobody reads it front to back. This chapter lists what you need, which parts to read for which job, how a chapter is laid out, and how to work through the exercises.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A terminal. You can change directories, run a command, read its output and edit a text file. Shell examples use Bash. On Windows, use Git Bash or WSL; the text notes where PowerShell differs.
  • Some programming. Variables, loops and functions should not be new. Python and JavaScript are taught from the start in parts 1 and 3, at a pace that assumes you know what a function is.
  • The ability to install software. Part 4 covers installing Odoo and PostgreSQL. You still deal with your system's package manager and a Python virtual environment.
  • Reading English. Error messages, source code and the Odoo community are in English.

You do not need to know Odoo as a user. "The Odoo mental model" explains what Odoo is made of before you write anything.

docs.title: Reading paths
docs.text:
You are Read first Then Skip or skim New to programming and to Odoo Start Here, Python for Odoo, the first four PostgreSQL chapters Web basics, Odoo architecture, Shell and debugging, The ORM, the first Blueprint Migration, until you need it A Python developer new to Odoo Start Here, the Odoo mental model, Odoo architecture The ORM, Data and views, Security, Shell and debugging Python for Odoo except decorators and super; skim the SQL part A web developer new to Odoo Start Here, Odoo architecture, The ORM Data and views, Frontend and JavaScript, Backend logic Web basics An Odoo user turning developer Start Here, Python for Odoo, Odoo architecture The ORM, Data and views, a Blueprint Frontend, until the ORM and views make sense An Odoo developer on older versions Migration and versions, Deprecations The frontend part (OWL) Python and SQL basics Maintaining production Shell and debugging, PostgreSQL (locks, transactions, psql), Backend logic (concurrency, queues) Security, Odoo.sh and deployment Frontend Building integrations Web basics (HTTP and JSON), Backend logic (APIs, webhooks, sync) Security, Testing Views and frontend

For a first working module quickly: the Odoo mental model, Anatomy of a module, Models and recordsets, Form views, Actions and menus, with the first Blueprint open next to them.

Parts depend only on earlier parts, with two exceptions. The ORM part uses SQL ideas from the joins and transactions chapters. "Data and views" mentions JavaScript behaviour that "Frontend and JavaScript" explains. A chapter that needs something from later points to it.

docs.title: How a chapter is laid out
docs.text:
1. Opening paragraph. The problem the chapter solves. If you do not have that problem, skip the chapter.
  2. Material. Concepts with the reason behind each rule, then examples you can run.
  3. Hints. Coloured boxes; the conventions chapter lists what each colour means.
  4. Versions. A section or hint, only where Odoo 16 to 20 differ.
  5. Pitfalls. Failures that cost real time.
  6. Try it. Three to five exercises, solutions behind a fold.

Reference chapters at the end (cheat sheets, catalogues, glossary) are for lookup and do not follow this layout.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
1. Read the exercise and keep the solution closed. Predict the answer or write the code.
  2. Run it with node, python, psql, curl or an Odoo shell. If your result differs from the solution, run both and compare the output.
  3. Open the solution and compare the approach as well as the result. Some exercises have more than one valid answer, and the solution names the trade-off.
  4. Break it: remove a closing tag, drop an await, rename a field, and read the error. The Shell and debugging part lists the common ones.

Keep a scratch folder outside any addons path and a scratch database you can drop. Data-changing commands in the book always come after the read-only query for the same data.

docs.title: Building a project alongside
docs.text: The Blueprints part builds complete modules on the library teaching module. Pick a small module you actually want (a loan tracker, a checklist on a standard form, a PDF with a total, a portal page) and build it as you read. When something is unclear, find the chapter in the table of contents, read the material and the pitfalls, and continue.

docs.title: Where each kind of work is covered
docs.text:
The work Where Understand a request and where it belongs in Odoo The Odoo mental model, Business logic design Set up a machine, a database, Odoo Odoo architecture; PostgreSQL for Odoo (psql and operations) Define data: models, fields, constraints The ORM; Fields reference; Constraints and defaults Decide who sees and does what Security Menus, forms, lists, search, kanban Data and views PDF reports, email templates QWeb templates; PDF reports; HTML and CSS Workflows, cron, server actions, queues State machines; Scheduled actions; Queues and background work New behaviour in the UI Frontend and JavaScript; Async and the DOM Other systems HTTP and JSON; External APIs; Webhooks; Bidirectional sync Finding out why it fails Shell and debugging; Common errors; Inspecting SQL Speed Cache and prefetch; Performance; Indexes and EXPLAIN; Profiling Tests and upkeep Testing and quality; Git workflow A new Odoo version Migration and versions Shipping and operating Odoo.sh and deployment; Safe bulk scripts

Real tasks cross several rows. Adding a field to the sales order and printing it on the PDF touches the ORM (the field), Data and views (inheritance), PDF reports (QWeb), Security (does it need a group?) and Testing. The Blueprints work through such combinations.

docs.title: Working habits
docs.text:
• Read the error first. Most failures print a traceback or an XML or JS error that names a file and a line. Read the last line, then the nearest frame in your code.
  • Reproduce on a scratch database with only your module installed: cleaner errors, faster restarts.
  • Read the source. When the book names a method or a template, find it under odoo/ and addons/ in your installation. The standard module that already does what you want is the best example.
  • Check the version. Run odoo-bin --version or read odoo/release.py before following a recipe.
  • Keep changes small and reversible. Commit often, run the read-only query before the write, test an upgrade on a copy.

docs.title: What is not covered
docs.text:
The functional side of Odoo (configuring accounting, designing a sales process), the user documentation of each standard app, and Odoo Studio. Reference chapters list what developers need often and show how to find the rest in the source.

If the book and the source of your installed version disagree, trust the source and report the difference.

docs.title: The Odoo mental model
docs.text: Odoo looks like a pile of folders, XML files and decorators until you see the five moving parts and the one rule that connects them: almost everything you write is either a Python class that becomes a table, or a data record that is loaded into one. This page gives you the map. Later chapters fill in each region.

docs.title: The five moving parts
docs.text:
Browser (web client, OWL/JS)
        |  HTTP: JSON-RPC (/web/dataset/call_kw), controllers, assets
        v
 +--------------------------------------------------------------+
 | Odoo server process (Python, one per worker)                 |
 |                                                              |
 |  HTTP layer (werkzeug) --> dispatch --> Environment (env)    |
 |                                            |                 |
 |  Registry (one per database)               v                 |
 |   - model classes, built from modules   ORM: recordsets,     |
 |   - fields, methods, inheritance chain  fields, domains,     |
 |   - view/ACL/rule caches                access checks        |
 +----------------------------|---------------------------------+
                              | SQL (psycopg2), one transaction per request
                              v
                        PostgreSQL
              tables, ir_model_data, ir_ui_view, ir_act_*, ir_rule ...

PostgreSQL holds everything: business data, and also the description of the application itself (views, actions, menus, access rights, translations). A database is an installation. Two databases on the same server can run different module sets.

The server is a Python process that serves HTTP, runs cron jobs and executes your code. It is stateless between requests apart from in-memory caches, which is why you can run several workers against one database. See workers, cron and longpolling.

The registry is a per-database object built at startup. It loads the installed modules in dependency order, collects every class that declares _name or _inherit, merges them into one final class per model, and creates or updates the tables to match. After that, env['library.book'] returns a recordset of the merged class. Details in registry and model loading.

The ORM is the only door to the data you should use. A recordset (self) is an ordered set of ids plus an environment (database cursor, user, context). Reading a field fetches from cache or SQL, writing goes through write(), and every call checks access rights and record rules for the environment's user. See models and recordsets.

The web client is a JavaScript application that knows nothing about your models. It asks the server for a view definition (get_views), then for data (web_search_read, web_read, web_save), and renders what comes back. A form you did not code in JS appears because an XML arch described it.

docs.title: A module is a unit of installation
docs.text:
A module is a directory with a __manifest__.py and a mix of Python, XML/CSV data and static assets:

library/
  __manifest__.py      # name, depends, data (ordered), assets
  models/              # Python classes -> tables, behaviour
  views/               # XML: ir.ui.view, ir.actions.*, ir.ui.menu
  security/            # groups, ir.model.access.csv, record rules
  data/                # reference or demo records
  report/              # QWeb templates and ir.actions.report
  wizard/              # TransientModel classes and their views
  static/              # JS, SCSS, images
  tests/

Installing a module does three things in order: loads its Python so the registry can build models, creates or alters the tables, then loads each file listed in data (and demo when enabled). Upgrading re-runs the data files, which is how an XML change reaches an existing database. See anatomy of a module.

docs.title: Code and data are two halves of one feature
docs.text:
This is the idea beginners miss. A feature is spread over several kinds of artifact, and each is stored differently:

Artifact Written as Stored in Loaded when Model, fields, methods Python class Python import; columns in the table Registry build View, action, menu, report XML record ir_ui_view, ir_act_window, ir_ui_menu, ir_act_report_xml Install / upgrade Access rights CSV or XML record ir_model_access, ir_rule Install / upgrade Reference data, demo data XML/CSV record The model's own table Install / upgrade Translations .po files ir_translation (16) / JSONB columns (17+) Language load

Two consequences follow. First, changing Python needs a server restart, changing XML needs a module upgrade (-u library), and changing both needs both. Second, every XML record gets an external id stored in ir_model_data, for example library.book_form. That row is how a later upgrade finds the record it created before and updates it instead of duplicating it. See XML ids and references.

Versions: translations of field values and view terms moved into JSONB columns in Odoo 16 for fields, and ir_translation was removed for most terms in 17. The mental model is the same: translations are data, not code.

docs.title: How the pieces point at each other
docs.text:
Follow one screen backwards:

  1. A menu (ir.ui.menu) points to an action (ir.actions.act_window).
  2. The action names a model (res_model) and the view types to offer (list, form, ...).
  3. Each view (ir.ui.view) holds an XML arch whose <field name="..."> tags must exist on that model.
  4. When the user opens the screen, the ORM reads those fields, but only after the security layer has answered two questions: may this user's groups read this model (ir.model.access), and which rows may they see (ir.rule)?
  5. A button in the form calls a method on the model by name (type="object"), or runs another action (type="action").

If a link in this chain is wrong you get a precise failure: a missing field breaks view validation at install time, a missing access line gives an access error at first use, a missing menu group makes the menu simply vanish.

docs.title: What happens on a click
docs.text:
A user presses a button labelled "Return". Roughly:

  1. The client sends a JSON-RPC call to /web/dataset/call_kw/library.loan/action_return with record ids and the context.
  2. The HTTP layer authenticates the session, opens a cursor and builds an Environment(cr, uid, context).
  3. The dispatcher looks up the model in the registry, browses the ids, checks that the method is public (no leading underscore), and calls it.
  4. Your method reads and writes through the ORM. Writes are flushed to SQL, computed fields are recomputed, constraints run.
  5. On success the transaction commits. On any exception it rolls back entirely, so a request never leaves half a change behind.
  6. The method returns True, a dict (an action to run next), or a value. The client renders the outcome.

The full path, including the type="http" controllers and report endpoints, is in request lifecycle.

docs.title: Inheritance is how you change what exists
docs.text:
You almost never edit the Odoo source. You extend it, in three forms:

  • Class inheritance (_inherit = 'res.partner') adds fields and overrides methods on an existing model. The registry merges your class into the chain.
  • View inheritance (inherit_id plus xpath) patches another module's XML arch without copying it.
  • Data override (a record with the same external id) replaces values on an existing record.

Because the result is one merged class per model, order matters: the depends list in your manifest decides who is applied first, and super() is how your override cooperates with the layers below. See inheritance.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Treating the database as the source of truth for views. The Python and XML in the module are the source. Editing a view in the UI works until the next upgrade resets it.
  • Forgetting the load order of data. Security files first, then views that reference groups, then menus that reference actions. An XML id used before it is defined fails at install.
  • Running code at import time that touches the database. The registry does not exist yet. Do work inside methods.
  • Bypassing the ORM with raw SQL for convenience. You lose access checks, cache invalidation and computed field triggers. Use it deliberately and flush first.
  • Assuming a restart picks up XML. It does not. Upgrade the module.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Read-only: list what the registry knows about one model and where its views come from.

psql -d mydb -c "select model, name from ir_model where model like 'library.%';"
psql -d mydb -c "select name, model, type, inherit_id from ir_ui_view where model = 'library.book';"
psql -d mydb -c "select module, name, res_id from ir_model_data where model = 'ir.ui.view' and module = 'library';"

The third query shows the external ids that tie your XML files to database rows. Next, see the wizard and report blueprint for all the parts working together in one feature.

docs.title: Classes and inheritance
docs.text: Every Odoo model is a Python class. library.book is a class, a record of it is an object, and a module that extends the model adds methods to it by inheriting. You cannot read or write Odoo code without understanding what self is, where attributes live, how a method is found when several classes define it, and what "overriding" means. This chapter teaches classes from the beginning and ends with the exact inheritance mechanics (the method resolution order) that super() explained builds on.

docs.title: Why classes
docs.text:
A dictionary can represent a book: {"title": "Dune", "pages": 612}. As soon as you want behaviour attached to that data, such as "is this long?", you start writing functions that take a dict and hope every caller builds the dict correctly. A class bundles the data (attributes) and the behaviour (methods) in one definition, and gives you a way to create many consistent objects from it.

>>> class Book:
...     def __init__(self, title, pages):
...         self.title = title
...         self.pages = pages
...
...     def is_long(self, threshold=500):
...         return self.pages > threshold
...
>>> dune = Book("Dune", 612)
>>> dune.title
'Dune'
>>> dune.is_long()
True
>>> Book("Emma", 474).is_long()
False

Terms: Book is the class. dune is an instance (an object) of it. title and pages are attributes. is_long is a method, a function defined inside a class.

docs.title: self and __init__
docs.text:
When you write dune.is_long(), Python calls Book.is_long(dune). The object before the dot becomes the first parameter, conventionally named self. That is all self is: the instance the method was called on.

>>> Book.is_long(dune)
True

__init__ is the initialiser. Python calls it right after creating a new instance, passing the arguments you gave to Book(...). Inside it you set the initial attributes. It must not return a value.

Attributes are created by assignment on self and can be added at any time, even outside the class:

>>> dune.isbn = "978-0441172719"
>>> dune.isbn
'978-0441172719'

That freedom is a trap. A typo creates a new attribute silently (dune.pagez = 5). Odoo models avoid this: fields are declared on the class and the ORM controls what a record has. For plain Python classes, __slots__ or dataclasses (below) tighten things.

docs.title: Instance versus class attributes
docs.text:
An attribute assigned inside a method on self belongs to that one instance. An attribute assigned in the class body belongs to the class and is shared:

>>> class Member:
...     max_loans = 3            # class attribute: shared
...     def __init__(self, name):
...         self.name = name     # instance attribute: one per object
...         self.loans = []
...
>>> ada, bob = Member("ada"), Member("bob")
>>> ada.max_loans, bob.max_loans, Member.max_loans
(3, 3, 3)
>>> Member.max_loans = 5
>>> ada.max_loans
5
>>> ada.max_loans = 1          # creates an instance attribute that hides the class one
>>> ada.max_loans, bob.max_loans
(1, 5)

Lookup goes instance first, then class, then base classes. In an Odoo model, the lines at class level (_name = "library.book", title = fields.Char()) are class attributes; the framework reads them when it builds the model, and records then read field values through a different mechanism, not as plain instance attributes.

Never put a mutable object (list, dict, set) in a class body expecting each instance to get its own. It is shared by all of them, which is the same bug as a mutable default argument. Create per-instance containers in __init__.

docs.title: Representing objects: __repr__ and __str__
docs.text:
By default an object prints as an unhelpful address:

>>> class Plain:
...     pass
...
>>> repr(Plain())[:15]
'<__main__.Plain'

Define __repr__ to return an unambiguous string, ideally one that looks like the constructor call. It is what the REPL, tracebacks, and log messages using %r show. __str__ is the friendlier text for print and str(); if absent, str() falls back to __repr__.

>>> class Book:
...     def __init__(self, title, pages):
...         self.title, self.pages = title, pages
...     def __repr__(self):
...         return f"Book({self.title!r}, {self.pages!r})"
...     def __str__(self):
...         return f"{self.title} ({self.pages} pages)"
...
>>> b = Book("Dune", 612)
>>> b
Book('Dune', 612)
>>> print(b)
Dune (612 pages)
>>> [b]
[Book('Dune', 612)]

Containers display their items with repr, so a good __repr__ makes debugging output readable. Odoo records give you library.book(1,) style reprs, showing the model name and ids, which you will see constantly in logs and the shell.

docs.title: Methods, class methods, static methods
docs.text:
An ordinary method gets the instance as self. Two decorators change that (Decorators explains the mechanism):

>>> class Book:
...     DEFAULT_PAGES = 100
...     def __init__(self, title, pages):
...         self.title, self.pages = title, pages
...
...     @classmethod
...     def from_line(cls, line):
...         """Alternative constructor: build a Book from 'title;pages'."""
...         title, pages = line.split(";")
...         return cls(title, int(pages))
...
...     @staticmethod
...     def normalise_title(raw):
...         return " ".join(raw.split()).title()
...
>>> b = Book.from_line("Dune;612")
>>> b.title, b.pages
('Dune', 612)
>>> Book.normalise_title("  the   hobbit ")
'The Hobbit'
  • @classmethod receives the class as cls. Use it for alternative constructors and for logic that concerns the class, not one object. It works correctly for subclasses, because cls is whichever class it was called on.
  • @staticmethod receives nothing extra. It is a plain function that lives in the class namespace for organisation. If it does not need the class or instance, a module-level function is often better.

Odoo has its own flavour: @api.model marks a method whose self is only a model-level recordset (no specific records), roughly the way classmethod marks "no instance". That relationship is worked out in Decorators.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
A property is a method accessed like an attribute. Use it for derived values and for validation on assignment:

>>> class Loan:
...     def __init__(self, days):
...         self.days = days
...
...     @property
...     def weeks(self):
...         return self.days / 7
...
...     @property
...     def days(self):
...         return self._days
...
...     @days.setter
...     def days(self, value):
...         if value < 0:
...             raise ValueError("days must be >= 0")
...         self._days = value
...
>>> loan = Loan(14)
>>> loan.weeks
2.0
>>> loan.days = 21
>>> loan.weeks
3.0
>>> loan.days = -1
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
ValueError: days must be >= 0

The underscore in _days is a convention: "internal, do not touch from outside". Python has no true private attributes. In Odoo, derived values are not properties but computed fields (fields.Float(compute="_compute_weeks")), because they must be stored, searched, and recomputed when dependencies change. A property is right for plain helper objects.

docs.title: Special ("dunder") methods
docs.text:
Names with double underscores let your class plug into the language:

Method Triggered by __repr__, __str__ repr(x), str(x), print(x) __len__ len(x) __iter__, __next__ for item in x, iter(x) __contains__ item in x __getitem__ x[key], x[1:3] __bool__ if x: (falls back to __len__) __eq__, __lt__, ... x == y, x < y __hash__ hash(x), use as dict key or set member __add__, __sub__, ... x + y, x - y __call__ x(...) __enter__, __exit__ with x:

A small collection class using several of them:

>>> class Shelf:
...     def __init__(self, books=()):
...         self._books = list(books)
...     def __len__(self):
...         return len(self._books)
...     def __iter__(self):
...         return iter(self._books)
...     def __getitem__(self, index):
...         return self._books[index]
...     def __contains__(self, title):
...         return title in self._books
...     def __add__(self, other):
...         return Shelf(self._books + list(other))
...     def __repr__(self):
...         return f"Shelf({self._books!r})"
...
>>> s = Shelf(["Dune", "Emma"])
>>> len(s), "Dune" in s, s[1], list(s)
(2, True, 'Emma', ['Dune', 'Emma'])
>>> s + ["Ulysses"]
Shelf(['Dune', 'Emma', 'Ulysses'])
>>> bool(Shelf()), bool(s)
(False, True)

This is close to how an Odoo recordset behaves: it has a length, iterates to single-record recordsets, supports in, indexing, slicing, + to concatenate, | and & for union and intersection, and is falsy when empty. Recordsets are one of the most important objects in Odoo, and their behaviour comes entirely from dunder methods on a Python class.

docs.title: Equality and hashing
docs.text:
By default two instances are equal only if they are the same object. Define __eq__ to compare by value. If you define __eq__ without __hash__, Python makes the class unhashable, because equal objects must have equal hashes:

>>> class Isbn:
...     def __init__(self, digits):
...         self.digits = digits
...     def __eq__(self, other):
...         return isinstance(other, Isbn) and self.digits == other.digits
...     def __hash__(self):
...         return hash(self.digits)
...
>>> Isbn("123") == Isbn("123"), len({Isbn("123"), Isbn("123")})
(True, 1)

Return NotImplemented (not False) from __eq__ when you do not know how to compare with the other type, so Python can try the reflected operation. The isinstance check above is the simple version.

docs.title: Dataclasses
docs.text:
For classes that mainly hold data, dataclasses writes __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ for you:

>>> from dataclasses import dataclass, field
>>> @dataclass
... class LoanLine:
...     book: str
...     days: int = 14
...     tags: list = field(default_factory=list)
...
>>> line = LoanLine("Dune")
>>> line
LoanLine(book='Dune', days=14, tags=[])
>>> line == LoanLine("Dune", 14)
True
>>> line.tags.append("new")
>>> LoanLine("Emma").tags
[]

field(default_factory=list) gives each instance its own list. A plain tags: list = [] is rejected by dataclasses with a ValueError, which protects you from the shared-mutable-default bug. Options: @dataclass(frozen=True) makes instances immutable and hashable, @dataclass(slots=True) (Python 3.10+) restricts attributes. Use dataclasses for helper structures in your own code, for example a result object from a parsing step. Do not use them for Odoo models.

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
A class can extend another. The new class (the subclass) gets all the attributes and methods of the base class (superclass) and can add or replace them:

>>> class Item:
...     def __init__(self, title):
...         self.title = title
...     def loan_days(self):
...         return 14
...     def describe(self):
...         return f"{self.title} ({self.loan_days()} days)"
...
>>> class Dvd(Item):
...     def loan_days(self):             # override
...         return 7
...
>>> Item("Dune").describe(), Dvd("Alien").describe()
('Dune (14 days)', 'Alien (7 days)')

Dvd did not define __init__ or describe, so it inherits them. Note that describe, defined in Item, calls self.loan_days(), and for a Dvd object self.loan_days finds the override. This is what makes inheritance useful: base code calls a method by name, and subclasses change the behaviour without touching the base code. The language feature that gives Odoo its extension model is exactly this.

isinstance and issubclass test relationships:

>>> d = Dvd("Alien")
>>> isinstance(d, Dvd), isinstance(d, Item), isinstance(d, str)
(True, True, False)
>>> issubclass(Dvd, Item)
True

docs.title: Calling the parent: super()
docs.text:
An override often wants to extend the parent's behaviour rather than replace it. super() gives access to the parent's version:

>>> class Dvd(Item):
...     def __init__(self, title, minutes):
...         super().__init__(title)       # let Item set up title
...         self.minutes = minutes
...     def describe(self):
...         base = super().describe()
...         return f"{base}, {self.minutes} min"
...     def loan_days(self):
...         return 7
...
>>> Dvd("Alien", 117).describe()
'Alien (7 days), 117 min'

Forgetting super().__init__(...) leaves the parent's attributes unset, and the object fails later with AttributeError. That is the single most common inheritance bug. The details of what super() resolves to are the subject of super() explained; here, read it as "the next class up the chain".

docs.title: Abstract-style base classes
docs.text:
Raise NotImplementedError in a base method that every subclass must provide:

>>> class Fee:
...     def amount(self, days_late):
...         raise NotImplementedError
...
>>> class Flat(Fee):
...     def amount(self, days_late):
...         return 2 if days_late > 0 else 0
...
>>> Flat().amount(3)
2
>>> Fee().amount(3)
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
NotImplementedError

The abc module goes further and forbids instantiating a class with unimplemented abstract methods. Odoo's models.AbstractModel is a different thing despite the name: it is a model without its own table, meant to be mixed into others. Read the ORM part for what it does.

docs.title: Multiple inheritance and the MRO
docs.text:
A class can have several bases:

>>> class Loggable:
...     def log(self, message):
...         return f"[{type(self).__name__}] {message}"
...
>>> class Item:
...     def __init__(self, title):
...         self.title = title
...
>>> class Dvd(Item, Loggable):
...     pass
...
>>> Dvd("Alien").log("created")
'[Dvd] created'

Loggable is a mixin: a class not meant to stand alone, providing a small piece of behaviour for others to combine. The mixin pattern is how Odoo composes features: a model inherits from mail.thread to get messaging, mail.activity.mixin for activities, and so on. Both of those are real standard mixins, used through the Odoo-level _inherit mechanism covered later, but the underlying idea is exactly the Python one above.

When several bases define the same method, Python needs a rule to pick one. That rule is the method resolution order (MRO), a linear list of all classes that Python searches in order. Inspect it:

>>> Dvd.__mro__
(<class '__main__.Dvd'>, <class '__main__.Item'>, <class '__main__.Loggable'>, <class 'object'>)
>>> [c.__name__ for c in Dvd.__mro__]
['Dvd', 'Item', 'Loggable', 'object']

Python computes the MRO with the C3 linearisation algorithm, which gives these guarantees:

  1. A class comes before its bases.
  2. The order of bases in the class statement is preserved.
  3. Each class appears once, even when reachable through several paths.

Diamonds show why this matters:

>>> class A:
...     def who(self): return "A"
...
>>> class B(A):
...     def who(self): return "B"
...
>>> class C(A):
...     def who(self): return "C"
...
>>> class D(B, C):
...     pass
...
>>> [c.__name__ for c in D.__mro__]
['D', 'B', 'C', 'A', 'object']
>>> D().who()
'B'

A is the common base. It must come after both B and C, so its who is reached only if neither B nor C has one. The order of the bases in class D(B, C) decides: swap them and who() returns "C".

If the constraints cannot be satisfied, Python refuses to create the class:

>>> class X(A, B):
...     pass
...
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order (MRO) for bases A, B

A before B contradicts B being a subclass of A.

docs.title: Odoo's model classes
docs.text:
When you write a model class in a module:

class LibraryBook(models.Model):
    _name = "library.book"
    _description = "Book"

you are writing a normal Python class that inherits models.Model. When another module extends the same model, it writes:

class LibraryBookExtra(models.Model):
    _inherit = "library.book"

This second class does not make a new model. At registry build time, Odoo collects every class that contributes to library.book, in module load order, and creates the final model class with all of them as base classes. Methods are then resolved through the MRO of that combined class, which is why each override can call super() and reach the previous module's version. The practical consequence: the order of module loading is the order of the inheritance chain, and an override placed in a module that loads later runs first. The detail of how the registry assembles these classes is in the architecture part of this book; what you need here is the MRO, because it explains everything that follows.

docs.title: Composition over inheritance
docs.text:
Inheritance expresses "is a". Composition expresses "has a", by holding another object in an attribute:

>>> class Clock:
...     def today(self):
...         from datetime import date
...         return date(2025, 3, 10)
...
>>> class LoanService:
...     def __init__(self, clock=None):
...         self.clock = clock or Clock()
...     def is_overdue(self, due):
...         return due < self.clock.today()
...
>>> from datetime import date
>>> LoanService().is_overdue(date(2025, 3, 1))
True

Passing the clock in makes the service testable, since a test can supply a fixed one. When a design feels like a deep inheritance tree, check whether a few small objects composed together would be simpler. Odoo itself leans heavily on inheritance for extensibility, because modules you do not control need a way to alter behaviour, but your own helper code usually does not need it.

docs.title: __slots__, briefly
docs.text:
__slots__ declares the allowed attributes and saves memory when you create many small objects. It also turns the "typo creates a new attribute" problem into an error:

>>> class Point:
...     __slots__ = ("x", "y")
...     def __init__(self, x, y):
...         self.x, self.y = x, y
...
>>> p = Point(1, 2)
>>> p.z = 3
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
AttributeError: 'Point' object has no attribute 'z'

Use it only where memory or strictness matters.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Forgetting self. A method defined as def total(): fails with TypeError: total() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given when called on an instance.
  • Forgetting self. inside a method. title = ... sets a local that disappears. self.title = ... sets the attribute.
  • Mutable class attributes. A list in the class body is shared by all instances. Create it in __init__.
  • Missing super().__init__(). The parent's setup never runs. The failure shows up later as AttributeError.
  • Overriding without calling the parent. In Odoo, replacing write or create without super() skips the framework's own logic and every other module's override. See super() explained.
  • Ignoring the return value in overrides. If the parent returns something and you drop it, every caller gets None.
  • Defining __eq__ and breaking hashing. Add __hash__, or accept that instances cannot be put in sets or used as dict keys.
  • Comparing with is. Use == for values. is tests identity.
  • Inheriting for code reuse only. If the subclass is not truly a kind of the base, use composition.
  • Deep or tangled hierarchies. Every extra layer adds an entry to the MRO that the reader must hold in their head. Prefer shallow trees and small mixins with one responsibility.
  • Mixin order. class D(B, C) and class D(C, B) differ when both define a method. Check D.__mro__ when behaviour surprises you.
  • Name mangling confusion. A name with two leading underscores (__x) is renamed inside the class to _ClassName__x and cannot be reached by a subclass under that name. Use one underscore for "internal".
  • Circular imports between class files. Two modules that import each other's classes at the top fail on load. See Modules and imports.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Write a Book class with title, pages, __repr__, and __eq__ (equal when title and pages match) and __hash__. Show that two equal books collapse to one in a set.
  2. Write Item and Dvd as above, then add Ebook(Item) whose loan_days() returns 21 and whose describe adds the file size using super(). Print describe() for one of each in a loop.
  3. Create classes A, B(A), C(A), D(B, C), each with a method chain() returning a list that starts with its own letter and extends with super().chain() if there is a parent. Predict D().chain() and D.__mro__, then run it.
  4. Implement Shelf with __len__, __iter__, __contains__, __getitem__, and __bool__-by-length, and verify bool(Shelf()) is False. Then add __or__ for union without duplicates, preserving order.
  5. Convert Book into a dataclass with frozen=True, and explain what changes about mutation and hashing.
Solution

1.

>>> class Book:
...     def __init__(self, title, pages):
...         self.title, self.pages = title, pages
...     def __repr__(self):
...         return f"Book({self.title!r}, {self.pages!r})"
...     def __eq__(self, other):
...         if not isinstance(other, Book):
...             return NotImplemented
...         return (self.title, self.pages) == (other.title, other.pages)
...     def __hash__(self):
...         return hash((self.title, self.pages))
...
>>> len({Book("Dune", 612), Book("Dune", 612), Book("Emma", 474)})
2

2.

>>> class Item:
...     def __init__(self, title):
...         self.title = title
...     def loan_days(self):
...         return 14
...     def describe(self):
...         return f"{self.title} ({self.loan_days()} days)"
...
>>> class Dvd(Item):
...     def loan_days(self):
...         return 7
...
>>> class Ebook(Item):
...     def __init__(self, title, mb):
...         super().__init__(title)
...         self.mb = mb
...     def loan_days(self):
...         return 21
...     def describe(self):
...         return super().describe() + f", {self.mb} MB"
...
>>> for item in [Item("Dune"), Dvd("Alien"), Ebook("Emma", 2)]:
...     print(item.describe())
Dune (14 days)
Alien (7 days)
Emma (21 days), 2 MB

3.

>>> class A:
...     def chain(self):
...         return ["A"]
...
>>> class B(A):
...     def chain(self):
...         return ["B"] + super().chain()
...
>>> class C(A):
...     def chain(self):
...         return ["C"] + super().chain()
...
>>> class D(B, C):
...     def chain(self):
...         return ["D"] + super().chain()
...
>>> D().chain()
['D', 'B', 'C', 'A']
>>> [k.__name__ for k in D.__mro__]
['D', 'B', 'C', 'A', 'object']

B's super() does not go to A; it goes to the next class after B in D's MRO, which is C. That behaviour is the key idea of the next chapter.

4.

>>> class Shelf:
...     def __init__(self, books=()):
...         self._books = list(books)
...     def __len__(self):
...         return len(self._books)
...     def __iter__(self):
...         return iter(self._books)
...     def __contains__(self, item):
...         return item in self._books
...     def __getitem__(self, index):
...         return self._books[index]
...     def __or__(self, other):
...         merged = list(self._books)
...         merged.extend(b for b in other if b not in merged)
...         return Shelf(merged)
...     def __repr__(self):
...         return f"Shelf({self._books!r})"
...
>>> bool(Shelf()), Shelf(["a"]) | Shelf(["a", "b"])
(False, Shelf(['a', 'b']))

When __bool__ is not defined, Python falls back to __len__, so an empty shelf is falsy.

5.

>>> from dataclasses import dataclass
>>> @dataclass(frozen=True)
... class Book:
...     title: str
...     pages: int
...
>>> b = Book("Dune", 612)
>>> b.pages = 700
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError: cannot assign to field 'pages'
>>> hash(b) == hash(Book("Dune", 612))
True

Frozen instances reject assignment and, because eq and frozen are both true, get a generated __hash__, so they can be set members and dict keys.

docs.title: Lists, tuples, dicts, sets
docs.text: A single value is rarely enough. A book has many loans, an order has many lines, a search returns many records. Python gives you four built-in containers for "many values": the list (ordered, changeable), the tuple (ordered, fixed), the dict (lookup by key), and the set (unique members). Odoo code uses all four constantly. Domains are lists of tuples, vals dictionaries feed create() and write(), context is a dict, and sets answer "which ids are in both groups". This chapter teaches each container, how to choose between them, and the grouping idioms that replace most manual bookkeeping.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text:
A list is an ordered, mutable sequence written with square brackets:

>>> books = ["Dune", "Emma", "Ulysses"]
>>> books[0], books[-1]
('Dune', 'Ulysses')
>>> len(books)
3
>>> books[1:]
['Emma', 'Ulysses']

Indexing and slicing work exactly as on strings (see Values and types). Unlike strings, lists can be changed in place:

>>> books[1] = "Persuasion"
>>> books.append("Hamlet")
>>> books.insert(0, "Beloved")
>>> books
['Beloved', 'Dune', 'Persuasion', 'Ulysses', 'Hamlet']
>>> books.remove("Dune")
>>> last = books.pop()
>>> last, books
('Hamlet', ['Beloved', 'Persuasion', 'Ulysses'])
>>> books.extend(["Emma", "Walden"])
>>> books
['Beloved', 'Persuasion', 'Ulysses', 'Emma', 'Walden']
Operation Effect Cost lst.append(x) add at the end fast lst.insert(i, x) add at position i slow for large lists lst.extend(other) add all items of other proportional to other lst.pop() remove and return the last item fast lst.pop(i) remove and return item i slow for large lists lst.remove(x) remove the first item equal to x scans the list x in lst membership test scans the list lst.index(x) position of first x scans the list lst.count(x) number of occurrences scans the list

The "scans the list" cost is the reason a membership test inside a loop over a large list gets slow: 10,000 items checked against a 10,000-item list is 100 million comparisons. Sets (below) answer the same question almost instantly.

docs.title: Operators on lists
docs.text:
>>> [1, 2] + [3]
[1, 2, 3]
>>> [0] * 4
[0, 0, 0, 0]
>>> 3 in [1, 2, 3]
True
>>> min([4, 1, 7]), max([4, 1, 7]), sum([4, 1, 7])
(1, 7, 12)
>>> list("abc")
['a', 'b', 'c']
>>> list(range(5))
[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]

+ builds a new list. lst += other modifies lst in place, which behaves differently when other names refer to the same list (next section).

docs.title: Mutation and shared references
docs.text:
A name refers to an object; assignment does not copy. For a list, that means two names can change the same data:

>>> a = [1, 2, 3]
>>> b = a
>>> b.append(4)
>>> a
[1, 2, 3, 4]
>>> c = a.copy()      # or a[:] or list(a)
>>> c.append(5)
>>> a, c
([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

copy() makes a shallow copy: a new outer list that holds the same inner objects. If the items are themselves lists or dicts, the copies share them:

>>> grid = [[0, 0], [0, 0]]
>>> shallow = grid.copy()
>>> shallow[0][0] = 9
>>> grid
[[9, 0], [0, 0]]

copy.deepcopy(obj) copies recursively when you need full independence.

The * operator has the same trap, because it repeats references:

>>> rows = [[0] * 2] * 3
>>> rows[0][0] = 1
>>> rows
[[1, 0], [1, 0], [1, 0]]
>>> rows = [[0] * 2 for _ in range(3)]
>>> rows[0][0] = 1
>>> rows
[[1, 0], [0, 0], [0, 0]]

The second form builds three separate inner lists using a comprehension (Comprehensions and generators).

docs.title: Sorting
docs.text:
sorted(iterable) returns a new sorted list. lst.sort() sorts in place and returns None.

>>> nums = [3, 1, 2]
>>> sorted(nums)
[1, 2, 3]
>>> nums
[3, 1, 2]
>>> nums.sort(reverse=True)
>>> nums
[3, 2, 1]
>>> result = nums.sort()
>>> result is None
True

Sorting by something other than the item itself uses key, a function that maps each item to the value to compare:

>>> words = ["pear", "Fig", "apple", "kiwi"]
>>> sorted(words)
['Fig', 'apple', 'kiwi', 'pear']
>>> sorted(words, key=str.lower)
['apple', 'Fig', 'kiwi', 'pear']
>>> sorted(words, key=len)
['Fig', 'pear', 'kiwi', 'apple']
>>> sorted(words, key=lambda w: (len(w), w))
['Fig', 'kiwi', 'pear', 'apple']

Python's sort is stable: items with equal keys keep their original order. That lets you sort in passes, least significant key first. A tuple key (len(w), w) compares the first element, then the second on ties. lambda is an anonymous one-expression function, introduced in Functions. Odoo's recordset.sorted(key=...) works on the same principle.

Mixing types in a sort fails:

>>> sorted([3, "a", 1])
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'

Odoo specific variant: a field that is False when empty cannot be compared with a date. Sorting records by an optional date with key=lambda r: r.date_due raises TypeError as soon as one record has no date. The fix is a key that maps missing values to a comparable placeholder, for example (r.date_due is False, r.date_due or date.min), which also decides whether empties come first or last.

docs.title: Unpacking
docs.text:
Assign several names at once:

>>> first, second = [10, 20]
>>> first, second
(10, 20)
>>> head, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4]
>>> head, rest
(1, [2, 3, 4])
>>> *init, tail = "abcd"
>>> init, tail
(['a', 'b', 'c'], 'd')
>>> x, y = 1, 2
>>> x, y = y, x        # swap without a temporary
>>> x, y
(2, 1)

The number of names must match unless one starred name absorbs the rest. A mismatch raises ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2).

docs.title: Tuples
docs.text:
A tuple is an ordered, immutable sequence written with parentheses (the commas make the tuple; the parentheses are mostly for grouping):

>>> point = (3, 4)
>>> point[0]
3
>>> point[0] = 9
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
>>> single = (5,)       # the trailing comma matters
>>> type(single), type((5))
(<class 'tuple'>, <class 'int'>)
>>> empty = ()
>>> a, b = point

Use a tuple when the number of items is fixed and the position carries meaning: (latitude, longitude), (field, operator, value). Use a list when the length varies and all items mean the same kind of thing. Tuples are hashable when their contents are, so they can be dictionary keys and set members, lists cannot.

Odoo's search domains are the standard example. A domain is a list of conditions, and each condition is a three-element tuple:

domain = [
    ("state", "=", "open"),
    ("date_due", "<", "2025-01-01"),
    ("book_id.title", "ilike", "dune"),
]

The list is long-lived and may be extended, the tuples are tiny fixed records. Domain operators ("&", "|", "!") are plain strings in the same list; domain syntax is covered in the ORM part. In Python terms you can build and filter such a list like any other.

docs.title: Named tuples
docs.text:
When positions carry meaning, names read better than indexes:

>>> from collections import namedtuple
>>> Loan = namedtuple("Loan", ["book", "member", "days"])
>>> loan = Loan("Dune", "ada", 14)
>>> loan.book, loan[2]
('Dune', 14)
>>> loan._replace(days=21)
Loan(book='Dune', member='ada', days=21)
>>> loan._asdict()
{'book': 'Dune', 'member': 'ada', 'days': 14}

typing.NamedTuple and dataclasses do similar jobs with type hints; they are covered in Classes and inheritance.

docs.title: One-item tuple trap
docs.text: (5) is just 5 in parentheses. (5,) is a tuple. Forgetting the comma bites when a function expects a tuple, for example IN clauses in SQL: cr.execute(..., (tuple(ids),)) needs the parameter list itself to be a tuple, and a single-parameter list is exactly the one-item case.

docs.title: Dictionaries
docs.text:
A dict maps keys to values. It is the workhorse container. Lookup by key is fast regardless of size.

>>> book = {"title": "Dune", "pages": 612, "available": True}
>>> book["title"]
'Dune'
>>> book["pages"] += 1
>>> book["author"] = "F. Herbert"      # add a new key
>>> book
{'title': 'Dune', 'pages': 613, 'available': True, 'author': 'F. Herbert'}
>>> "title" in book, "isbn" in book
(True, False)
>>> len(book)
4
>>> del book["available"]
>>> book.pop("author")
'F. Herbert'

Since Python 3.7 a dict remembers insertion order, and you can rely on it. Keys must be hashable: strings, numbers, tuples of hashables, and frozenset are fine, lists and dicts are not.

>>> hash([1, 2])
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

docs.title: Safe lookup
docs.text:
Indexing a missing key raises KeyError. get returns a default instead:

>>> book = {"title": "Dune", "pages": 612}
>>> book["isbn"]
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
KeyError: 'isbn'
>>> book.get("isbn")                 # None if absent
>>> book.get("isbn", "unknown")
'unknown'
>>> book.setdefault("tags", []).append("scifi")
>>> book
{'title': 'Dune', 'pages': 612, 'tags': ['scifi']}

setdefault(key, default) returns the existing value or inserts and returns the default. The one-line form above is the manual version of grouping, and defaultdict below does it better.

Choose between d[key] and d.get(key) by whether absence is an error. If a key must be there, index it, and a missing key fails loudly at the right place. If absence is normal, use get. In Odoo, vals.get("state") is the standard idiom inside create() and write() overrides, because the caller passes only the fields it wants to set.

docs.title: Iterating
docs.text:
>>> stock = {"Dune": 3, "Emma": 0, "Ulysses": 5}
>>> for title in stock:                       # keys
...     print(title)
Dune
Emma
Ulysses
>>> list(stock.keys()), list(stock.values())
(['Dune', 'Emma', 'Ulysses'], [3, 0, 5])
>>> for title, qty in stock.items():
...     print(f"{title}: {qty}")
Dune: 3
Emma: 0
Ulysses: 5

Do not add or remove keys while looping over the dict. Changing values of existing keys is fine, but changing the size raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration. Loop over a copy (list(d)) if you need to delete.

docs.title: Building and merging
docs.text:
>>> dict(a=1, b=2)
{'a': 1, 'b': 2}
>>> dict([("a", 1), ("b", 2)])
{'a': 1, 'b': 2}
>>> dict(zip(["a", "b"], [1, 2]))
{'a': 1, 'b': 2}
>>> defaults = {"state": "draft", "qty": 1}
>>> overrides = {"qty": 5}
>>> {**defaults, **overrides}
{'state': 'draft', 'qty': 5}
>>> defaults | overrides            # Python 3.9+
{'state': 'draft', 'qty': 5}
>>> merged = dict(defaults)
>>> merged.update(overrides)
>>> merged
{'state': 'draft', 'qty': 5}

{**a, **b} and a | b build a new dict in which the right side wins on conflicts. update changes in place. a | b needs Python 3.9. Dict comprehensions build dicts from an iterable:

>>> {title: len(title) for title in ["Dune", "Emma"]}
{'Dune': 4, 'Emma': 4}
>>> {k: v for k, v in stock.items() if v > 0}
{'Dune': 3, 'Ulysses': 5}

docs.title: Nested data and the JSON shape
docs.text:
Real data nests. JSON, the format used by APIs and Odoo's controllers, is made of dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans, and null (None), and maps one-to-one onto Python containers:

>>> order = {
...     "ref": "SO001",
...     "customer": {"name": "Ada", "country": "UK"},
...     "lines": [
...         {"sku": "A", "qty": 2, "price": 10.0},
...         {"sku": "B", "qty": 1, "price": 5.5},
...     ],
... }
>>> order["customer"]["name"]
'Ada'
>>> order["lines"][1]["sku"]
'B'
>>> sum(line["qty"] * line["price"] for line in order["lines"])
25.5

Chained indexing fails loudly when a level is missing. When parts of the structure are optional, chain get with an empty-dict default: order.get("customer", {}).get("name").

docs.title: vals dictionaries in Odoo
docs.text:
Odoo's create and write take a dict of field names to values. Writing one in plain Python looks like this:

vals = {
    "title": "Dune",
    "pages": 612,
    "author_ids": [(0, 0, {"name": "F. Herbert"})],
}

The tuples inside author_ids are x2many commands, a three-element tuple whose first element selects the operation (here 0 means "create a new record"). The command tuples are a convention of the ORM, not of Python, and later chapters spell out each one. What matters now is that vals is an ordinary dict, so everything above applies: you can merge defaults, copy it before changing it, and read optional keys with get.

Copying matters. If a method receives vals and modifies it, the caller's dictionary changes too, because only the reference was passed. When you override create and want to adjust values without surprising the caller, work on dict(vals).

>>> def normalise(vals):
...     vals = dict(vals)               # do not mutate the caller's dict
...     if "title" in vals:
...         vals["title"] = vals["title"].strip().title()
...     return vals
...
>>> original = {"title": "  the hobbit "}
>>> normalise(original), original
({'title': 'The Hobbit'}, {'title': '  the hobbit '})

docs.title: Sets
docs.text:
A set holds unique, hashable items with no order:

>>> s = {3, 1, 2, 3, 1}
>>> s == {1, 2, 3}
True
>>> len(s)
3
>>> 2 in s
True
>>> set([1, 1, 2]), set("hello") == {"h", "e", "l", "o"}
({1, 2}, True)
>>> empty = set()     # {} is an empty dict, not an empty set
>>> type({}), type(set())
(<class 'dict'>, <class 'set'>)

Membership tests on a set take roughly constant time. Converting a list of ids to a set before a loop turns a quadratic scan into a linear one.

>>> a = {1, 2, 3, 4}
>>> b = {3, 4, 5}
>>> a | b, a & b, a - b, a ^ b
({1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, {3, 4}, {1, 2}, {1, 2, 5})
>>> {1, 2} <= a, a.isdisjoint({9})
(True, True)
>>> a.add(10); a.discard(10); a.discard(99)     # discard never raises
>>> sorted(a)
[1, 2, 3, 4]

| is union, & intersection, - difference, ^ symmetric difference (in exactly one). Typical Odoo-flavoured uses: "which book ids were on the old list but not the new one", "do these two sets of group ids overlap", "deduplicate while I build a list of partner ids".

>>> old_ids = [1, 2, 3, 4]
>>> new_ids = [2, 3, 5]
>>> sorted(set(old_ids) - set(new_ids)), sorted(set(new_ids) - set(old_ids))
([1, 4], [5])

Sets are unordered, so printing a set of strings can give a different order on different runs (string hashing is randomised per process). If you need deterministic output, sorted() it. To deduplicate while keeping order, use a dict:

>>> list(dict.fromkeys(["b", "a", "b", "c", "a"]))
['b', 'a', 'c']

frozenset is the immutable set, usable as a dict key.

docs.title: Choosing the container
docs.text: You need Use Ordered items that grow or change list A fixed-size record, or a dict key made of several parts tuple Lookup by a key dict Uniqueness or fast membership; set arithmetic set A counter per key collections.Counter Group items by a key collections.defaultdict(list) A queue with fast removal at the front collections.deque

docs.title: Counter
docs.text:
>>> from collections import Counter
>>> c = Counter(["open", "open", "returned", "open", "lost"])
>>> c
Counter({'open': 3, 'returned': 1, 'lost': 1})
>>> c["open"], c["never"]
(3, 0)
>>> c.most_common(2)
[('open', 3), ('returned', 1)]
>>> c.update(["lost", "lost"])
>>> c["lost"]
3

A missing key counts as zero and is not inserted when read. Counter is the right tool for "how many of each state".

docs.title: defaultdict
docs.text:
A defaultdict creates a missing value with a factory the first time you ask for the key:

>>> from collections import defaultdict
>>> loans = [("ada", "Dune"), ("bob", "Emma"), ("ada", "Ulysses")]
>>> by_member = defaultdict(list)
>>> for member, title in loans:
...     by_member[member].append(title)
...
>>> dict(by_member)
{'ada': ['Dune', 'Ulysses'], 'bob': ['Emma']}
>>> totals = defaultdict(float)
>>> for sku, amount in [("A", 2.5), ("B", 1.0), ("A", 4.0)]:
...     totals[sku] += amount
...
>>> dict(totals)
{'A': 6.5, 'B': 1.0}

This is the standard grouping idiom, and it appears everywhere in Odoo code that processes records in Python: iterate once, append to groups[key], then handle each group. It replaces if key not in d: d[key] = [] boilerplate.

Reading d[key] on a defaultdict inserts the key. Calling d["x"] to "check" whether something exists silently creates an entry. Use "x" in d or d.get("x") for checks. When you finish grouping, convert with dict(...) before returning it to code that may probe it.

docs.title: deque
docs.text:
>>> from collections import deque
>>> queue = deque([1, 2, 3])
>>> queue.append(4)
>>> queue.popleft()
1
>>> queue
deque([2, 3, 4])

Popping from the front of a list is slow (pop(0) shifts everything). deque does it fast, and is the right structure for a work queue.

docs.title: Odoo-flavoured: grouping, indexing, set arithmetic
docs.text:
A recordset is not a list, but it iterates like one, and everything here applies to records as well as plain data. The examples below use plain dictionaries standing in for records so that they run anywhere. Later chapters show the same logic over real recordsets.

>>> loans = [
...     {"id": 1, "member": "ada", "book": "Dune", "state": "open", "days": 14},
...     {"id": 2, "member": "bob", "book": "Emma", "state": "returned", "days": 7},
...     {"id": 3, "member": "ada", "book": "Ulysses", "state": "open", "days": 21},
...     {"id": 4, "member": "cy", "book": "Dune", "state": "lost", "days": 30},
... ]

Filter is a loop with a condition. Odoo's recordset.filtered(lambda l: l.state == "open") is this:

>>> open_loans = [l for l in loans if l["state"] == "open"]
>>> [l["id"] for l in open_loans]
[1, 3]

Map extracts one field from each item, which Odoo's recordset.mapped("field") does:

>>> [l["book"] for l in loans]
['Dune', 'Emma', 'Ulysses', 'Dune']
>>> sorted({l["book"] for l in loans})            # unique, sorted
['Dune', 'Emma', 'Ulysses']

Group by a key with defaultdict:

>>> by_member = defaultdict(list)
>>> for loan in loans:
...     by_member[loan["member"]].append(loan)
...
>>> {m: [l["id"] for l in group] for m, group in by_member.items()}
{'ada': [1, 3], 'bob': [2], 'cy': [4]}

Aggregate per group:

>>> days_per_member = defaultdict(int)
>>> for loan in loans:
...     days_per_member[loan["member"]] += loan["days"]
...
>>> dict(days_per_member)
{'ada': 35, 'bob': 7, 'cy': 30}
>>> max(days_per_member, key=days_per_member.get)
'ada'

Index by id so that you can look records up without scanning:

>>> by_id = {l["id"]: l for l in loans}
>>> by_id[3]["book"]
'Ulysses'

Set arithmetic between two views of the data:

>>> borrowed = {l["book"] for l in loans if l["state"] == "open"}
>>> lost = {l["book"] for l in loans if l["state"] == "lost"}
>>> borrowed & lost
{'Dune'}

Many-to-many consistency is a set difference. Given a desired list of tag ids and the current ones, work out what to add and remove:

>>> current, wanted = {1, 2, 3}, {2, 3, 4}
>>> to_add, to_remove = wanted - current, current - wanted
>>> to_add, to_remove
({4}, {1})

docs.title: Identity of keys in a mapping
docs.text: Using a recordset or record as a dict key works because Odoo makes records hashable (they hash by model and id). For plain Python it means you can write groups[loan.member_id] and get one bucket per member, without first extracting ids. If you are not sure that an object is hashable, you can test it in the REPL with hash(obj); an unhashable object raises TypeError.

docs.title: Copying, and what "equal" means for containers
docs.text:
Lists, dicts, and sets compare by content:

>>> [1, 2] == [1, 2], {"a": 1} == {"a": 1}, {1, 2} == {2, 1}
(True, True, True)
>>> (1, 2) == [1, 2]
False

A tuple is never equal to a list holding the same items. This matters when a value round-trips through JSON: tuples become lists. A domain [("state", "=", "open")] sent over JSON-RPC arrives on the other side as [["state", "=", "open"]], and code comparing it with tuples will not match.

>>> import json
>>> json.loads(json.dumps(("a", 1)))
['a', 1]

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Mutable default aliasing. b = a does not copy. Use a.copy(), list(a), dict(a), or copy.deepcopy as needed.
  • Shallow copy of nested data. copy() shares inner lists and dicts. Use deepcopy for independence.
  • [[0] * n] * m. Builds m references to one inner list. Use a comprehension.
  • sort() returns None. items = items.sort() destroys the list reference. Use sorted() or call sort() on its own line.
  • Sorting mixed types. None, False, and dates or strings in one key raise TypeError. Normalise the key. This is common with Odoo optional fields.
  • Modifying a list while iterating. Removing items inside for x in lst: skips elements. Iterate over a copy or build a new list.
  • Modifying a dict while iterating. Changing its size raises RuntimeError.
  • d[key] on missing keys. Use get when absence is normal.
  • defaultdict reads insert keys. A "check" like if groups["x"]: creates the entry.
  • {} is a dict. An empty set is set().
  • Sets are unordered. Never rely on iteration order of a set. Sort before printing or comparing text output.
  • Unhashable keys. Lists and dicts cannot be keys or set members. Use tuples or frozenset.
  • One-item tuples. (x) is not a tuple. Write (x,).
  • Tuples become lists in JSON. Compare after normalising, or convert back explicitly.
  • Quadratic membership tests. if x in big_list inside a loop. Build a set once outside the loop.
  • Shared vals. Mutating a dict argument changes the caller's data. Copy first.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Given words = ["pear", "fig", "apple", "kiwi", "fig"], produce: the unique words sorted by length then alphabetically, and a dict from word to count.
  2. Given the loans list from this chapter, build a dict from member to the list of distinct book titles they borrowed, sorted alphabetically. Use defaultdict(set).
  3. Write diff_ids(old, new) that returns (added, removed, kept) as sorted lists, for two lists of ids that may contain duplicates.
  4. Sort the list [("ada", None), ("bob", 5), ("cy", 2)] by the second element with None last, ascending otherwise.
  5. Explain why rows = [[0] * 3] * 2; rows[0][0] = 7 changes both rows, and show two correct ways to build the grid.
Solution

1.

>>> words = ["pear", "fig", "apple", "kiwi", "fig"]
>>> sorted(set(words), key=lambda w: (len(w), w))
['fig', 'kiwi', 'pear', 'apple']
>>> from collections import Counter
>>> dict(Counter(words))
{'pear': 1, 'fig': 2, 'apple': 1, 'kiwi': 1}

2.

>>> from collections import defaultdict
>>> loans = [("ada", "Dune"), ("bob", "Emma"), ("ada", "Ulysses"), ("ada", "Dune")]
>>> books = defaultdict(set)
>>> for member, title in loans:
...     books[member].add(title)
...
>>> {m: sorted(t) for m, t in books.items()}
{'ada': ['Dune', 'Ulysses'], 'bob': ['Emma']}

3.

>>> def diff_ids(old, new):
...     old, new = set(old), set(new)
...     return sorted(new - old), sorted(old - new), sorted(old & new)
...
>>> diff_ids([1, 2, 2, 3], [2, 3, 3, 4])
([4], [1], [2, 3])
  1. The key puts None into a second tier: False sorts before True, so rows with a value come first.
>>> data = [("ada", None), ("bob", 5), ("cy", 2)]
>>> sorted(data, key=lambda row: (row[1] is None, row[1] or 0))
[('cy', 2), ('bob', 5), ('ada', None)]
  1. [[0] * 3] * 2 creates one inner list and repeats the reference to it twice, so both rows are the same object. Correct versions:
>>> rows = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]
>>> rows[0][0] = 7
>>> rows
[[7, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
>>> import copy
>>> template = [0, 0, 0]
>>> rows = [copy.copy(template) for _ in range(2)]
>>> rows[0][0] = 7
>>> rows
[[7, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]

docs.title: Comprehensions and generators
docs.text: Most loops in business code do one of two things: build a new collection from an old one, or walk through data without needing all of it in memory at once. Python has dedicated syntax for both. A comprehension builds a list, dict, or set from an iterable in one expression. A generator produces items one at a time, on demand. Odoo code uses comprehensions everywhere you see [x.name for x in records], and generators matter the moment you export or import tens of thousands of rows. This chapter explains both, shows where they pay off, and shows where plain loops are the better choice.

docs.title: List comprehensions
docs.text:
The loop

>>> squares = []
>>> for n in range(5):
...     squares.append(n * n)
...
>>> squares
[0, 1, 4, 9, 16]

is written as a comprehension:

>>> [n * n for n in range(5)]
[0, 1, 4, 9, 16]

The shape is [expression for name in iterable]. Read it as "the expression, for each name in the iterable". The result is always a new list.

docs.title: Filtering with if
docs.text:
An if after the for keeps only the items that satisfy it:

>>> nums = range(10)
>>> [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
[0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
>>> [n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
[0, 4, 16, 36, 64]
>>> titles = ["Dune", "", "Emma", "  "]
>>> [t.strip() for t in titles if t.strip()]
['Dune', 'Emma']

The filter decides which items enter; the expression decides what each becomes.

docs.title: Choosing between two values: if and else in the expression
docs.text:
An if/else that picks a value goes before the for:

>>> ["even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd" for n in range(4)]
['even', 'odd', 'even', 'odd']

The two positions differ. x for x in y if cond filters. a if cond else b for x in y transforms every item. Mixing them up is a syntax error or a wrong result, so check which one you mean.

docs.title: Several for clauses
docs.text:
Multiple for clauses nest, with the leftmost as the outermost loop:

>>> [(x, y) for x in range(3) for y in range(2)]
[(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0), (2, 1)]
>>> orders = [{"ref": "A", "lines": [1, 2]}, {"ref": "B", "lines": [3]}]
>>> [line for order in orders for line in order["lines"]]
[1, 2, 3]

The second example flattens a list of lists: for each order, for each line. This is the plain-Python equivalent of mapped("order_line") followed by iterating the result. More than two for clauses usually reads badly; use a loop.

docs.title: Using them on records
docs.text:
A recordset iterates like a list, so every comprehension applies to it. The records below are dictionaries standing in for them, to keep the examples runnable anywhere:

>>> loans = [
...     {"id": 1, "member": "ada", "state": "open", "days": 14},
...     {"id": 2, "member": "bob", "state": "returned", "days": 7},
...     {"id": 3, "member": "ada", "state": "open", "days": 21},
... ]
>>> [l["id"] for l in loans if l["state"] == "open"]
[1, 3]
>>> sum(l["days"] for l in loans if l["member"] == "ada")
35

In real Odoo code the same shapes read [l.id for l in loans if l.state == "open"]. For plain extraction, loans.mapped("id") or loans.ids is shorter. For filtering where you want records back, loans.filtered(...) is better than a comprehension because it returns a recordset you can keep working with. Use a comprehension when you want plain values or a different structure, such as a list of tuples or a dict.

docs.title: Dict and set comprehensions
docs.text:
Curly braces with a colon build a dict. Without the colon, they build a set:

>>> {l["id"]: l["member"] for l in loans}
{1: 'ada', 2: 'bob', 3: 'ada'}
>>> sorted({l["member"] for l in loans})
['ada', 'bob']
>>> {m: sum(l["days"] for l in loans if l["member"] == m) for m in {l["member"] for l in loans}} == {"ada": 35, "bob": 7}
True

The last line shows the problem with nesting: it works, but scans the list once per member and is hard to read. Group with defaultdict instead (Lists, tuples, dicts, sets).

Common dict comprehension uses:

>>> prices = {"A": 10.0, "B": 5.5}
>>> {sku: round(p * 1.2, 2) for sku, p in prices.items()}
{'A': 12.0, 'B': 6.6}
