WARNING library.import: item 0 failed: division by zero
([1, 2], [(0, 'division by zero')])

Catching Exception here is deliberate: the purpose is isolation of per-item failures, the failure is logged, and the information is returned. In Odoo you would add a savepoint around each item if the handler writes to the database.

  1. After a failed SQL statement the PostgreSQL transaction is aborted, so the following queries fail with an unrelated error, and pass hides why. Also, any partial work stays pending. Rewrite:
try:
    with self.env.cr.savepoint():
        record = self.env["library.loan"].create(vals)
except Exception:
    _logger.warning("loan creation failed for %s", vals, exc_info=True)
    record = self.env["library.loan"]

The savepoint rolls back just the failed creation, the log records the cause with a traceback, and the code continues with an empty recordset as a defined fallback.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: A function is a named, reusable block of code that takes inputs and gives back a result. Everything you write for Odoo is a function in one form or another: a compute method, a button action, an onchange handler, a cron entry point, a lambda that provides a field default. The details of how Python passes arguments are what make Odoo overrides work, because an override must accept whatever its parent accepts and hand it on unchanged. This chapter covers definition, argument passing, *args and **kwargs, scope, closures, and lambdas.

docs.title: Defining and calling
docs.text:
>>> def add(a, b):
...     return a + b
...
>>> add(2, 3)
5
>>> total = add(10, 5)
>>> total
15

def introduces the function name, its parameters in parentheses, and a colon, followed by an indented body. When you call it, the values you pass are arguments. return ends the function and hands a value back to the caller.

A function without a return, or with a bare return, gives back None:

>>> def greet(name):
...     print(f"Hello, {name}")
...
>>> result = greet("Ada")
Hello, Ada
>>> result is None
True

The distinction between printing and returning trips up beginners. print shows text to a human and the value is lost. return gives the value to the calling code, which can store it, test it, or pass it on. Code that is meant to be reused returns values; printing belongs at the outermost layer. In Odoo there is no terminal for a method to print to, and a method that "prints" its result writes into the server log at best. Return the value.

docs.title: Return multiple values
docs.text:
A function returns one object. To return several, return a tuple, and unpack at the call site:

>>> def min_max(values):
...     return min(values), max(values)
...
>>> low, high = min_max([4, 9, 2])
>>> low, high
(2, 9)
>>> min_max([4, 9, 2])
(2, 9)

docs.title: Early return
docs.text:
A return can sit anywhere, and the rest of the body is skipped. Use it for guard clauses (see Control flow).

>>> def safe_ratio(a, b):
...     if b == 0:
...         return None
...     return a / b
...
>>> safe_ratio(1, 4), safe_ratio(1, 0)
(0.25, None)

Be consistent. A function that sometimes returns a value and sometimes falls off the end returns None in the second case, which the caller will then fail on far from the cause. If some paths return a value, make every path say what it returns, even if that is an explicit return None.

docs.title: Docstrings
docs.text:
A string as the first statement of a function is its docstring. help() and editors display it.

>>> def late_fee(days_late, rate=0.5):
...     """Return the fee for a loan returned `days_late` days after the due date.
...
...     A loan returned on time (days_late <= 0) costs nothing.
...     """
...     return max(days_late, 0) * rate
...
>>> late_fee(4), late_fee(-3), late_fee(4, rate=1)
(2.0, 0.0, 4)
>>> late_fee.__doc__.splitlines()[0]
'Return the fee for a loan returned `days_late` days after the due date.'

Write the first line as a complete summary of what the function does. In Odoo, docstrings on model methods that are exposed to the client are shown in some tooling, and on public methods they are the only documentation your colleagues will find.

docs.title: Positional and keyword arguments
docs.text:
You can pass arguments by position or by name:

>>> def make_ref(prefix, year, number):
...     return f"{prefix}-{year}-{number:04d}"
...
>>> make_ref("LIB", 2025, 42)
'LIB-2025-0042'
>>> make_ref(prefix="LIB", number=42, year=2025)
'LIB-2025-0042'
>>> make_ref("LIB", number=42, year=2025)
'LIB-2025-0042'

Positional arguments come first, then keyword ones. Passing the same parameter twice, or too few or too many, is a TypeError:

>>> make_ref("LIB", 2025)
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
TypeError: make_ref() missing 1 required positional argument: 'number'
>>> make_ref("LIB", 2025, 42, year=2026)
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
TypeError: make_ref() got multiple values for argument 'year'

Keyword arguments make call sites self-documenting. create_loan(book, member, True) says nothing about the True; create_loan(book, member, renewable=True) does.

docs.title: Default values
docs.text:
A parameter with a default is optional:

>>> def make_ref(prefix, year, number=1, width=4):
...     return f"{prefix}-{year}-{number:0{width}d}"
...
>>> make_ref("LIB", 2025)
'LIB-2025-0001'
>>> make_ref("LIB", 2025, width=6)
'LIB-2025-000001'

Parameters with defaults must come after those without.

docs.title: The mutable default trap
docs.text:
Default values are evaluated once, when def runs, not at each call. For immutable defaults (numbers, strings, None) this is invisible. For a list or dict, every call that omits the argument shares the same object:

>>> def add_tag(tag, tags=[]):
...     tags.append(tag)
...     return tags
...
>>> add_tag("a")
['a']
>>> add_tag("b")
['a', 'b']

The second call returns ['a', 'b'], because the same list was reused. The standard fix is a None sentinel:

>>> def add_tag(tag, tags=None):
...     if tags is None:
...         tags = []
...     tags.append(tag)
...     return tags
...
>>> add_tag("a"), add_tag("b")
(['a'], ['b'])

This bug is nasty because the first call works. In Odoo it shows up when a default dict (for example, a context template) is declared in a signature and then modified by every caller.

docs.title: Keyword-only and positional-only parameters
docs.text:
A bare * in the parameter list means everything after it must be passed by keyword:

>>> def make_loan(book, member, *, days=14, renewable=True):
...     return (book, member, days, renewable)
...
>>> make_loan("Dune", "ada", days=7)
('Dune', 'ada', 7, True)
>>> make_loan("Dune", "ada", 7)
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
TypeError: make_loan() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given

This prevents mistakes with long parameter lists. A / marks the preceding parameters as positional-only (Python 3.8+):

>>> def clamp(value, low, high, /):
...     return max(low, min(value, high))
...
>>> clamp(15, 0, 10)
10

You will rarely write /, and you will see it in signatures printed by help().

docs.title: *args and **kwargs
docs.text:
A parameter prefixed with * collects extra positional arguments into a tuple. A parameter prefixed with ** collects extra keyword arguments into a dict:

>>> def show(*args, **kwargs):
...     print("args:", args)
...     print("kwargs:", kwargs)
...
>>> show(1, 2, x=3)
args: (1, 2)
kwargs: {'x': 3}
>>> show()
args: ()
kwargs: {}

The names args and kwargs are conventions, and the stars do the work. The same stars at the call site unpack a sequence or a dict into arguments:

>>> point = (3, 4)
>>> opts = {"width": 6}
>>> def fmt(x, y, width=2):
...     return f"{x:>{width}},{y:>{width}}"
...
>>> fmt(*point, **opts)
'     3,     4'
>>> fmt(*point)
' 3, 4'

The unpacking forms combine: f(*a, *b, **c, **d) is legal.

docs.title: Why Odoo cares
docs.text:
An override of a model method must pass through whatever arguments it does not understand. The usual form is:

def write(self, vals):
    # ... adjust vals or do something before
    result = super().write(vals)
    # ... do something after
    return result

This works because write takes exactly vals. For methods whose signature differs between Odoo versions or is extended by other modules (for example, create receives a list of dicts in recent versions and a single dict in older ones), overrides often accept *args, **kwargs and forward them untouched:

def action_confirm(self, *args, **kwargs):
    # pre-check
    return super().action_confirm(*args, **kwargs)

A wrapper written like this keeps working when another module adds a keyword argument to the method in the chain. A wrapper with a fixed narrow signature breaks the moment a caller passes something it did not anticipate. super() explained shows why the chain makes this necessary.

The pass-through pattern in plain Python:

>>> def base(a, b=0, *, scale=1):
...     return (a + b) * scale
...
>>> def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
...     print("calling base with", args, kwargs)
...     return base(*args, **kwargs)
...
>>> wrapper(1, 2, scale=10)
calling base with (1, 2) {'scale': 10}
30

docs.title: Argument passing: references, not copies
docs.text:
Python passes a reference to the object. If the object is mutable and the function changes it, the caller sees the change:

>>> def add_default(order):
...     order["state"] = "draft"
...
>>> o = {"ref": "SO1"}
>>> add_default(o)
>>> o
{'ref': 'SO1', 'state': 'draft'}

Reassigning the parameter name inside the function does not affect the caller, because it only rebinds the local name:

>>> def reset(items):
...     items = []
...
>>> data = [1, 2]
>>> reset(data)
>>> data
[1, 2]

Rule: a function should either return a new value or modify its argument in place, and the name and docstring should say which. Mixing both is how bugs hide. Python's own convention illustrates it: sorted(x) returns a new list, x.sort() mutates and returns None.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
A scope is where a name is visible. Python looks a name up in this order, nicknamed LEGB:

  1. Local: names assigned inside the current function.
  2. Enclosing: names in outer functions (for nested functions).
  3. Global: names at module level.
  4. Built-in: names such as len, print, sum.
>>> rate = 0.5            # global
>>> def fee(days):
...     cap = 10          # local
...     return min(days * rate, cap)
...
>>> fee(30)
10
>>> cap
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
NameError: name 'cap' is not defined

Reading a global from a function works. Assigning to a name inside a function creates a local, even if a global of the same name exists:

>>> counter = 0
>>> def bump():
...     counter = counter + 1
...
>>> bump()
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'counter' where it is not associated with a value

Because counter is assigned in the function, Python treats it as local for the whole function and complains when you read it before it is set. To rebind a module-level name, declare it global:

>>> def bump():
...     global counter
...     counter += 1
...
>>> bump(); bump()
>>> counter
2

Avoid global. State that changes at module level is shared by every request in the process, and Odoo servers run many requests in the same interpreter, sometimes in several threads. A module-level cache that two requests modify at once is a bug that appears only under load, and in Odoo it can also leak data between databases. If you need shared state, keep it on the registry or the environment as the framework provides, or in a database table.

Mutating a global list or dict does not need global, because that does not rebind the name. It is exactly as hazardous.

docs.title: Closures and nonlocal
docs.text:
A function defined inside another function can read the outer function's names, and keeps them alive after the outer function returns. That is a closure:

>>> def make_fee(rate):
...     def fee(days):
...         return days * rate
...     return fee
...
>>> daily = make_fee(0.5)
>>> daily(4)
2.0
>>> make_fee(2)(4)
8

fee remembers rate. To assign to an enclosing variable use nonlocal:

>>> def make_counter():
...     n = 0
...     def tick():
...         nonlocal n
...         n += 1
...         return n
...     return tick
...
>>> t = make_counter()
>>> t(), t(), t()
(1, 2, 3)

Closures are what decorators are built from.

docs.title: The late-binding trap
docs.text:
A closure looks up the variable when it is called, not when it is defined:

>>> funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
>>> [f() for f in funcs]
[2, 2, 2]
>>> funcs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
>>> [f() for f in funcs]
[0, 1, 2]

All three lambdas share the one i, which ends at 2. Binding it as a default argument (i=i) captures the current value. The same thing happens when you create callbacks in a loop in Odoo code.

docs.title: Functions are objects
docs.text:
A function is a value like any other. You can store it, pass it to other functions, and return it:

>>> def shout(s):
...     return s.upper() + "!"
...
>>> f = shout
>>> f("hi")
'HI!'
>>> [shout(w) for w in ["a", "b"]]
['A!', 'B!']
>>> list(map(shout, ["a", "b"]))
['A!', 'B!']
>>> handlers = {"loud": shout, "quiet": str.lower}
>>> handlers["loud"]("x"), handlers["quiet"]("X")
('X!', 'x')

A dict of functions is a clean replacement for a long if/elif chain. Passing a function to another function is how sorted(key=...), filter, and Odoo's filtered(...) work.

docs.title: lambda
docs.text:
lambda args: expression is a nameless function with a single expression as its body:

>>> square = lambda x: x * x
>>> square(5)
25
>>> sorted(["bb", "a", "ccc"], key=lambda s: -len(s))
['ccc', 'bb', 'a']
>>> list(filter(lambda n: n % 2, range(6)))
[1, 3, 5]

Use lambda for short throwaway functions passed as arguments. Do not assign a lambda to a name; use def, which gives the function a name that appears in tracebacks. A lambda cannot contain statements.

In Odoo you will write lambdas constantly:

recs.filtered(lambda r: r.state == "open")
recs.sorted(key=lambda r: r.date_due)
active = fields.Boolean(default=lambda self: True)

The third line shows a field default given as a function, so that the value is computed when each record is created and not once when the class is loaded. For a constant, default=True is fine. For a date or a value that depends on the current user, it must be a callable. A date default written as default=date.today() is evaluated once at server start and is stale from the next day on.

You can see the problem in plain Python:

>>> from datetime import datetime
>>> import time
>>> def stamp(at=datetime.now()):      # evaluated once, at definition
...     return at
...
>>> first = stamp()
>>> time.sleep(0.01)
>>> stamp() == first
True

docs.title: functools.partial
docs.text:
partial fixes some arguments of an existing function and gives you a new function:

>>> from functools import partial
>>> def fee(days, rate):
...     return days * rate
...
>>> weekly = partial(fee, rate=3.5)
>>> weekly(2)
7.0

It is cleaner than a lambda when you only want to pre-fill arguments.

docs.title: Type hints
docs.text:
Python lets you annotate parameters and return values. The interpreter does not enforce them, but editors and checkers use them, and they document intent:

>>> def late_fee(days_late: int, rate: float = 0.5) -> float:
...     return max(days_late, 0) * rate
...
>>> late_fee(3)
1.5
>>> late_fee.__annotations__
{'days_late': <class 'int'>, 'rate': <class 'float'>, 'return': <class 'float'>}

Common forms: list[str], dict[str, int], tuple[int, int] (Python 3.9+), str | None (3.10+; on older versions Optional[str] from typing). Odoo core code mostly omits annotations in model methods; some recent modules add them. Follow the style of the code base you work in. Wrong hints never raise errors at runtime, so a hint that lies is worse than none.

docs.title: Recursion
docs.text:
A function can call itself. It needs a base case that stops the recursion:

>>> def depth(node):
...     children = node.get("children", [])
...     return 1 + max((depth(c) for c in children), default=0)
...
>>> tree = {"name": "root", "children": [{"name": "a", "children": [{"name": "b"}]}, {"name": "c"}]}
>>> depth(tree)
3

This suits tree structures such as product categories or parent-child account hierarchies. Python limits recursion depth (about 1000 frames by default) and raises RecursionError beyond it. Hierarchies in Odoo data can contain a cycle by mistake (a category that is its own ancestor), which turns a recursive function into an infinite one; the ORM has a recursion check for parent_id fields, and your own traversal should track visited ids.

docs.title: Designing functions
docs.text:
• One job. A function that "validates and saves and sends email" is three functions. Test and reuse suffer otherwise.
  • Names are verbs for actions, nouns for values. compute_total, late_fee, is_overdue.
  • Return rather than print, and return rather than mutate unless the function's purpose is the mutation.
  • Few parameters. More than four or five suggests a group of values that should travel together, such as a dict or a small class (see Classes and inheritance).
  • Keyword-only for flags. Booleans passed positionally are unreadable.
  • No hidden globals. If the result depends on something other than the arguments, say so in the docstring.

A small worked example in the shape of Odoo business logic, without any Odoo dependency:

>>> from datetime import date, timedelta
>>> def due_date(start, days=14, *, skip_weekends=True):
...     """Return the due date for a loan that starts on `start`."""
...     due = start + timedelta(days=days)
...     if skip_weekends:
...         while due.weekday() >= 5:      # 5 = Saturday, 6 = Sunday
...             due += timedelta(days=1)
...     return due
...
>>> due_date(date(2025, 3, 3))          # Monday + 14 -> Monday
datetime.date(2025, 3, 17)
>>> due_date(date(2025, 3, 5))          # Wednesday + 14 -> Wednesday
datetime.date(2025, 3, 19)
>>> due_date(date(2025, 3, 8), days=7)  # Saturday + 7 -> Saturday -> Monday
datetime.date(2025, 3, 17)
>>> due_date(date(2025, 3, 8), days=7, skip_weekends=False)
datetime.date(2025, 3, 15)

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Mutable defaults. def f(x, items=[]) shares one list across calls. Use None and create inside.
  • Evaluated-once defaults. def f(at=datetime.now()) is frozen at import. In Odoo default=fields.Date.today() is the same mistake; pass the callable instead.
  • Printing instead of returning. The caller gets None.
  • Mutating arguments by accident. A function that changes the caller's dict or list surprises everyone. Copy first (dict(vals)), or document the mutation.
  • UnboundLocalError. Assigning to a name anywhere in a function makes it local everywhere in that function.
  • Late binding in closures and lambdas. Create callbacks in a loop with lambda i=i: ... or partial.
  • Narrow override signatures. An override of def method(self, a) breaks when another module in the chain passes an extra argument. Forward *args, **kwargs unless you are certain of the signature.
  • Forgetting to return the super() result. An override that calls the parent and does not return its value silently returns None to every caller. See super() explained.
  • Inconsistent returns. Some paths return a value, others fall off the end. The caller crashes with 'NoneType' object has no attribute ... far away.
  • Shadowing built-ins. A parameter named id, type, filter, or sum hides the built-in inside the function. Fine for id in most code, but a problem if you need the built-in on the next line.
  • Deep recursion. RecursionError on large hierarchies or cyclic data. Prefer a loop with an explicit stack and a visited set.
  • Overusing global. Module-level state is shared by all requests and threads.
  • Positional booleans. export(rows, True, False) cannot be reviewed. Use keyword-only flags.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Write fee(days_late, rate=0.5, *, cap=None) that returns days_late * rate, never negative, and no more than cap when cap is not None. Call it positionally and with keywords, and show that fee(3, 0.5, 2) fails.
  2. Write wrap(func) that returns a new function calling func with the same arguments and printing "calling <name>" first. Use *args, **kwargs. Apply it to fee.
  3. Predict the output, then run: def f(x, acc=[]): acc.append(x); return acc called as f(1), f(2), f(3, []), f(4). Fix the function.
  4. Build a list of three functions that return 10, 20, 30 using a loop, first incorrectly (all return 30), then correctly in two different ways.
  5. Write group_by(items, key) that takes an iterable and a function and returns a dict from key to list of items, preserving the input order inside each group.
Solution

1.

>>> def fee(days_late, rate=0.5, *, cap=None):
...     amount = max(days_late, 0) * rate
...     if cap is not None:
...         amount = min(amount, cap)
...     return amount
...
>>> fee(10), fee(10, 0.5), fee(10, rate=1, cap=4), fee(-2)
(5.0, 5.0, 4, 0.0)
>>> fee(3, 0.5, 2)
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
TypeError: fee() takes from 1 to 2 positional arguments but 3 were given

2.

>>> def wrap(func):
...     def inner(*args, **kwargs):
...         print("calling", func.__name__)
...         return func(*args, **kwargs)
...     return inner
...
>>> logged_fee = wrap(fee)
>>> logged_fee(4, cap=1)
calling fee
1
  1. f(1) gives [1], f(2) gives [1, 2] (shared default), f(3, []) gives [3], f(4) gives [1, 2, 4]. Fix:
>>> def f(x, acc=None):
...     if acc is None:
...         acc = []
...     acc.append(x)
...     return acc
...
>>> f(1), f(2)
([1], [2])

4.

>>> bad = [lambda: n * 10 for n in (1, 2, 3)]
>>> [g() for g in bad]
[30, 30, 30]
>>> good1 = [lambda n=n: n * 10 for n in (1, 2, 3)]
>>> [g() for g in good1]
[10, 20, 30]
>>> from functools import partial
>>> good2 = [partial(lambda n: n * 10, n) for n in (1, 2, 3)]
>>> [g() for g in good2]
[10, 20, 30]

5.

>>> def group_by(items, key):
...     groups = {}
...     for item in items:
...         groups.setdefault(key(item), []).append(item)
...     return groups
...
>>> group_by(["apple", "avocado", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry"], key=lambda w: w[0])
{'a': ['apple', 'avocado'], 'b': ['banana', 'blueberry'], 'c': ['cherry']}

docs.title: Modules and imports
docs.text: A program that fits in one file stops fitting quickly. Python splits code into modules (files) and packages (folders of modules), and connects them with import. Odoo takes this literally: an Odoo "module" is a Python package, its __init__.py files decide which model files get loaded and in what order, and cross-module code reuse is an ordinary import. Import mistakes, especially circular imports and missing __init__.py entries, are among the most common reasons a freshly written Odoo model does not appear. This chapter explains how imports work, how Python finds code, how packages are structured, and what that means for an Odoo addon.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
Any .py file is a module. Its name is the file name without the extension. Create fees.py:

RATE = 0.5

def late_fee(days_late):
    return max(days_late, 0) * RATE

Another file, in the same folder, can use it:

>>> import fees
>>> fees.late_fee(4)
2.0
>>> fees.RATE
0.5

import fees runs the file once, from top to bottom, and binds the name fees to a module object. The names defined in the file (RATE, late_fee) become attributes of that object.

docs.title: Import forms
docs.text:
import fees                       # use as fees.late_fee(...)
import fees as f                  # alias: f.late_fee(...)
from fees import late_fee         # bring one name in: late_fee(...)
from fees import late_fee, RATE   # several names
from fees import late_fee as fee  # alias for a name
from fees import *                # all public names: avoid

Which to use:

  • import module keeps the origin visible at the call site (fees.late_fee), avoids name clashes, and makes it obvious where something comes from. The standard library is usually imported this way: import os, import json.
  • from module import name is shorter and is the norm for frameworks: Odoo files begin with from odoo import api, fields, models, _.
  • from module import * pulls in everything not starting with an underscore (or everything listed in __all__), so a reader cannot tell where a name came from, and it can overwrite names you already defined. Do not use it in your code.

The PEP 8 convention is to put imports at the top of the file, in three groups separated by blank lines: standard library, third-party packages, then your own code. Odoo core follows it, in this order (standard library, odoo itself, then other addons):

import logging
from collections import defaultdict
from datetime import date, timedelta

from odoo import _, api, fields, models
from odoo.exceptions import UserError

docs.title: Modules run once, then are cached
docs.text:
Python stores every imported module in sys.modules, keyed by name. A second import fees anywhere in the program returns the same module object without re-running the file:

>>> import sys
>>> import fees
>>> sys.modules["fees"] is fees
True

This is why module-level code is a single-run initialisation, and why module-level variables are shared state across the whole process. In an Odoo server the process handles many requests, and often many databases, so a mutable module-level variable is global to all of them. See Functions on scope.

docs.title: Code runs at import time
docs.text:
Everything at module level executes during import: assignments, function and class definitions, and any statement you leave there.

# fees.py
print("fees loaded")          # runs on first import
RATE = 0.5

Keep module-level code to definitions and cheap constants. Do not open connections, read files, or call services at import time. A failure there breaks the import of every file that depends on it, and in Odoo it breaks the registry load for the whole database.

docs.title: __name__ and if __name__ == "__main__"
docs.text:
Every module has a __name__. When imported it is the module's name. When run as a script it is "__main__":

$ python3 mod.py          # mod.py contains: print(__name__)
__main__
$ python3 -c "import mod"
mod

So a file can serve both purposes:

def main():
    print("running")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The guarded block runs only when the file is executed directly, not when another file imports it. Odoo module files do not use this; Odoo imports them. You use it in standalone helper scripts that also expose reusable functions.

docs.title: How Python finds a module
docs.text:
When you write import fees, Python looks, in order, at:

  1. sys.modules, the cache of already imported modules.
  2. Built-in modules (compiled into the interpreter).
  3. Each folder in sys.path, in order, for fees.py or a fees package folder.

sys.path is a list of strings:

>>> import sys
>>> type(sys.path), isinstance(sys.path[0], str)
(<class 'list'>, True)

It starts with the script's folder (or an empty string in the REPL, meaning the current directory), followed by entries from the PYTHONPATH environment variable, then the standard library and the site-packages folder of the active environment (see Setup and running code).

The practical rules that follow:

  • A file named like a standard module (json.py, random.py, logging.py) placed next to your script shadows the real one, because the script's folder comes first.
  • ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'x' means no folder in sys.path contains x. Either it is not installed in the interpreter you are running, or your own folder is not on the path.
  • To use code from another folder, put the folder on the path (PYTHONPATH, or a package install), not by editing sys.path inside your files.

For Odoo, the addons path (set in the configuration file or with --addons-path) is how the server finds addons, and Odoo arranges the Python import side so that each addon in those folders is importable as odoo.addons.<module_name>. You do not edit sys.path yourself.

Inspect where something comes from:

>>> import json
>>> json.__name__, json.__file__.endswith("__init__.py")
('json', True)

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
A package is a folder that contains modules and, normally, a file named __init__.py. The folder name is the package name:

library/
    __init__.py
    models/
        __init__.py
        book.py
        loan.py

You import from it with dotted names:

import library.models.book
from library.models import loan
from library.models.book import register

__init__.py runs when the package is imported. It may be empty, or it may import the package's submodules. Whatever names it defines or imports become attributes of the package, which makes __init__.py the place to define the package's public face.

Since Python 3.3, a folder without __init__.py can still be imported as an implicit namespace package. It works until you need package-level initialisation, and for Odoo addons the file is required. A missing __init__.py is a classic cause of "my new folder is ignored".

docs.title: Relative imports
docs.text:
Inside a package you can refer to siblings relative to the current module:

# library/models/loan.py
from . import book              # sibling module: library.models.book
from .book import register      # a name from a sibling
from .. import wizard           # a module one level up: library.wizard
from ..tools import helpers     # a module in a sibling package

One dot means the current package, two dots the parent. Relative imports work only inside a package, not in a script run directly. They survive renaming the top-level package. Odoo code uses them heavily: from . import models in the addon's root __init__.py.

docs.title: Example: observing import order
docs.text:
With the package layout above, where models/__init__.py contains from . import book then from . import loan, and each file prints a line when loaded:

>>> import library
loading book
loading loan

import library ran library/__init__.py, which ran from . import models, which ran models/__init__.py, which imported book and then loan in the written order. Each module appears in sys.modules under its dotted name:

>>> sorted(m for m in sys.modules if m.startswith("library"))
['library', 'library.models', 'library.models.book', 'library.models.loan']

Import order is execution order, and execution order is what matters in Odoo, as the next section shows.

docs.title: Anatomy of an Odoo addon, as Python
docs.text:
An addon is a folder on the addons path containing a __manifest__.py and, for Python code, an __init__.py:

library/
    __manifest__.py
    __init__.py
    models/
        __init__.py
        book.py
        loan.py
    wizard/
        __init__.py
        return_wizard.py
    controllers/
        __init__.py
        main.py
    views/
        book_views.xml
    security/
        ir.model.access.csv

The root __init__.py is the entry point Odoo imports when it loads the addon, and it lists which subpackages to load:

# library/__init__.py
from . import models
from . import wizard
from . import controllers

# library/models/__init__.py
from . import book
from . import loan

Each model file defines classes inheriting models.Model. A model class exists in Odoo only if its file is imported. If you create models/fine.py and forget the line from . import fine in models/__init__.py, the file is never executed, the class is never defined, and nothing tells you: no error, and the model is simply absent. Views that reference its fields later fail with errors about unknown fields or models, which sends people looking in the wrong place. When a new model does not show up, check the __init__.py chain first.

The order of imports is also meaningful:

  • Inside one addon, classes are collected in the order in which their modules were imported. When two classes in the same addon extend one model, the order of from . import ... lines decides which is earlier in the chain (see super() explained).
  • A file that uses a class or constant from a sibling can import it, and Python will load the sibling first if it has not been loaded already.

The manifest, __manifest__.py, contains a single dictionary literal. Odoo reads it without importing the addon's code, to find the name, dependencies, data files, and so on. The fields that matter at this point:

{
    "name": "Library",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "depends": ["base", "mail"],
    "data": ["security/ir.model.access.csv", "views/book_views.xml"],
    "external_dependencies": {"python": ["lxml"]},
    "license": "LGPL-3",
}

depends lists other addons that must be loaded first, which is what decides module load order and therefore the order of the model chain. external_dependencies lists Python packages, and Odoo checks they are importable at install time and refuses to install the addon otherwise, with a message naming the missing library. The manifest keys are covered in the architecture part of this book.

docs.title: Importing from another addon
docs.text:
An addon that depends on another can import from it using the odoo.addons namespace:

from odoo.addons.library.models.book import SOME_CONSTANT

Use it for constants, helpers, and exceptions, not to bypass the ORM. Models of other addons are reached through the environment (self.env["library.book"]), not by importing the class. Importing an addon you do not list in depends may work on your machine, because it is on the addons path, and then fail on a database where it is not installed.

docs.title: Importing external libraries
docs.text:
A third-party package used only by some features should not break the whole addon when it is absent. The standard guarded import:

import logging

_logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

try:
    import xlsxwriter
except ImportError:
    _logger.warning("xlsxwriter is not installed; Excel export is disabled")
    xlsxwriter = None

and later:

def export_xlsx(self):
    if xlsxwriter is None:
        raise UserError(_("The xlsxwriter library is required for this export."))

For a hard requirement, list the package in external_dependencies so that installation fails clearly, rather than the failure happening at the first click.

docs.title: Circular imports
docs.text:
Module a imports b, and b imports a. Python starts loading a, hits import b, starts loading b, hits import a, finds a partially initialised in sys.modules (its remaining lines have not run yet), and the result depends on what b asks of it.

# circ/a.py
from circ.b import B_VALUE
A_VALUE = 1

# circ/b.py
from circ.a import A_VALUE
B_VALUE = 2

$ python3 -c "import circ.a"
  File ".../circ/b.py", line 1, in <module>
    from circ.a import A_VALUE
ImportError: cannot import name 'A_VALUE' from partially initialized module 'circ.a' (most likely due to a circular import)

from circ.a import A_VALUE needs the name A_VALUE to exist right now, but a has not reached the line that defines it. Note the traceback shows the error in b.py, though the design problem spans both files.

If the two files use import module and access attributes later, at call time rather than at import time, the same cycle works:

# circ/c.py
import circ.d

def c_value():
    return circ.d.D_VALUE + 1
C_VALUE = 1

# circ/d.py
import circ.c
D_VALUE = 10

def d_value():
    return circ.c.C_VALUE + D_VALUE

$ python3 -c "import circ.c, circ.d; print(circ.c.c_value(), circ.d.d_value())"
11 11

Here, nobody touches an attribute of the partially loaded module at import time, only inside functions that run later, when both modules are complete. This works, but it is fragile, and relying on it is a smell.

docs.title: Ways out
docs.text:
1. Move the shared piece to a third module that both import. This is almost always the right fix. If a and b both need a constant, a function, or a base class, put it in common.py and have both import from it. The dependency graph becomes a tree.
  2. Import inside the function that needs it (a deferred or local import):
def confirm(self):
    from .wizard import ConfirmWizard      # imported on first call, not at load
    return ConfirmWizard.run(self)

Works, and is acceptable for rare code paths. The cost is a hidden dependency and a tiny lookup on every call. 3. Use import module style and reference attributes lazily, as in the c/d example. 4. Reference by name, not by class. In Odoo you almost never need to import a model class from a sibling file, because self.env["library.book"] retrieves it by its model name at runtime. Many circular imports in addons come from importing a class that could have been looked up through env. Many-to-one fields reference other models by string (fields.Many2one("library.book")), which is exactly to avoid the import. 5. Type checking only: for type hints, from __future__ import annotations plus if TYPE_CHECKING: imports the name for editors without importing it at runtime.

docs.title: Reloading and importlib
docs.text:
Importing a name twice does not re-run the module. importlib.reload(module) forces it, and is useful in the REPL while developing a helper file, with caveats: objects created before the reload still refer to the old classes. Do not use it in production code. In Odoo, changes to Python files take effect after the server restarts, or in development when the server runs with auto-reload enabled.

importlib.import_module("library.models.book") imports a module by a name held in a string:

>>> import importlib
>>> mod = importlib.import_module("json")
>>> mod.dumps({"a": 1})
'{"a": 1}'

This is the building block for plugin systems and for code that picks an implementation at runtime from configuration.

docs.title: __all__
docs.text:
A module may define __all__, a list of the names that from module import * exports and that documentation tools treat as public:

__all__ = ["late_fee", "RATE"]

Names that begin with an underscore are also treated as private by convention. Python does not enforce privacy: anyone can import fees; fees._helper. The convention tells readers what is safe to depend on.

docs.title: Organising your own code
docs.text:
A few conventions that keep imports healthy:

  • One direction of dependency. If models imports from tools, then tools must not import from models. Draw the arrows; they should have no cycles.
  • Small, named modules. tools/dates.py and tools/money.py beat utils.py with 40 unrelated functions.
  • Pure helpers in their own modules. Functions that do not touch the ORM (parsing, formatting, calculations) go in plain Python modules. They can be tested without a database, and they import nothing from Odoo.
  • Explicit public names. Re-export what other files should use from __init__.py, so internal files can move.
  • Absolute imports in scripts, relative inside packages.
  • No work at import time. Module-level code defines things; functions do things.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Missing line in __init__.py. A new model or wizard file that is not imported does nothing, with no error. When something you wrote does not exist at runtime, check the import chain from the addon root.
  • Missing __init__.py in a new folder. The subpackage is not importable or not loaded.
  • Circular imports. Fix by extracting shared code, not by sprinkling local imports around.
  • Shadowing a standard module. json.py, logging.py, email.py, or types.py in your folder breaks unrelated imports. Delete __pycache__ after renaming.
  • from x import *. Hides origins and overwrites names silently.
  • Importing a class from another addon without declaring the dependency. Works locally where both are installed, fails elsewhere. Use depends, and prefer self.env[...].
  • Work at import time. Network calls or database access in module-level code slow down and can break server startup.
  • Mutable module-level state. Shared by all requests, and across databases in one process.
  • Optional library imports without a guard. A missing optional package breaks the whole addon load. Use the try/except ImportError pattern, or list a hard requirement in external_dependencies.
  • Relative import in a script. ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package when the file is run directly. Run it as a module (python -m package.module) or use absolute imports.
  • Stale .pyc or reload confusion. After moving files, stale __pycache__ folders can mask the change. Restarting the process is the reliable fix.
  • Different import paths for one file. Importing the same file as library.models.book in one place and as models.book in another creates two module objects with two copies of every class. Always import through the one canonical dotted path.
  • Assuming import order across addons. Do not rely on one addon being loaded before another unless the dependency is declared.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Create a package shop with __init__.py, prices.py (a function with_tax(amount, rate=0.2)), and report.py that imports with_tax with a relative import and defines line(label, amount) returning a formatted string. Import shop.report from a script one level above, and print a line.
  2. Add a print("loading prices") to prices.py. Import shop.report and shop.prices in the same script, and count how many times the message prints. Explain.
  3. Make a deliberate circular import with from ... import name in both modules, read the error, and fix it by moving the shared constant to a third module.
  4. Write a script tool.py with a function main() and the __main__ guard. Run it directly, then import it from the REPL, and observe the difference.
  5. Sketch the __init__.py files for an addon with models/book.py, models/loan.py, wizard/return_wizard.py, and controllers/main.py. Which line, if missing, hides a model silently, and which one hides a controller route?
Solution
  1. Layout and files:
project/
    main.py
    shop/
        __init__.py        (empty)
        prices.py
        report.py

# shop/prices.py
def with_tax(amount, rate=0.2):
    return round(amount * (1 + rate), 2)

# shop/report.py
from .prices import with_tax

def line(label, amount):
    return f"{label:<10}{with_tax(amount):>8.2f}"

# main.py
from shop.report import line
print(line("Book", 10))

$ python3 main.py
Book          12.00

  1. The message prints once. import shop.report loads shop.prices as a side effect of the relative import, and sys.modules caches it, so the later import shop.prices finds it already loaded and does not run the file again.

  2. With a.py doing from b import X and b.py doing from a import Y, the second import fails with ImportError: cannot import name ... from partially initialized module. Move X and Y to common.py and have both modules import from it; the dependency graph then has no cycle.

  3. Run directly, __name__ is "__main__" and the guarded block executes. Imported from the REPL, __name__ is "tool", the guarded block does not run, and main() is available to call by hand.

5.

# addon/__init__.py
from . import models
from . import wizard
from . import controllers

# addon/models/__init__.py
from . import book
from . import loan

# addon/wizard/__init__.py
from . import return_wizard

# addon/controllers/__init__.py
from . import main

Missing from . import loan in models/__init__.py hides the loan model silently. Missing from . import controllers in the root __init__.py (or from . import main in the controllers package) leaves the routes unregistered, and requests to them return a not-found response.

docs.title: Setup and running code
docs.text: Odoo is a Python program. Every model, every button handler, every scheduled job you will write is Python executed by an interpreter on a server. Before you write a line of business logic you need three things: a working interpreter, an isolated place to install libraries, and a feedback loop that tells you within seconds whether a line of code does what you think. This chapter builds those three things and introduces the vocabulary used for the rest of Part 1. It assumes you have never programmed.

docs.title: What "running Python" means
docs.text:
A computer executes machine instructions. Python source code is text, so something has to translate it. That something is the interpreter: a program called python (or python3) that reads your text file, converts it to an internal form, and executes it step by step. When you "run a script", you start the interpreter and hand it a file.

Python code lives in files ending in .py. A file is a script when you run it directly and a module when another file imports it (see Modules and imports). The distinction is about how the file is used, not about its content.

Odoo is started by running the interpreter on its entry point, conceptually python odoo-bin .... The server reads your module files, loads them as Python modules, and calls your code when users click things. Everything in this part of the book applies to those files.

docs.title: Which version
docs.text:
Each Odoo release states a minimum Python version, and the supported range moves with the release. Read the requirements.txt and the installation documentation of the release you target, then install an interpreter inside that range. This book uses syntax that needs Python 3.10 in a few places (match, X | Y in type hints) and says so each time. If your server runs an older interpreter, those snippets will not work there, and the text names the older equivalent.

Test on the same major.minor version your production server uses. A feature that exists on your laptop's interpreter and not on the server is a common way to break a deployment.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Download the installer from python.org. On the first screen tick Add python.exe to PATH. PATH is the list of folders the shell searches when you type a command name; without the tick, typing python finds nothing.

Open PowerShell and check:

> python --version
Python 3.12.4

Windows also ships a launcher called py that can choose between several installed versions:

> py -3.12 --version
Python 3.12.4
> py -0
 -V:3.12 *        Python 3.12 (64-bit)
 -V:3.10          Python 3.10 (64-bit)

py -0 lists installed versions and marks the default with *. With several Pythons installed, use py -3.10 to be explicit.

Windows has "App execution aliases" that make python open the Microsoft Store when no interpreter is installed. If python opens the Store, install from python.org and disable the alias under Settings, Apps, Advanced app settings, App execution aliases.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Most distributions ship Python. Check first:

$ python3 --version
Python 3.10.12

On Debian and Ubuntu you also need the venv module and the build tools that Odoo's dependencies need:

$ sudo apt install python3-venv python3-pip python3-dev build-essential

On Linux the command is python3. A bare python may not exist, or may point to something old. Inside a virtual environment (next section) python always exists and always means the right one.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: Install with Homebrew (brew install python@3.12) or from python.org. The command is python3.

docs.title: 1. The REPL
docs.text:
REPL means Read-Evaluate-Print Loop. Start the interpreter with no arguments:

$ python3
Python 3.12.4 (main, Jun  6 2024, 18:26:44) [GCC 13.2.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>>

>>> is the prompt. You type an expression, press Enter, and Python prints the result:

>>> 2 + 3
5
>>> "library" + " " + "book"
'library book'
>>> len("library.book")
12

Lines starting with >>> are what you type. Lines without a prefix are what Python prints. The book uses this format throughout; paste the >>> lines into a REPL and you see the same output.

A statement that needs more than one line shows the continuation prompt ...:

>>> for n in range(3):
...     print(n)
...
0
1
2

Press Enter on the empty ... line to finish the block. Leave the REPL with exit(), or Ctrl+D on Linux and macOS, or Ctrl+Z then Enter on Windows.

The REPL is the fastest way to answer "what does this expression do?". Use it constantly. Two built-ins make it better:

  • help(thing) shows documentation (press q to leave the pager). Try help(str.split).
  • dir(thing) lists the names an object offers.
>>> dir("abc")[-3:]
['title', 'translate', 'upper']

Both work on anything, including Odoo objects, which is why they matter later when you stand in front of an unfamiliar recordset.

The underscore _ holds the last printed result:

>>> 6 * 7
42
>>> _ + 1
43

docs.title: 2. Running a script file
docs.text:
Create a file hello.py:

name = "library"
count = 3
print("Module:", name)
print("Books:", count)

Run it from the folder that contains it:

$ python3 hello.py
Module: library
Books: 3

print() writes text to the terminal. A script that computes something and does not print it appears to do nothing. In the REPL the value of the last expression is printed automatically; in a script it is not.

A script is read top to bottom, once, and the interpreter exits at the end. Variables disappear. This is the main difference from the REPL, where state stays until you exit.

docs.title: 3. python -c for one-liners
docs.text:
-c runs a string as code:

$ python3 -c "print(sum(range(1, 101)))"
5050

This is useful for quick checks and for shell scripts. Quoting differs between shells; double quotes outside and single quotes inside works in Bash, PowerShell, and cmd:

$ python3 -c "print('a' * 3)"
aaa

docs.title: Running a module with -m
docs.text:
python -m name runs an installed module as a program. You will use these:

$ python3 -m venv .venv            # create a virtual environment
$ python3 -m pip install lxml      # run the pip that belongs to THIS interpreter
$ python3 -m json.tool data.json   # pretty-print a JSON file
$ python3 -m http.server 8000      # serve the current folder

python -m pip is better than a bare pip. A bare pip belongs to whichever Python appears first on PATH, which may not be the one you think. python -m pip installs into the interpreter you named.

docs.title: Virtual environments
docs.text:
Python libraries are installed into the interpreter's own folder, called site-packages. If every project installs there, two projects that need different versions of the same library collide. Odoo makes this concrete: different Odoo releases pin different versions of libraries such as lxml, Pillow, psycopg2, and Werkzeug. You cannot satisfy both in one folder.

A virtual environment (venv) is a self-contained folder holding a link to (or copy of) the interpreter plus its own empty site-packages. Install into it and nothing else on the machine changes. Give each Odoo version its own venv.

docs.title: Create and activate
docs.text:
$ cd ~/work/odoo-16
$ python3 -m venv .venv

Activation changes your shell's PATH for the current session so that python and pip resolve inside .venv:

# Linux / macOS
$ source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ which python
/home/me/work/odoo-16/.venv/bin/python

# Windows PowerShell
> .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
(.venv) > (Get-Command python).Source
C:\work\odoo-16\.venv\Scripts\python.exe

The (.venv) prefix tells you it is active. Leave with deactivate.

On Windows PowerShell, activation can fail with "running scripts is disabled on this system". Run Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned once, or skip activation and call the interpreter by its path: .venv\Scripts\python.exe script.py.

Activation is a convenience for humans. Services and cron jobs call the venv's interpreter by full path: /opt/odoo/.venv/bin/python /opt/odoo/odoo-bin -c /etc/odoo.conf.

docs.title: Installing packages with pip
docs.text:
pip downloads libraries from the Python Package Index (PyPI) and installs them in the active environment:

(.venv) $ python -m pip install --upgrade pip
(.venv) $ python -m pip install requests
(.venv) $ python -m pip list
Package            Version
------------------ ---------
certifi            2024.7.4
charset-normalizer 3.3.2
idna               3.7
pip                24.1.2
requests           2.32.3
urllib3            2.2.2

Pin versions in a text file. Odoo ships its own requirements.txt:

(.venv) $ python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

Each line names a package and optionally a version constraint, like lxml==4.9.3 or Pillow>=9.0,<11. If a package fails to build, the error usually names a missing system library (libpq-dev, libxml2-dev, libldap2-dev, libsasl2-dev on Debian-family systems). Install it with the system package manager and retry.

To record what you have installed:

(.venv) $ python -m pip freeze > frozen.txt

docs.title: Checking which Python is running
docs.text:
When something behaves oddly, ask the interpreter about itself:

>>> import sys
>>> sys.version_info[:2]
(3, 12)
>>> sys.executable
'/home/me/work/odoo-16/.venv/bin/python'
>>> sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix   # True inside a venv
True
>>> import lxml
>>> lxml.__file__
'/home/me/work/odoo-16/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/lxml/__init__.py'

sys.executable answers "which interpreter am I?". module.__file__ answers "which copy of this library did I import?". Those two questions resolve most "it works on my machine" confusion.

docs.title: Shadowing and isolated mode
docs.text:
When you run a script, Python searches the script's own folder first when resolving imports. A file named random.py or json.py next to your script therefore shadows the standard library module of the same name. Two defenses:

  • Never name your files after standard modules (json.py, random.py, logging.py, email.py, datetime.py).
  • Run throwaway code with python -I (isolated mode), which ignores the current directory and the PYTHON* environment variables:
$ python3 -I -c "import json; print(json.__file__)"
/usr/lib/python3.12/json/__init__.py

Keep a scratch folder outside any project for experiments, so stray files never end up on an addons path.

docs.title: Reading error messages
docs.text:
You will see errors every day. They describe what went wrong and where. Learn to read them bottom-up.

def total(prices):
    return sum(prices)

def report(data):
    return total(data["prices"])

print(report({"price": [1, 2, 3]}))

$ python3 report.py
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "report.py", line 7, in <module>
    print(report({"price": [1, 2, 3]}))
  File "report.py", line 5, in report
    return total(data["prices"])
KeyError: 'prices'

Read from the last line up. KeyError: 'prices' says what happened: a dictionary was asked for a key it does not have. The line above it shows the exact line of code. Lines above that show who called whom to get there, outermost call first. The last frame is where the error was raised, which is not always where the mistake was made. Here the typo is "price" in the data on line 7; the error surfaces at line 5.

Odoo prints this same traceback in its server log and, for errors the user can see, summarises it in a dialog. The skill is identical.

docs.title: Syntax errors versus runtime errors
docs.text:
A SyntaxError happens before any code runs, because the interpreter cannot parse the file:

  File "x.py", line 2
    if count > 3
                ^
SyntaxError: expected ':'

Everything else (NameError, TypeError, KeyError, ...) happens while running, so code before the faulty line has already executed. In Odoo a syntax error in a module file means the module fails to load at server start, and the log names the file and line. A runtime error inside a method appears only when a user triggers that method.

docs.title: Editors and tooling
docs.text:
You can write Python in any text editor, but three features save hours:

  1. Syntax highlighting and indentation handling. Python uses indentation as structure (see Control flow), so mixing tabs and spaces breaks code. Configure your editor to insert 4 spaces when you press Tab.
  2. A linter. flake8, pylint, or ruff flag undefined names, unused imports, and many bugs without running the code.
  3. A debugger. Covered in the Shell and debugging part of this book. For now print() is enough.

Install tools in the venv, not globally:

(.venv) $ python -m pip install ruff
(.venv) $ python -m ruff check hello.py
All checks passed!

docs.title: Your first useful script
docs.text:
A script that reads a text file and counts lines per state. Create loans.txt:

book-001 returned
book-002 open
book-003 open
book-004 returned
book-005 open

And count_loans.py:

from collections import Counter

counts = Counter()
with open("loans.txt", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    for line in handle:
        line = line.strip()
        if not line:
            continue
        book, state = line.split()
        counts[state] += 1

for state, number in counts.items():
    print(state, number)

$ python3 count_loans.py
returned 2
open 3

You do not need to understand every line yet. Notice the shape: read input, loop, compute, print. The next chapters explain each part until the whole script is obvious: import in Modules and imports, Counter and .items() in Lists, tuples, dicts, sets, for and continue in Control flow, and with open in Errors and exceptions and the Standard library toolbox.

docs.title: Where Odoo's Python runs
docs.text:
When you later start Odoo, several execution contexts exist, all using the same interpreter:

Context How it starts Typical use Server python odoo-bin -c config The long-running process that serves users. Shell python odoo-bin shell -d dbname An interactive REPL with a database environment loaded. Module install or update odoo-bin -d db -i module or -u module Runs your data files and migration scripts. Tests odoo-bin with test options Runs test classes.

The Odoo shell is a normal REPL with an extra variable (env) bound to a database environment. Everything you practise in a plain REPL transfers directly. Part 4 covers the command line in detail; the point here is that "Python for Odoo" is plain Python, run by a plain interpreter, inside a venv you control.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Wrong interpreter. pip install into the system Python, then running Odoo from a venv (or the reverse), gives ModuleNotFoundError for a package you "just installed". Use python -m pip and verify with sys.executable.
  • Forgetting to activate. A new terminal tab uses the system Python. The prompt prefix (.venv) is your confirmation.
  • Moving or renaming a venv folder. Venvs store absolute paths. Renaming the parent folder breaks the scripts inside .venv. Recreate the venv and reinstall from requirements.txt; venvs are disposable by design.
  • Committing the venv. Add .venv/ to .gitignore. Share requirements.txt, not the environment.
  • Shadowing standard modules. A local json.py or logging.py makes import json load your file. The error then looks unrelated (AttributeError: module 'json' has no attribute 'loads'). Rename the file and delete the __pycache__ folder next to it.
  • Mixed tabs and spaces. Python 3 raises TabError when they are mixed in a way it cannot interpret consistently. Configure the editor to use spaces.
  • Missing system libraries. pip install of psycopg2 or python-ldap fails with compiler errors when headers are absent. The fix is a system package, not a different pip command.
  • Different Python on the server. Developing on 3.12 and deploying on 3.10 means match works in both, while a newer standard library function may not exist on the server. Pin the same minor version.
  • File encoding on Windows. open("file.txt") without encoding= uses the system code page, so the same script reads a file differently on two machines. Always pass encoding="utf-8".
  • Print-less scripts. A script that computes and prints nothing looks broken. In a script, use print().

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Create a folder scratch, a virtual environment inside it, activate it, and print sys.prefix and sys.executable from the REPL. Confirm that they point inside the folder.
  2. Write squares.py that prints the squares of 1 to 5, one per line, then run it from the shell. Then do the same as a one-liner with -c.
  3. Deliberately cause a NameError, a KeyError, and a SyntaxError. For each, read the message bottom-up and state what the interpreter is telling you.
  4. In the scratch folder create json.py containing print("mine"). Run python -c "import json; print(json.__file__)", then python -I -c "import json; print(json.__file__)". Explain the difference, then delete the file.
  5. Install requests into the venv, then run python -m pip freeze. Create a second venv and check that requests is absent there.
Solution
  1. Typical commands:
$ mkdir scratch && cd scratch
$ python3 -m venv .venv
$ source .venv/bin/activate
(.venv) $ python
>>> import sys
>>> sys.prefix
'/home/me/scratch/.venv'
>>> sys.executable
'/home/me/scratch/.venv/bin/python'
  1. File:
for n in range(1, 6):
    print(n * n)

One-liner: python -c "print(*[n * n for n in range(1, 6)], sep=chr(10))" prints 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 on separate lines. (The for statement form does not fit after -c on one line when combined with other statements, which is why the list comprehension form is used; comprehensions are covered in Comprehensions and generators.)

  1. print(undefined_name) gives NameError: name 'undefined_name' is not defined: a name was used that was never assigned. {"a": 1}["b"] gives KeyError: 'b': the dictionary has no such key. if True print(1) gives SyntaxError, raised before anything runs. The last line names the type; the lines above give location.

  2. Without -I, the current directory comes first on the import path, so json.__file__ shows .../scratch/json.py (and importing it prints mine). With -I the standard library module is loaded and json.__file__ shows a path inside the Python installation. Remove the file and the __pycache__ folder afterwards.

  3. After installation, python -m pip freeze lists requests with its dependencies. In the second venv python -m pip freeze prints nothing, because each venv has its own site-packages.

docs.title: Standard library toolbox
docs.text: Python ships with a large library of ready-made modules, and most integration work in Odoo is a matter of knowing which one to reach for: parse a CSV an accountant sent, decode a base64 attachment, serialise a payload to JSON, pull a reference out of a free-text string with a regular expression, walk a folder of files. Reimplementing these by hand is slower and buggier than using the standard module. This chapter is a working tour of the modules you will use most, with the idioms and the failure modes that matter in Odoo code. Dates and money get their own chapter: Money, dates, and time zones.

docs.title: Which module for which job
docs.text:
Job Module Text patterns re Structured data exchange json, csv Binary-to-text encoding base64 Hashing, signatures hashlib, hmac, secrets Files and paths pathlib, os, tempfile, shutil In-memory files io Records and counting collections, dataclasses Iteration tools itertools Function tools functools, operator Logging logging URLs urllib.parse Dates, time datetime, zoneinfo Numbers decimal, math, statistics

Check the standard library before installing a package. Check Odoo's own odoo.tools before writing a helper; it contains utilities for dates, rounding, files, and mail that already handle Odoo's conventions. Where this chapter names an Odoo helper, it is one that is certain to exist; for others it stays with plain Python.

docs.title: re: regular expressions
docs.text:
A regular expression describes a text pattern. Use it when split, startswith, and in are not enough.

>>> import re
>>> text = "Loans LIB-2024-0042 and LIB-2025-0007 were returned."
>>> re.findall(r"LIB-\d{4}-\d{4}", text)
['LIB-2024-0042', 'LIB-2025-0007']
>>> m = re.search(r"LIB-(\d{4})-(\d{4})", text)
>>> m.group(0), m.group(1), m.group(2)
('LIB-2024-0042', '2024', '0042')
>>> m.span()
(6, 19)
>>> re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "too    many \n spaces")
'too many spaces'
>>> re.split(r"[;,]\s*", "a, b;c,d")
['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']

Always write patterns as raw strings (r"..."), so backslashes reach the regex engine instead of being consumed by Python's string escapes (see Values and types).

The syntax you need most:

Pattern Matches . any character except newline \d, \w, \s digit, word character, whitespace \D, \W, \S the opposites [abc], [a-z0-9], [^abc] one of the set, a range, not in the set *, +, ? zero or more, one or more, zero or one {n}, {n,m} exactly n, between n and m ^, $ start and end of the string (or line with re.MULTILINE) (...) capture group (?P<name>...) named group (?:...) group without capturing a\|b alternatives \b word boundary

docs.title: Named groups and compiled patterns
docs.text:
Compile a pattern you use repeatedly, and name groups instead of counting them:

>>> LOAN_REF = re.compile(r"LIB-(?P<year>\d{4})-(?P<seq>\d{4})")
>>> m = LOAN_REF.fullmatch("LIB-2024-0042")
>>> m.groupdict()
{'year': '2024', 'seq': '0042'}
>>> LOAN_REF.fullmatch("LIB-2024-0042 extra") is None
True

fullmatch requires the whole string to match. match anchors at the start only. search finds the pattern anywhere. Choosing among them wrongly is the most common regex bug: re.match(r"\d+", "abc123") is None, while re.search finds 123.

re.compile at module level means the pattern is built once at import. Python caches recently used patterns anyway, so the gain is small, but a named constant documents intent.

docs.title: Flags and greediness
docs.text:
>>> re.findall(r"^book", "Book one\nbook two", flags=re.IGNORECASE | re.MULTILINE)
['Book', 'book']
>>> re.findall(r"<.+>", "<a><b>")
['<a><b>']
>>> re.findall(r"<.+?>", "<a><b>")
['<a>', '<b>']

Quantifiers are greedy: they match as much as possible. Adding ? makes them lazy. The second example matches the whole string because .+ swallowed everything up to the last >.

Regular expressions are the wrong tool for HTML, XML, and JSON. Use a real parser (lxml, json). They are also easy to write with catastrophic backtracking: a pattern like (a+)+$ against a long string of a followed by b can run for minutes. Never run a regex you did not write against untrusted input without checking its structure.

docs.title: json
docs.text:
JSON maps onto Python containers: objects become dicts, arrays become lists, strings stay strings, numbers become int or float, true/false become True/False, null becomes None.

>>> import json
>>> payload = {"ref": "SO1", "lines": [{"sku": "A", "qty": 2}], "paid": False, "note": None}
>>> text = json.dumps(payload)
>>> text
'{"ref": "SO1", "lines": [{"sku": "A", "qty": 2}], "paid": false, "note": null}'
>>> json.loads(text) == payload
True
>>> print(json.dumps({"b": [1, 2], "a": None}, indent=2, sort_keys=True))
{
  "a": null,
  "b": [
    1,
    2
  ]
}

dumps and loads work on strings, dump and load on file objects. Useful options: indent=2 for readable output, sort_keys=True for stable output (useful in tests and diffs), ensure_ascii=False to keep non-ASCII characters unescaped, separators=(",", ":") for compact output.

JSON has no date, decimal, or set type. Passing one raises TypeError:

>>> from datetime import date
>>> from decimal import Decimal
>>> json.dumps({"due": date(2025, 3, 1)})
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
TypeError: Object of type date is not JSON serializable

Convert explicitly, or give dumps a default function:

>>> def encode(obj):
...     if isinstance(obj, (date,)):
...         return obj.isoformat()
...     if isinstance(obj, Decimal):
...         return str(obj)
...     raise TypeError(f"cannot encode {type(obj).__name__}")
...
>>> json.dumps({"due": date(2025, 3, 1), "total": Decimal("10.50")}, default=encode)
'{"due": "2025-03-01", "total": "10.50"}'

Money is written as a string here to avoid float rounding on the receiving side. Agree on the convention with whoever consumes the data.

Other facts that cause bugs: tuples come back as lists, dict keys always become strings ({1: "a"} returns as {"1": "a"}), and loads raises json.JSONDecodeError (a ValueError subclass) on invalid input:

>>> json.loads(json.dumps({1: "a"}))
{'1': 'a'}
>>> try:
...     json.loads("{bad json}")
... except json.JSONDecodeError as exc:
...     print("invalid:", exc.msg)
invalid: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes

In Odoo, JSON appears in controllers that return JSON, in webhook payloads, in fields that store structured data as text, and in the HTTP calls you make to other systems. Always wrap loads of external data in a try/except (see Errors and exceptions), and never trust the structure: use get with defaults.

docs.title: csv
docs.text:
csv reads and writes comma-separated (and similar) files, handling quoting for you. Never split lines on commas by hand: a field such as "Smith, John" contains a comma.

>>> import csv, io
>>> raw = 'title,pages,note\nDune,612,"Epic, long"\nEmma,474,\n'
>>> reader = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(raw))
>>> rows = list(reader)
>>> rows[0]
{'title': 'Dune', 'pages': '612', 'note': 'Epic, long'}
>>> rows[1]["note"]
''
>>> reader.fieldnames
['title', 'pages', 'note']

Every value from a CSV is a string. Convert explicitly: int(row["pages"]). Empty cells are empty strings, not None.

Writing:

>>> out = io.StringIO()
>>> writer = csv.DictWriter(out, fieldnames=["title", "pages", "note"], lineterminator="\n")
>>> writer.writeheader()
17
>>> writer.writerow({"title": "Dune", "pages": 612, "note": "Epic, long"})
22
>>> writer.writerow({"title": "Emma", "pages": 474, "note": ""})
10
>>> print(out.getvalue(), end="")
title,pages,note
Dune,612,"Epic, long"
Emma,474,

Hints for real files:

  • Open files with newline="" and an explicit encoding: open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8"). Without newline="" embedded newlines in quoted fields and Windows line endings misbehave.
  • Spreadsheet programs often write semicolon-separated files in regions that use comma as decimal separator, and may prefix UTF-8 files with a byte-order mark. Open those with encoding="utf-8-sig" and delimiter=";".
  • csv.Sniffer can guess the dialect, but an explicit delimiter is more reliable.
>>> raw = "title;pages\nDune;612\n"
>>> list(csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(raw), delimiter=";"))
[{'title': 'Dune', 'pages': '612'}]

In Odoo you will parse uploaded files from a Binary field. The content arrives as base64, so decode it first and wrap it in io.StringIO (see the base64 and io sections). For very large files, iterate the reader instead of building a list, so that memory use stays flat (see Comprehensions and generators).

docs.title: io: files in memory
docs.text:
io.StringIO and io.BytesIO behave like files but live in memory. They let you use file-based APIs (csv, json.dump, image libraries, spreadsheet writers) without touching the disk:

>>> buf = io.StringIO()
>>> buf.write("hello\n")
6
>>> buf.write("world\n")
6
>>> buf.getvalue()
'hello\nworld\n'
>>> buf.seek(0)
0
>>> buf.readline()
'hello\n'
>>> data = io.BytesIO(b"\x00\x01\x02")
>>> data.read(2)
b'\x00\x01'

After writing to a buffer, call seek(0) before reading from it, or the read position is at the end and returns nothing. Report generators in Odoo, for instance, write an Excel or PDF file into a BytesIO and then return its bytes for an attachment or an HTTP response.

docs.title: base64
docs.text:
base64 converts bytes to ASCII text and back. It exists because some channels (JSON, XML, email, database text columns) cannot carry raw bytes:

>>> import base64
>>> raw = "café".encode("utf-8")
>>> encoded = base64.b64encode(raw)
>>> encoded
b'Y2Fmw6k='
>>> base64.b64decode(encoded).decode("utf-8")
'café'
>>> encoded.decode("ascii")        # as a str, ready for JSON
'Y2Fmw6k='

Both functions take and return bytes. Convert to str with .decode("ascii") when you need text. Base64 inflates data by about a third.

Odoo uses this heavily. A Binary field exposes its content as base64, and attachments store file content the same way in their datas value. The round trip when reading a file from an uploaded field looks like:

raw_bytes = base64.b64decode(self.upload_file)       # bytes of the original file
text = raw_bytes.decode("utf-8")
rows = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text))

and when producing a download:

buffer = io.BytesIO()
# ... write a spreadsheet or PDF into buffer ...
self.write({"result_file": base64.b64encode(buffer.getvalue())})

Mistakes here are common: decoding something that was never encoded (binascii.Error: Incorrect padding), or encoding twice so that the user downloads text instead of the file. When a downloaded file is garbage, check the number of encode and decode steps. In recent versions the field value may already be a bytes object, and in other cases a str; base64.b64decode accepts either, and you should not assume more.

URL-safe variants (urlsafe_b64encode) use - and _ instead of + and /, and appear in tokens.

docs.title: hashlib, hmac, secrets
docs.text:
>>> import hashlib, hmac
>>> hashlib.sha256(b"hello").hexdigest()
'2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824'
>>> sig = hmac.new(b"shared-secret", b"payload", hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
>>> len(sig)
64
>>> hmac.compare_digest(sig, sig)
True
  • Use hashlib for checksums and fingerprints (is this the same file?). Do not use it to store passwords; Odoo handles passwords itself.
  • Use hmac to sign and verify messages with a shared secret, as webhook endpoints do. Compare signatures with hmac.compare_digest, never ==, to avoid timing attacks.
  • Use secrets (not random) for tokens and anything security-relevant: secrets.token_urlsafe(32). random is predictable by design.

docs.title: pathlib and the file system
docs.text:
pathlib.Path represents file paths as objects and replaces most of os.path:

>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> p = Path("exports") / "2025" / "loans.csv"
>>> p.name, p.stem, p.suffix, p.parent
('loans.csv', 'loans', '.csv', PosixPath('exports/2025'))
>>> p.with_suffix(".json").as_posix()
'exports/2025/loans.json'

(On Windows the parent displays as WindowsPath('exports/2025').) The / operator joins parts with the right separator for the platform, so never build paths with string concatenation or hard-coded backslashes.

Reading, writing, and listing, in a temporary folder so the example cleans up after itself:

>>> import tempfile
>>> with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
...     folder = Path(tmp)
...     (folder / "a.txt").write_text("one\n", encoding="utf-8")
...     (folder / "b.txt").write_text("two\n", encoding="utf-8")
...     (folder / "data").mkdir()
...     (folder / "data" / "c.csv").write_text("x,y\n", encoding="utf-8")
...     print(sorted(p.name for p in folder.glob("*.txt")))
...     print(sorted(str(p.relative_to(folder).as_posix()) for p in folder.rglob("*") if p.is_file()))
...     print((folder / "a.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8").strip())
...     print((folder / "missing.txt").exists())
4
4
4
['a.txt', 'b.txt']
['a.txt', 'b.txt', 'data/c.csv']
one
False

The three 4s are the return values of write_text (characters written) echoed by the REPL for the three file writes. glob("*.txt") matches in one folder, rglob("*") recurses.

Important details:

  • Always pass encoding="utf-8" to read_text, write_text, and open.
  • Path.exists() followed by an action has a race: the file can change in between. For files, prefer to just try and catch FileNotFoundError.
  • tempfile creates temporary files and folders that are cleaned up, and avoids collisions between concurrent requests. Never write temporary files to a fixed name like /tmp/export.csv in a server that handles several requests at once.
  • shutil copies, moves, and deletes trees: shutil.copy, shutil.move, shutil.rmtree. rmtree deletes recursively and without confirmation; double-check the path.
  • In a long-running Odoo process, do not rely on the current working directory: it is whatever the server was started from. Build paths from a known base.
  • Never build a path from user input without validating it. A file name of ../../etc/passwd escapes the intended folder. Take only Path(name).name, and check that the resolved path stays inside the base folder.

docs.title: itertools
docs.text:
itertools provides building blocks for iteration that work lazily:

>>> from itertools import chain, islice, groupby, accumulate, product, combinations, zip_longest, takewhile, count
>>> list(chain([1, 2], [3, 4]))
[1, 2, 3, 4]
>>> list(chain.from_iterable([[1, 2], [3], []]))
[1, 2, 3]
>>> list(islice(count(10), 3))
[10, 11, 12]
>>> list(accumulate([1, 2, 3, 4]))
[1, 3, 6, 10]
>>> list(product("ab", [1, 2]))
[('a', 1), ('a', 2), ('b', 1), ('b', 2)]
>>> list(combinations([1, 2, 3], 2))
[(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)]
>>> list(zip_longest([1, 2, 3], ["a"], fillvalue="-"))
[(1, 'a'), (2, '-'), (3, '-')]
>>> list(takewhile(lambda n: n < 3, [1, 2, 3, 1]))
[1, 2]

chain.from_iterable flattens one level of nesting; it is the usual way to flatten the lines of several orders. accumulate gives running totals. groupby needs input sorted by the key, as covered in Comprehensions and generators.

A batching helper (itertools.batched exists in Python 3.12+; for older versions write your own):

>>> from itertools import islice
>>> def batched(iterable, n):
...     it = iter(iterable)
...     while batch := list(islice(it, n)):
...         yield batch
...
>>> list(batched(range(7), 3))
[[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6]]

Unlike the slicing version in the generators chapter, this works on any iterable, including a generator or a database cursor.

docs.title: functools and operator
docs.text:
Beyond wraps and lru_cache from Decorators:

>>> from functools import reduce, partial, cmp_to_key
>>> reduce(lambda acc, n: acc * n, [1, 2, 3, 4], 1)
24
>>> from operator import itemgetter, attrgetter, add
>>> rows = [{"name": "b", "n": 2}, {"name": "a", "n": 2}, {"name": "c", "n": 1}]
>>> sorted(rows, key=itemgetter("n", "name"))
[{'name': 'c', 'n': 1}, {'name': 'a', 'n': 2}, {'name': 'b', 'n': 2}]
>>> reduce(add, [[1], [2, 3]], [])
[1, 2, 3]

itemgetter("n", "name") builds the key function lambda r: (r["n"], r["name"]). attrgetter("partner_id.name") does the same for attributes and supports dotted paths, which is the plain-Python analogue of walking relations on records. reduce folds a sequence into one value. Use it rarely: sum, max, "".join, and any cover most needs, and an explicit loop is often clearer.

functools.cached_property computes a value once per instance on first access, which suits helper objects (not Odoo models, whose cache is managed by the ORM).

docs.title: logging, briefly
docs.text: Covered with exceptions in Errors and exceptions. The rules to keep: _logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) at the top of each module, %s arguments instead of f-strings, _logger.exception inside except blocks, and levels used meaningfully. In Odoo the server configures handlers and formatting, so your code never calls basicConfig. In standalone scripts, call logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) once, at the entry point.

docs.title: urllib.parse
docs.text:
Build and take apart URLs without string slicing:

>>> from urllib.parse import urlparse, urlencode, quote, parse_qs, urljoin
>>> u = urlparse("https://example.org/api/v1/loans?state=open&page=2")
>>> u.scheme, u.netloc, u.path
('https', 'example.org', '/api/v1/loans')
>>> parse_qs(u.query)
{'state': ['open'], 'page': ['2']}
>>> urlencode({"q": "dune & co", "page": 2})
'q=dune+%26+co&page=2'
>>> quote("a b/c")
'a%20b/c'
>>> urljoin("https://example.org/api/", "v1/loans")
'https://example.org/api/v1/loans'

Always encode query parameters with urlencode (or pass params= to your HTTP library). Concatenating user input into a URL breaks on &, #, spaces, and non-ASCII text, and opens injection problems.

docs.title: A compact example: import a CSV of loans
docs.text:
