New York is four hours behind UTC in July (daylight saving), so the date stays the 1st. Tokyo is nine hours ahead, so it is already the next morning.

4.

>>> from datetime import date, time, timedelta
>>> def local_day_bounds_utc(day, zone_name):
...     zone = ZoneInfo(zone_name)
...     start = datetime.combine(day, time.min, tzinfo=zone)
...     end = datetime.combine(day + timedelta(days=1), time.min, tzinfo=zone)
...     return start.astimezone(timezone.utc), end.astimezone(timezone.utc)
...
>>> start, end = local_day_bounds_utc(date(2025, 11, 2), "America/New_York")
>>> (end - start).total_seconds() / 3600
25.0

The end of daylight saving gives a 25-hour day. Note that the end bound is built from the next day's local midnight, not by adding 24 hours to the start.

5.

>>> from dateutil.relativedelta import relativedelta
>>> def add_months(d, n):
...     return d + relativedelta(months=n)
...
>>> [add_months(date(2025, 1, 31), n).isoformat() for n in range(1, 5)]
['2025-02-28', '2025-03-31', '2025-04-30', '2025-05-31']

Each result is computed from the original date. Applying add_months(..., 1) repeatedly would produce 02-28, 03-28, 04-28, because the day of month is lost after the first clamp. For a monthly schedule, compute each date from the start date and the count.

docs.title: Aggregation and window functions
docs.text: Counting records per state, summing amounts per month, ranking customers, finding the previous row: these are the questions behind every Odoo list view with a "group by", every pivot, and most report SQL. Aggregates collapse many rows into one; window functions compute over a set of related rows without collapsing them. This chapter covers both, including the NULL and fan-out behaviours that make totals wrong, with the library schema from Relational basics and the extra tables from Joins.

docs.title: Aggregate functions
docs.text:
An aggregate reads many rows and returns one value. Without GROUP BY, the whole filtered table is one group:

SELECT count(*)                 AS all_rows,
       count(author_id)         AS with_author,
       count(DISTINCT author_id) AS distinct_authors,
       sum(price)               AS total_price,
       avg(price)               AS avg_price,
       min(price)               AS cheapest,
       max(price)               AS dearest,
       sum(pages)               AS total_pages
FROM books;

 all_rows | with_author | distinct_authors | total_price |      avg_price      | cheapest | dearest | total_pages
----------+-------------+------------------+-------------+---------------------+----------+---------+-------------
        6 |           5 |                3 |       71.40 | 11.9000000000000000 |     5.00 |   18.00 |        1770
(1 row)

Read the first three columns carefully, they are the core of the NULL behaviour:

  • count(*) counts rows.
  • count(expr) counts rows where expr is not NULL. Here one book has no author, so 5.
  • count(DISTINCT expr) counts different non-NULL values: authors 1, 2, 3.

Every aggregate except count(*) ignores NULL inputs. avg(price) divides by the number of non-NULL prices, not by the number of rows. If an input set is empty (or all NULL), sum, avg, min, max return NULL, while count returns 0:

SELECT count(*) AS n, sum(price) AS total FROM books WHERE status = 'missing';

 n | total
---+-------
 0 |
(1 row)

So sum(...) of nothing is NULL, not zero, and an application doing arithmetic on it will fail or, in Python, hit None. Write COALESCE(sum(price), 0).

avg of integers returns numeric, so it is safe. The integer-division surprise lives in sum(a) / sum(b): sum of an integer column is bigint, and dividing two bigints truncates. Cast one side to numeric.

docs.title: GROUP BY
docs.text:
GROUP BY splits rows into groups sharing the same value of the listed expressions, and each aggregate is computed per group:

SELECT status, count(*) AS n, round(avg(price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM books
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status;

  status   | n | avg_price
-----------+---+-----------
 available | 5 |     12.30
 lost      | 1 |      9.90
(2 rows)

Every column in SELECT must either appear in GROUP BY or sit inside an aggregate. Otherwise:

SELECT status, title, count(*) FROM books GROUP BY status;

ERROR:  column "books.title" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function

The error is correct: which title would represent five different books? There is one exception that you will see in Odoo SQL: if you group by a table's primary key, every other column of that table is functionally dependent and may be selected without listing it (GROUP BY b.id and then SELECT b.title). PostgreSQL knows this; MySQL-style laxness elsewhere does not exist.

NULL forms its own group:

SELECT author_id, count(*) AS books, sum(pages) AS pages
FROM books
GROUP BY author_id
ORDER BY author_id;

 author_id | books | pages
-----------+-------+-------
         1 |     2 |   730
         2 |     2 |   430
         3 |     1 |   520
           |     1 |    90
(4 rows)

The last row is the group of books with no author. In GROUP BY and DISTINCT, NULLs are treated as equal to each other, unlike in WHERE comparisons. This is exactly what the Odoo list view shows as "None" in a grouped list.

You can group by an expression, and GROUP BY 1 refers to the first select column:

SELECT to_char(date_trunc('month', loaned_on), 'YYYY-MM') AS month, count(*) AS loans
FROM loans
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

  month  | loans
---------+-------
 2024-01 |     1
 2024-02 |     1
 2024-03 |     2
 2024-04 |     1
 2024-05 |     2
(5 rows)

Months with no loans are absent, which is how charts end up with gaps. Fill them by joining against generate_series:

SELECT to_char(m, 'YYYY-MM') AS month, count(l.id) AS loans
FROM generate_series('2024-01-01'::timestamp, '2024-06-01'::timestamp, interval '1 month') AS m
LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.loaned_on >= m AND l.loaned_on < m + interval '1 month'
GROUP BY m
ORDER BY m;

  month  | loans
---------+-------
 2024-01 |     1
 2024-02 |     1
 2024-03 |     2
 2024-04 |     1
 2024-05 |     2
 2024-06 |     0
(6 rows)

docs.title: HAVING: filter groups
docs.text:
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation, and can use aggregates:

SELECT author_id, count(*) AS books
FROM books
GROUP BY author_id
HAVING count(*) > 1
ORDER BY author_id;

 author_id | books
-----------+-------
         1 |     2
         2 |     2
(2 rows)

Put every condition that does not need an aggregate in WHERE, since it removes rows before the work of grouping. HAVING status = 'available' returns the same rows as WHERE status = 'available' but computes all groups first.

docs.title: FILTER: conditional aggregates
docs.text:
Counting several conditions in one scan is common in dashboards. The standard SQL way is FILTER:

SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE returned_on IS NULL)      AS open,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE returned_on > due_on)     AS late,
       count(*)                                         AS total
FROM loans;

 open | late | total
------+------+-------
    2 |    1 |     7
(1 row)

The older idiom sum(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) works everywhere and you will see it in a lot of code; FILTER is clearer and keeps NULL out of the way (CASE without ELSE yields NULL, and sum of nothing is NULL).

docs.title: Collecting values: string_agg, array_agg
docs.text:
To read a group as a list rather than a count:

SELECT m.name,
       string_agg(b.title, ', ' ORDER BY l.loaned_on) AS titles,
       array_agg(b.id ORDER BY l.loaned_on)           AS book_ids
FROM members m
JOIN loans l ON l.member_id = m.id
JOIN books b ON b.id = l.book_id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
ORDER BY m.id;

 name  |                titles                | book_ids
-------+--------------------------------------+----------
 Nora  | Tidewater, Salt Roads, Quiet Engines | {1,2,5}
 Omar  | Tidewater, Quiet Engines             | {1,5}
 Petra | Paper Moons, Tidewater               | {4,1}
(3 rows)

The ORDER BY inside the aggregate makes the list order deterministic; without it the order is whatever the scan produced. string_agg skips NULL values. array_agg keeps them. A grouped array_agg(id) is what the ORM's read_group uses to return the ids of records in a group, and it is handy for answering "which records are in this bucket" while debugging.

Other useful aggregates: bool_and / bool_or (all/any true), percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x) for the median, mode(), stddev, and jsonb_agg/jsonb_object_agg for building JSON.

SELECT percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY price) AS median_price FROM books;

 median_price
--------------
        11.75
(1 row)

avg is 11.90 and the median 11.75: with six values the median is the mean of the middle two (11.00 and 12.50).

docs.title: Subtotals: ROLLUP and GROUPING SETS
docs.text:
GROUP BY ROLLUP (a, b) adds subtotal and grand-total rows; GROUPING SETS lists exactly the groupings you want:

SELECT member_id, count(*) AS loans
FROM loans
GROUP BY ROLLUP (member_id)
ORDER BY member_id;

 member_id | loans
-----------+-------
         1 |     3
         2 |     2
         3 |     2
           |     7
(4 rows)

The last row, with NULL in the grouping column, is the grand total. When the grouping column can itself be NULL, the subtotal row and a genuine NULL group look the same; use grouping(member_id) (1 on a subtotal row) to tell them apart. Odoo's pivot view works much like this, though it computes its totals in separate queries.

docs.title: Aggregates over joins: the fan-out again
docs.text:
Recall from Joins that a one-to-many join repeats the left row. Aggregating after the join multiplies. Compare:

-- authors, their book counts, and loan counts, done wrong
SELECT a.name, count(b.id) AS books, count(l.id) AS loans
FROM authors a
LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id
LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.book_id = b.id
GROUP BY a.id, a.name
ORDER BY a.id;

     name      | books | loans
---------------+-------+-------
 Ada Marlowe   |     4 |     4
 Boris Venn    |     2 |     1
 Chiara Lund   |     2 |     2
 Dmitri Okafor |     0 |     0
(4 rows)

Ada has two books, not four: Tidewater matched three loans, so it was counted three times. count(DISTINCT b.id) fixes the book count; the loan count is right because each loan row is unique. The clean method is to aggregate the many side first:

SELECT a.name, count(b.id) AS books, COALESCE(sum(lc.loans), 0) AS loans
FROM authors a
LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT book_id, count(*) AS loans FROM loans GROUP BY book_id) lc ON lc.book_id = b.id
GROUP BY a.id, a.name
ORDER BY a.id;

     name      | books | loans
---------------+-------+-------
 Ada Marlowe   |     2 |     4
 Boris Venn    |     2 |     1
 Chiara Lund   |     1 |     2
 Dmitri Okafor |     0 |     0
(4 rows)

Now Ada has 2 books and 4 loans, and Chiara 1 book and 2 loans, as in the data. (Check the first result again: Chiara showed 2 books, because her one book matched two loans.) Any time a "count" is larger than the number of records you can see in the UI, look for an unaggregated join.

docs.title: Window functions
docs.text: A window function computes a value for each row from a set of related rows (its window) but does not collapse the rows. The syntax is function(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... frame). PARTITION BY splits rows into independent groups (like GROUP BY without collapsing), ORDER BY orders rows inside each partition, and the optional frame narrows the rows considered for the current one.

docs.title: Aggregates as windows
docs.text:
Any aggregate becomes a window function with OVER. Compare each book with the overall average:

SELECT title, price,
       round(avg(price) OVER (), 2)             AS overall_avg,
       round(price - avg(price) OVER (), 2)     AS diff
FROM books
ORDER BY id;

      title      | price | overall_avg |  diff
-----------------+-------+-------------+-------
 Tidewater       | 12.50 |       11.90 |  0.60
 Salt Roads      | 15.00 |       11.90 |  3.10
 The Long Ledger |  9.90 |       11.90 | -2.00
 Paper Moons     | 11.00 |       11.90 | -0.90
 Quiet Engines   | 18.00 |       11.90 |  6.10
 Orphan Volume   |  5.00 |       11.90 | -6.90
(6 rows)

OVER () means one window containing all rows. With PARTITION BY, each author's books are compared to the author's best:

SELECT title, author_id, price,
       max(price) OVER (PARTITION BY author_id) AS best_in_author
FROM books
WHERE author_id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY id;

      title      | author_id | price | best_in_author
-----------------+-----------+-------+----------------
 Tidewater       |         1 | 12.50 |          15.00
 Salt Roads      |         1 | 15.00 |          15.00
 The Long Ledger |         2 |  9.90 |          11.00
 Paper Moons     |         2 | 11.00 |          11.00
 Quiet Engines   |         3 | 18.00 |          18.00
(5 rows)

This replaces a self-join or a correlated subquery, and the plan reads the table once.

docs.title: Ranking: row_number, rank, dense_rank, ntile
docs.text:
SELECT id, member_id, loaned_on,
       row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY loaned_on) AS nth_loan
FROM loans
ORDER BY member_id, loaned_on;

 id | member_id | loaned_on  | nth_loan
----+-----------+------------+----------
  1 |         1 | 2024-01-05 |        1
  2 |         1 | 2024-02-01 |        2
  7 |         1 | 2024-05-20 |        3
  3 |         2 | 2024-03-10 |        1
  4 |         2 | 2024-03-12 |        2
  5 |         3 | 2024-04-02 |        1
  6 |         3 | 2024-05-01 |        2
(7 rows)

row_number numbers rows 1, 2, 3 within each partition; ties get arbitrary but distinct numbers, so always add a tie-breaker (ORDER BY loaned_on, id) when the order must be reproducible. rank gives equal rows the same number and then skips; dense_rank does not skip; ntile(n) cuts the ordered rows into n buckets.

SELECT m.name, count(l.id) AS loans,
       rank()       OVER (ORDER BY count(l.id) DESC) AS rank,
       dense_rank() OVER (ORDER BY count(l.id) DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM members m
LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.member_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
ORDER BY rank, m.name;

 name  | loans | rank | dense_rank
-------+-------+------+------------
 Nora  |     3 |    1 |          1
 Omar  |     2 |    2 |          2
 Petra |     2 |    2 |          2
 Quinn |     0 |    4 |          3
(4 rows)

This query shows an important ordering: windows are evaluated after GROUP BY and HAVING, so a window function can rank aggregated results, as here (a window over count(l.id)). Omar and Petra tie at rank 2; rank then jumps to 4, dense_rank continues with 3.

docs.title: The top-N-per-group pattern
docs.text:
You cannot filter on a window function in WHERE (it is evaluated later than WHERE). Wrap the query:

SELECT id, member_id, loaned_on
FROM (
    SELECT id, member_id, loaned_on,
           row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY loaned_on DESC, id DESC) AS rn
    FROM loans
) t
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY member_id;

 id | member_id | loaned_on
----+-----------+------------
  7 |         1 | 2024-05-20
  4 |         2 | 2024-03-12
  6 |         3 | 2024-05-01
(3 rows)

That is the latest loan per member. It is the window-function sibling of DISTINCT ON and LATERAL; pick DISTINCT ON for brevity, LATERAL when an index can serve each probe, and the window form when you also need ranks or several rows per group.

docs.title: lag and lead: look at neighbouring rows
docs.text:
SELECT id, member_id, loaned_on,
       lag(loaned_on) OVER (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY loaned_on) AS previous_loan,
       loaned_on - lag(loaned_on) OVER (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY loaned_on) AS days_since
FROM loans
ORDER BY member_id, loaned_on;

 id | member_id | loaned_on  | previous_loan | days_since
----+-----------+------------+---------------+------------
  1 |         1 | 2024-01-05 |               |
  2 |         1 | 2024-02-01 | 2024-01-05    |         27
  7 |         1 | 2024-05-20 | 2024-02-01    |        109
  3 |         2 | 2024-03-10 |               |
  4 |         2 | 2024-03-12 | 2024-03-10    |          2
  5 |         3 | 2024-04-02 |               |
  6 |         3 | 2024-05-01 | 2024-04-02    |         29
(7 rows)

lag(x, n, default) looks back n rows (default 1), lead looks forward; the first row of a partition has no predecessor, hence NULL, or the default you pass. This is the standard way to compute gaps between events, durations between a record's states from a tracking table, or a running balance difference.

docs.title: Running totals and frames
docs.text:
Adding ORDER BY inside OVER turns an aggregate into a running one:

SELECT title, price, sum(price) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS running_total
FROM books
ORDER BY id;

      title      | price | running_total
-----------------+-------+---------------
 Tidewater       | 12.50 |         12.50
 Salt Roads      | 15.00 |         27.50
 The Long Ledger |  9.90 |         37.40
 Paper Moons     | 11.00 |         48.40
 Quiet Engines   | 18.00 |         66.40
 Orphan Volume   |  5.00 |         71.40
(6 rows)

The default frame with an ORDER BY is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, and RANGE includes all peers: rows that tie on the ordering value. Order by something that is not unique and you see it:

SELECT title, author_id, pages,
       sum(pages) OVER (ORDER BY author_id) AS running_pages
FROM books
ORDER BY author_id, title;

      title      | author_id | pages | running_pages
-----------------+-----------+-------+---------------
 Salt Roads      |         1 |   420 |           730
 Tidewater       |         1 |   310 |           730
 Paper Moons     |         2 |   180 |          1160
 The Long Ledger |         2 |   250 |          1160
 Quiet Engines   |         3 |   520 |          1680
 Orphan Volume   |           |    90 |          1770
(6 rows)

Both of author 1's books show 730, not 420 and then 730, because they are peers. For a true row-by-row running total use a unique ordering (add id) or an explicit ROWS frame:

SELECT id, price,
       sum(price) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS two_book_sum
FROM books
ORDER BY id;

 id | price | two_book_sum
----+-------+--------------
  1 | 12.50 |        12.50
  2 | 15.00 |        27.50
  3 |  9.90 |        24.90
  4 | 11.00 |        20.90
  5 | 18.00 |        29.00
  6 |  5.00 |        23.00
(6 rows)

That is a moving sum over the current and previous row. Frames can also look ahead (1 FOLLOWING) or cover everything (UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING). first_value, last_value, and nth_value read values from the frame, and be careful with last_value: with the default frame it returns the current row's value, not the partition's last. Specify the frame if you want the end of the partition.

docs.title: Named windows
docs.text:
Repeating the same OVER (...) is tedious and error-prone. Define it once:

SELECT id, member_id,
       row_number() OVER w AS rn,
       lag(loaned_on) OVER w AS previous_loan
FROM loans
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY loaned_on, id)
ORDER BY member_id, loaned_on;

The WINDOW clause goes after HAVING and before ORDER BY.

docs.title: Where this shows up in Odoo
docs.text:
_read_group and read_group compile into GROUP BY queries with count(*) and sum(...) columns; your debugging queries are just the same thing written by hand. Accounting reports use window functions for running balances and previous-period comparison, and SQL-view reports often use row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) to pick "the latest" row. Know these shapes so you can read and fix them.

Versions. The Python API of read_group changed in Odoo 17 to 18 (a new _read_group signature with groupby/aggregates names, and formatted_read_group appearing later). That is ORM territory, covered in the ORM part. The SQL it produces is still GROUP BY plus aggregates.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Forgetting that count(col) skips NULLs. count(*) counts rows; count(col) counts values. Mixing them gives "off by the empty ones".
  • Empty aggregates return NULL. sum over no rows is NULL; wrap with COALESCE(..., 0) before arithmetic.
  • Aggregating after a one-to-many join. The fan-out doubles or triples sums and counts. Pre-aggregate the many side, or move the measure into a subquery.
  • HAVING for what belongs in WHERE. Same rows, more work.
  • avg of a rate. The average of per-row percentages is not the percentage of the totals. Compute sum(a) / sum(b), cast to numeric, and guard the division with NULLIF.
  • Window function in WHERE. Not allowed ("window functions are not allowed in WHERE"). Wrap in a subquery or CTE and filter outside.
  • Ties in row_number. Without a unique tie-breaker the numbering differs between runs, and "top 1" picks a random row among equals.
  • Default frame surprises. last_value returns the current row, and sum(...) OVER (ORDER BY non_unique) lumps ties together.
  • NULLs in GROUP BY. They form one group; a "None" bucket is data, not a bug. A NULL subtotal row in ROLLUP is confusable with it, use grouping().
  • Group by timestamp. GROUP BY create_date groups by the microsecond. Truncate: date_trunc('day', create_date), and mind the UTC issue from the previous chapter.
  • Counting distinct on huge sets. count(DISTINCT x) sorts or hashes every value; for large tables, aggregate in stages.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. For each member, return the number of loans, the number returned late, and the date of the first loan, including members without any loans.

  2. Which author has the highest average book price? Return the name and the average. Then return the full ranking including authors with no books, ranking them last.

  3. For each book, return the loan count and its rank by loan count (ties share a rank), showing only books ranked in the top 3.

  4. For each member's loans in order, return the loan id, the days kept (returned minus loaned) and a running total of the days kept so far for that member. Open loans have no days; use a unique ordering.

  5. Produce a month-by-month table for January to June 2024 showing how many loans were started and how many were returned in that month, with zeros for empty months.

Solution 

  1. SELECT m.name,
       count(l.id)                                   AS loans,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE l.returned_on > l.due_on) AS late,
       min(l.loaned_on)                              AS first_loan
FROM members m
LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.member_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
ORDER BY m.id;

     name  | loans | late | first_loan
-------+-------+------+------------
 Nora  |     3 |    1 | 2024-01-05
 Omar  |     2 |    0 | 2024-03-10
 Petra |     2 |    0 | 2024-04-02
 Quinn |     0 |    0 |
(4 rows)
    The FILTER condition is false for the NULL row that the left join creates for Quinn, so count(*) FILTER (...) is 0 and not 1. Using count(l.id) for the plain total avoids counting that placeholder row.

  2. SELECT a.name, round(avg(b.price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM authors a
JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.id, a.name
ORDER BY avg_price DESC
LIMIT 1;
    Chiara Lund, 18.00 (Ada: 13.75, Boris: 10.45). For the full ranking with the empty author last, use a left join and ORDER BY avg(b.price) DESC NULLS LAST; the empty author's average is NULL.

  3. SELECT title, loans, rnk
FROM (
    SELECT b.title, count(l.id) AS loans,
           rank() OVER (ORDER BY count(l.id) DESC) AS rnk
    FROM books b
    LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.book_id = b.id
    GROUP BY b.id, b.title
) t
WHERE rnk <= 3
ORDER BY rnk, title;

         title     | loans | rnk
---------------+-------+-----
 Tidewater     |     3 |   1
 Quiet Engines |     2 |   2
 Paper Moons   |     1 |   3
 Salt Roads    |     1 |   3
(4 rows)
    Four rows because of the tie at rank 3.

  4. SELECT id, member_id, loaned_on, returned_on - loaned_on AS days,
       sum(returned_on - loaned_on) OVER (
           PARTITION BY member_id ORDER BY loaned_on, id
       ) AS running_days
FROM loans
ORDER BY member_id, loaned_on, id;
    sum skips NULL days (open loans). Member 1 shows running days 13, 32, 44. Member 2's first row is NULL (its only input so far is the open loan 3) and the second is 13. Member 3 is NULL, then 9.

  5. SELECT to_char(m, 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM loans l WHERE l.loaned_on   >= m AND l.loaned_on   < m + interval '1 month') AS started,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM loans l WHERE l.returned_on >= m AND l.returned_on < m + interval '1 month') AS returned
FROM generate_series('2024-01-01'::timestamp, '2024-06-01'::timestamp, interval '1 month') AS m
ORDER BY m;

      month  | started | returned
---------+---------+----------
 2024-01 |       1 |        1
 2024-02 |       1 |        1
 2024-03 |       2 |        1
 2024-04 |       1 |        0
 2024-05 |       2 |        1
 2024-06 |       0 |        1
(6 rows)
    Two independent counts per month are done as scalar subqueries on purpose: joining loans twice would multiply rows.

docs.title: Indexes and EXPLAIN
docs.text:
A slow Odoo screen, a cron job that takes hours, a report that times out: almost every case ends with the same two tools. EXPLAIN ANALYZE tells you what PostgreSQL did and where the time went; an index (or a rewritten query) fixes it. This chapter teaches how to read a plan, how B-tree and the other index types work, which indexes Odoo creates, when the planner refuses to use yours, and how to add an index to a live system without blocking it.

The plans below are representative output from a 500,000-row lab table. Costs and timings differ on your machine; what matters is the node types, the estimate-versus-actual comparison, and the reasoning. The plan shapes are what you will meet on real Odoo databases.

docs.title: A table big enough to matter
docs.text:
On six-row tables PostgreSQL correctly ignores every index, because reading one page is cheaper than any lookup. To see the effects you need volume. Create a synthetic log of loans in the lab database:

CREATE TABLE loan_log AS
SELECT g                                       AS id,
       (g % 5000) + 1                          AS book_id,
       (g % 800) + 1                           AS member_id,
       date '2020-01-01' + (g % 1500)          AS loaned_on,
       CASE WHEN g % 50 = 0 THEN NULL
            ELSE date '2020-01-01' + (g % 1500) + 10 END AS returned_on
FROM generate_series(1, 500000) AS g;

ALTER TABLE loan_log ADD PRIMARY KEY (id);

CREATE TABLE catalog AS
SELECT g AS id, 'Book ' || g AS title FROM generate_series(1, 5000) AS g;
ALTER TABLE catalog ADD PRIMARY KEY (id);

ANALYZE loan_log;
ANALYZE catalog;

It has 500,000 rows; each book_id appears 100 times, each member_id 625 times, and 2% of rows (10,000) have returned_on NULL, so they are "still open". ANALYZE collects the statistics the planner needs. Without it, the first plans are made on guesses.

docs.title: EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE
docs.text:
EXPLAIN shows the plan the planner would choose, without running the query:

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM loan_log WHERE book_id = 42;

                        QUERY PLAN
-----------------------------------------------------------
 Seq Scan on loan_log  (cost=0.00..9435.00 rows=100 width=20)
   Filter: (book_id = 42)
(2 rows)

EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs it and adds measured numbers:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM loan_log WHERE book_id = 42;

 Seq Scan on loan_log  (cost=0.00..9435.00 rows=100 width=20) (actual time=0.021..38.412 rows=100 loops=1)
   Filter: (book_id = 42)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 499900
   Buffers: shared hit=3185
 Planning Time: 0.084 ms
 Execution Time: 38.455 ms
(5 rows)

EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement. On an UPDATE, DELETE, or INSERT it changes data. Wrap it: BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE ...; ROLLBACK;. On a production database, run it on a copy, or on a SELECT you know is safe. A heavy SELECT still takes as long as it takes.

How to read one node:

  • Seq Scan on loan_log is the operation (a full table scan) and its target.
  • cost=0.00..9435.00 are the planner's estimates in arbitrary units: startup cost (before the first row) and total cost. They only compare plans to each other; they are not milliseconds. The default unit: one sequential page read costs 1.0.
  • rows=100 is the estimated number of output rows; width=20 the estimated bytes per row.
  • actual time=0.021..38.412 is real time in milliseconds: first row, last row. rows=100 the real output, loops=1 how many times the node ran. For a node inside a nested loop, multiply actual time and rows by loops.
  • Rows Removed by Filter: 499900 is the work thrown away. A large number next to a small result is the signature of a missing index.
  • Buffers: shared hit=3185 counts 8 kB pages read from the shared cache (hit) or from disk or the OS cache (read). It is the most stable measure when timings vary.

Two comparisons find 90% of problems:

  1. Estimated rows against actual rows. If rows=100 but actual rows=250000, the planner worked from wrong statistics and may have chosen a poor plan. Fix the statistics (ANALYZE), not the query.
  2. Where the time goes. In a tree of nodes, the actual time of a node includes its children. Find the deepest node whose own time (its time minus its children's) is large.

Read a plan from the innermost, most-indented node outward. Data flows up the tree; an arrow -> marks a child.

docs.title: Sequential scan
docs.text: Read the whole table in physical order. Cheap per row, but proportional to table size. It is the right choice for tiny tables and for queries that need a large fraction of the rows (above roughly 5-10% selectivity it often beats an index).

docs.title: Index scan
docs.text:
Create an index on the column and run the same query:

CREATE INDEX loan_log_book_id_idx ON loan_log (book_id);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM loan_log WHERE book_id = 42;

 Bitmap Heap Scan on loan_log  (cost=5.30..342.00 rows=100 width=20) (actual time=0.060..0.311 rows=100 loops=1)
   Recheck Cond: (book_id = 42)
   Heap Blocks: exact=100
   Buffers: shared hit=103
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on loan_log_book_id_idx  (cost=0.00..5.27 rows=100 width=0) (actual time=0.037..0.037 rows=100 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (book_id = 42)
         Buffers: shared hit=3
 Planning Time: 0.120 ms
 Execution Time: 0.352 ms
(9 rows)

38 ms became 0.35 ms, and 3,185 buffers became 103. The plan uses a bitmap scan here: the index finds the 100 matching row locations, they are sorted by page, and the heap pages are visited once each. A plain Index Scan walks the index and visits each row's heap page immediately; PostgreSQL picks it for very few rows or when the order of the index is useful (for ORDER BY ... LIMIT). Both are "using the index".

docs.title: Index Only Scan
docs.text:
If the index contains every column the query needs, PostgreSQL answers from the index alone and skips the table:

EXPLAIN SELECT book_id FROM loan_log WHERE book_id BETWEEN 10 AND 12;

 Index Only Scan using loan_log_book_id_idx on loan_log  (cost=0.42..30.12 rows=300 width=4)
   Index Cond: ((book_id >= 10) AND (book_id <= 12))

It depends on the visibility map being current (VACUUM maintains it); on a freshly loaded table you may see Heap Fetches: 300, meaning it still had to check the table.

docs.title: Bitmap scans combine indexes
docs.text: Bitmap Index Scan nodes can be combined with BitmapAnd and BitmapOr to use two single-column indexes for one query. That is why many single-column indexes can serve many query shapes reasonably, and also why a purpose-built multicolumn index is better for the hot query.

docs.title: What a B-tree index serves
docs.text:
The default index type is a B-tree. It keeps keys sorted, so it supports:

  • equality: col = x, col IN (...)
  • ranges: <, <=, >, >=, BETWEEN
  • sorting: ORDER BY col and ORDER BY col DESC (a B-tree is scannable backwards), min() and max()
  • prefix matching: col LIKE 'abc%', but only if the database collation is C, or the index is created with the text_pattern_ops operator class
  • IS NULL and IS NOT NULL (NULLs are stored in the index)

It does not help col LIKE '%abc', col ILIKE '%abc%', or any condition that applies a function to col.

Indexes cost something on every write: each INSERT adds an entry to every index, each UPDATE of an indexed column too, and they occupy disk and memory. Add indexes for queries you actually run, not for every column.

docs.title: Multicolumn indexes and column order
docs.text:
An index on (member_id, loaned_on) is sorted by member_id, and within equal member_id by loaned_on. It serves a query that constrains the leftmost columns:

CREATE INDEX loan_log_member_loaned_idx ON loan_log (member_id, loaned_on);

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM loan_log
WHERE member_id = 7 AND loaned_on >= '2023-01-01'
ORDER BY loaned_on;

 Index Scan using loan_log_member_loaned_idx on loan_log  (cost=0.42..216.30 rows=380 width=20)
   Index Cond: ((member_id = 7) AND (loaned_on >= '2023-01-01'::date))

One index handled the equality, the range, and the sort (no Sort node appears). The rules:

  • The index is usable for a query that constrains member_id alone, or member_id and loaned_on.
  • It is poor for a query on loaned_on alone, because dates are scattered across all the member_id groups. A leading-column filter is what makes the key range narrow.
  • Put equality columns first, then the range or sort column. Among equality columns, put the more selective one first unless other queries need another prefix.
  • A separate single-column index on member_id is redundant after this one and just adds write cost.

docs.title: Partial, expression, and covering indexes
docs.text:
Partial index. Index only the rows you search for. The 10,000 open loans are 2% of the table, and "open loans per book" is the question an application asks all day:

CREATE INDEX loan_log_open_idx ON loan_log (book_id) WHERE returned_on IS NULL;

SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('loan_log_book_id_idx')) AS full_index,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('loan_log_open_idx'))    AS partial_index;

 full_index | partial_index
------------+---------------
 11 MB      | 264 kB
(1 row)

The partial index is 40 times smaller and cheaper to maintain. The query must contain the index predicate (or something that implies it) to be eligible: WHERE book_id = 42 AND returned_on IS NULL can use it; WHERE book_id = 42 cannot. A partial UNIQUE index also expresses rules like "one open loan per member and book" (the exercise in chapter 1).

Expression index. Index the value the query computes. A case-insensitive email lookup:

-- fragment: against a table with an email column
CREATE INDEX members_lower_email_idx ON members (lower(email));
SELECT id FROM members WHERE lower(email) = 'nora@example.com';

The query must use the identical expression, lower(email). A plain index on email is useless for lower(email) = ..., and ILIKE 'x' without wildcards does not use it either.

Covering index (INCLUDE, PostgreSQL 11+). Add payload columns that are not part of the search key so that an index-only scan can return them:

CREATE INDEX loan_log_member_cover_idx ON loan_log (member_id) INCLUDE (loaned_on);

Use it sparingly: it enlarges the index.

docs.title: Unique indexes
docs.text: UNIQUE constraints and primary keys are unique indexes. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... WHERE ... gives conditional uniqueness. Odoo's _sql_constraints entries of the form unique(a, b) create a unique constraint with its backing index; Odoo does that, the index is a side effect you do not manage separately.

docs.title: Index types beyond B-tree
Joins in plans
docs.text:
The planner picks one of three join algorithms for each join:

  • Nested Loop: for each row of the outer side, look up matches on the inner side. Excellent when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index on the join column. Terrible when both are large and there is no index.
  • Hash Join: build a hash table from one input, probe it with the other. Good for large unsorted inputs and equality joins, needs memory (work_mem).
  • Merge Join: both inputs sorted on the join key, walk them together. Good when they are already sorted (from indexes).

A hash join in a plan:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
SELECT c.title, count(*)
FROM loan_log l
JOIN catalog c ON c.id = l.book_id
WHERE l.loaned_on >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY c.title;

 HashAggregate  (cost=11112.33..11162.33 rows=5000 width=40) (actual time=41.2..42.3 rows=5000 loops=1)
   Group Key: c.title
   ->  Hash Join  (cost=143.00..11047.00 rows=13000 width=32) (actual time=1.4..37.8 rows=13000 loops=1)
         Hash Cond: (l.book_id = c.id)
         ->  Seq Scan on loan_log l  (cost=0.00..10685.00 rows=13000 width=4) (actual time=0.02..31.9 rows=13000 loops=1)
               Filter: (loaned_on >= '2024-01-01'::date)
               Rows Removed by Filter: 487000
         ->  Hash  (cost=80.50..80.50 rows=5000 width=36) (actual time=1.3..1.3 rows=5000 loops=1)
               Buckets: 8192  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 372kB
 Planning Time: 0.3 ms
 Execution Time: 43.1 ms

(catalog is the 5,000-row table created above.) The inner Hash builds the small side (5,000 rows); the scan of loan_log probes it. Batches: 1 means the hash fit in work_mem; Batches above 1 means it spilled to disk, a common cause of mysterious slowness that raising work_mem for the session cures. The seq scan removed 487,000 rows to keep 13,000, so an index on loaned_on is the likely improvement here.

docs.title: Why the planner ignores your index
docs.text:
You create an index, the plan still shows Seq Scan. In rough order of frequency:

  1. The query returns a large share of the table. Reading 30% of the rows through an index is slower than a sequential scan. The planner is right.
  2. A function or cast on the column. WHERE lower(name) = 'x', WHERE created::date = '2024-01-01', WHERE amount + 0 > 10. Rewrite the condition so the column stands alone (created >= '2024-01-01' AND created < '2024-01-02'), or create an expression index.
  3. Type mismatch. Comparing an integer column to a numeric or text parameter may force a cast of the column. Pass parameters with the right type.
  4. Leading wildcard. LIKE '%x' or ILIKE '%x%' needs a trigram index.
  5. Stale statistics. After a bulk load or a big delete, run ANALYZE table. Autovacuum does it eventually, "eventually" being the problem right after your script.
  6. The table is small. Under a few hundred rows no index is worth it.
  7. OR across columns. a = 1 OR b = 2 needs both columns indexed to use a BitmapOr; otherwise it scans.
  8. Wrong multicolumn order. The query constrains the second column only.
  9. The index is invalid or not built yet. A failed CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY leaves an INVALID index (\d table marks it); drop and recreate it.

To test whether an index could help, you can discourage sequential scans for one session:

SET enable_seqscan = off;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM loan_log WHERE member_id = 7;
RESET enable_seqscan;

If the plan with the index has a lower cost and is faster when you run it, the planner underestimated something (statistics, random_page_cost). If it is slower, the planner was right. This is a diagnostic only; never leave enable_* switches on in application code or postgresql.conf.

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
The planner's estimates come from pg_stats, filled by ANALYZE: the number of distinct values, the most common values and their frequencies, and a histogram of the rest.

SELECT attname, n_distinct, null_frac
FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'loan_log' AND attname IN ('book_id', 'member_id', 'returned_on');

   attname   | n_distinct | null_frac
-------------+------------+-----------
 book_id     |       5000 |         0
 member_id   |        800 |         0
 returned_on |       1500 |      0.02
(3 rows)

null_frac = 0.02 is exactly the 2% of open loans: the planner knows returned_on IS NULL matches about 10,000 rows. When estimates are wrong, fix them in this order: ANALYZE the table; for skewed columns raise the sample with ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET STATISTICS 500 and analyze again; for correlated columns create extended statistics (CREATE STATISTICS ... (dependencies) ON a, b FROM t).

docs.title: Building and removing indexes safely
docs.text:
CREATE INDEX takes a lock that blocks all writes to the table for the duration. On a live database use the concurrent form:

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY loan_log_loaned_on_idx ON loan_log (loaned_on);

It scans the table twice and waits for open transactions, so it takes longer, but writers keep working. Rules: it cannot run inside a transaction block (so no BEGIN, and not inside a psql script run with --single-transaction); if it fails or is cancelled it leaves an INVALID index which you must DROP INDEX and retry; and long-running transactions elsewhere make it wait. DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY and REINDEX CONCURRENTLY (PostgreSQL 12+) exist as well.

To find indexes that are never used, ask the statistics (collected since the last stats reset):

SELECT relname AS table, indexrelname AS index, idx_scan,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE idx_scan = 0
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;

An index with idx_scan = 0 over a long, representative period is a candidate for removal. Do not drop an index that backs a constraint (a primary key or unique constraint), and check that a monthly report is not its only user. The statistics reset on some operations (a crash recovery, pg_stat_reset), so a young counter proves little.

Indexes also go stale in another way: heavy update and delete patterns bloat them. A REINDEX CONCURRENTLY rebuilds one without blocking.

docs.title: Indexes on foreign keys
docs.text:
PostgreSQL indexes the referenced side (a primary key) but not the referencing column. Odoo does create indexes for many2one fields declared with index=True, and does not for the rest. Two things follow:

  • Joins and filters on an unindexed many2one column read the whole child table.
  • Deleting a parent row needs to check the child table for references (or to set them NULL), a scan per delete when the foreign key column has no index. Deleting 10,000 records from a parent table with an unindexed child of 5 million rows can take hours. If you see a slow DELETE, check the foreign keys that reference the table (the query from INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and whether each child column is indexed.

docs.title: Odoo workflow: find the query, then explain it
docs.text:
1. Get the slow SQL: from the Odoo log with --log-sql or the odoo.sql_db logger at DEBUG, from pg_stat_activity while it runs, or from pg_stat_statements if the extension is enabled (psql and operations). The tools are covered in Inspecting SQL.
  2. Replace the %s placeholders with real values, in psql.
  3. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on a copy of the database with realistic data.
  4. Find the node with large time and Rows Removed by Filter, or the estimate error.
  5. Prefer fixing the query (a sargable condition, a narrower domain) before adding an index; then add the index, rerun, compare the buffers.
  6. In a module, declare the index in code (index=True on the field) rather than hand-creating it in production, so that every database gets it on update. Build it concurrently by hand on a large live database first, if the update step would block writes for too long.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Testing on tiny data. Plans on a 100-row development database say nothing about production. The planner chooses by size.
  • Forgetting ANALYZE after a bulk load. The first plans run on defaults; estimates are far off.
  • Indexing every column. Each index slows writes and fills the cache. Index for real query patterns.
  • Function on the indexed column. lower(col), col::date, col + 1: the plain index is unusable.
  • LIKE '%x' expected to be fast. It needs trigrams. ILIKE on a name field without a trigram index scans.
  • Trusting cost as time. Costs are for comparing alternative plans of the same query, not for comparing queries.
  • Reading EXPLAIN without ANALYZE. Estimates only; the error you need to find is estimate against actual.
  • Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a write. It writes. Use a transaction and ROLLBACK.
  • Index-only scan expected but not happening. The visibility map is stale after heavy writes; VACUUM the table.
  • Plain CREATE INDEX on a busy table. It blocks writes for the build. Use CONCURRENTLY, and clean up an INVALID leftover.
  • Leaving a half-built invalid index. It slows writes without helping reads.
  • Missing index on a foreign key. Slow parent deletes and slow joins on the child column.
  • Raising work_mem globally. It applies per sort or hash per query per connection: 200 connections with 1 GB each is an out-of-memory crash. Raise it for the one session (SET work_mem = '256MB') running the heavy report.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Use the 500,000-row loan_log table and its indexes as created in this chapter. Drop the extra ones as needed to reproduce each scenario.

  1. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for WHERE member_id = 7 with no index on member_id. Note the rows removed. Create the right index and run it again. Compare buffers.

  2. Which of these queries can use loan_log_member_loaned_idx (member_id, loaned_on) efficiently, and which cannot: (a) WHERE member_id = 5, (b) WHERE loaned_on = '2023-05-05', (c) WHERE member_id = 5 AND loaned_on > '2023-01-01', (d) WHERE member_id > 700 ORDER BY loaned_on?

  3. A query SELECT count(*) FROM loan_log WHERE returned_on IS NULL AND book_id = 42 is run thousands of times a day. Design the smallest suitable index and justify it.

  4. SELECT * FROM loan_log WHERE loaned_on::text LIKE '2024-03%' is slow despite an index on loaned_on. Explain why, and rewrite it to be index-friendly.

  5. You must add an index to a 200 million row table on a system that cannot stop writes. Write the statement, the check afterwards that it is valid, and what to do if it failed halfway.

Solution

  1. Without an index you get a Seq Scan with Rows Removed by Filter: 499375 (625 rows match) and Buffers: shared hit=3185 or similar. After 

    CREATE INDEX loan_log_member_id_idx ON loan_log (member_id);
    the plan is a Bitmap Heap Scan on 625 rows touching a few hundred pages; execution drops from tens of milliseconds to around one. (Drop it later if you keep the composite one: DROP INDEX loan_log_member_id_idx;.)

  2. (a) yes: it constrains the leading column. (b) no: it does not constrain member_id, so the matching rows are spread through the whole index; the planner will use a seq scan or a different index. (c) yes: equality then range on the second column. (d) partially: it can scan the member_id range, but the order by loaned_on is not guaranteed by the index across multiple member_id values, so there will be a Sort node.

  3. A partial index on the filter that is always present, keyed on the equality column: 

    CREATE INDEX loan_log_open_book_idx ON loan_log (book_id) WHERE returned_on IS NULL;
    Only the 2% of open loans are indexed (about 264 kB instead of 11 MB), and the query's returned_on IS NULL implies the predicate, so it is eligible. count(*) can then be answered as an index-only scan if the visibility map is current.

  4. loaned_on::text applies a cast to the column, so the plain index on loaned_on cannot be used and every row is converted to text. Rewrite as a range on the original type: 

    SELECT * FROM loan_log
WHERE loaned_on >= '2024-03-01' AND loaned_on < '2024-04-01';


  5. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY loan_log_xxx_idx ON loan_log (xxx);
    (Use the real column.) Run it outside a transaction block. Afterwards check validity: 
    SELECT indexrelid::regclass, indisvalid FROM pg_index WHERE indrelid = 'loan_log'::regclass;
    indisvalid = false means it failed; run DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY loan_log_xxx_idx; and start again, after finding out why it failed (a deadlock, a cancelled statement, a unique violation for a unique index). Run it at a quiet hour, since it waits for existing transactions to finish.

docs.title: Joins
docs.text: A single Odoo record is spread over several tables: the sale order points at a partner, the partner at a country, a product at several tags through a relation table. Reading anything meaningful from the database means following those keys, and the join is the tool. This chapter covers inner and outer joins, the difference between ON and WHERE in an outer join, the anti-join and semi-join patterns, many-to-many traversal, the row multiplication that corrupts totals, LATERAL, and set operations. Examples use the library schema from Relational basics and SELECT, FROM, WHERE.

docs.title: Two more tables for many-to-many
docs.text:
A book can have several genres and a genre several books. Add the pair of tables:

CREATE TABLE genres (
    id    serial PRIMARY KEY,
    name  varchar NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE book_genre (
    book_id   integer NOT NULL REFERENCES books (id)  ON DELETE CASCADE,
    genre_id  integer NOT NULL REFERENCES genres (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    PRIMARY KEY (book_id, genre_id)
);

INSERT INTO genres (name) VALUES ('Fiction'), ('History'), ('Poetry');

INSERT INTO book_genre (book_id, genre_id) VALUES
    (1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1), (3, 1), (5, 1), (5, 3);

book_genre is the shape Odoo gives a Many2many field: two key columns, one row per pair. Odoo would call this table library_book_library_genre_rel (naming rules in The Odoo schema); the short name keeps the lab readable.

docs.title: What a join does
docs.text: A join combines rows from two sources according to a condition and emits one output row for each pair that satisfies it. Conceptually, the database forms every pair (the Cartesian product) and keeps the ones matching ON. Physically it does nothing of the kind: the planner picks a nested loop, a hash join, or a merge join (see Indexes and EXPLAIN) and produces the same rows far faster. You reason with the conceptual model and let the planner pick the physical one.

docs.title: INNER JOIN
docs.text:
SELECT b.id, b.title, a.name AS author
FROM books b
JOIN authors a ON a.id = b.author_id
ORDER BY b.id;

 id |      title      |   author
----+-----------------+-------------
  1 | Tidewater       | Ada Marlowe
  2 | Salt Roads      | Ada Marlowe
  3 | The Long Ledger | Boris Venn
  4 | Paper Moons     | Boris Venn
  5 | Quiet Engines   | Chiara Lund
(5 rows)

JOIN alone means INNER JOIN. Only pairs that match survive: Orphan Volume has no author and vanishes, Dmitri Okafor has no book and vanishes. That is the single most common cause of "my report is missing rows" in hand-written SQL, and it is silent.

Table aliases (b, a) are not decoration. Both tables have id and name-like columns; an unqualified id raises column reference "id" is ambiguous. Qualify every column in a join, always, even those that are unambiguous today: a column added later to the other table breaks an unqualified reference.

docs.title: LEFT JOIN
docs.text:
A left join keeps every row of the left table, and fills the right-side columns with NULL when nothing matches:

SELECT b.id, b.title, a.name AS author
FROM books b
LEFT JOIN authors a ON a.id = b.author_id
ORDER BY b.id;

 id |      title      |   author
----+-----------------+-------------
  1 | Tidewater       | Ada Marlowe
  2 | Salt Roads      | Ada Marlowe
  3 | The Long Ledger | Boris Venn
  4 | Paper Moons     | Boris Venn
  5 | Quiet Engines   | Chiara Lund
  6 | Orphan Volume   |
(6 rows)

Rule for Odoo: a join from a record to an optional many2one must be a LEFT JOIN. A required many2one (NOT NULL) can safely be an inner join, but inner joining an optional one deletes the records without a value from your result. The ORM always uses LEFT JOIN when a domain walks through a many2one path (when it joins at all; see the hint below).

RIGHT JOIN is a left join with the tables swapped; nobody needs it, since you can swap the tables yourself and the reading order stays natural. FULL JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides:

SELECT a.name AS author, b.title
FROM authors a
FULL JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id
ORDER BY a.id, b.id;

    author     |      title
---------------+-----------------
 Ada Marlowe   | Tidewater
 Ada Marlowe   | Salt Roads
 Boris Venn    | The Long Ledger
 Boris Venn    | Paper Moons
 Chiara Lund   | Quiet Engines
 Dmitri Okafor |
               | Orphan Volume
(7 rows)

(NULL sorts last in ascending order, so Orphan Volume ends the list.) A full join is the right tool for reconciling two lists: "in A but not B, in B but not A, in both" in one pass.

Versions. When a search domain contains a path like [('partner_id.country_id.code', '=', 'IT')], Odoo 16 to 18 normally compiles each many2one step into a subquery (partner_id IN (SELECT id FROM res_partner WHERE ...)), and into real LEFT JOINs only for fields declared with auto_join=True. Print the SQL with the odoo.sql_db logger at DEBUG to see what your domain generates; the techniques are in the shell-and-debugging part.

docs.title: ON versus WHERE in an outer join
docs.text:
For an inner join, a condition in ON and the same condition in WHERE give identical results. For an outer join they do not, and the difference is the classic mistake. Compare:

-- condition in ON: the filter applies while matching
SELECT a.name, b.title
FROM authors a
LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id AND b.status = 'available'
ORDER BY a.id, b.id;

     name      |     title
---------------+---------------
 Ada Marlowe   | Tidewater
 Ada Marlowe   | Salt Roads
 Boris Venn    | Paper Moons
 Chiara Lund   | Quiet Engines
 Dmitri Okafor |
(5 rows)

-- condition in WHERE: the filter applies after the join
SELECT a.name, b.title
FROM authors a
LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id
WHERE b.status = 'available'
ORDER BY a.id, b.id;

     name     |     title
--------------+---------------
 Ada Marlowe  | Tidewater
 Ada Marlowe  | Salt Roads
 Boris Venn   | Paper Moons
 Chiara Lund  | Quiet Engines
(4 rows)

In the first, Dmitri stays with an empty title: the ON clause decides which books match an author, and an author with no matching book is still emitted. In the second, the join first produced the Dmitri row with b.status NULL, and WHERE b.status = 'available' threw it away. Filtering the right-hand table in WHERE quietly converts your left join into an inner join.

The rule: conditions that describe which right-hand rows may match go in ON; conditions that filter the final result go in WHERE. The one deliberate exception is the anti-join below, where you test the right side for NULL in WHERE.

docs.title: Anti-join: rows with no match
docs.text:
"Authors without books", "partners without invoices", "products never sold". Two idioms:

-- NOT EXISTS
SELECT a.name FROM authors a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM books b WHERE b.author_id = a.id);

-- LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL
SELECT a.name
FROM authors a
LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id
WHERE b.id IS NULL;

Both return:

     name
---------------
 Dmitri Okafor
(1 row)

Test the right table's primary key (or any NOT NULL column) for NULL, never a nullable column, whose NULL could be real data. Both forms are optimized into the same anti-join by the planner; NOT EXISTS states the intent more directly, and NOT IN is the one to avoid when the subquery column is nullable (see the previous chapter).

docs.title: Semi-join: rows with at least one match
docs.text:
"Members who ever borrowed something". Using JOIN returns a member once per loan; what you want is a membership test:

SELECT m.name FROM members m
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM loans l WHERE l.member_id = m.id)
ORDER BY m.id;

 name
-------
 Nora
 Omar
 Petra
(3 rows)

WHERE m.id IN (SELECT member_id FROM loans) gives the same rows. Each member appears once however many loans they have. Choose EXISTS/IN whenever you do not need columns from the other table.

docs.title: Joining more than two tables
docs.text:
Chain joins; each ON relates the new table to something already present:

SELECT l.id, b.title, m.name AS member, l.loaned_on
FROM loans l
JOIN books b   ON b.id = l.book_id
JOIN members m ON m.id = l.member_id
ORDER BY l.id;

 id |     title     | member | loaned_on
----+---------------+--------+------------
  1 | Tidewater     | Nora   | 2024-01-05
  2 | Salt Roads    | Nora   | 2024-02-01
  3 | Tidewater     | Omar   | 2024-03-10
  4 | Quiet Engines | Omar   | 2024-03-12
  5 | Paper Moons   | Petra  | 2024-04-02
  6 | Tidewater     | Petra  | 2024-05-01
  7 | Quiet Engines | Nora   | 2024-05-20
(7 rows)

Joins are logically associative for inner joins, so the order you write them does not change the result and the planner reorders freely (up to the join_collapse_limit, default 8 tables; Odoo's reports sometimes exceed it). Mixing inner and outer joins is different: order matters, and a later inner join on a column from the right side of an earlier left join kills the NULL rows, like the WHERE example above. When mixing, put the outer joins last, or use parentheses.

Chain with an optional step in the middle:

SELECT b.title, a.name AS author, count(l.id) AS loans
FROM books b
LEFT JOIN authors a ON a.id = b.author_id
LEFT JOIN loans l   ON l.book_id = b.id
GROUP BY b.id, b.title, a.name
ORDER BY b.id;

      title      |   author    | loans
-----------------+-------------+-------
 Tidewater       | Ada Marlowe |     3
 Salt Roads      | Ada Marlowe |     1
 The Long Ledger | Boris Venn  |     0
 Paper Moons     | Boris Venn  |     1
 Quiet Engines   | Chiara Lund |     2
 Orphan Volume   |             |     0
(6 rows)

count(l.id) counts only non-NULL values, so the unlucky books show 0. count(*) would show 1 for them; keep that distinction in mind for the next chapter.

docs.title: Many-to-many through the relation table
docs.text:
Join from one side to the relation table to the other side:

SELECT b.title, g.name AS genre
FROM books b
JOIN book_genre bg ON bg.book_id = b.id
JOIN genres g      ON g.id = bg.genre_id
ORDER BY b.id, g.id;

      title      |  genre
-----------------+---------
 Tidewater       | Fiction
 Tidewater       | History
 Salt Roads      | Fiction
 The Long Ledger | Fiction
 Quiet Engines   | Fiction
 Quiet Engines   | Poetry
(6 rows)

Books with several genres appear several times: the output has one row per pair. Books without a genre (Paper Moons, Orphan Volume) are missing, again because of the inner join. Find them with an anti-join:

SELECT b.title
FROM books b
LEFT JOIN book_genre bg ON bg.book_id = b.id
WHERE bg.book_id IS NULL
ORDER BY b.id;

     title
---------------
 Paper Moons
 Orphan Volume
(2 rows)

This is how you find orphans in Odoo's own relation tables, for instance partners without any category or users without any group.

docs.title: Row multiplication: the join that inflates totals
docs.text:
A join with a one-to-many or many-to-many relation yields several rows per left-hand row. Every aggregate computed over the joined result then counts each left-hand value several times.

SELECT sum(b.price) AS wrong_total
FROM books b
JOIN book_genre bg ON bg.book_id = b.id;

 wrong_total
-------------
       85.90
(1 row)

The books in book_genre cost 55.40 in total (12.50 + 15.00 + 9.90 + 18.00); the join counted Tidewater and Quiet Engines twice because each has two genres. The same effect hits you whenever you join two independent one-to-many relations in one query:

SELECT b.title,
       count(*)              AS joined_rows,
       count(DISTINCT l.id)  AS loans
FROM books b
JOIN book_genre bg ON bg.book_id = b.id
JOIN loans l       ON l.book_id = b.id
GROUP BY b.id, b.title
ORDER BY b.id;

     title     | joined_rows | loans
---------------+-------------+-------
 Tidewater     |           6 |     3
 Salt Roads    |           1 |     1
 Quiet Engines |           4 |     2
(3 rows)

Tidewater has 2 genres and 3 loans: the join emits 2 x 3 = 6 rows. Any sum over loan columns would be doubled, any sum over genre columns tripled. The remedies, in order of preference:

  1. Aggregate each many-side separately, then join the one-row-per-key results.
  2. Use a correlated scalar subquery for a single number per row.
  3. Use count(DISTINCT ...) for counts only, and only when you understand why; it does not fix sums.
-- 1. aggregate first, join after
SELECT b.title, COALESCE(lc.loans, 0) AS loans, COALESCE(gc.genres, 0) AS genres
FROM books b
LEFT JOIN (SELECT book_id, count(*) AS loans  FROM loans      GROUP BY book_id) lc ON lc.book_id = b.id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT book_id, count(*) AS genres FROM book_genre GROUP BY book_id) gc ON gc.book_id = b.id
ORDER BY b.id;

      title      | loans | genres
-----------------+-------+--------
 Tidewater       |     3 |      2
 Salt Roads      |     1 |      1
 The Long Ledger |     0 |      1
 Paper Moons     |     1 |      0
 Quiet Engines   |     2 |      2
 Orphan Volume   |     0 |      0
(6 rows)

-- 2. scalar subquery
SELECT b.id, b.title,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM loans l WHERE l.book_id = b.id) AS loans
FROM books b
ORDER BY b.id;

Odoo reporting code (_read_group, SQL views for reports) fights this all the time: a sale report joining order lines and invoice lines multiplies amounts unless each side is pre-aggregated. When a figure from your SQL differs from the UI, suspect row multiplication first.

docs.title: Self-joins
docs.text:
A table joined to itself needs two aliases. Pairs of loans of the same book:

SELECT x.id AS loan_a, y.id AS loan_b, x.book_id
FROM loans x
JOIN loans y ON y.book_id = x.book_id AND x.id < y.id
ORDER BY loan_a, loan_b;

 loan_a | loan_b | book_id
--------+--------+---------
      1 |      3 |       1
      1 |      6 |       1
      3 |      6 |       1
      4 |      7 |       5
(4 rows)

The x.id < y.id condition keeps each unordered pair once and excludes a loan paired with itself. Odoo's own self-referencing tables are res_partner (parent_id), product_category, account_account groups, and stock_location; "children and their parent's name" is a self join:

-- fragment against an Odoo database
SELECT c.id, c.name, p.name AS parent_name
FROM res_partner c
LEFT JOIN res_partner p ON p.id = c.parent_id
LIMIT 10;

docs.title: CROSS JOIN, and the accidental one
docs.text:
CROSS JOIN returns every pair. It is sometimes what you want (all months times all products for a grid), and otherwise a disaster:

SELECT m.name, b.title
FROM members m
CROSS JOIN books b
WHERE m.id <= 2 AND b.id <= 2
ORDER BY m.id, b.id;

 name |   title
------+------------
 Nora | Tidewater
 Nora | Salt Roads
 Omar | Tidewater
 Omar | Salt Roads
(4 rows)

The accidental version is FROM members, books with the join condition forgotten in WHERE: 4 members x 6 books gives 24 rows here; on res_partner x sale_order_line it gives billions and a query that eats the server until statement_timeout. A missing join condition is a bug whose symptom is "the query never finishes". Prefer the explicit JOIN ... ON syntax: it makes the condition mandatory, since the parser rejects a JOIN without ON (except CROSS JOIN).

docs.title: USING and NATURAL
docs.text:
When the join columns have the same name on both sides, JOIN ... USING (col) is a shorter ON and returns the column once. Our schema uses book_id in both loans and book_genre:

SELECT bg.genre_id, l.id AS loan_id
FROM loans l
JOIN book_genre bg USING (book_id)
ORDER BY l.id, bg.genre_id;

Odoo columns are named <field>_id, usually with a different name from the target's id, so USING rarely fits; spell out ON. Avoid NATURAL JOIN entirely: it joins on every same-named column, so adding a column such as create_date to either table changes the meaning of the query without any edit to it. Every Odoo table has id, create_uid, create_date, write_uid, write_date, and NATURAL JOIN would try to match all of them.

docs.title: LATERAL: a subquery that sees the row to its left
docs.text:
A LATERAL subquery may refer to columns of earlier tables in the same FROM. It is the natural tool for "top N per row", the newest loan for each member, the latest price per product, the last message per record:

SELECT a.name, b.title, b.published_year
FROM authors a
JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT title, published_year
    FROM books
    WHERE author_id = a.id
    ORDER BY published_year DESC
    LIMIT 1
) b ON true
ORDER BY a.id;

     name     |     title     | published_year
--------------+---------------+----------------
 Ada Marlowe  | Salt Roads    |           2004
 Boris Venn   | Paper Moons   |           2015
 Chiara Lund  | Quiet Engines |           2019
(3 rows)

JOIN LATERAL (...) ON true behaves like an inner join (authors without books drop out); LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) ON true keeps them with NULLs:

SELECT a.name, b.title
FROM authors a
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT title FROM books WHERE author_id = a.id ORDER BY published_year DESC LIMIT 1
) b ON true
ORDER BY a.id;

     name      |     title
---------------+---------------
 Ada Marlowe   | Salt Roads
 Boris Venn    | Paper Moons
 Chiara Lund   | Quiet Engines
 Dmitri Okafor |
(4 rows)

With an index on (author_id, published_year) this does one index probe per author, usually far better than sorting all books; with window functions (next chapter) it is a second option.

docs.title: Combining result sets: UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT
docs.text:
Set operators stack queries with the same column count and compatible types:

SELECT title FROM books WHERE author_id = 1
UNION
SELECT title FROM books WHERE status = 'lost'
ORDER BY title;

      title
-----------------
 Salt Roads
 The Long Ledger
 Tidewater
(3 rows)

UNION removes duplicates (it sorts or hashes to do so); UNION ALL keeps all rows and is much cheaper, so use it whenever duplicates are impossible or acceptable. INTERSECT keeps rows found in both; EXCEPT rows in the first but not the second:

SELECT member_id FROM loans WHERE book_id = 1
INTERSECT
SELECT member_id FROM loans WHERE book_id = 5
ORDER BY 1;

 member_id
-----------
         1
         2
(2 rows)

Swap INTERSECT for EXCEPT and the result is member 3: borrowed book 1, never book 5. The column names come from the first query. Odoo uses UNION ALL heavily in SQL-view reports (CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT ... UNION ALL SELECT ...).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Inner join on an optional key. Records with NULL in the foreign key vanish from the result. Use LEFT JOIN for anything that is not NOT NULL.
  • Filtering the right table in WHERE after a left join. It turns the join into an inner join. Put the condition in ON.
  • Fan-out in aggregates. Two one-to-many joins in one query multiply rows; sums and counts inflate. Pre-aggregate each side.
  • count(*) over a left join. The unmatched row counts as 1. Count a column of the right table.
  • A missing join condition. The query returns the product of the two tables, or never returns. Always write ON, and always check row counts on a first run with LIMIT or count(*).
  • NATURAL JOIN and SELECT * across joins. Shared column names (id, name, audit columns) collide; clients that read result rows into a dict silently keep one of them. Alias what you select.
  • Unqualified column names. They work until someone adds a same-named column to another joined table.
  • Joining on translated fields or JSON. In Odoo 16+ name of product_template is jsonb; JOIN ... ON a.name = b.name compares JSON documents, not display names.
  • Assuming a join ordering you wrote is the order of execution. The planner reorders inner joins; you are describing the result, not the procedure.
  • UNION where UNION ALL is meant. Deduplication hides legitimate duplicate rows and costs a sort.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. List each loan with the book title, the author's name (or unknown when the book has none), and the member's name. Keep all seven loans.

  2. Which members have never borrowed anything? Write it twice: once with LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL and once with NOT EXISTS.

  3. For each author, return the number of books and the total price of those books, including authors without books (show 0 for both). Then add a join to loans to count loans per author and explain what happens to the price total if you join naively.

  4. For every member, show the title of the book they borrowed most recently. Members with no loans should appear with an empty title. Use LATERAL.

  5. List the genres that have no books. Then list pairs of distinct genres that occur together on at least one book (each pair once).

Solution 

  1. SELECT l.id, b.title, COALESCE(a.name, 'unknown') AS author, m.name AS member
FROM loans l
JOIN books b   ON b.id = l.book_id
LEFT JOIN authors a ON a.id = b.author_id
JOIN members m ON m.id = l.member_id
ORDER BY l.id;
    The books in all loans have an author, so unknown does not appear; the left join is still the correct choice. Seven rows.

  2. SELECT m.name FROM members m
LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.member_id = m.id
WHERE l.id IS NULL;

SELECT m.name FROM members m
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM loans l WHERE l.member_id = m.id);
    Both return Quinn.

  3. SELECT a.name, count(b.id) AS books, COALESCE(sum(b.price), 0) AS total_price
FROM authors a
LEFT JOIN books b ON b.author_id = a.id
GROUP BY a.id, a.name
ORDER BY a.id;

         name      | books | total_price
---------------+-------+-------------
 Ada Marlowe   |     2 |       27.50
 Boris Venn    |     2 |       20.90
 Chiara Lund   |     1 |       18.00
 Dmitri Okafor |     0 |           0
(4 rows)
    Adding LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.book_id = b.id repeats each book once per loan: Tidewater (12.50) appears 3 times, so Ada's total becomes 12.50 x 3 + 15.00 x 1 = 52.50 and her book count 4 unless you use count(DISTINCT b.id). The price sum cannot be repaired with DISTINCT: aggregate loans per book first in a subquery and join that.

  4. SELECT m.name, last_loan.title
FROM members m
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT b.title
    FROM loans l JOIN books b ON b.id = l.book_id
    WHERE l.member_id = m.id
    ORDER BY l.loaned_on DESC, l.id DESC
    LIMIT 1
) last_loan ON true
ORDER BY m.id;

     name  |     title
-------+---------------
 Nora  | Quiet Engines
 Omar  | Quiet Engines
 Petra | Tidewater
 Quinn |
(4 rows)


  5. SELECT g.name FROM genres g
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM book_genre bg WHERE bg.genre_id = g.id);
    Returns no rows: every genre has a book (History belongs to Tidewater). For pairs: 
    SELECT DISTINCT g1.name AS genre_a, g2.name AS genre_b
FROM book_genre x
JOIN book_genre y ON y.book_id = x.book_id AND x.genre_id < y.genre_id
JOIN genres g1 ON g1.id = x.genre_id
JOIN genres g2 ON g2.id = y.genre_id
ORDER BY 1, 2;

     genre_a | genre_b
---------+---------
 Fiction | History
 Fiction | Poetry
(2 rows)
    The x.genre_id < y.genre_id condition is the self-join trick from above that yields each pair once.

docs.title: Locks
docs.text: MVCC lets readers and writers run side by side, but two transactions that want to change the same row cannot both win, and some operations (schema changes, index builds) need exclusive access to a whole table. PostgreSQL arbitrates with locks. When Odoo "hangs" for a minute and then recovers, when an update of a module freezes the whole system, when a cron job and a user trip over each other, you are looking at locks. This chapter explains which locks exist, how to see who is waiting for whom, how to take locks deliberately (FOR UPDATE, NOWAIT, SKIP LOCKED, advisory locks), how deadlocks arise, and how to avoid them. It follows Transactions and isolation and uses the library schema.

docs.title: Why locks exist, and the two scales
docs.text:
Locks live at two levels:

  • Row locks protect individual rows. UPDATE and DELETE take them automatically, and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes them on request. They are held until the transaction ends (commit or rollback).
  • Table locks protect a table as a whole. Every statement takes one automatically, in a mode matching what it does. Most are harmless (a plain SELECT takes ACCESS SHARE, which conflicts with almost nothing); a few, notably ALTER TABLE, take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, which conflicts with everything including SELECT.

A lock is released only when the transaction ends. A long transaction therefore keeps every lock it ever took, which is why "do not leave transactions open" appears in so many places.

docs.title: Row locks in action
docs.text:
Two sessions again, A and B. B tries to update the row A has just updated:

Session A                                     Session B
BEGIN;
UPDATE books SET price = 13.00 WHERE id = 1;
                                              UPDATE books SET price = 14.00 WHERE id = 1;
                                              (waits; no output)
COMMIT;
                                              (continues: UPDATE 1)

B did not fail. It waited for A's transaction to end and then proceeded. In READ COMMITTED it applied its update to the row as A left it. In REPEATABLE READ (Odoo's level) B would instead fail with could not serialize access due to concurrent update once A committed, and a retry would follow. If A had issued ROLLBACK, B would have proceeded with the original row.

What B waits on is a lock held on the row version A created, taken by writing it. Note that readers are not blocked: a plain SELECT from a third session during all this simply sees the old committed row.

docs.title: Which updates conflict
docs.text:
Row locks come in four strengths:

Mode Taken by Conflicts with FOR KEY SHARE foreign-key checks (an insert into a child table locks the parent row) FOR UPDATE only FOR SHARE explicit FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR UPDATE FOR NO KEY UPDATE UPDATE that does not change key columns FOR SHARE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR UPDATE FOR UPDATE DELETE, UPDATE of key columns, explicit SELECT ... FOR UPDATE all of them

The split exists for foreign keys: inserting a loan locks the book row in KEY SHARE mode (to make sure the book is not deleted meanwhile), and a concurrent UPDATE books SET price = ... takes NO KEY UPDATE, which does not conflict with KEY SHARE. So price changes on a book do not block loans of that book. Before PostgreSQL 9.3 this combination blocked.

docs.title: Locking on purpose: SELECT FOR UPDATE
docs.text:
To read a row and then change it based on what you read, lock it at read time, so nobody else can change it in between:

BEGIN;
SELECT copies FROM book_stock WHERE book_id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
-- decide in the application ...
UPDATE book_stock SET copies = copies - 1 WHERE book_id = 1;
COMMIT;

(book_stock is the small table from the previous chapter: CREATE TABLE book_stock (book_id integer PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES books (id), copies integer NOT NULL CHECK (copies >= 0)); INSERT INTO book_stock VALUES (1, 3);.) A second session running the same SELECT ... FOR UPDATE waits until the first one commits or rolls back, and then sees the updated value.

Details that matter:

  • It locks only the rows returned. With LIMIT, only the rows actually returned are locked (but the rows examined may be more, so be careful with ordering and filters).
  • With joins, lock only the table you mean: SELECT ... FROM loans l JOIN books b ON ... FOR UPDATE OF l. Without OF, every table in the join is locked.
  • FOR UPDATE cannot be applied to the nullable side of an outer join (FOR UPDATE cannot be applied to the nullable side of an outer join); lock before joining, in a subquery or a separate statement.
  • Locks are on the row, not on "the absence of a row". SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a key that does not yet exist locks nothing, so two sessions can both see "not found" and both insert. Use a unique constraint plus ON CONFLICT, or lock a parent row, for existence checks.
  • FOR NO KEY UPDATE is enough when you will not change key columns and want to avoid blocking foreign-key checks from other sessions; it is the lock a plain UPDATE takes.

docs.title: NOWAIT and lock_timeout
docs.text:
By default a lock request waits indefinitely. Two ways to refuse waiting:

SELECT * FROM book_stock WHERE book_id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;

ERROR:  could not obtain lock on row in relation "book_stock"

NOWAIT fails immediately with SQLSTATE 55P03 (lock_not_available) if another transaction holds the row. SET lock_timeout = '2s' applies a deadline to any lock wait in the session, with the same error on expiry. Odoo's retry mechanism treats 55P03 as retryable, so a NOWAIT that loses just reruns the request later. It also makes a good guard for anything that must not queue (a cron job that does the same work every minute should skip a minute, not pile up).

docs.title: SKIP LOCKED: the work queue
docs.text:
SKIP LOCKED ignores rows that are currently locked, returning only the free ones. It turns a table into a queue that many workers drain without waiting on each other. Create a queue of notifications:

CREATE TABLE notify_queue (
    id       serial PRIMARY KEY,
    loan_id  integer NOT NULL,
    sent     boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false
);
INSERT INTO notify_queue (loan_id) SELECT g FROM generate_series(1, 6) g;

Each worker claims a batch inside a transaction:

Worker A                                      Worker B
BEGIN;                                        BEGIN;
SELECT id FROM notify_queue
 WHERE NOT sent
 ORDER BY id LIMIT 2
 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
  -> 1, 2
                                              SELECT id FROM notify_queue
                                               WHERE NOT sent
                                               ORDER BY id LIMIT 2
                                               FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
                                                -> 3, 4
UPDATE notify_queue SET sent = true           UPDATE notify_queue SET sent = true
 WHERE id IN (1, 2);                           WHERE id IN (3, 4);
COMMIT;                                       COMMIT;

B was not delayed by A's locks, and got different rows. If a worker crashes mid-batch, its locks vanish with its transaction and the rows return to the pool automatically. The cost: results are not a consistent view of the queue ("skipped" rows are invisible to that query), so use it for work distribution only, never for reports.

Odoo uses row locking for scheduled actions: the cron runner locks the ir_cron row of a job while it runs, so that two workers (or two Odoo servers on one database) never run the same job simultaneously. If a job's row is locked, the other worker skips it. Whether it is NOWAIT or SKIP LOCKED depends on the release; the effect is the same.

docs.title: Seeing who blocks whom
docs.text:
When something hangs, find the blocker. pg_stat_activity lists sessions and what they wait for; pg_blocking_pids() (PostgreSQL 9.6+) names the sessions blocking one:

SELECT a.pid                          AS blocked_pid,
       pg_blocking_pids(a.pid)        AS blocked_by,
       a.wait_event_type,
       a.wait_event,
       now() - a.query_start          AS waiting_for,
       left(a.query, 50)              AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity a
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(a.pid)) > 0;

 blocked_pid | blocked_by | wait_event_type |  wait_event   |  waiting_for  |                       query
-------------+------------+-----------------+---------------+---------------+----------------------------------------------------
        4121 | {4107}     | Lock            | transactionid | 00:00:41.2    | UPDATE books SET price = 14.00 WHERE id = 1
(1 row)

wait_event_type = Lock and wait_event = transactionid is the signature of waiting for a row lock: the waiter waits for the blocker's transaction to finish. Now look at the blocker:

SELECT pid, state, now() - xact_start AS xact_age, left(query, 60) AS last_query
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE pid = 4107;

 pid  |        state        |  xact_age  |                          last_query
