------+---------------------+------------+--------------------------------------------------------------
 4107 | idle in transaction | 00:03:02.1 | UPDATE books SET price = 13.00 WHERE id = 1

The blocker is idle in transaction: someone updated a row, forgot to commit, and walked away. last_query is the last statement it ran, not necessarily the one holding the lock, but it is the best clue. Who is it? usename, application_name, client_addr in the same view. Resolve it by having that person commit or roll back. As a last resort a DBA can end the session:

SELECT pg_cancel_backend(4107);     -- cancel the running statement, keep the session
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(4107);  -- end the session; its transaction rolls back

Terminating a session rolls back whatever it did. On a production Odoo database, check that the session is not a worker in the middle of a legitimate long job, and ask first.

The complete picture of what is locked is pg_locks:

SELECT l.pid, l.locktype, l.mode, l.granted, c.relname
FROM pg_locks l
LEFT JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid = l.relation
WHERE l.pid = 4107;

 pid  |   locktype    |       mode       | granted |  relname
------+---------------+------------------+---------+-----------
 4107 | relation      | RowExclusiveLock | t       | books_pkey
 4107 | relation      | RowExclusiveLock | t       | books
 4107 | virtualxid    | ExclusiveLock    | t       |
 4107 | transactionid | ExclusiveLock    | t       |
(4 rows)

You will not read pg_locks often; pg_blocking_pids answers the question you actually have. (Row locks themselves are stored in the row version, not in pg_locks, which is why you see the transactionid instead.)

docs.title: Table locks and the lock queue
docs.text:
Every statement takes a table-level lock. The ones to know:

Mode Taken by Blocks ACCESS SHARE SELECT only ACCESS EXCLUSIVE ROW EXCLUSIVE INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE SHARE and stronger (index builds, DDL) SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE VACUUM, ANALYZE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY itself and stronger; ordinary reads and writes continue SHARE plain CREATE INDEX writes (ROW EXCLUSIVE) ACCESS EXCLUSIVE DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE, VACUUM FULL, most ALTER TABLE forms everything, reads included

The behaviour that surprises people is the queue. Locks are granted in request order, and a request waits for the locks held and for the earlier waiters it conflicts with. Suppose a report is running a ten-minute SELECT on books (holding ACCESS SHARE). A migration then issues ALTER TABLE books ADD COLUMN ..., which needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and must wait for the report. While it waits, every new SELECT on books queues behind the ALTER: the table is unreadable although nothing has been changed yet. Users see the application freeze, and it recovers the moment the report ends or the ALTER is cancelled.

This is the classic cause of "we updated the module and the whole system froze". Odoo's module update runs ALTER TABLE statements for new columns and constraints; if a long transaction (a stuck cron, a long report, a forgotten shell) holds even a read lock on a table it touches, the update queues and blocks everyone. Defences:

-- before any manual DDL on a busy system
SET lock_timeout = '5s';
ALTER TABLE books ADD COLUMN subtitle varchar;

If the lock is not available within five seconds the statement fails instead of freezing everyone; retry later, ideally after finding and ending the long transaction (see the query above and the one in the previous chapter). Before an Odoo update on a live database, look for long transactions and make sure no cron job is running.

Other DDL notes:

  • ADD COLUMN with a constant default is quick since PostgreSQL 11 (no table rewrite), but still takes the exclusive lock briefly. Adding a column with a volatile default, or changing a column type, rewrites the table under the exclusive lock.
  • ADD FOREIGN KEY validates existing rows while holding a strong lock. For big tables add it NOT VALID (instant) and run ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT afterwards, which takes a weaker lock.
  • CREATE INDEX blocks writes; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY does not (see Indexes and EXPLAIN).
  • LOCK TABLE books IN SHARE MODE; takes a table lock explicitly, which you rarely want in application code.

docs.title: Deadlocks
docs.text:
A deadlock is a cycle: A waits for B, B waits for A. Neither can proceed ever, so PostgreSQL resolves it: after waiting for deadlock_timeout (1 second by default) it checks for a cycle and, if found, aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40P01.

Session A                                     Session B
BEGIN;                                        BEGIN;
UPDATE books SET price = 1 WHERE id = 1;
                                              UPDATE books SET price = 2 WHERE id = 2;
UPDATE books SET price = 1 WHERE id = 2;
(waits for B)
                                              UPDATE books SET price = 2 WHERE id = 1;
                                              (waits for A: a cycle)
                                              ERROR:  deadlock detected

The full error, as it appears in the log and to the aborted session:

ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL:  Process 4121 waits for ShareLock on transaction 8123; blocked by process 4107.
Process 4107 waits for ShareLock on transaction 8124; blocked by process 4121.
HINT:  See server log for query details.
CONTEXT:  while updating tuple (0,1) in relation "books"

The victim rolls back; the other continues. Odoo retries the aborted request, so occasional deadlocks cost a delay, not an error, but frequent ones mean contention that wants fixing.

Where do they come from in Odoo? Two flows updating the same set of records in different orders. The ORM's own writes to a recordset are issued as UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (...), and the order in which PostgreSQL locks the rows inside such a statement follows the physical scan order, not the id list. Two requests writing overlapping sets (a cron recomputing stock, a user confirming an order) can lock rows in opposing order. The cure is the standard one: always acquire locks in a consistent global order.

BEGIN;
SELECT id FROM books WHERE id IN (1, 2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;   -- lock in id order
UPDATE books SET price = price + 1 WHERE id IN (1, 2);
COMMIT;

If every flow that touches several rows locks them sorted by id first, no cycle can form. In Python: records.sorted('id') before the loop of writes, or a SELECT ... ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE before a raw bulk update.

Other ways to reduce deadlocks: keep transactions short, do not mix long computation or network calls between the first lock and the commit, and avoid unnecessary updates (every UPDATE, even to the same value, takes the row lock).

docs.title: Unique indexes also make you wait
docs.text: Two sessions inserting the same unique key serialize: the second INSERT waits for the first to finish. If the first commits, the second fails with a unique violation; if the first rolls back, the second proceeds. This is correct behaviour, but it is a lock wait: you will see wait_event = transactionid in pg_stat_activity for an INSERT. It is why an import that creates the same partner or XML ID from two parallel workers stalls and then fails.

docs.title: Advisory locks: a mutex you name
docs.text:
Advisory locks are locks on numbers you choose, with meaning only to your code. PostgreSQL stores and arbitrates them, but guards no data. They are the tool for "only one of these may run at a time" where no row exists to lock: a singleton job, a per-customer critical section, an import.

SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(4711);   -- true if acquired, false if held by another session

 pg_try_advisory_xact_lock
---------------------------
 t
(1 row)

A second session running the same statement while the first transaction is open gets f. The lock releases automatically at the end of the transaction (the xact variants). The family:

Function Waits? Released pg_advisory_xact_lock(k) yes at transaction end pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(k) no, returns boolean at transaction end pg_advisory_lock(k) yes when explicitly unlocked, or the session ends pg_try_advisory_lock(k) no same

Prefer the transaction-level variants. A session-level lock outlives the transaction, and Odoo reuses pooled connections, so a lock taken in one request with pg_advisory_lock and not released stays on that pooled connection, blocking other requests for as long as the connection lives, with no sign in pg_stat_activity's transaction age. Always release session-level locks in a finally, or avoid them.

Keys are 64-bit integers (or two 32-bit). To lock by a string or a record, hash it: pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('library.import')), or combine a namespace and an id: pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(1001, record_id) where the first number identifies your feature. Choose keys that cannot collide with other code using advisory locks on the same database (Odoo itself or a third-party module may use them); a distinctive two-number form with your own namespace is the safest.

docs.title: Choosing between the tools
docs.text: Need Use change numbers based on current value UPDATE ... SET x = x - 1 (atomic) read, decide in Python, then write one row SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on that row distribute work among workers FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED do not queue, fail fast NOWAIT or lock_timeout rule across several rows or a missing row unique/partial index; or lock a parent row singleton job with no natural row pg_try_advisory_xact_lock avoid deadlock on many rows lock in a fixed order (ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE)

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Open transactions holding row locks. The most common cause of "the system hangs when I edit this record". Look for idle in transaction in pg_stat_activity.
  • DDL on a busy table with no lock_timeout. It queues behind a long reader and blocks all new queries on the table. Always set a short lock_timeout for manual DDL, and check for long transactions before module updates.
  • Locking more than you need. FOR UPDATE on a join locks every table; add OF. A broad FOR UPDATE on a hot parent row serializes the whole system.
  • Locking in inconsistent order. The root of nearly all deadlocks. Sort ids first.
  • Using FOR UPDATE to guard a row that does not exist. It locks nothing. Use a unique constraint or lock a parent.
  • Session-level advisory locks through a pool. They leak across requests. Use xact locks.
  • SKIP LOCKED for consistent reads. It returns an arbitrary subset by design.
  • Catching 40001/40P01/55P03 in application code. They must propagate to the retry layer, or you must implement an equivalent.
  • Holding locks across slow work. An HTTP call, an email, or time.sleep between the lock and the commit multiplies every other transaction's wait.
  • Killing a backend without looking. pg_terminate_backend rolls the transaction back. Check what the session was doing and ask before using it on production.
  • Assuming SELECT never blocks. It takes ACCESS SHARE, which conflicts with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; under a pending DDL even reads wait.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Use two psql windows A and B on handbook_lab.

  1. In A start a transaction and update a book's price without committing. In B try the same update, and while it waits, run the blocking query from this chapter in a third window (or from A). Identify the blocked pid, the blocker, and the wait event. Then roll back in A.

  2. Show that SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT in B fails immediately while A holds the row, and that a plain SELECT still works. Then repeat with SET lock_timeout = '2s' and a plain UPDATE.

  3. Create a deadlock between two sessions on books 1 and 2. Read the error and log lines. Then rewrite both sessions so that they cannot deadlock.

  4. Build the queue from this chapter with six rows and have two sessions claim two rows each with SKIP LOCKED. Show that they get different rows, and what happens to a claim whose session you disconnect before commit.

  5. With A holding a transaction that has run SELECT * FROM books;, run ALTER TABLE books ADD COLUMN subtitle varchar; in B and then a SELECT on books in a third session. Explain what you see and how lock_timeout changes it. Roll back and, if the column was added, drop it.

Solution 

  1. A: BEGIN; UPDATE books SET price = 13.00 WHERE id = 1;
B: UPDATE books SET price = 14.00 WHERE id = 1;     -- waits
C: SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid), wait_event_type, wait_event, left(query, 40)
   FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;
    B's pid appears with blocked_by equal to A's pid, wait_event_type = Lock, wait_event = transactionid. ROLLBACK in A lets B finish.

  2. With A holding the row, B's SELECT * FROM books WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT; fails at once with could not obtain lock on row in relation "books"; a plain SELECT returns the committed row, because readers do not block. With SET lock_timeout = '2s'; the UPDATE waits two seconds and then fails with canceling statement due to lock timeout (SQLSTATE 55P03).

  3. A: BEGIN; UPDATE books SET price = 1 WHERE id = 1;
B: BEGIN; UPDATE books SET price = 2 WHERE id = 2;
A: UPDATE books SET price = 1 WHERE id = 2;    -- waits
B: UPDATE books SET price = 2 WHERE id = 1;    -- after about 1 s: ERROR: deadlock detected
    One session is aborted; the other continues. Fix: both sessions begin with SELECT id FROM books WHERE id IN (1, 2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE; before their updates. Then the second session simply waits for the first to finish and no cycle exists.

  4. After CREATE TABLE notify_queue ... and the insert, session A's SELECT ... LIMIT 2 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED returns ids 1 and 2, and B's, run while A is open, returns 3 and 4. If A disconnects before COMMIT, its transaction rolls back, the locks disappear, and a later claim returns ids 1 and 2 again. Clean up with DROP TABLE notify_queue;.

  5. B's ALTER TABLE waits for A's ACCESS SHARE lock to be released. The third session's SELECT also waits, queueing behind the pending ALTER, although A is only reading. That is the lock queue. With SET lock_timeout = '3s'; in B before the ALTER, B fails after three seconds with canceling statement due to lock timeout, the queue drains, and the SELECT in the third session completes. After ROLLBACK in A, retry; if it was added, remove with ALTER TABLE books DROP COLUMN subtitle;.

docs.title: psql and operations
docs.text:
The earlier chapters of this part taught SQL. This one covers the tools and routines around it: connecting to a database, getting around in psql efficiently, making and restoring backups (including the copy-for-testing workflow that every Odoo developer uses weekly), keeping the database healthy, and a set of diagnostic queries to keep in a file. Most of it is operational hygiene; the habit that matters most is treating production as read-only by default and doing risky work on a copy.

Hosts, users, database names, and paths below are placeholders. Never put real passwords on a command line or in a script you commit. Use the mechanisms in the connection section (~/.pgpass, environment variables, a service file).

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
psql takes the same five parameters as every PostgreSQL client: host, port, user, database, and a password if the server asks for one.

psql -h db.internal.example -p 5432 -U odoo -d mydb
psql "host=db.internal.example port=5432 user=odoo dbname=mydb sslmode=require"
psql "postgresql://odoo@db.internal.example:5432/mydb"

Omitted parameters fall back to environment variables and then to defaults: PGHOST, PGPORT, PGUSER, PGDATABASE (and PGPASSWORD, which you should avoid because other users on the machine can see the environment of your processes in some setups). With nothing set, psql connects through the local Unix socket as your operating-system user to a database named like that user.

Passwords belong in ~/.pgpass (on Windows %APPDATA%\postgresql\pgpass.conf), one line per server, with the file readable only by you (chmod 600):

db.internal.example:5432:mydb:odoo:the-password-goes-here

Fields are host:port:database:user:password, and * is a wildcard. psql then never prompts. A service file (~/.pg_service.conf) names a whole connection:

[odoo-staging]
host=db.internal.example
port=5432
dbname=mydb
user=odoo

and psql service=odoo-staging connects with it.

Odoo's own settings are in its configuration file (db_host, db_port, db_user, db_password, db_name, dbfilter). When you must connect "the way Odoo does" to see what it sees, read those values from the file instead of guessing, and use the same role, because role permissions differ (the Odoo role is usually not a superuser).

On a Linux server the common local patterns are:

sudo -u postgres psql                 # superuser, via peer authentication
sudo -u odoo psql -d mydb             # as the odoo OS user, whose role has the same name

Peer authentication maps the operating-system user to the database role of the same name, which is why these work without a password. Remote access is governed by pg_hba.conf on the server: which hosts, which users, which databases, which authentication method. "no pg_hba.conf entry for host" is the error when the server was not told to accept your address; "password authentication failed" means the entry matched but the credentials did not.

List databases and check where you are connected:

\l
\conninfo

You are connected to database "mydb" as user "odoo" via socket in "/var/run/postgresql" at port "5432".

docs.title: Working in psql
docs.text:
psql's own commands start with a backslash and are not SQL: they are handled by the client, need no semicolon, and are not sent to the server. The ones worth knowing by heart:

Command Does \? list all backslash commands; \h CREATE INDEX gives SQL syntax help \c dbname connect to another database \l list databases \dt, \dt+ list tables (with sizes) \dt library_* list tables matching a pattern \d name describe a table: columns, indexes, constraints, referencing tables \d+ name the same with storage, statistics target, comments \di, \dv, \ds, \df indexes, views, sequences, functions \du roles \x or \x auto expanded display: one column per line, for wide rows \timing print the time each statement took \e edit the current query in $EDITOR \i file.sql run a file of commands \o file send results to a file; \o alone restores the screen \copy ... client-side COPY (see INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) \set name value, :name psql variables \watch 2 repeat the previous query every 2 seconds \g, \gset run the query buffer; store a one-row result in variables \q quit

Wide rows read badly in a table; \x flips to a vertical layout:

\x on
SELECT * FROM members WHERE id = 1;

-[ RECORD 1 ]-------------------
id        | 1
name      | Nora
email     | nora@example.com
joined_on | 2023-01-10
active    | t

\x auto switches to vertical only when the row would not fit the screen. \timing shows the elapsed time of each statement, which is the fastest way to compare two versions of a query before reaching for EXPLAIN. \watch re-runs the previous statement periodically; it turns a query on pg_stat_activity into a live monitor:

SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;
\watch 2

\gset turns a one-row result into psql variables, so a script can feed one query's result into the next:

SELECT max(id) AS last_book_id FROM books \gset
SELECT * FROM books WHERE id = :last_book_id;

docs.title: Running SQL non-interactively
docs.text:
psql -d handbook_lab -c "SELECT count(*) FROM books"            # one statement
psql -d handbook_lab -f fix.sql                                 # a file
psql -d handbook_lab -At -c "SELECT id FROM books ORDER BY id"  # unaligned, tuples only: script-friendly
psql -d handbook_lab -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -1 -f fix.sql           # stop at first error; wrap in one transaction

By default psql continues after an error, so a script that fails at statement 3 happily runs statements 4 to 40 against a half-changed database. For any script that changes data use -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1, and -1 (--single-transaction) to wrap the file in one BEGIN ... COMMIT, which then rolls back entirely on failure. (A file that contains CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY or VACUUM cannot use -1.)

-A (unaligned) and -t (tuples only) give clean output for shell pipelines; --csv produces CSV with a header, a quick way to export.

docs.title: A useful ~/.psqlrc
docs.text:
psql reads ~/.psqlrc at startup. A conservative set:

\set QUIET 1
\pset null '[NULL]'
\x auto
\timing on
\set HISTSIZE 5000
\set ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK interactive
\set PROMPT1 '%n@%m/%/%R%x%# '
\unset QUIET
  • \pset null '[NULL]' makes NULL visible instead of an empty cell that looks like an empty string. It prevents a real class of misreadings.
  • ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK interactive wraps each statement you type inside an open transaction in an implicit savepoint, so a typo does not abort your whole transaction.
  • %x in the prompt prints * when you are inside an open transaction, and ! when it is aborted: at a glance you can see that you left a BEGIN open, which is the leading cause of long-held locks.

Do not set \set AUTOCOMMIT off in your rc file. It makes every statement open a transaction that nothing closes, so a harmless SELECT leaves a session idle in transaction on a production database for hours. The inverse safety, a prompt that shows the host and database in a conspicuous way, is worth setting: you must know whether you are on staging or production before you press Enter. Many teams use per-environment service files with a distinct prompt.

docs.title: Pointing psql safely at a database you do not own
docs.text:
For a database you only intend to read:

PGOPTIONS='-c default_transaction_read_only=on -c statement_timeout=60000 -c lock_timeout=5000 -c idle_in_transaction_session_timeout=600000' \
  psql -h db.internal.example -U odoo -d mydb

Read-only default, a one-minute statement limit, a five-second limit on lock waits, and a ten-minute limit on idle open transactions. It is not a security boundary (the session can SET the option back), but it removes accidents. For a real boundary create a role with pg_read_all_data (PostgreSQL 14+) or SELECT grants on specific tables and connect as it.

docs.title: Backups: pg_dump and pg_restore
docs.text:
pg_dump makes a consistent snapshot of one database while it is in use (it runs in a REPEATABLE READ transaction, the same mechanism as the previous chapters). It does not block other users, though it adds read load.

Format Flag Properties plain SQL -Fp (default) a text file of SQL; restore with psql -f; no parallelism or selective restore custom -Fc compressed, one file, pg_restore can list, select, and parallelize directory -Fd one file per table; supports parallel dump (-j) tar -Ft rarely useful

The everyday choice is custom format:

pg_dump -h db.internal.example -U odoo -Fc -f mydb_2026-11-13.dump mydb

Inspect before trusting it:

pg_restore --list mydb_2026-11-13.dump | head -30
ls -l mydb_2026-11-13.dump

pg_restore --list prints the table of contents (tables, indexes, constraints, data); a dump that lists nothing, or is a few hundred bytes, is a failed one. The only real test of a backup is a restore.

Restore into a fresh database, never over a live one:

createdb -h db.internal.example -U odoo mydb_copy
pg_restore -h db.internal.example -U odoo -d mydb_copy --no-owner --no-privileges -j 4 mydb_2026-11-13.dump
  • --no-owner --no-privileges ignore the ownership and GRANTs recorded in the dump, so everything is owned by the user running the restore. It avoids "role does not exist" errors when you restore on a machine without the original roles.
  • -j 4 restores with four parallel jobs (custom and directory formats only). It speeds up index builds substantially.
  • Errors: pg_restore continues past errors by default and prints a count at the end. Read the messages, because "ignoring errors" can mean a missing extension (unaccent, pg_trgm) or a failed constraint. --exit-on-error stops at the first one.

For small databases or when you want to read the dump, plain SQL works: pg_dump -Fp -f mydb.sql mydb, restored with psql -d mydb_copy -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f mydb.sql.

Compatibility rules: pg_dump must be the same or a newer major version than the server it dumps. A dump can be restored to the same or a newer server major version; restoring a dump from a newer server into an older one is not supported. Roles and tablespaces are cluster-wide, not in a per-database dump; pg_dumpall --globals-only captures them.

docs.title: Cloning a database on the same server
docs.text:
If no one is connected to the source, the fastest copy is a template:

CREATE DATABASE mydb_copy TEMPLATE mydb;

It fails with source database "mydb" is being accessed by other users while connections exist. Odoo's workers, cron, and any open sessions count. Disconnecting them is a decision for whoever owns the system, not a statement to run casually.

docs.title: The Odoo-specific part: the filestore
docs.text:
A PostgreSQL dump contains the database only. Attachments and binary fields stored with the default settings live as files in the filestore, a directory per database under the data directory (data_dir, e.g. ~/.local/share/Odoo/filestore/<dbname> or /var/lib/odoo/filestore/<dbname>), and ir_attachment.store_fname names the file. A database restored without its filestore opens, but every attachment, report logo, and image gives a missing-file error. A complete backup is the dump plus the filestore directory, taken close together in time:

tar czf mydb_filestore_2026-11-13.tgz -C /var/lib/odoo/filestore mydb

and a complete restore puts the directory back under the new database's name (filestore/mydb_copy). Odoo's web database manager and its db command line (available from Odoo 16; check odoo-bin db --help on your version) produce a zip containing both dump.sql and the filestore, which is convenient and equivalent.

docs.title: A restored copy is a live clone: neutralize it
docs.text:
A copy of a production database contains scheduled actions, outgoing mail servers, payment provider credentials, webhooks, and integrations. Started as is, it can send real emails to real customers and process real payments. Before the first start of a copy, neutralize it. Odoo 16 and later ship a command for this:

odoo-bin neutralize -d mydb_copy

which disables the relevant scheduled actions, mail servers, and payment providers (the exact set depends on the installed modules). Otherwise do it by hand, always looking first:

SELECT id, cron_name, active FROM ir_cron WHERE active ORDER BY id;
SELECT id, name, active FROM ir_mail_server;

BEGIN;
UPDATE ir_cron SET active = false WHERE active;
UPDATE ir_mail_server SET active = false WHERE active;
COMMIT;

(The cron_name column and the other table names vary by version; use \d ir_cron first.) Also change web.base.url in ir_config_parameter so that links in emails and reports do not point at production, and reset anything that identifies the instance to external services. This is the same read-first, change-in-a-transaction discipline as in INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, with one extra rule: do it on the copy, before anyone starts Odoo on it.

docs.title: Keeping the database healthy
docs.text:
MVCC leaves dead row versions behind (see Transactions and isolation); VACUUM reclaims them for reuse, ANALYZE refreshes planner statistics, and autovacuum does both automatically in the background. Usually you do nothing. You check:

SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,
       round(100.0 * n_dead_tup / nullif(n_live_tup + n_dead_tup, 0), 1) AS dead_pct,
       last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC
LIMIT 10;

  relname   | n_live_tup | n_dead_tup | dead_pct |       last_autovacuum        |       last_autoanalyze
------------+------------+------------+----------+------------------------------+------------------------------
 mail_message |    812344 |      30112 |      3.6 | 2026-11-13 02:14:55+00       | 2026-11-13 02:15:10+00
 bus_bus      |     12000 |      98000 |     89.1 | 2026-11-12 21:03:12+00       | 2026-11-12 21:03:13+00
(2 rows)

(Illustrative.) A high dead_pct with an old last_autovacuum means vacuum is not keeping up or is blocked by a long transaction. Run it by hand on one table: VACUUM (ANALYZE, VERBOSE) mail_message;. It does not block normal reads and writes.

VACUUM FULL rewrites the table into a new file to return space to the operating system. It takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the whole duration (the table is unusable), needs free disk space equal to the table, and is almost never the right call on a live system. Plain VACUUM makes space reusable, and pg_repack is the usual tool when real shrinking is needed without downtime.

Bulk operations leave stale statistics: after a big import, a mass update, or a restore, run ANALYZE; (restores do not carry statistics over). Sluggish first queries after a restore are very often this.

docs.title: Diagnostic queries worth keeping
docs.text:
Save these in a file (for example diag.sql) and run them with \i. All are read-only.

What is running now (excluding your own session), longest first:

SELECT pid, usename, application_name, state,
       now() - query_start AS running_for,
       wait_event_type, wait_event,
       left(query, 80) AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid()
ORDER BY query_start;

Sessions stuck in a transaction (from the previous chapters):

SELECT pid, usename, now() - xact_start AS xact_age, state, left(query, 60) AS last_query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL AND state = 'idle in transaction'
ORDER BY xact_start;

Who blocks whom: the query using pg_blocking_pids() from Locks.

Connections against the limit. Each Odoo worker holds connections to the database, so the sum across all Odoo servers must stay below PostgreSQL's max_connections (default 100), minus the connections other tools need:

SELECT count(*) AS connections,
       current_setting('max_connections')::int AS max_connections,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE state = 'idle in transaction') AS idle_in_tx
FROM pg_stat_activity;

The Odoo option db_maxconn (default 64) is a per-process pool limit, not a global one; with several workers it multiplies. "FATAL: sorry, too many clients already" is this limit being exceeded.

Database and table sizes:

SELECT datname, pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size(datname)) AS size
FROM pg_database WHERE NOT datistemplate ORDER BY pg_database_size(datname) DESC;

SELECT relname,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(oid)) AS total,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid))       AS table_only,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_indexes_size(oid))        AS indexes
FROM pg_class
WHERE relkind = 'r' AND relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(oid) DESC
LIMIT 10;

Cache hit ratio (below about 99% on a database that should fit in memory means too little shared_buffers or an unusually scan-heavy workload):

SELECT round(100.0 * sum(blks_hit) / nullif(sum(blks_hit) + sum(blks_read), 0), 2) AS hit_pct
FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = current_database();

Unused and duplicate indexes: see Indexes and EXPLAIN.

Sequences approaching the integer limit. Odoo ids are int4, so a sequence near 2.1 billion is a time bomb, usually on log-like tables:

SELECT schemaname, sequencename, last_value, max_value,
       round(100.0 * last_value / max_value, 1) AS pct_used
FROM pg_sequences
WHERE last_value IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY last_value DESC
LIMIT 5;

Transaction-id age (rarely a problem with working autovacuum, fatal if ignored for long):

SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid) AS xid_age FROM pg_database ORDER BY 2 DESC;

Values approaching two billion need immediate attention, though normal systems stay in the low hundreds of millions.

Slowest queries overall need the pg_stat_statements extension, which must be in shared_preload_libraries (a restart) and created per database:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_stat_statements;

SELECT calls,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric, 0) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2)  AS mean_ms,
       rows,
       left(query, 80)                     AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;

(Column names are total_exec_time and mean_exec_time from PostgreSQL 13; older servers call them total_time and mean_time.) The statements appear with parameters replaced by $1, $2, grouped by shape, so one slow ORM pattern called a million times surfaces at the top. SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset(); clears the counters before an experiment.

docs.title: Server settings worth knowing
docs.text:
SHOW shared_buffers;
SHOW work_mem;
SHOW max_connections;
SHOW log_min_duration_statement;

Settings live in postgresql.conf and can be changed for the server with ALTER SYSTEM SET name = value; followed by SELECT pg_reload_conf(); (many take effect on reload, a few need a restart; SELECT name, pending_restart FROM pg_settings WHERE pending_restart; shows which). For troubleshooting, three logging settings pay for themselves:

  • log_min_duration_statement = 500 logs every statement slower than 500 ms with its duration.
  • log_lock_waits = on logs when a statement waits longer than deadlock_timeout for a lock, naming the blocker.
  • log_temp_files = 0 logs every query that spilled a sort or hash to disk, the cue to raise work_mem for that query.

Tuning memory and checkpoints for a production server is a topic of its own; start from a tool such as PGTune for the baseline and change one thing at a time. Odoo's own advice: keep max_connections consistent with workers, and give shared_buffers about a quarter of the memory of a dedicated database host.

docs.title: Roles and ownership
docs.text:
\du

                                   List of roles
 Role name |                         Attributes                         | Member of
-----------+------------------------------------------------------------+-----------
 odoo      | Create DB                                                  | {}
 postgres  | Superuser, Create role, Create DB, Replication, Bypass RLS | {}

Odoo's role needs CREATEDB for the database manager (creating, duplicating, restoring databases through the web UI or odoo-bin db), and does not need to be a superuser. Extensions that Odoo wants (unaccent, pg_trgm) need a superuser to create in older PostgreSQL versions; PostgreSQL 13 marks some as trusted so that a database owner may create them. After a restore with --no-owner all objects belong to the restoring role; to move ownership use REASSIGN OWNED BY old_role TO new_role; and ALTER DATABASE mydb OWNER TO odoo;.

docs.title: Cleaning up the lab
docs.text:
When you finish the exercises of this part, remove what you created:

dropdb handbook_lab

dropdb fails if anyone is connected, which in a lab is only your other psql windows. If you want to keep the lab but remove the heavy tables: DROP TABLE loan_log, catalog, book_stock, notify_queue; (each IF EXISTS if unsure).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Running a script without ON_ERROR_STOP. After the first error psql carries on, and the rest of the file runs against a half-applied state. Always -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1, and -1 for data changes.
  • An open BEGIN you forgot. Locks held, vacuum blocked. Show the transaction state in the prompt (%x).
  • AUTOCOMMIT off in .psqlrc. Turns every session into an idle-in-transaction session.
  • Connecting to production by habit. Use distinct service names and prompts, and a read-only default for everything that is not a deliberate change.
  • Password on the command line. Visible in process listings and shell history. Use .pgpass or a service file.
  • Dump without the filestore. The restore opens but attachments and images are missing. Back up both and restore both.
  • Untested backups. A backup is a guess until restored. Restore into a scratch database regularly and open it.
  • Starting a restored copy un-neutralized. It sends production mail and runs production crons. Neutralize before the first start, and keep copies off networks that can reach real integrations.
  • Restoring over a live database. Restore into a new name, check, then switch. pg_restore --clean against the wrong database drops production tables.
  • Version mismatch. pg_dump older than the server refuses; a dump from a newer server does not load into an older one.
  • VACUUM FULL on a live table. An exclusive lock for the duration. Plain VACUUM and autovacuum tuning are the right tools.
  • Skipping ANALYZE after a restore. The planner has no statistics; first queries are slow.
  • Counting connections wrongly. Workers times pool size, across all servers, must stay below max_connections, with room for cron, backup, and your own sessions.
  • pg_terminate_backend as a reflex. It rolls back whatever the session was doing. Look at the session first.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Create a ~/.psqlrc with the settings from this chapter. Open psql, BEGIN;, and notice the prompt. Run a bad statement and notice the prompt again. Roll back.

  2. Take a custom-format dump of handbook_lab, list its contents with pg_restore --list, restore it into handbook_lab_copy with --no-owner, and verify that the row counts of books and loans match in both databases. Drop the copy.

  3. Write a diag.sql with the five queries you would run first when a user says "Odoo is slow": running statements, idle-in-transaction sessions, blockers, connection count, and the largest tables. Run it with psql -f against the lab.

  4. Run a script that deliberately fails halfway, first without and then with -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -1, and compare the state of the database afterwards.

  5. Describe, as a checklist, how you would produce a safe test copy of a production Odoo database from backups, including everything that must happen before the first start.

Solution

  1. With the %x prompt, handbook_lab=# becomes handbook_lab=*# after BEGIN;, and handbook_lab=!# after an error inside the transaction (until ROLLBACK). With ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK interactive the ! does not appear on errors you type interactively, because each statement is wrapped in a savepoint and the transaction survives; unset it temporarily if you want to see the aborted state.

  2. pg_dump -Fc -f lab.dump handbook_lab
pg_restore --list lab.dump | head
createdb handbook_lab_copy
pg_restore -d handbook_lab_copy --no-owner lab.dump
psql -d handbook_lab -At -c "SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM books), (SELECT count(*) FROM loans)"
psql -d handbook_lab_copy -At -c "SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM books), (SELECT count(*) FROM loans)"
dropdb handbook_lab_copy
    The two count lines should be identical, for example 6|7 on a pristine lab.

  3. Put the queries of this chapter and the blocker query from the Locks chapter in the file, separated by \echo '--- title ---' lines so the output is readable, and run psql -d handbook_lab -f diag.sql.

  4. Create broken.sql with three statements, the second invalid (for example UPDATE books SET nosuchcolumn = 1;) and the first and third valid updates. Without the options, the first and third apply and only the second fails. With -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -1 the script stops at the error and the whole transaction rolls back: no statement leaves a trace.

  6. Take the dump (custom format) and a filestore archive at the same time.
  7. createdb a new name; pg_restore --no-owner -j N into it; ANALYZE.
  8. Copy the filestore under the new database name.
  9. Neutralize before starting: odoo-bin neutralize -d newname, or manually deactivate crons, mail servers, payment providers, webhooks; change web.base.url.
  10. Start Odoo against it on a different port with a configuration that has no outgoing mail, then log in and check a few records and an attachment.
  11. Never put the copy on a network path where it can reach live integrations.

docs.title: Relational basics
docs.text: Odoo keeps every record in PostgreSQL, and sooner or later you will need to look at the rows themselves: to see what a script really wrote, to find out why a constraint fired, or to repair data the ORM cannot reach. This chapter gives you the vocabulary (table, row, key, constraint, type, sequence), a lab database you can break freely, and the habits that keep a relational schema honest. Every later chapter in this part runs against the lab schema defined here.

docs.title: The model in five sentences
docs.text:
A database holds tables. A table has a fixed list of named, typed columns and any number of rows. Each row is one record; each column holds one value per row. Rows have no inherent order, and a table is a set in spirit: if you need an order you ask for it. Tables refer to each other by storing the key of the row they point at.

That last sentence is the whole "relational" idea. A loan does not contain a copy of the book; it contains the book's id. Change the title once, and every loan sees it. The cost is that you need a join to read the title next to the loan (chapter Joins), and the benefit is that there is exactly one place where each fact lives.

Odoo's ORM is a translation layer over this model. A model is a table, a record is a row, a field is a column, a Many2one is a stored key. When the ORM misbehaves, the table is the ground truth.

docs.title: A lab database
docs.text:
Install PostgreSQL 14 or newer locally (Odoo 16 to 18 support 12 and up; 14+ is a safe baseline for this book). Create a scratch database that you never confuse with a real one:

createdb handbook_lab
psql -d handbook_lab

createdb and psql connect through the local socket (Linux/macOS) or TCP on localhost:5432 (Windows) as your operating-system user, unless you pass -h, -p, -U. If your install needs a password, psql -h localhost -U postgres -d handbook_lab will ask for it. When you finish with the book you remove everything with dropdb handbook_lab.

Run the exercises of this part only on a database you created for it. Several examples delete rows and hold locks on purpose. Never point them at a database that belongs to a running system, and never at a customer or production database.

You are in the psql prompt when you see handbook_lab=#. Two things to know right now: every SQL statement ends with a semicolon, and backslash commands (\dt, \d table, \q) are psql's own, not SQL. The full tour of psql is in psql and operations.

docs.title: Column types you will meet
docs.text:
PostgreSQL has dozens of types. These cover almost everything Odoo creates and everything this book uses:

Type Holds Odoo field that produces it integer (int4) whole numbers, about +/- 2.1 billion Integer, Many2one key columns, id bigint (int8) whole numbers, about +/- 9.2e18 rarely; some counters numeric(p,s) exact decimals Monetary; Float with digits (see hint) double precision (float8) binary floating point Float without digits varchar / text strings; no practical length difference Char, Selection (varchar); Text, Html (text) boolean true, false, or NULL Boolean date a calendar day Date timestamp (without time zone) a date and time, no zone attached Datetime (stored as UTC by convention) timestamptz an absolute instant not used by Odoo fields; common in logs bytea raw bytes Binary stored in the database jsonb parsed JSON Json; translated Char/Text/Html fields since Odoo 16

Versions. The jsonb storage for translatable fields arrived in Odoo 16: before that, translations lived in the separate ir_translation table and the column held the source term as plain text. Whether a Float with digits becomes numeric or stays double precision has also changed over time. Do not guess; run \d your_table on your own database and read the column type.

Two rules about types save a lot of grief.

First, money and anything where 0.1 + 0.2 must equal 0.3 belongs in numeric, never in floating point:

SELECT 0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8 AS float_sum,
       0.1::numeric + 0.2::numeric AS numeric_sum;

      float_sum      | numeric_sum
---------------------+-------------
 0.30000000000000004 |         0.3
(1 row)

Second, varchar(n), varchar, and text are stored identically. The length limit is only a check. Odoo's Char fields create an unbounded varchar unless size is set, so do not invent length limits in your own tables for "performance"; there is none.

docs.title: The teaching schema
docs.text:
The library schema has four tables: authors, books, members, loans. A book has at most one author (the key may be empty), a loan ties a member to a book for a period. It is small enough to hold in your head and rich enough to need every kind of join.

Paste this into psql. It is the only setup the rest of the part needs; if you drop and recreate the lab, run it again.

CREATE TABLE authors (
    id         serial PRIMARY KEY,
    name       varchar NOT NULL,
    born_year  integer,
    country    varchar
);

CREATE TABLE books (
    id              serial PRIMARY KEY,
    title           varchar NOT NULL,
    author_id       integer REFERENCES authors (id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
    published_year  integer,
    price           numeric(8,2),
    pages           integer,
    status          varchar NOT NULL DEFAULT 'available',
    CONSTRAINT books_pages_positive CHECK (pages > 0)
);

CREATE TABLE members (
    id         serial PRIMARY KEY,
    name       varchar NOT NULL,
    email      varchar UNIQUE,
    joined_on  date NOT NULL,
    active     boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true
);

CREATE TABLE loans (
    id           serial PRIMARY KEY,
    book_id      integer NOT NULL REFERENCES books (id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    member_id    integer NOT NULL REFERENCES members (id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    loaned_on    date NOT NULL,
    due_on       date NOT NULL,
    returned_on  date
);

INSERT INTO authors (name, born_year, country) VALUES
    ('Ada Marlowe',   1950, 'UK'),
    ('Boris Venn',    1962, 'US'),
    ('Chiara Lund',   1975, 'IT'),
    ('Dmitri Okafor', 1981, NULL);

INSERT INTO books (title, author_id, published_year, price, pages, status) VALUES
    ('Tidewater',       1,    1998, 12.50, 310, 'available'),
    ('Salt Roads',      1,    2004, 15.00, 420, 'available'),
    ('The Long Ledger', 2,    2010,  9.90, 250, 'lost'),
    ('Paper Moons',     2,    2015, 11.00, 180, 'available'),
    ('Quiet Engines',   3,    2019, 18.00, 520, 'available'),
    ('Orphan Volume',   NULL, 2001,  5.00,  90, 'available');

INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined_on, active) VALUES
    ('Nora',  'nora@example.com',  '2023-01-10', true),
    ('Omar',  'omar@example.com',  '2023-03-05', true),
    ('Petra', NULL,                '2024-02-20', true),
    ('Quinn', 'quinn@example.com', '2024-06-01', false);

INSERT INTO loans (book_id, member_id, loaned_on, due_on, returned_on) VALUES
    (1, 1, '2024-01-05', '2024-01-19', '2024-01-18'),
    (2, 1, '2024-02-01', '2024-02-15', '2024-02-20'),
    (1, 2, '2024-03-10', '2024-03-24', NULL),
    (5, 2, '2024-03-12', '2024-03-26', '2024-03-25'),
    (4, 3, '2024-04-02', '2024-04-16', NULL),
    (1, 3, '2024-05-01', '2024-05-15', '2024-05-10'),
    (5, 1, '2024-05-20', '2024-06-03', '2024-06-01');

Check that it landed:

SELECT id, title, author_id, price FROM books ORDER BY id;

 id |      title      | author_id | price
----+-----------------+-----------+-------
  1 | Tidewater       |         1 | 12.50
  2 | Salt Roads      |         1 | 15.00
  3 | The Long Ledger |         2 |  9.90
  4 | Paper Moons     |         2 | 11.00
  5 | Quiet Engines   |         3 | 18.00
  6 | Orphan Volume   |           |  5.00
(6 rows)

The empty cell in author_id is NULL. Three properties of this data are deliberate, and later chapters depend on them:

  • Author 4 (Dmitri) wrote no book, so a join from authors to books must decide what to do with him.
  • Book 6 has no author, so a join from books to authors must decide what to do with it.
  • Loans 3 and 5 are not returned yet (returned_on is NULL), and member 4 never borrowed anything.

Real Odoo data has exactly these gaps everywhere: optional many2one fields, unreturned or unposted documents, partners that never bought anything.

docs.title: Primary keys
docs.text:
A primary key is a column (or set of columns) whose value identifies a row uniquely and is never NULL. PostgreSQL enforces it with a unique index. Odoo gives every table an id primary key and nothing else; compound keys do not exist in Odoo models, and uniqueness over several fields is expressed as a separate UNIQUE constraint.

Why a surrogate integer id rather than "the real key" such as an ISBN or an email? Real-world identifiers change, get reused, or turn out to be non-unique. An id the database generates never changes meaning. Keep the natural identifier as an ordinary UNIQUE column.

docs.title: Foreign keys and what happens on delete
docs.text:
A foreign key says "this column must contain the key of an existing row in that table, or be NULL". The database refuses anything else:

INSERT INTO books (title, author_id) VALUES ('Ghost Writer', 99);

ERROR:  insert or update on table "books" violates foreign key constraint "books_author_id_fkey"
DETAIL:  Key (author_id)=(99) is not present in table "authors".

The second half of the contract is what happens when the referenced row is deleted. You pick the behaviour per foreign key:

ON DELETE Effect on the referencing row Typical Odoo use RESTRICT / NO ACTION the delete of the parent fails required many2one without a better idea SET NULL the child's column becomes NULL optional many2one (Odoo's usual default) CASCADE the child row is deleted too lines owned by their header (ondelete='cascade')

books.author_id is SET NULL; loans.book_id is RESTRICT. Try both. First the read-only look at what would be affected:

SELECT id, title, author_id FROM books WHERE author_id = 3;

 id |     title     | author_id
----+---------------+-----------
  5 | Quiet Engines |         3
(1 row)

Now delete the author inside a transaction you will roll back, so the lab data stays intact (transactions are covered properly in Transactions and isolation; for now BEGIN opens one and ROLLBACK throws it away):

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM authors WHERE id = 3;
SELECT id, title, author_id FROM books WHERE id = 5;
ROLLBACK;

DELETE 1
 id |     title     | author_id
----+---------------+-----------
  5 | Quiet Engines |
(1 row)

The book survived and lost its author. Now the same experiment on RESTRICT:

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM books WHERE id = 1;
ROLLBACK;

ERROR:  update or delete on table "books" violates foreign key constraint "loans_book_id_fkey" on table "loans"
DETAIL:  Key (id)=(1) is still referenced from table "loans".

In a failed transaction PostgreSQL refuses further commands until you finish it; the ROLLBACK clears the state. You will meet this in Odoo as InFailedSqlTransaction ("current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block") when code catches an SQL error and carries on without a savepoint. Chapter Transactions and isolation explains the fix.

Versions. In Odoo 16 to 18 a Many2one creates the foreign key with ON DELETE SET NULL unless you pass ondelete=, and Odoo refuses set null on a required field at model setup. Check the actual constraint with \d table rather than trusting memory; modules can and do override it.

docs.title: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK
docs.text:
Three more constraints round out the toolkit. They all fire at the moment of the write, inside the statement.

INSERT INTO books (title, pages) VALUES (NULL, 100);

ERROR:  null value in column "title" of relation "books" violates not-null constraint
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (8, null, null, null, null, 100, available).

INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined_on) VALUES ('Nora II', 'nora@example.com', '2024-07-01');

ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "members_email_key"
DETAIL:  Key (email)=(nora@example.com) already exists.

INSERT INTO books (title, pages) VALUES ('Empty Book', 0);

ERROR:  new row for relation "books" violates check constraint "books_pages_positive"
DETAIL:  Failing row contains (9, Empty Book, null, null, null, 0, available).

Note the ids in the DETAIL lines: 8 and 9. The failed inserts still consumed sequence values (7 went to the foreign-key failure earlier). We come back to that below.

A UNIQUE constraint treats NULLs as distinct. Petra has no email, and so does any number of other members, without violating members_email_key:

INSERT INTO members (name, joined_on) VALUES ('Rhea', '2024-07-02'), ('Sven', '2024-07-03');
SELECT id, name, email FROM members ORDER BY id;

INSERT 0 2
 id | name  |       email
----+-------+-------------------
  1 | Nora  | nora@example.com
  2 | Omar  | omar@example.com
  3 | Petra |
  4 | Quinn | quinn@example.com
  6 | Rhea  |
  7 | Sven  |
(6 rows)

(Rhea is 6 and not 5 because the failed duplicate insert burned value 5 of the members sequence. Your numbers depend on how many failures you triggered; the shape is what matters.) Remove them to keep later results as printed:

SELECT id, name FROM members WHERE id > 4;
DELETE FROM members WHERE id > 4;

On PostgreSQL 15 and newer, UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT flips that behaviour. Odoo's _sql_constraints (up to 18) creates ordinary UNIQUE constraints named <table>_<constraint name>, so they behave like members_email_key above: several NULLs pass.

docs.title: Sequences: where the ids come from
docs.text:
serial is shorthand. id serial PRIMARY KEY expands into: an integer column, a sequence called books_id_seq, a default of nextval('books_id_seq'), and NOT NULL. Odoo creates id SERIAL NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY(id) for every model, and its sequence is <table>_id_seq. You can see all of it:

\d books

                                     Table "public.books"
     Column     |       Type        | Collation | Nullable |              Default
----------------+-------------------+-----------+----------+-----------------------------------
 id             | integer           |           | not null | nextval('books_id_seq'::regclass)
 title          | character varying |           | not null |
 author_id      | integer           |           |          |
 published_year | integer           |           |          |
 price          | numeric(8,2)      |           |          |
 pages          | integer           |           |          |
 status         | character varying |           | not null | 'available'::character varying
Indexes:
    "books_pkey" PRIMARY KEY, btree (id)
Check constraints:
    "books_pages_positive" CHECK (pages > 0)
Foreign-key constraints:
    "books_author_id_fkey" FOREIGN KEY (author_id) REFERENCES authors(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
Referenced by:
    TABLE "loans" CONSTRAINT "loans_book_id_fkey" FOREIGN KEY (book_id) REFERENCES books(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT

Sequences are non-transactional by design. A rolled-back insert does not give its number back, because another session may already have taken the next one. Consequences:

  • Gaps in id are normal and carry no meaning. Never write code that assumes ids are consecutive, and never "fix" a gap.
  • Two sessions inserting concurrently get distinct ids without waiting for each other. That is why sequences scale.

The other end of the same fact is the classic post-restore bug. If you load rows with explicit ids (an INSERT ... (id, ...), a COPY, a data migration), the sequence does not move. The next ordinary insert then collides with an existing row:

SELECT max(id) AS max_id, (SELECT last_value FROM books_id_seq) AS seq_last FROM books;

If seq_last is lower than max_id, you are one insert away from duplicate key value violates unique constraint "books_pkey". The repair, after you have looked at the numbers above:

SELECT setval('books_id_seq', (SELECT max(id) FROM books));

pg_dump and a restore handle this for you; hand-rolled imports do not.

PostgreSQL 10 added the standard GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY column. It behaves the same for our purposes and is what you would choose in a new non-Odoo schema. Odoo still creates serial, so this book does too.

docs.title: Why tables get split: a short normalization story
docs.text:
Suppose you wanted to avoid the authors table and stored the author's name and country directly in each book row:

 id |     title     | author_name | author_country
----+---------------+-------------+----------------
  1 | Tidewater     | Ada Marlowe | UK
  2 | Salt Roads    | Ada Marlowe | UK

Now Ada moving country means updating every one of her books, and forgetting one leaves the data contradicting itself. A book whose author is spelled "Ada Marlow" is a different author as far as any GROUP BY is concerned. Splitting the author into its own table and pointing at it by key removes the whole class of contradiction: one fact, one row.

The rule of thumb: a column should depend on the key of its own row and nothing else. If a column's value is determined by another column in the same row (country by author), it belongs in the table that column is the key of.

The same logic explains many-to-many relations. A book can have several authors and an author several books; a single author_id column cannot express that. You create a third table whose rows are pairs:

CREATE TABLE book_author_rel (
    book_id    integer NOT NULL REFERENCES books (id)   ON DELETE CASCADE,
    author_id  integer NOT NULL REFERENCES authors (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    PRIMARY KEY (book_id, author_id)
);

Odoo's Many2many creates exactly this: a relation table with two integer columns, two cascading foreign keys, a unique index over the pair, and one extra index. The Odoo schema covers the naming rules. The table above is only to show the pattern; you will not need it for the exercises, and you can drop it (DROP TABLE book_author_rel;).

The opposite mistake exists too: splitting without reason. Odoo accepts denormalized, stored computed fields (store=True) on purpose, trading the contradiction risk for read speed, and keeps them in sync through the ORM. When you edit such a column with raw SQL you take on the job of the recompute. More on that in INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and in the ORM part.

docs.title: Looking around: the catalog
docs.text:
PostgreSQL describes itself in ordinary tables you can query. You will use these all the time against Odoo databases:

SELECT table_name, column_name, data_type, is_nullable
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND table_name = 'loans'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;

 table_name | column_name | data_type         | is_nullable
------------+-------------+-------------------+-------------
 loans      | id          | integer           | NO
 loans      | book_id     | integer           | NO
 loans      | member_id   | integer           | NO
 loans      | loaned_on   | date              | NO
 loans      | due_on      | date              | NO
 loans      | returned_on | date              | YES
(6 rows)

And the list of tables with an estimate of their row counts:

SELECT relname AS table_name, reltuples::bigint AS approx_rows
FROM pg_class
WHERE relkind = 'r' AND relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace
ORDER BY relname;

 table_name | approx_rows
------------+-------------
 authors    |          -1
 books      |          -1
 loans      |          -1
 members    |          -1
(4 rows)

-1 (PostgreSQL 14 and later) means "never analyzed yet"; after ANALYZE or autovacuum, it holds the estimate. reltuples is an estimate, never an exact count. For an exact number use SELECT count(*) FROM ..., which on a large table is a full scan.

docs.title: Schemas and databases
docs.text: A PostgreSQL server hosts several databases; a connection belongs to exactly one, and you cannot query across them. Inside a database, tables live in schemas, and public is the default. The search_path setting decides which schema an unqualified name like books resolves in. Odoo uses a single schema and one database per Odoo "database" (the thing you pick on the login screen). When a script says "the database", it means this: one connection, one Odoo instance's worth of tables, with no schema prefixes needed.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Treating row order as stable. SELECT * FROM books without ORDER BY often returns insertion order today and something else after an UPDATE or a vacuum. Odoo's _order always adds an ORDER BY; in raw SQL you must too.
  • Float for money. double precision sums drift. If a computed total is off by 0.000000001, look at the column type first.
  • Counting on gapless ids. Rollbacks, failed inserts, and concurrent sessions leave holes. Use a dedicated ir.sequence (Odoo) or a locking scheme if you need gapless numbering, and expect it to serialize writers.
  • Setting ids by hand and forgetting the sequence. After any import with explicit ids, compare max(id) with the sequence's last_value.
  • Assuming a unique constraint blocks duplicate NULLs. It does not (before PostgreSQL 15's NULLS NOT DISTINCT, and not by default after). A "unique code" field with several empty values is legal.
  • Relying on ON DELETE CASCADE you did not read. A cascade from res.partner can remove far more than you expect. Read \d table and the "Referenced by" list before any delete.
  • Mixing up the failed-transaction state. After an SQL error inside a transaction every later statement fails with "current transaction is aborted". The cure is ROLLBACK or a SAVEPOINT, never "just try again".
  • Case-sensitive names by accident. CREATE TABLE "Books" with quotes makes a table you must always quote. Odoo's names are lowercase with underscores; keep yours the same.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Work in handbook_lab with the schema above loaded. Wrap anything that changes data in BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK; unless told otherwise.

  1. List every column of members with its type and whether it accepts NULL, using information_schema.columns. Which column has a default, and what is it?

  2. Make the sequence trap happen on purpose: insert a book with an explicit id of 100, then insert one without an id, and read the ids. Then insert one more explicit id equal to the sequence's next value and observe the error. (Do it in a transaction you roll back; note that the sequence itself does not roll back.)

  3. Find out which tables reference members, and with what ON DELETE rule, using only \d members and then using the catalog view information_schema.referential_constraints together with information_schema.table_constraints.

  4. Add a constraint so that loans.due_on can never be earlier than loans.loaned_on. First check that no existing row would violate it. Then add it, and show the error you get for an invalid insert.

  5. A member can only have one open (unreturned) loan of the same book at a time. Express this as a database rule, without adding any column.

Solution 

  1. SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable, column_default
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND table_name = 'members'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;
    id has nextval('members_id_seq'::regclass) and active has true. email, name and joined_on have no default.

  2. BEGIN;
INSERT INTO books (id, title) VALUES (100, 'Hand-numbered');
INSERT INTO books (title) VALUES ('Sequence-numbered') RETURNING id;
    The second insert returns the next sequence value (7 or higher in a lab that has seen failures), not 101: the explicit id 100 did not move the sequence. To force the collision, still inside the transaction: 
    SELECT setval('books_id_seq', 99);
INSERT INTO books (title) VALUES ('Collision');
ROLLBACK;
    The INSERT takes id 100 from the sequence and fails with duplicate key value violates unique constraint "books_pkey". The setval is not undone by ROLLBACK, since sequences are non-transactional, so repair it with SELECT setval('books_id_seq', (SELECT max(id) FROM books));.

  3. \d members ends with "Referenced by: TABLE "loans" CONSTRAINT "loans_member_id_fkey" FOREIGN KEY (member_id) REFERENCES members(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT". With the catalog: 

    SELECT tc.table_name, tc.constraint_name, rc.delete_rule
FROM information_schema.referential_constraints rc
JOIN information_schema.table_constraints tc
  ON tc.constraint_name = rc.constraint_name AND tc.constraint_schema = rc.constraint_schema
JOIN information_schema.table_constraints ref
  ON ref.constraint_name = rc.unique_constraint_name AND ref.constraint_schema = rc.unique_constraint_schema
WHERE ref.table_name = 'members';
    Result: loans | loans_member_id_fkey | RESTRICT.

  4. SELECT id FROM loans WHERE due_on < loaned_on;   -- expect 0 rows
ALTER TABLE loans ADD CONSTRAINT loans_due_after_loan CHECK (due_on >= loaned_on);
INSERT INTO loans (book_id, member_id, loaned_on, due_on) VALUES (3, 1, '2024-07-10', '2024-07-01');
    The insert fails with new row for relation "loans" violates check constraint "loans_due_after_loan". If the SELECT had returned rows, ADD CONSTRAINT would fail on them; you would fix the data first, or add the constraint NOT VALID and validate later.

  5. A partial unique index: 

    CREATE UNIQUE INDEX loans_one_open_per_member_book
    ON loans (book_id, member_id) WHERE returned_on IS NULL;
    Rows with returned_on filled are outside the index, so history is unrestricted. Chapter Indexes and EXPLAIN covers partial indexes. (Drop it afterwards if you want the lab data to behave as printed in later chapters: DROP INDEX loans_one_open_per_member_book;.)

docs.title: SELECT, FROM, WHERE
docs.text: Most of your SQL as an Odoo developer is SELECT: finding out what is really in a table, counting the records a domain would match, checking which rows a bug touched. This chapter covers a single-table SELECT thoroughly, including the three-valued logic of NULL that causes more wrong results than any other feature, and ends with subqueries and common table expressions. Joins across tables come next. The queries use the library schema from Relational basics; load it first.

docs.title: Anatomy and evaluation order
docs.text:
SELECT   title, price
FROM     books
WHERE    status = 'available'
ORDER BY price DESC
LIMIT    3;

     title     | price
---------------+-------
 Quiet Engines | 18.00
 Salt Roads    | 15.00
 Tidewater     | 12.50
(3 rows)

You write SELECT first, but the database thinks in a different order, and knowing it explains most "why can't I use this alias here" errors:

  1. FROM picks the source rows (and joins, next chapter).
  2. WHERE throws away rows that do not match.
  3. GROUP BY collapses rows into groups; aggregates are computed.
  4. HAVING throws away groups.
  5. SELECT computes the output expressions.
  6. DISTINCT removes duplicate output rows.
  7. ORDER BY sorts.
  8. LIMIT / OFFSET cut the result.

Consequence: a column alias defined in SELECT does not exist yet in WHERE, but it does in ORDER BY:

SELECT title, price * 2 AS double_price FROM books WHERE double_price > 20;

ERROR:  column "double_price" does not exist
LINE 1: SELECT title, price * 2 AS double_price FROM books WHERE dou...

Repeat the expression in WHERE, or wrap the query (a subquery or a CTE, below).

docs.title: Choosing columns
docs.text:
SELECT * returns every column and is fine in psql while exploring. In code it is a liability: a new column changes your result shape, and on tables with bytea or large text columns (Odoo's ir_attachment with db_datas, mail_message bodies) it pulls megabytes you did not want. Name your columns.

Expressions and aliases:

SELECT title,
       price,
       pages,
       round(price / pages * 100, 2) AS price_per_100_pages
FROM books
ORDER BY id;

      title      | price | pages | price_per_100_pages
-----------------+-------+-------+---------------------
 Tidewater       | 12.50 |   310 |                4.03
 Salt Roads      | 15.00 |   420 |                3.57
 The Long Ledger |  9.90 |   250 |                3.96
 Paper Moons     | 11.00 |   180 |                6.11
 Quiet Engines   | 18.00 |   520 |                3.46
 Orphan Volume   |  5.00 |    90 |                5.56
(6 rows)

Beware of integer division: pages / 100 between two integers truncates (310 / 100 is 3). Cast one side (pages / 100.0 or pages::numeric / 100). The :: cast operator is PostgreSQL's shorthand for CAST(x AS type); you will see both in Odoo code.

A SELECT without FROM is legal and useful as a calculator:

SELECT 7 / 2 AS int_div, 7 / 2.0 AS dec_div, 7 % 2 AS remainder;

 int_div |      dec_div       | remainder
---------+--------------------+-----------
       3 | 3.5000000000000000 |         1
(1 row)

docs.title: WHERE: comparing and combining
docs.text:
Comparison operators are =, <> (also !=), <, <=, >, >=. Note the single = for equality. Beyond those:

-- range, inclusive on both ends
SELECT title, price FROM books WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 15 ORDER BY price;

    title    | price
-------------+-------
 Paper Moons | 11.00
 Tidewater   | 12.50
 Salt Roads  | 15.00
(3 rows)

-- membership
SELECT title FROM books WHERE author_id IN (1, 3) ORDER BY title;

     title
---------------
 Quiet Engines
 Salt Roads
 Tidewater
(3 rows)

IN (...) is shorthand for a chain of OR. The array form author_id = ANY(ARRAY[1,3]) is equivalent and is how drivers pass a Python list as one parameter; Odoo's cr.execute("... WHERE id = ANY(%s)", [ids]) uses it.

docs.title: AND, OR, NOT and precedence
docs.text:
AND binds tighter than OR. Without parentheses the next query does not mean what it appears to:

SELECT title, published_year, price FROM books
WHERE status = 'available' AND published_year < 2005 OR price > 17
ORDER BY id;

     title     | published_year | price
---------------+----------------+-------
 Tidewater     |           1998 | 12.50
 Salt Roads    |           2004 | 15.00
 Quiet Engines |           2019 | 18.00
 Orphan Volume |           2001 |  5.00
(4 rows)

It parses as (available AND old) OR expensive. It happens to produce the same rows as the parenthesized variant on this data, which is exactly how this bug survives code review. Parenthesize every mixed AND/OR; Odoo domains do the same with their prefix notation, and the SQL it generates is always fully parenthesized.

docs.title: Pattern matching
docs.text:
SELECT name FROM members WHERE email LIKE '%@example.com' ORDER BY id;

 name
-------
 Nora
 Omar
 Quinn
(3 rows)

% matches any run of characters, _ exactly one. LIKE is case sensitive; ILIKE ignores case. Odoo's ilike operator compiles to ILIKE (and, where a field opts in and the unaccent extension is installed, wraps both sides in unaccent()). A pattern with a leading % cannot use an ordinary btree index (see Indexes and EXPLAIN). Escape a literal % or _ with a backslash. PostgreSQL also has regular expression operators: ~ (match), ~* (case-insensitive), !~.

SELECT title FROM books WHERE title ~ '^[A-Q]' ORDER BY title;

     title
---------------
 Orphan Volume
 Paper Moons
 Quiet Engines
(3 rows)

docs.title: NULL: the value that is not a value
docs.text:
NULL means "unknown" or "absent", not zero or empty string. Every comparison with NULL yields neither true nor false but NULL, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true. This is three-valued logic, and it is the source of a family of bugs.

SELECT title FROM books WHERE author_id = NULL;

 title
-------
(0 rows)

author_id = NULL is NULL for every row, so nothing matches, including the book that has a NULL author. The correct test:

SELECT title FROM books WHERE author_id IS NULL;

     title
---------------
 Orphan Volume
(1 row)

The second trap: <> also drops NULL rows.

SELECT title FROM books WHERE author_id <> 1 ORDER BY id;

      title
-----------------
 The Long Ledger
 Paper Moons
 Quiet Engines
(3 rows)

"Not by author 1" intuitively includes Orphan Volume; SQL leaves it out, because NULL <> 1 is NULL. If you want the intuitive meaning, use IS DISTINCT FROM, which treats NULL as an ordinary comparable value:

SELECT title FROM books WHERE author_id IS DISTINCT FROM 1 ORDER BY id;

      title
-----------------
 The Long Ledger
 Paper Moons
 Quiet Engines
 Orphan Volume
(4 rows)

When you translate an Odoo domain like [('author_id', '!=', 1)], the ORM adds the NULL handling for you (it generates author_id IS NULL OR author_id != 1). Written by hand, that is your job.

The logic tables, because they explain what you see:

a b a AND b a OR b true NULL NULL true false NULL false NULL NULL NULL NULL NULL

and NOT NULL is NULL.

docs.title: The NOT IN trap
docs.text:
x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) means x <> 1 AND x <> 2 AND x <> NULL. The last term is NULL for every x, so the whole expression is never true:

SELECT title FROM books WHERE author_id NOT IN (1, NULL);

 title
-------
(0 rows)

This bites when the list comes from a subquery whose column can be NULL. Here the subquery excludes NULLs naturally, so it works:

SELECT title FROM books
WHERE author_id NOT IN (SELECT author_id FROM books WHERE status = 'lost')
ORDER BY id;

     title
---------------
 Tidewater
 Salt Roads
 Quiet Engines
(3 rows)

Put a book with an unknown author in the lost set, and the inner query returns a NULL: now the outer query returns nothing, silently. Prefer NOT EXISTS, which has no such surprise (shown below), or add WHERE author_id IS NOT NULL inside the subquery.

docs.title: COALESCE and NULLIF
docs.text:
COALESCE(a, b, ...) returns the first non-NULL argument; NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL if the two are equal, else a.

SELECT name, COALESCE(email, '(none)') AS email FROM members ORDER BY id;

 name  |       email
-------+-------------------
 Nora  | nora@example.com
 Omar  | omar@example.com
 Petra | (none)
 Quinn | quinn@example.com
(4 rows)

NULLIF is the standard defence against division by zero: total / NULLIF(count, 0) yields NULL instead of an error. Odoo stores unset Char, Date, and many2one fields as NULL, not as empty string or zero; a boolean that was never written is NULL too (not false) on rows created before the column existed, which matters for WHERE NOT active. Write COALESCE(active, false) when you read such columns, or compare with IS NOT TRUE.

Aggregates ignore NULL, which we use in the next chapters, and NULL || 'text' is NULL (use concat() or COALESCE to build strings from nullable parts).

docs.title: Sorting and paging
docs.text:
SELECT title, author_id FROM books ORDER BY author_id, title;

      title      | author_id
-----------------+-----------
 Salt Roads      |         1
 Tidewater       |         1
 Paper Moons     |         2
 The Long Ledger |         2
 Quiet Engines   |         3
 Orphan Volume   |
(6 rows)

In PostgreSQL, NULL sorts as larger than any value: last in ascending order, first in descending. Control it explicitly with NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST:

SELECT title, author_id FROM books ORDER BY author_id DESC NULLS LAST, title LIMIT 3;

      title      | author_id
-----------------+-----------
 Quiet Engines   |         3
 Paper Moons     |         2
 The Long Ledger |         2
(3 rows)

ORDER BY can use column numbers (ORDER BY 2) and expressions, and accepts a different direction per key. Sorting strings follows the database's collation: with a en_US.UTF-8 collation, 'a' < 'B', with C collation, uppercase sorts before lowercase. Odoo databases are created with whatever the cluster default is (often en_US.UTF-8, sometimes C), so the same query can sort differently on two servers.

docs.title: LIMIT, OFFSET, and keyset paging
docs.text:
SELECT id, title FROM books ORDER BY id LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2;

 id |     title
----+-----------------
  3 | The Long Ledger
  4 | Paper Moons
(2 rows)

OFFSET n still reads and discards the first n rows, so page 5000 of a long list is slow, and if rows are inserted between page requests you see duplicates or gaps. For stable deep paging remember where you stopped and seek from there:

SELECT id, title FROM books WHERE id > 3 ORDER BY id LIMIT 2;

 id |    title
----+---------------
  4 | Paper Moons
  5 | Quiet Engines
(2 rows)

With a unique, indexed sort key this reads only the rows it returns. Always combine LIMIT with ORDER BY: without it you get "some" rows, and not necessarily the same ones next time. Odoo's search_read with limit/offset and its default _order = 'id' has the same trade-offs; batch jobs that walk a large table should page by id.

docs.title: DISTINCT and DISTINCT ON
docs.text:
SELECT DISTINCT status FROM books;

  status
-----------
 available
 lost
(2 rows)

(Row order is not guaranteed without ORDER BY.) DISTINCT compares whole output rows and treats NULLs as equal to each other.

DISTINCT ON (expr) is a PostgreSQL extension that keeps the first row for each value of expr, "first" decided by ORDER BY. It answers "latest row per group" in one clause:

SELECT DISTINCT ON (member_id) member_id, book_id, loaned_on
FROM loans
ORDER BY member_id, loaned_on DESC;

 member_id | book_id | loaned_on
-----------+---------+------------
         1 |       5 | 2024-05-20
         2 |       5 | 2024-03-12
         3 |       1 | 2024-05-01
(3 rows)

The ORDER BY must start with the DISTINCT ON expression(s), or PostgreSQL refuses the query. Window functions give the same result more flexibly (next-but-one chapter).

docs.title: Dates and times
docs.text:
Dates are first-class types with arithmetic. Subtracting two date values gives an integer number of days; adding an integer to a date adds days:

SELECT id, returned_on - due_on AS days_late
FROM loans
WHERE returned_on > due_on;

 id | days_late
----+-----------
  2 |         5
(1 row)

SELECT id, due_on, due_on + 7 AS extended_to, loaned_on + interval '1 month' AS plus_month
FROM loans WHERE id <= 2;

 id |   due_on   | extended_to |      plus_month
----+------------+-------------+---------------------
  1 | 2024-01-19 | 2024-01-26  | 2024-02-05 00:00:00
  2 | 2024-02-15 | 2024-02-22  | 2024-03-01 00:00:00
(2 rows)

Adding an interval turns a date into a timestamp. Truncate or extract to bucket:

SELECT id,
       date_trunc('month', loaned_on) AS month_start,
       extract(year FROM loaned_on)   AS yr,
       to_char(loaned_on, 'YYYY-MM')  AS ym
FROM loans WHERE id <= 3 ORDER BY id;

 id |     month_start     | yr   |   ym
----+---------------------+------+---------
  1 | 2024-01-01 00:00:00 | 2024 | 2024-01
  2 | 2024-02-01 00:00:00 | 2024 | 2024-02
  3 | 2024-03-01 00:00:00 | 2024 | 2024-03
(3 rows)

current_date and now() give today and the transaction start time. Note that now() is frozen for the whole transaction: it does not advance while the transaction runs. clock_timestamp() returns the real current time. Odoo's own create_date and write_date are set from the ORM's Python clock (fields.Datetime.now()) in most cases, not from now(), and the column is timestamp without time zone holding UTC. When you compare it to a local date, convert explicitly:

SELECT now() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AS utc_now;

timestamp AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' on a plain timestamp reinterprets it as UTC and returns a timestamptz; timestamptz AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' returns a plain timestamp. The direction flips depending on the input type, and almost everyone gets it wrong once. To convert an Odoo UTC datetime to a local wall-clock time in a given zone:

SELECT create_date AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Rome' FROM some_odoo_table LIMIT 1;

The first AT TIME ZONE makes the stored value a proper UTC instant, the second renders it in the target zone. (some_odoo_table is a placeholder; the lab schema has no timestamp column.)

docs.title: Ranges: use half-open intervals
docs.text:
To select "everything in March" on a timestamp column, BETWEEN '2024-03-01' AND '2024-03-31' silently excludes anything after midnight on the 31st. Use a half-open range:

SELECT id, loaned_on FROM loans
WHERE loaned_on >= '2024-03-01' AND loaned_on < '2024-04-01'
ORDER BY id;

 id | loaned_on
----+------------
  3 | 2024-03-10
  4 | 2024-03-12
(2 rows)
