The same pattern is correct for dates and timestamps, and composes with adjacent ranges without gaps or overlaps. It is also what you want when the end boundary is the start of the next period.

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
SELECT title, upper(title) AS up, length(title) AS len, substring(title FROM 1 FOR 4) AS first4,
       position('o' IN title) AS pos_o
FROM books WHERE id <= 2 ORDER BY id;

   title    |     up     | len | first4 | pos_o
------------+------------+-----+--------+-------
 Tidewater  | TIDEWATER  |   9 | Tide   |     0
 Salt Roads | SALT ROADS |  10 | Salt   |     7
(2 rows)

Other tools you will use: lower, trim, replace, split_part(str, ',', 2), left/right, lpad, regexp_replace, string_agg (an aggregate, later), and format('%s (%s)', title, published_year) for building text. || concatenates but returns NULL when either side is NULL; concat(a, b) skips NULLs.

SELECT 'a' || NULL AS with_pipes, concat('a', NULL, 'b') AS with_concat;

 with_pipes | with_concat
------------+-------------
            | ab
(1 row)

docs.title: CASE
docs.text:
CASE is the expression form of if/else, usable anywhere an expression is:

SELECT title,
       CASE WHEN pages < 200 THEN 'short'
            WHEN pages < 400 THEN 'medium'
            ELSE 'long' END AS length
FROM books ORDER BY id;

      title      | length
-----------------+--------
 Tidewater       | medium
 Salt Roads      | long
 The Long Ledger | medium
 Paper Moons     | short
 Quiet Engines   | long
 Orphan Volume   | short
(6 rows)

Branches are tried in order; without ELSE, no match yields NULL.

docs.title: Subqueries
docs.text:
A scalar subquery returns one value and can sit wherever a value can:

SELECT title, price FROM books
WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM books)
ORDER BY id;

     title     | price
---------------+-------
 Tidewater     | 12.50
 Salt Roads    | 15.00
 Quiet Engines | 18.00
(3 rows)

(The average is 11.90.) If a scalar subquery returns more than one row, PostgreSQL raises more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression.

EXISTS asks "is there at least one matching row", and is the safe way to express "has none":

SELECT name FROM authors a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM books b WHERE b.author_id = a.id);

     name
---------------
 Dmitri Okafor
(1 row)

The inner query refers to the outer row a; that is a correlated subquery. What it selects is irrelevant (SELECT 1 by convention). NOT EXISTS stops at the first match and, unlike NOT IN, is not fooled by NULLs.

docs.title: Common table expressions
docs.text:
A WITH clause names an intermediate result, so you can read the query top to bottom:

WITH late AS (
    SELECT id, book_id, member_id
    FROM loans
    WHERE returned_on > due_on
)
SELECT late.id AS loan_id, b.title
FROM late
JOIN books b ON b.id = late.book_id;

 loan_id |   title
---------+------------
       2 | Salt Roads
(1 row)

(The JOIN is the subject of the next chapter.) Since PostgreSQL 12, a non-recursive CTE that is referenced once and has no side effects is inlined into the outer query, as if you had written a subquery, so it costs nothing and the planner optimizes across it. Before 12 every CTE was an optimization fence, materialized once. You can force either behaviour with WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (...) or AS NOT MATERIALIZED (...). Odoo 16 to 18 require PostgreSQL 12 or newer, so the inlining is the norm.

WITH RECURSIVE walks hierarchies; Odoo's parent_path mostly spares you from it, but res_company/res_partner trees and category trees are classic uses. A minimal one counting 1 to 3:

WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (
    SELECT 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 3
)
SELECT i FROM n;

 i
---
 1
 2
 3
(3 rows)

docs.title: Arrays and jsonb, briefly
docs.text:
Odoo uses two compound types you will hit when reading data. Arrays appear as parameters (= ANY(%s)). jsonb is where translated field values live from Odoo 16 on: one key per language.

SELECT '{"en_US": "Tidewater", "fr_FR": "Maree"}'::jsonb ->> 'en_US' AS en,
       '{"en_US": "Tidewater"}'::jsonb ->> 'de_DE'                     AS missing;

    en     | missing
-----------+---------
 Tidewater |
(1 row)

-> returns jsonb, ->> returns text; a missing key yields NULL. So SELECT name->>'en_US' FROM product_template is how you read a product name, and a translated field with no entry for your language is NULL, not the English fallback (the ORM adds the fallback in Python). Chapter The Odoo schema returns to this.

docs.title: Reading production data safely
docs.text:
For the first look at any database you do not own, make the session incapable of writing:

psql "dbname=handbook_lab options='-c default_transaction_read_only=on -c statement_timeout=30000'"

Or inside a session:

SET default_transaction_read_only = on;
SET statement_timeout = '30s';

statement_timeout ends runaway queries (a join missing its ON condition returns millions of rows). Add LIMIT to exploratory queries on big tables, and prefer count(*) or EXPLAIN first to see how large the answer will be.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• = NULL and <> value with NULLs. Both silently drop NULL rows. Use IS NULL, IS NOT NULL, IS DISTINCT FROM.
  • NOT IN against a subquery that can return NULL. One NULL empties the result. Use NOT EXISTS.
  • Unparenthesized AND/OR. The result looks right on your sample and is wrong on the full table.
  • Integer division. count / total between integers is 0 for any fraction below one. Cast to numeric.
  • BETWEEN on timestamps. Excludes the last day's time of day. Use >= start AND < next_start.
  • LIMIT without ORDER BY. You get arbitrary rows, and the set changes between runs and after an UPDATE.
  • Deep OFFSET. Page 10,000 reads 10,000 pages of rows to throw them away. Page by key.
  • SELECT * on big tables. Binary and HTML columns make a harmless-looking query move gigabytes.
  • Time zones. Odoo's datetime columns are UTC without a zone marker. A report grouped with date_trunc('day', create_date) groups UTC days, so evening records in a positive-offset zone land on the next day. Convert before you truncate.
  • Case and accents. = is exact. Names in Odoo come in any capitalization; use ILIKE or lower() and expect no index help.
  • Sort order differences across servers. Collation decides string order; do not write tests that depend on it unless you set it.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Use the library schema.

  1. List the titles of books that are not lost and cost more than 10 but at most 15, cheapest first.

  2. List members whose email is missing or whose account is inactive. Return name and a column reason that says no email or inactive, with no email taking priority if both apply.

  3. For every loan, show the loan id, the number of days it was kept (returned minus loaned, or NULL if not returned) and a column state that reads open, late or on time. A loan is late if it was returned after its due date.

  4. Return the three most recently published books after skipping the newest one, with OFFSET. Then explain what goes wrong if a book is inserted between two page requests, and how keyset paging avoids it.

  5. Find the authors who have at least one book that is lost, using EXISTS, and then write the same with IN. Predict what each returns if you add a lost book with no author.

Solution 

  1. SELECT title, price FROM books
WHERE status <> 'lost' AND price > 10 AND price <= 15
ORDER BY price;

        title    | price
-------------+-------
 Paper Moons | 11.00
 Tidewater   | 12.50
 Salt Roads  | 15.00
(3 rows)
    status is NOT NULL, so <> is safe here.

  2. SELECT name,
       CASE WHEN email IS NULL THEN 'no email' ELSE 'inactive' END AS reason
FROM members
WHERE email IS NULL OR NOT active
ORDER BY id;

     name  |  reason
-------+----------
 Petra | no email
 Quinn | inactive
(2 rows)


  3. SELECT id,
       returned_on - loaned_on AS days_kept,
       CASE WHEN returned_on IS NULL THEN 'open'
            WHEN returned_on > due_on THEN 'late'
            ELSE 'on time' END AS state
FROM loans ORDER BY id;

     id | days_kept |  state
----+-----------+---------
  1 |        13 | on time
  2 |        19 | late
  3 |           | open
  4 |        13 | on time
  5 |           | open
  6 |         9 | on time
  7 |        12 | on time
(7 rows)


  4. SELECT id, title, published_year FROM books
ORDER BY published_year DESC, id LIMIT 3 OFFSET 1;

     id |      title      | published_year
----+-----------------+----------------
  4 | Paper Moons     |           2015
  3 | The Long Ledger |           2010
  2 | Salt Roads      |           2004
(3 rows)
    If a newer book is inserted after you fetched the first page, the next OFFSET window shifts by one row and you see a row twice (or, after a delete, skip one). Keyset: remember (published_year, id) of the last row and ask for WHERE (published_year, id) > (...) in the appropriate direction. Tie-break on id so the order is total.

  5. SELECT a.name FROM authors a
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM books b WHERE b.author_id = a.id AND b.status = 'lost');

SELECT a.name FROM authors a
WHERE a.id IN (SELECT author_id FROM books WHERE status = 'lost');
    Both return Boris Venn. A lost book without an author adds a NULL to the inner list of the IN version, which still matches correctly (IN only needs one true), so both keep returning the same row. The problem would appear with NOT IN: a.id NOT IN (SELECT author_id ...) would return no rows at all once that NULL is in the list, while NOT EXISTS keeps working.

docs.title: The Odoo schema
docs.text:
Odoo never asks you to write CREATE TABLE. You declare a model in Python, and at install or update time the framework creates and alters tables to match. The mapping is regular enough to learn once: a model name gives a table name, a field type gives a column type, a Many2many gives a relation table, and a small set of ir_* tables record what the framework did and why. Knowing the rules lets you go from a Python class to the SQL (and back), find the rows behind a screen, and write a correct diagnostic query without opening the source. This chapter states the rules for Odoo 16 to 18, flags the points that differ by version, and finishes with a toolbox of discovery queries.

The teaching module library is used throughout: models library.book, library.author, library.loan, library.tag. The standard tables mentioned (res_partner, ir_model, ...) are the same in every Odoo database.

Everything here describes behaviour of the Odoo 16, 17, and 18 series. Where a detail changed between them it is marked, and where it is stated without a marker it holds for all three. Whenever the exact column type or constraint matters to you, confirm it on your own database with \d table_name (the discovery habit this chapter teaches) rather than trusting a book.

docs.title: From model name to table name
docs.text:
The table name is the model's _name with dots replaced by underscores:

Model Table res.partner res_partner sale.order.line sale_order_line library.book library_book library.loan library_loan

A model can override this with _table = 'my_table', and a few standard models do. For a model you do not know, ask the registry instead of guessing (query below).

Not every model has a table:

  • Regular models (models.Model) get a table.
  • Transient models (models.TransientModel, used for wizards) get a table too. Odoo vacuums old rows from it periodically, so rows are short-lived.
  • Abstract models (models.AbstractModel, mixins like mail.thread) have no table. Their fields are copied into the concrete models that inherit them.
  • Models with _auto = False have no automatically created table. Reports commonly define one as a database view in init() (CREATE VIEW sale_report AS ...). They are listed by \dv, not \dt.

docs.title: The columns every table has
docs.text:
Each regular model table starts with an id primary key and four audit columns:

Column Type Meaning id integer, from <table>_id_seq (serial) primary key create_uid integer, foreign key to res_users(id), ON DELETE SET NULL user who created the row create_date timestamp without time zone creation time, UTC write_uid integer, foreign key to res_users(id), ON DELETE SET NULL user of the last write write_date timestamp without time zone time of the last write, UTC

The audit columns exist because _log_access defaults to true; a model that sets _log_access = False (typical of high-volume technical tables, such as ir_attachment-like or log tables, and of _auto = False views) has none. Because create_uid and write_uid point at res_users, deleting a user is allowed even though their ids appear everywhere: the audit columns become NULL.

Other columns that appear by convention, not by rule: active (boolean, makes the ORM hide rows with false), name, sequence, company_id, parent_id and parent_path (when _parent_store = True, a varchar like 1/5/12/ that makes subtree queries a prefix match), and state (selection stored as its key). They are ordinary fields; they just recur.

docs.title: Field type to column type
docs.text:
Field Column type Notes Integer int4 Float float8 (double precision) with digits, may be numeric; see hint Monetary numeric no digits limit in the column Char varchar size=n adds a limit: varchar(n) Text, Html text Boolean bool may be NULL on rows from before the field existed Date date Datetime timestamp (without time zone) stored as UTC Selection varchar holds the key, e.g. 'available'; no check constraint Binary bytea, or no column default attachment=True stores the file in ir_attachment and the field has no column Image like Binary Json jsonb Many2one int4 plus a foreign key column name equals the field name, e.g. author_id Reference varchar text 'model,id', no foreign key Many2oneReference int4 an id into a model named by another field; no foreign key One2many no column the column is on the other model (the inverse_name) Many2many no column on either table a separate relation table (below) computed, not stored no column computed in Python on read computed with store=True, related with store=True a normal column maintained by the ORM; stale if you write SQL Properties jsonb free-form properties (Odoo 17 and later)

A column exists only for stored fields. When a field is "missing" from the table, check whether it is computed without store, a One2many, a Many2many, or an attachment-backed binary.

Versions. Whether Float(digits=...) creates a numeric or a float8 column has varied; use \d on the real table. Translated Char/Text/Html fields (translate=True) are jsonb from Odoo 16, holding one entry per language code ({"en_US": "Tidewater", "fr_FR": "..."}); in Odoo 15 and earlier they are plain varchar/text and translations sit in ir_translation. Company-dependent fields (company_dependent=True) are stored in ir_property rows up to Odoo 17; from Odoo 18 they are, to my knowledge, a jsonb column on the model's own table keyed by company id (confirm in the release notes). In all versions reading them with SQL needs care.

docs.title: Many2one: the foreign key column
docs.text:
author_id = fields.Many2one('library.author') creates author_id integer and a foreign key library_book_author_id_fkey referencing library_author(id). The ondelete argument sets the foreign-key action:

ondelete= Foreign key action (not given) SET NULL for an optional field; RESTRICT for a required one (Odoo refuses set null on a required field) 'set null' ON DELETE SET NULL 'restrict' ON DELETE RESTRICT 'cascade' ON DELETE CASCADE (lines that cannot live without their header)

index=True adds a B-tree index library_book_author_id_index. Without it, there is no index on the foreign key column, so joins from library_author to its books and deletes of an author need a scan of library_book. The index habits of Indexes and EXPLAIN apply.

A One2many has no column. loan_ids = fields.One2many('library.loan', 'book_id') is a view of the book_id many2one on library_loan. To read it in SQL you query library_loan WHERE book_id = ....

docs.title: Many2many: the relation table
docs.text:
tag_ids = fields.Many2many('library.tag') on library.book creates a table named from the two table names sorted alphabetically, joined, with _rel appended:

library_book_library_tag_rel

The two columns are named <table>_id for each side: library_book_id and library_tag_id. Both are integer NOT NULL, with foreign keys ON DELETE CASCADE to their parents, a unique constraint over the pair, and an index on the second column (so lookups from either side are indexed). Each row is one link; there is no id, no audit column, and so no way to know who linked what or when.

You can override any of the three names in the field definition:

tag_ids = fields.Many2many('library.tag', relation='library_book_tag_rel',
                           column1='book_id', column2='tag_id')

Standard Odoo does this all the time, so the alphabetical rule describes the default, not every table. For example res.users and res.groups are linked by res_groups_users_rel with columns gid and uid. Never assume; ask the registry (query below).

PostgreSQL limits identifiers to 63 bytes, and Odoo refuses to create a relation table whose name would exceed it. For long model names the symptom is an error at module load telling you to pass relation= explicitly.

Reading a many2many in SQL is the join from Joins:

SELECT b.id, b.name->>'en_US' AS book, t.name->>'en_US' AS tag
FROM library_book b
JOIN library_book_library_tag_rel r ON r.library_book_id = b.id
JOIN library_tag t                  ON t.id = r.library_tag_id
ORDER BY b.id, t.id;

(That assumes translated name fields on both models; for a non-translated Char write b.name.)

docs.title: A worked example: Python to DDL
docs.text:
class LibraryBook(models.Model):
    _name = 'library.book'
    _description = 'Book'

    name = fields.Char(required=True, translate=True)
    isbn = fields.Char(size=13)
    state = fields.Selection([('available', 'Available'), ('lost', 'Lost')],
                             default='available', required=True)
    active = fields.Boolean(default=True)
    weight = fields.Float()
    author_id = fields.Many2one('library.author', ondelete='set null', index=True)
    tag_ids = fields.Many2many('library.tag')
    loan_ids = fields.One2many('library.loan', 'book_id')
    loan_count = fields.Integer(compute='_compute_loan_count', store=True)

    _sql_constraints = [
        ('isbn_unique', 'unique(isbn)', 'The ISBN must be unique.'),
    ]

After installing the module, \d library_book shows (abridged, with details that vary by release):

                                          Table "public.library_book"
    Column    |            Type             | Nullable |                 Default
--------------+-----------------------------+----------+------------------------------------------
 id           | integer                     | not null | nextval('library_book_id_seq'::regclass)
 create_uid   | integer                     |          |
 create_date  | timestamp without time zone |          |
 write_uid    | integer                     |          |
 write_date   | timestamp without time zone |          |
 name         | jsonb                       | not null |
 isbn         | character varying(13)       |          |
 state        | character varying           | not null |
 active       | boolean                     |          |
 weight       | double precision            |          |
 author_id    | integer                     |          |
 loan_count   | integer                     |          |
Indexes:
    "library_book_pkey" PRIMARY KEY, btree (id)
    "library_book_author_id_index" btree (author_id)
    "library_book_isbn_unique" UNIQUE CONSTRAINT, btree (isbn)
Foreign-key constraints:
    "library_book_author_id_fkey" FOREIGN KEY (author_id) REFERENCES library_author(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
    "library_book_create_uid_fkey" FOREIGN KEY (create_uid) REFERENCES res_users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
    "library_book_write_uid_fkey" FOREIGN KEY (write_uid) REFERENCES res_users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
Referenced by:
    TABLE "library_book_library_tag_rel" CONSTRAINT "library_book_library_tag_rel_library_book_id_fkey" ...
    TABLE "library_loan" CONSTRAINT "library_loan_book_id_fkey" ...

Note what is not in the table: tag_ids (a relation table) and loan_ids (a column on library_loan). Note also the constraint name: _sql_constraints entries become <table>_<constraint name>, here library_book_isbn_unique. That name is what appears in the error text, which is how you map a raw database error back to the declaration: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "library_book_isbn_unique".

Odoo also writes a comment on each column with the field's label and on the table with the model's _description. These come out in the descriptive form of \d:

\d+ library_book
SELECT col_description('library_book'::regclass, attnum) AS label, attname
FROM pg_attribute
WHERE attrelid = 'library_book'::regclass AND attnum > 0 AND NOT attisdropped
ORDER BY attnum;

The labels give the screen name for each column, which helps when you meet an unfamiliar table.

Versions. Up to Odoo 18, _sql_constraints is the mechanism. Later versions replace it with constraint objects declared on the class; the database objects and their naming stay close, but check the release notes of the version you work on.

docs.title: Inheritance and the table
docs.text:
How a model extends another decides what happens in the database.

  • Extension in place (_inherit = 'res.partner' without a new _name): the new fields become columns on the same table res_partner. This is how modules add fields to standard models, and why res_partner grows wide.
  • Prototype inheritance (_name = 'x.y' with _inherit = 'a.b'): a new model with its own new table, copying a's fields.
  • Delegation (_inherits = {'res.partner': 'partner_id'}): the child has its own table with a required many2one to the parent table, and reads and writes of the inherited fields transparently go to the parent row. res_users is the standard example: a user row has a partner_id, and the user's name, email, and image live in res_partner.
  • Mixins (abstract): no table of their own. mail.thread adds no column to your table; its data lives in mail_message, mail_followers, and friends, tied to your records by model and res_id.

Custom fields created through the UI or Studio are model fields too: their names start with x_ and their rows in ir_model_fields have state = 'manual', and they produce columns like any other stored field. They are not part of any module's Python, which is why they are easy to lose when a database is copied without the right database dump of the metadata tables.

docs.title: Odoo's own metadata tables
docs.text: The ir_* tables are Odoo's catalogue about itself. These are the ones a developer reads.

docs.title: ir_model and ir_model_fields
docs.text:
ir_model lists every model; ir_model_fields lists every field, including those with no column:

SELECT m.model, m.name->>'en_US' AS label, m.transient
FROM ir_model m
WHERE m.model LIKE 'library.%'
ORDER BY m.model;

      model      |  label  | transient
-----------------+---------+-----------
 library.author  | Author  | f
 library.book    | Book    | f
 library.loan    | Loan    | f
 library.tag     | Tag     | f
(4 rows)

(name is jsonb from Odoo 16; in 15 and earlier read it as plain text.) The table behind a model:

SELECT model, replace(model, '.', '_') AS expected_table
FROM ir_model WHERE model = 'library.book';

replace(model, '.', '_') is right unless the model sets _table; confirm with \dt library_book.

List the fields of a model, stored or not:

SELECT name, ttype, relation, store, required, index, compute IS NOT NULL AS computed
FROM ir_model_fields
WHERE model = 'library.book'
ORDER BY name;

     name     |   ttype   |    relation    | store | required | index | computed
--------------+-----------+----------------+-------+----------+-------+----------
 active       | boolean   |                | t     | f        | f     | f
 author_id    | many2one  | library.author | t     | f        | t     | f
 create_date  | datetime  |                | t     | f        | f     | f
 create_uid   | many2one  | res.users      | t     | f        | f     | f
 display_name | char      |                | f     | f        | f     | t
 id           | integer   |                | t     | f        | f     | f
 isbn         | char      |                | t     | f        | f     | f
 loan_count   | integer   |                | t     | f        | f     | t
 loan_ids     | one2many  | library.loan   | f     | f        | f     | f
 name         | char      |                | t     | t        | f     | f
 state        | selection |                | t     | t        | f     | f
 tag_ids      | many2many | library.tag    | f     | f        | f     | f
 weight       | float     |                | t     | f        | f     | f
 write_date   | datetime  |                | t     | f        | f     | f
 write_uid    | many2one  | res.users      | t     | f        | f     | f
(15 rows)

The inherited technical field display_name is listed too, with no column. Some releases also list __last_update (non-stored). Fields you did not declare, such as message_ids, appear as soon as the model inherits a mixin.

store = f fields have no column. For a many2many the same table records the relation table and its two column names, so you never need to infer them:

SELECT name, relation, relation_table, column1, column2
FROM ir_model_fields
WHERE model = 'res.users' AND ttype = 'many2many';

Selection values live in ir_model_fields_selection (columns field_id, value, name, sequence), one row per option.

docs.title: ir_model_data: XML IDs
docs.text:
Every record created from a data file, and many created in code, has a row in ir_model_data that maps a stable name to a database id:

Column Meaning module the module that owns the record, e.g. base name the local part of the XML ID model the model of the record, e.g. res.groups res_id the record's id in that model's table noupdate if true, module updates do not overwrite this record's data

The full XML ID is module.name. Resolve one in either direction:

-- XML ID to record id
SELECT model, res_id FROM ir_model_data WHERE module = 'base' AND name = 'group_user';

-- record to XML ID(s)
SELECT module || '.' || name AS xml_id, noupdate
FROM ir_model_data
WHERE model = 'res.groups' AND res_id = 1;

This is how you find the row behind env.ref('base.group_user') without a shell. It is also the first place to look when a "record was deleted" error appears at module update: an ir_model_data row exists, but its target is gone (a raw DELETE somewhere), and the update stops with a missing-reference error.

docs.title: ir_ui_view and the others
docs.text:
Table Content Useful columns ir_ui_view every view name, model, type, arch_db (the XML), inherit_id, mode (primary or extension), key, priority, active ir_act_window window actions name, res_model, view_mode, domain, context ir_ui_menu the menu tree name, parent_id, action (a reference string ir.actions.act_window,<id>), sequence ir_attachment files name, res_model, res_id, res_field, type, store_fname, file_size, mimetype, db_datas ir_config_parameter system parameters key, value ir_cron scheduled actions cron_name (or the linked action), active, interval_number, interval_type, nextcall ir_module_module installed modules name, state, latest_version ir_model_access ACL rows model_id, group_id, perm_read, perm_write, perm_create, perm_unlink ir_rule record rules model_id, domain_force, global, groups ir_sequence numbering sequences code, prefix, padding, number_next

A view's XML is in arch_db, which is how you see what a view really looks like after all inheritance is stored (but not applied; the combined view is built at load). Find the extensions of a view:

SELECT v.id, v.name, v.mode, v.priority
FROM ir_ui_view v
WHERE v.inherit_id = (SELECT id FROM ir_ui_view WHERE key = 'library.view_book_form')
ORDER BY v.priority, v.id;

(Use a real view key from your database; keys are module.xmlid.) Installed modules and their states:

SELECT name, state, latest_version
FROM ir_module_module
WHERE state IN ('installed', 'to upgrade', 'to install', 'to remove')
ORDER BY name;

Module state takes the values uninstalled, installed, to install, to upgrade, to remove, and uninstallable. A module stuck in to upgrade after an interrupted update is a common reason an instance refuses to start cleanly.

Be careful with attachment files: ir_attachment.db_datas holds file contents when ir.attachment.location is db; otherwise store_fname names a file on disk (the filestore) and the column is NULL. Select without db_datas unless you want megabytes.

docs.title: The core business tables
docs.text:
You will read these constantly. The names are stable across 16 to 18:

Table Notes res_partner every contact, company, and address. parent_id links a contact to its company; is_company; type (contact, invoice, delivery, ...); active; company_id optional res_users one row per login (login, active, partner_id, company_id, share). The person's name, email, and image are on the linked res_partner row. Never select the password column res_company companies, linked to a partner_id; parent_id for hierarchies res_groups security groups. Memberships in res_groups_users_rel (gid, uid); implied groups in another relation table res_country, res_currency, res_lang reference data. res_currency_rate has the exchange rates mail_message chatter messages and logged notes: model, res_id, body, message_type, author_id, date mail_followers followers: res_model, res_id, partner_id product_template, product_product product and its variants; the variant has product_tmpl_id account_move, account_move_line invoices, bills, journal entries and their lines (all in one table pair, told apart by move_type) sale_order, sale_order_line, purchase_order, stock_picking, stock_move, stock_quant the usual document tables

Two modelling patterns explain many joins:

  • Generic references from mail_message, ir_attachment, and mail_followers use a pair of columns: the model name as a string, and the id as an integer, with no foreign key. "All messages of this partner" is WHERE model = 'res.partner' AND res_id = 42. Such rows are not removed by database cascades; the ORM deletes them when the owning record is unlinked, so a raw delete of the owner leaves orphans.
  • The header/line pattern: a *_line table has a many2one to its header (order_id, move_id, picking_id), usually ondelete='cascade', and the money totals on the header are stored computed fields maintained from the lines.

docs.title: Discovery queries
docs.text:
Keep these in a snippet file. They answer the first questions about any Odoo database.

Row counts of the largest tables (estimates, instant):

SELECT relname, reltuples::bigint AS approx_rows,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(oid)) AS total_size
FROM pg_class
WHERE relkind = 'r' AND relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(oid) DESC
LIMIT 15;

On a database that has run for years, ir_attachment (when stored in the database), mail_message, mail_tracking_value, bus_bus, and accounting lines typically lead the list.

Which tables reference res_partner (and with what delete rule), the reason a contact cannot be deleted:

SELECT conrelid::regclass AS referencing_table,
       a.attname           AS column,
       CASE confdeltype WHEN 'a' THEN 'NO ACTION' WHEN 'r' THEN 'RESTRICT'
                        WHEN 'c' THEN 'CASCADE'  WHEN 'n' THEN 'SET NULL'
                        WHEN 'd' THEN 'SET DEFAULT' END AS on_delete
FROM pg_constraint c
JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = c.conrelid AND a.attnum = c.conkey[1]
WHERE c.contype = 'f' AND c.confrelid = 'res_partner'::regclass
ORDER BY 1, 2;

Columns that exist in the table but not in the registry, a sign of removed fields (Odoo does not drop the column when a field disappears; it only drops the NOT NULL):

SELECT c.column_name
FROM information_schema.columns c
WHERE c.table_name = 'library_book'
  AND c.column_name NOT IN (SELECT name FROM ir_model_fields WHERE model = 'library.book' AND store)
ORDER BY 1;

Which module defines a model. ir_model_data rows for the model's model_* xml ids name the owners:

SELECT module, name FROM ir_model_data WHERE model = 'ir.model' AND res_id = (SELECT id FROM ir_model WHERE model = 'library.book');

A record's chatter. Messages of a record:

SELECT id, date, message_type, left(regexp_replace(body, '<[^>]+>', '', 'g'), 80) AS text
FROM mail_message
WHERE model = 'library.book' AND res_id = 1
ORDER BY date DESC
LIMIT 5;

The regexp_replace strips HTML tags so the body is readable in a terminal.

Which cron jobs will run next:

SELECT id, active, nextcall, interval_number, interval_type
FROM ir_cron
ORDER BY nextcall
LIMIT 10;

The ir_cron columns that name the job and its code differ between versions (the job's name is on the linked ir_act_server row in recent releases), so join accordingly or \d ir_cron first.

The company of a record, the stored translation of a term, the properties of a record: all of these follow the same recipe: find the model in ir_model, list its fields in ir_model_fields, then query the table.

docs.title: Reading translated and JSON values
docs.text:
In Odoo 16 and later a translated field is a JSON object:

SELECT id, name, name->>'en_US' AS en, name->>'fr_FR' AS fr
FROM library_book
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 3;

 id |                   name                    |     en     |       fr
----+-------------------------------------------+------------+-----------------
  1 | {"en_US": "Tidewater"}                    | Tidewater  |
  2 | {"en_US": "Salt Roads", "fr_FR": "Routes de sel"} | Salt Roads | Routes de sel

A missing language key gives NULL, not a fallback to English; the ORM applies the fallback in Python. When you filter with ILIKE against a translated field in SQL, filter on the key: name->>'en_US' ILIKE '%road%'. And when you update, use jsonb_set to change one language without erasing the others (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Assuming model.name is table_name. It is, until a model sets _table. Check ir_model and \dt.
  • Looking for a column that does not exist. One2many, Many2many, non-stored computed fields, and attachment-backed binaries have none. Query ir_model_fields for store.
  • Guessing relation-table names. Standard modules override them. Read relation_table, column1, and column2 from ir_model_fields.
  • Writing a stored computed or related field in SQL and not its dependants. The ORM will not recompute. Update both, or recompute in the shell.
  • Treating jsonb names as text. On 16+, WHERE name = 'x' compares to a JSON value. Use name->>'en_US'.
  • Selecting binary columns by accident. SELECT * on ir_attachment or res_partner (image fields in attachments) can transfer huge data. Name your columns.
  • Raw deletes leaving orphans. No foreign key protects mail_message, ir_attachment, or ir_model_data rows that reference a deleted record by model name and id.
  • Believing active means deleted. Archived rows are still there; a count that ignores active includes them. Odoo's UI count excludes them.
  • Joining res_users to res_partner incorrectly. A user's display name is the partner's name. res_users has no name column of its own.
  • Reading local time out of UTC columns. create_date and write_date are UTC. Convert deliberately.
  • Unique error names read as noise. A constraint named library_book_isbn_unique tells you the module, the model, and the declaration; search the code for the suffix.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Use any Odoo database you may read (a throwaway development database, or a restored copy; never a live production system), or reason from the library_book example if you have none.

  1. Find the table and the stored columns of the model res.partner using ir_model and ir_model_fields (your database must be Odoo 16 or later to see jsonb labels; otherwise drop the ->>). Which of its relational fields have no column?

  2. For res.users, find every many2many field, with its relation table and the two column names. Then write the SQL join listing user logins and their group names for one user.

  3. Resolve the XML ID base.user_root (or base.main_company) to a record id and a table, then fetch the row from that table.

  4. Write a query that lists, for the model library.book, the foreign keys declared on its table, using pg_constraint, and compare with the many2one rows of ir_model_fields. Which foreign keys have no counterpart among the fields, and why?

  5. Given the error duplicate key value violates unique constraint "library_loan_book_member_uniq", work out the table, the likely _sql_constraints name, and the columns involved, using only the catalog.

Solution 

  1. SELECT name, ttype, relation, store
FROM ir_model_fields
WHERE model = 'res.partner'
ORDER BY store DESC, name;
    The model's table is res_partner. Fields with store = f and ttype of one2many or many2many (for example child_ids, category_id, user_ids) have no column on res_partner, and non-stored computed fields (many) have none either. The remaining stored fields are the columns of \d res_partner.

  2. SELECT name, relation, relation_table, column1, column2
FROM ir_model_fields
WHERE model = 'res.users' AND ttype = 'many2many';
    For the groups, groups_id points at res.groups with relation table res_groups_users_rel and columns uid, gid. The join: 
    SELECT u.login, g.name->>'en_US' AS grp
FROM res_users u
JOIN res_groups_users_rel r ON r.uid = u.id
JOIN res_groups g           ON g.id = r.gid
WHERE u.login = 'someone'
ORDER BY 2;
    On Odoo 16 and later res_groups.name is jsonb; in earlier versions use g.name.

  3. SELECT model, res_id FROM ir_model_data WHERE module = 'base' AND name = 'user_root';
    The result names res.users and an id. The table is res_users: SELECT id, login, partner_id FROM res_users WHERE id = <res_id>;.

  4. SELECT conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid)
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE conrelid = 'library_book'::regclass AND contype = 'f';

SELECT name, relation FROM ir_model_fields
WHERE model = 'library.book' AND ttype = 'many2one' AND store;
    Both lists contain author_id, create_uid, and write_uid: every stored many2one has one foreign key, named <table>_<column>_fkey. The foreign keys that are not many2one fields live on other tables: the relation table library_book_library_tag_rel carries two (to library_book and library_tag), and library_loan carries one pointing at library_book. They appear under "Referenced by" in \d library_book, not in its own constraint list.

  5. SELECT conrelid::regclass AS table_name, conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid)
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE conname = 'library_loan_book_member_uniq';
    The result gives the table library_loan and a definition such as UNIQUE (book_id, member_id). The Odoo name is the part after library_loan_: the _sql_constraints entry called book_member_uniq in the library.loan model.

docs.title: Transactions and isolation
docs.text: Every Odoo request, cron run, and shell session works inside a database transaction, and every strange concurrency bug in Odoo is, underneath, a question about what a transaction can see and when it fails. "Could not serialize access due to concurrent update", a record that is invisible although another user just saved it, a stock quantity that went negative, a total that lost an update: all of them are explained by the material in this chapter. It covers atomicity and savepoints, MVCC, the three isolation levels PostgreSQL offers, the anomalies each allows (demonstrated with two sessions), and how Odoo's default level shapes the code you write. It builds on the library schema from Relational basics.

docs.title: Transactions: all or nothing
docs.text:
A transaction groups statements so that they take effect together or not at all. Without BEGIN, psql runs each statement as its own transaction (autocommit). With it:

BEGIN;
UPDATE books SET status = 'lost' WHERE id = 2;
UPDATE books SET status = 'lost' WHERE id = 99999;   -- matches nothing, no error
SELECT id, status FROM books WHERE id = 2;
ROLLBACK;

BEGIN
UPDATE 1
UPDATE 0
 id | status
----+--------
  2 | lost
(1 row)

ROLLBACK

Inside the transaction you see your own change. After ROLLBACK, it is as if it never happened. COMMIT makes it permanent and visible to others. The four properties, "ACID":

  • Atomicity: all statements apply or none do.
  • Consistency: constraints hold at commit (an update violating a CHECK fails and aborts).
  • Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work; how strongly is a setting (below).
  • Durability: after COMMIT returns, the data survives a crash (it is in the write-ahead log on disk).

DDL is transactional in PostgreSQL too: ALTER TABLE, CREATE INDEX (not the concurrent kind), DROP TABLE can be rolled back. That makes schema migrations safer here than on most databases. Sequences are the exception (a nextval never rolls back), which is why ids have gaps.

docs.title: Aborted transactions
docs.text:
When a statement inside a transaction raises an error, the transaction enters the aborted state. Everything after is refused until you end it:

BEGIN;
SELECT 1 / 0;
SELECT 1;

ERROR:  division by zero
ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block

The only way out is ROLLBACK (a COMMIT of an aborted transaction is silently turned into a rollback). In Odoo this shows up as psycopg2.errors.InFailedSqlTransaction, almost always because Python code caught the first exception, swallowed it, and continued using the same cursor.

docs.title: Savepoints: a partial rollback
docs.text:
A savepoint marks a point inside a transaction that you can roll back to without abandoning the whole transaction:

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined_on) VALUES ('Tess', 'tess@example.com', '2024-07-01');

SAVEPOINT before_risky;
INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined_on) VALUES ('Dup', 'tess@example.com', '2024-07-01');

ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "members_email_key"

ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_risky;
SELECT name FROM members WHERE email = 'tess@example.com';
COMMIT;

  name
--------
 Tess
(1 row)

Tess survived and the duplicate attempt vanished, and the transaction is usable again. Odoo wraps this in with self.env.cr.savepoint():. Use it around any code that may legitimately fail on a database error (an unlink that may be blocked by a foreign key, a create that may hit a unique constraint) and that you intend to survive:

# fragment: inside an Odoo method
for vals in vals_list:
    try:
        with self.env.cr.savepoint():
            self.env['library.book'].create(vals)
    except Exception:
        _logger.exception("skipping %s", vals)

Without the savepoint the first failure poisons the transaction and every later create fails with InFailedSqlTransaction. Savepoints are cheap, but not free: tens of thousands of them in one transaction slow it down (each one is a subtransaction), so do not wrap each of a million records.

(Remove the lab row afterwards: DELETE FROM members WHERE email = 'tess@example.com';.)

docs.title: MVCC: why readers do not block writers
docs.text:
PostgreSQL keeps multiple versions of each row. An UPDATE does not overwrite: it writes a new version and marks the old one as ended by your transaction. Each row version records the id of the transaction that created it (xmin) and the one that deleted or replaced it (xmax); you can look:

SELECT xmin, xmax, id, price FROM books WHERE id = 1;

 xmin | xmax | id | price
------+------+----+-------
  742 |    0 |  1 | 12.50
(1 row)

(Your numbers differ.) A query reads through a snapshot: a description of which transactions had committed at a certain moment. For each row version the query asks "was its creator committed in my snapshot, and was its deleter not?", and uses only versions that satisfy that. The consequences:

  • Readers never wait for writers, and writers never wait for readers. A long report does not block order entry.
  • Two writers to the same row do conflict, and one has to wait or fail (the locks chapter).
  • Old row versions pile up until VACUUM removes the ones nobody can see. A transaction that stays open forever keeps its snapshot, and nothing newer than it can be cleaned up.

The isolation level decides when a snapshot is taken: per statement or per transaction.

docs.title: The isolation levels
docs.text: PostgreSQL implements three levels (a fourth, READ UNCOMMITTED, behaves as READ COMMITTED). Check the current one with SHOW transaction_isolation;.

docs.title: READ COMMITTED (the PostgreSQL default)
docs.text:
Each statement takes a fresh snapshot, so a transaction sees data committed by others between its statements. Two sessions, A and B, on a lab row, with time flowing downward:

Session A                                     Session B
BEGIN;
SELECT price FROM books WHERE id = 1;
  -> 12.50
                                              UPDATE books SET price = 13.00 WHERE id = 1;
                                              (autocommit: committed)
SELECT price FROM books WHERE id = 1;
  -> 13.00     (the same query, a different answer)
COMMIT;

This is a non-repeatable read: within one transaction the same query returned different results. For a report that runs several queries it means the numbers may not add up to each other. Restore the price (UPDATE books SET price = 12.50 WHERE id = 1;) before going on.

docs.title: REPEATABLE READ (what Odoo uses)
docs.text:
The snapshot is taken at the first statement of the transaction and kept until the end. The transaction sees a frozen view of the database, plus its own changes:

Session A                                     Session B
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT price FROM books WHERE id = 1;
  -> 12.50
                                              UPDATE books SET price = 13.00 WHERE id = 1;
                                              (committed)
SELECT price FROM books WHERE id = 1;
  -> 12.50     (still the old value)
UPDATE books SET price = price + 1 WHERE id = 1;
  -> ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update
ROLLBACK;

The two points to understand:

  1. The snapshot is taken at the first query, not at BEGIN. A BEGIN followed by idle time sees data as of the first SELECT.
  2. If A tries to modify a row that another transaction changed and committed after A's snapshot, PostgreSQL cannot apply A's change on top of a version A never saw, so it aborts A with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure). The correct reaction is to roll back and run the whole transaction again from the start, where the new snapshot sees the new row.

PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ is stronger than the SQL standard requires: it also prevents phantom reads (rows appearing in a repeated range query), because the snapshot is a complete view.

Odoo sets its connections to REPEATABLE READ. Hence:

  • A request sees a consistent view of the database as of its first query. A record that another worker committed while your request ran stays invisible to it. A scheduled action that loops for twenty minutes without committing works on twenty-minute-old data.
  • Writing to a row that someone else has modified since your snapshot fails with a serialization error instead of silently overwriting. That is safer than READ COMMITTED, and it makes retries a core part of the framework.
  • A cr.commit() ends the transaction; the next statement begins a new one with a fresh snapshot. That is the legitimate reason to commit in a long batch, and the reason it breaks atomicity (below).

docs.title: SERIALIZABLE
docs.text:
The strictest: the outcome is as if the transactions had run one at a time in some order. PostgreSQL implements it (SSI) by tracking read and write dependencies and aborting a transaction when it would produce a result no serial order could. Anything that goes wrong becomes a 40001, so applications must retry. Odoo does not use it, but it is the level that stops write skew (next section). You choose it per transaction: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;.

Anomaly READ COMMITTED REPEATABLE READ SERIALIZABLE Dirty read (see uncommitted data) no no no Non-repeatable read possible no no Phantom read possible no (in PostgreSQL) no Lost update possible prevented by failure prevented by failure Write skew possible possible prevented by failure

docs.title: Lost updates
docs.text:
The most common real-life concurrency bug is "read, compute in the application, write back". Set up a stock table:

CREATE TABLE book_stock (
    book_id  integer PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES books (id),
    copies   integer NOT NULL CHECK (copies >= 0)
);
INSERT INTO book_stock VALUES (1, 3);

Two clerks each check out a copy at the same moment. Application code reads copies, subtracts one, and writes the result. In READ COMMITTED:

Session A                                     Session B
BEGIN;                                        BEGIN;
SELECT copies FROM book_stock WHERE book_id=1;
  -> 3
                                              SELECT copies FROM book_stock WHERE book_id=1;
                                                -> 3
UPDATE book_stock SET copies = 2 WHERE book_id=1;
COMMIT;
                                              UPDATE book_stock SET copies = 2 WHERE book_id=1;
                                              COMMIT;

Two copies went out, and the stock fell from 3 to 2 instead of 1. Neither session errored. This is a lost update. There are three standard cures, in increasing strength:

1. A single atomic statement. Let the database do the arithmetic:

UPDATE book_stock SET copies = copies - 1 WHERE book_id = 1 AND copies > 0;

In READ COMMITTED, B's update waits for A's lock, and when A commits B re-evaluates the WHERE and the expression on the new row version: copies = 2 - 1 = 1. The row-count tag (UPDATE 1 or UPDATE 0) tells the application whether a copy was available. No read step exists to go stale.

2. Lock the row when you read it:

BEGIN;
SELECT copies FROM book_stock WHERE book_id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
-- compute in the application
UPDATE book_stock SET copies = 1 WHERE book_id = 1;
COMMIT;

FOR UPDATE makes B's SELECT wait until A finishes, then return the new value. See Locks.

3. Rely on REPEATABLE READ to fail loudly. Under Odoo's level, B's UPDATE fails with could not serialize access due to concurrent update, and the request is retried from scratch against fresh data. The lost update becomes a retry. This is the safety net under every ORM write(), but it only works if the retry actually re-reads the data. An application that catches the error and re-applies the same stale computation defeats it.

docs.title: Write skew: the anomaly REPEATABLE READ allows
docs.text:
Two transactions read overlapping data, each makes a decision, and each writes a different row. No row is updated twice, so there is no conflict, yet the combination violates a rule neither checked alone. Rule: at least one member must stay active.

Session A                                     Session B
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;        BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT count(*) FROM members WHERE active;    SELECT count(*) FROM members WHERE active;
  -> 3                                          -> 3
UPDATE members SET active = false WHERE id=1; UPDATE members SET active = false WHERE id=2;
COMMIT;                                       COMMIT;

Both transactions saw "3 active, deactivating one leaves 2" and both committed; no database constraint tells them about each other. (The lab has three active members: Nora, Omar, Petra; extend the scenario to all three and the end result is none.) Under REPEATABLE READ both commit. Under SERIALIZABLE one COMMIT fails:

ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
DETAIL:  Reason code: Canceled on identification as a pivot, during commit attempt.
HINT:  The transaction might succeed if retried.

Odoo runs REPEATABLE READ, so such invariants are your problem. Typical examples: "only one default record per company", "stock must not go below zero across several lines", "this sequence number must be unique". The remedies:

  • Express the rule as a database constraint (UNIQUE, a partial unique index, CHECK) so that the database enforces it regardless of isolation. The losing transaction fails with a unique violation. Note that Odoo does not retry unique violations automatically, since a duplicate is usually a real error; the caller sees an error and decides.
  • Take a lock on a shared parent row (SELECT ... FROM res_company WHERE id = ... FOR UPDATE) at the start of the check-then-act sequence, so concurrent attempts queue. Cheap and effective for low-contention rules.
  • Use pg_advisory_xact_lock(key) as a named mutex (see Locks).

docs.title: How Odoo uses transactions
docs.text:
A few facts about the framework, all of which follow from the above:

One transaction per request. An HTTP request or RPC call gets a cursor; at the end of the request Odoo commits, or rolls back if an exception escapes. All ORM writes in the request, including those done by overridden methods and by mail automations, are one atomic unit.

Retries on concurrency errors. When a request fails with a serialization failure, a deadlock, or a lock that could not be acquired, the RPC layer rolls back and runs the request again, a small number of times (five in the versions this book targets; look for PG_CONCURRENCY_ERRORS_TO_RETRY and MAX_TRIES_ON_CONCURRENCY_FAILURE in odoo/service/model.py). This is why a rare "could not serialize" error is normally invisible to users, and why you will see it in logs as a WARNING or INFO line followed by a successful completion.

Retrying a request means running your controller or method again from scratch. Everything must therefore be safe to repeat: no side effect outside the database (an email sent, a payment API called, a file written) may happen before the commit unless it is idempotent. The retry logic only works while the request body can be replayed, which is another reason to keep side effects at the very end or in a post-commit hook (cr.postcommit.add(...), available in recent versions; check yours).

Never catch database errors blindly.

# fragment: the bug
try:
    self.env['library.loan'].create(vals)
except Exception:
    pass          # the cursor is now unusable; the next statement raises InFailedSqlTransaction

Either let the error propagate, or wrap the risky call in with self.env.cr.savepoint():. And never swallow psycopg2.errors.SerializationFailure or DeadlockDetected: catching them stops the framework from retrying, and turns a harmless collision into lost work.

cr.commit() in your code is rarely right. It ends the transaction, makes everything so far permanent, and means that an error later leaves half the work done. It is legitimate in long cron jobs that process thousands of independent records, committing after each batch so progress survives a failure and locks are released. It is wrong in the middle of a business flow that must be atomic. Also remember: after a commit() the ORM cache may hold records from the old snapshot; Odoo invalidates what it knows about, but your own SQL results do not refresh themselves.

Reading your own raw SQL writes. If you cr.execute("UPDATE ...") and then browse().field for a record already in the cache, you may read the stale cached value. Call self.env.invalidate_all() (or the recordset's invalidate_recordset) after raw writes. Details in the ORM part under Cache and prefetch and Raw SQL from the ORM.

Autocommit cursors. A few operations run outside a transaction (creating or dropping a database, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, VACUUM), because PostgreSQL refuses them inside one. Odoo does these through a cursor in autocommit mode (cr._cnx.autocommit = True). If you must run such a statement from a script, open a plain psycopg2 connection with autocommit = True.

Versions. The retry policy and its helper function have been reorganized between Odoo releases (the retry decorator moved, the maximum count and wait differ, and newer versions retry also in odoo.http dispatch). Treat the numbers above as "a few attempts" and read your version's service/model.py and http.py before relying on exact behaviour.

docs.title: Long transactions and idle in transaction
docs.text:
A transaction that stays open does damage even if it does nothing:

  • Its snapshot holds back vacuum: dead row versions cannot be removed while any transaction might still need to see them. Tables bloat.
  • It holds every lock it took, so others wait on rows it has modified.
  • A transaction that has not committed prevents some DDL and makes CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY wait.

Find them:

SELECT pid,
       usename,
       state,
       now() - xact_start  AS xact_age,
       now() - state_change AS in_state_for,
       left(query, 60)      AS last_query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY xact_start;

  pid  | usename |        state        |    xact_age     |  in_state_for   |        last_query
-------+---------+---------------------+-----------------+-----------------+--------------------------
 18211 | odoo    | idle in transaction | 02:14:09.331    | 02:14:08.920    | SELECT "res_users"."id" FROM ...
 18390 | odoo    | active              | 00:00:00.041    | 00:00:00.041    | SELECT ...
(2 rows)

idle in transaction for hours means a client (a forgotten psql window, a shell session that did env['x'].create(...) and never committed or exited, a crashed worker connection) is holding a transaction open. Set a safety net on the server or on the role:

ALTER ROLE odoo SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '10min';

That setting terminates sessions idle in a transaction for too long; choose a value that exceeds the slowest legitimate pause (an Odoo worker between statements) with a wide margin, and note that it also kills a developer who thinks at the prompt during a debugging session. Apply it deliberately and tell the team.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Assuming a transaction sees the latest data. Under REPEATABLE READ it sees data as of its first query. Long jobs process stale input; start a new transaction (commit) per batch if freshness matters.
  • Catching an SQL error and continuing. The transaction is aborted; use a savepoint, or let the error propagate.
  • Swallowing serialization failures. They are signals to retry, not bugs to hide.
  • Side effects before commit. Emails, webhooks, and payment calls inside a transaction that may be retried or rolled back leave the world and the database disagreeing. Do them after commit, and make them idempotent.
  • Read-modify-write in Python. Under any level but SERIALIZABLE, stale-read logic can still produce wrong results between rows. Use atomic SQL expressions, FOR UPDATE, or a unique constraint.
  • Relying on application checks for cross-row rules. Two concurrent requests both pass the check. Enforce it in the database or serialize with a lock.
  • cr.commit() mid-flow. Breaks atomicity and leaves partial results after an error; also surprises tests, which run in one transaction.
  • Open transactions in shells. A psql or Odoo shell session left at an open BEGIN blocks vacuum and other people's updates. Always end with COMMIT or ROLLBACK, or enable the idle timeout.
  • Counting on sequence gaplessness. Rollbacks and retries burn numbers.
  • Reading now() as "the current time". It is the transaction start time and does not advance; in a long transaction it is old. clock_timestamp() is the wall clock.
  • Running VACUUM, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY or CREATE DATABASE in a transaction. PostgreSQL refuses ("cannot run inside a transaction block"); use autocommit.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
You need two psql windows connected to handbook_lab; call them A and B.

  1. Reproduce a non-repeatable read in READ COMMITTED, then repeat the exact sequence with BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ in A and note the difference. Restore the price afterwards.

  2. In A (REPEATABLE READ) read book 1's price, then in B update and commit its price, then in A update the same row. Record the error and its SQLSTATE (\set VERBOSITY verbose shows it). What should the application do next?

  3. Using book_stock, show a lost update with two sessions in READ COMMITTED that each do read, then UPDATE ... SET copies = <value computed in the shell>. Then redo it with UPDATE ... SET copies = copies - 1. Explain the difference in the final value.

  4. Demonstrate that an error inside a transaction aborts it, then use a savepoint so the transaction survives and commits the first insert.

  5. Write a psql or Python snippet that retries a transaction up to five times on SQLSTATE 40001 and 40P01, with a short random wait between attempts. Say what must be true of the transaction body for retrying to be safe.

Solution

  1. In READ COMMITTED, A's second SELECT returns 13.00 after B's committed update; in REPEATABLE READ it still returns 12.50, and only a new transaction in A shows 13.00. Restore with UPDATE books SET price = 12.50 WHERE id = 1;.

  2. A fails with 

    ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update
    SQLSTATE 40001. A's transaction is aborted. The application must ROLLBACK and run the whole transaction again from the start, including reading, because its snapshot was stale. A new transaction in A sees B's value and applies the change on top of it.

  3. Read-modify-write: both read 3, A writes 2 and commits, B writes 2 and commits; final value 2 although two copies left. With SET copies = copies - 1, B waits for A's row lock and, when A commits, recomputes copies - 1 from the new row (2), ending with 1. Under REPEATABLE READ the second form instead fails with 40001 for B, and B retries to reach 1. Clean up with DROP TABLE book_stock; afterwards.

  4. BEGIN;
INSERT INTO members (name, joined_on) VALUES ('Savepoint Test', '2024-07-01');
SAVEPOINT s;
INSERT INTO members (name, joined_on) VALUES (NULL, '2024-07-01');   -- NOT NULL violation
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s;
COMMIT;
    After ROLLBACK TO the transaction is usable and the first insert commits. Without the savepoint, the COMMIT would behave as a ROLLBACK. Remove the row afterwards.

  5. import random, time
import psycopg2
from psycopg2 import errors

def run_with_retry(dsn, work, tries=5):
    for attempt in range(1, tries + 1):
        conn = psycopg2.connect(dsn)
        try:
            with conn:                      # commit on success, rollback on exception
                with conn.cursor() as cur:
                    cur.execute("SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ")
                    return work(cur)
        except (errors.SerializationFailure, errors.DeadlockDetected):
            if attempt == tries:
                raise
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0.05, 0.3) * attempt)
        finally:
            conn.close()
    (Use a database that is the lab only.) Retrying is safe only if work has no effect outside the transaction (no emails, no external calls), re-reads everything it depends on at the start of each attempt, and does not carry computed state over from a previous attempt.

docs.title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
docs.text:
Sooner or later a script has to change data without going through the ORM: a migration backfills a new column, a bad import needs undoing, a stuck state needs resetting, a million rows need a fix that write() would take hours to apply. This chapter covers the three write statements, RETURNING, upserts, and joins inside writes. It also covers what raw SQL skips (the ORM's recomputes, audit columns, caches, and constraints), and a repeatable workflow in which every change is preceded by its read-only twin and wrapped in a transaction. It uses the library schema from Relational basics and Joins.

Every statement in this chapter changes data. Run them in your handbook_lab database only. For the exercises on a real Odoo database, use a copy restored from a backup (see psql and operations), never the live system, and never without the read-only SELECT first.

docs.title: The workflow, before the syntax
docs.text:
Fix data in four steps:

  1. Write the SELECT that returns exactly the rows you intend to change. Read the result.
  2. Open a transaction (BEGIN) and run the write with the same WHERE.
  3. Compare the reported row count with your expectation, and re-SELECT to look at the result.
  4. COMMIT if it matches, ROLLBACK if it does not.

Here it is for real. Which loans are still open?

SELECT id, book_id, member_id, due_on FROM loans WHERE returned_on IS NULL ORDER BY id;

 id | book_id | member_id |   due_on
----+---------+-----------+------------
  3 |       1 |         2 | 2024-03-24
  5 |       4 |         3 | 2024-04-16
(2 rows)

Two rows. Now extend their due date by a week, inside a transaction, and look at the outcome before deciding:

BEGIN;

UPDATE loans
SET due_on = due_on + 7
WHERE returned_on IS NULL
RETURNING id, due_on;

 id |   due_on
----+------------
  3 | 2024-03-31
  5 | 2024-04-23
(2 rows)

UPDATE 2

Two rows updated, as predicted. If you were satisfied you would type COMMIT;. Here we are only practicing:

ROLLBACK;

Until COMMIT, no other session sees your change, and ROLLBACK discards it as if nothing had happened (apart from sequence values consumed). This single habit prevents most data incidents. An unexpected UPDATE 4817 where you expected 2 is the cheapest possible warning, and only if the transaction is still open.

psql runs each statement in its own transaction unless you issue BEGIN. That is "autocommit": a bare UPDATE is committed the instant it finishes. Some GUI clients do the opposite and open a transaction silently, which is why an UPDATE you ran "yesterday" can still be uncommitted and holding locks today. Know which mode your tool is in.

docs.title: INSERT
docs.text:
The basic form names the columns and gives the values:

INSERT INTO authors (name, born_year, country)
VALUES ('Eve Quill', 1990, 'UK');

INSERT 0 1

INSERT 0 1 means: oid 0 (obsolete, always 0), one row inserted. Name the columns every time. A column list protects the statement from later ALTER TABLE changes and lets the columns you leave out take their defaults (id from the sequence, status from 'available').

Several rows in one statement are faster than several statements:

INSERT INTO authors (name, born_year, country) VALUES
    ('Fay Rowan',  1985, 'US'),
    ('Gus Heller', 1971, NULL);

docs.title: RETURNING
docs.text:
RETURNING hands back the rows the statement wrote, including defaults and generated values. It removes the need for a second query to find the new id:

INSERT INTO books (title, author_id, published_year, price, pages)
VALUES ('Small Hours', 5, 2023, 13.00, 220)
RETURNING id, title, status;

 id |    title    |  status
----+-------------+-----------
  7 | Small Hours | available
(1 row)

(The id depends on how many failed inserts consumed sequence values earlier. After the failing examples of the first chapter it is 10; on a fresh lab it is 7.) Odoo's ORM uses exactly this, INSERT ... RETURNING id, in create().

These example rows stay in your lab. Leave them for now; the section "Cleaning up the lab" near the end of the chapter removes them.

docs.title: INSERT from a SELECT
docs.text:
Any query can feed an insert, as long as the columns line up:

CREATE TABLE loans_archive (LIKE loans INCLUDING ALL);

SELECT id FROM loans WHERE returned_on < '2024-03-01' ORDER BY id;

 id
----
  1
  2
(2 rows)

INSERT INTO loans_archive
SELECT * FROM loans WHERE returned_on < '2024-03-01';

INSERT 0 2

LIKE ... INCLUDING ALL copies column definitions, defaults, indexes and check constraints, but not foreign keys. INSERT INTO t SELECT * depends on both tables having identical column order, which is brittle; in real code list the columns on both sides. CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT is the quick way to take a snapshot before a risky change:

CREATE TABLE fix_backup_loans AS
SELECT * FROM loans WHERE returned_on IS NULL;

It copies the data but no constraints or indexes, which is what you want from a throwaway safety copy. Remember to drop such tables when the fix is verified (after asking whoever owns the database, because on a shared system someone may be using it).

docs.title: Upsert: ON CONFLICT
docs.text:
"Insert, or update if it exists" is a single atomic statement:

SELECT id, name, email FROM members WHERE email = 'nora@example.com';

 id | name |      email
----+------+------------------
  1 | Nora | nora@example.com
(1 row)

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined_on)
VALUES ('Nora Renamed', 'nora@example.com', '2024-07-01')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name
RETURNING id, name;
ROLLBACK;

 id |     name
----+--------------
  1 | Nora Renamed
(1 row)

ON CONFLICT (email) names the unique index to check. If a row with that email exists, the DO UPDATE branch runs, and EXCLUDED refers to the row you tried to insert. DO NOTHING skips the conflict silently and returns no row (INSERT 0 0). The conflict target must be backed by a unique index or constraint, otherwise PostgreSQL errors with there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification.

ON CONFLICT is safe under concurrency: two sessions upserting the same key do not both insert, and neither gets a duplicate-key error. The conflicting loser waits for the winner to commit and then takes the update branch. That is what you want in code that registers something "if it is not there yet" while other workers do the same. Note that a skipped or updated insert still consumed a sequence value, so ids have gaps.

Versions. PostgreSQL 15 added the standard MERGE statement. Odoo 16 to 18 officially support PostgreSQL 12 and later, so code that has to run on all of them must stick to ON CONFLICT. For one-off scripts on a known newer server, MERGE is available.

docs.title: UPDATE
docs.text:
BEGIN;
UPDATE books SET price = price * 1.10 WHERE author_id = 1 RETURNING id, title, price;
ROLLBACK;

 id |   title    |  price
----+------------+---------
  1 | Tidewater  | 13.7500
  2 | Salt Roads | 16.5000
(2 rows)

(numeric(8,2) * 1.10 gives a result with more decimals in RETURNING; the column itself would round to two places when stored: 13.75 and 16.50.)

The SET list can reference current column values and several columns at once (SET a = b, b = a swaps them, since the right sides all see the old row). A missing WHERE updates every row of the table. Leaving the WHERE off on a production table is the classic disaster, which is why the workflow starts with a transaction and a row-count check.

docs.title: UPDATE ... FROM: updating using another table
docs.text:
To set values from, or select rows by, another table, list it in FROM and join it in WHERE. Mark books that are currently out on loan. Read-only version first:

SELECT DISTINCT b.id, b.title, b.status
FROM books b
JOIN loans l ON l.book_id = b.id
WHERE l.returned_on IS NULL AND b.status = 'available'
ORDER BY b.id;

 id |    title    |  status
----+-------------+-----------
  1 | Tidewater   | available
  4 | Paper Moons | available
(2 rows)

BEGIN;

UPDATE books b
SET status = 'on_loan'
FROM loans l
WHERE l.book_id = b.id
  AND l.returned_on IS NULL
  AND b.status = 'available'
RETURNING b.id, b.title, b.status;

 id |    title    | status
----+-------------+---------
  1 | Tidewater   | on_loan
  4 | Paper Moons | on_loan
(2 rows)

UPDATE 2

ROLLBACK;

A hidden trap: if a target row matches several rows of the FROM table, PostgreSQL updates it once, using an arbitrary one of the matches, and does not warn you. Here each book has at most one open loan, but a book with two open loans would be updated with whichever came first; if the SET used a value from loans the result would be unpredictable. When values come from the joined table, make sure the join produces one row per target, by aggregating first or using DISTINCT ON.

The alternative is a correlated subquery in SET, which makes uniqueness explicit: a subquery returning more than one row raises more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression, which is the failure you want instead of a silent arbitrary pick. Use it for single-value lookups; use UPDATE ... FROM when you set several columns from the same joined row.

docs.title: What an UPDATE really does
docs.text:
PostgreSQL does not overwrite a row in place. An UPDATE writes a new version of the row and marks the old one dead (this is MVCC, which the transactions chapter builds on). Consequences you can feel:

  • Updating every row of a table doubles its physical size until VACUUM reclaims the dead versions ("table bloat"). A big backfill on a large table leaves a lot of work for autovacuum.
  • Every index containing a changed column gets a new entry per updated row, too. Updating an indexed column of millions of rows is much heavier than updating an unindexed one.
  • A no-op update (SET x = x) still creates a row version. Add AND x IS DISTINCT FROM new_value to the WHERE to skip rows that already hold the target value; it makes scripts idempotent and cheaper:
BEGIN;
UPDATE books SET status = 'available'
WHERE status IS DISTINCT FROM 'available' AND id = 3;
ROLLBACK;

docs.title: DELETE
docs.text:
SELECT id, returned_on FROM loans WHERE returned_on < '2024-03-01' ORDER BY id;

 id | returned_on
----+-------------
  1 | 2024-01-18
  2 | 2024-02-20
(2 rows)

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM loans WHERE returned_on < '2024-03-01' RETURNING id;
ROLLBACK;

 id
----
  1
  2
(2 rows)

DELETE 2

RETURNING on DELETE returns the deleted rows, so you can capture exactly what disappeared. A pattern worth using on any manual delete is to move rows into a log table in the same statement, via a data-modifying CTE:

BEGIN;
WITH gone AS (
    DELETE FROM loans WHERE returned_on < '2024-03-01' RETURNING *
)
INSERT INTO loans_archive SELECT * FROM gone;
ROLLBACK;

The delete and the insert are one atomic statement: either both happen or neither does.

To delete using another table, USING plays the role of FROM in an update:

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM book_genre bg
USING books b
WHERE bg.book_id = b.id AND b.status = 'lost'
RETURNING bg.book_id, bg.genre_id;
ROLLBACK;

 book_id | genre_id
---------+----------
       3 |        1
(1 row)

Foreign keys apply on delete: a referenced row with ON DELETE RESTRICT blocks the delete with an error, CASCADE removes the children too, SET NULL clears their keys. Before deleting rows from a parent table, list what references it, with \d table ("Referenced by") or this catalog query:

SELECT conrelid::regclass AS referencing_table,
       conname,
       pg_get_constraintdef(oid) AS definition
FROM pg_constraint
WHERE contype = 'f' AND confrelid = 'books'::regclass;

 referencing_table |         conname         |                          definition
-------------------+-------------------------+---------------------------------------------------------------
 loans             | loans_book_id_fkey      | FOREIGN KEY (book_id) REFERENCES books(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT
 book_genre        | book_genre_book_id_fkey | FOREIGN KEY (book_id) REFERENCES books(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
(2 rows)

On an Odoo database this query, run against res_partner, returns many dozens of rows, which is the real answer to "why can't I delete this contact".

docs.title: TRUNCATE
docs.text: TRUNCATE table empties a table instantly, without scanning it, and unlike DELETE leaves no dead rows behind. It also takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock (blocks every reader and writer), skips row-level triggers, and TRUNCATE ... CASCADE truncates every table that references the target. It is transactional in PostgreSQL, so inside BEGIN you can roll it back, but do not touch it on an Odoo database: with CASCADE it reaches tables you did not know existed. Use it for your own staging tables.

docs.title: Bulk loading: COPY
docs.text:
For loading many rows from a file, COPY is an order of magnitude faster than inserts:

COPY books_stage (title, price) FROM '/var/lib/postgresql/books.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true);

That form reads the file on the database server and needs superuser rights or the pg_read_server_files role. In practice you use psql's client-side \copy, which reads the file on your machine and streams it through the connection:

\copy books_stage (title, price) FROM 'books.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true)

The reliable import pattern is to load into a staging table with plain text columns, check and clean it with SELECTs, and only then INSERT ... SELECT into the real table with casts. That way one bad cell produces a row you can inspect instead of an aborted load. COPY (SELECT ...) TO STDOUT WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER) works in the other direction and is the quickest export.

docs.title: What raw SQL bypasses in Odoo
docs.text:
Everything above works on any PostgreSQL table. On an Odoo table the same statements skip the ORM, and the ORM does more than store values. Know what you give up:

What the ORM does Effect of raw SQL sets create_uid, create_date, write_uid, write_date the columns keep old values or stay NULL on insert; "last modified" filters and incremental syncs miss your change recomputes stored computed fields (store=True) dependants keep stale values, e.g. a total does not follow its lines runs @api.constrains and _sql_constraints in Python only database constraints apply applies access rights and record rules none; you act as the database owner invalidates the record cache running workers keep the old value in memory until restart or cache clear; this applies to cached models such as ir.config_parameter and ir.rule creates mail.message tracking, activities, chatter nothing is logged maintains ir_model_data, ir_attachment links, translations a raw delete leaves XML-id rows pointing at nothing fires ondelete logic implemented in Python (unlink overrides) skipped

So the rule is: change data through the ORM (the Odoo shell, covered in The Odoo shell and Safe bulk scripts) whenever the volume allows it, and use SQL for what the ORM cannot do reasonably. When you must use SQL:

  • Set the audit columns yourself. Odoo stores datetimes as UTC without a zone:
SELECT count(*) FROM library_book WHERE state IS NULL;   -- read-only counterpart first

UPDATE library_book
SET state = 'available',
    write_uid = 1,
    write_date = now() AT TIME ZONE 'utc'
WHERE state IS NULL;

(library_book is the teaching module's table; user id 1 is the system user in standard Odoo, you can use the id of an administrative user instead.)

  • If the changed column feeds stored computed fields, either update those too in SQL, or afterwards trigger the recompute from the shell: records.modified(['state']) followed by env.flush_all() (the exact API name has moved between versions; check the source of your release).
  • Restart the workers, or call the cache clearing for the registry, when you changed a cached setting.
  • Update translated fields as jsonb, not text. In Odoo 16 to 18 a translated name is a JSON object keyed by language code, so replacing it with a plain string breaks the column's type contract:
UPDATE library_book
SET name = jsonb_set(name, '{en_US}', to_jsonb('New title'::text))
WHERE id = 1;

jsonb_set replaces one key and leaves the other languages intact; assigning name = '"New title"'::jsonb would wipe them.
