  • Never write to ir_model_data or delete from ir_model, ir_model_fields, ir_ui_view by hand to "clean up" a module: the next update will recreate or orphan things in confusing ways. Uninstall properly.

Never run UPDATE or DELETE on a live production Odoo database as a first attempt. Reproduce on a restored copy, check the Odoo UI and a module update against that copy, and only then repeat in production, in a transaction, with the row count you predicted.

docs.title: Large updates in batches
docs.text:
One UPDATE over ten million rows holds its row locks and a transaction snapshot until it ends, generates a single enormous WAL burst, and if it fails at the end throws all the work away. Batch it, committing between batches. Each batch picks a limited set of rows that still need the change:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# fragment: batched backfill against a scratch database
while true; do
  n=$(psql -d handbook_lab -q -At -c "
    WITH batch AS (
      SELECT id FROM books
      WHERE status IS DISTINCT FROM 'available' AND status <> 'lost'
      LIMIT 1000
      FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
    )
    UPDATE books b SET status = 'available'
    FROM batch WHERE b.id = batch.id
    RETURNING 1" | wc -l)
  echo "updated $n rows"
  [ "$n" -eq 0 ] && break
done

Each psql -c is its own transaction, so each batch commits. The WHERE excludes rows already processed, which makes the loop restartable and ends it with 0. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (next chapters) avoids waiting on rows another session holds. Pause between batches on a busy system, and run VACUUM (ANALYZE) on the table afterwards.

Create new indexes after a large backfill rather than before it, when the backfill rewrites many rows; and do not change a column's type with ALTER TABLE ... TYPE on a big table at a busy time, because most type changes rewrite the whole table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.

docs.title: Guarding scripts: expecting a row count
docs.text:
When a fix runs as a script rather than interactively, do not rely on eyes: assert the row count and abort the whole transaction otherwise.

BEGIN;

DO $$
DECLARE
    n integer;
BEGIN
    UPDATE loans SET due_on = due_on + 7 WHERE returned_on IS NULL;
    GET DIAGNOSTICS n = ROW_COUNT;
    IF n <> 2 THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'expected to touch 2 loans, touched %', n;
    END IF;
END
$$;

COMMIT;

If the count is wrong, the RAISE EXCEPTION puts the transaction in the aborted state, and the final COMMIT is turned into a rollback (psql prints ROLLBACK). Run with psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f fix.sql so that a failure stops the script instead of continuing to later statements.

docs.title: Cleaning up the lab
docs.text:
The inserts and helper tables above were committed. Remove them so that later chapters match their printed results:

DELETE FROM books   WHERE title = 'Small Hours';
DELETE FROM authors WHERE name IN ('Eve Quill', 'Fay Rowan', 'Gus Heller');
DROP TABLE loans_archive, fix_backup_loans;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS members_removed;

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE. Changes every row. Always begin a transaction, read the UPDATE n count, and ROLLBACK if it is not the number you expected.
  • Autocommit misunderstanding. A statement outside BEGIN is committed immediately in psql; in some GUIs a hidden open transaction holds locks for hours. Check SELECT now() - xact_start FROM pg_stat_activity (see psql and operations).
  • UPDATE ... FROM with several matches. The target row gets one arbitrary match. Make the join one-to-one.
  • Setting a value but not its dependants. A stored computed field, a denormalized counter, a parent_path, or an ir_model_data row left stale. Update all of them, or recompute through the ORM.
  • Forgetting write_date and write_uid. Incremental exports, "modified since" filters and cache validation keys depend on them.
  • Raw delete on a table with ON DELETE CASCADE children. The children disappear with no log. List the referencing foreign keys first.
  • Not accounting for NULLs. WHERE state <> 'done' skips rows where state is NULL; the fix script silently leaves part of the data untouched. Use IS DISTINCT FROM.
  • Running big writes in one transaction. Long-held locks, replication lag, a huge rollback if it fails. Batch.
  • Inserting rows with explicit ids. The sequence does not move. Run setval afterwards, and in Odoo prefer not to insert into model tables at all.
  • Assuming RETURNING shows the final state. It shows the row as written by the statement; AFTER triggers or later statements in the same transaction can still change it.
  • Leaving backup tables lying around. fix_backup_* tables accumulate in production databases. Name them with a date and a ticket reference and drop them after sign-off.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Add a member Rhea with no email, return the generated id, and then add a second member with the email of an existing member using ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, observing the command tag. Roll everything back.

  2. Mark all books by authors born before 1970 as status = 'classic'. Write the read-only SELECT first, then run the update in a transaction, check the count, and roll back.

  3. Delete members who are inactive and have no loans, but capture the deleted rows into a table members_removed in the same statement. Do it inside a transaction and show the content of members_removed before rolling back.

  4. A migration must set loans.returned_on = due_on for every open loan whose book is flagged lost. First list affected loans (probably none in the lab data), then write the update with an UPDATE ... FROM form and a guard that aborts if more than 5 rows would be touched.

Solution 

  1. BEGIN;
INSERT INTO members (name, joined_on) VALUES ('Rhea', '2024-07-02') RETURNING id;
INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined_on)
VALUES ('Impostor', 'omar@example.com', '2024-07-02')
ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING;
ROLLBACK;
    The first statement returns the new id; the second prints INSERT 0 0 because the email already exists (nothing inserted, no error).

  2. SELECT b.id, b.title, a.born_year
FROM books b JOIN authors a ON a.id = b.author_id
WHERE a.born_year < 1970 ORDER BY b.id;
    This returns books 1 to 4 (authors Ada born 1950 and Boris born 1962). Then: 
    BEGIN;
UPDATE books b SET status = 'classic'
FROM authors a
WHERE a.id = b.author_id AND a.born_year < 1970
RETURNING b.id;
ROLLBACK;
    UPDATE 4. Note that book 3 was lost: this update overwrites that status. A real script would add AND b.status = 'available', which is the point of reading the SELECT first.

  3. CREATE TABLE members_removed (LIKE members);

BEGIN;
WITH gone AS (
    DELETE FROM members m
    WHERE NOT m.active
      AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM loans l WHERE l.member_id = m.id)
    RETURNING m.*
)
INSERT INTO members_removed SELECT * FROM gone;

SELECT id, name FROM members_removed;
ROLLBACK;
    Result: one row, 4 | Quinn. (The CREATE TABLE is outside the transaction in this sketch, so the empty table stays.) Check the read-only version first: the same WHERE in a SELECT.

  4. SELECT l.id, l.book_id
FROM loans l JOIN books b ON b.id = l.book_id
WHERE l.returned_on IS NULL AND b.status = 'lost';
    In the lab, book 3 is lost but has no loans, so the query returns zero rows. The guarded update: 
    BEGIN;
DO $$
DECLARE n integer;
BEGIN
    UPDATE loans l SET returned_on = l.due_on
    FROM books b
    WHERE b.id = l.book_id AND l.returned_on IS NULL AND b.status = 'lost';
    GET DIAGNOSTICS n = ROW_COUNT;
    IF n > 5 THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'refusing to touch % loans', n;
    END IF;
END
$$;
COMMIT;
    With zero matching rows it commits without changing anything. To see the guard fire, change the threshold to n > 0 after making a loan of book 3 in a transaction.

docs.title: Async and the DOM
docs.text:
A browser runs your JavaScript on a single thread, and almost everything interesting (a server call, a timer, a click) happens later. Odoo's client is one long chain of "ask the server, wait, update the screen". This chapter covers the event loop, promises, async/await, error handling for concurrent work, and the DOM: selecting elements, handling events, and changing the page safely. The last section maps these onto OWL, which does most DOM work for you, so you know what it saves you from and when you still need the raw API.

The Node-runnable snippets were executed with Node.js 20+ as .mjs files. DOM snippets run in a browser console or in a page; they are marked.

docs.title: The event loop
docs.text:
JavaScript has one call stack. A long synchronous loop blocks everything, including rendering and clicks. Asynchronous operations hand work to the environment (timers, network, file system) and register a callback; when the stack is empty, the event loop picks the next callback from a queue.

There are two queues you need to distinguish:

  • Macrotasks: timers (setTimeout, setInterval), I/O callbacks, user events.
  • Microtasks: promise callbacks (then, await continuations) and queueMicrotask. All pending microtasks run before the next macrotask, and before the browser renders.
console.log("1 sync");
setTimeout(() => console.log("5 timeout"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3 microtask"));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log("4 microtask 2"));
(async () => {
  console.log("2 async start (runs synchronously until the first await)");
  await null;
  console.log("4b after await (a microtask)");
})();
console.log("2b sync end");

Output order: 1 sync, 2 async start..., 2b sync end, 3 microtask, 4 microtask 2, 4b after await, 5 timeout. Even with a delay of 0 the timeout runs last, because the synchronous code and the whole microtask queue go first.

Two things follow. An async function runs synchronously until its first await. And a microtask loop that keeps scheduling microtasks starves rendering, so a while with await on an already-resolved promise can freeze the page.

docs.title: Callbacks, and why promises replaced them
docs.text:
The old style passes a function to be called when the work is done:

setTimeout(() => console.log("later"), 100);

Nesting a few of these produces a pyramid where each level handles its own errors. A promise is an object that represents a value that will exist later, and it can be passed around, combined, and awaited.

A promise has three states: pending, fulfilled (with a value), rejected (with a reason). It settles once and never changes.

const sleep = (ms, value, fail = false) =>
  new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => (fail ? reject(new Error(value)) : resolve(value)), ms)
  );

sleep(10, "a")
  .then((v) => v + "b")          // returns a value: next then gets it
  .then((v) => sleep(10, v + "c"))   // returns a promise: next then waits for it
  .then(console.log)             // abc
  .catch((e) => console.log("failed", e.message))
  .finally(() => console.log("always"));

A .then returns a new promise. Whatever the callback returns (or throws) settles that new promise. A .catch at the end catches a rejection from any step before it.

docs.title: async/await
docs.text:
async/await is promise syntax that reads like synchronous code.

async function loanReport() {
  const a = await sleep(10, "A");
  const b = await sleep(10, "B");
  return a + b;                 // an async function always returns a promise
}
loanReport().then(console.log);  // AB
  • async function f() returns a promise. return x resolves it with x; a throw rejects it.
  • await p pauses the function until p settles, then gives the fulfilled value or throws the rejection reason. It does not block the thread; other code runs meanwhile.
  • await is allowed only inside an async function or at the top level of an ES module.
  • Arrow functions and methods can be async: const f = async () => {}, async refresh() {}.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Use try/catch/finally:

async function safe() {
  try {
    await sleep(5, "server said no", true);
  } catch (err) {
    console.log("caught:", err.message);
    return "fallback";
  } finally {
    console.log("cleanup");        // always runs: reset a loading flag here
  }
}
safe().then(console.log);

The finally block is the right place to reset a "loading" state, so a failed request does not leave a spinner on forever.

The main hazard is forgetting await or forgetting to handle a rejection. A promise whose rejection nobody handles ends as an "unhandled rejection": the browser logs it, and Node (15 and later) terminates the process. In a UI the failure is silent: the button just does nothing.

async function save() { throw new Error("nope"); }
save();                 // missing await and catch: unhandled rejection
await save();           // propagates to the caller, which must handle it

Odoo's RPC layer turns server errors into rejections with an error object, and the web client shows a dialog for uncaught ones. In a component method, catch only what you can act on and let the rest propagate to that global handler.

docs.title: Sequential versus parallel
docs.text:
Awaiting in sequence adds the durations. Starting the work first and awaiting together overlaps it.

console.time("seq");
await sleep(50, "a");
await sleep(50, "b");
console.timeEnd("seq");   // about 100 ms

console.time("par");
const results = await Promise.all([sleep(50, "a"), sleep(50, "b")]);
console.timeEnd("par");   // about 50 ms
console.log(results);     // [ 'a', 'b' ]

The combinators:

Function Resolves when Rejects when Promise.all([...]) all fulfil, with an array of values in input order the first one rejects Promise.allSettled([...]) all settle, with {status, value\|reason} objects never Promise.race([...]) the first settles (fulfil or reject) first to settle rejects Promise.any([...]) the first fulfils all reject (AggregateError) 
console.log(await Promise.allSettled([sleep(5, "ok"), sleep(5, "bad", true)]));
// [ { status: 'fulfilled', value: 'ok' }, { status: 'rejected', reason: Error: bad ... } ]
try {
  await Promise.all([sleep(5, "ok"), sleep(5, "bad", true)]);
} catch (e) { console.log("caught", e.message); }     // caught bad
console.log(await Promise.race([sleep(30, "slow"), sleep(5, "fast")]));   // fast

Use all when every result is required, allSettled when partial failure is acceptable (for example, loading optional side panels). Note that Promise.all does not cancel the others when one rejects; they keep running.

A trap with loops: array.forEach(async (x) => { await work(x); }) does not wait for anything, because forEach ignores the returned promises. Use for...of with await for sequential work, or await Promise.all(array.map(async (x) => work(x))) for parallel.

for (const book of books) {
  await returnBook(book);              // one at a time, in order
}
await Promise.all(books.map(returnBook));   // all at once; mind server load

For many items, concurrent calls to one server hit database limits and Odoo's worker limits; batch in the ORM call instead of sending hundreds of requests.

docs.title: Timers, debounce, and cancellation
docs.text:
const id = setTimeout(fn, 300);  clearTimeout(id);
const tick = setInterval(fn, 1000);  clearInterval(tick);

Debounce delays a call until input has settled. It is the standard fix for "search on every keystroke":

function debounce(fn, ms) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms);
  };
}
const search = debounce((q) => console.log("search for", q), 20);
search("d"); search("du"); search("dun");   // prints once: search for dun

To abandon a request, use an AbortController. fetch accepts its signal:

const controller = new AbortController();
const promise = fetch("/library/api/books", { signal: controller.signal });
controller.abort();                // promise rejects with an AbortError
promise.catch((e) => console.log(e.name));   // AbortError

Components that start requests should cancel or ignore results when they are destroyed, so a late response does not update a component that no longer exists.

docs.title: Talking to a server
docs.text:
fetch returns a promise of a Response. A response is available when the headers arrive; reading the body is another promise. fetch rejects only on network failure; an HTTP 404 or 500 is a successful fetch with response.ok === false.

async function getJson(url, options) {
  const response = await fetch(url, options);
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status} for ${url}`);
  }
  return response.json();
}

const created = await getJson("/library/api/books", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title: "Dune" }),
});

The HTTP chapter covers methods, headers, and JSON-RPC in detail. In Odoo's web client you rarely use fetch directly for model data. The framework gives you the ORM service for CRUD and an rpc helper for custom routes, both returning promises:

// in an OWL component, fragment
setup() {
  this.orm = useService("orm");
}
async loadBooks() {
  const books = await this.orm.searchRead(
    "library.book", [["year", "<", 2000]], ["name", "year"], { limit: 20 }
  );
  this.state.books = books;
}

searchRead(model, domain, fields, kwargs) is part of the ORM service in the versions covered by this book.

Versions: how you call a custom route differs by release. In Odoo 16 the rpc service is obtained with useService("rpc"); from 17 there is also a standalone rpc function you can import from the web module's network folder. Verify the exact import path in your version's source before copying.

Plain fetch is appropriate for non-JSON endpoints (file downloads, static assets) and for code outside the web client, such as a standalone portal script. Remember that Odoo controllers of type="http" that accept POST need a CSRF token; type="json" routes use the JSON-RPC envelope described in the next chapter.

docs.title: The DOM
docs.text: The DOM is the browser's in-memory tree of the page. JavaScript reads and changes it; the browser re-renders. document is the root and every element is an object.

docs.title: Selecting
docs.text:
// browser
const title = document.querySelector("h1");                  // first match or null
const rows = document.querySelectorAll("table.items tr");     // NodeList (static)
const byId = document.getElementById("total");
const inCard = card.querySelector(".price");                  // scoped to an element
const row = event.target.closest("tr");                       // nearest ancestor match
Array.from(rows).map((r) => r.dataset.id);                    // NodeList to array

querySelector returns null if nothing matches, so document.querySelector(".x").textContent throws when .x is absent. Guard with ?..

docs.title: Reading and changing
docs.text:
// browser
el.textContent = "Dune";                    // text; safe, no HTML parsing
el.innerHTML = "<b>Dune</b>";               // parses HTML; dangerous with untrusted text
el.classList.add("text-muted");
el.classList.toggle("d-none", isHidden);
el.setAttribute("href", "/my/loans/1");
el.dataset.bookId = "7";                    // writes data-book-id="7"
el.style.display = "none";
const input = document.querySelector("input[name=q]");
console.log(input.value);                   // current value, a string

Creating and inserting:

// browser
const li = document.createElement("li");
li.textContent = "Emma";
list.append(li);                  // end of list
list.prepend(li.cloneNode(true)); // start
list.insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", "<li>Static markup you wrote</li>");
li.remove();

docs.title: innerHTML and cross-site scripting
docs.text: If any part of an innerHTML string comes from a user (a book title, a partner name, a note), an attacker can put <img src=x onerror=...> there and run script in the viewer's session, including an administrator's. Use textContent for text. When you must insert markup, build elements with createElement, or sanitise through the framework's Markup mechanism. In OWL and QWeb, t-out escapes by default, and only values marked as markup are inserted raw; fields of type Html are the sanctioned source of markup.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
// browser
const button = document.querySelector("button.save");
button.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();       // stop default (link navigation, form submit)
  console.log("clicked", event.target);
});

An event travels in three phases: capture (window down to the target), target, and bubble (target back up to window). Most handlers run in the bubble phase. event.stopPropagation() stops it from travelling further, and should be rare, because it breaks other code listening higher up (including Odoo's own global handlers).

Because events bubble, one listener on a container can serve many children. This is event delegation, and it is the right tool for lists that change:

// browser
document.querySelector("table.loans").addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const btn = event.target.closest("button[data-action='return']");
  if (!btn) return;
  const loanId = Number(btn.closest("tr").dataset.id);
  console.log("return loan", loanId);
});

Remove listeners you add to long-lived objects (window, document) when the owner goes away, or they leak and fire on stale state:

// browser
function onResize() { /* ... */ }
window.addEventListener("resize", onResize);
// later
window.removeEventListener("resize", onResize);

The listener passed to removeEventListener must be the same function reference. An inline arrow cannot be removed, so keep it in a variable. AbortController gives a tidy alternative: pass { signal } when adding, and controller.abort() removes all of them.

Common events: click, input (every change to a field value), change (on commit), submit, keydown, focus/blur, DOMContentLoaded, scroll, resize. input fires per keystroke, so combine with debounce for server calls.

docs.title: Observers
docs.text:
For things that happen later without an event, observers watch the DOM:

// browser
const mo = new MutationObserver((records) => console.log(records.length, "changes"));
mo.observe(container, { childList: true, subtree: true });
// mo.disconnect() when done

const io = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {
  for (const e of entries) if (e.isIntersecting) console.log("visible", e.target);
});
io.observe(document.querySelector(".card"));

MutationObserver reports DOM changes; IntersectionObserver reports visibility (lazy loading, infinite scroll). Both batch and run as microtasks, so they do not fire inside your synchronous code.

docs.title: Layout reads and writes
docs.text: Reading offsetHeight or getBoundingClientRect() forces the browser to compute layout. Alternating reads and writes in a loop makes this happen repeatedly ("layout thrashing"). Read everything, then write everything.

docs.title: Waiting for the page
docs.text:
A script in a page head runs before the body exists. Either place the script at the end, use defer, or listen for readiness:

// browser
if (document.readyState === "loading") {
  document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", init);
} else {
  init();
}

In Odoo you do not write this; the framework mounts components when the page is ready and calls your hooks at the right time.

docs.title: OWL does the DOM for you
docs.text:
In an OWL component the DOM is a function of state. You change state; the framework patches the DOM. Compare a hand-written counter with the component form:

// browser, manual DOM
let count = 0;
const label = document.querySelector("#count");
document.querySelector("#plus").addEventListener("click", () => {
  count++;
  label.textContent = String(count);
});

<!-- OWL template (fragment) -->
<t t-name="library.Counter">
    <button class="btn btn-primary" t-on-click="increment">
        Count: <t t-out="state.count"/>
    </button>
</t>

// OWL component (fragment)
import { Component, useState } from "@odoo/owl";
export class Counter extends Component {
  static template = "library.Counter";
  setup() { this.state = useState({ count: 0 }); }
  increment() { this.state.count++; }
}

What you stop doing: selecting elements, creating nodes, keeping the DOM in sync, removing listeners (t-on-* handlers are managed with the component's life). What you still need:

  • useRef("name") with t-ref="name" to get an element when you need a native API (focus, measuring, a third-party widget).
  • Lifecycle hooks for effects that touch the outside world: onMounted(() => ...) after the first render, onWillUnmount(() => ...) to remove what you added, onWillStart(async () => ...) to load data before the first render, onWillUpdateProps when inputs change.
  • useEffect-style hooks (available in the web library) to run code when specific dependencies change.
// fragment
setup() {
  this.inputRef = useRef("search");
  onMounted(() => this.inputRef.el.focus());
  onWillStart(async () => {
    this.books = await this.orm.searchRead("library.book", [], ["name"]);
  });
}

onWillStart accepts an async callback and the component does not render until it settles, which is how you load initial data. Setting this.state.x in onMounted triggers a second render, which is fine for data that arrives later but flickers for data you could have loaded in onWillStart.

Rule: if you find yourself calling document.querySelector inside an OWL component, stop and check whether a t-ref, a t-on-*, or state can do it.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Forgotten await. const books = this.orm.searchRead(...) gives a promise, and books.length is undefined. Linters with a "floating promise" rule catch it.
  • forEach(async ...). Does not wait. Use for...of or Promise.all(map(...)).
  • Sequential awaits that should be parallel, and the opposite: parallel requests that must be ordered (a write followed by a read of the same record).
  • Treating fetch as failing on 4xx/5xx. It does not. Check response.ok.
  • Swallowed errors. catch (e) {} hides bugs. Catch to recover or to add context, then rethrow if you cannot recover.
  • State after unmount. A response arriving after the component is destroyed writes into dead state. Cancel with AbortController or check a flag.
  • innerHTML with user data. Cross-site scripting. Use textContent or escaped templates.
  • querySelector returning null. Elements may not exist yet or at all.
  • Listeners that are never removed, especially on window and document, and listeners registered inside a component method that runs on every render.
  • stopPropagation as a fix. It hides the event from code that depended on it. Prefer checking event.target.
  • Blocking the thread. A big synchronous loop over thousands of records freezes the page. Process on the server, or chunk the work with await between chunks.
  • Updating state in a loop and expecting an immediate DOM change. Rendering is batched; DOM reflects state after the next render, not on the next line.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Order of output. Predict the output order, then run it.

setTimeout(() => console.log("A"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("B"));
(async () => { console.log("C"); await 1; console.log("D"); })();
console.log("E");
Solution

C, E, B, D, A. C runs synchronously inside the async function until await; E follows. Then the microtask queue drains in registration order: the then callback (B), then the continuation after await (D). The timeout, a macrotask, goes last.

2. Parallel loading. You have loadBooks(), loadMembers(), and loadSettings(), all returning promises; settings are optional. Write one async function that loads all three in parallel and returns { books, members, settings }, with settings as null when it fails.

Solution 
async function loadAll() {
  const [books, members, settings] = await Promise.all([
    loadBooks(),
    loadMembers(),
    loadSettings().catch(() => null),
  ]);
  return { books, members, settings };
}

The .catch on the optional request converts its rejection to null so Promise.all does not fail; a failure of books or members still rejects the whole call.

3. Fix the loop. This function returns before the books are returned. Fix it in two ways.

async function returnAll(books) {
  books.forEach(async (b) => { await returnBook(b); });
}
Solution

Sequential:

async function returnAll(books) {
  for (const b of books) await returnBook(b);
}

Parallel:

async function returnAll(books) {
  await Promise.all(books.map((b) => returnBook(b)));
}

forEach ignores the promises its callback returns, so the outer function finishes immediately.

4. Delegation. A table of loans gets rows added dynamically. Write one listener so that clicking any button.renew inside a row calls renew(id), where id is the row's data-id.

Solution 
// browser
document.querySelector("table.loans").addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const button = event.target.closest("button.renew");
  if (!button) return;
  renew(Number(button.closest("tr").dataset.id));
});

The listener lives on the table, which exists once, so rows added later work without new listeners. closest handles clicks on elements inside the button, such as an icon.

5. Debounced search with cancellation. Write makeSearcher(url) returning a function search(q) that waits 200 ms after the last call, aborts any request still in flight, and returns nothing. Sketch it with fetch and AbortController.

Solution 
function makeSearcher(url, onResult) {
  let timer, controller;
  return (q) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(async () => {
      controller?.abort();
      controller = new AbortController();
      try {
        const res = await fetch(`${url}?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}`, { signal: controller.signal });
        if (res.ok) onResult(await res.json());
      } catch (err) {
        if (err.name !== "AbortError") throw err;
      }
    }, 200);
  };
}

encodeURIComponent protects the query string from characters such as & and spaces. Aborted requests reject with AbortError, which is expected and ignored; other errors propagate.

docs.title: HTML and CSS you need
docs.text:
You do not need to be a front-end designer to build Odoo modules, but you do need enough HTML and CSS to read a QWeb template, lay out a PDF report so it does not split a table row across pages, and make a portal page look like it belongs on the site. This chapter covers the subset that repeatedly shows up: document structure, the box model, selectors and specificity, flexbox, the Bootstrap grid and utilities that Odoo ships, and print CSS for the wkhtmltopdf engine behind PDF reports.

Everything here is plain web technology. Odoo specifics are limited to class names and behaviours I name explicitly; for anything version-sensitive there is a hint.

docs.title: HTML in five minutes
docs.text:
HTML is a tree of elements like XML, but with a forgiving parser and a fixed vocabulary.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Book card</title>
  <style>
    .card { border: 1px solid #ccc; padding: 12px; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <article class="card">
    <h2>Dune</h2>
    <p>Published <time datetime="1965">1965</time>.</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Frank Herbert</li>
      <li>Science fiction</li>
    </ul>
  </article>
</body>
</html>

Save it as card.html and open it in a browser; it is the fastest way to try any snippet in this chapter.

Elements fall into two groups by default layout:

  • Block elements (div, p, h1-h6, ul, table, section, form) start on a new line and stretch to the width of their container.
  • Inline elements (span, a, strong, em, img, code) flow within a line of text. Width and height do not apply to a plain inline element.

The semantic elements you will meet in Odoo templates:

Element Use div, span Generic block and inline containers h1...h6 Headings; one h1 per page p, ul, ol, li Paragraphs and lists table, thead, tbody, tfoot, tr, th, td Tabular data. Reports are mostly tables a href Links img src alt Images; always provide alt form, input, label, button, select, textarea Forms on website and portal pages section, article, header, footer, nav Structure for portal and website pages

Attributes worth knowing: class (a space-separated list of CSS classes), id (unique per page), style (inline CSS), data-* (custom data, read in JavaScript through element.dataset), and aria-* / role for accessibility.

docs.title: HTML versus XML
docs.text:
QWeb templates are XML files that produce HTML, so they must be well-formed XML even though the output is HTML. In templates:

  • Every tag is closed. Write <br/>, <img src="..." alt=""/>, <input type="text"/>, never <br>.
  • Attributes are always quoted and always have a value. Use <input disabled="disabled"/> instead of <input disabled>.
  • Raw < and & in text must be escaped (see the XML chapter).

The browser sees the output of the template, so the output is HTML. But the file you author is XML.

docs.title: The box model
docs.text:
Every element is a rectangle with four layers, from the inside out: content, padding, border, margin.

.box {
  width: 200px;
  padding: 10px;
  border: 2px solid #333;
  margin: 20px;
}

By default (box-sizing: content-box), width: 200px is the content width; the rendered box is 200 + 210 + 22 = 224px wide. With box-sizing: border-box, width includes padding and border and the box is 200px wide. Bootstrap, which Odoo uses, sets border-box globally, so inside Odoo pages widths behave the way you expect. In a standalone test file, add * { box-sizing: border-box; }.

Vertical margins between block siblings collapse: two stacked blocks with margin-bottom: 20px and margin-top: 30px are 30px apart, not 50px. Margins do not collapse inside flex containers.

Units you will use:

Unit Meaning Where px CSS pixel Screens rem Multiple of the root font size Spacing and type in portal pages % Percentage of the parent Widths mm, cm, pt Physical units PDF reports vw, vh Percent of the viewport Full-screen layouts; not useful in PDFs

docs.title: Selectors, the cascade, and specificity
docs.text:
A rule is selector { property: value; }. Common selectors:

p              /* all p elements */
.note          /* elements with class="note" */
#total         /* the element with id="total" */
table.items td /* td inside a table having class "items" */
ul > li        /* direct children only */
h2 + p         /* p right after an h2 */
a[href^="http"]/* attribute starts with */
li:first-child /* pseudo-classes */
li:nth-child(even)
p::first-line  /* pseudo-elements */

When several rules target one element and set the same property, the winner is chosen by:

  1. Importance (!important wins; avoid it).
  2. Specificity: inline style beats an id selector, which beats class/attribute/pseudo-class selectors, which beat element selectors. #a .b beats .a .b .c. Each level is counted separately; ten classes never beat one id.
  3. Order: for equal specificity, the later rule wins.
p { color: black; }          /* specificity 0,0,1 */
.note { color: gray; }       /* 0,1,0 wins over p */
article .note { color: red; }/* 0,1,1 wins over .note */

Inherited properties (color, font-*, line-height, text-align) flow down to children; box properties (margin, padding, border, background) do not.

In Odoo you almost never fight specificity by hand. Add your own class prefixed with your module (for example o_library_card) and write a selector one level more specific than the rule you override. If you reach for !important, you have usually picked the wrong selector.

docs.title: Flexbox
docs.text:
Flexbox lays children out along one axis. The container sets the rules:

<style>
  .row-demo { display: flex; gap: 12px; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; }
  .row-demo > .grow { flex: 1 1 auto; }
</style>
<div class="row-demo">
  <span>Dune</span>
  <span class="grow">1965</span>
  <button>Open</button>
</div>

The properties that cover 90% of cases:

Property Where Effect display: flex container Children become flex items flex-direction: row \| column container Main axis; row is the default justify-content container Distribution along the main axis (flex-start, center, space-between, flex-end) align-items container Alignment across the cross axis (stretch default, center, flex-start) flex-wrap: wrap container Allow items to wrap onto new lines gap container Space between items flex: grow shrink basis item flex: 1 means "share leftover space equally" margin-left: auto item Pushes the item (and followers) to the far end

A common point of confusion: justify-content is main axis, align-items is cross axis. When you switch flex-direction to column, they swap geometric directions.

CSS Grid exists for two-dimensional layouts, but Odoo's own CSS and the Bootstrap grid do not require it, and PDF rendering does not support it at all (see below). Learn flexbox first.

docs.title: Bootstrap as Odoo uses it
docs.text:
Odoo's backend and website both build on Bootstrap. The website and the QWeb reports rely on its grid, spacing, and utility classes directly, so you write them in your templates.

Versions: Odoo 16 and later use Bootstrap 5; Odoo 15 and earlier use Bootstrap 4. Several utility names changed between the two. Where it matters below, both are listed. Check your version's bundled Bootstrap before copying a snippet from the web, because the wrong generation silently does nothing.

docs.title: The grid
docs.text:
A row has 12 columns. Columns declare their span at a breakpoint and up.

<div class="container">
  <div class="row">
    <div class="col-12 col-md-8">Main content</div>
    <div class="col-12 col-md-4">Sidebar</div>
  </div>
</div>
  • container centres content with a maximum width (container-fluid uses the full width).
  • row is a flex container with negative side margins that offset the column gutters.
  • col-N takes N of 12 columns at all widths; col-md-N applies from the md breakpoint (768px) upward. Below that the column stacks to full width if col-12 or nothing is set.
  • The breakpoints are sm 576, md 768, lg 992, xl 1200, xxl 1400 (in Bootstrap 5).
  • col alone shares remaining width equally; col-auto sizes to content.
  • offset-md-2 adds two columns of left space (same name in Bootstrap 4 and 5).
  • Columns must be direct children of a row, and rows go inside a container or a column.

Bootstrap's grid is mobile-first: unprefixed rules apply everywhere, and each larger breakpoint overrides upward. Design the narrow layout first.

docs.title: Utility classes
docs.text:
Utilities are single-purpose classes. Learn these and you rarely need custom CSS:

<!-- Spacing: m = margin, p = padding; t/b/s/e/x/y sides; 0-5 scale -->
<div class="mt-3 mb-2 px-4 py-2">...</div>

<!-- Flex helpers -->
<div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center gap-2">
  <span class="fw-bold">Dune</span>
  <span class="text-muted">1965</span>
</div>

<!-- Text -->
<p class="text-center text-uppercase small">...</p>
<span class="text-end">right aligned in BS5</span>

<!-- Display and visibility -->
<div class="d-none d-md-block">Hidden on phones</div>

<!-- Tables -->
<table class="table table-sm table-bordered">...</table>

Names that differ between Bootstrap 4 and 5:

Purpose BS 4 (Odoo 15 and earlier) BS 5 (Odoo 16+) Margin left / right ml-2, mr-2 ms-2, me-2 Padding left / right pl-2, pr-2 ps-2, pe-2 Text align right / left text-right, text-left text-end, text-start Float float-left float-start Font weight font-weight-bold fw-bold Gap between flex items not available gap-2 Badge colours badge badge-primary badge text-bg-primary or badge bg-primary

If a spacing class has no visible effect, the generation mismatch is the first suspect.

docs.title: Colours and components in views
docs.text:
Contextual colour classes (text-success, text-danger, bg-light, alert alert-warning, btn btn-primary, badge) are the supported way to colour text and boxes. They follow the database's theme, which a custom hex colour does not.

Odoo's own widgets use classes beginning with o_ (for example o_form_view, o_list_view). Treat these as internal: reading them in the browser inspector to find a hook is fine, but depending on one in module CSS ties you to a particular release. Prefer your own class on your own element.

docs.title: Where CSS lives in a module
docs.text: CSS and SCSS files ship under static/src and are registered in the manifest assets key (assets are covered in the frontend part). For a quick edit in a QWeb template or a report you can use an inline style attribute, which also guarantees the rule reaches wkhtmltopdf. Inline styles have the highest specificity, so use them for report-only tweaks and keep reusable styles in a stylesheet.

docs.title: QWeb reports and wkhtmltopdf
docs.text:
A PDF report is not a page-sized screenshot. Odoo renders your QWeb template to HTML, then passes it to the wkhtmltopdf program, which uses an old fork of the WebKit engine to paginate it. That engine is years behind a modern browser, and it explains most report layout bugs.

What you can count on:

  • Tables, floats, block layout, position: absolute, and fixed-width layouts work.
  • Bootstrap's grid works in reports, because Odoo's report layouts load Bootstrap, but the engine's flexbox implementation is partial and prefixed. Rows and columns generally render; elaborate flex layouts (nested flex, gap, flex-wrap with many items) do not render reliably.
  • CSS Grid does not work.
  • CSS custom properties (var(--x)) do not work.
  • @media print rules apply; wkhtmltopdf emulates print media by default.

Rule of thumb for reports: use tables for tabular content and Bootstrap rows of a few col-N columns for the header and totals; test in the real PDF, not in the browser preview.

The HTML preview of a report (the ?debug or report/html/... route) is rendered by the browser with modern CSS. It looks right when the PDF does not. Always judge a layout from the PDF.

docs.title: Print CSS essentials
docs.text:
/* Keep a table row together */
tr, .no-break { page-break-inside: avoid; }

/* Repeat the table header on every page */
thead { display: table-header-group; }
tfoot { display: table-footer-group; }

/* Force a page break before each section */
.new-page { page-break-before: always; }

/* Keep a heading with the content after it */
h2, h3 { page-break-after: avoid; }

/* Physical units for margins inside the page */
.signature { margin-top: 15mm; width: 60mm; border-top: 1px solid #000; }

page-break-inside: avoid on a div containing a long table is ignored when the table is longer than a page; apply it to rows or to small blocks, not to large containers. In PDF reports, page breaks inside tables are the most common source of ugly output: a total row orphaned alone at the top of a new page. Wrapping the totals in a block with page-break-inside: avoid and placing it after the table helps.

An example report fragment for a library loan sheet:

<template id="report_loan_sheet_document">
    <t t-call="web.external_layout">
        <div class="page">
            <h2>Loan <span t-field="o.name"/></h2>
            <div class="row mb-3">
                <div class="col-6">
                    <strong>Member</strong>
                    <div t-field="o.member_id"/>
                </div>
                <div class="col-6 text-end">
                    <strong>Date out</strong>
                    <div t-field="o.date_out"/>
                </div>
            </div>
            <table class="table table-sm">
                <thead>
                    <tr><th>Book</th><th class="text-end">Copies</th></tr>
                </thead>
                <tbody>
                    <tr t-foreach="o.line_ids" t-as="line" style="page-break-inside: avoid;">
                        <td><span t-field="line.book_id"/></td>
                        <td class="text-end"><span t-field="line.copies"/></td>
                    </tr>
                </tbody>
            </table>
        </div>
    </t>
</template>

The t-call, t-foreach, and t-field directives are explained in the QWeb and PDF reports chapters. For layout, note: div.page is the content wrapper, the row/col-6 pair is plain Bootstrap, and the row-level style attribute keeps each line unbroken. text-end is the Bootstrap 5 name; use text-right in versions with Bootstrap 4.

docs.title: Fonts, colours, images in PDFs
docs.text:
• Fonts must be installed on the machine that runs wkhtmltopdf, or loaded from a path it can read. A missing font silently falls back to a default and changes the layout. Stick to the fonts the report layout already uses unless you control the server.
  • Background colours on table cells and rows normally print; background images are less reliable. Check the actual PDF.
  • Images: give an explicit width or max-width. An unconstrained image taller than a page breaks pagination. Use t-att-src with image_data_uri(...) for binary fields in reports, and always include alt.
  • Wide tables: wkhtmltopdf will not shrink content to fit; a table wider than the page is cut off. Set table-layout: fixed, give column widths in %, and use word-wrap: break-word.

docs.title: Portal and website pages
docs.text:
Portal and website templates render inside Odoo's website layout, which already loads Bootstrap, so the grid and utilities work as in any Bootstrap page. The structure you will write most often:

<template id="portal_my_loans" name="My loans">
    <t t-call="portal.portal_layout">
        <div class="o_portal_my_loans">
            <t t-if="not loans">
                <p class="alert alert-info">No loans yet.</p>
            </t>
            <div t-else="" class="table-responsive">
                <table class="table table-hover">
                    <tbody>
                        <tr t-foreach="loans" t-as="loan">
                            <td><a t-attf-href="/my/loans/#{loan.id}" t-out="loan.name"/></td>
                            <td class="text-end"><span t-field="loan.date_out"/></td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </table>
            </div>
        </div>
    </t>
</template>

A few points that apply regardless of version:

  • Wrap wide tables in table-responsive so phones can scroll them sideways.
  • A portal page is viewed on a phone more often than you expect. Test at 375px wide with the browser's responsive mode.
  • Forms posted to Odoo controllers need a CSRF token; the controller chapter covers it. In a form the hidden input is <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" t-att-value="request.csrf_token()"/>.
  • Link and button text should be real text, not images, so translations pick them up.
  • Avoid id attributes derived from record ids unless you need them; duplicated ids make anchors and label for= links misbehave.

docs.title: Debugging CSS
docs.text:
1. Right-click the element, Inspect. The Styles pane lists the winning rules and the crossed-out losers.
  2. The Computed tab shows the final value of every property, which ends most "why is my padding ignored" questions.
  3. Toggle a rule off with its checkbox to see which one is responsible.
  4. For reports, produce the PDF and view it; the browser preview misleads. Download a sample PDF, then change one thing at a time.
  5. To see the HTML wkhtmltopdf received, open the report's HTML route in the browser with developer mode, and inspect what Odoo produced.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Treating the browser preview as the PDF. Different engines. Final judgement is always from the PDF.
  • Flexbox and grid in reports. Partial or absent in wkhtmltopdf. Use tables and Bootstrap rows of simple columns.
  • Bootstrap generation mismatch. ml-2 on Odoo 16+ does nothing; ms-2 on Odoo 15 does nothing.
  • position: fixed footers in reports repeat in unpredictable ways. Use the layout's footer facility.
  • Row-breaking. Without page-break-inside: avoid, a single row may split between two pages.
  • Overriding with !important. It wins today and makes the next override impossible. Write a more specific selector.
  • Depending on Odoo's internal o_ classes. They change between releases; add your own class.
  • Unclosed tags in templates. <br> is valid HTML and a fatal XML error in a QWeb file.
  • Units. Pixels in a PDF depend on the engine's DPI assumptions. Use mm and pt for anything that must be sized physically.
  • Big images. A 4000px photo inside a report makes the PDF huge and slow to generate. Resize in code.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Box model. An element has width: 300px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid;. How wide is it on screen with content-box, and with border-box?

Solution

content-box: 300 + 220 + 25 = 350px. border-box: 300px, because the width includes padding and border and the content shrinks to 250px.

2. Header row. Write HTML using Bootstrap utilities (no custom CSS) for a row where the title "Loans" is left and a button "New" is right, vertically centred.

Solution 
<div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center">
  <h2 class="mb-0">Loans</h2>
  <a class="btn btn-primary" href="/my/loans/new">New</a>
</div>

d-flex makes it a flex container, justify-content-between pushes the two items to opposite ends, align-items-center centres them across the cross axis, mb-0 removes the heading's default bottom margin so the centring looks right.

3. Responsive columns. Make a two-column layout (8/4) that stacks on phones. Then change it so the sidebar is hidden on phones.

Solution 
<div class="row">
  <div class="col-12 col-md-8">Main</div>
  <div class="col-12 col-md-4 d-none d-md-block">Sidebar</div>
</div>

Below md both columns are col-12; d-none d-md-block hides the sidebar until md and then displays it as a block.

4. Report table. Write CSS that repeats a table header on every page, never splits a row, and keeps a div.totals block together.

Solution 
thead { display: table-header-group; }
tr { page-break-inside: avoid; }
.totals { page-break-inside: avoid; }

Test it with a table of 100 rows in a real PDF. The thead rule is what makes the header repeat; some engines already do it by default, wkhtmltopdf is more reliable when you state it.

5. Specificity. Given .note { color: gray }, p.note { color: blue }, #x { color: red }, and <p id="x" class="note" style="color: green">, what colour is the text, and what if the inline style is removed?

Solution

Green: the inline style beats everything without !important. Without it, red: the id selector (specificity 1,0,0 in id, class, element order) outranks p.note (0,1,1) and .note (0,1,0).

docs.title: HTTP and JSON
docs.text:
Every integration you will build around Odoo, and the web client itself, speaks HTTP carrying JSON. Browser to server, Odoo to a payment provider, a script to the external API, a webhook arriving from another system: it is all requests, responses, headers, and cookies. If you can read a raw exchange and say what each line means, most integration bugs shrink to a diff between what you expected and what is on the wire. This chapter covers the protocol, JSON as a format, sessions and cookies, CORS, the JSON-RPC shape Odoo uses, REST design for your own endpoints, and curl as the debugging tool.

The examples were run against a small local server written with Node.js (a throwaway scratch script, not part of Odoo). The Odoo-specific facts are limited to routes and envelopes that are stable across the versions covered by this book.

docs.title: A request and a response
docs.text:
HTTP is text over a connection. A client sends a request; a server sends one response.

POST /books HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8765
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
Content-Length: 18

{"title":"Ulysses"}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Location: /books/3
Content-Length: 27

{"id":3,"title":"Ulysses"}

Anatomy:

  • Request line: method, target (path plus query string), protocol version.
  • Headers: Name: value lines. One blank line ends the headers.
  • Body: optional bytes, described by Content-Type and Content-Length.
  • Status line (response): protocol, status code, reason phrase. Clients act on the code, not the phrase.

HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone, and anything that looks like a session (a logged-in user) is carried by something the client sends each time, normally a cookie or an Authorization header.

docs.title: URLs
docs.text:
https://shop.example.com:8069/library/books?year=1965&tag=sf#reviews
 scheme      host        port   path           query string   fragment

The fragment (#reviews) never reaches the server. The query string is key=value pairs separated by &, and values must be percent-encoded: a space is %20 (or + in form encoding), & is %26. In JavaScript, encodeURIComponent("a&b") gives a%26b, and new URL(...).searchParams handles building and parsing. In Python, use urllib.parse.urlencode and never string concatenation.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Meaning Body Safe Idempotent GET Read a resource no yes yes HEAD Like GET, headers only no yes yes POST Create, or run an action yes no no PUT Replace a resource at a known URL yes no yes PATCH Partial update yes no not guaranteed DELETE Remove rarely no yes OPTIONS Ask what is allowed (CORS preflight) no yes yes

Safe means it should not change server state; idempotent means repeating the request has the same effect as sending it once. These words matter in practice: browsers, proxies, and retry logic may repeat idempotent requests automatically, and a GET that deletes data will be triggered by a link prefetcher or a crawler. Never perform a state change on GET. Odoo's own type="http" routes accept both methods unless restricted with methods=["POST"] in the route declaration.

A network timeout on a POST leaves you not knowing if it happened. Safe retrying of non-idempotent calls requires an idempotency key (see REST design below).

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text:
The first digit gives the class.

Code Name Use 200 OK Success with a body 201 Created A resource was created; send Location 204 No Content Success, nothing to return (DELETE, OPTIONS) 301 / 302 Moved permanently / found Redirect to Location. Browsers turn a POST into GET on 302 303 See Other Redirect after POST to a GET page 304 Not Modified Cached copy is valid (ETag, If-None-Match) 400 Bad Request Malformed request or JSON 401 Unauthorized Not authenticated (missing or bad credentials) 403 Forbidden Authenticated but not allowed 404 Not Found No such resource (also used to hide existence) 405 Method Not Allowed Wrong method for this URL 409 Conflict State conflict, such as a duplicate or stale update 415 Unsupported Media Type Wrong Content-Type 422 Unprocessable Content Well-formed but fails validation 429 Too Many Requests Rate limited; honour Retry-After 500 Internal Server Error Unhandled server bug 502 / 503 / 504 Bad gateway / unavailable / gateway timeout Proxy or upstream trouble

A useful rule: 4xx means "you must change the request", 5xx means "the server failed; the same request might work later". Retry logic retries 5xx and 429 with backoff, and never 4xx.

Odoo specifics you will hit:

  • A type="json" route (the RPC style) answers with HTTP 200 even when the call failed; the failure is reported inside the JSON body under an error key. A client that only looks at the HTTP status will treat errors as success. Verify the shape on your version, but the convention has been stable for years.
  • A type="http" route returns real status codes. An access error from the framework becomes 403, a missing record routed through request.not_found() becomes 404, an unhandled exception becomes 500.
  • A request for a protected page without a session is redirected (302) to /web/login, so scripts that follow redirects can end up "successfully" downloading the login page. Check the final URL and Content-Type.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
Headers carry metadata about the message. The ones you will actually look at:

Header Direction Purpose Host request Which site on this server; Odoo's dbfilter can use it to pick a database Content-Type both Format of the body: application/json, application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, text/html; charset=utf-8 Accept request What formats the client wants Authorization request Credentials: Bearer <token> or Basic <base64(user:pass)> Cookie / Set-Cookie request / response Session state Location response Redirect target or the URL of a created resource Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified response Caching User-Agent request Client identification X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Forwarded-Host request via proxy Real client IP, scheme, host as seen by the proxy Retry-After response When to retry (429, 503)

Header names are case-insensitive. Values are not always.

The forwarded headers matter on every real Odoo deployment, because Odoo sits behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS. If the proxy does not send them and Odoo is not configured to trust them (proxy_mode in the configuration file), Odoo generates http:// links, loses client IPs, and cookies marked Secure misbehave. Misconfigured proxy headers are the most common cause of "login works on the server but redirects to the wrong URL".

docs.title: Content types for bodies
docs.text:
• application/json: the body is JSON. This is what you send to JSON endpoints.
  • application/x-www-form-urlencoded: a=1&b=two%20words. Traditional HTML form posts.
  • multipart/form-data: forms with file uploads; each part has its own headers.
  • A response may be text/html, application/pdf, image/png, text/csv, or a download with Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="loans.csv".

If a JSON endpoint receives application/x-www-form-urlencoded, it typically returns 400 or 415, or sees an empty body. Always send the header that matches the body.

docs.title: Cookies, sessions, and CSRF
docs.text:
A cookie is a small value the server stores in the browser with Set-Cookie; the browser sends it back on every later request to that site.

Set-Cookie: session_id=abc123; HttpOnly; Path=/; SameSite=Lax; Secure; Max-Age=604800

Attributes:

  • HttpOnly: JavaScript cannot read it. Protects the session ID from theft by injected scripts.
  • Secure: sent only over HTTPS.
  • SameSite: Lax (default in modern browsers) withholds the cookie on cross-site sub-requests such as images and POSTs from another site, Strict withholds it more broadly, None allows cross-site (and requires Secure).
  • Path and Domain: where the cookie applies.
  • Max-Age / Expires: lifetime; without it the cookie dies when the browser closes.

How Odoo uses them: after login, the server creates a session, stores it server-side (files in the data directory by default, or a configured store), and sets a cookie holding the session ID. The cookie name is session_id. Every request sends it; the server looks up the session to find the user, database, and context. Authentication via cookie is what lets a script reuse a login:

# 1. Authenticate (JSON-RPC style); -c saves the session cookie
curl -s -c cookies.txt -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"call","params":{"db":"<db>","login":"<login>","password":"<password>"}}' \
  http://localhost:8069/web/session/authenticate

# 2. Reuse it; -b sends the saved cookies
curl -s -b cookies.txt http://localhost:8069/web/session/get_session_info \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"call","params":{}}'

(<db>, <login>, <password> are placeholders, as everywhere in this book. Never put real credentials into scripts you commit.)

The session cookie lets a request act as the user. That is both the feature and the attack surface:

  • CSRF (cross-site request forgery): a malicious page makes the victim's browser send a request to your server, and the browser attaches the cookie automatically. Defences: SameSite cookies, and a secret token that a legitimate page embeds and a foreign page cannot read. Odoo type="http" routes that change data with POST check a csrf_token form field by default, which templates provide with request.csrf_token(). Turning that check off (csrf=False on the route) is legitimate for webhooks that authenticate by other means (a signature), and never for browser-facing forms.
  • Session fixation and theft: keep cookies HttpOnly and Secure, serve everything over HTTPS.

Cookies versus tokens: browsers use cookies naturally; server-to-server integrations prefer an explicit credential in the Authorization header, an API key or a bearer token, which does not require a login dance and is not subject to CSRF. Odoo supports API keys for external API use (generated by the user in their account security settings), usable in place of the password in RPC calls.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
Browsers enforce the same-origin policy: a script on https://a.example cannot read responses from https://b.example unless b opts in. An origin is scheme + host + port. CORS (cross-origin resource sharing) is that opt-in, done with response headers. The browser, not the server, enforces it, so curl is never blocked, which is why "works in curl, fails in the browser" is the classic symptom.

A cross-origin request is either simple or needs a preflight. If the request uses a method other than GET/HEAD/POST, or a custom header, or a Content-Type such as application/json, the browser first sends an OPTIONS request:

OPTIONS /books HTTP/1.1
Origin: https://portal.example
Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type

and expects:

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://portal.example
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type
Access-Control-Max-Age: 600

Only if the preflight passes does it send the real request, whose response must also carry Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Rules worth remembering:

  • Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * allows any origin but cannot be combined with credentials. For requests that send cookies (fetch(..., { credentials: "include" })), the server must name the exact origin and send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
  • Browsers hide response headers from scripts unless listed in Access-Control-Expose-Headers.
  • A CORS error does not mean the server rejected the call. The request often reached the server and ran; only the response was withheld from the script. For a POST that creates a record, you may have created it and not seen the result.

Odoo's route decorator has a cors parameter (@http.route("/library/api/books", type="json", auth="public", cors="*")) that adds the headers. Use a specific origin rather than * for anything that is not public data.

Same-origin is the easy case: a portal page served by Odoo calling Odoo's own routes needs no CORS at all. You only configure CORS when a different site's JavaScript calls Odoo.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
JSON is the data format of the web: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, true, false, null.

{
  "id": 3,
  "title": "Dune",
  "year": 1965,
  "price": 12.5,
  "available": true,
  "tags": ["sf", "classic"],
  "author": { "id": 7, "name": "F. Herbert" },
  "series": null
}

Strict rules, a stricter grammar than JavaScript object literals:

  • Keys are double-quoted strings. Strings use double quotes; 'single' is invalid.
  • No comments, no trailing commas, no undefined, no NaN/Infinity, no functions.
  • Numbers are decimal; no leading zeros and no hex. There is no integer type, only a number; very large integers lose precision in JavaScript (above 2^53), a concern for 64-bit identifiers. Send them as strings if you control the format.
  • There is no date type. Dates travel as strings. Use ISO 8601 (2025-03-01T10:00:00Z) in your own APIs, always with an explicit time zone or Z. Odoo's own Datetime fields serialise to "2025-03-01 10:00:00" in UTC, with a space and no zone marker, and Date fields as "2025-03-01"; convert deliberately.
  • There is no binary type. Binary data is base64 text, with a 33% size cost. Odoo Binary fields come over RPC as base64 strings.

Parsing and writing:

const text = '{"a":[1,2,{"b":null}]}';
const data = JSON.parse(text);              // throws SyntaxError on bad JSON
console.log(data.a[2].b);                   // null
console.log(JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)); // pretty print with 2 spaces
console.log(JSON.stringify({ d: new Date(0), u: undefined, n: null }));
// {"d":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z","n":null}   undefined keys are dropped, dates become strings

import json

payload = json.loads('{"a": [1, 2, {"b": null}]}')   # null -> None
print(payload["a"][2]["b"] is None)                 # True
print(json.dumps({"ok": True, "n": None}, indent=2, sort_keys=True))
print(json.dumps({"price": 12.5, "d": "é"}, ensure_ascii=False))

Mappings between Python and JSON: True/False to true/false, None to null, dict to object, list and tuple to array. Python's json does not serialise datetime, Decimal, or recordsets by default: convert them first, or pass default=str consciously. Odoo's json route type serialises standard cases for you; for your own type="http" responses, convert dates with fields.Date.to_string and friends before json.dumps.

Practical checks on JSON on the command line:

curl -s http://localhost:8765/books | python -m json.tool    # pretty printing
curl -s http://localhost:8765/books | jq '.items[].title'    # if jq is installed

docs.title: JSON-RPC and Odoo
docs.text:
JSON-RPC 2.0 is a tiny protocol on top of JSON over HTTP: the client sends a method name and params with an id; the server returns the same id with either a result or an error.

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "call", "params": { "a": 1 }, "id": 7 }

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "result": { "echo": { "a": 1 } } }

{ "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "error": { "code": 200, "message": "Odoo Server Error", "data": { "name": "odoo.exceptions.UserError", "message": "Cannot loan a book twice." } } }

In Odoo, type="json" routes use this envelope with method "call": whatever params carry becomes the keyword arguments of the controller method, and the return value becomes result. The web client calls model methods through /web/dataset/call_kw with params of the form { "model": "library.book", "method": "search_read", "args": [[["year", "<", 2000]]], "kwargs": { "fields": ["name"] } }. For external scripts, Odoo exposes the /jsonrpc endpoint and its execute_kw:

curl -s http://localhost:8069/jsonrpc -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "call", "id": 1,
  "params": {
    "service": "object", "method": "execute_kw",
    "args": ["<db>", <uid>, "<password_or_api_key>", "library.book", "search_read",
             [[["year", "<", 2000]]], {"fields": ["name", "year"], "limit": 5}]
  }
}'

<uid> is the numeric user id returned by a prior call to {"service": "common", "method": "login", "args": ["<db>", "<login>", "<password>"]}. The positional args after the credentials are the model, the method, the positional arguments of the ORM method, and a dictionary of keyword arguments. This is the same mechanism as the XML-RPC interface under /xmlrpc/2/, which accepts the same arguments in XML. The external API chapter later in the book builds complete clients; the shape is what matters here: model, method, args, kwargs.

The first two lines worth memorising when debugging an RPC call in the browser's network tab: the response status is 200 even for a failure, and the failure is in error.data.message (the text the user sees) and error.data.debug (the traceback, present in developer deployments).

Versions: the /jsonrpc and /xmlrpc/2/ endpoints, call_kw, and the envelope above are available across the versions covered here. Newer releases add other external API styles; consult the target version's documentation before choosing one for a new integration.

docs.title: Designing HTTP APIs (REST style)
docs.text:
When you add routes to Odoo for another system to call, you design a small API. The conventions of REST-style design keep it predictable:

  • Resources are nouns, methods are verbs. GET /library/api/v1/books, GET /library/api/v1/books/3, POST /library/api/v1/books, PATCH /library/api/v1/books/3, DELETE /library/api/v1/books/3. Not /getBook or /deleteBook.
  • Version the path (/v1/) so a breaking change does not break existing clients.
  • Filtering, sorting, paging in the query string: ?year_lt=2000&sort=-year&limit=20&offset=40. Return the total, or a cursor, so clients can page. Always put a default and a maximum on limit.
  • Consistent response shapes. List: { "items": [...], "total": 120 }. Error: { "error": { "code": "validation_failed", "message": "title is required", "fields": { "title": "required" } } }. Pick one error shape and keep it.
  • Correct status codes. 201 plus Location on creation, 204 on delete, 400/422 on bad input, 401 versus 403 as defined above, 404 for unknown ids, 409 for conflicts.
  • Authentication in a header, not in the URL (URLs end up in logs). API key or bearer token for server-to-server use.
  • Idempotency for POSTs that must not repeat. Accept an Idempotency-Key header, store the key with the result, and on a repeat return the stored result. This is how a client can safely retry after a timeout.
  • Dates in ISO 8601 with a zone, money as strings or integer minor units with a currency code, never floats.
  • Do not expose database ids if you have a better identifier and do not leak internal field names you may rename.
  • Rate limits and payload limits exist because someone will send a million rows. Check Content-Length, cap list sizes.
  • Return only what the caller is allowed to see. Routes with auth="public" and sudo() inside are a data leak waiting to happen; use record rules and fetch with the caller's user, as the security part explains.

Exposing everything an ORM model has is rarely a good API: shape the response explicitly.

# fragment of a controller; models, security and routing are covered in later parts
@http.route("/library/api/v1/books", type="http", auth="user", methods=["GET"])
def list_books(self, limit=20, offset=0, **kw):
    ...

The auth values and API-key handling are covered in the controller chapter; with auth="user" the caller needs a valid session, which an external client obtains by logging in first.

docs.title: curl: the debugging tool
docs.text:
curl shows what the wire carries. These commands were run against the scratch server.

# GET with response headers
curl -i http://localhost:8765/books

# Only the status code
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:8765/books

# POST JSON
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8765/books \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Ulysses"}'

# Validation failure: 422
curl -s -w ' -> %{http_code}\n' -X POST http://localhost:8765/books \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'

# Show the request and response in full, including TLS details
curl -v http://localhost:8765/books

# Preflight, as a browser would send it
curl -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:8765/books \
  -H 'Origin: https://portal.example' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST'

# Save and reuse cookies
curl -c jar.txt -X POST http://localhost:8765/login
curl -b jar.txt http://localhost:8765/books

# Send a body from a file
curl -X POST http://localhost:8765/books -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @book.json

# Follow redirects and show the final URL
curl -sL -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective} %{http_code}\n' http://localhost:8069/my

Useful flags: -i include response headers, -s silent, -v verbose, -X method, -H header, -d data (implies POST), -b/-c cookies in/out, -o output file, -w write-out format, -L follow redirects, -k skip TLS verification (never in scripts that matter), -u user:pass Basic auth.

Shell quoting breaks JSON on Windows cmd and PowerShell; use Git Bash, put the JSON in a file and use -d @file, or use PowerShell's Invoke-RestMethod. The browser's developer tools (Network tab, "Copy as cURL") give you a working command for any request the browser made, which is the fastest way to reproduce what the Odoo web client sends.

A minimal Python client with requests, for scripts:

import requests

BASE = "http://localhost:8765"
s = requests.Session()
s.post(f"{BASE}/login").raise_for_status()           # cookie kept in the session
r = s.post(f"{BASE}/books", json={"title": "Ulysses"}, timeout=10)
if r.status_code == 422:
    print("validation:", r.json())
else:
    r.raise_for_status()
    print(r.status_code, r.headers["Location"], r.json())

Always pass timeout; the library default is to wait forever, and a stuck remote call stalls an Odoo worker until it is killed.

docs.title: Debugging checklist
docs.text:
1. Reproduce with curl -v or the browser's Network tab. Look at the status, the Content-Type you sent and received, and the body.
  2. Status 200 from a JSON route: read the error key.
  3. Redirect to a login page: your session or credentials are missing; check the cookie.
  4. 403 versus 401: 401 means "who are you", 403 means "you may not". For Odoo, 403 on a controller often is a CSRF failure or an access rule.
  5. Works in curl, fails in the browser: CORS or cookies (SameSite, Secure, third-party restrictions).
  6. Works locally, wrong URLs in production: proxy headers and proxy_mode.
  7. Empty body received: wrong Content-Type, or the body was sent on a method that drops it.
  8. Timeouts: look at the server side first; a 504 from the proxy means the proxy gave up while Odoo kept working.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Trusting the status of JSON-RPC calls. HTTP 200 with an error key is a failure.
  • State change on GET. Prefetchers, crawlers, and email scanners will trigger it.
  • Missing Content-Type: application/json on a JSON body; the server reads nothing.
  • Following a redirect to the login page and treating the HTML as data.
  • Credentials in URLs and logs. Query strings are logged by proxies. Use headers.
  • csrf=False on browser-facing routes. Only for endpoints authenticated by a signature or token.
  • CORS as a security control. It restricts browsers only. Anyone with curl ignores it; authenticate and authorise on the server regardless.
  • Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with cookies. Browsers reject it. Name the origin.
  • Floats for money and large integer ids in JSON. Precision loss. Use strings or integer minor units.
  • Naive datetimes. A date string without a zone is ambiguous. State UTC or an offset, and know what Odoo stores.
  • No timeouts on outbound calls. A slow upstream ties up a worker.
  • Retrying non-idempotent requests blindly and creating duplicates. Add idempotency keys.
  • Unbounded list endpoints. No limit means one client can take the server down.
  • Returning tracebacks to clients. Log them; return a short error.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Read a response. Without running anything, say what each part of this response means and what a client should do next.

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
Content-Type: application/json

{"error":{"code":"rate_limited","message":"slow down"}}
Solution

Status 429: the client sent too many requests. Retry-After: 30 says to wait 30 seconds before trying again. The body is JSON with an error object whose code is machine-readable and whose message is for humans. The client should pause for 30 seconds (adding some random jitter), then retry the same request; a 4xx other than 429 would not be retried.

2. curl a JSON-RPC call. Write the curl command that calls a type="json" route at /library/api/ping with params {"name": "Ann"} on a local server, and say how to tell if it failed.

Solution 
curl -s http://localhost:8069/library/api/ping \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"call","params":{"name":"Ann"},"id":1}'

The HTTP status will be 200 either way. Failure is the presence of an error key in the response JSON, whose data.message holds the text. Success has a result key.

3. Choose status codes. For each case pick the best status code: (a) a client posts {"title": ""} to create a book and title is required; (b) a client asks for /books/9999 which does not exist; (c) a logged-in portal user requests another member's loan; (d) a client sends invalid JSON; (e) a client creates a loan successfully.

Solution

(a) 422 (or 400 if you do not distinguish validation from malformed input). (b) 404. (c) 403, or 404 if you prefer not to reveal that the loan exists. (d) 400. (e) 201 with a Location header pointing at the new loan.

4. Explain a CORS failure. A page at https://portal.example calls fetch("https://erp.example/library/api/ping", { method: "POST", headers: {"Content-Type": "application/json"}, credentials: "include" }). The browser console says the request was blocked, but the Odoo log shows a request arrived. What happened, and which headers must the response carry?

Solution

The request is cross-origin, uses application/json, so the browser sends a preflight OPTIONS first, then the real request. A request arrived, but the browser withheld the response from the script because the CORS headers were missing or insufficient. With credentials: "include" the server must send Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://portal.example (not *) and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true; the preflight response must also send Access-Control-Allow-Methods including POST and Access-Control-Allow-Headers including Content-Type.

5. Build and call. Run a scratch HTTP server of your own in Node with a GET /books route that returns a JSON list and a POST /books route that returns 422 when title is missing. Call both with curl and confirm the status codes.

Solution 
// server.mjs: run with `node server.mjs`
import http from "node:http";
const books = [{ id: 1, title: "Dune" }];
const send = (res, code, body, headers = {}) => {
  res.writeHead(code, { "Content-Type": "application/json", ...headers });
  res.end(JSON.stringify(body));
};
http.createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (req.url === "/books" && req.method === "GET") return send(res, 200, { items: books });
  if (req.url === "/books" && req.method === "POST") {
    let raw = "";
    for await (const chunk of req) raw += chunk;
    let data;
    try { data = JSON.parse(raw); } catch { return send(res, 400, { error: "invalid JSON" }); }
    if (!data.title) return send(res, 422, { error: "title required" });
    const book = { id: books.length + 1, title: data.title };
    books.push(book);
    return send(res, 201, book, { Location: `/books/${book.id}` });
  }
  send(res, 404, { error: "not found" });
}).listen(8765);

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' localhost:8765/books                                   # 200
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST localhost:8765/books -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'   # 422
curl -i -X POST localhost:8765/books -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"title":"Emma"}'  # 201 + Location

docs.title: JavaScript fundamentals
docs.text:
Odoo's web client, website, and portal are written in modern JavaScript: ES modules, classes, arrow functions, destructuring, and (from version 16 on) the OWL component framework. A Python developer can read most of it after a day and still be bitten for weeks by this, by ==, and by await forgotten in the wrong place. This chapter teaches the language as it is used in current Odoo code, and ends by showing what an OWL component looks like so the next parts of the book read naturally.

Every runnable snippet was executed with Node.js (version 20 or later). Save a snippet as demo.mjs and run node demo.mjs; the .mjs extension makes Node treat the file as an ES module, which is the same module system Odoo uses. Browser-only examples are marked.

docs.title: Values, variables, and types
docs.text:
Declare with const by default and let when you reassign. Do not use var.
