const name = "Dune";      // cannot be rebound
let copies = 3;           // can be rebound
copies += 1;
// name = "Emma";         // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable

const stops rebinding, not mutation: a const array can still be pushed to.

Primitive types: string, number (one type for integers and floats, a 64-bit float), bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol. Everything else is an object: plain objects, arrays, functions, dates, maps, sets.

console.log(typeof "x", typeof 1, typeof true, typeof undefined);   // string number boolean undefined
console.log(typeof null, typeof [], typeof {}, typeof (() => 1));   // object object object function
console.log(Array.isArray([]));                                      // true
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);                                              // 0.30000000000000004

Two consequences. typeof null is "object", a historical accident, so test for null explicitly. And all numbers are floats, so money must be handled in integer cents or by the server, never accumulated as JavaScript floats. Odoo monetary values arrive as numbers already rounded by the server; display them with the framework's formatting helpers instead of toFixed where available.

undefined means "no value was provided" (a missing property, an uninitialised variable, a function without return). null means "deliberately empty". Python's None maps to JSON null.

docs.title: Equality and truthiness
docs.text:
Use === and !==. The loose == converts types and produces results nobody remembers:

console.log(0 == "", "1" == 1, null == undefined, [] == false);  // true true true true
console.log(0 === "", "1" === 1, null === undefined);            // false false false
console.log(NaN === NaN, Object.is(NaN, NaN));                   // false true

Falsy values are false, 0, -0, "", null, undefined, NaN, 0n. Everything else is truthy, including [], {}, and "0". This differs from Python, where an empty list is falsy:

if ([]) console.log("empty array is truthy");
if (!Array.isArray(list) || list.length === 0) { /* check emptiness explicitly */ }

Two operators to know:

console.log(0 || "default");      // "default"  (|| replaces any falsy value)
console.log(0 ?? "default");      // 0          (?? replaces only null and undefined)
const user = { profile: null };
console.log(user.profile?.name);  // undefined  (optional chaining, no TypeError)
console.log(user.profile?.name ?? "anonymous");  // anonymous
let cache;
cache ??= new Map();              // assign only if null or undefined

Use ?? when 0 or "" are legitimate values. ?. also works on calls (obj.method?.()) and indexes (list?.[0]).

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
Template literals use backticks, support embedded expressions and multiple lines:

const book = { title: "Dune", year: 1965 };
const line = `${book.title} (${book.year ?? "n/a"})`;
console.log(line.toUpperCase(), line.length, line.includes("Dune"));
console.log("a-b-c".split("-"), "a-b-c".replaceAll("-", "+"), "7".padStart(3, "0"));

Strings are immutable and compared by value. In Odoo the translation helper _t("text") marks a string for translation. It needs a literal string, not a template literal with embedded expressions, because the extractor reads the source text. The details sit in the frontend part.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Three forms, all common:

function add(a, b) { return a + b; }            // declaration, hoisted
const mul = function (a, b) { return a * b; };  // expression
const sub = (a, b) => a - b;                    // arrow function

Arrow functions with a single expression return it implicitly; with a block they need return. Returning an object literal from an arrow needs parentheses: () => ({ a: 1 }).

Parameters can have defaults and a rest parameter collects the remainder:

function loan(book, { days = 14, renew = false } = {}, ...notes) {
  return { book, days, renew, notes };
}
console.log(loan("Dune"));
console.log(loan("Dune", { days: 7 }, "late fee", "call member"));

Passing an options object, with destructuring in the parameter list, is the idiom for any function with more than two or three parameters. Odoo code does it everywhere.

Functions are values. You pass them, return them, and store them in objects:

const apply = (fn, x) => fn(x);
console.log(apply((n) => n * 2, 21));  // 42

docs.title: Scope and closures
docs.text:
let and const are block scoped; var is function scoped and hoisted, which creates a classic bug:

const withVar = [];
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) withVar.push(() => i);
console.log(withVar.map((f) => f()));   // [ 3, 3, 3 ]   one shared i

const withLet = [];
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) withLet.push(() => j);
console.log(withLet.map((f) => f()));   // [ 0, 1, 2 ]   a fresh j per iteration

A closure is a function that remembers the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished:

function makeCounter() {
  let n = 0;
  return {
    inc: () => ++n,
    get value() { return n; },
  };
}
const c = makeCounter();
c.inc(); c.inc();
console.log(c.value);   // 2

n is private: only the two functions can reach it. Closures are the reason event handlers can use variables from the function that registered them, and the reason a stale variable in a handler is a common bug: the closure captures the variable, and in frameworks that re-run code per render, you can capture an old value.

A useful closure pattern is memoising:

function once(fn) {
  let done = false, result;
  return (...args) => (done ? result : ((done = true), (result = fn(...args))));
}
const init = once((x) => x * 2);
console.log(init(2), init(5));   // 4 4

docs.title: this
docs.text:
this is the object a function is called on, decided at call time, not at definition time. This is the largest difference from Python's self, which is an explicit parameter.

const obj = {
  name: "a",
  hello() { return this?.name; },
};
console.log(obj.hello());      // "a"   called as a method: this is obj
const detached = obj.hello;
console.log(detached());       // undefined   no object: this is undefined (module code is strict)

Rules, in order:

  1. new F(): this is the new object.
  2. obj.method(): this is obj.
  3. A plain call fn(): this is undefined in modules and strict mode (in sloppy scripts it was the global object).
  4. fn.call(x, ...), fn.apply(x, [...]), fn.bind(x): this is x.
  5. Arrow functions have no this of their own. They use the this of the enclosing code, fixed at definition.

Rule 5 is why arrows fit callbacks inside methods:

class Timer {
  seconds = 0;
  start() {
    const id = setInterval(() => {
      this.seconds++;          // arrow: this is the Timer instance
      if (this.seconds === 3) { clearInterval(id); console.log("done", this.seconds); }
    }, 10);
  }
}
new Timer().start();

With function () { this.seconds++ } the this would be wrong. The failure mode for the reverse, passing a method as a callback, is just as common:

class Counter {
  count = 0;
  inc = () => { this.count++; };   // class field holding an arrow: bound once per instance
  dec() { this.count--; }          // normal method: depends on the caller
}
const k = new Counter();
const { inc, dec } = k;
inc();
console.log(k.count);              // 1  works
try { dec(); } catch (e) { console.log(e.constructor.name); }   // TypeError: this is undefined

In OWL components, handlers referenced from templates (t-on-click="onClick") are bound to the component for you, so you can write ordinary methods. Handlers you register yourself on a DOM node or a timer in setup should be arrows or explicitly bound.

docs.title: Objects
docs.text:
const book = { title: "Dune", year: 1965, tags: ["sf"] };
book.author = "Herbert";          // add
delete book.year;                 // remove
console.log("title" in book, Object.keys(book), Object.values(book));
console.log(Object.entries(book).map(([k, v]) => `${k}=${v}`).join("&"));
console.log(Object.fromEntries([["a", 1], ["b", 2]]));   // { a: 1, b: 2 }

Shorthand and computed keys:

const title = "Dune", field = "year";
const rec = { title, [field]: 1965, describe() { return `${this.title}`; } };

Objects are references: assigning copies the reference, not the content.

const a = { n: 1, inner: { x: 1 } };
const b = a;                  // same object
const shallow = { ...a };     // new top level, shared inner
const deep = structuredClone(a);   // full copy (no functions)
shallow.inner.x = 9;
console.log(a.inner.x);       // 9: shallow copy shares the nested object
console.log(deep.inner.x);    // 1

JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) is the older deep copy trick; it loses undefined, functions, and turns dates into strings. Prefer structuredClone.

The Map and Set types are better than plain objects for dynamic keys and uniqueness:

const m = new Map([["a", 1]]);
m.set("b", 2);
console.log([...m], m.size, m.get("a"), m.has("z"));
console.log([...new Set([1, 1, 2, 3, 3])]);   // [ 1, 2, 3 ]

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
The array methods replace most loops. They return new arrays and do not mutate unless stated.

const loans = [
  { member: "Ann", book: "Dune", days: 3 },
  { member: "Bob", book: "Emma", days: 10 },
  { member: "Ann", book: "Ulysses", days: 7 },
];

loans.filter((l) => l.days > 5).map((l) => l.book);      // [ 'Emma', 'Ulysses' ]
loans.find((l) => l.member === "Bob");                    // first match or undefined
loans.some((l) => l.days > 9);                            // true
loans.every((l) => l.days > 0);                           // true
loans.map((l) => l.days).reduce((sum, d) => sum + d, 0);  // 20
loans.at(-1).book;                                        // 'Ulysses'
loans.flatMap((l) => [l.member, l.book]);                 // flattened one level

Grouping with reduce, the long-standing form, and totals per key:

const totals = loans.reduce(
  (acc, { member, days }) => ({ ...acc, [member]: (acc[member] ?? 0) + days }),
  {}
);
console.log(totals);   // { Ann: 10, Bob: 10 }

Newer runtimes also have Object.groupBy(loans, (l) => l.member). It is not available in the oldest browsers, so check the browsers you support before using it in a module that ships to users.

Mutating methods: push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse. sort sorts as strings by default:

console.log([10, 9, 1].sort());                 // [ 1, 10, 9 ]
console.log([10, 9, 1].sort((a, b) => a - b));  // [ 1, 9, 10 ]

Another classic trap:

console.log(["1", "2", "3"].map(parseInt));     // [ 1, NaN, NaN ]  map passes (value, index)
console.log(["1", "2", "3"].map(Number));       // [ 1, 2, 3 ]

Iterate with for...of (values) or Object.entries for pairs. Avoid for...in over arrays: it yields keys and inherited properties.

for (const [i, loan] of loans.entries()) console.log(i, loan.book);

There is no negative indexing with brackets; arr[-1] is undefined. Use .at(-1).

docs.title: Destructuring, spread, and rest
docs.text:
Destructuring unpacks arrays and objects into variables:

const [first, , third = "none", ...others] = ["a", "b", undefined, "d", "e"];
console.log(first, third, others);   // a none [ 'd', 'e' ]

const { title, author: writer = "?", meta: { pages } = { pages: 0 } } =
  { title: "Dune" };
console.log(title, writer, pages);   // Dune ? 0

Spread expands an iterable or object into another one:

const a = [1, 2], b = [...a, 3];                  // [1, 2, 3]
const defaults = { days: 14, renew: false };
const options = { ...defaults, days: 7 };         // later keys win
const { id, ...rest } = { id: 1, x: 2, y: 3 };    // rest = { x: 2, y: 3 }

The pattern { ...state, field: newValue } produces a changed copy without mutating the original. It is how you update objects in code that must not mutate (for example, a value passed in as props).

Swap two variables: [x, y] = [y, x].

docs.title: Control flow in brief
docs.text:
if (a) { } else if (b) { } else { }
switch (state) { case "draft": /* ... */ break; default: break; }
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { }
for (const x of iterable) { }
while (cond) { }
try { risky(); } catch (err) { handle(err); } finally { cleanup(); }

Ternary: cond ? a : b. Short-circuit: ready && start(). Labels exist for breaking out of nested loops (outer: for (...) { ... continue outer; }), rarely needed.

Errors are objects: throw new Error("message"). Throwing strings loses the stack trace.

try {
  JSON.parse("{bad json}");
} catch (err) {
  console.log(err.name, err.message);   // SyntaxError ...
}

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
class Book {
  static count = 0;     // class-level
  #id;                  // private field
  constructor(title, { author = "?", year } = {}) {
    this.title = title;
    this.author = author;
    this.year = year;
    this.#id = ++Book.count;
  }
  get label() { return `${this.title} (${this.year ?? "n/a"})`; }
  get id() { return this.#id; }
  toString() { return this.label; }
  static fromObject(o) { return new Book(o.title, o); }
}

class Ebook extends Book {
  constructor(title, opts) {
    super(title, opts);                 // must be called before using this
    this.format = opts?.format ?? "epub";
  }
  get label() { return `${super.label} [${this.format}]`; }
}

const e = new Ebook("Dune", { year: 1965 });
console.log(e.label, e.id, String(e));        // Dune (1965) [epub] 1 Dune (1965) [epub]
console.log(e instanceof Book, Object.getPrototypeOf(Ebook) === Book);

Compared to Python classes: the constructor is constructor, super(...) must run before this is used in a subclass, methods are defined without self, static members belong to the class, getters are declared with get, and #name fields are truly private. Class fields (count = 0;) are initialised per instance before the constructor body.

Underneath, classes are syntax over prototypes: methods live on Class.prototype, and an instance finds a missing property by walking the prototype chain. You can ignore this until you read framework code that patches a method; the patch helper in Odoo's frontend replaces methods on a class prototype and calls the original through super.

Mixed-in behaviour via functions that return classes is also used in framework code, but you will write plain subclasses 95% of the time. Composition (holding a helper object) is usually simpler than deep inheritance.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
A module is a file. export names what is public; import brings names in.

// math.mjs
export const TAX = 0.2;
export function net(gross) { return gross / (1 + TAX); }
export default class Ledger { }

// main.mjs
import Ledger, { TAX, net as netAmount } from "./math.mjs";
import * as math from "./math.mjs";
console.log(net === math.net, TAX);

Rules: named exports are imported by their name in braces; a default export without braces under any name; paths are relative (./) or a module specifier a loader resolves. A module executes once, on first import, and every importer shares its exports (live bindings). Imports are hoisted: they are evaluated before the code in the file.

Odoo has its own module loader. In the web client you do not write relative paths between modules; you import by module name:

import { Component, useState } from "@odoo/owl";
import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";
import { useService } from "@web/core/utils/hooks";
import { _t } from "@web/core/l10n/translation";
import { LibraryCard } from "@library/components/card/card";

@odoo/owl is the OWL library, @web/... is the web addon's static/src folder, and @library/... is your own module's static/src. The file path inside the addon's static/src becomes the module name.

Versions: in Odoo 16 and 17, a JavaScript file in an asset bundle is recognised as an ES module only if its first line is the comment /** @odoo-module **/. Later versions relax this for files that use import/export; verify on your build, and note that keeping the annotation is always harmless. If a new file seems not to load in 16 or 17, a missing annotation is the first thing to check.

Node does not know Odoo's @web/... specifiers, so your own pure-logic helper files (formatting, calculations) are best written without importing from @web so you can test them with node directly.

docs.title: Date, numbers, JSON
docs.text:
const d = new Date("2025-03-01T10:00:00Z");
console.log(d.toISOString(), d.getTime(), d.getUTCFullYear());
console.log(JSON.stringify({ d: new Date(0), u: undefined, n: null }));
// {"d":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z","n":null}
console.log(JSON.parse('{"a":[1,2,{"b":null}]}').a[2].b);  // null
console.log(Number("12.5"), parseInt("12px", 10), (1234.5).toFixed(1), Number.isInteger(2));
console.log(Number("abc"), Number(""), Number(null));        // NaN 0 0

new Date("2025-03-01") (date only) parses as UTC midnight, while new Date("2025-03-01T00:00") (no zone) parses as local time. Odoo stores datetimes in UTC and transmits them as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS" strings, which are not ISO and must be converted by the framework's helpers (a luxon DateTime in recent versions) rather than new Date(string). Treat all date conversions as "use the framework helper" in Odoo code.

docs.title: What OWL component code looks like
docs.text:
You have now seen every language feature that an OWL component uses. A fragment of a component for a library card, written for Odoo 17/18 style (this is a fragment: it needs the template and an asset bundle to run, covered in the frontend part):

import { Component, useState } from "@odoo/owl";
import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";
import { useService } from "@web/core/utils/hooks";

export class LoanCounter extends Component {
  static template = "library.LoanCounter";
  static props = {
    bookId: Number,
    label: { type: String, optional: true },
  };

  setup() {
    this.orm = useService("orm");
    this.state = useState({ count: 0, loading: false });
  }

  async refresh() {
    this.state.loading = true;
    try {
      this.state.count = await this.orm.searchCount("library.loan", [
        ["book_id", "=", this.props.bookId],
      ]);
    } finally {
      this.state.loading = false;
    }
  }
}

registry.category("actions").add("library.loan_counter", LoanCounter);

Map each line to this chapter: import from a named module; class ... extends with static fields; setup() instead of a constructor (the framework calls it); a destructuring-free options object for props; this.state as reactive object where assignment triggers a re-render; async/await with try/finally for the request; the registry call at the bottom registering the component under a key. The matching template is XML with t- directives, and the next chapter covers async/await and the DOM.

You can feel what useState does with a tiny model, runnable in Node. A Proxy intercepts assignments, and the framework re-renders when it sees one:

function reactive(target, onChange) {
  return new Proxy(target, {
    set(obj, key, value) {
      obj[key] = value;
      onChange(key, value);
      return true;
    },
  });
}
const state = reactive({ count: 0 }, (k, v) => console.log("render", k, v));
state.count++;       // render count 1
state.count += 2;    // render count 3

OWL's useState is built on the same idea, with batching and dependency tracking. The practical rules follow from it: mutate state through the reactive object, replace values rather than keeping a separate reference to a plain object you created before wrapping, and do not expect changes to non-reactive fields to re-render anything.

Versions: The component style shown here targets Odoo 17 and 18. Odoo 16 also uses OWL 2 but some helpers, hooks, and service access differ between releases. Check the target version's source for any hook you rely on.

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text:
• Run snippets: node file.mjs. For quick experiments, node opens a REPL; paste code and see results.
  • The browser console (F12) runs modern JavaScript too; in Odoo, developer mode adds an asset debugging option that loads unminified code, which makes stack traces readable.
  • A formatter and a linter save time: Prettier formats, ESLint finds undefined variables and unused imports. Odoo's own repository uses ESLint with a project config; copy its habits (double quotes, semicolons, 4-space indentation, const).
  • Check syntax without running: node --check file.mjs.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• this lost when passing a method as a callback. setTimeout(obj.method) calls it detached. Use an arrow wrapper, a bound class field, or .bind.
  • Arrow functions as object methods. { f: () => this.x } uses the outer this, not the object.
  • == and truthiness. Use ===; test emptiness of arrays explicitly (list.length), and use ?? when 0 or "" are valid.
  • sort() without a comparator sorts numbers as strings.
  • map(parseInt) passes the index as the radix.
  • for...in on arrays and mutating an array while iterating it.
  • Shallow copies. { ...obj } and slice() share nested objects; mutating them changes the original. Prefer structuredClone for real copies.
  • Mutating props or state you do not own. In frameworks with reactivity, mutate only state you created; treat props as read-only.
  • Floating-point money. 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3. Let the server round, or work in integer minor units.
  • new Date(string) guessing. Different formats parse as different time zones. Use the framework's date helpers for Odoo's string format.
  • Forgetting await. A promise is truthy; if (check()) on an async function always passes. The next chapter covers it.
  • Unhandled undefined. a.b.c throws if b is missing. Use ?. where absence is legitimate, and let it throw where absence is a bug.
  • Missing the module annotation in Odoo 16/17, which results in a file that is bundled but whose import lines fail with a syntax error in the browser console.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Closure. Write makeLimiter(max) returning a function that returns true the first max times it is called and false afterwards.

Solution 
function makeLimiter(max) {
  let calls = 0;
  return () => calls++ < max;
}
const lim = makeLimiter(2);
console.log(lim(), lim(), lim());   // true true false

calls lives in the closure; each limiter has its own counter.

2. this. Why does this code throw, and give two fixes?

class Btn {
  label = "Save";
  onClick() { return this.label; }
}
const { onClick } = new Btn();
onClick();
Solution

onClick is detached from the instance, so this is undefined in module code and this.label throws a TypeError. Fix 1: define the handler as a class field arrow, onClick = () => this.label;. Fix 2: bind at the point of use, const b = new Btn(); const f = b.onClick.bind(b); or call it as b.onClick().

3. Array pipeline. Given the loans array above, produce an object with the total days per member, for loans of 5 days or more, using one reduce and one filter.

Solution 
const totals = loans
  .filter((l) => l.days >= 5)
  .reduce((acc, { member, days }) => ({ ...acc, [member]: (acc[member] ?? 0) + days }), {});
console.log(totals);   // { Bob: 10, Ann: 7 }

4. Destructuring. Write a function describe taking one argument shaped like { title, meta: { pages = 100, tags: [firstTag = "none"] = [] } = {} } and returning "title: pages, firstTag". What does describe({ title: "Dune" }) return?

Solution 
const describe = ({ title, meta: { pages = 100, tags: [firstTag = "none"] = [] } = {} }) =>
  `${title}: ${pages}, ${firstTag}`;
console.log(describe({ title: "Dune" }));   // Dune: 100, none

Each default applies when its part is undefined: meta missing gives {}, tags missing gives [], and firstTag missing gives "none".

5. Reactive helper. Extend the reactive function so onChange is not called when the new value equals the old one.

Solution 
function reactive(target, onChange) {
  return new Proxy(target, {
    set(obj, key, value) {
      const changed = obj[key] !== value;
      obj[key] = value;
      if (changed) onChange(key, value);
      return true;
    },
  });
}
const s = reactive({ n: 1 }, (k, v) => console.log("render", k, v));
s.n = 1;   // nothing
s.n = 2;   // render n 2

docs.title: XML for Odoo
docs.text: Almost everything an Odoo module ships besides Python and JavaScript is XML: views, menus, security groups, report templates, email templates, demo data. A single stray & or an unclosed tag stops module installation with a parser error that points at a line you did not write. This chapter teaches XML as a language, then shows exactly how Odoo reads a data file, so that the errors become predictable and the eval, ref, and noupdate attributes stop looking like magic.

docs.title: What XML is
docs.text:
XML is a tree of elements. Every document has exactly one root element, every element is closed, and the text between tags is data. There is no built-in meaning for any tag name: <record> means something only because Odoo's loader says so.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<odoo>
    <record id="book_dune" model="library.book">
        <field name="name">Dune</field>
        <field name="year">1965</field>
    </record>
</odoo>

The pieces:

  • Declaration <?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>: optional, but Odoo files always carry it. It must be the very first thing in the file, with no blank line or space before it. If you declare an encoding, the file must actually be saved in that encoding. Use UTF-8 everywhere.
  • Element: <field name="year">1965</field> has a start tag, text content, and an end tag. An element with no content can be self-closing: <field name="year"/>.
  • Attribute: name="year". Values are always quoted, with double or single quotes. <field name=year> is invalid, and so is an attribute without a value (<button disabled> is HTML, not XML).
  • Text: everything between tags, including whitespace and newlines.
  • Comment: <!-- ... -->. A comment cannot contain -- and cannot nest.
  • Root: one element wraps everything. In Odoo data files it is <odoo>.

docs.title: Well-formed
docs.text:
A document is well-formed if tags are properly nested and closed, attribute values are quoted, there is exactly one root, and special characters are escaped. A parser rejects everything else outright; XML has no "best effort" mode, unlike HTML.

<!-- Not well-formed: wrong nesting -->
<b><i>text</b></i>

<!-- Not well-formed: unclosed -->
<field name="year">1965

<!-- Not well-formed: two roots -->
<odoo/><odoo/>

Tag names are case-sensitive: <Field> and <field> are different elements, and the end tag must match the start tag exactly.

Well-formed and valid are two different checks. Well-formed means the syntax is right. Valid means the document also follows a schema. Odoo validates view architectures against a RelaxNG schema shipped with the base addon, so a view can be well-formed XML and still be rejected at load time for an unknown tag or attribute.

docs.title: Escaping
docs.text:
Five characters are special. Two of them are always dangerous in text and attributes.

Character Write it as Notes < < Always escape in text and attribute values & & Always escape. The most common cause of load failures > > Legal raw in text, but escape it for consistency " " Required inside a double-quoted attribute ' ' Required inside a single-quoted attribute

The place this bites in Odoo is domains and Python expressions that live in attributes:

<!-- Broken: raw '<' inside an attribute -->
<field name="domain">[('year', '<', 2000)]</field>   <!-- text content: also broken -->

<!-- Correct -->
<field name="domain">[('year', '<', 2000)]</field>

The symptom is lxml.etree.XMLSyntaxError: StartTag: invalid element name (for a <) or xmlParseEntityRef: no name (for an &). The line number it reports is usually right.

The same applies to view attributes in Odoo 17 and later, where visibility is a Python-like expression:

<field name="year" invisible="year < 1000 and state != 'done'"/>

Python's and/or need no escaping. The operators <, <=, and a bitwise & do.

Escaping works through numeric references too: < is < and € is the euro sign. You rarely need them, because UTF-8 lets you type the character directly.

docs.title: CDATA
docs.text:
A CDATA section says "everything until ]]> is literal text":

<field name="code"><![CDATA[
for rec in records:
    if rec.year < 2000 and rec.copies > 1:
        rec.flag = True
]]></field>

This is the readable way to embed Python or SQL that contains many < and &. Two limits: CDATA cannot contain the sequence ]]>, and it works only in text content, never in attribute values. Odoo's server action code field is the typical user.

docs.title: Attributes versus text
docs.text:
Both carry data, with one practical difference: attribute values are normalised by the parser. Newlines and tabs inside an attribute value become spaces, so a multi-line domain or invisible expression still works, but a multi-line attribute can never carry meaningful line breaks. Put anything that needs newlines (Python code, HTML, an email body) in element text.

Text keeps whitespace as written. In Odoo most field loaders strip surrounding whitespace for simple types (Char, Integer), but not inside HTML or text content you intend to be exact. Do not rely on indentation inside text you care about; for Text and Html fields keep the content flush with the tag if the exact bytes matter.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
A namespace prefixes tag names so that vocabularies do not collide: <svg:rect> versus <html:rect>. A prefix is bound to a URI with xmlns:prefix="...", and a default namespace with plain xmlns="..." applies to every unprefixed element below it.

Odoo data files and views use no namespaces. Elements like <record>, <field>, <t> and attributes like t-if and t-foreach are plain names; the t- prefix is a naming convention, not an XML namespace. The places you meet namespaces:

  • Inline SVG in a QWeb template: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 10 10">...</svg>. Without xmlns, the browser treats the contents as unknown HTML elements.
  • Reading other people's XML with Python: {http://example.org/ns}tag is how a namespaced tag looks in ElementTree and lxml.
  • Electronic invoice formats and SOAP: heavy namespace use. In Python you write explicit namespace maps.
from lxml import etree

doc = etree.fromstring(b'<a xmlns="urn:x" xmlns:p="urn:y"><p:b/><c/></a>')
print([el.tag for el in doc.iter()])
# ['{urn:x}a', '{urn:y}b', '{urn:x}c']
print(doc.findall('{urn:y}b'))
print(doc.xpath('//x:c', namespaces={'x': 'urn:x'}))

Note xpath('//c') would find nothing: unprefixed names in XPath mean "no namespace", not "the default namespace". This is the reason people think XPath on invoice XML is broken.

docs.title: How Odoo parses a data file
docs.text:
Files listed in the manifest data or demo keys with the extension .xml go to Odoo's XML loader (odoo/tools/convert.py), which builds a tree with lxml and walks it element by element. It does not execute the file as a whole; it interprets each top-level element as a command.

manifest 'data': ['views/book_views.xml']
   |
   v
lxml parses the file -> tree
   |
   v
for each child of <odoo> (or of <data>):
     <record>   -> create or update a database row
     <template> -> create a QWeb view row (ir.ui.view)
     <menuitem> -> create menu rows (ir.ui.menu)
     <function> -> call a model method
     <delete>   -> remove records by id or search

docs.title: Root and noupdate
docs.text:
The root element is <odoo>. Older files wrap their content as <odoo><data>...</data></odoo>, and older still, <openerp><data>. All forms load; the inner <data> is optional and only matters when you need noupdate:

<odoo>
    <data noupdate="1">
        <record id="seq_loan" model="ir.sequence">
            <field name="name">Loan</field>
            <field name="code">library.loan</field>
        </record>
    </data>
    <record id="book_dune" model="library.book">...</record>
</odoo>

noupdate="1" means: create the record when the module is first installed, but never overwrite it on later module updates (-u library). It exists for records the user is expected to edit, such as sequences, email templates, and default configuration. Records without it are overwritten from the file on every update, so a manual edit in the UI is lost. Both the <odoo noupdate="1"> and <data noupdate="1"> forms work. Records are marked per record in ir.model.data, and the flag is only applied when the record is created or updated by the loader.

docs.title: The record element
docs.text:
<record id="loan_demo_1" model="library.loan">
    <field name="book_id" ref="book_dune"/>
    <field name="member_id" ref="base.partner_demo"/>
    <field name="date_out" eval="(datetime.now() - timedelta(days=3)).strftime('%Y-%m-%d')"/>
    <field name="copies" eval="1"/>
    <field name="note">Reserved by phone.</field>
</record>
  • model: the technical model name. If it does not exist at load time (the module that defines it is not in depends), loading fails.
  • id: the XML ID suffix. Odoo stores it as <module>.<id> in ir.model.data. Without a dot, the module name is prefixed automatically. With a dot (other_module.some_id), you refer to or overwrite a record from another module. IDs must be unique per module.
  • <field name="x">text</field>: the text is the field value. For Char, Text, Selection it is used as a string. For Integer, Float, Boolean Odoo converts the string, but it is cleaner to use eval.
  • ref="xml_id": resolves an XML ID to a database ID. Use it for Many2one.
  • eval="python expr": evaluates a Python expression and uses the result.
  • search="[domain]": finds the record(s) by domain, used for rare cases when no XML ID exists.
  • type="xml" or type="html": the element's children are the value, serialised back to a string. This is how a view's arch is stored.
  • file="path" with type="base64": reads a file relative to the module and stores it base64-encoded, as for an image.

docs.title: eval in detail
docs.text:
eval is a Python expression, not a statement, evaluated with a restricted set of names in scope. The set includes ref (a function returning a database ID from an XML ID), time, datetime, timedelta, relativedelta, and a few more. Treat anything beyond ref, datetime, timedelta, and time as unavailable until you have checked your version's convert.py.

<!-- Boolean, integer, float: eval keeps the type -->
<field name="active" eval="False"/>
<field name="copies" eval="3"/>
<field name="price" eval="12.5"/>

<!-- A Many2one as an id -->
<field name="member_id" eval="ref('base.partner_demo')"/>

<!-- Many2many and One2many: list of command tuples -->
<field name="tag_ids" eval="[(6, 0, [ref('tag_fiction'), ref('tag_classic')])]"/>
<field name="line_ids" eval="[(0, 0, {'name': 'Line 1', 'qty': 2})]"/>

The command tuples are (0, 0, vals) create, (1, id, vals) update, (2, id) delete, (3, id) unlink, (4, id) link, (5,) unlink all, and (6, 0, ids) replace. In Python code you can also use Command.create(...); in XML data the tuples are the portable form.

A frequent mistake is putting a bare number or word without eval: <field name="active">False</field> stores a string, and whether the loader converts it to a boolean depends on the version. Use eval="False" and the question never arises.

ref as an attribute versus ref() in eval is the same lookup. Prefer the attribute; use the function when you build a list or dictionary.

docs.title: Dates and times in data
docs.text:
Fixed dates are plain text in ISO format: <field name="date_out">2025-03-01</field> and 2025-03-01 14:30:00 for datetimes. For demo data that should always look recent, compute from datetime:

<field name="date_out" eval="(DateTime.today() - relativedelta(days=2)).strftime('%Y-%m-%d')"/>

DateTime and relativedelta are available in the eval context in standard data files. If you are not sure in your version, datetime.now() and timedelta are the safe pair.

docs.title: Views as records
docs.text:
A view is a record of ir.ui.view whose arch field contains the view XML:

<record id="library_book_view_form" model="ir.ui.view">
    <field name="name">library.book.form</field>
    <field name="model">library.book</field>
    <field name="arch" type="xml">
        <form string="Book">
            <sheet>
                <group>
                    <field name="name"/>
                    <field name="year"/>
                </group>
            </sheet>
        </form>
    </field>
</record>

type="xml" is what tells the loader to serialise the child elements into the arch text. When the view is read, the server parses arch again, validates it against the schema, and applies inheritance. Form, list, and search structure are covered in the data and views part; here the point is that the file you write is a record wrapper around an XML document, so two parsers are involved: the file parser at install time and the view parser at read time.

docs.title: Template shortcut
docs.text:
QWeb templates have shorthand: <template> is expanded to an ir.ui.view record with type="qweb".

<template id="report_book_card">
    <t t-call="web.html_container">
        <t t-foreach="docs" t-as="o">
            <div class="page">
                <h2 t-out="o.name"/>
            </div>
        </t>
    </t>
</template>

Attributes of <template> include id, name, inherit_id, priority, active, customize_show, and t-name-less operation: the id becomes the template's name. The body of <template> is the template content, so any <, & in expressions needs escaping exactly as above: t-if="o.year < 2000".

Versions: t-esc and t-raw were the output directives up to 14. From 15 onward t-out is the output directive and t-esc/t-raw are deprecated aliases that still work in many versions. Write t-out in new code. The template and QWeb chapters cover the distinction.

docs.title: Menus
docs.text:
<menuitem> is shorthand for creating ir.ui.menu rows:

<menuitem id="menu_library_root" name="Library" sequence="30"/>
<menuitem id="menu_library_books" name="Books"
          parent="menu_library_root" action="action_library_book" sequence="10"/>

Omitting parent makes a top-level app entry. Menu structure follows from parent XML IDs, and groups restricts visibility.

docs.title: function, delete
docs.text:
<function model="library.book" name="_demo_populate"/>
<delete model="ir.ui.view" search="[('name', '=', 'library.book.legacy')]"/>

<function> calls a model method (by name, on the model, with no records unless you pass ids). Because <function> runs on every load of the file, the method must be idempotent. <delete> removes by id or by search and appears mostly in migration-style cleanup.

docs.title: Inheritance in XML
docs.text:
Extending someone else's view is XML-level editing: the new record names its parent and describes edits as XPath operations.

<record id="library_book_view_form_inherit" model="ir.ui.view">
    <field name="name">library.book.form.inherit</field>
    <field name="model">library.book</field>
    <field name="inherit_id" ref="library.library_book_view_form"/>
    <field name="arch" type="xml">
        <xpath expr="//field[@name='year']" position="after">
            <field name="isbn"/>
        </xpath>
    </field>
</record>

expr is an XPath 1.0 expression evaluated against the parent arch. The mechanics (positions, attributes, priorities, and why a broad XPath breaks on update) have a chapter of their own; the syntax you need here is XPath's: // any depth, [@name='x'] attribute test, [1] first match, .. parent.

You can try XPath outside Odoo to learn it:

from lxml import etree
arch = etree.fromstring("""
<form><sheet><group>
  <field name="name"/><field name="year"/>
</group></sheet></form>""")
print(arch.xpath("//field[@name='year']"))      # one element
print(arch.xpath("//group/field[1]/@name"))     # ['name']
print(arch.xpath("//field[@name='missing']"))   # [] -> in Odoo this raises at view-combine time

docs.title: Checking a file before you start the server
docs.text:
Starting Odoo to find a typo costs a minute. Check well-formedness first:

# libxml2 tools (Linux, macOS; Windows via WSL or a package)
xmllint --noout library/views/book_views.xml

# No xmllint? Python is already installed
python -c "import sys, lxml.etree as e; e.parse(sys.argv[1]); print('ok')" library/views/book_views.xml

Both report the line and column of the first error. This catches syntax only; unknown fields in a view, bad XML IDs, and schema errors surface when Odoo loads the file. Running the module with a throwaway database speeds that cycle:

odoo-bin -d scratch -i library --stop-after-init

docs.title: A mental checklist for a failing data file
docs.text:
1. Is the parse error XMLSyntaxError? It is a syntax problem: escaping, unclosed tag, or a character before the XML declaration. Look at the reported line.
  2. Is the error ValueError: External ID not found in the system: module.name? A ref points at a record that does not exist yet. Check the file order in the manifest (a file can only reference records created by files earlier in the list or by modules in depends) and the module prefix.
  3. Is the error Invalid field 'x' on model 'y' in a view? The field name is wrong, or the field belongs to a module not in depends.
  4. Did the record load but not change after -u? It is under noupdate, or an XML ID with a different prefix created a second record.
  5. Did the whole view vanish? It may be active=False, or an inheriting view failed and was skipped in a way you did not see; read the server log from top.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Unescaped < and & in domains, eval, t-if, and invisible. Always < and &. A text editor with XML syntax highlighting makes the mistake visible.
  • Text before the XML declaration (BOM aside): a blank first line causes XML or text declaration not at start of entity.
  • noupdate surprises. You change a record in the XML, upgrade, and nothing happens. Either the record is in a noupdate block, or someone edited it manually and the loader respects that for noupdate records only. Check ir.model.data.noupdate for the XML ID. The inverse also hurts: a QWeb template you wanted users to customise gets overwritten on every update.
  • Wrong file order in the manifest. Security files first, then data that other files reference, then views, then menus and actions that reference views. A menu that references an action defined in a later file fails.
  • Same id in two files of one module. The second silently becomes an update of the first. Use a naming scheme such as <model>_view_<type> so collisions are visible.
  • Whitespace-sensitive content. An Html field or a Text field with newlines picks up your indentation. Put it flush-left, or strip it in code.
  • Boolean and number as text. <field name="active">False</field> is a string. Use eval.
  • Putting < in CDATA inside an attribute. CDATA works only in text nodes.
  • Tabs and mixed encodings. A file saved as Latin-1 with an encoding="utf-8" declaration fails on the first accented character, usually in a translated string.
  • Assuming the data file is run like a script. Records are created in document order, but a <function> earlier in the file runs when the loader reaches it, before records below it exist.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Find the errors. This file fails to load. List every problem.

 <?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<odoo>
    <record id="book_a" model="library.book">
        <field name="name">Rock & Roll</field>
        <field name="year">1999
        <field name="active">False</field>
    </record>
    <record id=book_b model="library.book"/>
</odoo>
Solution
  1. A space before <?xml: the declaration must be the first bytes of the file.
  2. Rock & Roll: raw &, write Rock & Roll.
  3. <field name="year">1999 is never closed (</field> missing), so the following <field> nests inside it and the tags no longer match.
  4. id=book_b is missing quotes around the value.
  5. Not a syntax error but wrong: <field name="active">False</field> stores the string; use eval="False".

Check with xmllint --noout file.xml; it reports problems one at a time, so fix and rerun.

2. Write a record with relations. Write a library.loan record whose book_id points to the XML ID book_dune and whose tag_ids (Many2many to library.tag) links two records with XML IDs tag_fiction and tag_classic, and whose date_out is three days ago.

Solution 

<record id="loan_demo_1" model="library.loan">
    <field name="book_id" ref="book_dune"/>
    <field name="tag_ids" eval="[(6, 0, [ref('tag_fiction'), ref('tag_classic')])]"/>
    <field name="date_out" eval="(datetime.now() - timedelta(days=3)).strftime('%Y-%m-%d')"/>
</record>

ref as an attribute works for the Many2one; the Many2many needs a command list in eval. The (6, 0, ids) command replaces the whole set.

3. Escape a domain. A window action needs the domain "year before 2000 and copies at least 2". Write it as a <field name="domain"> of a ir.actions.act_window record.

Solution 

<field name="domain">[('year', '<', 2000), ('copies', '>=', 2)]</field>

< is required. > is legal raw, but keeping both escaped makes the pattern uniform.

4. Namespaces. Parse <root xmlns="urn:a"><item>1</item><item>2</item></root> in Python and print the text of both items.

Solution 

from lxml import etree
root = etree.fromstring(b'<root xmlns="urn:a"><item>1</item><item>2</item></root>')
print([e.text for e in root.xpath('//a:item', namespaces={'a': 'urn:a'})])
# ['1', '2']

root.xpath('//item') returns an empty list because unprefixed XPath names mean "no namespace". Bind a prefix, or use {urn:a}item with findall.

5. Update behaviour. You mark <data noupdate="1"> around an email template, install the module, edit the template body in the UI, change the body in the XML, and run -u library. What does the UI show, and how do you force the XML version?

Solution

The UI keeps the edited body, because the loader skips updating noupdate records. To force the XML version, delete the record (or its ir.model.data row so the record is recreated), or temporarily remove the noupdate flag and update; do this on a copy of the database first, because the manual edits are lost.

?>

docs.title: Anatomy of a module
docs.text: A module is a Python package plus a manifest and a set of data files. The manifest tells Odoo what to load and in which order; the folders are convention, except for the few names the framework treats specially. Knowing which parts are convention and which are contract saves you from cargo-culting a layout that does not matter and ignoring one that does.

docs.title: The smallest useful module
docs.text:
library/
  __init__.py
  __manifest__.py
  models/
    __init__.py
    book.py
  security/
    ir.model.access.csv
  views/
    book_views.xml

# __manifest__.py
{
    'name': 'Library',
    'version': '18.0.1.0.0',
    'summary': 'Books and loans',
    'category': 'Services/Library',
    'license': 'LGPL-3',
    'depends': ['base', 'mail'],
    'data': [
        'security/ir.model.access.csv',
        'views/book_views.xml',
    ],
    'application': True,
    'installable': True,
}

# __init__.py
from . import models

# models/__init__.py
from . import book

# models/book.py
from odoo import fields, models


class LibraryBook(models.Model):
    _name = 'library.book'
    _description = 'Library Book'

    name = fields.Char(required=True)
    isbn = fields.Char(copy=False)

Every Python file must be imported from an __init__.py chain starting at the module root. A model file that is not imported is simply not part of the registry; there is no error.

docs.title: Manifest keys
docs.text:
Key Purpose name Display name. Required. version Convention: <series>.<major>.<minor>.<patch>, e.g. 18.0.1.0.0. If you give a short version, Odoo prefixes the series. Migration scripts are selected by comparing this. summary, description, category, author, website, license Metadata. A missing license logs a warning and defaults to LGPL-3. depends Modules that must be loaded first. Defaults to ['base']. This is the only thing that decides load order. data Files loaded at install and at every update, in the listed order. demo Files loaded only when demo data is enabled. assets JS, SCSS, and XML bundles (from 16; earlier versions used QWeb templates in data). application Shows the module as an app in the Apps list. installable False hides it from installation. auto_install True, or a list of modules: installed automatically once all dependencies are installed. external_dependencies Python packages and binaries checked at install. pre_init_hook, post_init_hook, uninstall_hook, post_load Python hooks, names of functions in the module's __init__.py.

Versions: hook signatures changed. In 16, pre_init_hook and post_init_hook receive (cr, registry); from 17 they receive env. A module that supports both needs a compatibility shim or separate branches. Check the odoo/modules/loading.py of your branch.

docs.title: Standard folders
docs.text:
Only some names mean something to the framework. The rest are convention.

Folder Role models/ Python models. Convention. views/ XML views, actions, menus. Convention; files are loaded because they are in data. security/ ir.model.access.csv and record rule XML. Convention, but ir.model.access.csv is the expected name of the ACL file. data/ Records with noupdate data, sequences, cron jobs, mail templates. demo/ Demo data listed under demo. wizard/ (or wizards/) Transient models. Convention. report/ QWeb report templates and report models. controllers/ HTTP controllers. Convention; imported from __init__.py. static/ Served to the browser as /library/static/.... This name is contract. static/description/icon.png is the app icon and index.html the Apps page description. static/src/ Frontend sources, referenced in assets. i18n/ .po and .pot translation files, loaded by language code. Contract. tests/ Test classes. Test discovery imports tests/__init__.py. Contract. migrations/ Upgrade scripts. Contract, see below.

docs.title: Load order inside a module
docs.text:
1. Dependencies are loaded first, recursively. Order among independent dependencies is not specified; do not rely on it.
  2. The module's Python package is imported, which defines the model classes.
  3. The registry is built for the models (see Registry and model loading).
  4. On install or update, the data files are processed in the order listed, then demo files if demo is enabled.
  5. Hooks run: pre_init_hook before data on install, post_init_hook after.

Within data, order is yours to get right. Security CSV first, so that views and menus that reference groups do not fail; views before the menus and actions that reference them; data records before anything that points at them by XML id.

'data': [
    'security/library_security.xml',     # groups
    'security/ir.model.access.csv',      # ACLs reference groups and models
    'data/library_sequence.xml',
    'views/book_views.xml',              # views and actions
    'views/menus.xml',                   # menus reference actions
],

docs.title: XML IDs and noupdate
docs.text: Records created from data files get an XML ID module.name stored in ir.model.data. On update, Odoo matches records by that ID and overwrites them, unless the record sits in a noupdate="1" block. noupdate is for data that users are expected to edit (mail templates, sequences). If you change a noupdate record in code and update the module, nothing happens on databases that already have it. That is the single most common "my data change is not applied" report.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
library/migrations/18.0.1.1.0/pre-migrate.py
library/migrations/18.0.1.1.0/post-migrate.py

A script runs when the installed version is lower than the folder version and the manifest version is equal or higher. pre- runs before the module's data and schema are updated, post- after. Each script defines migrate(cr, version). Forgetting to bump the manifest version means the script never runs.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Missing depends. A module works on your database because another module happened to load first, then fails on a clean install with "model or field not found" or an XML ID error. Test installs on an empty database with only your dependencies.
  • Wrong order in data. A view referencing a group defined in a later file raises ValueError: External ID not found.
  • File not listed in data. The file exists, is never loaded, and nothing complains.
  • Tab or space style in CSV. ir.model.access.csv must have the exact header and one blank-free line per rule; a stray empty column makes the whole file fail.
  • Models with no access rule. In 16 and later a model with no ACL logs a warning at load and is unreachable for non-superusers. Add the ACL in the same change as the model.
  • Renaming a module directory. XML IDs, ir_model_data rows, and installed state all carry the old name. Rename through a migration, not just the folder.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
odoo-bin scaffold library_demo /tmp/addons     # compare its output with the layout above
psql -d dev -c "select module, name, noupdate from ir_model_data where module='library' limit 10;"

docs.title: Command line reference
docs.text: odoo-bin --help prints a wall of options. In daily work about twenty matter, and a handful of them are routinely misused. This chapter groups them by task and says what each one does in the framework. Option definitions live in odoo/tools/config.py in each branch; when a switch behaves differently from what you read here, that file is the authority for your version.

docs.title: Selecting the database
docs.text:
Switch Meaning -d, --database Database to operate on. A comma-separated list is accepted for batch -i / -u. -r, --db_user / -w, --db_password PostgreSQL credentials. --db_host, --db_port Connection target. An empty host means the Unix socket. --db-filter Regular expression limiting which databases the web client shows and accepts. %d expands to the first label of the host name, %h to the full host. --no-database-list Hide the database manager and selector (list_db = False). --db_maxconn Connection pool size per process.

--db-filter is the multi-database switch that causes the most support tickets. If a login page keeps returning to the database selector, the filter matches zero or several databases for that host name. In production, aim for one filter that matches exactly one database per host name.

docs.title: Modules: install, update, test
docs.text:
odoo-bin -d dev -i library --stop-after-init          # install
odoo-bin -d dev -u library --stop-after-init          # update
odoo-bin -d dev -u all --stop-after-init              # update everything (slow, upgrade day)
  • -i installs modules and their dependencies. If a module is already installed, it is skipped; use -u to apply changes.
  • -u reloads the module's data files and applies schema changes for the models it defines or extends. It does not reload Python code in a running server; restart the process (or use --dev=reload in development).
  • -u on a module also updates the modules that depend on it, which is why updating base is effectively updating everything.
  • --without-demo=all (or a module list) controls demo data at install time.

-u changes the database. On anything that is not a disposable copy, run it first on a restored backup and keep the previous dump. A failed update can leave a half-migrated schema.

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
odoo-bin -d test_db -i library --test-enable --stop-after-init --log-level=test
odoo-bin -d test_db -u library --test-tags /library:TestLoan.test_overdue --stop-after-init

--test-enable runs the tests of the modules being installed or updated. --test-tags filters; the grammar is [-][tag][/module][:Class][.method]. Tags include at_install and post_install; a leading - excludes. Pass both --test-enable and --test-tags unless you have verified in your branch that tags alone enable tests.

docs.title: HTTP and process model
docs.text:
Switch Meaning -p, --http-port Port for HTTP. Default 8069. --http-interface Bind address. Use 127.0.0.1 behind a reverse proxy. --gevent-port (older: --longpolling-port) Port of the separate process for live updates (bus, chat). Odoo 18 documents only --gevent-port (verified in odoo/tools/config.py); 16 uses --longpolling-port. Default 8072. --workers Number of HTTP worker processes. 0 means threaded mode. --max-cron-threads Number of cron threads (threaded mode) or cron workers (multi-process). --proxy-mode Trust X-Forwarded-* headers. Only behind a proxy that sets them. --limit-memory-soft, --limit-memory-hard Per-worker memory ceilings in bytes. --limit-time-cpu, --limit-time-real, --limit-time-real-cron Per-request CPU and wall-clock limits in seconds. --limit-request Requests a worker serves before being recycled.

The last group is explained in Workers, cron, and longpolling.

docs.title: Development switches
docs.text:
odoo-bin -c dev.conf -d dev --dev=all
odoo-bin -c dev.conf -d dev --dev=xml,reload

--dev takes a comma-separated list. In Odoo 18 the help text lists all, reload, qweb, xml (verified in odoo/tools/config.py): reload restarts on Python file change, xml reads views and QWeb templates from disk on each request, qweb enables template debugging, and all is the shorthand. Older branches also document werkzeug (browser debugger, never on a reachable server) and pdb (post-mortem debugger); check --help on your branch before relying on them.

Two details save time. reload depends on the watchdog package being installed; without it, expect a warning and no reload. And xml re-reads only views that come from files: a view edited through the UI lives in the database and is unaffected.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
--log-level=debug_sql
--log-handler=odoo.addons.library:DEBUG
--log-handler=odoo.sql_db:DEBUG
--logfile=/var/log/odoo/odoo.log

--log-level accepts, among others, critical, error, warn, info, debug, debug_rpc, debug_rpc_answer, debug_sql, and test. debug_sql prints every query with its duration and is the fastest way to find an N+1 pattern. --log-handler takes logger:LEVEL pairs and is repeatable, which is how you raise one module to debug without drowning in the rest.

Without --logfile, logs go to stderr, which is what you want under systemd or in containers.

docs.title: Subcommands
docs.text:
odoo-bin has subcommands beside the server:

odoo-bin shell -d dev                       # interactive shell with env
odoo-bin scaffold library ./custom          # module skeleton
odoo-bin db dump dev dev.zip                # database management
odoo-bin db load newdev dev.zip
odoo-bin populate -d dev --models library.book --size small

shell opens a Python console with env bound to the database. It runs in a transaction that is not committed unless you call env.cr.commit().

Versions: in Odoo 18 the db subcommand offers load, dump, duplicate, rename and drop (verified in odoo/cli/db.py), and the other built-in commands are shell, scaffold, server, start, deploy, neutralize, populate, cloc and upgrade_code. The db subcommand (dump, load, duplicate, drop) and the way translation export is invoked have changed between 16, 17 and 18. Run odoo-bin --help and odoo-bin db --help in your checkout before scripting against them. On older branches translations are exported with --i18n-export=file --modules=... -l ....

docs.title: Configuration precedence
docs.text:
1. Command line switch.
  2. Value in the -c config file (or the file named by the ODOO_RC environment variable, or ~/.odoorc).
  3. Built-in default.

-s writes the effective values back to the config file, including passwords given on the command line. Check the file afterwards and never commit it.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• -u with a misspelled module name logs a warning and carries on. Read the log after a scripted update.
  • -i on an installed module is skipped. Use -u.
  • --stop-after-init forgotten in a deploy script: the "update" step never returns because the server stays up.
  • --workers on a developer machine gets in the way of --dev=reload and debuggers. Develop in threaded mode.
  • --db-filter and -d together. -d names the database for batch operations; the filter still applies to web requests.
  • --test-enable on a populated database. Tests roll back, but side effects such as queued mails and external calls can leave traces. Use a copy.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
odoo-bin --help | grep -E "dev|workers|limit|gevent|longpolling"
odoo-bin -c dev.conf -d dev -u library --stop-after-init --log-level=debug_sql 2>&1 | tail -50

docs.title: Installing and running
docs.text: A from-source checkout gives you a debugger, a git history you can bisect, and the freedom to run several versions side by side. This chapter sets up a development environment you can throw away and rebuild in ten minutes, and explains the three things that make a first run fail: Python version, PostgreSQL access, and the addons path.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Component Odoo 16 Odoo 17 Odoo 18 Python 3.7 to 3.10 (3.10 recommended) 3.10+ 3.10+ PostgreSQL 12+ 12+ 12+ wkhtmltopdf 0.12.6 with patched Qt same same Node (rtlcss, for right-to-left languages only) optional optional optional

Check the exact floor in requirements.txt and setup/ of the branch you checked out; the supported range moves with each release and distribution packages lag. Treat the table as a starting point, not a contract.

wkhtmltopdf matters only for PDF reports. A missing or unpatched build does not stop the server; it produces PDFs without headers and footers, which is a confusing symptom to meet for the first time on someone else's machine.

docs.title: Layout on disk
docs.text:
Keep Odoo itself, your own addons, and the virtualenv in separate directories. Never put your modules inside the Odoo checkout: upgrading the checkout (git pull, branch switch) must not touch your code.

~/odoo/
  16.0/            # git clone --branch 16.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/odoo/odoo
  18.0/
  venv-16/
  venv-18/
  custom/          # your addons repositories
  conf/
    dev-18.conf

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
git clone --branch 18.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/odoo/odoo ~/odoo/18.0
python3 -m venv ~/odoo/venv-18
. ~/odoo/venv-18/bin/activate
pip install -U pip wheel
pip install -r ~/odoo/18.0/requirements.txt

On Debian-family systems, install the build dependencies first (libpq-dev, libldap2-dev, libsasl2-dev, libxml2-dev, libxslt1-dev, libjpeg-dev, zlib1g-dev), otherwise psycopg2, python-ldap, or lxml fail to compile. The failure surfaces halfway through pip install, and the error text points at a missing header, not at the package you need to install.

A shallow clone (--depth 1) is fast and fine for running. If you need git blame or git log -S on the framework, which you will, drop the flag or run git fetch --unshallow later.

docs.title: PostgreSQL role
docs.text:
Odoo refuses to run as the postgres superuser. Create a dedicated role that may create databases:

sudo -u postgres createuser --createdb --pwprompt odoo_dev

Without --createdb the database manager and -d newdb -i base fail with a permission error. Do not make the role a superuser. If a module needs an extension such as unaccent or pg_trgm, creating it once as postgres in template1 is cleaner than widening the role. (Whether a given module needs one depends on the version and your configuration; check the log of the first install.)

docs.title: The configuration file
docs.text:
Every command line switch can live in a config file. Generate one from the current switches with --save (short -s), then edit it:

~/odoo/18.0/odoo-bin -c ~/odoo/conf/dev-18.conf -s \
  --addons-path=$HOME/odoo/18.0/addons,$HOME/odoo/custom/library \
  --db_host=localhost --db_user=odoo_dev --db_password=secret \
  --stop-after-init

A minimal dev-18.conf:

[options]
addons_path = /home/dev/odoo/18.0/odoo/addons,/home/dev/odoo/18.0/addons,/home/dev/odoo/custom/library
db_host = localhost
db_user = odoo_dev
db_password = secret
http_port = 8069
log_level = info
dbfilter = ^dev_.*$
list_db = True

Note the two core directories. odoo/addons holds base and a few framework modules; addons holds the rest. Leaving out odoo/addons makes the first run fail because base cannot be found. Copying addons_path from a generated config is the safest approach.

Config keys use underscores (db_host). On the command line, most options accept both hyphens and underscores (--db_host, --db-host); the hyphenated form is the one the help output shows for newer options. When in doubt, run odoo-bin --help.

docs.title: First run
docs.text:
~/odoo/18.0/odoo-bin -c ~/odoo/conf/dev-18.conf -d dev_library -i base --without-demo=all --stop-after-init
~/odoo/18.0/odoo-bin -c ~/odoo/conf/dev-18.conf -d dev_library --dev=xml,reload

The first command creates the database, loads base, and exits. The second starts the server on http://localhost:8069. --stop-after-init is how you run installation and upgrade as a batch step; it is also the only sane way to run them in CI or a deploy script.

--without-demo=all skips demo data. Demo data is useful when you learn the standard apps and harmful when you want to see how your module behaves on a realistic database, because demo records hide missing-data bugs. Decide per database at creation time: the demo flag is recorded when modules are first installed, and flipping it later means recreating the database.

The login after -i base is admin / admin. Change it before the database is reachable from anywhere but your laptop.

docs.title: Multiple versions side by side
docs.text: One virtualenv, one config file, and one database name prefix per version. A database created by 16 cannot be opened by 18 without a migration: the server sees modules with older versions and tries to upgrade them or fails. A dbfilter prefix (dev16_, dev18_) keeps the wrong server from listing the wrong databases.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Run the server as an unprivileged account, never as root. A stray odoo-bin shell as root writes filestore files that the service account cannot read afterwards.

  • Port already in use. A forgotten server on 8069 makes the new one fail at bind time. ss -ltnp | grep 8069 first.
  • -u without -d. With no database selected, the update has nothing to act on; the server starts and waits. Always pass -d in scripts.
  • Wrong virtualenv. The framework is run from the checkout, not installed. pip list | grep -i odoo should show nothing; an old odoo package in the venv can shadow the checkout.
  • Filestore location. Attachments live outside the database, in data_dir (default under your user's local share directory). Copying only a database dump gives a copy with missing images and attachments. Set --data-dir explicitly for every instance.
  • Two instances, one database. Two servers on the same database both run the crons. Never start a second dev server against a shared database without disabling crons (see Workers, cron, and longpolling).

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# read-only: what does this build think its options are?
~/odoo/18.0/odoo-bin --help | head -40
# does the role connect, and what databases exist?
psql -U odoo_dev -h localhost -l
# after the first run, which modules are installed?
psql -U odoo_dev -d dev_library -c "select name, state, latest_version from ir_module_module where state='installed' order by name limit 10;"

docs.title: Odoo.sh and deployment
docs.text: Whether you deploy to a hosted platform or to your own server, the shape of the job is the same: code arrives from version control, an environment builds from it, modules are updated against a database, and processes restart. This chapter describes the hosted platform's model (branches, builds, three stages) and then the checklist for a self-managed server. Where the platform's behaviour is documented by the vendor and not by the framework source, details can change; confirm against the vendor documentation.

docs.title: The hosted model
docs.text:
On Odoo.sh, a Git repository is the source of truth and every branch can become a running environment ("build"). Branches have one of three stages:

Stage Database Purpose Development Fresh, demo or restored data, destroyed on rebuild Try a change, run tests Staging A copy of production data, mail and crons neutralised Validate a change on real data Production The real database Serving users

Pushing to a branch triggers a build: the platform checks out the commit, installs requirements, creates or updates the database, and starts the server. On a development branch the build installs modules on an empty database and runs tests. On a staging branch the database is a restored copy of production on which the changed modules are updated, which is the closest rehearsal of an upgrade you get. Production builds update the existing database in place after a push.

A build has states you will read in the build list: green (succeeded), yellow (succeeded with warnings in the log), red (failed). A failed update on production leaves the previous build still serving; read the failure before pushing again.

docs.title: Repository conventions
docs.text:
The platform scans the repository for modules; top-level directories with a manifest are modules, and submodules are supported for third-party code. Add a requirements.txt at the root for Python dependencies; it is installed during the build, not on a running instance. Keep the module layout described in Project layout and addons path, and pin third-party submodules to a commit so a build is reproducible.

Branch naming follows the series: a branch whose name the platform recognises with a version prefix is built for that Odoo version. Check the vendor documentation for the exact rule before branching.

docs.title: Day-to-day workflow
docs.text:
1. Create a feature branch from production. It builds as development.
  2. Push commits; each push is a build with logs and test results.
  3. Open the web client of that build, the shell, and the logs in the platform interface.
  4. Merge to a staging branch, or promote the feature branch to staging; validate on production data.
  5. Merge to production. The platform updates the modules that changed (it detects them from the diff and manifest versions) and restarts.

The platform updates only the modules whose files changed. If you rely on a data record that changed in a module you did not touch, it will not be updated. Bumping the manifest version of the affected module makes the intent explicit and triggers migrations.

docs.title: Logs and shell
docs.text:
Each build has log files and a browser-based shell attached to the instance. The useful logs: the server log (odoo.log), the install/update log from the build, the PostgreSQL log, and the HTTP access log. Search with grep in the shell; logs rotate, so a failure from three days ago may be gone.

The shell gives you odoo-bin shell against the build's database, same as locally. On production, the shell is not a place to experiment: anything you commit there is production data.

docs.title: Backups and restores
docs.text:
Production databases are backed up automatically; the platform keeps several daily backups and lets you restore into a staging branch or download them. Rules that follow from the model:

  • Restore to a staging branch to test migrations, not directly onto production.
  • A restored database on staging carries production data. Respect privacy rules for that environment.
  • Test a restore periodically. A backup you have not restored is a hope, not a backup.

docs.title: Self-managed deployment checklist
docs.text:
For a server you run yourself, build the same discipline by hand.

  1. Package. A tagged commit of your repositories and the exact Odoo checkout commit. Deploy artifacts, not "git pull on the server".
  2. Install dependencies in a versioned virtualenv from requirements.txt.
  3. Back up the database and the filestore, and check that the dump is readable.
  4. Update on a copy first. Restore the production dump to a scratch database, run odoo-bin -d copy -u module --stop-after-init, read the log, and run smoke tests. Time it: the duration is your downtime estimate.
  5. Maintenance window. Stop the service, or route traffic to a maintenance page.
  6. Update production: odoo-bin -c prod.conf -d prod -u module1,module2 --stop-after-init. The update runs without worker limits.
  7. Start the service under systemd; check logs for warnings that were not there before.
  8. Verify with a scripted login and a few model reads.
  9. Rollback plan: the previous code tag plus the pre-update dump. Rolling back code without the dump rarely works, since the schema has changed.

A minimal systemd unit:

[Unit]
Description=Odoo
After=postgresql.service

[Service]
User=odoo
ExecStart=/srv/odoo/venv/bin/python /srv/odoo/18.0/odoo-bin -c /etc/odoo/odoo.conf
Restart=on-failure
KillMode=mixed

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Behind a reverse proxy, set --proxy-mode, bind HTTP to localhost, enable --workers, and route the live-update port as described in Workers, cron, and longpolling. Set list_db = False and a strict dbfilter, and put the master password (admin_passwd) in a file readable only by the service account.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Pushing to production with a red staging build. The same update will fail on production. Do not.
  • Migrations that work on demo data only. Development builds use small data. Test on the staging copy, where volumes, nulls, and odd historic records exist.
  • Forgetting the filestore when copying an instance by hand: the database restores, images and attachments are gone.
  • Staging sending real mail. On the platform, outgoing mail is blocked on non-production builds; on your own staging, disable ir.mail_server and crons yourself.
  • Long updates. A recompute of a stored field on a large table can hold locks for many minutes. Estimate on the staging copy; consider a migration script that fills the column in batches.
  • Version drift. Production on one commit of the framework, staging on another. Pin the Odoo commit as well as your own.
  • Uncommitted shell changes. Fixing data in a production shell without recording the script in the repository makes the next environment differ. Put one-off fixes in a migration script.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# rehearse an update on a restored copy (self-managed)
createdb -T template0 copy && pg_restore -d copy prod.dump
odoo-bin -c prod.conf -d copy -u library --stop-after-init --log-level=info 2>&1 | tee update.log
grep -E "WARNING|ERROR|CRITICAL" update.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

docs.title: Project layout and addons path
docs.text: Odoo finds modules by scanning directories listed in addons_path. Everything else about project layout follows from that one rule: a module is a directory with a manifest, directly inside one of the listed directories. This chapter covers how to structure repositories around it, how the scan resolves duplicates, and what breaks when the path is wrong.

docs.title: How the scan works
docs.text:
At startup (and when you click "Update Apps List") Odoo walks each directory in addons_path, one level deep. A subdirectory is a module if it contains __manifest__.py (older code used __openerp__.py; ignore it). The directory name is the technical module name and must be a valid Python identifier, because it becomes the package odoo.addons.<name>.

addons_path = /srv/odoo/18.0/odoo/addons,/srv/odoo/18.0/addons,/srv/custom/library,/srv/custom/third-party

Consequences:

  • Modules are not found recursively. /srv/custom/library/library/ is a module only if /srv/custom/library is in the path, and /srv/custom alone would not find it.
  • Order matters for duplicates. If two directories contain a module with the same name, the first one in the path wins and the other is silently ignored. A fork of a standard module placed earlier than the core directory shadows the original; placed later, it is never loaded and you wonder why your change has no effect.
  • Names are global across all directories. Two repositories that both ship sale_extra collide.
  • The scan only decides what is available. What is loaded is decided by what is installed in the database, plus dependencies.

docs.title: Repository layout that scales
docs.text:
One repository per concern, each a directory of modules, none of them nested:

~/odoo/custom/
  library/               # a repository, added to addons_path
    library/             # a module (library.book, library.loan)
      __manifest__.py
      __init__.py
      models/ views/ security/ data/ static/ tests/
    library_portal/
    library_reports/
  third-party/
    some_oca_module/

Practical conventions:

  • Prefix module names with a project or domain token (library_) so they sort together and cannot collide with standard or community names.
  • One feature per module. A module with depends on half the system cannot be installed in a test database cheaply.
  • A thin "glue" module per customer or deployment, last in the dependency chain, with settings and data that only matter there. Reusable logic stays in other modules.
  • Keep dependencies as an acyclic graph that you can draw. Circular depends are rejected at load time with a clear message; indirect cycles through auto_install are harder to spot.

docs.title: Environment-specific paths
docs.text:
Keep paths out of the repository. The repository holds code; the config file on each machine holds addons_path. Using --addons-path on the command line overrides the config file, which is useful in CI:

odoo-bin -d ci --addons-path=odoo/addons,addons,$PWD --test-enable -i library --stop-after-init

Relative paths are resolved against the current working directory, not against the config file, so a relative addons_path in a config used from two directories behaves differently. Use absolute paths in long-lived configs.

docs.title: What else Odoo adds to the path
docs.text:
Odoo appends its own odoo/addons directory automatically in recent versions, and base is always available, but relying on it is fragile across versions and distributions. Listing both core directories explicitly is clearer and costs nothing.

On hosted platforms the platform assembles the path for you from the repository (every top-level module directory and submodule is scanned). See Odoo.sh and deployment.

docs.title: Python dependencies
docs.text:
A module declares pip dependencies with external_dependencies in its manifest:

'external_dependencies': {'python': ['openpyxl'], 'bin': ['pdftotext']},

Odoo checks them at install time and refuses with an explicit error if one is missing. This only protects the machine where you install; a missing package on production after a deploy shows up as a failed upgrade. Keep a requirements.txt next to the modules and install it as part of every deploy.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
A duplicate module name does not raise an error. The earlier path entry wins. If a change in your fork "does nothing", print the module's real location from a shell: import odoo.addons.library; print(odoo.addons.library.__path__).

  • Module added but not listed. The Apps list is cached in ir.module.module. After adding a directory, update the list (Apps menu in developer mode) or start with -u base. Merely restarting does not rescan for the web UI.
  • Directory name with a hyphen (library-portal) is not importable. Rename the directory; the Git repository name can keep the hyphen.
  • Symlinks work, but deployments that copy trees without following links lose them silently.
  • Stale .pyc or removed modules. Deleting a directory of an installed module leaves the database record in state installed; the next start logs "module not found" and later updates can fail on its dependants. Uninstall first, then remove the code.
