  • Nested addons directories. Putting custom/ inside addons/ of the core checkout makes upgrades of the checkout destroy or conflict with your code.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# which directories does this server scan?
odoo-bin shell -d dev <<'PY'
from odoo.modules import module
print(module.ad_paths)
PY
# where does a given module come from?
odoo-bin shell -d dev <<'PY'
print(env['ir.module.module'].search([('name', '=', 'library')]).mapped('state'))
import odoo.addons.library as m; print(m.__path__)
PY

docs.title: Registry and model loading
docs.text: An Odoo model is not a single Python class. It is the result of combining every class that declares or extends the same _name, across every installed module, into one class built at runtime. That combined set of models, one per database, is the registry. Most "my override is ignored" and "field not found" problems are explained by how the registry is built, so this chapter walks through it.

docs.title: One registry per database
docs.text:
Each database served by a process has its own Registry object (odoo.modules.registry.Registry). It holds the final model classes, the field definitions, the SQL constraints, the cache, and signals for cross-process invalidation. Two databases on the same server can have different modules installed, so env['library.book'] is a different class in each.

Consequences you will meet:

  • Code at module import time cannot know which database it is for. Never read the database at import. Do it in methods or in _register_hook.
  • Memory grows with the number of loaded databases. Multi-database servers with many large registries need an eye on --limit-memory-* and on --db-filter.

docs.title: From classes to a model
docs.text:
When Odoo loads a module, importing its Python files defines classes. A metaclass records each one in the module's list. Then, for each model in the module, the registry runs _build_model:

class LibraryBook(models.Model):            # defines
    _name = 'library.book'
    name = fields.Char()

class LibraryBookExt(models.Model):         # extends in place
    _inherit = 'library.book'
    isbn = fields.Char()

class LibraryBookMixin(models.Model):       # inherits another model by copy
    _name = 'library.rare.book'
    _inherit = ['library.book', 'mail.thread']
  • A class with _name only defines a new model.
  • A class with _inherit and no _name, or with _name equal to one of the parents, extends that model in place.
  • A class with a new _name and _inherit creates a new model that copies the parents' fields and methods (prototype inheritance). The new table is separate.
  • _inherits = {'parent.model': 'parent_id'} is delegation: the child has its own table and exposes the parent's fields through a many2one. It is a different mechanism, rarely what you want.

The final class is built by creating a new Python class whose bases are all the extension classes in load order, followed by the original definition. That is why super() in an override reaches the code from modules loaded earlier: the MRO is the module load order, reversed.

docs.title: Load order decides override order
docs.text:
Modules are loaded in dependency order. Among modules at the same depth, the order is by sequence and then by name; it is deterministic but you should not depend on it. If module A and B both override library.book.write and neither depends on the other, which runs first is unspecified.

class LibraryBook(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'library.book'

    def write(self, vals):
        # runs before the code of every module loaded earlier
        res = super().write(vals)
        # runs after
        return res

Rule: if you need to run after or before another module's override, depend on that module in depends. Do not rely on alphabetical order.

docs.title: What happens at startup
docs.text:
The loader in odoo/modules/loading.py does this for each database, in simplified order:

  1. Load base and set up the registry.
  2. For each module in dependency order: import Python package, build its models, create or update tables and columns (_auto_init), load data files, run hooks.
  3. After all modules of the batch are loaded, finalize: _setup_complete, add constraints, create indexes, compute stored fields that were added, and call _register_hook on every model.
  4. Run post-install tests if enabled.
  5. When the registry is ready, the server starts serving requests for the database.

Schema changes are made during step 2, per module. A field added in your module gets its column on update, not at ordinary startup. That is why Python code changes need only a restart, while model changes need -u.

Versions: from 17 on, many tables and column definitions follow the same flow but index creation and some constraint handling moved into dedicated steps (for example, _sql_constraints is still honoured in 17 and 18; check your branch if you are touching the schema code itself). The registry-building idea is identical across 16, 17 and 18.

docs.title: Lazy loading and reload
docs.text:
On first request after startup, registries are created lazily per database. If a request arrives for a database whose registry is not loaded, it is loaded then and the user waits. On large installations, this means the first request after a restart can take tens of seconds.

When a module is installed, updated or uninstalled in a running multi-process server, the process that did it reloads its own registry and records a signal in the database (the ir_sequence rows named base_registry_signaling and base_cache_signaling). Other workers check those sequences at the start of each request and reload when they changed. This is how a running pool converges after an update without restarts. It is also why a long-running worker can briefly use stale code or stale cache after another process changed the database.

docs.title: Registry hooks you can use
docs.text: Hook When Use _register_hook After the registry is complete, every time it is loaded Patching methods dynamically, setting up one-time per-registry state _auto_init During schema update Rarely overridden; use init() to create SQL views init() After table creation Create database views or indexes for _auto = False models post_init_hook (manifest) After install, once Data fixups

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Never import another module's models in a way that creates a hard dependency without declaring it in depends. The import works when the module is installed, and crashes the registry build when it is not.

  • Class-level state. Mutable class attributes are shared by every database in the process. Keep state on the environment or in the database, not on the class.
  • Overriding without super(). The extension chain is a chain only if everyone calls super(). Skipping it silently disables every module loaded earlier.
  • Field type change in an extension. Redefining a field with a different type is allowed and rebuilds the column on update; for large tables this is a long, locking migration.
  • _inherit typo. An unknown _inherit name raises at load: Model 'library.bok' does not exist in registry. A correct name from a module you forgot to put in depends raises the same.
  • Computed stored fields on update. Adding a stored computed field recomputes it for all rows during -u. On large tables, set the column first in a migration, or compute in batches.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
odoo-bin shell -d dev <<'PY'
Book = env['library.book']
print(type(Book).__mro__)           # the combined class and its bases
print(env.registry.models.keys() & {'library.book', 'library.loan'})
print([c.__module__ for c in type(Book).__mro__ if c.__module__.startswith('odoo.addons')])
PY

The last line lists the modules contributing to the model, in override order.

docs.title: Request lifecycle
docs.text: Every interaction with Odoo that is not a cron job or a shell session is an HTTP request. Understanding what happens between the socket and the COMMIT tells you where transactions begin and end, why an exception rolls back everything, and where to put code that must run once per request or once per transaction.

docs.title: The path of a request
docs.text:
1. WSGI entry. A worker (or thread) receives the request. The framework's odoo.http.Application (a WSGI application on top of Werkzeug) handles it.
  2. Session and database. The session cookie is loaded; the database is selected from the session, the db parameter, or the --db-filter matching the host name.
  3. Routing. The request is matched to a controller method registered with @http.route. Routes from all installed modules are collected at registry load, so an uninstalled module has no routes.
  4. Dispatch. Depending on type= ('http' or 'json' in 16 and 17; 18 renames the JSON type to 'jsonrpc' while keeping 'json' as an alias, so verify in your branch), a dispatcher parses the body and prepares arguments.
  5. Authentication. auth='user', 'public', 'none'. The result is a user id and an environment.
  6. Cursor and environment. For database-bound routes, the framework opens a cursor and creates request.env. One cursor per request.
  7. Handler runs. Your controller code executes ORM calls inside that single transaction.
  8. Commit or rollback. On normal return the cursor commits; on an exception it rolls back. Both happen after your handler returns, not at each ORM call.
  9. Response. Rendered, headers set, session saved.

A controller in its simplest form:

from odoo import http
from odoo.http import request


class LibraryController(http.Controller):

    @http.route('/library/books', type='http', auth='user')
    def books(self, **kw):
        books = request.env['library.book'].search([], limit=20)
        return request.render('library.book_list', {'books': books})

docs.title: The ORM RPC path
docs.text:
The web client does not call controllers for most things. It calls two generic JSON routes that expose model methods:

  • /web/dataset/call_kw (and /web/dataset/call_kw/<model>/<method>) calls model.method(*args, **kwargs) on the server.
  • /web/dataset/call_button is the older sibling for buttons.

Both end up in odoo.service.model.execute_kw, which opens a cursor, builds an environment for the user, calls the public method, and commits. The external XML-RPC and JSON-RPC endpoints (/xmlrpc/2/object, /jsonrpc) use the same machinery. This is why every public model method (not starting with an underscore) is callable by any user who can reach the server, and why you must check access in methods, not only in views.

Methods that start with _ are not exposed through RPC. Put helpers there. Anything public is an endpoint: if it does sudo() internally, an authenticated user can trigger it.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
One request is one transaction on one database cursor. This has practical effects:

  • A raise anywhere rolls back every write in the request. Expected, and the reason a UI error leaves no half-written data.
  • Writes become visible to other transactions only at commit. Another worker handling a concurrent request cannot see your changes during the handler.
  • Code that sends an email or calls an external service from inside the handler cannot be undone if the transaction later fails. Queue the side effect, or trigger it after commit.
def action_confirm(self):
    self.write({'state': 'confirmed'})
    # runs after the transaction commits, not before
    self.env.cr.postcommit.add(lambda: self._notify_external())

cr.postcommit and cr.precommit are available as callback registries on the cursor in recent versions (introduced around 14). Verify the exact API in your branch before depending on it, and keep callbacks idempotent.

env.cr.commit() inside request code ends the transaction early. After it, a later error cannot roll back what came before. Use it only in batch jobs that deliberately process in chunks, never in business logic reached from the UI.

docs.title: Concurrency errors
docs.text:
PostgreSQL runs at REPEATABLE READ in Odoo. Two requests that update the same row concurrently produce a serialization failure (could not serialize access due to concurrent update). The framework catches psycopg2.errors.SerializationFailure and LockNotAvailable in the RPC layer and retries the call a few times (MAX_TRIES_ON_CONCURRENCY_FAILURE, 5 in current code), so your method may run more than once.

Therefore:

  • Do not do non-idempotent external work (payments, emails) in the same method as the writes that can be retried; or make the external call detect duplicates.
  • Do not catch broad Exception around ORM calls. Swallowing a database error leaves the transaction aborted: every later statement fails with current transaction is aborted.
  • Wrap deliberate error handling in a savepoint: with self.env.cr.savepoint(): ....

docs.title: Environment and context
docs.text: request.env is built from the session: user, company, language, timezone, and context. The web client sends its context with each call (lang, tz, allowed_company_ids, defaults such as default_partner_id). Methods that behave differently from the shell and from the UI usually differ in context. allowed_company_ids in particular controls which companies' records are visible through record rules, so a test in the shell without it sees a different world.

docs.title: Static files and assets
docs.text: Requests for /<module>/static/... are served by the framework from disk; in production put them behind the reverse proxy cache. Bundles under /web/assets/... are generated on first demand from the assets manifest keys and stored as attachments; deleting them forces regeneration and is the first thing to try when a frontend change does not appear.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Calling sudo() and trusting the result. sudo() skips ACLs and record rules; the data you return to the user is whatever it returns. Filter explicitly.
  • auth='public' routes with csrf=False. Public routes that change state without CSRF protection are open to cross-site calls. Keep CSRF on for POST forms; for JSON routes, require a token or signature.
  • Long handlers. A request holds its transaction and often row locks for its whole duration. A 60-second import in a request blocks concurrent writers and may hit --limit-time-real.
  • Reading data written by another transaction in the same request. With REPEATABLE READ, a snapshot starts at the first query. Polling in a loop never sees new rows.
  • Multiple databases and db parameter. A route called without a database selected and with auth='none' has no request.env for models. Use request.env only after request.update_env(...) or via odoo.registry(db).cursor() explicitly.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# watch the SQL of one request
odoo-bin -c dev.conf -d dev --log-level=debug_sql
# call the same method through external RPC, outside the web client
python3 - <<'PY'
import xmlrpc.client as x
common = x.ServerProxy('http://localhost:8069/xmlrpc/2/common')
uid = common.authenticate('dev', 'admin', 'admin', {})
models = x.ServerProxy('http://localhost:8069/xmlrpc/2/object')
print(models.execute_kw('dev', uid, 'admin', 'library.book', 'search_count', [[]]))
PY

docs.title: Workers, cron, and longpolling
docs.text: Odoo runs in one of two process models, and the choice changes what your code may assume: whether a request can run for ten minutes, whether a cron job shares memory with the web server, and how a browser learns that something changed. Development usually runs in threaded mode; production should not. Behaviour that works on a laptop can fail the first week on a server.

docs.title: Threaded mode
docs.text:
With --workers=0 (the default), one process serves HTTP requests on a pool of threads and runs cron jobs on --max-cron-threads additional threads. Characteristics:

  • Easy to debug; --dev=reload, breakpoints, and the Werkzeug debugger work.
  • All threads share one Python process, so one CPU-bound request competes for the GIL with everything else.
  • --limit-memory-* and --limit-time-* are not enforced. A runaway request runs forever.
  • Live-update traffic (chat, bus notifications) is served by the same process on the same port.

docs.title: Multi-process mode
docs.text:
With --workers=N where N is greater than 0, Odoo starts a prefork server:

  • N HTTP worker processes, each handling one request at a time.
  • --max-cron-threads cron worker processes (the option sets the number of cron workers in this mode).
  • A separate process for live updates (gevent), listening on its own port (default 8072).

Each worker is killed and replaced if it exceeds its limits:

Option Effect --limit-memory-soft Worker finishes its current request, then is recycled. --limit-memory-hard Worker is killed immediately. --limit-time-cpu CPU seconds per request. --limit-time-real Wall-clock seconds per request. --limit-time-real-cron Wall-clock limit for cron workers. Defaults to -1, meaning it falls back to --limit-time-real; 0 removes the limit (verified in Odoo 18). --limit-request Requests served before the worker is recycled.

Sizing is rough arithmetic. A worker process uses a few hundred MB under load. A common starting rule is workers around (CPU cores * 2) + 1 for web traffic, memory budget workers * soft limit plus the gevent process plus PostgreSQL, and --db_maxconn large enough for workers and cron combined. Measure under real traffic; the rule is a place to start, not an answer.

Versions: the gevent process serves /websocket in 16 and later for the bus on Odoo 17 and 18; on 16, the bus used HTTP long polling at /longpolling/poll with the same separate process. Port naming also changed (longpolling_port to gevent_port). The deployment shape stays the same: a second port that the reverse proxy must route to.

docs.title: Why your code must care
docs.text:
A request that exceeds limit-time-real is killed with no chance to clean up; the transaction rolls back. This applies to:

  • Imports triggered from a button.
  • "Recompute everything" actions on large tables.
  • Reports that aggregate a year of data.

Move long work out of the request: into a cron job processing in batches, or into a queued job that the request creates and returns immediately.

A worker serves one request at a time. A handler that calls an external service with a 30-second timeout occupies a worker for that time. With four workers, four slow calls make the whole site stall while the CPU is idle.

docs.title: Cron jobs
docs.text:
A scheduled action is a record of ir.cron with a model, a method, an interval, and a number of calls. Define it in data:

<odoo>
  <record id="cron_library_overdue" model="ir.cron">
    <field name="name">Library: flag overdue loans</field>
    <field name="model_id" ref="model_library_loan"/>
    <field name="state">code</field>
    <field name="code">model._cron_flag_overdue()</field>
    <field name="interval_number">1</field>
    <field name="interval_type">days</field>
    <field name="active" eval="True"/>
  </record>
</odoo>

In 16 you could also set numbercall and doall. Neither appears in ir_cron.py of Odoo 18 (verified); check 17 yourself if you migrate through it. The job runs as the user in the user_id field (a superuser-equivalent internal user by default).

How the scheduler works:

  1. A cron worker wakes every minute (or on a trigger, see below), lists ir_cron rows whose nextcall is due.
  2. It locks one row with SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so only one worker runs a given job, even across processes and servers.
  3. It runs the job in its own transaction and commits.
  4. It updates nextcall and lastcall.

Failure semantics: an exception rolls back that run and is logged; the job stays active and runs again at the next interval. In recent versions a job that keeps failing may be deactivated after a threshold (in 17 and later, repeated failures can disable the job; verify the thresholds in ir_cron.py of your branch).

docs.title: Writing a safe cron method
docs.text:
@api.model
def _cron_flag_overdue(self, batch_size=500):
    domain = [('state', '=', 'out'), ('due_date', '<', fields.Date.today())]
    loans = self.search(domain, limit=batch_size)
    loans.write({'state': 'overdue'})
    # tell the scheduler there is more to do (17 and later)
    remaining = self.search_count(domain)
    if remaining and hasattr(self.env['ir.cron'], '_trigger'):
        self.env.ref('library.cron_library_overdue')._trigger()

Process a bounded batch, commit the progress, and ask to be run again. From 16 ir.cron._trigger() schedules an additional run at a given time (the ir.cron.trigger model). Large single-run jobs hit the real-time limit and roll back completely, losing all progress.

Cron also commits per job, not per record. In 17 and later the helper self.env['ir.cron']._commit_progress() (mentioned in newer documentation) exists for progress tracking; do not assume it on 16.

docs.title: Cron on non-production copies
docs.text:
A database restored from production carries its cron jobs, outgoing mail servers, and external webhook configuration. Starting a staging server on it sends real mail and calls real services. Before first start of a copy:

update ir_cron set active = false;
update ir_mail_server set active = false;

Platforms that manage staging do this for you; self-hosted copies do not. Read the first query as a SELECT with the same WHERE to see what is active before changing anything.

docs.title: Longpolling, websocket, and the bus
docs.text:
The browser needs to learn about events (new chat message, notification, a record changed by someone else) without polling constantly. The bus module keeps rows in bus_bus and a long-lived connection to the gevent process delivers them.

  • The gevent process holds many idle connections cheaply; HTTP workers cannot (one request per worker).
  • It uses its own database connections, so it appears as extra connections to PostgreSQL.
  • The reverse proxy must route the live endpoint to port 8072 and the rest to 8069:
location /websocket { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8072; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade"; }
location /longpolling { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8072; }
location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8069; }

Use only the location that matches your version; keep proxy_read_timeout generous for it.

Sending a notification from code:

self.env['bus.bus']._sendone(user.partner_id, 'library/loan_overdue', {'loan_id': loan.id})

The message is written in the transaction and delivered after commit. In Odoo 18 the signature is _sendone(self, target, notification_type, message) (verified in addons/bus/models/bus.py); older branches used sendone.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
In multi-process mode, live updates do not work unless the proxy routes the live endpoint to the gevent port. Symptom: chat and notifications silent, nothing in the Odoo log, everything else fine.

  • Workers set, no proxy. Workers without --proxy-mode and a proxy that sets the right headers cause wrong URLs and lost client IPs.
  • Cron in dev against shared database. Two servers, two cron runners on the same data. Locks prevent the same job running twice at once, but not twice in succession on the dev side with half-finished code.
  • Global variables across requests. Each worker has its own memory. A module-level cache filled in one worker is invisible to the next; use @tools.ormcache and the registry invalidation, or the database.
  • Time limits too low for a deploy-time update. Update commands (-u) run in a separate process without worker limits; do not run updates through the web server.
  • limit-memory-hard too tight. Workers killed mid-request look like random 502s from the proxy. Check kernel logs and Odoo logs for "Virtual memory limit reached".
  • Slow crons delaying others. With one cron worker, a ten-minute job delays every job due behind it.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# how many workers do we actually have, and who is listening where?
ps -eo pid,ppid,rss,cmd | grep odoo-bin
ss -ltnp | grep -E ":(8069|8072)"
# which crons are due, read-only
psql -d dev -c "select cron_name, nextcall, active from ir_cron order by nextcall limit 10;"

docs.title: Common errors catalog
docs.text: Each entry gives the message as you will see it, the cause, and the fix. Message wording varies slightly between versions.

docs.title: ValueError: Expected singleton: library.book(1, 2)
docs.text: Cause: code written for one record received several (or none) and accessed a field or called a method as if single. Fix: loop (for book in self:), or ensure_one() where one record is the contract and let it fail loudly. For zero records, check if not self.

docs.title: AttributeError: 'library.book' object has no attribute 'x'
docs.text: Cause: the field is not defined on this model, the defining module is not installed in this database, or the code was not reloaded. Fix: check env['library.book']._fields, check the module state, restart or update.

docs.title: KeyError: 'library.book' / Object library.book doesn't exist
docs.text: Cause: model not in the registry. The module is not installed, not loaded by --load/-u, or failed to import. Fix: check the module state and the log at startup for an import error.

docs.title: MissingError: Record does not exist or has been deleted
docs.text: Cause: an id outlived its record, often from a cached id in a wizard, a stale browser tab, or an unlink earlier in the same flow. Fix: exists() before use, or re-read the ids.

docs.title: RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
docs.text: Cause: a compute reading its own result, parent and child dependencies that loop, or write inside write without a guard. Fix: break the cycle; use @api.depends with the minimal set; guard with a context key.

docs.title: TypeError: ... missing 1 required positional argument after a version change
docs.text: Cause: an overridden method's signature changed upstream. Fix: read the parent's signature in the target version; use *args, **kwargs in overrides that only wrap.

docs.title: Compute method failed to assign library.book(5,).total
docs.text: Cause: a compute method did not set the field on every record in self, including the branch with no data. Fix: assign in all branches, or set a default first: rec.total = 0.0.

docs.title: odoo.exceptions.AccessError: You are not allowed to access 'Book' (library.book) records
docs.text: Cause: no ir.model.access line gives the user's groups the operation. Common in a new model without ir.model.access.csv, or with a wrong model_id:id name. Fix: add the access row; update the module; check the CSV loads in the manifest data list, in the right order.

docs.title: AccessError: ... due to security restrictions (record rule)
docs.text: Cause: a record rule excludes the record for this user, often a company rule. Fix: inspect Record Rules for the model; test with env(user=...). Use sudo() in code only when bypassing is intended and reviewed.

docs.title: ValidationError from a constraint
docs.text: Cause: an @api.constrains method or a _sql_constraints check rejected the data. Fix: the message is yours; check the values passed. In scripts, catch it per batch (see Safe bulk scripts).

docs.title: UserError: You cannot delete ...
docs.text: Cause: an ondelete override or @api.ondelete(at_uninstall=False) blocks it. Fix: archive instead of deleting, or satisfy the condition stated in the message.

docs.title: psycopg2.errors.UniqueViolation: duplicate key value violates unique constraint
docs.text: Cause: a duplicate on a unique index. The DETAIL line names the field and value. Fix: deduplicate before the insert, or use the existing record. When adding a new _sql_constraints unique to a table with duplicates, the module update fails; clean the data first.

docs.title: psycopg2.errors.NotNullViolation: null value in column
docs.text: Cause: a required field not set, often a new required=True on a table that has rows. Fix: provide a default and, in a migration, fill existing rows before the column constraint applies.

docs.title: psycopg2.errors.ForeignKeyViolation
docs.text: Cause: deleting a record that is still referenced with ondelete='restrict', or inserting a bad id. Fix: remove or reassign dependants first.

docs.title: psycopg2.errors.InFailedSqlTransaction: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
docs.text: Cause: a previous SQL error in this transaction was caught and ignored, and the code continued. Fix: wrap the risky statement in with env.cr.savepoint():, or roll back. Find the first error in the log; this message is the follow-up.

docs.title: psycopg2.errors.SerializationFailure: could not serialize access due to concurrent update
docs.text: Cause: two transactions changed the same row. Odoo retries the request a few times. Fix: keep transactions short; avoid hot rows such as a global counter; commit batches in scripts.

docs.title: psycopg2.errors.DeadlockDetected
docs.text: Cause: two transactions lock rows in opposite order. Fix: process records in a consistent order (order="id"); smaller batches.

docs.title: psycopg2.OperationalError: connection ... too many clients already
docs.text: Cause: more connections than PostgreSQL's max_connections; too many workers or leaked scripts. Fix: lower db_maxconn and workers, close stray scripts, or raise max_connections with care.

docs.title: ParseError: while parsing ... or Invalid view definition
docs.text: Cause: XML error in a data file; the message names the file and line. Fix: fix the XML; check field names exist on the model.

docs.title: Element '<xpath expr="...">' cannot be located in parent view
docs.text: Cause: an inherited view's locator matches nothing, because the parent changed, the module order is wrong, or the expression is wrong. Fix: inspect the combined parent arch (see Developer mode); use a more stable anchor such as a field name; add the parent module to depends.

docs.title: ValueError: External ID not found in the system: library.view_book_form
docs.text: Cause: a reference to an XML ID in a module not in depends, or loaded later in the manifest. Fix: add the dependency, order the data files.

docs.title: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'x' at startup
docs.text: Cause: a Python dependency is not installed in the virtualenv, or the addon is outside the addons path. Fix: pip install into the right environment; check addons_path.

docs.title: Some modules are not loaded, some dependencies or manifest may be missing
docs.text: Cause: a module in depends is not found. Fix: check the addons path and spelling in the manifest.

docs.title: Field "x" does not exist in model "y" (view validation)
docs.text: Cause: a view references a field not defined, or defined in a module that is not a dependency. Fix: add the field or the dependency.

docs.title: werkzeug.exceptions.NotFound / 404
docs.text: Cause: wrong route, wrong database selection when several databases exist, or a missing --db-filter. Fix: set dbfilter, or pass the db in the session.

docs.title: odoo.exceptions.AccessDenied on RPC
docs.text: Cause: wrong login, expired or revoked API key, or two-factor requirement on the account with a password. Fix: generate a new key; use it as the password.

docs.title: Object ... doesn't exist via RPC on a private method
docs.text: Cause: methods starting with _ are not callable remotely. Fix: expose a public method.

docs.title: TypeError: cannot marshal None unless allow_none is enabled
docs.text: Cause: XML-RPC with a None value. Fix: allow_none=True, or send False.

docs.title: Worker (pid) CPU time limit (limit_time_cpu) reached or Virtual memory limit (limit_memory_hard) reached
docs.text: Cause: a request or cron exceeded limits. Fix: reduce the work per call, chunk it, or run it from the shell. Raise limits only for a measured need.

docs.title: Pitfalls when reading this catalog
docs.text:
• A message in the UI may be translated. Search the log, which is in English, rather than the dialog text.
  • The last error is often a follow-up. Look for the first ERROR of the request.
  • A fix that makes the message disappear without explaining the cause usually moves the failure.

docs.title: Debugging with pdb and debugpy
docs.text: A print statement tells you what you thought to print. A debugger lets you inspect everything at the moment of failure. Odoo runs normal Python, so both the standard pdb and an IDE debugger through debugpy work, with a few constraints about workers and threads.

docs.title: Run single-process first
docs.text:
Breakpoints are only useful in a process you can see. Start the server with no workers, so one process handles every request:

./odoo-bin -c odoo.conf -d mydb --workers=0 --dev=all

--dev=all enables reload and the post-mortem debugger. The values are comma-separated and include reload (restart on Python change), qweb, xml (read views from disk) and pdb (drop into the debugger on exception). In recent versions --dev=all implies all of them; check ./odoo-bin --help in your version.

docs.title: pdb: breakpoints in code
docs.text:
def action_confirm(self):
    for loan in self:
        breakpoint()          # or: import pdb; pdb.set_trace()
        loan._check_availability()

The server stops on that line and the prompt appears in the terminal that started it. This does not work under systemd, in Docker without -it, or when output is piped. Run it in the foreground.

Commands you need:

Command Effect n Next line s Step into c Continue r Run until the current function returns l / ll Show code around the line / the whole function p expr / pp expr Print / pretty-print w Show the stack u / d Move up / down the stack b file:line Set a breakpoint q Quit (raises, so the request fails)

Inside the prompt, self, self.env and the local variables are live:

(Pdb) self.env['library.loan'].search_count([])
(Pdb) pp self.read(['state'])
(Pdb) self.env.cr.execute("select 1"); self.env.cr.fetchall()

Do not call self.env.cr.commit() from a debugger session unless you mean it.

docs.title: Post-mortem: stop where it crashes
docs.text:
./odoo-bin -c odoo.conf -d mydb --workers=0 --dev=pdb

On an unhandled exception the process drops into pdb at the failing frame, with the exception state intact. Use w to see the stack and u to climb to the frame whose variables you need. This is usually quicker than guessing a breakpoint position.

docs.title: debugpy: attach an IDE
docs.text:
pip install debugpy

Add near the start of the code you want to debug, or in a small local addon:

import debugpy
debugpy.listen(("127.0.0.1", 5678))
print("waiting for debugger")
debugpy.wait_for_client()

Or start the server through debugpy without touching code:

python -m debugpy --listen 127.0.0.1:5678 --wait-for-client ./odoo-bin -c odoo.conf -d mydb --workers=0

In VS Code add an "attach" configuration:

{
  "name": "Attach to Odoo",
  "type": "debugpy",
  "request": "attach",
  "connect": {"host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 5678},
  "justMyCode": false
}

Older VS Code versions use "type": "python". Set justMyCode to false to step into Odoo's own code. PyCharm uses a "Python Debug Server" or attaches by process.

docs.title: Debugging a remote or containerised server
docs.text:
Bind to 0.0.0.0 only in a private network, and prefer an SSH tunnel:

ssh -L 5678:127.0.0.1:5678 user@devserver

debugpy has no authentication. Never expose it to the internet. In Docker publish the port and map source paths with pathMappings so breakpoints line up.

docs.title: Debugging the shell and tests
docs.text:
./odoo-bin shell -d mydb --no-http          # then call breakpoint() in your own code
./odoo-bin -d mytest -i library --test-tags=/library:TestLoan --stop-after-init --workers=0

A test stops at breakpoint() the same way. Use --test-tags to run only the test you debug.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Workers. With --workers>0 requests run in child processes without a terminal; the breakpoint hangs or is skipped. Use --workers=0.
  • Request timeouts. A request paused in a debugger can hit --limit-time-real. Raise it for the session.
  • Leftover breakpoints. A breakpoint() committed to production blocks a worker forever. Set PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 in production environments as a safety net.
  • Locks. A stopped transaction holds row locks. Others wait.
  • Reload during debugging. --dev=reload restarts on file save and drops your session. Disable it when stepping.

docs.title: Developer mode and tools
docs.text: Developer mode exposes the metadata Odoo keeps about itself: models, fields, views, access rules, XML IDs. Most "why does this behave like that" questions are answered by one click there, faster than reading source.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
• URL: append ?debug=1 to the address. Use ?debug=assets to serve unminified assets, useful when debugging JavaScript. ?debug=0 turns it off.
  • Settings: Settings, Developer Tools, Activate the developer mode (with variants for assets).
  • Keep it on while developing; do not leave it on for ordinary users, since it exposes technical menus and raw fields.

In recent versions a bug icon appears in the top bar when active. It opens the debug menu with the items for the current view.

docs.title: The debug menu on a form
docs.text:
Open any record with debug active and you get entries such as:

  • Edit View: Form and the equivalent for list, search, kanban: opens the view's arch for editing. Edits are stored in the database as a customised view and are lost or conflict when the module is updated. Use it to experiment, then move the change to your module's XML.
  • View Fields: the fields of the model with their types and technical names.
  • View Metadata: the record's id, XML ID, creator and write date, and whether it is noupdate.
  • Manage Attachments, Set Defaults, Edit Action, View Access Rights, View Record Rules.
  • Run Tour, Start Tour and Disable Tours when working with tours.

Labels differ slightly by version.

docs.title: Technical menu
docs.text:
Settings, Technical (visible only in debug mode) contains the tables behind the system:

Menu Model Typical use Models, Fields ir.model, ir.model.fields Find a field's technical name, type, stored or not Views ir.ui.view See inherited views and their priority; the combined arch Actions ir.actions.* Check domain, context, view mode of a menu entry Scheduled Actions ir.cron Run now, change interval, see last call Automation Rules base.automation Triggers on create and write Server Actions ir.actions.server Code that menus and buttons run Sequences ir.sequence Fix numbering Parameters, System Parameters ir.config_parameter web.base.url, mail settings Access Rights, Record Rules ir.model.access, ir.rule Why a user cannot see something Outgoing Mail Servers, Emails ir.mail_server, mail.mail Stuck mail Translations ir.translation / ir.model.fields.translate storage Wrong labels (storage changed in 16/17)

docs.title: Finding out why a user cannot do something
docs.text:
1. Reproduce as the user: Settings, Users, pick the user, then Action, Impersonate (debug mode; in older versions log in with the user's credentials or use the shell with env(user=...)).
  2. Check Access Rights for the model and the user's groups.
  3. Check Record Rules for the model: a rule with a domain that excludes the record shows as "record does not exist" or an access error.
  4. Check for a field with groups= that hides it in the view.

docs.title: Inspecting a view that does not do what you expect
docs.text:
The combined view is what the client receives. In debug mode, Edit View shows the source of the current view; the inheritance chain is under Settings, Technical, Views, with the "Inherited Views" tab. When your xpath does not apply you get an error at update time naming the view and the locator that failed.

From the shell you can see the final arch:

>>> env['library.book'].get_view(view_type='form')['arch']

(get_view exists from 16; older versions use fields_view_get.)

docs.title: Metadata from the shell
docs.text:
>>> rec = env['library.book'].browse(7)
>>> rec.get_metadata()
>>> rec.get_external_id()

Both are the same data as View Metadata.

docs.title: Developer shortcuts in the UI
docs.text:
• Hovering a field label in debug mode shows its technical name, type, and model.
  • The list view's column selector and "Export" dialog show technical field names.
  • Pressing the QWeb or "Inspect" tools shows which template rendered a block in a report; the "Edit Template" entry in a website or report context opens the QWeb source.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Editing views in the UI on a database that gets updated. Your change is overwritten or conflicts after -u. Treat UI edits as scratch work.
  • noupdate data. Records in noupdate="1" are not refreshed by module updates; View Metadata shows the flag when you wonder why your XML change did not arrive.
  • Debug assets in production. ?debug=assets is slower and not meant for users.
  • Changing system parameters casually. web.base.url and mail parameters affect links in outgoing mail.

docs.title: Inspecting SQL
docs.text: Most Odoo performance problems are query problems: too many queries (N+1), or a few queries that scan a large table. You find both by looking at what the database actually receives.

docs.title: Log every query
docs.text:
./odoo-bin -d mydb --log-level=debug_sql
# or one handler only
./odoo-bin -d mydb --log-handler=odoo.sql_db:DEBUG

Each statement is logged with its duration. It is very verbose, so use it against one action on a development database, not for a day of traffic.

In the shell:

./odoo-bin shell -d mydb --no-http --log-handler=odoo.sql_db:DEBUG

docs.title: Count queries in code
docs.text:
The cursor counts them:

cr = env.cr
before = cr.sql_log_count   # verified in Odoo 18 (odoo/sql_db.py, used by odoo/tools/profiler.py)
env['library.loan'].search([]).mapped('book_id.name')
print(cr.sql_log_count - before)

If the attribute is missing in your version, wrap the call with odoo.tools.misc.mute_logger-style logging, or compare counts from the debug log. A more portable approach is a small context manager that patches cr.execute:

import contextlib

@contextlib.contextmanager
def count_queries(cr):
    original = cr.execute
    stats = {"n": 0}
    def wrapper(query, params=None, *a, **kw):
        stats["n"] += 1
        return original(query, params, *a, **kw)
    cr.execute = wrapper
    try:
        yield stats
    finally:
        cr.execute = original

In tests, with self.assertQueryCount(admin=12): asserts a budget and fails when code regresses.

docs.title: Recognising N+1
docs.text:
for loan in loans:
    print(loan.book_id.name)   # fine: prefetching loads books for the whole recordset

The ORM prefetches fields for all records of the recordset, so this is normally fine. N+1 appears when the recordset is rebuilt each iteration:

for loan_id in ids:
    loan = env['library.loan'].browse(loan_id)   # new recordset, no shared prefetch
    print(loan.book_id.name)

Fix: browse once (env['library.loan'].browse(ids)) and iterate over that. Also watch for search inside a loop, and for read per record. Batch with search(domain_in) and group in Python, or use read_group (renamed _read_group / formatted_read_group in later versions) for aggregates.

docs.title: Get the SQL of a search
docs.text:
>>> query = env['library.loan']._search([('state', '=', 'open')])
>>> print(query.select())          # (sql, params)

Query internals changed between versions (_where_calc, Query.get_sql in older ones). Treat the exact method as version-specific. The log is the reliable source.

docs.title: Explain it
docs.text:
Copy the statement from the log into psql against a copy of the database:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT "library_loan".id FROM "library_loan"
WHERE "library_loan"."state" = 'open'
ORDER BY "library_loan"."id" DESC LIMIT 80;

Read it for:

  • Seq Scan on a large table where you expected an index.
  • Estimated rows far from actual rows (stale statistics; run ANALYZE).
  • Sort with disk use, large Rows Removed by Filter.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement. On UPDATE or DELETE, wrap in BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;.

docs.title: Find slow queries on the server
docs.text:
-- requires the pg_stat_statements extension
SELECT calls, round(total_exec_time::numeric) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS mean_ms, left(query, 120)
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 20;

PostgreSQL's log_min_duration_statement = 500 logs every statement slower than 500 ms. Locks:

SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, now() - query_start AS age, left(query, 100)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = 'mydb' AND state <> 'idle' ORDER BY age DESC;

docs.title: Indexes
docs.text: A frequently searched stored field benefits from index=True on the field definition. Indexes cost writes and disk, so add them for measured cases. For ilike '%text%' a btree index does not help; the field option index='trigram' (available in recent versions) needs the pg_trgm extension.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Measuring on an empty database. Plans differ with data volume.
  • Judging by count alone. One query with a bad plan costs more than fifty indexed ones.
  • Related and computed stored fields. A write may trigger recomputes of dependants, a burst of queries you did not write.
  • Raw SQL bypasses the ORM. No access rules, no recomputes, stale cache.
  • Logging SQL with parameters in production. Parameters can contain personal data.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Run a list search in the shell with --log-handler=odoo.sql_db:DEBUG, then paste the statement into EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on a development copy.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Odoo logs through Python's logging module, one logger per Python module name. Knowing the logger names lets you turn on exactly the detail you need, and knowing the log format lets you find the line that matters in a file of a hundred thousand.

docs.title: The log line
docs.text:
2026-01-15 10:22:31,412 4821 INFO mydb odoo.addons.library.models.library_book: Loaded 12 books

Fields: timestamp, process id, level, database, logger name, message. The logger name tells you where the line came from: odoo.modules.loading for module loading, odoo.sql_db for SQL, odoo.http for requests, odoo.addons.<module>... for addon code. werkzeug logs access lines.

docs.title: Levels and switches
docs.text:
./odoo-bin -d mydb --log-level=debug                       # everything, very noisy
./odoo-bin -d mydb --log-level=warn
./odoo-bin -d mydb --log-handler=odoo.addons.library:DEBUG  # one namespace
./odoo-bin -d mydb --log-handler=:INFO --log-handler=odoo.sql_db:DEBUG
./odoo-bin -d mydb --logfile=/var/log/odoo/odoo.log

--log-handler takes LOGGER:LEVEL, repeatable, and an empty logger name means the root. Specific values: --log-level=debug_sql logs queries, debug_rpc and debug_rpc_answer log RPC calls and their answers, test is used for test runs. These shortcuts set a preset combination of handlers; check --help in your version for the list.

The same options go in the config file as log_level and log_handler = odoo.addons.library:DEBUG.

docs.title: Logging from your code
docs.text:
import logging
_logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class LibraryBook(models.Model):
    _inherit = "library.book"

    def action_import(self):
        _logger.info("importing %d books", len(self))
        try:
            self._do_import()
        except Exception:
            _logger.exception("import failed for books %s", self.ids)
            raise

Rules that matter:

  • Use lazy formatting ("%s", value), not f-strings. With f-strings the string is built even when the level is disabled.
  • _logger.exception(...) inside an except block adds the traceback. Outside one it adds nothing useful.
  • Do not log secrets, tokens, or full customer records. Log ids.
  • _logger.warning for things an operator should read, info for milestones, debug for developer detail. A module that logs per record at info makes the log unreadable.

docs.title: Reading a log
docs.text:
# Errors with a few lines before them
grep -n -B2 -A25 " ERROR " /var/log/odoo/odoo.log | less

# One database, one time window
grep "mydb" odoo.log | awk '$2 >= "10:20" && $2 <= "10:25"'

# Follow live
tail -f odoo.log | grep --line-buffered -E "ERROR|CRITICAL|WARNING"

# Slow requests and slow queries
grep -E "took|slow" odoo.log

When requests run in parallel, lines from different workers interleave. Follow one request by its process id (the second field) rather than reading top to bottom.

docs.title: Useful loggers
docs.text: Logger Why odoo.sql_db at DEBUG Every query, see Inspecting SQL odoo.modules.loading Why a module failed to load odoo.modules.registry Registry setup, missing dependencies odoo.models.unlink What cascades on delete odoo.addons.base.models.ir_cron Cron execution, failures odoo.addons.mail.models.mail_mail Outgoing mail odoo.http Request errors

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Debug level in production. debug on the root logger slows the server and fills the disk. Scope it to a namespace and revert.
  • Logs split across workers and files. With several workers and a reverse proxy, the failing request may be in another worker's output.
  • Rotating logs. Without logrotate, --logfile grows forever. If you rotate, Odoo reopens the file on SIGHUP.
  • Exceptions swallowed. except Exception: pass removes the only evidence. Log and re-raise.
  • Messages that vary per record. They defeat searching and alerting. Keep the message constant and put variable data last.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
./odoo-bin shell -d mydb --no-http --log-handler=odoo.sql_db:DEBUG <<'PY'
env['res.partner'].search_count([])
PY

docs.title: The Odoo shell
docs.text: The shell loads the registry of one database and gives you an env in a Python prompt. It is the fastest way to test an ORM expression, reproduce a bug against real data, or run a one-off fix without writing a module. It is also the easiest way to damage a database, so this chapter spends as much time on transactions as on syntax.

docs.title: Starting it
docs.text:
./odoo-bin shell -d mydb -c /etc/odoo/odoo.conf

The shell reads the same configuration as the server: addons path, database host, credentials. Pass -c with the file the server uses, otherwise you land on defaults and get a confusing "module not found" or connection error.

# pick the interface (ipython, ptpython, bpython, python)
./odoo-bin shell -d mydb --shell-interface=ipython

# skip the http listener; the shell does not need it
./odoo-bin shell -d mydb --no-http

# run a script from stdin and exit
./odoo-bin shell -d mydb < fix_titles.py

pip install ipython is worth the ten seconds: tab completion on records and fields is what makes the shell pleasant. If the requested interface is missing, Odoo falls back to another one.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
Name Meaning env An Environment for the database, running as the superuser self The current user record, handy as a one-record recordset odoo The top-level odoo package 
>>> env.user
res.users(1,)
>>> env['library.book'].search_count([])
42
>>> env.ref('base.main_company')
res.company(1,)

The superuser bypasses record rules and access rights. A query that returns records in the shell may return nothing for a real user. To see what a user sees:

>>> user = env['res.users'].search([('login', '=', 'demo')])
>>> env_u = env(user=user.id)
>>> env_u['library.book'].search_count([])

For multi-company behaviour pass the companies explicitly:

>>> Book = env['library.book'].with_context(allowed_company_ids=[1, 2])
>>> Book2 = env['library.book'].with_company(2)

docs.title: Transactions: nothing is saved until you commit
docs.text:
The shell keeps one transaction open. Writes are visible in your session and invisible to everyone else until you commit:

>>> book = env['library.book'].browse(7)
>>> book.write({'name': 'Draft title'})
True
>>> env.cr.commit()     # now it is permanent

If you leave without committing, the transaction is rolled back. That is the safe default and why a shell experiment normally leaves nothing behind. Two consequences:

  • A long session ended with Ctrl-D loses all its work. You learn this once.
  • env.cr.rollback() discards everything since the last commit. Follow it with env.invalidate_all() (older versions: env.clear() or invalidate_cache()), otherwise cached records show values that no longer exist.

ORM writes run computes, constraints and write overrides. env.cr.execute does none of that and leaves the ORM cache stale. Prefer the ORM, and use SQL only when you have measured a need.

docs.title: Locks on a live database
docs.text: Locking is by row. If your shell holds an uncommitted update and a user saves the same record, their request waits and may fail with a lock timeout or a concurrent update error. Keep experiments read-only, or commit quickly, when the instance is in use.

docs.title: Installing and upgrading
docs.text:
The shell inspects; the server entry point installs and updates:

./odoo-bin -d mydb -u library --stop-after-init
./odoo-bin -d mydb -i library_extra --stop-after-init

-u takes a comma-separated list. -u all updates everything and is slow; avoid it on production. The shell does not pick up edits to Python files, so restart it after changing code.

docs.title: The shell as a lab
docs.text:
# What does this domain match?
>>> env['library.loan'].search([('state', '=', 'open')], limit=5).mapped('book_id.name')

# Field definitions
>>> env['library.book']._fields['isbn'].type
'char'

# Stored values
>>> env['library.book'].browse(7).read(['name', 'isbn'])

# XML ID of a record
>>> env['ir.model.data'].search([('model', '=', 'library.book'), ('res_id', '=', 7)]).complete_name

For the SQL behind a search see Inspecting SQL. Any addon is importable: from odoo.addons.library.models.library_book import LibraryBook. A ModuleNotFoundError means the addons path of your config does not contain that addon.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Forgetting -c. The shell connects with defaults and shows no addons.
  • Stale cache after SQL or rollback. Call env.invalidate_all().
  • Assuming a user's view. The superuser sees everything; test with env(user=...).
  • Committing in a loop. One commit per record is slow and leaves a half-applied state if you stop. See Safe bulk scripts.
  • Mail side effects. Tracked-field writes post messages and may queue emails. Use with_context(tracking_disable=True) for data repair, and make sure a copy of production cannot send mail.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
./odoo-bin shell -d mydb -c /etc/odoo/odoo.conf --no-http <<'PY'
print(env.user.login, env.company.name)
print(env['ir.module.module'].search_count([('state', '=', 'installed')]))
PY

docs.title: Profiling
docs.text: Logging queries shows what the database did. Profiling shows where the time went in Python and SQL together, per call stack. Use it when a screen or method is slow and you do not yet know why.

docs.title: The profiler in the UI
docs.text:
In developer mode, the debug menu has a profiling entry (a bug icon with a stopwatch in recent versions). Open it, enable recording, optionally select options, then reproduce the slow action. Disable it again. The recordings are stored in the model ir.profile and listed under Settings, Technical, Profiling.

Options you can toggle:

  • Memory: sample allocations (heavier).
  • Sync and Async collectors: stack sampling of the running code, and sampling of asynchronous work.
  • SQL: record every query with its stack.
  • Traces: full call tracing, very slow, for short actions.

Open a recording and choose "Open in Speedscope" to browse flame graphs in the browser. The SQL view lists queries by the line of Python that issued them.

docs.title: Profiling from code
docs.text:
from odoo.tools import profiler

def heavy(self):
    with profiler.Profiler(description="heavy export", db=self.env.cr.dbname):
        self._build_export()

The recording ends up in ir.profile. In the shell:

>>> from odoo.tools.profiler import Profiler
>>> with Profiler(description="loans listing", db=env.cr.dbname):
...     env['library.loan'].search([]).mapped('book_id.name')

Without a database, Profiler can write to the log or to a file depending on options. The module and arguments changed over versions; read odoo/tools/profiler.py in your release.

docs.title: Command-line profiling with cProfile
docs.text:
Works on any version, and is good for scripts:

python -m cProfile -o /tmp/run.prof ./odoo-bin shell -d mydb --no-http < scripts/export.py
python - <<'PY'
import pstats
pstats.Stats("/tmp/run.prof").sort_stats("cumulative").print_stats(30)
PY

Or inside code, for a block:

import cProfile, pstats, io
pr = cProfile.Profile()
pr.enable()
records._compute_totals()
pr.disable()
out = io.StringIO()
pstats.Stats(pr, stream=out).sort_stats("cumulative").print_stats(25)
print(out.getvalue())

cumulative shows where time is spent including callees; tottime shows the cost of the function itself. Look at cumulative to find the area, tottime to find the culprit.

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
• A wide flame graph block around cr.execute or psycopg2: database time. Go to Inspecting SQL.
  • Many narrow repeated blocks under one parent: a loop issuing small queries (N+1), or a compute running per record.
  • Time in fields.py __get__ and _fetch: reading fields in a way that defeats the prefetch.
  • Time in _recompute_* or modified: write triggered recomputes of stored dependants.
  • Time in ir_qweb or _render: template cost; check the number of records rendered.
  • Time in safe_eval: rules and automations evaluated per record.

docs.title: Measuring method
docs.text:
1. Fix one scenario and data set. Profile it before changing anything.
  2. Change one thing. Profile again, with the same data.
  3. Compare totals, not feelings. Keep the numbers in the commit message.

A quick wall-clock check beats a profiler for before and after:

import time
t = time.perf_counter()
...
print(round(time.perf_counter() - t, 3))

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Profiling with debug logging on. The logging overhead distorts the result.
  • Cold cache. The first run reads from disk; run twice and measure the second.
  • Profiler overhead. Tracing and memory options slow the code several times; relative shapes stay useful, absolute times do not.
  • Production recordings. A profile contains code paths and, with SQL collection, query text with data. Delete recordings when finished and do not share them.
  • Optimising the wrong layer. If one query takes 90 percent of the time, no Python change matters.

docs.title: Reading tracebacks
docs.text: An Odoo traceback can run to fifty frames of framework code. The cause is almost never at the top and rarely at the bottom alone. This chapter gives a method for reading one quickly.

docs.title: Anatomy
docs.text:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "odoo/http.py", line 1989, in _transactioning
    return service_model.retrying(func, env=self.env)
  File "odoo/service/model.py", line 133, in retrying
    result = func()
  ...
  File "odoo/addons/library/models/library_loan.py", line 54, in action_confirm
    loan._check_availability()
  File "odoo/addons/library/models/library_loan.py", line 71, in _check_availability
    if loan.book_id.copies_available < 1:
  File "odoo/fields.py", line 1201, in __get__
    ...
AttributeError: 'library.book' object has no attribute 'copies_available'

Python prints the oldest call first and the failing line last. The final line is the exception type and message. Read it first, then go up.

docs.title: The method
docs.text:
1. Read the last line. Exception class and message. ValidationError, UserError, AccessError, MissingError are Odoo's own; psycopg2.errors.* are from the database; the rest are Python.
  2. Find the last frame in your code. Scan upward for the first path under your addons (not odoo/, werkzeug, psycopg2). Framework frames show the route, your frame shows the decision.
  3. Read the frame just below it. If your line calls into the ORM and it fails, the cause is the data or the arguments you passed.
  4. Ignore the repetitive middle. _transactioning, retrying, call_kw, _call_kw_multi, dispatch are plumbing.
  5. Check whether it is the first exception. Chained errors print "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred". The cause is the first block, not the last.
psycopg2.errors.UniqueViolation: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "library_book_isbn_uniq"
DETAIL:  Key (isbn)=(9780000000000) already exists.

During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:
...

Here the database message names the constraint and the value. Everything after is cleanup.

docs.title: Frames that tell you something
docs.text: Frame Meaning odoo/models.py _compute_field_value / fields.py __get__ A computed field raised; the next frame down is its compute method models.py _check_* / _validate_fields A @api.constrains method failed models.py create / write Your override, or an inherited one, runs between this and the caller odoo/addons/base/models/ir_qweb.py A template failed; the message includes the template and expression odoo/tools/safe_eval.py A domain, server action or automation expression failed odoo/sql_db.py execute A query failed; the exception below is a psycopg2 error

docs.title: Client errors versus server errors
docs.text: The browser dialog shows a trimmed version. The full text is in the server log, and the dialog's "Copy" or "See details" button gives the server-side traceback in recent versions. JavaScript errors appear in the browser console, with source maps only in debug assets mode.

docs.title: Reproduce it in the shell
docs.text:
Once you know the record and method, call it directly:

>>> loan = env['library.loan'].browse(12)
>>> loan.action_confirm()

You get the same traceback without the HTTP frames, and you can add breakpoint() (see Debugging).

docs.title: What the exception class suggests
docs.text:
• KeyError: 'name' on a dict: missing key in values or a context; print the dict.
  • AttributeError: ... has no attribute: field not defined on this model, module not loaded in this database, or a typo.
  • TypeError: ... got an unexpected keyword argument: override signature mismatch after a version change.
  • ValueError: Expected singleton: self holds zero or several records; see the catalog.
  • RecursionError: a compute depending on itself, or an @api.onchange and write loop.
  • MissingError: the record was deleted since the id was read.
  • psycopg2.errors.SerializationFailure / DeadlockDetected: concurrency; Odoo retries these a few times before giving up.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Fixing the symptom at the top. Wrapping the failing line in try/except hides the cause.
  • Reading only the dialog. It omits the chain and the SQL detail.
  • Stale code. A traceback line number that does not match the file means the server runs older code; restart.
  • Truncated logs. Reverse proxies and log shippers can cut long tracebacks; read the file on the server.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Trigger a unique violation from the shell on a throwaway database and read both blocks of the chained traceback.

docs.title: Remote scripts over RPC
docs.text: When you cannot or should not log in to the server, a script can drive Odoo over its external API. The calls go through the normal ORM with the permissions of one user, so record rules apply, which is both the limit and the safety.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
Create a key under Preferences, Account Security, New API Key (user menu, in developer mode if the option is hidden). Use it in place of the password. Treat it as a password: keep it in an environment variable or a secrets file outside the repository, never in the script.

export ODOO_URL=https://odoo.example.test
export ODOO_DB=mydb
export ODOO_LOGIN=api.user@example.test
export ODOO_KEY=...   # from your secret store

Use a dedicated user with only the groups the script needs. An automation running as an administrator can do anything the administrator can.

docs.title: XML-RPC
docs.text:
import os
import xmlrpc.client

url, db = os.environ["ODOO_URL"], os.environ["ODOO_DB"]
common = xmlrpc.client.ServerProxy(f"{url}/xmlrpc/2/common")
uid = common.authenticate(db, os.environ["ODOO_LOGIN"], os.environ["ODOO_KEY"], {})
if not uid:
    raise SystemExit("authentication failed")

models = xmlrpc.client.ServerProxy(f"{url}/xmlrpc/2/object")

def call(model, method, *args, **kwargs):
    return models.execute_kw(db, uid, os.environ["ODOO_KEY"], model, method, list(args), kwargs)

print(common.version()["server_version"])
ids = call("library.book", "search", [("isbn", "=", False)], limit=100)
rows = call("library.book", "read", ids, fields=["name", "isbn"])

Shortcuts: search_read returns dicts directly, search_count counts, create takes a dict or a list of dicts, write takes ids, values, unlink takes ids.

new_id = call("library.book", "create", {"name": "Test book"})
call("library.book", "write", [new_id], {"isbn": "9780000000000"})

docs.title: JSON-RPC
docs.text:
The /jsonrpc endpoint exposes the same services:

import json, os, urllib.request

def rpc(service, method, *args):
    payload = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "call", "id": 1,
               "params": {"service": service, "method": method, "args": args}}
    req = urllib.request.Request(os.environ["ODOO_URL"] + "/jsonrpc",
                                 json.dumps(payload).encode(),
                                 {"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    out = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req))
    if "error" in out:
        raise RuntimeError(out["error"]["data"]["message"])
    return out["result"]

uid = rpc("common", "authenticate", db, login, key, {})
count = rpc("object", "execute_kw", db, uid, key, "library.book", "search_count", [[]])

Odoo 18 contains no /json/2 route (searched odoo and addons/base of the 18.0 source). Releases after 18 may add a REST-style endpoint; check the documentation of the version you target before building something long-lived on XML-RPC or /jsonrpc.

docs.title: Context, companies and languages
docs.text:
Pass context as a keyword argument:

call("library.book", "search_read", [], fields=["name"],
     context={"lang": "fr_FR", "allowed_company_ids": [1, 2]})

docs.title: Reading and writing in batches
docs.text:
Each call is an HTTP round trip. Read in pages, write in chunks, and never loop one call per record for thousands of records:

offset = 0
while True:
    rows = call("library.book", "search_read", [], fields=["name"], limit=500, offset=offset, order="id")
    if not rows:
        break
    offset += len(rows)

Paginating with offset over a table that changes underneath you can skip or repeat rows. Prefer paging by id ([("id", ">", last_id)], order="id") for long jobs.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A failure raises xmlrpc.client.Fault; fault.faultString holds the server traceback. Access errors, validation errors and constraint violations all arrive this way. Log the model, ids and values before each write, so a failure at record 4,000 is diagnosable.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Secrets in the repository. Use the environment.
  • Methods that return recordsets. Only plain data crosses RPC. A method returning a recordset fails to serialize; return ids or True.
  • Private methods. Methods starting with an underscore cannot be called over RPC.
  • None in XML-RPC. XML-RPC cannot marshal None by default; use ServerProxy(url, allow_none=True) or send False.
  • Dry run. RPC has no transaction to roll back; each call commits. Test against a copy, and add a --apply switch that skips writes by default.
  • Timeouts. Long server-side methods hit worker time limits. Chunk the work.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: python -c "import xmlrpc.client,os;print(xmlrpc.client.ServerProxy(os.environ['ODOO_URL']+'/xmlrpc/2/common').version())"

docs.title: Running scripts
docs.text: A script is a repeatable change you can review, version and re-run. This chapter covers the ways to run one against a database you have shell access to, and when each fits. For a remote instance see Remote scripts over RPC.

docs.title: Option 1: pipe a file into the shell
docs.text:
./odoo-bin shell -d mydb -c /etc/odoo/odoo.conf --no-http < scripts/fix_isbn.py

The file sees env as an interactive session does. Be explicit about the transaction, and make the dry run the default:

# scripts/fix_isbn.py
import logging
import os

_logger = logging.getLogger("script.fix_isbn")
APPLY = os.environ.get("APPLY") == "1"

books = env["library.book"].search([("isbn", "=", False), ("legacy_code", "!=", False)])
_logger.info("candidates: %d", len(books))

for book in books:
    book.isbn = book.legacy_code.replace("-", "")

if APPLY:
    env.cr.commit()
    _logger.info("committed")
else:
    env.cr.rollback()
    _logger.info("dry run: rolled back")

./odoo-bin shell -d mydb --no-http < scripts/fix_isbn.py            # dry run
APPLY=1 ./odoo-bin shell -d mydb --no-http < scripts/fix_isbn.py    # real

Forgetting the variable is harmless. A traceback ends the script and the transaction is rolled back, which is what you want.

docs.title: Option 2: a standalone script that loads Odoo
docs.text:
When you need arguments or exit codes, build the environment yourself:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys
import odoo
from odoo.api import Environment
from odoo.tools import config

config.parse_config(["-c", "/etc/odoo/odoo.conf"])
registry = odoo.registry(sys.argv[1])
with registry.cursor() as cr:
    env = Environment(cr, odoo.SUPERUSER_ID, {})
    print(env["res.users"].search_count([]))
    # the cursor commits when the block exits cleanly

Run it with the Python that runs Odoo and with odoo importable (PYTHONPATH=/opt/odoo). Registry and environment construction changed slightly between releases; check the signatures in your version before copying this.

With registry.cursor(), leaving the block normally commits and an exception rolls back. The interactive shell rolls back at the end of the session. State the commit policy in a comment at the top of every script.

docs.title: Option 3: a method in a module
docs.text:
Logic that others must review, or that cron will run, belongs in a model method:

env["library.book"]._cron_fix_isbn()

A script run three times should become a method: it is then tested and deployed with the module.

docs.title: Migration scripts
docs.text:
A fix that belongs to an upgrade runs once per database when the module version increases:

library/migrations/17.0.1.2/post-fix_isbn.py

def migrate(cr, version):
    cr.execute("UPDATE library_book SET isbn = replace(isbn, '-', '') WHERE isbn LIKE '%-%'")

pre- scripts run before the module's models load, post- after. Both get a cursor; build Environment(cr, SUPERUSER_ID, {}) if you need the ORM.

docs.title: Running on a server
docs.text:
• Use tmux, screen or nohup so a dropped SSH session does not kill a half-finished job.
  • Run as the service user with the service's virtualenv. A script run as root creates root-owned filestore files the service cannot read.
  • Keep a log: ... 2>&1 | tee run-$(date +%F-%H%M).log.
  • Take a backup before any run that commits.
sudo -u odoo nohup /opt/odoo/venv/bin/python /opt/odoo/odoo-bin shell \
  -d mydb -c /etc/odoo/odoo.conf --no-http < scripts/fix_isbn.py \
  > /var/log/odoo/fix_isbn.log 2>&1 &

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Editing the script on the server. What ran no longer matches the repository.
  • Buffered output. Use logging, and python -u for standalone scripts.
  • Wrong Python. System Python lacks Odoo's dependencies.
  • Unbounded search. search([]) on a million rows loads every id; batch it.
  • Multi-company blindness. Superuser scripts have no allowed_company_ids, so company-dependent fields can resolve to the wrong company. Pass the context.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: Write a script that logs how many books lack an ISBN and rolls back. Run it piped, then add the APPLY switch.

docs.title: Safe bulk scripts
docs.text: A script that touches thousands of records fails in the middle, or succeeds and is wrong. The patterns here make both survivable: look before you write, write in bounded batches, isolate failures, and leave a record of what changed.

docs.title: The order of work
docs.text:
1. Read-only counterpart first. Count and list what the script would touch.
  2. Dry run on a copy of production.
  3. Backup, then run on production in batches, with a log.
  4. Verify with a query that proves the end state.
domain = [("state", "=", "draft"), ("create_date", "<", "2025-01-01")]
Loan = env["library.loan"]
print(Loan.search_count(domain))
print(Loan.search(domain, limit=10).read(["name", "state", "create_date"]))

docs.title: Skeleton
docs.text:
import logging
import os

_logger = logging.getLogger("script.archive_old_loans")
APPLY = os.environ.get("APPLY") == "1"
BATCH = 500

Loan = env["library.loan"].with_context(tracking_disable=True, mail_notrack=True)
ids = Loan.search([("state", "=", "draft"), ("create_date", "<", "2025-01-01")], order="id").ids
_logger.info("to process: %d (apply=%s)", len(ids), APPLY)

done = failed = 0
for start in range(0, len(ids), BATCH):
    chunk = Loan.browse(ids[start:start + BATCH])
    try:
        with env.cr.savepoint():
            chunk.write({"active": False})
        if APPLY:
            env.cr.commit()
        else:
            env.cr.rollback()
        done += len(chunk)
    except Exception:
        _logger.exception("batch starting at %d failed, ids %s", start, chunk.ids[:5])
        env.cr.rollback()
        failed += len(chunk)
    env.invalidate_all()
    _logger.info("progress %d/%d (failed %d)", start + len(chunk), len(ids), failed)

_logger.info("finished: done=%d failed=%d", done, failed)

Why each part exists:

  • Ids first, then browse per chunk. The id list is fixed up front, so the script does not chase a domain that changes as it writes, and memory stays bounded.
  • Batches with a commit release locks and make a stop recoverable: the next run's domain no longer matches processed records.
  • savepoint() lets a failed statement roll back without poisoning the whole transaction. After a SQL error the transaction is aborted until you roll back to a savepoint.
  • invalidate_all() between batches keeps the cache from growing without limit.
  • tracking_disable and mail_notrack stop chatter messages and mail for every record.

docs.title: Isolating a bad record
docs.text:
When a batch fails, retry it record by record to find the offender instead of losing the batch:

def process(records):
    try:
        with env.cr.savepoint():
            records.write({"active": False})
    except Exception:
        if len(records) == 1:
            _logger.error("record %s failed", records.id, exc_info=True)
            return
        mid = len(records) // 2
        process(records[:mid])
        process(records[mid:])

This bisects: a thousand-record batch with one bad record costs about twenty extra writes, not a thousand.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text:
A script must be safe to run twice. Build the domain so processed records drop out, or mark them:

Loan.search([("x_migrated", "=", False)])

If you cannot, compute the target value from the current data, so a second run writes the same value.

docs.title: Record what changed
docs.text:
Before a destructive step, save the old values:

import csv
with open("old_values.csv", "w", newline="") as fh:
    w = csv.writer(fh)
    w.writerow(["id", "name", "state"])
    for r in Loan.browse(ids).read(["name", "state"]):
        w.writerow([r["id"], r["name"], r["state"]])

That file is your undo. Keep it with the run log. Store it outside the repository when it contains personal data.

docs.title: Choosing ORM or SQL
Guardrails
docs.text:
• Refuse to run without an explicit target: assert os.environ.get("ODOO_DB"), or compare env.cr.dbname to the expected name.
  • Cap the damage: assert len(ids) < 10000, "unexpectedly many records".
  • Run outside business hours when locks matter; check pg_stat_activity for waiters.
  • Stop switch: check for a file such as /tmp/stop_script per batch and exit cleanly.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• One giant transaction. Memory grows, locks last, one error discards hours.
  • Commit per record. Needlessly slow; batch.
  • Savepoint misuse. A savepoint protects the database, not the ORM cache; invalidate after a failure.
  • Writes that trigger side effects. Mail, webhooks, and automations fire on write. Check automation rules and disable tracking.
  • Search with limit and no order. Pages shift while you write. Fix the ids first.
  • Dry run that differs from the real run. Keep one code path and switch only the commit.

docs.title: Cache and prefetch
docs.text: The ORM keeps a per-transaction cache of field values. Reading one field of one record normally loads many records and many fields in a single query, so most Python loops over recordsets cost far fewer queries than they appear to. When they do not, the cause is almost always one of a short list of mistakes.

docs.title: How a read works
docs.text:
books = self.env['library.book'].search([('shelf', '=', 'A')])
for book in books:
    print(book.name)

search returns ids only. The first book.name finds the value missing from the cache and issues one SELECT for the stored fields of all records in the same prefetch set (the ids that came from the same search), up to 1000 records per batch (PREFETCH_MAX in odoo/models.py). The remaining iterations read from the cache.

Details:

  • Only stored, non-relational-heavy fields are loaded in that query: columns of the table. Many2one values are loaded as ids; the related record's own fields are loaded when you first read them, again for the whole prefetch set of that related model.
  • One2many and Many2many are fetched with a query per field, for the whole set.
  • Computed non-stored fields are computed on first access for all records in the prefetch set at once. A compute method must therefore loop over self.
  • The cache is per environment transaction: sudo(), with_context and with_user create new environments that share the underlying cache storage, but entries for context-dependent fields are keyed by their context.

docs.title: The N+1 shapes
docs.text:
# Bad: one query per book, no prefetch set
for book_id in ids:
    book = self.env['library.book'].browse(book_id)
    print(book.name)

browse(single_id) in a loop builds one-record sets. Browse once with the whole list: self.env['library.book'].browse(ids).

# Bad: search inside the loop
for partner in partners:
    loans = self.env['library.loan'].search([('partner_id', '=', partner.id)])

Replace with one search or a grouped read:

loans = self.env['library.loan'].search([('partner_id', 'in', partners.ids)])
by_partner = loans.grouped('partner_id')

grouped(key) returns a dictionary of recordsets (18 has it; earlier versions use itertools.groupby after sorting or _read_group).

For counts and sums, do not load records at all: use _read_group or read_group, covered in the grouping chapter.

docs.title: Prefetch control
docs.text:
books = books.with_context(prefetch_fields=False)   # read only the requested field

prefetch_fields=False makes a read load only the field you asked for. Use it when records have heavy columns you will not use, such as images or long text.
