fields.Binary(attachment=True) is excluded from the default prefetch group, and fields with prefetch=False are loaded only on explicit access. Set prefetch=False on large Text or HTML fields that are rarely read.

To read specific columns in bulk without building records:

rows = books.read(['name', 'isbn'])          # list of dicts
names = books.mapped('name')                  # list of values

docs.title: Flush and invalidate
docs.text:
Writes in the ORM are not sent to PostgreSQL immediately. They sit in the cache as dirty values and are flushed before any query that could depend on them (search, read_group, execute_query), at the end of the request, and by explicit calls:

self.env.flush_all()                       # everything pending
books.flush_recordset(['state'])           # specific fields, specific records
self.env['library.book'].flush_model(['state'])

Invalidate is the reverse: drop cached values so that the next read goes to the database.

self.env.invalidate_all()
self.env['library.book'].invalidate_model(['state'])
books.invalidate_recordset(['state'])

invalidate_model and invalidate_recordset accept flush=True by default, so pending writes are saved before the cache is dropped. You need these calls when you change data behind the ORM's back, which is mostly raw SQL and external processes in a long transaction.

Versions: flush_model, flush_recordset, invalidate_model and invalidate_recordset exist in 16, 17 and 18. The older flush() and refresh() methods are removed. Environment.invalidate_all(flush=True) also takes the flag.

docs.title: Measuring
docs.text:
Count queries rather than guessing:

with self.assertQueryCount(__system__=3):
    process(books)

In tests, assertQueryCount fails with the executed queries printed. Interactively, enable query logging with --log-sql on a development server, or run:

import logging
logging.getLogger('odoo.sql_db').setLevel(logging.DEBUG)

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Looping over a recordset inside sudo() or with_context() created per iteration. Each call produces a new environment and a new prefetch set. Apply sudo() once, before the loop.

  • Reading a relational field on a record before it is flushed: search flushes for you, a raw cr.execute does not.
  • After raw SQL that writes, the cache still holds the old values. Call invalidate_model(['field']) for the affected model.
  • mapped('partner_id.name') is efficient; a Python loop with if book.partner_id.name is too. A loop that calls search or create per row is not.
  • Computed stored fields recompute lazily. Reading one forces the recompute of the whole pending set, which can look like a slow read.
  • Unbounded search([]) on a large table loads ids only, but a following loop will prefetch in batches of 1000: memory is bounded, time is not.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
In odoo shell on a throwaway database with --log-sql enabled, run:

books = env['library.book'].search([])
[b.name for b in books]

You should see one SELECT for the table, not one per record. Replace it with [env['library.book'].browse(b.id).name for b in books] and compare.

docs.title: Computed and related fields
docs.text: A computed field's value comes from a Python method, not from user input. A related field is a computed field that follows a path through relations. Both depend on a correct dependency declaration: get @api.depends wrong and stored values go stale without any error.

docs.title: A minimal computed field
docs.text:
class Loan(models.Model):
    _name = 'library.loan'
    _description = 'Loan'

    due_date = fields.Date()
    returned_on = fields.Date()
    days_late = fields.Integer(compute='_compute_days_late', store=True)

    @api.depends('due_date', 'returned_on')
    def _compute_days_late(self):
        today = fields.Date.context_today(self)
        for loan in self:
            end = loan.returned_on or today
            loan.days_late = max((end - loan.due_date).days, 0) if loan.due_date else 0

Rules the framework enforces:

  • The method must assign the field on every record of self, including the cases where the result is "empty". Skipping a record raises on read.
  • The method receives a recordset. Loop over it, or write the logic over the whole set.
  • Do not call write or create on self inside a compute. Assign the attribute.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
@api.depends takes field names and dotted paths:

@api.depends('line_ids.amount', 'partner_id.country_id')
def _compute_total(self): ...

For stored fields, a change of any listed field triggers recomputation at the next flush. For non-stored fields, it invalidates the cache.

Miss a dependency and the stored value stays wrong until something else touches the record. Typical causes:

  • Reading a field in the method that is not in depends.
  • Depending on line_ids when you read line_ids.amount. The first only reacts to adding or removing lines, not to amount changes.
  • Using a field of another record found by search inside the method. The ORM cannot see that dependency at all.

@api.depends_context('company', 'uid') declares context keys that change the result of a non-stored compute, so the cache is keyed correctly.

docs.title: Stored versus non-stored
docs.text:
store=False (default) store=True Computed when read, per cache miss dependency changes, at flush Searchable only with search= yes, as a column Groupable no yes Indexable no yes Cost on every uncached read on writes of dependencies

Store a field when you search, sort, or group on it, or when the computation is expensive and the dependencies change rarely. Keep it non-stored when the value depends on "now", the current user, or context, since a stored value would be stale the next day.

A stored field depending on fields.Date.today() never updates by itself. The ORM only recomputes on dependency changes. Compute it non-stored, or recompute it with a cron.

docs.title: precompute and compute_sudo
docs.text:
• precompute=True computes a stored field before the INSERT during create, so it exists in the first write and can carry required=True without a default. Dependencies must then be readable from the values being created.
  • compute_sudo defaults to True for stored computed fields and related fields (confirmed in the 18 source: attrs.get('compute_sudo', attrs.get('related_sudo', True))). The method runs as superuser, so users who cannot read the dependencies still see the result. Set compute_sudo=False when the result must respect the caller's rights.

docs.title: inverse
docs.text:
An inverse method makes a computed field writable. It runs after write on the field and must push the value back into the real source fields.

full_name = fields.Char(compute='_compute_full_name', inverse='_inverse_full_name')

def _inverse_full_name(self):
    for rec in self:
        first, _sep, last = (rec.full_name or '').partition(' ')
        rec.first_name, rec.last_name = first, last

Without inverse, writing a non-stored computed field has no lasting effect. For a stored computed field, the written value is kept until the next recomputation overwrites it, which is a confusing half-state; add an inverse or make the field readonly.

docs.title: search
docs.text: A non-stored computed field is searchable only if you provide search. The chapter on search and domains shows the method shape: it receives (operator, value) and returns a domain over stored fields.

docs.title: Related fields
docs.text:
author_country_id = fields.Many2one(related='author_id.country_id')
author_name = fields.Char(related='author_id.name', store=True)

A related field is a compute plus an inverse plus a search, generated from the path. Defaults from the 18 source and framework behaviour:

  • readonly=True by default. Pass readonly=False to let a write go through to the target record.
  • store=False by default. With store=True it is a real column that recomputes when the path changes.
  • copy=False by default.
  • compute_sudo is on, so the value shows even when the user cannot read the target model. Be careful when the path crosses into data the user should not see.
  • Attributes such as string, help, required are taken from the target field unless overridden.

Writing a related field with readonly=False writes to the target record, possibly shared by many records. Writing author_name on one book renames the author for every book.

docs.title: Recursive dependencies
docs.text:
For hierarchies (parent_id, child_ids), set recursive=True on the field and depend on the parent path:

@api.depends('parent_id.level')
def _compute_level(self): ...
level = fields.Integer(compute='_compute_level', store=True, recursive=True)

Without recursive=True, a dependency chain that returns to the same field raises a cycle error at setup.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• Write computes over the whole recordset. A search per record inside the loop multiplies queries.
  • For aggregates over children, use _read_group once for all of self, then assign:
@api.depends('loan_ids.fine')
def _compute_total_fines(self):
    data = dict(self.env['library.loan']._read_group(
        [('member_id', 'in', self.ids)], ['member_id'], ['fine:sum']))
    for member in self:
        member.total_fines = data.get(member, 0.0)
  • Stored fields with deep paths recompute on every change of any path element. Keep stored dependency chains short.
  • A stored compute on a model with millions of rows makes module installation slow, since it fills the whole column. Plan for it, or add the field via a pre-install SQL column and a batch fill.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Forgetting to assign the field on some branch: ValueError: Compute method failed to assign ....
  • Putting @api.depends on a method that is also used elsewhere with different dependencies. Keep compute methods single-purpose.
  • Relying on onchange instead of compute. Onchange runs only in the form UI; API and import writes skip it. Business invariants belong in compute or constraints.
  • Changing store=True to False later orphans a column that stays in the database, harmless but untidy; the reverse requires a migration to fill values.
  • depends on a field of a model reachable only by a dotted path through a non-stored computed field. Dependency tracing works through stored and computed alike, but a cycle in that chain is hard to debug; read the setup log.

Versions. compute_sudo defaulting to true for related fields and precompute are in 16 through 18. In 18, company_dependent fields are stored as jsonb on the model table, which affects raw SQL; check the field attribute in your version before writing SQL against it.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Check how a standard field is wired, in a development shell:

f = env['res.partner']._fields['display_name']
print(f.compute, f.store, f.depends)
g = env['res.partner']._fields['country_code']
print(g.related, g.store, g.readonly)

docs.title: Constraints, defaults, and onchange
docs.text: Three mechanisms keep data valid and convenient: constraints reject bad data, defaults fill in values on creation, onchange methods update a form while the user types. They run at different moments and enforce different guarantees, and only constraints are guarantees.

docs.title: SQL constraints
docs.text:
Declared on the model, enforced by PostgreSQL, so they hold for every writer: ORM, import, raw SQL, other tools.

class LibraryBook(models.Model):
    _name = 'library.book'
    _description = 'Book'

    name = fields.Char(required=True)
    isbn = fields.Char()
    pages = fields.Integer()

    _sql_constraints = [
        ('isbn_unique', 'UNIQUE(isbn)', 'The ISBN must be unique.'),
        ('pages_positive', 'CHECK(pages >= 0)', 'Pages cannot be negative.'),
    ]

Each tuple is (name, definition, message). The constraint is created at module update as <table>_<name>. The message is shown when PostgreSQL reports a violation.

Limits: the definition is a single static expression. It cannot call Python, cannot see other tables except through a subquery-free CHECK, and a UNIQUE on a nullable column allows many NULLs. For a partial or conditional unique, create a unique index in init().

Versions: _sql_constraints is the form in 16, 17 and 18. Adding a constraint to a table that already holds violating rows fails with a warning in the log and the constraint is simply not created. The module update still succeeds.

docs.title: Python constraints
docs.text:
from odoo import api, models
from odoo.exceptions import ValidationError


@api.constrains('isbn')
def _check_isbn(self):
    for book in self:
        if book.isbn and len(book.isbn.replace('-', '')) not in (10, 13):
            raise ValidationError(self.env._("ISBN %s is not valid.", book.isbn))

@api.constrains triggers after create and after write on the listed fields, once per call, on the affected records. Points that matter:

  • It is triggered only by the fields you name. Constraints on a related path, 'loan_ids.date_due', are not triggered by changes on the other model in older versions; do not rely on dotted names and name local fields.
  • It runs after the write, inside the transaction. Raising rolls everything back.
  • A constraint on a field not present in vals does not run on write, so an unchanged invalid record is not re-validated.
  • It is not a security measure; code that uses sudo() or raw SQL bypasses nothing, but code that writes with SQL skips it entirely.

Python constraints are for rules SQL cannot express. If CHECK can say it, use SQL: it holds for imports and SQL scripts too.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
state = fields.Selection([('draft', 'Draft'), ('active', 'Active')], default='draft')
date = fields.Date(default=fields.Date.context_today)
user_id = fields.Many2one('res.users', default=lambda self: self.env.user)
company_id = fields.Many2one('res.company', default=lambda self: self.env.company)

A default is a constant or a callable taking the recordset. Never write default=fields.Date.today() with parentheses: it is evaluated at import and every record gets the date the server started. A lambda or fields.Date.today (no call) is evaluated on each create.

Defaults apply on create for fields absent from vals, and in default_get for forms. Resolution order, highest first:

  1. Values in vals.
  2. Context keys default_<field>.
  3. User defaults set by ir.default.
  4. Field default.

ir.default is how Settings configure defaults, and per-company defaults for company-dependent fields use the same table. It is why changing a Python default in code does not change a value an administrator already set.

docs.title: onchange
docs.text:
@api.onchange('book_id')
def _onchange_book_id(self):
    if self.book_id:
        self.due_days = self.book_id.default_loan_days

@api.onchange runs only in the form view, on a virtual record, when the user changes the field. It does nothing on create, write, import or API calls. Use it for convenience only.

When the value should always follow another field, use a computed field with store=True, readonly=False. It runs everywhere, is recomputed when the dependency changes, and the user can still override it:

due_days = fields.Integer(compute='_compute_due_days', store=True, readonly=False)

@api.depends('book_id')
def _compute_due_days(self):
    for loan in self:
        loan.due_days = loan.book_id.default_loan_days or 14

Onchange can also return a warning:

return {'warning': {'title': self.env._("Careful"), 'message': self.env._("Rare book.")}}

docs.title: Company consistency
docs.text: For models with several company_id-bound relations, set _check_company_auto = True and check_company=True on the relational fields. The ORM then validates on write that records belong to compatible companies.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
A constraint that reads many records per record (search inside the loop) turns an import of ten thousand rows into ten thousand searches. Group the work: one read_group or one search with in.

  • required=True on a field is a NOT NULL column, but only for stored fields that are not set in the view as required by a states-like condition. A view-level required is client-side only.
  • Raising in a constraint with a plain Exception produces an internal error dialog; use ValidationError (or UserError) for messages meant for people.
  • A default that depends on self.env.company evaluated in a cron or in sudo uses the company of the environment, not of the user in the form.
  • Defaults on create do not apply to write. Setting a field to False later does not restore the default.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
SELECT conname, pg_get_constraintdef(oid)
FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'library_book'::regclass;

Each _sql_constraints entry appears as library_book_<name>.

docs.title: Create, read, write, unlink
docs.text: The persistence methods are the supported way to change data through the ORM. They run access checks, record rules, constraints, computed field recomputation, and tracking. This chapter covers signatures, batch behaviour, and the command tuples used for relational fields. Overriding them is covered in a separate chapter.

docs.title: create
docs.text:
In Odoo 18 the signature is create(self, vals_list), a batch method that takes a list of dicts and returns one recordset.

books = self.env['library.book'].create([
    {'title': 'First', 'pages': 120},
    {'title': 'Second', 'pages': 340},
])

A single dict is still accepted and wrapped into a list. Pass a list in new code: one call with N dicts does batched INSERTs and one round of recomputation, where N calls repeat the overhead N times.

Missing values are filled from field defaults. Context keys default_<field> override model defaults, which is how actions prefill forms.

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
Python code rarely calls read(). Attribute access fetches and caches values, and prefetching loads the same field for the other records of the recordset in one query.

for book in books:
    print(book.title)     # one SELECT for all books, not one per book

read(fields) returns a list of dicts and is what RPC clients use. Many2one values come back as (id, display_name) pairs, x2many fields as lists of ids. When a search needs values immediately, use search_read (RPC style) or search_fetch (exists in the 18 source) to fetch named fields in the same query:

rows = self.env['library.book'].search_fetch(
    [('pages', '>', 300)], ['title', 'pages'], limit=50)

docs.title: write
docs.text:
books.write({'pages': 100})      # one UPDATE for the whole set
book.pages = 100                 # same, via the descriptor, singleton only

write applies the same values to all records and returns True. Values are converted by field type, constraints (@api.constrains) run once for the set, and dependent computed fields are marked for recomputation. Writing an unchanged value is not skipped for you; compare first if the extra UPDATE and write_date bump matter.

docs.title: The Command API
docs.text:
x2many fields are written with commands. In Odoo 18 Command is an IntEnum in odoo.fields, imported with from odoo import Command. The codes below are from the 18 source.

Helper Tuple Effect Command.create(vals) (0, 0, vals) create a record and link it Command.update(id, vals) (1, id, vals) write on a linked record Command.delete(id) (2, id, 0) unlink and delete the record Command.unlink(id) (3, id, 0) remove the link, keep the record Command.link(id) (4, id, 0) link an existing record Command.clear() (5, 0, 0) remove all links Command.set(ids) (6, 0, ids) replace all links with ids 
member.write({
    'loan_ids': [
        Command.create({'book_id': book.id}),
        Command.update(old_loan.id, {'state': 'returned'}),
        Command.unlink(cancelled_loan.id),
    ],
})

Differences by field type:

  • On a One2many, unlink detaches the child by clearing its inverse Many2one (the child is deleted if the inverse is required), while delete removes the child row.
  • On a Many2many, delete removes the comodel record itself, not only the relation. Use unlink to detach and delete only when the target must go.
  • Command.set on a One2many unlinks children missing from the list. Prefer explicit link and unlink when the intent is partial.

Use the named helpers. Raw tuples work and fill old code, but (4, id) versus (4, id, 0) makes readers stop; Command.link(id) does not.

docs.title: unlink
docs.text:
books.unlink()

Before the DELETE the ORM checks access rights and record rules, then applies ondelete of every Many2one pointing at the records:

  • restrict: refuse if referenced.
  • set null: clear the reference (the default for optional Many2one).
  • cascade: delete the referencing rows.

A required Many2one cannot use set null; state ondelete explicitly there. After unlink, any recordset still holding those ids raises MissingError on the next read; guard with exists().

docs.title: copy
docs.text:
new_book = book.copy({'title': book.title + ' (copy)'})

copy(default) duplicates a record and honours the copy= attribute of every field. One2many fields default to copy=False, so child lines are not duplicated unless the field says so. Fields under a unique constraint need an overriding value in default.

docs.title: Batching
docs.text:
• One create with 1000 dicts is far cheaper than 1000 create calls.
  • One write with a shared dict beats a loop of per-record writes.
  • Do not search inside a loop. Search once and use grouped() or filtered().
  • For very large changes, process in chunks of about 1000 ids. Call cr.commit() only in cron or script context, never inside a web request.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
write({'tag_ids': [1, 2, 3]}) is a bug. A plain list of ids is not a command list. Use Command.set([1, 2, 3]).

  • An override of create must keep the batch signature (@api.model_create_multi, vals_list) or a list call breaks it. See the overriding chapter.
  • Writing a non-stored computed field without inverse has no stored effect; the value is recomputed on the next read.
  • A database integrity error aborts the whole transaction. Catching it inside a loop and continuing does not work unless you wrap the step in with self.env.cr.savepoint():.
  • Do not assume zip(vals_list, records) alignment after an override that reorders or filters.
  • Deleting a Many2many comodel record with Command.delete when you meant Command.unlink loses data for every other record linked to it.

Versions. Command and create batching work the same in 16, 17, and 18. search_fetch is in the 18 source; I did not verify it in 16 or 17.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Inspect the command tuples in a development shell:

from odoo import Command
print(Command.link(5), Command.set([1, 2]), Command.clear())

docs.title: Environment, context, and sudo
docs.text: Every recordset carries an environment: the cursor, the user, the context dictionary and (in 17 and 18) the company set. Changing any of them creates a new recordset bound to a new environment. The original is untouched.

docs.title: What env holds
docs.text:
self.env.cr          # database cursor, one transaction
self.env.uid         # user id
self.env.user        # res.users record
self.env.context     # frozen dict
self.env.company     # current company
self.env.companies   # allowed companies, selected in the UI
self.env.lang        # context['lang']

env.context is immutable. You never modify it; you derive a new one.

docs.title: with_context
docs.text:
books = self.with_context(active_test=False).search([])      # include archived
books = self.with_context(lang='fr_FR')                      # read translations

with_context(**kw) merges keys into the existing context. with_context(dict) replaces the whole context, dropping lang, tz, allowed_company_ids and everything else. Merge on purpose:

ctx = dict(self.env.context, default_state='draft')

Context keys with a meaning in the framework:

Key Effect active_test False makes search ignore active lang, tz translation and timezone of reads allowed_company_ids companies the user selected; first one is the current company default_<field> default for that field on create and default_get tracking_disable, mail_notrack no chatter tracking prefetch_fields False disables fetching other fields when you read one

docs.title: with_user and sudo
docs.text:
self.with_user(other_user)   # runs with that user's rights and rules
self.sudo()                  # superuser: bypasses access rights and record rules

sudo() returns a recordset in superuser mode: access rights and record rules do not apply. In Odoo 13 and later it does not switch the user: self.env.user stays the same, and create_uid / write_uid still record the real user. Only env.su becomes True.

self.env.su          # True inside sudo
self.env.is_superuser()
self.env.is_admin()  # user is in base.group_system, or superuser

sudo(False) goes back to normal mode. Use with_user(SUPERUSER_ID) only when you need the superuser as the actual user; it behaves differently from sudo() for create_uid and for rules that mention user.

Records read through a sudo recordset keep the superuser flag when you follow relations, so book.sudo().partner_id.company_id is entirely unrestricted.

docs.title: with_company and companies
docs.text:
self.with_company(company)   # changes env.company and prepends it in allowed_company_ids

Company-dependent fields (company_dependent=True) and multi-company record rules read the context, so a method that works for one company silently returns another company's values if you forget with_company. Many fields use @api.depends_context('company') for exactly this reason.

docs.title: with_env and new cursors
docs.text:
with_env(env) rebinds records to another environment. A new cursor is for work that must commit independently of the caller, such as logging an error that survives a rollback:

from odoo import api, registry

with self.pool.cursor() as cr:
    env = api.Environment(cr, self.env.uid, self.env.context)
    env['library.log'].create({'message': 'failed'})

The new cursor sees only committed data and commits on exit. Records created in the parent transaction are invisible to it, and it can deadlock against rows the parent holds.

docs.title: Access checks in 18
docs.text:
check_access_rights and check_access_rule still exist, but Odoo 18 adds records.check_access('read') which does both in one call, and records.has_access('read') which returns a boolean. Use those in new code.

Versions: check_access and has_access exist from 18. In 16 and 17, use check_access_rights(op) plus check_access_rule(op).

docs.title: When sudo is the wrong answer
docs.text:
sudo() is a decision about trust. Reach for it when the code runs on behalf of the system for a legitimate reason: reading a sequence, reading a configuration record, posting a technical message. Do not use it to make an error go away.

Narrower options:

  • with_user to a service user with the minimum groups.
  • Add a record rule or an access line that expresses the real requirement.
  • Have the method run in a controller with auth='public' plus an explicit lookup, not a blanket sudo() on an entire search.
  • Sudo a single read, not the whole method: self.env['ir.config_parameter'].sudo().get_param(...) instead of self = self.sudo() at the top.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
self.sudo().write(vals) where vals came from a request is privilege escalation. Validate which fields are allowed, then sudo the minimum.

  • Records created with sudo() have create_uid of the real user, so rules based on ownership still match, but company rules read the context and may not.
  • self.env.user inside sudo is not the superuser. Code that tests self.env.user.has_group(...) is evaluated against the real user.
  • with_context(dict) replaces the context. Forgetting to merge loses lang and allowed_company_ids.
  • A recordset passed to another method keeps its environment. A sudo recordset leaks the privilege to every callee.
  • ir.rule evaluation caches by context; changing allowed_company_ids mid-method invalidates it.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
print(env.su, env.uid, env.user.name)
sudo_books = env['library.book'].sudo()
print(sudo_books.env.su, sudo_books.env.uid)   # True, same uid

docs.title: Fields reference
docs.text: Choosing the right field type and attributes decides the column type, the index, the UI widget, and how the field behaves in search, grouping, and export. This chapter lists the types in the Odoo 18 odoo/fields.py and the attributes that matter in daily work.

docs.title: Basic types
docs.text:
Type Column Notes Boolean bool Never NULL semantics; unset reads False. Integer int4 aggregator defaults to sum. Float numeric digits=(total, decimals) or a decimal.precision name. Monetary numeric Needs currency_field (default currency_id) on the model. Char varchar size, translate, trim. Text text Multi-line, translate supported. Html text Sanitised on write unless sanitize=False. Date / Datetime date / timestamp Datetime is stored in UTC and shown in the user's timezone. Binary / Image attachment or bytea attachment=True by default; stored as ir.attachment. Selection varchar List of (value, label) pairs, or a method name. Json jsonb Opaque to search except via = on the whole value. Properties jsonb User-defined fields, defined on a parent record. Reference varchar Value is "model,id".

Relational types: Many2one (FK column), One2many (inverse of a Many2one, no column), Many2many (relation table), Many2oneReference (id column plus a model field).

class Book(models.Model):
    _name = 'library.book'
    _description = 'Book'

    title = fields.Char(required=True, index='trigram', translate=True)
    isbn = fields.Char(copy=False)
    pages = fields.Integer()
    price = fields.Monetary(currency_field='currency_id')
    currency_id = fields.Many2one('res.currency')
    state = fields.Selection(
        [('draft', 'Draft'), ('available', 'Available'), ('lost', 'Lost')],
        default='draft', required=True)
    author_id = fields.Many2one('res.partner', ondelete='restrict', index=True)
    tag_ids = fields.Many2many('library.tag')
    loan_ids = fields.One2many('library.loan', 'book_id')

docs.title: Attributes that apply to every field
docs.text:
From the Field class in the 18 source:

  • string, help: label and tooltip.
  • required, readonly: readonly is a UI and write-through rule on the field definition, not a database constraint. Server code can still write it.
  • default: a value or a callable lambda self: ....
  • store: False for non-stored computed or related fields.
  • index: see below.
  • copy: whether copy() duplicates the value. True by default for simple fields, False for One2many, computed, and related fields.
  • groups: comma-separated group XML ids. Users outside the groups cannot read or write the field, and it disappears from the form view. This is field-level access, not record-level.
  • compute, inverse, search, related, compute_sudo, precompute, recursive: see the computed fields chapter.
  • aggregator: how read_group aggregates the field (sum, avg, max, min, count_distinct, and others PostgreSQL allows).
  • group_expand: name of a method that adds empty groups to grouped views, used by kanban stages.
  • prefetch: set False for heavy fields you do not want fetched along with their siblings.
  • company_dependent: the value is stored per company, in a jsonb column in 18.
  • tracking: from mail.thread; see the mail chapter.

Versions. In 18 the aggregation attribute is aggregator; passing group_operator still works but emits a DeprecationWarning and is mapped to aggregator (confirmed in the 18 source). In 16 and 17 the name is group_operator.

docs.title: Index values
docs.text:
index accepts a string, not only True. The 18 source maps index=True to 'btree_not_null' (btree that skips NULL rows). Other values are 'btree', and 'trigram' for ilike search on Char and Text.

Index what you filter or sort on: foreign keys you search through, state fields with selective values, and Char fields searched with ilike. Do not index everything; every index slows writes and costs disk.

docs.title: Selection
docs.text:
state = fields.Selection([...], default='draft')

When a module extends a selection with selection_add, it must say what happens to existing rows if that module is uninstalled:

state = fields.Selection(selection_add=[('archived', 'Archived')],
                         ondelete={'archived': 'set default'})

The 18 source requires an ondelete policy for added values on required fields and rejects policies that are invalid for the field. A dynamic list is a method name string: selection='_get_states'.

docs.title: Many2one
docs.text:
Key attributes: comodel_name, domain, context, ondelete, check_company, auto_join.

  • ondelete: set null (default for optional), restrict, cascade. Required fields must not use set null.
  • domain on the field is a UI filter plus a default for search; it is not enforced on write. Enforce with a constraint.
  • check_company=True validates that the target belongs to the same company, using a _check_company pass on write.

docs.title: One2many and Many2many
docs.text:
• One2many(comodel, inverse_name): the inverse Many2one must exist. No column. Writes go through commands.
  • Many2many(comodel, relation, column1, column2): the relation table name is derived from the two model names if omitted. When two Many2many fields on the same pair of models need separate storage, name relation explicitly or they share one table.
  • Neither can be sorted in SQL.

docs.title: Monetary and Float
docs.text: Monetary rounds by the currency's rounding on write. Reading it as Float elsewhere loses that rounding. Float(digits=...) rounds on write by the precision; use float_compare, float_is_zero, and float_round from odoo.tools to compare. Never compare floats with ==.

docs.title: Date and Datetime
docs.text: Date.today(), Date.context_today(record), Datetime.now() and Datetime.to_datetime() are the safe helpers. Datetime.now() is naive UTC. Date.context_today(record) gives the date in the user's timezone, which differs from Date.today() near midnight.

docs.title: Choosing: quick rules
docs.text:
• Status with a fixed set of values: Selection, not Char.
  • Reference to another record: Many2one, not an integer.
  • Free structured data per record that users define: Properties, not Json.
  • Long text indexed for search: Char with index='trigram'.
  • Money: Monetary, never Float.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Changing a field's type on an existing database does not migrate data automatically for all type pairs. Changing Integer to Float works; Char to Many2one does not. Write a migration script.

  • required=True on a field with existing NULL rows breaks module update. Add a default or a pre-migration.
  • readonly=True does not stop write() from Python. Use access rights or groups to block writes.
  • A One2many without a matching Many2one raises at registry load.
  • default=fields.Date.today() with parentheses evaluates once at import. Pass the callable: default=fields.Date.today.
  • translate=True on Char changes the column to jsonb in 16 and later; raw SQL against it must use the language key.
  • A Many2many shared relation table between two fields causes each to show the other's links.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
List the attributes a field carries on a development shell:

f = env['res.partner']._fields['name']
print(f.type, f.required, f.index, f.translate)
print(env['res.partner'].fields_get(['name'], attributes=['type', 'string', 'required']))

docs.title: Grouping and aggregation
docs.text: When you need counts, sums, or averages over many records, do it in PostgreSQL, not in a Python loop. Odoo 18 has two entry points: the public read_group, which serves the web client, and _read_group, the typed API you use in Python code.

docs.title: _read_group
docs.text:
Signature in the 18 source:

_read_group(self, domain, groupby=(), aggregates=(), having=(), offset=0, limit=None, order=None)

It returns a list of tuples: the group values first, then the aggregate values, in the order you asked for them. Many2one group values come back as recordsets, not (id, name) pairs.

rows = self.env['library.loan']._read_group(
    domain=[('state', '=', 'late')],
    groupby=['member_id', 'due_date:month'],
    aggregates=['__count', 'fine:sum', 'book_id:count_distinct'],
    order='member_id',
)
for member, month, loans, fines, books in rows:
    ...

Rules from the source:

  • A groupby item is 'field' or 'field:granularity'. Granularities for date and datetime are day, week, month, quarter, year; the source also defines number-style granularities (such as day of week) in READ_GROUP_NUMBER_GRANULARITY.
  • An aggregates item is 'field:agg' or the special '__count'. Aggregate functions are those of PostgreSQL, plus count_distinct and recordset.
  • recordset as an aggregate returns the related records of each group as a recordset, handy when you need both the number and the records.
  • having is a domain over the aggregates, for example [('fine:sum', '>', 100)].
  • With no groupby, PostgreSQL still returns one row, and so does this method, even on an empty set.
  • When the domain is provably false, the method returns early without querying.

Access is checked through check_access('read') on the model, and the domain gets record rules like search.

docs.title: Typical patterns
docs.text:
Count per key into a dict:

counts = {
    book: count
    for book, count in self.env['library.loan']._read_group(
        [('book_id', 'in', books.ids)], ['book_id'], ['__count'])
}

Total of one field with no grouping:

[(total,)] = self.env['library.loan']._read_group(domain, [], ['fine:sum'])

Doing this over a stored computed field works. Over a non-stored field it fails, because the aggregate is computed by SQL.

docs.title: read_group
docs.text:
read_group(self, domain, fields, groupby, offset=0, limit=None, orderby=False, lazy=True)

It returns a list of dicts and exists mainly for the web client's list, pivot, graph, and kanban views. The dicts contain the group values, __domain (the domain selecting that group), __count (named <field>_count in lazy single groupby mode), and the aggregated fields. With lazy=True only the first groupby level is evaluated, so drill-down is a second call using __domain.

Prefer _read_group in module code: it is typed, returns recordsets for relations, and supports having. Use read_group only when you need the web-client dict shape, for example to feed a custom view, or when the code must run on 16.

Versions. _read_group exists in 16, 17, and 18, but the shape changed. In 16 it was a private helper returning dicts with the old read_group conventions. From 17 it is the tuple-based API with the aggregates list. Code written for 17 and 18 does not run on 16. In 18 the field attribute for the default aggregate is aggregator; group_operator is deprecated (a DeprecationWarning in the source), and in 16 and 17 group_operator is the name.

docs.title: Field-level aggregation
docs.text:
The aggregator attribute of a field sets what the web client uses when it totals that column, and what read_group uses for it when you list the field in fields without an explicit function:

fine = fields.Monetary(aggregator='sum')
rating = fields.Float(aggregator='avg')
days_late = fields.Integer(aggregator=False)   # no total shown

Set it to a falsy value to stop a column from being summed in lists, which is right for rates, percentages, and ids.

docs.title: Grouping on related and computed fields
docs.text:
Group on stored fields. Related fields that are stored (store=True) group like normal columns. A Many2one path in groupby such as 'member_id.country_id' is not supported; group on member_id and read the country in Python, or add a stored related field member_country_id.

Fields whose groupable description is false in fields_get cannot be grouped. Non-stored computed fields are the usual cause.

docs.title: group_expand and empty groups
docs.text:
Kanban stages show columns with no records. That is done with group_expand on the grouping field, a method name that returns the extra values:

stage_id = fields.Many2one('library.stage', group_expand='_read_group_stage_ids')

@api.model
def _read_group_stage_ids(self, stages, domain):
    return stages.search([], order=stages._order)

It applies to read_group and the web client path, not to a plain _read_group call.

docs.title: In-memory grouping
docs.text: For records already loaded, use recordset.grouped('field') or grouped(lambda r: ...); it returns a dict of key to recordset and runs no SQL. Choose by size: SQL for scans over many rows, grouped when the set is already in memory.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
_read_group returns tuples ordered by your groupby then aggregates. Unpacking in the wrong order gives no error when types are compatible, and wrong numbers.

  • A group value for an empty Many2one is an empty recordset, not False. For dates, an empty value comes back as False.
  • Date groups return the first day of the period as a date or datetime, not a label. Format it yourself.
  • Datetime grouping uses the user's timezone from the context (tz). Running the same call in a cron with no tz groups on UTC and shifts rows near midnight.
  • Lazy read_group with a list of groupby returns only the first level. Passing lazy=False returns all levels in one go but loses the __domain drill-down convenience.
  • Do not loop over read_group results to build a search per group. The __domain is for one-off drill-downs.
  • __count is the count of rows in the group, not distinct values. Use field:count_distinct for that.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
rows = env['res.partner']._read_group(
    [('active', '=', True)], ['country_id'], ['__count'], order='__count desc', limit=5)
for country, count in rows:
    print(country.display_name or 'none', count)

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text: Odoo has three inheritance mechanisms, and they differ in one thing that matters: what ends up in PostgreSQL. Picking the wrong one is the usual source of "why is there a second table" and "why did my field not show up on the child".

docs.title: Extension: _inherit without _name
docs.text:
The most common form. You add fields and methods to an existing model. No new table, no new model; the registry builds one class from the original plus every extension, in module dependency order.

from odoo import fields, models


class ResPartner(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'res.partner'

    library_card = fields.Char(index='btree_not_null')
    loan_ids = fields.One2many('library.loan', 'partner_id')

On module update, library_card becomes a column on res_partner. Every record of the model gets it, including partners created by other modules.

docs.title: Classical: _inherit plus a new _name
docs.text:
Copies the parent definition into a new model with its own table. The two share nothing at runtime: records of the parent do not appear in the child.

class LibraryRareBook(models.Model):
    _name = 'library.rare.book'
    _inherit = 'library.book'
    _description = 'Rare book'

    insured_value = fields.Monetary(currency_field='currency_id')

Result: a table library_rare_book with all columns of library_book plus insured_value. Methods come through the Python class chain, so super() works as usual. Views, access rules and record rules are not copied: the new model needs its own.

You can inherit from several models at once, which is how mixins work:

_inherit = ['library.book', 'mail.thread', 'mail.activity.mixin']

Mixins are abstract models (models.AbstractModel): no table of their own, only fields and methods that concrete models absorb. The fields of a mixin become columns on the table of the model that uses it.

docs.title: Delegation: _inherits
docs.text:
Composition, not copying. The child holds a required Many2one to the parent and exposes the parent's fields as if they were its own.

class LibraryMember(models.Model):
    _name = 'library.member'
    _description = 'Library member'
    _inherits = {'res.partner': 'partner_id'}

    partner_id = fields.Many2one('res.partner', required=True, ondelete='restrict')
    joined_on = fields.Date(default=fields.Date.today)

member.name reads member.partner_id.name. Creating a member with name in the values creates a partner first, then the member row pointing at it. Two tables, one join. This is how res.users relates to res.partner.

Rules worth knowing:

  • Only fields are delegated. Methods of the parent are not reachable on the child.
  • Writing a delegated field writes to the parent record, which may be shared by other children.
  • Set ondelete on the link field explicitly. restrict protects a shared parent; cascade removes the child when the parent goes.
  • Searching on a delegated field works and produces a join.
  • Delegated fields are related fields (inherited=True); the value is stored once, on the parent.

docs.title: Which one
docs.text:
You want Use New fields or behaviour on an existing model extension (_inherit only) Reusable behaviour (chatter, activities) abstract mixin A specialised variant with separate records and table classical A new record type that must also be a partner or product delegation

A fourth option, often missed: do not inherit. If the new model only needs a link to res.partner, a Many2one is simpler than any of the above.

docs.title: Method resolution order
docs.text:
Extensions are applied in load order, so super() in your override calls the version from the module loaded before yours. Declaring dependencies in __manifest__.py is therefore part of correctness, not just packaging: if module B must wrap module A's method, B must depend on A.

class ResPartner(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'res.partner'

    def _get_name(self):
        name = super()._get_name()
        return f'{name} ({self.library_card})' if self.library_card else name

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Forgetting _name when you meant a classical inheritance modifies the parent for everybody. Forgetting _inherit when you meant an extension creates an unrelated model that merely shares the name.

  • Classical inheritance copies _sql_constraints of the parent. Constraint names are keyed per table, but reusing a name with a different definition in the child is a silent override: check the update log.
  • Redefining a field in an extension replaces only the attributes you pass. name = fields.Char(string='Title') on an existing Char keeps required, translate and the rest.
  • Changing a field's type in an extension is not supported cleanly; the column conversion can lose data.
  • With _inherits, creating a child creates a parent, so the parent's defaults and constraints run on child creation. A batch create produces one parent per child.
  • Extend a mixin through _inherit; never copy its class into your module.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Look at the schema each mechanism produced, read only, from psql:

SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_name IN ('library_book', 'library_rare_book', 'library_member');
\d library_member

The _inherits model has a partner_id column and nothing for name; the classical model has every column of its parent.

docs.title: Mail thread and activities
docs.text: Two mixins give a model its chatter: mail.thread (messages, followers, tracking) and mail.activity.mixin (scheduled to-dos). Inheriting them is one line, but what they do on every create and write is worth understanding, because it is the main reason bulk operations on tracked models are slow.

docs.title: Adding them
docs.text:
class LibraryLoan(models.Model):
    _name = 'library.loan'
    _description = 'Loan'
    _inherit = ['mail.thread', 'mail.activity.mixin']

    name = fields.Char(required=True, tracking=True)
    state = fields.Selection(
        [('open', 'Open'), ('late', 'Late'), ('done', 'Done')],
        default='open', tracking=True)
    user_id = fields.Many2one('res.users', tracking=True)

Add message_follower_ids, message_ids and activity_ids to the form view, or the shorthand <chatter/> element in Odoo 18 (16 and 17 use the explicit <div class="oe_chatter"> block).

docs.title: Tracking
docs.text:
tracking=True on a field logs its changes as a message with a before and after value. An integer value orders the fields in the message. A tracked change triggers on write, not on raw SQL, and not when the context has tracking_disable or mail_notrack.

@api.model_create_multi
def create(self, vals_list):
    return super().create(vals_list).with_context(tracking_disable=True)

Disable tracking for imports and large batch creates by passing tracking_disable=True on the call that creates, not by editing the model. On creation, mail_create_nolog=True removes the "created" message and mail_create_nosubscribe=True stops adding the creator as a follower.

Override _track_subtype(self, initial_values) to choose the message subtype (for example a "Loan became late" subtype) so followers can subscribe to it selectively.

docs.title: Posting messages
docs.text:
loan.message_post(
    body=self.env._("Loan marked late."),
    subtype_xmlid='mail.mt_note',
)

message_post is keyword-only. Main parameters: body, subject, message_type ('notification' by default, 'comment' for something a user wrote), subtype_xmlid (mail.mt_comment notifies followers, mail.mt_note is internal), partner_ids, attachment_ids.

Other entry points:

  • message_notify(...) sends a message to given partners without making them followers, and without writing in the thread.
  • _message_log(body=...) writes a log note with no notification.
  • message_post_with_source(...) renders a template or view as the body.

Bodies are HTML. Pass plain strings only when they are already escaped; for user input, use Markup and markupsafe.escape, or the body gets sanitised.

docs.title: Followers
docs.text:
loan.message_subscribe(partner_ids=[partner.id])
loan.message_unsubscribe(partner_ids=[partner.id])

Followers receive notifications for subtypes they chose. Odoo adds the author of a message as a follower unless mail_post_autofollow is disabled in context. Default subtypes per model come from mail.message.subtype records whose res_model matches.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
Activities are scheduled to-dos for a user on a record: a call, a reminder, an approval.

loan.activity_schedule(
    'mail.mail_activity_data_todo',
    date_deadline=fields.Date.add(fields.Date.today(), days=7),
    summary=self.env._("Check return"),
    user_id=loan.user_id.id,
)

The signature is activity_schedule(act_type_xmlid='', date_deadline=None, summary='', note='', **act_values). Extra values (such as user_id) go straight into mail.activity. When user_id is not given, the activity type's default user, then the current user, is used. The activity type is referenced by XML ID; defining your own type in data lets managers rename and reconfigure it.

Closing activities:

loan.activity_feedback(['mail.mail_activity_data_todo'], feedback=self.env._("Returned"))
loan.activity_unlink(['mail.mail_activity_data_todo'])

activity_feedback(act_type_xmlids, user_id=None, feedback=None, attachment_ids=None) marks done and posts the feedback in the chatter; activity_unlink removes without trace. Prefer feedback: it leaves an audit trail.

The mixin also adds stored fields such as activity_state and activity_date_deadline, which power the list-view activity widget and the "My activities" filters.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Each tracked write creates a message, tracking values and notifications; each create subscribes followers. A loop with write per record on a tracked model is far slower than one write on the recordset.

  • Tracking a computed field works only if it is stored.
  • Tracking a One2many or Many2many does not produce a before and after; the ORM tracks columns. Post a message by hand.
  • message_post from a cron or sudo() is authored by the environment user (often the superuser, shown as a system user). Pass author_id for human-looking messages.
  • Notifications go out by email through the mail queue. A test or staging database with outgoing mail enabled will email real followers. Check outgoing mail servers before running a data load.
  • activity_schedule with a missing XML ID raises; guard custom types with raise_if_not_found=False through env.ref.
  • Mail sending errors are logged by the queue, not raised in your method, so a post can succeed while the email fails.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
On a throwaway database:

loan = env['library.loan'].create({'name': 'Test loan'})
loan.message_post(body='Hello', subtype_xmlid='mail.mt_note')
loan.activity_schedule('mail.mail_activity_data_todo', summary='Check')
print(loan.message_ids.mapped('body'), loan.activity_ids.mapped('summary'))

Then open the form to see both in the chatter.

docs.title: Models and recordsets
docs.text: Every ORM call returns or consumes a recordset: an ordered collection of record ids bound to an environment. Most ORM bugs come from misunderstanding what a recordset is, so this chapter fixes the mental model before the API chapters build on it.

docs.title: Three model classes
docs.text:
from odoo import models, fields

class Book(models.Model):                 # persistent, one table
    _name = 'library.book'
    _description = 'Book'

class LoanWizard(models.TransientModel):  # persistent, vacuumed automatically
    _name = 'library.loan.wizard'
    _description = 'Loan wizard'

class LoanHelpers(models.AbstractModel):  # no table, mixin or service
    _name = 'library.loan.helpers'
    _description = 'Loan helpers'
  • Model creates a table library_book with the standard columns id, create_uid, create_date, write_uid, write_date.
  • TransientModel has a table, but rows are removed by a scheduled vacuum. Use it for wizards, never for data you need tomorrow.
  • AbstractModel has no table. Use it as a mixin (_inherit = ['library.loan.helpers']) or as a namespace for methods.

_description is required in practice: without it the registry logs a warning at load, and the model has no readable label in the UI or in access errors.

docs.title: What a recordset is
docs.text:
self.env['library.book'] is an empty recordset of the model. browse(ids) builds one without touching the database. search() builds one from a query. There is no separate "record" class.

books = self.env['library.book'].search([('pages', '>', 300)])
books.ids          # [3, 8, 11]
len(books)         # 3
books[0]           # recordset of length 1, a "singleton"
books[:2]          # slicing returns a recordset
bool(books)        # False when empty

A recordset behaves like an immutable ordered set of ids. It is hashable, iterable, and supports:

a | b      # union, no duplicates
a & b      # intersection
a - b      # difference
a + b      # concatenation, keeps duplicates
x in a     # membership of a singleton

Two recordsets are equal if model, ids, and order match.

docs.title: Singletons and ensure_one
docs.text:
Reading a field on a multi-record set raises ValueError: Expected singleton. Iterating yields singletons.

books.title                       # ValueError if len(books) > 1
books.write({'active': False})    # fine, one UPDATE for all
for book in books:
    book.title                    # fine

Call self.ensure_one() at the top of any method that needs exactly one record, such as a button action. It fails loudly instead of silently reading the wrong record.

An empty recordset is falsy and field reads on it return the empty value (False, 0, an empty recordset). That is why book.author_id.name is safe when author_id is unset.

docs.title: Batch the write
docs.text:
# Bad: one UPDATE per record
for loan in loans:
    loan.state = 'returned'

# Good: one UPDATE
loans.write({'state': 'returned'})

When values differ per record a loop is unavoidable, but group first (filtered, grouped) and write once per group.

docs.title: mapped
docs.text:
loans.mapped('book_id')                 # recordset of books, deduplicated
loans.mapped('book_id.title')           # list of strings
loans.mapped(lambda l: l.days_late)     # list of values

With a relational path mapped returns a recordset without duplicates; with a scalar field it returns a list and keeps duplicates.

docs.title: filtered, filtered_domain, sorted
docs.text:
late = loans.filtered(lambda l: l.days_late > 0)
late = loans.filtered('is_late')                      # by truthiness of a field
late = loans.filtered_domain([('days_late', '>', 0)])
by_due = loans.sorted('due_date', reverse=True)

filtered_domain evaluates the domain in Python over records already in memory. No SQL runs, so it is cheap for small sets and wrong tool for large ones.

docs.title: grouped
docs.text:
Partition a recordset in memory by a field name or a callable. The method exists in the 18 source (models.py, def grouped(self, key)).

for member, member_loans in loans.grouped('member_id').items():
    ...

The result is a dict from key to recordset, and all values share one prefetch set, so field reads in the loop stay cheap. It is a partition, not an aggregation; for sums and counts over many rows use _read_group.

docs.title: exists
docs.text:
if not record.exists():
    return

browse(id) never checks that the row is present. After a concurrent unlink, a cached recordset still holds the id and the first field read raises MissingError. exists() returns the subset that still exists.

docs.title: Environments travel with the recordset
docs.text:
Each recordset carries env (cursor, user, context, su flag). with_context, with_user, sudo, and with_company return a new recordset over the same ids; they never mutate the original.

book = book.with_context(lang='fr_FR')   # rebind, do not drop the result

Calling book.with_context(...) without using the result does nothing, a common mistake. The environment chapter covers sudo and context rules.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
if record: is true for a stale record. A recordset with one id is truthy even if the row was deleted. Use exists().

  • search(...)[0] raises IndexError on an empty result. Use search(..., limit=1) and test truthiness, or ensure_one() when exactly one is required.
  • record == 5 is always False. Compare record.id.
  • a + b keeps duplicates, a | b does not. Merging search results with + can process records twice.
  • Building a big recordset by repeated |= is quadratic. Collect ids in a list and browse once.
  • Do not keep recordsets in module-level variables or class attributes. They are bound to a cursor that will be closed.
  • Do not call len(search(...)) just to count; use search_count.

Versions. grouped and search_fetch are present in 18; I did not check 16 and 17 for them, so verify before using in a module that must run on those. filtered_domain, mapped, sorted, exists, and ensure_one are available in 16 through 18.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
In an Odoo shell on a development database:

partners = env['res.partner'].search([], limit=5)
print(partners.ids, len(partners))
print(partners.mapped('name'))
print((partners[:2] | partners[1:3]).ids)

docs.title: Overriding CRUD methods
docs.text: Overriding create, write, unlink and copy is the usual way to hook business rules into the record lifecycle. It is also where the subtle bugs live: wrong signature, per-record logic that breaks on batches, side effects that run before validation.

docs.title: create
docs.text:
create receives a list of dictionaries (create(self, vals_list: list[dict]) -> Self). Decorate your override with @api.model_create_multi and treat the argument as a list.

from odoo import api, models


class LibraryBook(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'library.book'

    @api.model_create_multi
    def create(self, vals_list):
        for vals in vals_list:
            if not vals.get('isbn'):
                vals['isbn'] = self.env['ir.sequence'].next_by_code('library.book')
        books = super().create(vals_list)
        books._notify_new_books()
        return books

The decorator also lets legacy callers pass a single dictionary: it is wrapped into a list before your code runs.

Rules:

  • Change values before super(), act on records after it. Records do not exist before super() returns.
  • Return the recordset super() returned.
  • Never loop super().create([vals]) per item; you lose the batch insert.
  • Values can contain context defaults, False for empty relational fields, and command tuples for x2many. Do not assume plain ids.

docs.title: write
docs.text:
def write(self, vals):
    if vals.get('state') == 'lost':
        if self.loan_ids.filtered(lambda l: not l.returned):
            raise UserError(self.env._("Return open loans before marking a book lost."))
    old_shelf = {book.id: book.shelf for book in self}
    result = super().write(vals)
    if 'shelf' in vals:
        self.filtered(lambda b: old_shelf[b.id] != b.shelf)._reindex_shelf()
    return result

write runs on a recordset with one dictionary applied to every record. Read old values before super(); they are gone afterwards. It returns True.

self.env._() for translation is available in Odoo 18. In 16 and 17 use from odoo import _ and call _("...").

docs.title: unlink
docs.text:
For cleanup, override unlink:

def unlink(self):
    self.env['library.loan'].search([('book_id', 'in', self.ids)]).unlink()
    return super().unlink()

For validation, prefer @api.ondelete:

@api.ondelete(at_uninstall=False)
def _unlink_except_on_loan(self):
    if any(book.state == 'on_loan' for book in self):
        raise UserError(self.env._("You cannot delete a book that is on loan."))

Methods marked at_uninstall=False are skipped when the module is being uninstalled. A raise in a plain unlink override can make the module impossible to uninstall because its own records cannot be deleted.

docs.title: copy and copy_data
docs.text:
Override copy_data to change what is copied, copy to react to the new record.

def copy_data(self, default=None):
    default = dict(default or {})
    default.setdefault('isbn', False)
    return super().copy_data(default)

copy_data returns a list of dictionaries, one per record. If you only want to exclude a field, set copy=False on it instead of overriding anything.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Always call super(). A missing call silently removes behaviour from every module loaded earlier.
  • Context keys such as tracking_disable, mail_notrack and mail_create_nolog change the behaviour of the mail mixin further down the chain. Pass them with with_context, not through values.
  • _write and _create are the low-level methods. They skip access checks and tracking; use them only for internal bookkeeping.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
self.ensure_one() in write crashes on mass edits, imports and any save that touches several records. Loop or use filtered.

  • Writing to self inside write recurses. Guard with a context key, or put the extra values into vals before super().
  • Side effects in create (HTTP calls, emails) run inside the transaction. A later error rolls back the data but not the action. Defer with self.env.cr.postcommit.add(callback) when it must happen only after commit.
  • Validation belongs in @api.constrains, not in write: constraints also run on create and during import.
  • Reading a stored computed field before super().create() returns nothing useful; it has not been computed.
  • An override on create that returns early without calling super() for some vals breaks the order of the returned recordset relative to vals_list.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
On a throwaway database, in odoo shell, check that your override is batch-safe:

books = env['library.book'].create([{'name': f'Book {i}'} for i in range(5)])
books.write({'shelf': 'A'})

Add a log line in each override. You should see one create call and one write call, not five.

docs.title: Raw SQL from the ORM
docs.text: Most code never needs SQL. Reach for it when the ORM cannot express the query (window functions, CTEs, aggregate filters), or when a set-based update replaces a loop over a hundred thousand records. When you do, three things have to be right: parameterisation, flushing before the query, and invalidating the cache after it.

docs.title: The SQL helper
docs.text:
odoo.tools.SQL is a composable wrapper that keeps code and parameters together and discourages string concatenation:

from odoo.tools import SQL

query = SQL(
    "SELECT book_id, COUNT(*) FROM %s WHERE state = %s GROUP BY book_id",
    SQL.identifier('library_loan'),
    'open',
)

Arguments are either parameters (bound by the driver) or other SQL objects, which are merged with their own parameters. SQL.identifier(name) quotes a table or column name; use it for anything that is not a literal. Named arguments work too: SQL("... %(state)s", state='open'). Literal percent signs cannot be escaped in this form.

Fragments combine:

where = SQL("state = %s", 'open')
if partner:
    where = SQL("%s AND partner_id = %s", where, partner.id)
query = SQL("SELECT id FROM library_loan WHERE %s", where)

The model API also produces SQL objects for you, which keeps field names and company-dependent or translated columns right:

Loan = self.env['library.loan']
sql_state = Loan._field_to_sql('library_loan', 'state')

_field_to_sql(alias, field_expr, query=None) returns the SQL for a field, handling translations and related paths. Use it instead of hardcoding column names for anything translated or inherited.

docs.title: Executing
docs.text:
rows = self.env.execute_query(query)            # list of tuples
dicts = self.env.execute_query_dict(query)      # list of dicts

env.execute_query(SQL) flushes the fields declared in the query's metadata and fetches the result. Pass an SQL object, not a string; there is an assertion on the type. The older, lower-level form still works:

self.env.cr.execute(query)
rows = self.env.cr.fetchall()

cr.execute accepts an SQL object as well as the (string, params) form. With the raw cursor, flushing is your job.

Versions: the SQL class and env.execute_query exist in 17 and 18. In 16, call cr.execute(query_string, params) and flush by hand. Query objects returned by _search convert to SQL through query.subselect() or by passing the query itself as an argument to SQL(...) in 18.

docs.title: Flush before, invalidate after
docs.text:
The ORM writes lazily (see the cache chapter). Before a raw read, pending values must reach the database. After a raw write, cached values are stale.

Loan = self.env['library.loan']
Loan.flush_model(['state', 'date_due'])      # before reading state and date_due

self.env.cr.execute(SQL(
    "UPDATE library_loan SET state = 'late' WHERE state = 'open' AND date_due < %s",
    fields.Date.today(),
))

Loan.invalidate_model(['state'])             # after writing state

execute_query does the flush step for you only for the fields it knows about, so it is still worth naming them for hand-written SQL. Flush the model whose columns you touch, and every model you join. A computed stored field that depends on the changed column is not recomputed by raw SQL: neither dependants nor tracking nor constraints run.

docs.title: Reading from the ORM, then joining in SQL
docs.text:
Use ORM for the access-controlled part, then SQL for the rest. _search returns a Query that applies record rules:

query = self.env['library.loan']._search([('state', '=', 'open')])
ids = [row[0] for row in self.env.execute_query(query.select())]

Going through _search keeps record rules and company filters in the SQL. Raw SQL by itself sees every row of every company.

docs.title: When raw SQL is justified
docs.text:
• Reports on large tables with window functions or CTEs.
  • Bulk updates that need not trigger business logic (denormalised counters after an import).
  • Migrations in pre- and post-migration scripts where the ORM models may not match the schema yet.
  • Locking, such as SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED in a queue worker.

It is not justified to avoid learning search or _read_group, or to skip access rights.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Never build SQL with f-strings or % on user input. Pass values as parameters and identifiers through SQL.identifier. A bare string in cr.execute that contains user input is an injection.

  • Skipping the invalidate after a write: the next read in the same transaction returns the old value and the bug disappears in the next request.
  • Skipping the flush before a read: your query misses records the same method created a moment ago.
  • Raw INSERT bypasses defaults, sequences, create_uid, create_date, translations and access checks. The columns the ORM fills automatically are NOT NULL without defaults in the table.
  • Raw SQL ignores company and user record rules.
  • A failed statement aborts the transaction in PostgreSQL. To catch the error and continue, wrap the statement in with self.env.cr.savepoint():.
  • Translated columns (translate=True) are JSONB in 16 and later; WHERE name = 'x' does not work, use _field_to_sql.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Read-only, in odoo shell:

from odoo.tools import SQL
print(env.execute_query(SQL("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM %s", SQL.identifier('res_partner'))))

Compare with env['res.partner'].search_count([]); the SQL count ignores record rules and the active filter.

docs.title: Search and domains
docs.text: A domain is a list that filters records. The ORM compiles it to SQL in search, evaluates it in Python in filtered_domain, and clients send it as JSON. This chapter covers the syntax, the operators in the Odoo 18 source, and the habits that keep searches fast and correct.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
A domain is a list of conditions and logical operators in prefix (Polish) notation. A condition is a tuple (field_path, operator, value).

[('state', '=', 'available'), ('pages', '>', 300)]       # implicit AND
['|', ('state', '=', 'draft'), ('state', '=', 'lost')]    # OR of two
['!', ('title', 'ilike', 'guide')]                        # NOT
['&', ('a', '=', 1), '|', ('b', '=', 2), ('c', '=', 3)]   # a AND (b OR c)

Logical operators are &, |, !. & and | take two operands, ! takes one. Conditions with no operator between them are ANDed, so the leading & is rarely written. The common mistake is forgetting that | binds only the next two items:

# Intended: (a OR b) AND c. This is not it.
['|', ('a', '=', 1), ('b', '=', 2), ('c', '=', 3)]   # fine here: c is ANDed after
# Intended: a OR b OR c needs two '|'.
['|', '|', ('a', '=', 1), ('b', '=', 2), ('c', '=', 3)]

odoo.osv.expression has helpers: AND([d1, d2]), OR([d1, d2]), NOT_OPERATOR, normalize_domain. Prefer them when composing domains from parts, since concatenating lists by hand breaks the prefix structure when one part is already an OR.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
These are the term operators defined in the 18 source (TERM_OPERATORS in odoo/osv/expression.py):

=, !=, <, <=, >, >=, =?, =like, =ilike, like, not like, ilike, not ilike, in, not in, child_of, parent_of, any, not any.

Behaviour worth knowing:

  • like and ilike wrap the value in %...%. =like and =ilike do not, so you provide the wildcards yourself.
  • =? means "equals unless the value is falsy": ('partner_id', '=?', False) is ignored. Useful for optional filters.
  • in takes a list or tuple. ('id', 'in', []) matches nothing, and ('id', 'not in', []) matches everything.
  • = False on a Many2one or Char matches both NULL and, for Char, the empty string in some paths. For stricter logic, test with ('field', '=', False) and check the result set, or use a custom search.
  • child_of and parent_of follow _parent_name (default parent_id) over the hierarchy, using parent_path when _parent_store is on.
  • any and not any test the comodel with a sub-domain:
[('loan_ids', 'any', [('state', '=', 'late')])]
[('author_id', 'any', [('country_id.code', '=', 'FR')])]

any is the clear way to say "at least one related record matches these conditions together". A dotted path with two conditions on the same x2many does not guarantee the same related record satisfies both.

Versions. In 16 any and not any exist as well, but the domain was a plain list with a normalize_domain-style pass. Odoo 18 still uses odoo/osv/expression.py for this; I did not check any other module layout. Do not rely on a Domain class in code that must run on 16 to 18.

docs.title: Dotted paths
docs.text:
[('book_id.author_id.name', 'ilike', 'tolstoy')]

A path through Many2one joins or sub-selects automatically, subject to the access rules of the comodel. Through x2many the result is "any related record", and the ORM runs a sub-query. Paths over non-stored computed fields work only if the field has a search method.

docs.title: The search methods
docs.text:
Book = self.env['library.book']
Book.search(domain, offset=0, limit=None, order=None)
Book.search_count(domain, limit=None)
Book.search_read(domain, fields, offset=0, limit=None, order=None)   # RPC oriented
Book.search_fetch(domain, field_names, offset=0, limit=None, order=None)

search_count accepts a limit in 18, which stops counting early; use it for "are there at least N" checks. _search returns a Query object instead of records, used when building sub-selects or in overrides that must not load ids.

docs.title: Active records
docs.text: For models with an active field, search adds ('active', '=', True) automatically. Override with with_context(active_test=False), or put an explicit ('active', ...) condition in the domain.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text: order is a comma-separated string: 'pages desc, title'. If omitted, _order of the model applies. The ORM appends id to make the order stable. Sorting is on stored fields only (or related fields that resolve to stored ones).

docs.title: Access rules are part of search
docs.text: search applies record rules of the current user. Under sudo() it does not. A search that returns a record for an admin and nothing for a regular user is almost always a record rule, not a bug in the domain.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• Search on indexed columns. A filter on an unindexed Char with ilike '%x%' is a sequential scan; give the field index='trigram'.
  • search([...]) followed by len() loads ids; search_count runs COUNT.
  • Do not search inside loops. Collect keys, search once with in, and grouped().
  • Large in lists (tens of thousands of ids) are slow. Use a sub-domain with any or restructure.
  • Use limit=1 when you need existence, or search_count(domain, limit=1).
  • Non-stored computed fields in a domain need a search method, and that method decides the cost.

docs.title: Writing a search method for a computed field
docs.text:
is_late = fields.Boolean(compute='_compute_is_late', search='_search_is_late')

def _search_is_late(self, operator, value):
    if operator not in ('=', '!=') or not isinstance(value, bool):
        raise UserError(_("Unsupported search on is_late."))
    positive = (operator == '=') == value
    domain = [('due_date', '<', fields.Date.context_today(self))]
    return domain if positive else ['!'] + domain

The method returns a domain; return only fields that are stored or themselves searchable. Validate the operator instead of assuming =.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Unsaved changes are flushed before a search that depends on them, but only for fields the ORM can detect from the domain. A search through a raw SQL path, or after cr.execute writes, sees stale data. Call flush_model() first.

  • ('field', '=', record) works for Many2one, but passing a multi-record recordset to = is wrong; use in with .ids.
  • Concatenating domains with + is correct for AND only when both parts are complete. A part starting with | that has fewer terms than needed corrupts the result.
  • ('name', 'ilike', False) is not "no filter". Use =? or build the domain conditionally.
  • A domain stored as a string in a record (filters, rules) is evaluated with a limited context; user, time, and company_ids exist, arbitrary names do not.
  • search with limit but no order uses _order; without a stable order, pagination can skip or repeat rows.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
domain = ['|', ('is_company', '=', True), ('email', '!=', False)]
print(env['res.partner'].search_count(domain))
from odoo.osv import expression
print(expression.AND([domain, [('active', '=', True)]]))

docs.title: Sequences and translations
docs.text: Two unrelated topics that every model with a user-facing reference eventually meets: generating document numbers, and making text show up in the user's language.

docs.title: ir.sequence
docs.text:
A sequence is a configurable number generator stored in ir.sequence. Define one in data:

<odoo>
    <data noupdate="1">
        <record id="seq_library_loan" model="ir.sequence">
            <field name="name">Loan</field>
            <field name="code">library.loan</field>
            <field name="prefix">LN/%(year)s/</field>
            <field name="padding">5</field>
            <field name="company_id" eval="False"/>
        </record>
    </data>
</odoo>

Use it in create:

@api.model_create_multi
def create(self, vals_list):
    for vals in vals_list:
        if not vals.get('name') or vals['name'] == '/':
            vals['name'] = self.env['ir.sequence'].next_by_code('library.loan') or '/'
    return super().create(vals_list)

next_by_code(sequence_code) picks the sequence by code, preferring one of the current company and falling back to one with no company. It returns False when none matches, hence the or '/'. next_by_id() on a sequence record takes no code.

Prefix and suffix support interpolation: %(year)s, %(month)s, %(day)s, %(y)s, and the range_* variants for date ranges. Enable use_date_range for yearly or monthly resets: each range keeps its own counter.

docs.title: Standard and no-gap
docs.text:
The implementation field has two values (odoo/addons/base/models/ir_sequence.py):

  • standard: backed by a PostgreSQL sequence. Fast, never blocks, and never rolls back. A failed transaction burns a number.
  • no_gap: a counter row locked and incremented in the transaction. No number is skipped by a rollback, but concurrent creators wait for each other.

Choose no_gap only when the law or the auditor requires contiguous numbers, and expect contention. Even then, deleted records leave gaps.

Accounting documents do not use ir.sequence in recent versions; they build their own sequence from the journal and the previous record. Use ir.sequence for the rest.

docs.title: Translations
docs.text: User-visible strings in Python code and in view XML are extracted into .po files per module (i18n/fr.po). Two kinds of text need to be handled differently:

docs.title: Static strings in code
docs.text:
raise UserError(self.env._("Loan %s is already closed.", loan.name))

self.env._() translates into the user's language (env.lang) at call time and takes %s arguments that it substitutes after translation. It is available in Odoo 18; in 16 and 17 use from odoo import _ and _("...", arg). Never format before translating: _("Loan %s" % name) produces a string that exists in no catalogue.

Strings defined at import time, such as selection labels or module-level constants, need a lazy form, since the language is not known yet:

from odoo.tools import LazyTranslate
_lt = LazyTranslate(__name__)

STATES = [('open', _lt("Open")), ('done', _lt("Done"))]

Selection labels and field string= values in field definitions are extracted automatically; you do not wrap them.

docs.title: Translatable field values
docs.text:
translate=True on a Char, Text or Html field stores one value per language.

name = fields.Char(translate=True)
