In Odoo 16 and later such a column is JSONB, with a key per language code, instead of rows in ir_translation. That table is gone. Consequences:

  • book.with_context(lang='fr_FR').name reads the French value, falling back to the source value (en_US) when the French one is missing.
  • Writing with a context language writes that language only. Writing without one (English) updates the source and, for Html and Text, tries to keep existing translations aligned.
  • To set several languages in one call, use update_field_translations:
book.update_field_translations('name', {'fr_FR': 'Dune', 'it_IT': 'Dune'})
  • Searching on a translated field compares against the user's language with fallback.
  • Raw SQL must address the JSON: use _field_to_sql, as in the raw SQL chapter.

Loading a language, exporting and importing .po files, and updating terms are done from Settings, Translations, or the command line with odoo-bin -d db -l fr_FR --i18n-export style options. Do these on staging first.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Translating at import time. A string wrapped with _() at module level is evaluated once, in no language, and the extracted term is attached to nothing useful. Use the lazy form or translate inside the method.

  • Sequences with company_id set are invisible to other companies. next_by_code then returns False, and the name falls back to /.
  • The sequence code must be unique per intent. Two modules using 'sale.order' as a code share the counter.
  • noupdate="1" on the sequence record keeps the live counter from being reset by module updates. Without it, an update can overwrite the prefix an administrator changed.
  • Changing the prefix of an existing sequence does not renumber existing records.
  • Translating a field value with translate=True that holds an identifier, such as a code or a technical name, makes lookups depend on the user's language. Leave identifiers untranslated.
  • A .po file entry with a changed source term no longer matches; terms are matched on exact source text.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
seq = env['ir.sequence'].search([('code', '=', 'library.loan')], limit=1)
print(seq.implementation, seq.prefix, seq.number_next_actual)

number_next_actual shows the next value without consuming it (unlike next_by_code, which burns one).

docs.title: XML IDs and references
docs.text: A database id changes between databases; an XML ID does not. Every reference from code, data files, views and migrations to a specific record should go through an XML ID. They live in the ir.model.data model, one row per identifier.

docs.title: Anatomy
docs.text:
An XML ID is module.name. The row in ir_model_data stores module, name, the target model, res_id, and a noupdate flag.

<odoo>
    <data noupdate="1">
        <record id="loan_type_default" model="library.loan.type">
            <field name="name">Standard</field>
        </record>
    </data>
</odoo>

This creates library.loan_type_default (the module prefix is added when you omit it, inside the module that owns the file). Inside the same module you can reference it as loan_type_default; from another module use the full form.

docs.title: Resolving in Python
docs.text:
type_ = self.env.ref('library.loan_type_default')                  # record, raises if missing
type_ = self.env.ref('library.loan_type_default', raise_if_not_found=False)

env.ref(xml_id, raise_if_not_found=True) returns a recordset of the right model. It is cached for the transaction. For just the id, or when you do not want to build a record:

res_id = self.env['ir.model.data']._xmlid_to_res_id('library.loan_type_default')

_xmlid_to_res_id(xmlid, raise_if_not_found=False) returns the id, or 0 when missing. And the other direction:

book.get_external_id()          # {book.id: 'library.book_dune'} or '' per record
book.get_metadata()             # includes xmlid, noupdate, create/write info

get_external_id() on a recordset returns a dictionary keyed by id. It is a query per call, so do not use it in a loop over thousands of records.

docs.title: Access checks
docs.text: env.ref does not check access rights on the result beyond what a later read does. If you need to verify, use check_access on the record. The model-level helper ir.model.data.check_object_reference(module, xml_id, raise_on_access_error=False) returns (model, res_id) after checking read access.

docs.title: In views and data files
docs.text:
<field name="partner_id" ref="base.main_partner"/>
<field name="category_ids" eval="[(6, 0, [ref('library.cat_fiction')])]"/>
<field name="groups_id" eval="[Command.link(ref('library.group_librarian'))]"/>

ref="..." sets a Many2one. ref('...') in eval returns the id. In 17 and 18 use Command objects in eval; the numeric tuple forms still work but are harder to read.

Actions, menus and views refer to each other by XML ID: action="library.action_books", parent="library.menu_root". A missing or mistyped ID fails the module update, which is how typos get caught.

docs.title: Creating XML IDs from code
docs.text:
Records you create in Python have no XML ID. When another module or a later upgrade must find them, create one:

self.env['ir.model.data'].create({
    'module': 'library',
    'name': 'default_shelf',
    'model': 'library.shelf',
    'res_id': shelf.id,
    'noupdate': True,
})

Use this sparingly, in post_init_hook or migration scripts. For batch creation from data, _load_records is what the XML loader uses and it handles updates of existing IDs.

docs.title: noupdate
docs.text:
noupdate="1" means the record is created on install and left alone on module updates. Without it, every -u rewrites the record from the XML, discarding user changes. Use noupdate for data users are expected to edit (templates, sequences, default configuration) and plain records for technical data (views, actions, security groups).

To change a noupdate record deliberately, write a migration script or use a <function> in a data file. Editing the XML will not do it.

docs.title: Module uninstall and renaming
docs.text: Uninstalling a module deletes the records for every XML ID it owns, which is how data cleans itself. Renaming an XML ID in a later version creates a new record and, after the old row is no longer in the data files, deletes the old one at the end of the update. If other records point to it, they break. Rename with a pre-migration script that updates ir_model_data.name, or keep the old ID.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
self.env.ref('module.name') in the body of a method that runs during module loading, before that module's data is loaded, raises. Prefer lazy lookup or raise_if_not_found=False.

  • Referencing an XML ID from a module that is not in your depends. It works on your database, fails on a clean install.
  • Hardcoding database ids (browse(3)). They differ between staging and production.
  • ref returns a recordset in the current environment. Calling it under sudo() and returning the record leaks the sudo flag to the caller.
  • Two files declaring the same ID in the same module: the later one overwrites the earlier, silently.
  • Using noupdate on a view or action and then wondering why a fix does not arrive on update.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Read only, in psql:

SELECT module, name, model, res_id, noupdate
FROM ir_model_data
WHERE module = 'base' AND name LIKE 'group_%'
ORDER BY name LIMIT 10;

Then check one in the shell:

env.ref('base.group_user')
env['ir.model.data']._xmlid_to_res_id('base.group_user')

docs.title: Field-level security
docs.text:
Sometimes the model is open but one column is not: a member's phone number, a loan's internal notes, a price. A field's groups attribute removes the field from every user outside the listed groups.

Checked against odoo/fields.py (Field.is_accessible, NO_ACCESS) and odoo/models.py (check_field_access_rights, fields_get, _fetch_field) of Odoo 18, and the 20 tree where noted.

docs.title: The attribute
docs.text:
class LibraryMember(models.Model):
    _name = "library.member"

    name = fields.Char(required=True)
    phone = fields.Char(groups="library.group_library_manager")
    internal_note = fields.Text(groups="library.group_library_manager,base.group_system")
    legacy_token = fields.Char(groups=fields.NO_ACCESS)     # nobody, ever, but the superuser

groups is a comma-separated list of fully-qualified group external ids. A user passes if they are in at least one of them. Each id may be preceded by ! to exclude a group (groups="base.group_user,!base.group_system"), the same syntax as in views. The constant fields.NO_ACCESS is the string '.': a field with it is accessible to nobody but superuser mode.

The rule, in one function (Field.is_accessible):

if not self.groups or env.is_superuser():
    return True
if self.groups == '.':
    return False
return env.user.has_groups(self.groups)

The check applies to every ORM path below. It does not apply to raw SQL, and it does not apply in sudo() mode.

docs.title: What the ORM does
docs.text:
Operation Behaviour for a user outside the groups fields_get() the field is not in the result, so it is also unknown to the web client read() / search_read() with no field list returns only the accessible fields read(["phone"]) naming the field raises AccessError: "You do not have enough rights to access the fields ..." record.phone triggers a read of that field: AccessError write({"phone": ...}) / create({"phone": ...}) AccessError search([("phone", "=", ...)]), order or groupby on it AccessError: every use of a column in SQL goes through _field_to_sql, which calls check_field_access_rights('read', ...) _fetch_field / prefetch fields the user cannot access are excluded from the prefetch group, so touching name never pulls phone into the cache

The message names the fields. For users with base.group_no_one (technical features, debug mode) it adds the groups that would give access, or "always forbidden" for NO_ACCESS, which helps administrators and nobody else.

Two things follow:

  • Leaking by absence is not a leak. A form view that contains <field name="phone"/> is processed for the user; because the field is not in fields_get for them, the node is dropped. You need no groups on the view node for the protection to hold, but you should add it so the view is self-explanatory and the arch stays valid for users who lack the field.
  • Code that reads the field must expect AccessError. A method that does self.phone runs as the calling user. If any ordinary user may trigger it, it fails for them. Either do not read the field there, or use a deliberate escalation (below).

docs.title: Reading a protected value on purpose
docs.text:
When a feature must use a protected value without revealing it, read it in a narrow sudo() and return only what is safe:

def _phone_is_set(self):
    # exposes whether a phone exists, never the number
    return bool(self.sudo().phone)

def action_call_member(self):
    self.ensure_one()
    self.check_access("read")                    # record rules still apply to the caller
    return {"type": "ir.actions.act_url", "url": f"tel:{self.sudo().phone}"}

The second example deliberately returns the number to anyone who can reach the button. If only managers should do that, check has_group first. Field groups stops accidental exposure; it is not an authorization system for features.

docs.title: Computed and related fields
docs.text:
A computed field is its own field with its own groups (none by default). If it derives from a protected field, it can leak it:

# Leaks: anyone can read masked_phone, and the mask may reveal too much.
phone_last4 = fields.Char(compute="_compute_phone_last4")

@api.depends("phone")
def _compute_phone_last4(self):
    for rec in self:
        rec.phone_last4 = (rec.phone or "")[-4:]

Questions to ask, in order:

  1. Does the compute method run as the reading user? For a non-stored field, yes: the method reads rec.phone as that user, so for an unauthorised user the computation raises AccessError. That is safe but turns into an error. For a stored field the recompute runs as superuser (see 2), so the value is stored and readable by everyone who can read the new field, which is a leak.
  2. compute_sudo=True makes the compute run elevated. That is what you need when the value is meant for everybody, and what makes a leak possible. In the 18 source the default is compute_sudo = store: stored computed fields recompute as superuser, non-stored ones run as the reading user.
  3. Put the same groups on the derived field when it carries the sensitive information, or reduce what it carries so that publishing it is harmless.

A related field is different: when it sets up, it copies string, help, groups and a few other attributes from the target field unless you set them yourself (setup_related in fields.py only copies an attribute that is not explicitly defined on the related field). So related="member_id.phone" inherits the target's groups. Two cautions: the copy happens only when you did not pass groups= yourself, so passing a weaker one on purpose overrides the protection, and related fields default to compute_sudo=True (through related_sudo), so the value is read with elevated rights and only the copied groups stands between the user and the number. State it explicitly so the intent is visible:

member_phone = fields.Char(related="member_id.phone", groups="library.group_library_manager")

docs.title: Hiding in views versus protecting
Exports and reports
docs.text: The standard export dialog uses the ORM, so protected fields are not offered to users without access. A QWeb report reads fields as whoever renders it. If the report prints a protected field, restrict the report action itself to the authorised groups, and review any custom route that renders a report under sudo(): elevated rendering bypasses field access.

docs.title: Raw SQL, search_read on _rec_name, and other bypasses
docs.text:
• self.env.cr.execute("SELECT phone FROM library_member") bypasses ACLs, rules and field groups. Raw SQL is for trusted code and needs its own checks, covered in the raw SQL and secure coding chapters.
  • display_name is computed from the record's _rec_name field. If that field is protected, users without access cannot build a display name for the record. Do not protect the field used as the record name.
  • Many2one widgets read the display name through name_search. Make sure the comodel's _rec_name is accessible to everyone who can reach the relation.
  • A default_get or an onchange that reads a protected field runs as the user and raises for those without access.

docs.title: Odoo 20
docs.text: The mechanism is the same in the Odoo 20 tree: is_accessible, the '.' value (NO_ACCESS) and the groups syntax. Group external ids themselves differ per application (the groups chapter shows the privilege-based layout). Re-check group ids you name in groups= when you port.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
A computed field that derives from a protected field is a new field with its own access. Give it the same groups, or make sure it carries nothing sensitive.

  • Protecting only in the view. The data is one search_read away.
  • A protected _rec_name. display_name fails for everyone outside the groups.
  • A stored computed field with compute_sudo=True over a protected field. The value is computed with elevated rights and is readable by all.
  • Overriding groups on a related field with something weaker than the target's. The related read runs elevated, so the related field's own groups is the only guard.
  • Business methods reading a protected field for ordinary users. They raise AccessError. Test as an ordinary user.
  • Searching or grouping by a protected field in a default filter shipped to everyone. It raises for those without access and the whole view fails.
  • Typos in group ids. A wrong id makes has_groups fail or the field inaccessible for all; install-time checks do not always catch it.
  • Relying on field groups for the superuser case. sudo() bypasses them entirely.
  • Assuming translations or attachments are covered. Attachments have their own access through ir.attachment and the record they belong to.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
16 and 17: groups works the same way. The NO_ACCESS constant should not be assumed on 16; the string '.' is what it stands for.

18: fields.NO_ACCESS exists and Field.is_accessible is the single check.

20: same semantics.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Add phone with groups as above. As a plain user, run env["library.member"].with_user(user).fields_get() and look for phone.
  2. As the same user, call search_read([], []), then read(["phone"]). Compare.
  3. Add the phone_last4 computed field without groups, read it as the plain user, and then with compute_sudo=True.
  4. Add groups to the view node but not to the field. Confirm the data is still reachable over read.
Solution notes
  1. phone is absent from the result.
  2. The first returns only accessible fields; the second raises an AccessError naming phone.
  3. Without compute_sudo the compute raises for the plain user because it reads phone; with it the value is computed elevated and the last four digits become readable, which is the leak.
  4. The form hides the field but read(["phone"]) succeeds, because only the field attribute protects data.

docs.title: Groups and access rights
docs.text:
Groups answer "who", access rights (ACLs) answer "what on which model".

Checked against odoo/addons/base/models/res_users.py, ir_model.py, security/base_groups.xml (18) and models/res_groups.py, security/base_groups.xml, addons/hr/security/hr_security.xml (20).

docs.title: What a group is
docs.text:
A res.groups record has, in 18:

Field Meaning name label, translatable category_id the application (ir.module.category) the group is shown under implied_ids groups granted automatically to its members trans_implied_ids computed: everything implied, transitively users its members model_access the ir.model.access rows granting this group rights rule_groups the ir.rule records scoped to this group menu_access, view_access menus and views restricted to this group comment description shown on the user form share marks a group created for sharing, not a real role

Names are unique per application (name_uniq on (category_id, name)).

A user's effective groups are the groups assigned plus everything they imply. On 18 the user field is groups_id; user._get_group_ids() returns its ids as a cached tuple.

docs.title: Defining groups in a module (Odoo 17 and 18)
docs.text:
<odoo>
    <record id="module_category_library" model="ir.module.category">
        <field name="name">Library</field>
        <field name="sequence">40</field>
    </record>

    <record id="group_library_user" model="res.groups">
        <field name="name">User</field>
        <field name="category_id" ref="module_category_library"/>
        <field name="implied_ids" eval="[(4, ref('base.group_user'))]"/>
        <field name="comment">Can borrow and return books.</field>
    </record>

    <record id="group_library_manager" model="res.groups">
        <field name="name">Manager</field>
        <field name="category_id" ref="module_category_library"/>
        <field name="implied_ids" eval="[(4, ref('group_library_user'))]"/>
        <field name="comment">Manages the catalogue and all loans.</field>
        <field name="users" eval="[(4, ref('base.user_root')), (4, ref('base.user_admin'))]"/>
    </record>
</odoo>

What the pieces do:

  • category_id puts the groups of one application together. On the user form, an application with two or more groups where each implies the previous becomes a single selection field (Library: none, User, Manager). Groups that are not in a ladder appear as separate checkboxes. The form is generated from the groups, which is why changing groups needs a view refresh.
  • implied_ids makes membership transitive. A manager gets the user group, which gets base.group_user (internal user). When you add a user to a group, the implied groups are added too.
  • The users line puts the superuser (base.user_root) and the administrator in the top group so a fresh install is usable. (4, id) is the "link" command.
  • base.group_user is the Internal User group. Making your lowest group imply it is what turns a role into "an employee who may log into the backend".

docs.title: Defining groups in Odoo 20
docs.text:
Odoo 20 replaces the category with a privilege: a named scope for a family of groups, itself filed under an application category. Groups point at the privilege, and the user-side fields were renamed. From addons/hr/security/hr_security.xml in the 20 tree:

<record model="res.groups.privilege" id="res_groups_privilege_employees">
    <field name="name">Employees</field>
    <field name="sequence">9</field>
    <field name="category_id" ref="base.module_category_human_resources"/>
</record>

<record id="group_hr_user" model="res.groups">
    <field name="name">Officer: Manage all employees</field>
    <field name="sequence">10</field>
    <field name="privilege_id" ref="res_groups_privilege_employees"/>
    <field name="implied_ids" eval="[(6, 0, [ref('base.group_user')])]"/>
</record>

<record id="group_hr_manager" model="res.groups">
    <field name="name">Administrator</field>
    <field name="privilege_id" ref="res_groups_privilege_employees"/>
    <field name="implied_ids" eval="[(4, ref('group_hr_user'))]"/>
    <field name="user_ids" eval="[(4, ref('base.user_root')), (4, ref('base.user_admin'))]"/>
</record>

Differences you will hit when porting 18 to 20, all read from the two source trees:

Concept Odoo 18 Odoo 20 Group's home category_id on res.groups privilege_id on res.groups; category_id is on res.groups.privilege Group members users user_ids User's explicit groups groups_id on res.users group_ids; all_group_ids adds implied groups Ordering by name sequence field, ordered by privilege, sequence, name

A module that must support both versions needs two group files, one per layout, chosen by branch. Odoo 19 is not covered here because its source was not available to check.

docs.title: Access rights: ir.model.access
docs.text:
A row grants four permissions on a model to a group:

Field Meaning model_id the model group_id the group; empty means everyone (deprecated, logged as a warning) perm_read, perm_write, perm_create, perm_unlink the four permissions name label, required active switch an ACL off without deleting it

The usual way to write them is security/ir.model.access.csv:

id,name,model_id:id,group_id:id,perm_read,perm_write,perm_create,perm_unlink
access_library_book_user,library.book user,model_library_book,group_library_user,1,0,0,0
access_library_book_manager,library.book manager,model_library_book,group_library_manager,1,1,1,1
access_library_loan_user,library.loan user,model_library_loan,group_library_user,1,1,1,0
access_library_loan_manager,library.loan manager,model_library_loan,group_library_manager,1,1,1,1
access_library_member_user,library.member user,model_library_member,group_library_user,1,0,0,0
access_library_member_manager,library.member manager,model_library_member,group_library_manager,1,1,1,1

Rules for the file:

  • model_id:id is the external id model_<model name with dots replaced by underscores>, which Odoo creates for every model when it registers the model.
  • group_id:id is the group's external id. A group of another module needs its module prefix (base.group_user).
  • A row's id must be unique across modules, so prefix it with the module name.
  • List the file in the manifest data after the XML that defines the groups.
  • Transient models (wizards) need ACL rows too: _check_access in 18 has no exception for them, so without a row an ordinary user cannot use the wizard. Grant it to the lowest group that opens it.
  • A model without any ACL row is closed to everyone but the superuser: check only passes for models in the set computed from the ACL rows of the user's groups.

docs.title: How rights combine
docs.text:
Rights are additive. A user in several groups gets the union of all rows. There is no deny. Therefore:

  • Design groups as a ladder, with each ACL row granted to the lowest group that needs it, and let implied_ids give the higher groups the same.
  • If a user can do something you did not intend, find which of their groups grants it. A SQL query makes that quick, see Try it.
  • You cannot revoke a permission another module grants. You can only change which groups the user belongs to, or add a record rule that restricts the rows.

docs.title: Access rights in Odoo 20
docs.text:
In the Odoo 20 tree there is no ir.model.access. A row of security/ir.access.csv carries operation (letters from crud) and an optional domain, and a row with a group is a permission:

id,name,model_id,group_id/id,operation,domain
access_library_book_user,library.book user,library.book,group_library_user,r,
access_library_book_manager,library.book manager,library.book,group_library_manager,crud,

model_id is the model's technical name. Permissions of a user's groups are OR-ed, so a user gets the widest domain among them, and having no permission for an operation means no access. The security model chapter explains the combination, and odoo-bin upgrade_code converts 18 data (see the migration chapter).

docs.title: User types
docs.text:
Beyond application groups there are three mutually exclusive user types in the category base.module_category_user_type:

Group Meaning base.group_user Internal user: backend access, subject to the ACLs of their other groups base.group_portal Portal: external users who see the portal pages only base.group_public Public: the anonymous website visitor (a single shared user)

A constraint (_check_one_user_type) rejects a user with more than one of them, which could otherwise happen through implied_ids. Never make a portal-visible group imply base.group_user.

Other base groups worth knowing: base.group_system (Settings: administration), base.group_erp_manager (Access Rights), base.group_multi_company, base.group_multi_currency, base.group_no_one (technical features, effective only in debug mode), base.group_allow_export, base.group_partner_manager (Contact Creation), base.group_sanitize_override (may bypass HTML sanitisation on fields that allow it).

docs.title: Assigning access to menus, actions, views
docs.text:
groups on ir.ui.menu hides the menu from other users. groups on an action or a view makes it unavailable. On a node inside a view, groups="library.group_library_manager" removes the node for others:

<menuitem id="menu_library_config" name="Configuration" parent="menu_library_root"
          groups="group_library_manager"/>

<button name="action_write_off" type="object" string="Write off"
        groups="library.group_library_manager"/>

groups in a view accepts the same syntax as the field attribute: comma-separated external ids, each optionally preceded by ! (groups="base.group_user,!base.group_system"). The 18 has_groups docstring gives that exact example.

Remember the earlier chapter: this controls what is shown. It is not enforcement.

docs.title: Checking groups in code
docs.text:
# the current user
if self.env.user.has_group("library.group_library_manager"):
    ...

# several groups, with negation, same syntax as the attribute
if self.env.user.has_groups("library.group_library_user,!library.group_library_manager"):
    ...
  • has_group takes a fully qualified external id; there is no implicit module. has_groups takes a comma-separated spec with optional ! negations, returns true if the user belongs to at least one positive group and none of the negated ones (or if there are only negatives and none matched).
  • base.group_no_one is effective only in debug mode for these methods.
  • The first call per group queries; the result is cached per user.
  • A record method that acts on behalf of a group should use the ORM checks, not group membership, when the real question is "may this user write this record":
def action_write_off(self):
    self.check_access("write")                      # model ACL + record rules
    if not self.env.user.has_group("library.group_library_manager"):
        raise AccessError(_("Only librarians can write off a loan."))
    ...

AccessError comes from odoo.exceptions. Use has_group for business policy ("only managers may do this step"); use check_access for data access.

docs.title: Data files for access rights
docs.text:
ACLs and groups are data. They load at install and update. Two consequences:

  • They are noupdate-sensitive. A group or an ACL created from XML in a file without noupdate is reset to the file's values whenever the module is updated. Tune them in the UI only for experiments.
  • Order matters on first install. The groups XML must load before the CSV that names them, and both before views that reference the group ids in groups attributes. List them in the manifest in that order:
"data": [
    "security/library_groups.xml",
    "security/ir.model.access.csv",
    "security/library_rules.xml",
    "views/book_views.xml",
    "views/loan_views.xml",
    "views/menus.xml",
],

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Giving the lowest group write access "for now". It stays. Grant to the lowest group that needs it.
  • Empty group_id. Grants everyone, portal and public included if the model is reachable. Odoo warns when you create one; do not ignore it.
  • A missing ACL row for a transient model. The wizard opens for administrators and fails for everyone else.
  • Typo in the model's external id. model_library_loans instead of model_library_loan fails the whole data load with a message naming the id.
  • A group implying base.group_user that is also given to portal users. The user-type constraint rejects the combination.
  • Using has_group in a view attrs. Not available there; use the groups attribute.
  • Deleting an ACL line from the CSV and expecting the right to disappear. An update does not remove rows that no longer appear in the file, it only creates or updates the ones that do. Remove the record explicitly, or set perm_* to 0.
  • Relying on users or groups_id field names across versions. They changed in 20.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
16 and 17: category_id, users, groups_id as in 18. check_access_rights is the access check method.

18: as described here; check_access is the new method.

20: groups use privilege_id; members are user_ids; the user's groups are group_ids and all_group_ids. A ladder of groups under one privilege plays the role that a category did.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. List who can write library.loan and why, in SQL (read-only):
SELECT g.id, g.name, a.perm_read, a.perm_write, a.perm_create, a.perm_unlink
FROM ir_model_access a
JOIN ir_model m ON m.id = a.model_id
LEFT JOIN res_groups g ON g.id = a.group_id
WHERE m.model = 'library.loan' AND a.active
ORDER BY g.name;
  1. In an Odoo shell, print the transitive groups of a user and check one: u = env.ref("base.user_admin"); u.groups_id.mapped("full_name") (on 18).
  2. Add a user to group_library_manager only, open the form and check that they also show as User and Internal User.
Solution notes
  1. Rows with a null group name are ACLs granting everyone; the rest are the groups that can write. Remember the union rule when reading the result.
  2. full_name shows application and group names; the list includes groups implied through implied_ids.
  3. The manager group implies the library user group, which implies base.group_user, so all three show.

docs.title: Multi-company
docs.text:
One Odoo database can serve several companies whose data must stay apart: their own invoices, stock, sequences, prices, while sharing users, products and partners where that is useful. Multi-company is not a switch you flip; it is a set of conventions that your models must follow.

Checked against odoo/api.py, odoo/models.py, odoo/fields.py and odoo/addons/base/security/base_security.xml (18).

docs.title: How the environment knows the company
docs.text:
The user belongs to one or more companies (user.company_ids) and has a main one (user.company_id). The web client has a company switcher; the companies ticked there are enabled. The client sends them in the context as allowed_company_ids, with the first id being the current company. Server code reads them from the environment:

self.env.company      # the current company (a res.company record)
self.env.companies    # all enabled companies (a recordset)
self.env.user.company_ids   # all companies the user may switch to

From the 18 source (api.py):

  • env.company returns the first id of allowed_company_ids from the context, or user.company_id when the context has none.
  • For a non-superuser environment, if allowed_company_ids contains a company that is not among the user's own companies, reading env.company or env.companies raises AccessError("Access to unauthorized or invalid companies."). A tampered context cannot pick companies the user does not have.
  • In sudo() mode the check is skipped, and the docstring warns: "When in sudo mode, a user can access any company, even if not in his allowed companies." That is useful for inter-company transactions and dangerous everywhere else.

with_company(company) returns the recordset with a modified context so that env.company is the given company and env.companies includes it:

invoice = self.with_company(other_company).create({...})

The docstring warns that using a company the current user is not allowed to use may raise AccessError unless the environment is sudoed. It returns self unchanged when company is empty.

docs.title: The model pattern
docs.text:
A model whose records belong to one company gets a company_id and a rule:

class LibraryLoan(models.Model):
    _name = "library.loan"
    _description = "Loan"
    _check_company_auto = True

    company_id = fields.Many2one(
        "res.company", string="Company", required=True, index=True,
        default=lambda self: self.env.company,
    )
    member_id = fields.Many2one("library.member", check_company=True, required=True)
    book_id = fields.Many2one("library.book", check_company=True, required=True)

and in security/library_security.xml a global rule:

<record id="library_loan_rule_company" model="ir.rule">
    <field name="name">Library loan: multi-company</field>
    <field name="model_id" ref="model_library_loan"/>
    <field name="domain_force">['|', ('company_id', '=', False), ('company_id', 'in', company_ids)]</field>
</record>

Three details are easy to get wrong:

  • The default lambda self: self.env.company is the current company, not the user's main company. Records created while the switcher is on company B belong to B.
  • The rule is global (no groups). A group rule would not restrict users outside the group; the record rules chapter explains why. This is the case where a global rule is exactly right.
  • The rule uses company_ids, the enabled companies from the switcher, not all the user's companies. Records from companies the user has not ticked do not appear, which is what makes the switcher meaningful.

For shared data (a product visible to every company) allow an empty company: ('company_id', '=', False) in the domain above, and leave company_id optional on the model. For a company hierarchy, the base res.partner rule uses ('company_id', 'parent_of', company_ids) alongside the partner-share condition, so a company can see records of its parents.

docs.title: check_company: keeping relations consistent
docs.text:
A loan in company A that points at a book of company B is a data leak and a source of impossible accounting. Two switches prevent it:

  • _check_company_auto = True on the model: on every create and write the ORM calls _check_company().
  • check_company=True on each relational field to verify.

_check_company verifies that the company of each related record is compatible with the company of the record: allowed are the same company or no company. The comodel's _check_company_domain(companies) is [('company_id', 'in', company_ids + [False])], or [('company_id', '=', False)] when there are no companies. If a record fails the check you get UserError: Incompatible companies on records: with a line per offending field naming the company of each record. Records are checked with active_test=False, so archived records are judged too.

check_company=True has a second effect: it generates a default domain for the field (_description_domain in fields.py), so the many2one dropdown offers only compatible records. When the model has company_id the domain reads, in effect: if the record has a company, offer comodel records whose company is that one or empty; if it has none, offer only records without a company. With company_ids it uses that field the same way; if the model has neither, the framework logs a warning that it could not generate the company-dependent domain. Your own domain= on the field is appended to it.

The check is skipped for fields that are not marked, so a missing check_company=True is a silent hole: the domain is also missing and the form lets users pick wrong records.

docs.title: Company-dependent fields
docs.text:
Some values differ per company on the same record: a product's cost price, a partner's receivable account. company_dependent=True stores one value per company:

class LibraryBook(models.Model):
    _inherit = "library.book"

    replacement_cost = fields.Float(company_dependent=True)
    shelf_account_id = fields.Many2one("account.account", company_dependent=True, check_company=True)

In the Odoo 18 source:

  • The value is stored in the model's own table as a jsonb dictionary keyed by company id, not in a separate table. (Older versions used ir.property rows, which is why old tutorials describe them differently.) Defaults for companies without a value come from ir.default.
  • It is read and written for env.company, the current company. Switching company changes what the same record shows.
  • Allowed types are char, float, boolean, integer, text, many2one, date, datetime, selection, html. A company-dependent field cannot be required and cannot be translated; Odoo warns at definition.
  • With check_company=True on a company-dependent field, the check uses the currently active company instead of the record's company, and the generated domain uses the first enabled company.
  • A model with company-dependent fields should have a company_id or company_ids field, or the framework logs "Skipping a company check ... the model doesn't have a company_id".

Because of the jsonb storage, a SQL query on such a field needs the key: replacement_cost->>'1' for company 1. When you read in SQL, remember this and that the value for a company without an entry is null, not the default.

docs.title: Where multi-company breaks
docs.text:
sudo(). It ignores record rules, so a sudo().search([]) returns all companies' records mixed together, and env.company skips its sanity check. The sudo docstring in 18 spells it out: "could cause data access to cross the boundaries of record rules, possibly mixing records that are meant to be isolated (e.g. records from different companies)", and "methods which select one record among many - for example getting the default company, or selecting a Bill of Materials" can behave unintuitively. In a multi-company database every sudo() in a search is a bug report waiting to happen. Add the company explicitly when you must elevate:

loans = self.env["library.loan"].sudo().search([
    ("company_id", "in", self.env.companies.ids),
    ("state", "=", "open"),
])

Cron jobs and server actions. They run as the user configured on the job (often the superuser, base.user_root), so env.company is the superuser's main company and rules do not apply. A cron that processes "all open loans" will process every company with whatever company context the first record happens to give. Loop over companies explicitly:

@api.model
def _cron_send_reminders(self):
    for company in self.env["res.company"].search([]):
        loans = self.with_company(company).search([
            ("company_id", "=", company.id),
            ("state", "=", "open"),
        ])
        loans._send_reminders()

Sequences. An ir.sequence has its own company_id. If the sequence has no company, all companies share one numbering. Use company_id on the sequence and search it with the right with_company, or invoices of different companies will interleave. See the sequences chapter in the ORM part.

Reports and emails. Reports render with the company of the record; templates should read object.company_id, not user.company_id, for letterheads and legal data.

Default values. default=lambda self: self.env.company evaluates at creation, in the creator's current company. Imports and automated creation under sudo take the superuser's. Pass company_id explicitly in automated creation.

Unique constraints. An SQL UNIQUE (name) is global across companies. If names only need to be unique per company use UNIQUE (company_id, name); remember null company_id values are distinct in PostgreSQL unique constraints.

Domains in actions. Do not filter by company in an action domain for isolation; use the rule. The rule applies everywhere (list, kanban, search, RPC), a domain only in that action.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Create two companies and a user belonging to both, and test with the switcher in each state:

@tagged("post_install", "-at_install")
class TestLoanCompanies(TransactionCase):

    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        super().setUpClass()
        cls.company_a = cls.env.company
        cls.company_b = cls.env["res.company"].create({"name": "Company B"})
        cls.user = cls.env["res.users"].create({
            "name": "Multi", "login": "multi",
            "company_id": cls.company_a.id,
            "company_ids": [(6, 0, [cls.company_a.id, cls.company_b.id])],
            "groups_id": [(6, 0, [cls.env.ref("library.group_library_user").id])],
        })
        Loan = cls.env["library.loan"]
        cls.loan_b = Loan.with_company(cls.company_b).create({
            "company_id": cls.company_b.id,
            "member_id": cls.env["library.member"].create({"name": "M", "company_id": cls.company_b.id}).id,
            "book_id": cls.env["library.book"].create({"name": "Dune", "company_id": cls.company_b.id}).id,
        })

    def test_only_enabled_companies_are_visible(self):
        Loan = self.env["library.loan"].with_user(self.user)
        only_a = Loan.with_context(allowed_company_ids=[self.company_a.id]).search([])
        both = Loan.with_context(
            allowed_company_ids=[self.company_a.id, self.company_b.id]
        ).search([])
        self.assertNotIn(self.loan_b, only_a)
        self.assertIn(self.loan_b, both)

    def test_incompatible_company_is_rejected(self):
        book_a = self.env["library.book"].create({"name": "A", "company_id": self.company_a.id})
        with self.assertRaises(UserError):
            self.loan_b.write({"book_id": book_a.id})

The first test exercises the global rule through allowed_company_ids, exactly as the web client sends it. The second exercises _check_company. Also test a user who tries allowed_company_ids with a company they do not own: reading env.company raises AccessError.

docs.title: Odoo 20
docs.text: The isolation rule is an ir.access row without a group in the 20 tree (a restriction), for example hr_employee_comp_rule in hr: empty group, operation crud, domain [('company_id', 'in', company_ids + [False])]. The mechanisms above (env.company, env.companies, with_company, check_company) exist unchanged in the Odoo 20 tree. The group layout for base.group_multi_company follows the new privilege structure, which affects only the group XML you write, not the ORM behaviour.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
sudo() plus search in a multi-company database mixes companies. Add the company condition explicitly, or avoid elevation.

  • A group rule for companies. It does not restrict users outside the group. Companies need a global rule.
  • Forgetting check_company=True. No consistency check and no filtered dropdown; wrong-company records can be linked.
  • company_id without index=True. The rule domain is on every query.
  • Defaulting company_id to user.company_id. Use env.company: records follow the switcher.
  • Crons that ignore companies. They run as the superuser. Loop over companies and use with_company.
  • Company-dependent fields in SQL. They are jsonb keyed by company id in 18; old ir.property queries do not apply.
  • A company-dependent field marked required. Not supported; Odoo warns.
  • Shared sequences across companies by leaving the sequence company empty.
  • env.company on a tampered context. Raises AccessError for normal users; sudo skips the check.
  • Unique constraints without the company. Global uniqueness blocks legitimate duplicates across companies.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
16 and 17: company-dependent fields are stored as ir.property rows; company_ids rule context and check_company exist. Verify the storage claim on your branch before writing SQL against these fields.

18: company-dependent fields are jsonb columns on the model table, with defaults from ir.default. check_company and _check_company_auto as above.

20: same environment API.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Create two companies and a user in both. Open the switcher with only A ticked, then both. Count library.loan records.
  2. In a shell, as that user, set allowed_company_ids to a company the user does not own and read env.company. Then repeat with sudo().
  3. Add replacement_cost as company-dependent, set it in A and in B for one book, and read it in each company. Then inspect the column in SQL: SELECT replacement_cost FROM library_book WHERE id = ....
Solution notes
  1. With only A ticked the rule hides B's loans; with both ticked they appear.
  2. The non-sudo access raises AccessError: Access to unauthorized or invalid companies.; with sudo() it returns the company.
  3. The value follows the current company, and the column holds a JSON object such as {"1": 12.5, "2": 14.0}.

docs.title: Record rules
docs.text:
ACLs say whether a user may touch a model at all. Record rules (ir.rule) narrow that to specific rows. A rule is a domain, a set of operations it applies to, and optionally a set of groups.

Checked against odoo/addons/base/models/ir_rule.py, odoo/models.py and odoo/osv/expression.py of Odoo 18, and the Odoo 20 tree where noted.

docs.title: The fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning name label model_id the model the rule restricts (rules on ir.rule itself are forbidden) domain_force the domain, as a Python expression string groups groups the rule is scoped to; empty means a global rule perm_read, perm_write, perm_create, perm_unlink which operations it applies to (all default to true) active switch it off without deleting it

global is a computed field: true when groups is empty.

docs.title: Defining rules
docs.text:
<odoo>
    <data noupdate="1">

        <!-- group rule: a library user sees only their own loans -->
        <record id="library_loan_rule_own" model="ir.rule">
            <field name="name">Library loan: own loans</field>
            <field name="model_id" ref="model_library_loan"/>
            <field name="domain_force">[('member_id.user_id', '=', user.id)]</field>
            <field name="groups" eval="[(4, ref('library.group_library_user'))]"/>
            <field name="perm_unlink" eval="False"/>
        </record>

        <!-- group rule: managers see everything; ORed with the rule above -->
        <record id="library_loan_rule_manager" model="ir.rule">
            <field name="name">Library loan: managers see all</field>
            <field name="model_id" ref="model_library_loan"/>
            <field name="domain_force">[(1, '=', 1)]</field>
            <field name="groups" eval="[(4, ref('library.group_library_manager'))]"/>
        </record>

        <!-- global rule: nobody sees loans of other companies -->
        <record id="library_loan_rule_company" model="ir.rule">
            <field name="name">Library loan: multi-company</field>
            <field name="model_id" ref="model_library_loan"/>
            <field name="domain_force">['|', ('company_id', '=', False), ('company_id', 'in', company_ids)]</field>
        </record>

    </data>
</odoo>

noupdate="1" matters: rules are data, and without it a module update resets any rule you tuned in the UI.

docs.title: The evaluation context
docs.text:
domain_force is evaluated by safe_eval with exactly these names (from _eval_context):

Name Value user the current user record, taken with an empty context so evaluation does not depend on the request context time the Python time module company_ids the ids of the companies currently enabled in the company switcher (env.companies.ids) company_id the id of the current company (env.company.id)

Everything else is undefined. uid does not exist; use user.id. The domain can use any field path of the model, any attribute path on user (user.partner_id.id, user.commercial_partner_id.id, user.company_ids.ids), and time.strftime(...) for date comparisons.

company_ids is not "all companies the user may use", it is those the user has ticked in the switcher: "These companies are filtered and trusted", says the source comment. The domain cache is keyed on the context key allowed_company_ids for this reason.

A rule's domain is validated when it is saved (_check_domain compiles it against the model with safe_eval and the expression parser), so a typo in a field name is rejected at install time with Invalid domain: ....

docs.title: How the final domain is built
docs.text:
For one model and one operation, _compute_domain does this, in order:

  1. For each parent model in _inherits, compute that parent's domain recursively and add (parent_field, 'any', parent_domain) as a global domain. Delegation inheritance therefore inherits the restrictions of the parent.
  2. _get_rules fetches the active rules for the model whose perm_<operation> is true and that are either global or belong to a group the user is in. In superuser mode it returns nothing.
  3. Each rule's domain is evaluated and normalised. A rule without groups goes to the global list; a rule with groups the user belongs to goes to the group list.
  4. If there are no applicable group domains, the result is AND(global_domains). Otherwise it is AND(global_domains + [OR(group_domains)]).

The result is cached per user, su flag, model, operation and the context values from _compute_domain_keys (just allowed_company_ids), and the cache is cleared whenever a rule is created, written or deleted.

Step 4 is the sentence to remember. Consider a model whose only rules are group rules: "library users see their own loans" and "managers see all". A user who belongs to neither group, but whose ACL lets them in through some third group, has no applicable group rules. The OR part disappears and nothing restricts them: they see every loan. Group rules narrow nothing for people outside their groups. To restrict everyone, you need a global rule.

Practical consequences:

  • To widen access for a group, add a group rule with a permissive domain; it is ORed with the others.
  • To restrict everyone (companies, archived data, tenant isolation), use a global rule. Another group's rule cannot widen past it.
  • A global rule is ANDed with the OR of the group rules, so combining the two is the normal pattern: global rules draw the outer fence, group rules open specific gates inside it.
  • A group rule can never override a global rule.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Operation What the rule does read, and search The domain is added to the SQL query. Non-matching rows silently disappear. search_count and read_group obey the same domain. write, unlink The selected records are checked; if any is not matched by the domain, an AccessError names the failing rule. create The new records are checked after they are created (records.check_access('create') at the end of create). If a record does not satisfy the domain, the creation fails and rolls back.

Because reads filter silently, "my record disappeared" is most often a rule. And because create checks after the fact, a rule like [('state', '=', 'draft')] with perm_create makes it impossible to create a record in any other state, which is easy to forget when a wizard creates in confirmed.

The check on write and unlink is filtered_domain over the records, run as superuser: forbidden := self - self.sudo().filtered_domain(domain).

docs.title: Reading the failure message
docs.text:
_get_failing builds the explanation: it re-evaluates the rules with active_test disabled on the failing records, so a record that is archived is judged on its fields, not hidden. It returns every failing global rule and, if the group rules as a whole fail, all of them. Then _make_access_error produces the message. Users without the technical-features group (base.group_no_one, effective only in debug mode) and portal or public users get the generic text ("Uh-oh! Looks like you have stumbled upon some top-secret records. Sorry, doesn't have 'write' access to: ..."), which names the user, the operation and the model but not the records or rules. Internal users in debug mode also see the first records and the failing rules. When a failing rule's domain mentions company_id, the message adds a multi-company hint and, if it can tell, the company to switch to.

Odoo also logs at INFO level: Access Denied by record rules for operation: write on record ids: [...], uid: ..., model: .... When a user reports "access error", that log line tells you which model and operation.

docs.title: Patterns that cover most needs
docs.text:
Own records.

[('create_uid', '=', user.id)]
[('user_id', '=', user.id)]

Through a parent, with any (Odoo 17 and 18; also not any):

[('loan_id', 'any', [('member_id.user_id', '=', user.id)])]

any turns into a subquery. It evaluates the sub-domain with the comodel's own record rules applied, so if the user cannot see the parent loans at all, the child rows disappear too, which is usually what you want and sometimes a surprise. The 18 expression.py knows only any and not any. In the Odoo 20 tree there is also an internal any! that skips the comodel rules; it is listed as an internal operator, so do not use it in rule XML.

Company isolation. The shape used by the core for shared master data:

['|', ('company_id', '=', False), ('company_id', 'in', company_ids)]

and for hierarchies of companies, ('company_id', 'parent_of', company_ids), as the base res.partner rule does.

Portal users' own documents. The core rule for partners available to portal and public groups reads [('id', 'child_of', user.commercial_partner_id.id)] with write, create and unlink disabled. Your portal rules follow the same pattern: group base.group_portal, perm_read only, the domain anchored on the user's partner:

<record id="library_loan_rule_portal" model="ir.rule">
    <field name="name">Library loan: portal sees own</field>
    <field name="model_id" ref="model_library_loan"/>
    <field name="domain_force">[('member_id.partner_id', '=', user.partner_id.id)]</field>
    <field name="groups" eval="[(4, ref('base.group_portal'))]"/>
    <field name="perm_write" eval="False"/>
    <field name="perm_create" eval="False"/>
    <field name="perm_unlink" eval="False"/>
</record>

Hide archived or finished rows from non-managers. A group rule can not do this (see step 4), a global rule can, with an exception built into the domain only if you have a way to identify managers in the domain. Usually the better tool is a default active_test filter in the action, not a rule.

Time-based.

[('date', '>=', time.strftime('%Y-%m-01'))]

time.strftime is evaluated each time the rule is computed. The domain cache key does not include the date, so a long-running worker can keep a stale month until the cache is cleared. Avoid time in rules for anything that must roll over exactly.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
A rule domain is appended to every query on the model by every user in its scope. Dotted paths such as member_id.user_id become joins or subqueries on every list, search and read, and a rule on res.partner or res.users touches almost everything because most models join those. Keep rule domains:

  • indexable: compare stored columns (many2one ids, company, create_uid);
  • shallow: one hop where possible, any over deep dotted paths;
  • not dependent on non-stored computed fields, which cannot be searched anyway and will fail at save.

Look at the SQL the rule produces with env.cr logging (see the shell chapters) before shipping a rule on a table with millions of rows. Editing a rule clears the registry cache, so changing rules on a busy production database causes a short stall.

docs.title: sudo() and rules
docs.text:
sudo() ignores record rules entirely, because _get_rules returns an empty set when env.su is true. A sudo().search(...) returns rows the rules were meant to hide. If you must elevate, do it narrowly and check access first as the real user, as in the security model chapter.

with_user(user) returns an environment in which rules apply for that user, which is what tests need.

docs.title: Testing rules
docs.text:
Rule bugs appear only when you run as the right user. A minimal test:

from odoo.exceptions import AccessError
from odoo.tests import TransactionCase, tagged


@tagged("post_install", "-at_install")
class TestLoanRules(TransactionCase):

    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        super().setUpClass()
        group_user = cls.env.ref("library.group_library_user")
        cls.user_a = cls.env["res.users"].create({
            "name": "Member A", "login": "member_a",
            "groups_id": [(6, 0, [group_user.id])],
        })
        cls.user_b = cls.env["res.users"].create({
            "name": "Member B", "login": "member_b",
            "groups_id": [(6, 0, [group_user.id])],
        })
        cls.loan_a = cls.env["library.loan"].create({
            "member_id": cls._member_for(cls.user_a).id,
            "book_id": cls.env["library.book"].create({"name": "Dune"}).id,
        })

    @classmethod
    def _member_for(cls, user):
        return cls.env["library.member"].create({"name": user.name, "user_id": user.id})

    def test_user_sees_only_own_loans(self):
        loans = self.env["library.loan"].with_user(self.user_a).search([])
        self.assertEqual(loans, self.loan_a)
        self.assertFalse(self.env["library.loan"].with_user(self.user_b).search([]))

    def test_other_user_cannot_write(self):
        with self.assertRaises(AccessError):
            self.loan_a.with_user(self.user_b).write({"state": "returned"})

Notes: use with_user and never sudo or the default admin in the assertions. groups_id is the 18 field name (group_ids in 20). Assert both directions, that allowed users see what they should and that others do not. Test the unlisted-group case too: a user in neither group.

docs.title: Inspecting rules in a database
docs.text:
-- read-only: the rules of a model, with their groups
SELECT r.id, r.name, r.domain_force, r.global,
       r.perm_read, r.perm_write, r.perm_create, r.perm_unlink,
       (SELECT string_agg(g.name->>'en_US', ', ')
          FROM rule_group_rel rg
          JOIN res_groups g ON g.id = rg.group_id
         WHERE rg.rule_group_id = r.id) AS groups
FROM ir_rule r
JOIN ir_model m ON m.id = r.model_id
WHERE m.model = 'library.loan' AND r.active
ORDER BY r.global DESC, r.id;

In 18, res_groups.name is a translatable column stored as jsonb, hence ->>'en_US'. In an Odoo shell the effective domain for a user is one call:

env["ir.rule"].with_user(user)._compute_domain("library.loan", "read")

It returns the normalised domain the ORM will append, or an empty list when nothing restricts the user.

docs.title: Odoo 20: ir.access
docs.text:
In the Odoo 20 tree a record rule is an ir.access row: model_id, group_id, operation (a subset of crud) and domain. The three rules of this chapter become:

id,name,model_id,group_id/id,operation,domain
library_loan_own,Library loan: own loans,library.loan,group_library_user,cru,"[('member_id.user_id', '=', user.id)]"
library_loan_manager,Library loan: managers see all,library.loan,group_library_manager,crud,
library_loan_company,Library loan: multi-company,library.loan,,crud,"['|', ('company_id', '=', False), ('company_id', 'in', company_ids)]"

The first two have a group, so they are permissions and are OR-ed; the third has none, so it is a restriction and is AND-ed. The effect is OR(own, all) & company. Two behaviours differ from 18:

  • With no applicable permission the result is the empty set, not "no restriction". The surprise described under "How the final domain is built" is gone.
  • A permission without a domain grants every record. A user who is in a group with r and no domain and in another group with r and a narrowing domain gets everything. Give each group's permission its own domain.

The evaluation context, _get_failed_accesses (the 20 name of _get_failing) and the error text are otherwise the same idea as in 18.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
A model with only group rules is unrestricted for users outside those groups. Restrict everyone with a global rule.

  • A global rule meant for one group. It restricts every user of the model, including managers. Only the superuser is exempt.
  • A leftover global rule with a real domain, copied from a demo, blocks everyone silently.
  • Rules on res.partner and res.users. Nearly every model joins them, so a tight rule changes behaviour system-wide and can make display_name fail or show empty for related records.
  • noupdate missing. Tuned rules revert on the next module update.
  • create rule that rejects your own creates. The check runs after creation against the final values.
  • Time in domains. Cached, so it does not roll over exactly at midnight.
  • Testing as admin. The administrator is in many groups and passes most group rules; use plain users with with_user.
  • Using any!. It is an internal operator in the 20 tree and does not exist in 18.
  • Assuming read rules apply to sudo background jobs. They do not; check what runs as superuser (crons, server actions with a configured user).
  • Tuning rules in production by hand. Every change clears the registry cache. Keep rules in code.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
16: the any operator does not exist (it is absent from the 16 expression.py); use dotted paths or in with a sub-search. The rule context has the same names.

17 and 18: any and not any are available (present in the 17 expression.py). 18 applies parent rules for _inherits through any in _compute_domain.

20: ir.rule and ir.model.access no longer exist as separate models. Both are ir.access records (odoo/addons/base/models/ir_access.py): a record with a group is a permission, a record without one is a restriction, and the final domain is OR(permissions) & AND(restrictions). A rule written for 18 has to be converted, and the semantics of group rules change (no permission means no access). See "Odoo 20: ir.access" below. The ORM code was also moved to odoo/orm/.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Create the three rules above for library.loan. As a plain user in the library user group, run search_count([]). Then remove the user from the group, give them read access to the model through some other group, and repeat. What changed, and why?
  2. Remove the global company rule, keep the two group rules, and repeat with a user in neither group.
  3. Print _compute_domain for the same user before and after.
  4. Write the second test of the testing section and make it fail by adding perm_write=False to the wrong rule.
Solution notes
  1. In the group the user sees only their own loans (and only those passing the global company rule). Outside it, no group rule applies, so only the global company domain remains: the user sees every loan of their companies.
  2. With only group rules, a user in neither group sees every loan the ACL lets them reach. This is the case step 4 describes.
  3. The first domain is AND(global, OR(group domains)); after the change it is the global domain alone.
  4. The write attempt by another user raises AccessError only while the owner rule applies to write; changing the wrong flag turns the test into a pass on the wrong rule, which is why testing each operation separately matters.

docs.title: Secure coding
docs.text:
The ORM's three access layers protect you only while your code goes through them. Custom modules leak data in a handful of recurring ways: a SQL string built with formatting, a sudo() that returns what rules were hiding, a controller route that trusts a parameter, HTML marked safe that came from a user, a token compared with ==. It is a checklist you can run on any module before it goes to production.

Checked against Odoo 18 (odoo/tools/sql.py, odoo/sql_db.py, odoo/api.py, odoo/http.py, odoo/tools/misc.py, odoo/fields.py, odoo/tools/mail.py) and the 20 tree where noted.

docs.title: 1. SQL injection
docs.text:
Any SQL built by formatting user-influenced text into the query is injectable:

# WRONG: the text becomes SQL.
self.env.cr.execute("SELECT id FROM library_book WHERE name = '%s'" % name)
self.env.cr.execute(f"SELECT id FROM library_book WHERE isbn = '{isbn}'")
self.env.cr.execute("SELECT id FROM library_book WHERE name = '" + name + "'")

The safe form passes values as parameters, and since Odoo 17 the preferred container is the SQL object, which refuses to mix code and values:

from odoo.tools import SQL

# Parameters.
self.env.cr.execute("SELECT id FROM library_book WHERE name = %s", (name,))

# The SQL object: code is a literal, values are parameters.
query = SQL("SELECT id FROM library_book WHERE name = %s AND state = %s", name, "available")
rows = self.env.execute_query(query)        # returns a list of tuples

How the SQL class works (from tools/sql.py in 18):

  • SQL("... %s ...", value, ...) takes a %-format string and the parameters. query.code is the text with placeholders, query.params the values.
  • If code is a string literal (not a dynamic string), the object is guaranteed to be safe, provided the objects it embeds are SQL objects too. Passing a computed string as code is exactly what bypasses the protection, so it is the one thing never to do.
  • SQL.identifier(name) quotes a table or column name. Use it when an identifier must vary:
column = "name" if by_name else "isbn"
query = SQL(
    "SELECT id FROM %s WHERE %s = %s",
    SQL.identifier("library_book"),
    SQL.identifier(column),
    value,
)
  • SQL.join(parts) combines several SQL fragments, for example a list of conditions.
  • cr.execute accepts an SQL object (it unpacks code and params and asserts no extra parameters were given); env.execute_query(sql) additionally flushes the fields mentioned in the query's metadata and returns rows.

Identifiers that come from the user, such as a sort column, must be validated against an allow-list and quoted with SQL.identifier; parameters cannot carry identifiers.

Raw SQL also bypasses every access layer: ACLs, record rules and field groups. Every raw query on a model with rules needs its own company and ownership conditions. The raw SQL chapter in the ORM part covers the cache and flush implications.

docs.title: 2. Domains and eval
docs.text:
A domain is data, not code. If it comes from outside, parse it as data:

# WRONG: executes whatever arrives.
domain = eval(self.env.context["domain_text"])

# Better: safe_eval, restricted to a whitelist of operations.
from odoo.tools.safe_eval import safe_eval
domain = safe_eval(text, {"user": self.env.user, "time": time})

# Best: build the domain yourself from validated pieces.
domain = [("state", "=", "open")]
if member_id:
    domain.append(("member_id", "=", int(member_id)))

eval on request data is remote code execution. safe_eval removes most dangerous builtins, and the record rules use it for domain_force, but it is still meant for administrators' input, not anonymous visitors'. For filters coming from a web form, accept a field name from an allow-list and a value, and build the leaf yourself. Convert numbers with int() so a string cannot change the meaning of a condition, and do not allow arbitrary operators or paths: ('partner_id.user_ids.password', '!=', False) is a way to probe data through a relational path.

docs.title: 3. sudo() and privilege escalation
docs.text:
sudo() is the largest source of leaks because it makes the right thing and the wrong thing look identical. Concrete rules, drawn from what the ORM does in superuser mode (ACL, record rules and field groups are skipped, env.company sanity checks are skipped):

# WRONG: a public route that returns every loan.
@http.route("/library/loans", auth="public", type="json")
def loans(self):
    return request.env["library.loan"].sudo().search_read([], ["name", "member_id"])

# RIGHT: a user route, no elevation, rules do their job.
@http.route("/my/loans", auth="user", type="json")
def my_loans(self):
    return request.env["library.loan"].search_read([], ["name", "state"])

Guidelines:

  1. Before any sudo(), name the reason in a comment, and ask whether the check can be done with check_access instead.
  2. Check first, elevate second. If a portal user must trigger a write to a model they cannot touch, check that they may act on this record, then write the minimum:
def action_extend(self, days):
    self.ensure_one()
    self.check_access("write")                 # as the caller
    self.sudo().write({"due_date": self.due_date + timedelta(days=days)})
  1. Elevate the smallest scope: record.sudo().field, not self.sudo() for a whole method.
  2. Never return a sudoed recordset or its data straight to the caller without deciding which fields are safe.
  3. Never elevate based on a model name or record id from the request. request.env[model].sudo().browse(id) with both taken from parameters reads any record of any model.
  4. In multi-company databases add the company explicitly to sudoed searches (see the multi-company chapter).
  5. with_user(SUPERUSER_ID) is superuser mode by convention; treat it like sudo().

docs.title: 4. Controllers
docs.text:
A route is the boundary between the world and your ORM code. For each route decide, from odoo/http.py:

Decision Options Guidance Authentication auth='user' / 'bearer' (18) / 'public' / 'none' user unless the content is truly public. public runs as the shared public user (or the logged-in one). none has no user at all. Method methods=['POST'] restrict; state changes belong to POST CSRF csrf=True (default for type='http') keep it. It is off by default for type='json' CORS cors='*' only for APIs meant for other origins

CSRF protection for http routes means forms must include the token:

<form method="post" action="/library/return">
    <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" t-att-value="request.csrf_token()"/>
    ...
</form>

Disabling it (csrf=False) is acceptable only for endpoints authenticated by something other than the browser session, such as a signature on a webhook, and then the signature check replaces it:

from werkzeug.exceptions import Forbidden
from odoo import http
from odoo.http import request
from odoo.tools import consteq, hmac


@http.route("/library/webhook", type="http", auth="public", methods=["POST"], csrf=False)
def webhook(self, **kw):
    body = request.httprequest.get_data()
    sent = request.httprequest.headers.get("X-Signature", "")
    expected = hmac(request.env(su=True), "library-webhook", body)
    if not consteq(sent, expected):
        raise Forbidden()
    ...

Here the route is auth="public", not none: with auth="none" there is no database environment to build the superuser environment from. (A real webhook from an external service signs with a secret shared with that service; use the secret= argument of hmac for that.)

Input handling rules:

  • Treat every parameter as untrusted text. Convert with int() and catch ValueError; never pass **kw straight into write or create (mass assignment lets a caller set state, user_id, company_id):
# WRONG
loan.write(kw)
# RIGHT
allowed = {"note"}
loan.write({k: v for k, v in kw.items() if k in allowed})
  • Load records through the user's environment and let rules decide. For a record accessed with a token, use the portal helper that checks the token and then renders read-only, as the portal chapter shows.
  • Do not echo exception messages from the database to the client.
  • Redirect targets taken from parameters (?redirect=/path) must be validated, or the route is an open redirect. Accept only relative paths that start with a single /.
  • type='json' routes receive JSON; routes that accept file uploads must check size, type and name.

docs.title: 5. HTML output and XSS
docs.text:
QWeb escapes by default: t-out and t-esc escape text. The danger is values wrapped as safe:

from markupsafe import Markup

# WRONG: a user-controlled string marked safe.
body = Markup(user_text)

# RIGHT: escape, or build with Markup.format, which escapes arguments.
body = Markup("<p>%s</p>") % user_text
body = Markup("<b>{}</b>").format(user_text)
from odoo.tools import html_escape         # markupsafe.escape in 18
safe_text = html_escape(user_text)

Rules:

  • Markup(x) is a promise that x is already safe HTML. Applying it to user text breaks the promise. Interpolate into a Markup template with % or .format; both escape the arguments.
  • t-out of a Markup value is not escaped. In OWL JavaScript, t-out renders HTML only for values wrapped with markup(); never wrap user text.
  • t-raw and t-esc are marked deprecated in the QWeb reference of 18 ("please use t-out"). If you meet t-raw in an old module, replace it with t-out and check that every value rendered unescaped is intended.
  • fields.Html sanitises by default. The parameters in 18 are sanitize (default True), sanitize_overridable (default False; when true, users in base.group_sanitize_override may bypass it), sanitize_tags, sanitize_attributes, sanitize_style (default False), sanitize_form, sanitize_conditional_comments (default True). Turning sanitisation off (sanitize=False) for a field that users can edit is stored XSS for everyone who views it. Leave the default unless the content comes only from trusted staff.
  • html_sanitize(src) in odoo.tools.mail is the function the field uses; call it explicitly when you accept HTML into a non-Html field.
  • Do not put user data into <script> blocks, href="javascript:" URLs, or inline event handlers. Encode data attributes with t-att- instead of string concatenation.
  • Mail templates: values rendered into HTML bodies are escaped; subject and Markup handling follow the same rules.

docs.title: 6. Secrets, tokens and comparisons
docs.text:
• Never store credentials in code or in the repository. Use system parameters (ir.config_parameter) read through the ORM as superuser, or environment variables, or the configuration file. System parameters are readable only by the Settings group; do not expose ir.config_parameter to ordinary users.
  • Tokens must be unguessable. Use secrets.token_urlsafe(32) or uuid.uuid4().hex for access tokens, not a counter, a timestamp, or an id.
  • Compare secrets in constant time. tools.misc.consteq is hmac.compare_digest; use it for tokens and signatures, never ==.
  • Sign, do not just encode. odoo.tools.hmac(env, scope, message) computes a SHA-256 HMAC with the database's database.secret as key. The mandatory non-empty scope makes the same message produce different signatures in different features, so a token minted for one purpose cannot be replayed for another. env must be a sudo environment (it reads the config parameter). For tokens that carry data, odoo.tools.hash_sign(env, scope, message_values, expiration=None, expiration_hours=None) produces a URL-safe signed payload with optional expiry (the docstring compares it to a JWT), and verify_hash_signed checks it.
  • API keys of users (res.users.apikeys) are managed by core. Do not invent a parallel scheme; for outbound calls from your module, store third-party keys in a protected system parameter or a field with groups= and read it with sudo() in the one method that needs it.
  • Do not log secrets, request bodies containing passwords, or full tokens. Logging a truncated hash is fine.

docs.title: 7. Files and paths
docs.text:
• tools.file_open(name, mode, filter_ext) opens a file located inside an addons path directory and rejects anything else; prefer it to open() for module resources. Pass filter_ext to restrict extensions.
  • When you build a path from a request parameter, join it with werkzeug.security.safe_join(directory, path) (the web controller does exactly this for static files). It returns None for a path that escapes the directory.
  • Never use a user-supplied name directly as a filename or as ir.attachment name for a file served back with that name. Strip path separators and control characters.
  • Uploaded files: check size and content type; remember attachments are served by /web/content according to the access of the record they belong to, and a public=True attachment is readable by anyone with the URL.
  • Do not unpickle, yaml.load, or eval uploaded data. Use json or yaml.safe_load.
  • Temporary files: use tempfile and delete them; file_open_temporary_directory exists for code that must read from a temp directory.

docs.title: 8. Denial of service and resource abuse
docs.text:
• A public route that does unbounded work (search without limit, export of all records, PDF generation) is a free DoS. Add limits and pagination, and put expensive endpoints behind authentication.
  • Do not search([]) an unbounded model inside a request.
  • Sleeping, long loops or external calls inside a request hold a worker. Move them to a queue or cron (the queues chapter).
  • Regular expressions on user input can backtrack catastrophically; prefer simple parsing.

docs.title: 9. Logging and information disclosure
docs.text:
• Do not return Python tracebacks or SQL errors to clients. The framework's default error handling for http routes hides them in production; a route that catches Exception and returns str(e) undoes that.
  • AccessError messages are designed to be shown to the user; do not replace them with a message that reveals record ids or rule domains.
  • Keep debug mode off in production: it adds the developer menu and technical details to access errors for users with base.group_no_one.

docs.title: A review checklist
docs.text:
Run this against every module before it ships:

  1. grep -rn "execute(" --include=*.py and read each one: parameters or SQL, never %/format/f-string on the query.
  2. grep -rn "sudo()" --include=*.py: for each, the reason, the scope, the check done before.
  3. grep -rn "eval(" --include=*.py and grep -rn "Markup(" --include=*.py: where does the argument come from?
  4. Every @http.route: auth, methods, csrf, what is read from kw, what is returned.
  5. Every fields.Html(sanitize=False) and every t-out of a value that came from a user.
  6. Every secret and token: how generated, how compared, where stored.
  7. Every file access built from a parameter.
  8. Every ACL row with an empty group, every global rule's domain, every groups= on a field holding personal data.
  9. The test that logs in as an ordinary user and as a portal user and tries to read another user's record.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Markup(user_text) is not escaping. It is the opposite: it tells the template engine not to escape.

  • cr.execute(query % value) and f-strings in queries.
  • A dynamic string passed as SQL code. The safety guarantee is for literals.
  • **kw into write or create.
