  • If a module throws while loading, the module and everything depending on it silently never exists, and the loader prints one console error naming the failed module. Always open the browser console after you add JavaScript. Look for "The following modules failed to load because of an error".

The loader itself is plain code you can inspect in the console:

// any backend page
odoo.loader.modules.size                 // started modules
[...odoo.loader.failed]                  // names of modules that threw
[...odoo.loader.jobs]                    // modules waiting for a missing dependency
odoo.loader.modules.get("@web/core/registry")

jobs is the most useful: a module listed there is waiting for a dependency that no bundle provides, which usually means a typo in an import path or a file that is not in any bundle.

docs.title: Module names
docs.text:
Every file under an addon's static/src (and static/tests) becomes an ES module whose name is derived from its path:

File Module name web/static/src/core/registry.js @web/core/registry library/static/src/book_list/book_list.js @library/book_list/book_list library/static/src/components/card.js @library/components/card

The pattern is @<addon>/<path under static/src without extension>. Relative imports (./card) work inside one addon; across addons always use the @addon/... form so a file move in your module does not break someone else's import.

docs.title: The @odoo-module header
docs.text:
Older code starts with this comment:

/** @odoo-module **/

The transpiler (odoo/tools/js_transpiler.py) turns files that are "Odoo modules" into loader definitions. In 16 and 17 a file is an Odoo module only if the header is present. In 18 and 20 every file under <addon>/static/src and <addon>/static/tests is transpiled as a module whether or not the header is there; the header only matters for files outside those folders, and /** @odoo-module ignore **/ opts a file out.

Keep writing the header. It costs one line, it makes the module work on 16 and 17 as well, and it tells readers that the file is an ES module.

docs.title: Registries, services, components
docs.text:
Three ideas cover almost everything in the backend client.

Components are OWL classes with an XML template. Pages, field widgets, list renderers, dialogs and systray buttons are all components.

Registries are ordered key-value stores. Nothing in the client hard-codes "the list of field widgets" or "the list of view types"; it looks them up in a registry, so you extend the client by adding an entry. The categories actually used by the 18 web addon, from most to least populated:

Category What lives there fields field widgets (char, many2one, your custom ones) services singletons started with the client (orm, action, dialog, ...) formatters, parsers text conversions for field values views view types (list, form, kanban, your own) view_widgets widgets used with <widget name="..."/> in views main_components components mounted once next to the web client (notification container, dialog container) actions client actions (tag values of ir.actions.client) systray items in the top right bar debug entries of the developer menu command_provider command palette sources user_menuitems entries in the user menu public_components OWL components for website pages

Print the real list for your build:

odoo.loader.modules.get("@web/core/registry").registry.category("services").getEntries().map(([k]) => k)

Services hold shared state and do shared work. The built-in ones in 18 include orm, action, dialog, notification, user (a plain module in 18, not a registry service), hotkey, ui, view, field, name, menu, command, popover, title, http, localization, company, currency, effect, file_upload, datetime_picker, sortable, tooltip. A component asks for one with useService("orm").

The next chapters cover each in depth: OWL in "OWL fundamentals", registries and services in their own chapter, and the three ways to change existing behaviour (registry entry, subclass, patch).

docs.title: Choosing the right extension technique
docs.text:
Work down this list and stop at the first that fits:

  1. Add a new entry to a registry. A new field widget, a new client action, a new systray item. Zero coupling with existing code. This is the only technique that survives every upgrade intact.
  2. Subclass and register a replacement. For example, extend ListRenderer, then register a new view type library_list that uses it, and select it with js_class="library_list" on the <list> tag of one view. Only the views that opt in change.
  3. patch() an existing class. This changes behaviour for everyone, everywhere, which is what you want only when the existing class has no registry hook and you really need the global change. See the patching chapter.
  4. Template inheritance (t-inherit, t-inherit-mode="extension") for markup changes only.
  5. Replacing a file through the manifest (("replace", ...)). Last resort, breaks on renames.

The order is not about elegance. It is about blast radius: number 2 changes one view; number 3 changes every form in the database, including those from modules you never read.

docs.title: A module with a frontend: the file layout
docs.text:
This is the layout this book uses for every teaching module. Names are the conventional ones; nothing forces them except the globs in your manifest.

library/
  __manifest__.py
  static/
    src/
      js/                     # or one folder per feature
        book_counter.js
      xml/
        book_counter.xml
      scss/
        library.scss
    tests/
      tours/
        library_tour.js
      unit/
        book_counter.test.js

And the manifest part that makes it load:

"assets": {
    "web.assets_backend": [
        "library/static/src/**/*",
        ("remove", "library/static/src/**/*.test.js"),
    ],
    "web.assets_tests": [
        "library/static/tests/tours/**/*",
    ],
},

The remove line keeps unit-test files out of the production backend bundle. The assets chapter explains globs and directives in detail.

docs.title: A first end-to-end change
docs.text:
Show the number of open loans in the systray. This is a complete, working extension (18 and 20; see Versions for 16/17).

library/static/src/systray/loan_counter.js:

/** @odoo-module **/
import { Component, onWillStart, useState } from "@odoo/owl";
import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";
import { useService } from "@web/core/utils/hooks";

export class LoanCounter extends Component {
    static template = "library.LoanCounter";
    static props = {};

    setup() {
        this.orm = useService("orm");
        this.action = useService("action");
        this.state = useState({ open: 0 });
        onWillStart(() => this.refresh());
    }

    async refresh() {
        this.state.open = await this.orm.searchCount("library.loan", [
            ["state", "=", "open"],
        ]);
    }

    openLoans() {
        this.action.doAction("library.action_loan");
    }
}

registry.category("systray").add(
    "library.LoanCounter",
    { Component: LoanCounter },
    { sequence: 25 }
);

library/static/src/systray/loan_counter.xml:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<templates xml:space="preserve">
    <t t-name="library.LoanCounter">
        <div class="o_nav_entry">
            <button class="btn btn-link" t-on-click="openLoans">
                Loans: <t t-out="state.open"/>
            </button>
        </div>
    </t>
</templates>

Add both files to web.assets_backend, update the module, hard-reload. If nothing appears, the order of checks is: browser console for a failed module, then odoo.loader.modules.has("@library/systray/loan_counter"), then registry.category("systray").getEntries().

library.action_loan is the xml id of a window action in the teaching module. doAction accepts an xml id string, a numeric id, or an action dictionary.

docs.title: Reading the real implementation
docs.text:
You will spend more time reading Odoo's JavaScript than writing yours. Three techniques, in the order you should try them.

1. Debug assets in the browser. Add ?debug=assets to any backend URL. Odoo stops bundling and minifying; every module is served as its own file, and the Sources tab of the developer tools shows @web/... paths with readable code. Set breakpoints there. (?debug=1 gives the developer menu and some tooling; assets additionally serves unbundled files and regenerates the bundle when a source file changes.) A tests value adds the test bundle and enables tours to run from the debug menu.

2. grep a checkout. Keep a checkout of the branch you run. Searching beats browsing:

grep -rn "registry.category(\"fields\").add(\"many2one\"" addons/web/static/src
grep -rn "static template = \"web.ListRenderer\"" addons/web/static/src

For the XML half of a component, search by template name, which is global (t-name="web.ListRenderer").

3. Ask the running client. In the console, with debug on:

const { registry } = odoo.loader.modules.get("@web/core/registry");
registry.category("views").getEntries().map(([k]) => k);     // view types
registry.category("fields").get("many2one");                 // the widget definition

docs.title: Debug modes at a glance
docs.text:
URL parameter Effect ?debug=1 developer menu, technical names in tooltips, view editing tools ?debug=assets everything of 1 plus unbundled, unminified assets, regenerated on change ?debug=tests everything of 1 plus the test bundle for tours ?debug=0 leave debug mode

They combine: ?debug=assets,tests. Debug state lives in the URL and is also kept in the session cookie for the rendered pages that need it, so a plain link without the parameter drops it.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Old tutorials use odoo.define("module.name", function (require) {...}). It still exists in the loader (odoo.define = loader.define.bind(loader)) and runs in 16 and in some website code, but backend code in 17 and later is written as ES modules. Do not mix: a legacy require("web.core") returns nothing useful in a modern backend.

  • Looking for a global to reach services. There is none you should use. Inside components use useService; outside them use env.services.
  • Writing jQuery in backend components. It is not guaranteed to be loaded by the modern client. Use OWL refs and plain DOM APIs.
  • Putting a backend file in web.assets_frontend (or the reverse). The module @web/views/... does not exist on a public page, and the module is added to odoo.loader.jobs forever.
  • Forgetting the template file. A component whose template is not in any bundle fails at mount with "Missing template", not at load time. Templates and scripts live in the same assets list.
  • Editing a file and expecting a change without debug=assets. The compiled bundle is cached under a hash; you are running the old copy.
  • Adding a registry entry inside setup(). It runs once per component instance; the second instance throws "Cannot add key ... already in registry".
  • Naming a template or registry key without your module prefix. Both are global namespaces. t-name="LoanCounter" can collide with someone else's; library.LoanCounter cannot.
  • Trusting console.log ordering across modules. Module start order follows dependencies, not file names.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
16: OWL 2 and the legacy widget system coexist. Fields and views have separate legacy and OWL registries (legacy_registries), and a /** @odoo-module **/ header is required for a file to be an ES module. The backend URL is /web, and there is no web.assets_web bundle (the client loads web.assets_backend directly).

17: the legacy layer is gone from the backend. web.assets_web exists and includes web.assets_backend. The URL is still /web. The header is still required.

18: URLs are /odoo/... (the /web route still works). Files under static/src and static/tests are transpiled without the header.

20: ships OWL 3 (3.0.0-alpha.50 in the source checked), where 18 ships OWL 2.8.4. The web client keeps the same registries and services, but some hook signatures changed. For example useAutofocus takes a ref instead of a refName, and useBus names its arguments target, type, listener. The registry validation in 20 uses assertType from OWL instead of validate. Treat any 18 snippet as a starting point and run it on a 20 database before trusting it. The chapters that follow mark each known difference.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Open any backend page with ?debug=assets. In the Sources tab find web/static/src/core/registry.js and read the add method. Note what happens when the key already exists.
  2. In the console run odoo.loader.modules.get("@web/core/registry").registry.category("systray").getEntries() and compare with the icons in the top bar.
  3. Build the systray counter above. Then break it on purpose by misspelling the import @web/core/utils/hooks and read what odoo.loader.jobs and the console say.
Solution notes
  1. add(key, value, { force, sequence }) throws if the key is already present and force is not set, and keeps the previous sequence when you replace with force.
  2. The entries come back ordered by sequence; the default sequence is 50, which is why items you add without one land after the built-in ones that use lower numbers.
  3. A wrong import path leaves your module in odoo.loader.jobs, and the console reports that the module is waiting for an unknown dependency. A syntax error instead puts it in odoo.loader.failed.

docs.title: OWL fundamentals
docs.text:
OWL is the component framework of the web client. You write a class, an XML template and some hooks; the framework re-renders the component when reactive state changes. Odoo 20 ships OWL 3, which changes props, state and refs; that is covered in the next chapter, and the differences are flagged here where they bite.

Examples target Odoo 18, which ships OWL 2.8.4 (addons/web/static/lib/owl), and use the teaching module library.

docs.title: Anatomy of a component
docs.text:
/** @odoo-module **/
import { Component, onWillStart, useState } from "@odoo/owl";
import { useService } from "@web/core/utils/hooks";

export class BookList extends Component {
    static template = "library.BookList";
    static props = {
        title: { type: String, optional: true },
        limit: { type: Number, optional: true },
    };
    static defaultProps = { limit: 10 };

    setup() {
        this.orm = useService("orm");
        this.state = useState({ books: [], loading: true });
        onWillStart(async () => {
            this.state.books = await this.orm.searchRead(
                "library.book", [], ["name", "isbn"], { limit: this.props.limit }
            );
            this.state.loading = false;
        });
    }
}

<templates xml:space="preserve">
  <t t-name="library.BookList">
    <div class="o_library_book_list">
      <h4 t-if="props.title" t-out="props.title"/>
      <ul>
        <li t-foreach="state.books" t-as="book" t-key="book.id">
          <t t-out="book.name"/> <small class="text-muted" t-out="book.isbn"/>
        </li>
      </ul>
    </div>
  </t>
</templates>

Four things make a component: a class that extends Component, a static template naming a template, an optional static props description, and a setup() method. The template has the component as its rendering context: props, state (anything you assigned to this) and methods are reachable by name.

docs.title: setup(), not the constructor
docs.text:
Hooks only work while the component is being set up. They register themselves on "the component currently being built", and that pointer exists only during setup().

setup() {
    this.state = useState({ q: "" });         // fine
    const ref = useRef("input");              // fine
    onMounted(() => ref.el.focus());          // fine
}

async onClick() {
    const s = useState({});                   // throws: no current component
}

Never await before a hook call, and never make setup async. A hook after an await runs outside the setup window. Do asynchronous loading in onWillStart and keep setup synchronous.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
OWL templates are QWeb. A template file is a <templates> root with one <t t-name="..."> per template, listed in the same bundle as the JavaScript. Template names are a single global namespace. Prefix them with the module name.

The directives you will use daily:

Directive Meaning t-if, t-elif, t-else conditionals t-foreach="items" t-as="item" t-key="item.id" loops. t-key is mandatory for lists that change; use a stable id, not the index t-out="expr" output, escaped unless the value is wrapped by markup() t-esc="expr" same as t-out for plain values. Works in 17/18, deprecated in 20 (console warning) t-att-name="expr" dynamic attribute. false/null/undefined omits the attribute t-attf-class="a #{expr} b" attribute with interpolation t-att-class="{ active: state.on, 'text-danger': state.err }" class object t-on-click="method" event handler. Also t-on-input, t-on-keydown, ... t-ref="name" element reference, read through useRef("name") t-set="x" t-value="expr" local variable inside the template t-call="other.template" include another template, sharing the current scope t-component="Comp" dynamic component (see below) t-props="obj" spread an object as props t-slot, t-call-slot slots (see below) t-model="state.q" two-way binding for inputs

Expressions are a restricted JavaScript subset. You can call methods and use ternaries, &&, || and !, but you cannot declare functions or use if statements. The template compiler also rewrites some words: and, or, not, lt, gt are accepted as aliases for operators, which is why you may see props.a and props.b in core templates.

docs.title: Event handlers
docs.text:
<button t-on-click="save">Save</button>
<button t-on-click="() => this.remove(book.id)">Delete</button>
<form t-on-submit.prevent="onSubmit">...</form>
<div t-on-click.stop="noop">...</div>

A bare method name is bound to the component and receives the DOM event. An arrow function receives nothing unless you pass it. Modifiers .prevent, .stop, .capture, .self, .synthetic are available.

Handlers in a loop capture the loop variable, so the arrow form is the normal way to pass the row:

<li t-foreach="state.books" t-as="book" t-key="book.id">
    <a t-on-click="() => this.open(book.id)" t-out="book.name"/>
</li>

docs.title: Binding inputs
docs.text:
<input class="form-control" t-model="state.q" placeholder="Search"/>
<input t-model.trim="state.name"/>
<input type="number" t-model.number="state.qty"/>
<input t-model.lazy="state.note"/>

t-model updates state.q on every input event (on change with .lazy). It needs state to be reactive, otherwise nothing re-renders.

docs.title: State and reactivity
docs.text:
useState(obj) returns a reactive proxy around obj. Reading a key inside a render subscribes the component to it, and writing it later schedules a re-render of the components that read it.

this.state = useState({ q: "", books: [], editing: null });
this.state.q = "dune";                // re-render
this.state.books.push({ id: 7 });     // re-render (arrays and nested objects are reactive)
this.state.editing = { id: 7 };       // re-render

Rules that explain most "my UI does not update" reports:

  • Only the proxy is reactive. Keep the original object out of reach, and never destructure state at the top of a method: let { q } = this.state; q = "x" writes to a local variable.
  • Replacing the proxy, as in this.state = {...}, discards reactivity. Assign to its keys.
  • Class instances and values set via markRaw are not proxied. Wrap a big object (a chart instance, a library handle) in markRaw(obj) to avoid the cost and the surprises.
  • A key that was never present is not tracked until written. Initialise every key you will read.
  • Renders are batched. After this.state.x = 1 the DOM is not updated yet; it updates on the next microtask. If you need the DOM after a change, do the work in an onPatched callback (or a useEffect that depends on the changed value).

docs.title: Sharing state between components
docs.text:
Use reactive(obj, callback) from @odoo/owl for state that lives outside a component, and useState on it inside each consumer:

import { reactive, useState } from "@odoo/owl";

export const basket = reactive({ ids: [], add(id) { this.ids.push(id); } });

// in a component
this.basket = useState(basket);

For anything application-wide, a service is a better home (see the registries chapter).

docs.title: Props
docs.text:
Props come from the parent and are read-only from the child's point of view.

static props = {
    title: { type: String, optional: true },
    book: { type: Object, shape: { id: Number, name: String } },
    onPick: { type: Function, optional: true },
    "*": true,                    // allow any other prop
};
static defaultProps = { title: "Books" };
  • Types: String, Number, Boolean, Object, Array, Function, Date, a class, or a union [String, Number]. { type: Array, element: Object } and { type: Object, shape: {...} } validate contents.
  • optional: true allows undefined. defaultProps fills in missing values before validation.
  • "*": true accepts anything extra. Without it, an unknown prop is a validation error.
  • Validation runs only in debug mode (the Odoo environment passes dev: env.debug) and in test mode. In production a wrong prop is silently accepted, so read the warnings in ?debug=1 while you develop.
  • A component with no static props triggers the warning "Component 'X' does not have a static props description" (warnIfNoStaticProps is on outside test mode). Declare props even for components with none: static props = {};.

Callbacks are the only way a child tells its parent anything. Name them onSomething, and pass them in:

<BookRow t-foreach="state.books" t-as="book" t-key="book.id"
         book="book" onPick.bind="pick"/>

The .bind suffix on a prop binds the method to the parent component, so this is right when the child calls it. A prop name that is an attribute in an XML template must be a valid XML name; onPick.bind is the only place a dot is allowed.

docs.title: Children and dynamic components
docs.text:
Child components are registered in static components and used by name:

import { BookRow } from "./book_row";

export class BookList extends Component {
    static template = "library.BookList";
    static components = { BookRow };
    static props = {};
}

When the component class is decided at runtime, use t-component:

<t t-component="state.editor" t-props="editorProps"/>

where state.editor holds a class. This is how the web client renders any field widget, any view and any action: it looks up the class in a registry and drops it into a t-component. Keep class references out of useState or wrap them with markRaw; a class is not meant to be proxied.

docs.title: Slots
docs.text:
Slots let the parent pass markup into the child.

<!-- child: library.Card -->
<t t-name="library.Card">
  <div class="card">
    <div class="card-header"><t t-slot="header"/></div>
    <div class="card-body"><t t-slot="default"/></div>
  </div>
</t>

<!-- parent -->
<Card>
  <t t-set-slot="header">Overdue loans</t>
  <p>Three books are late.</p>
</Card>

Content outside any t-set-slot becomes the default slot. A slot can receive values from the child:

<!-- child --> <t t-slot="row" book="book"/>
<!-- parent --> <t t-set-slot="row" t-slot-scope="s"><b t-out="s.book.name"/></t>

In the child class, declare slots: { type: Object, optional: true } in static props if you want validation to accept them. The core uses t-call-slot for the same purpose inside templates that are called with t-call.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
In order of occurrence:

Hook When Typical use setup() construction register hooks, create state onWillStart(fn) before the first render, may be async load data the first render needs onWillRender / onRendered before/after the template is evaluated rare onMounted(fn) after the component is in the DOM DOM libraries, focus, measure onWillUpdateProps(fn) before a re-render caused by new props, may be async reload when a prop changes onWillPatch / onPatched around DOM updates restore scroll positions onWillUnmount(fn) before removal remove listeners, destroy library objects onWillDestroy(fn) after unmount, children included last cleanup onError(fn) an error in a descendant error boundary

Parents render before children and mount after them: onMounted of a child fires before onMounted of its parent, and a parent waits for the onWillStart promises of all children to resolve before anything shows. A slow request in a deep child delays the whole screen; start non-essential loads in onMounted instead.

Reacting to a changed prop is the classic place to go wrong:

setup() {
    this.state = useState({ lines: [] });
    onWillStart(() => this.load(this.props.loanId));
    onWillUpdateProps((next) => {
        if (next.loanId !== this.props.loanId) {
            return this.load(next.loanId);       // returning the promise delays the render
        }
    });
}
async load(id) {
    this.state.lines = await this.orm.searchRead(
        "library.loan.line", [["loan_id", "=", id]], ["book_id", "due_date"]
    );
}

Note that onWillUpdateProps receives the next props; this.props still holds the old ones.

docs.title: References and DOM work
docs.text:
import { useRef, onMounted, useEffect } from "@odoo/owl";

setup() {
    this.input = useRef("search");           // <input t-ref="search"/>
    onMounted(() => this.input.el.focus());
}

ref.el is null until mount and while the element is not rendered (inside a false t-if). For code that must re-run when a dependency changes, use useEffect:

useEffect(
    (el, open) => {
        if (open) el.focus();
        return () => { /* cleanup before the next run */ };
    },
    () => [this.input.el, this.state.open]
);

The second argument computes the dependency list. The effect runs after mount and after any patch where a dependency changed. An empty list () => [] means once. Omitting the argument means "after every patch" (OWL uses [NaN], which never equals itself).

Odoo provides ready-made hooks on top of these. The ones you will use, all in @web/core/utils/hooks: useService, useBus, useAutofocus, useOwnedDialogs, useChildRef, useForwardRefToParent, useRefListener. useBus(bus, "EVENT", cb) subscribes for the component lifetime. useAutofocus({ refName: "search" }) focuses t-ref="search" on mount. Timing helpers in @web/core/utils/timing: useDebounced(callback, delay) and debounce.

Listeners on window or document go through useExternalListener(window, "resize", cb), which removes them for you. Writing window.addEventListener in setup leaks the component.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
An exception thrown while rendering or in a hook destroys the app unless some ancestor catches it:

export class SafeBox extends Component {
    static template = xml`<t t-if="state.error">Could not display this.</t><t t-else="" t-slot="default"/>`;
    static props = { slots: Object };
    setup() {
        this.state = useState({ error: false });
        onError(() => { this.state.error = true; });
    }
}

xml is a tagged template from @odoo/owl that compiles a template string. It is handy for tiny inline templates and in tests; real modules put templates in files because only file templates can be inherited by other modules.

docs.title: Rendering HTML safely
docs.text:
t-out escapes. To render trusted HTML wrap it with markup:

import { markup } from "@odoo/owl";
this.state.html = markup(htmlFromTheServer);   // only when the server sanitised it

Never mark user-provided text. A html-typed field value from the ORM is sanitised by the server for display purposes; anything else is not.

docs.title: Translating strings
docs.text:
Static strings in templates are extracted for translation automatically, and data-tooltip is registered as translatable by the web client. In JavaScript use _t:

import { _t } from "@web/core/l10n/translation";
this.notification.add(_t("Book returned"), { type: "success" });

_t must be called with a literal string for the extraction to find it. For strings with values: _t("%s is overdue", name). A top-level const LABEL = _t("Hello") runs before translations are loaded; use it inside functions, or build it lazily.

docs.title: A complete worked example
docs.text:
A debounced search box over library.book, with a loading state, using only what this chapter introduced.

/** @odoo-module **/
import { Component, onWillStart, useState } from "@odoo/owl";
import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";
import { useService } from "@web/core/utils/hooks";
import { useDebounced } from "@web/core/utils/timing";

export class BookSearch extends Component {
    static template = "library.BookSearch";
    static props = { "*": true };

    setup() {
        this.orm = useService("orm");
        this.action = useService("action");
        this.state = useState({ q: "", rows: [], busy: false });
        this.search = useDebounced(this.runSearch, 300);
        onWillStart(() => this.runSearch());
    }

    onInput() {
        this.search();
    }

    async runSearch() {
        this.state.busy = true;
        const domain = this.state.q
            ? ["|", ["name", "ilike", this.state.q], ["isbn", "ilike", this.state.q]]
            : [];
        this.state.rows = await this.orm.searchRead(
            "library.book", domain, ["name", "isbn"], { limit: 20, order: "name" }
        );
        this.state.busy = false;
    }

    open(id) {
        this.action.doAction({
            type: "ir.actions.act_window",
            res_model: "library.book",
            res_id: id,
            views: [[false, "form"]],
        });
    }
}

registry.category("actions").add("library.book_search", BookSearch);

<templates xml:space="preserve">
  <t t-name="library.BookSearch">
    <div class="o_action p-3">
      <input class="form-control mb-3" placeholder="Title or ISBN"
             t-model="state.q" t-on-input="onInput"/>
      <div t-if="state.busy" class="text-muted">Searching...</div>
      <div class="list-group">
        <a t-foreach="state.rows" t-as="row" t-key="row.id"
           href="#" class="list-group-item list-group-item-action"
           t-on-click.prevent="() => this.open(row.id)">
          <t t-out="row.name"/>
          <small class="float-end text-muted" t-out="row.isbn"/>
        </a>
      </div>
    </div>
  </t>
</templates>

Registering it as actions entry library.book_search makes it a client action. Pair it with a menu:

<record id="action_book_search" model="ir.actions.client">
    <field name="name">Book search</field>
    <field name="tag">library.book_search</field>
</record>
<menuitem id="menu_book_search" name="Book search"
          parent="library.menu_root" action="action_book_search"/>

tag is the registry key. If the menu opens a blank screen, the key in the registry and the tag differ, and the console shows "Could not find client action".

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Mutating props. OWL does not stop you, but the parent never learns about the change and its next render overwrites it. Copy a prop into state, or call a callback prop that asks the parent to change it.

  • await before a hook, or an async setup. The hook has no current component and throws.
  • Missing t-key in a t-foreach over changing data. OWL falls back to positions: input contents and focus jump to the wrong row after a reorder.
  • t-key="row_index" has the same problem. Use the record id.
  • Destructuring state loses reactivity.
  • Reusing a template name. The last registered wins, silently. Always prefix: library.BookList.
  • Holding a service call across destruction. Methods of orm and friends are wrapped by useService: if the component is destroyed while a request is pending, the returned promise never resolves. Code after the await simply does not run. Do not stash the wrapped service in a global.
  • Heavy onWillStart in many siblings. They run in parallel but the screen waits for the slowest.
  • A static props that omits something you pass. Silent in production, a loud error in debug mode, which is why you develop with debug on.
  • Forgetting .bind on a callback prop passed to a child: this inside the callback is the child's, or undefined.
  • Putting a class instance in useState. Proxying breaks private fields and identity checks. Use markRaw.
  • Writing to state in a template or getter. Rendering must be pure. A write during a render triggers a render loop.
  • jQuery in the backend. Not guaranteed to be loaded; use refs.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
16: the client mixes OWL 1-style legacy widgets with OWL 2 code. Check what a file uses before copying: static template plus useState from @odoo/owl is the OWL 2 style used here.

17 and 18: OWL 2 only. 18 ships OWL 2.8.4. In 18 the @odoo-module header is optional under static/src.

20: OWL 3 (3.0.0-alpha.50 in the checked source). static props and defaultProps are rejected (Component "X" defines a static "props" or "defaultProps", which Owl 3 ignores), useState is gone in favour of proxy, useRef in favour of signal.ref(), and templates address members as this.props.x. Read the next chapter before porting.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Build BookSearch above. Open it from the menu with ?debug=1. Delete static props and read the warning. Add it back.
  2. Remove t-key from the list, type a search that reorders results while one row is focused, and watch what happens. Put it back.
  3. Change useDebounced(this.runSearch, 300) to call this.runSearch directly from t-on-input and watch the network tab while typing. Count requests.
Solution notes
  1. Without static props the console shows a warning that the component has no props description; with it, there is no output. Passing a prop you did not declare produces a validation error unless "*": true is present.
  2. Without t-key, rows are reused by position, so DOM state such as focus belongs to the position rather than the record. With a stable key the DOM node follows the record.
  3. One request per keystroke versus one request per pause. useDebounced also cancels a pending call when the component unmounts.

docs.title: OWL 3 and the Odoo 20 web client
docs.text:
Odoo 20 replaces OWL 2 with OWL 3. Most of the vocabulary of the previous chapter survives (components, templates, slots, lifecycle hooks, registries) but the way you declare props, hold state, reference elements and write services changes. Code written for Odoo 18 does not run unchanged.

Everything here was read from the Odoo 20 source tree available to the author, whose bundled library reports 3.0.0-alpha.50 (addons/web/static/lib/owl/owl.js). The source contains @todo owl3 migration markers and a temporary compatibility layer, so details can still move between that tree and a release you install. Where something is marked temporary in the source, this chapter says so. Always re-check an API against your own checkout before relying on it.

docs.title: What you notice first
docs.text:
A component from the Odoo 20 core, web/static/src/core/checkbox/checkbox.js, trimmed:

import { Component, signal, t, useProps } from "@odoo/owl";

export class CheckBox extends Component {
    static template = "web.CheckBox";
    props = useProps({
        value: t.boolean().optional(),
        disabled: t.boolean().optional(),
        onChange: t.function().optional(() => () => {}),
        slots: t.object().optional(),
    });

    rootRef = signal.ref();

    onChange(ev) {
        if (!this.props.disabled) {
            this.props.onChange(ev.target.checked);
        }
    }
}

<t t-name="web.CheckBox">
    <div class="o-checkbox form-check" t-ref="this.rootRef">
        <input type="checkbox" t-att-checked="this.props.value"
               t-att-disabled="this.props.disabled" t-on-change="this.onChange"/>
        <label class="form-check-label"><t t-call-slot="default"/></label>
    </div>
</t>

Compared with the 18 version of the same component, four things are different:

  1. Props are declared as a class field with useProps(...) and a schema built from t.* types, not with static props.
  2. Elements are referenced through a signal: signal.ref() in the class, t-ref="this.rootRef" in the template, and this.rootRef() to read the element.
  3. Templates address component members with an explicit this. prefix: this.props.value, this.onChange.
  4. There is no useState in sight: component state is a proxy, described below.

docs.title: Props
docs.text:
The old and new forms:

// Odoo 17 / 18 (OWL 2)
static props = {
    title: { type: String, optional: true },
    limit: { type: Number, optional: true },
    onPick: { type: Function, optional: true },
};
static defaultProps = { limit: 10 };

// Odoo 20 (OWL 3)
props = useProps({
    title: t.string().optional(),
    limit: t.number().optional(10),
    onPick: t.function().optional(),
});
  • Defaults move into .optional(default). For a function-valued default the source passes a factory that returns the function (t.function().optional(() => () => {})), so the value is not shared.
  • static props and static defaultProps are errors in Odoo 20: the compatibility layer throws Component "X" defines a static "props" or "defaultProps", which Owl 3 ignores. Declare the props schema through "useProps" instead. This is intentional, so a half-ported component fails at once instead of silently skipping validation.
  • The type vocabulary, from the library's types export: string, number, boolean, function, object, array, tuple, record, strictObject, any, literal, selection (one of a list of values), instanceOf, constructor, promise, ref, signal, combined with or([...]) and and([...]), plus customValidator(type, fn). t.object({...}) takes a shape.
  • Some classes keep their schema as a separate constant so subclasses can reuse it, for example static propsSchema = dialogProps next to props = useProps(this.constructor.propsSchema) in Dialog. The source comments that this is a temporary measure, so do not build on that pattern.

A component with no props still declares them, as props = useProps({}).

docs.title: State: proxy instead of useState
docs.text:
// OWL 2
import { useState } from "@odoo/owl";
this.state = useState({ q: "", rows: [] });

// OWL 3
import { proxy } from "@odoo/owl";
this.state = proxy({ q: "", rows: [] });

proxy is the reactive-object primitive; the Odoo 20 core uses it directly (this.state = proxy({...}) in autocomplete.js, barcode_dialog.js and others) and useState is no longer exported by the library. Reactivity rules from the previous chapter carry over: write through the proxy, do not replace it, initialise every key.

OWL 3 adds other reactive primitives that the web client uses:

Primitive Use signal(value) a reactive cell; read by calling sig(), write with sig.set(v) or through helpers signal.ref() a reactive element reference (replaces useRef) signal.Array, signal.Map, signal.Object, signal.Set reactive collections computed(fn) derived value, recomputed when its inputs change effect(fn) side effect that re-runs when the signals it reads change untrack(fn) read signals without subscribing markRaw, toRaw opt out of, or unwrap, the proxy

Which one to use in your own code: a plain proxy object for component state is the closest match to what you know and what most of the core does. Reach for signal when you need a value that several components or plugins share and depend on.

docs.title: Refs and listeners
docs.text:
// OWL 2
this.input = useRef("search");           // <input t-ref="search"/>
onMounted(() => this.input.el.focus());

// OWL 3
this.input = signal.ref();               // <input t-ref="this.input"/>
onMounted(() => this.input().focus());

For global listeners, OWL 3 exports useListener(target, eventName, handler, params), where target can be an element or a function returning one (it then wires itself with an effect). In the checked source useExternalListener is no longer part of the library exports.

useEffect still exists in the library. The Odoo compatibility layer wraps the old two-argument form as useLayoutEffect(effect, computeDependencies), with the same semantics as the OWL 2 hook (runs after mount and after patches when a dependency changed).

docs.title: Templates: the this. prefix
docs.text:
In the Odoo 20 core, templates read members through this:

<!-- Odoo 18 -->
<button t-on-click="save" t-att-disabled="state.busy" t-out="props.label"/>

<!-- Odoo 20 core style -->
<button t-on-click="this.save" t-att-disabled="this.state.busy" t-out="this.props.label"/>

A template that still uses the bare form is what the compatibility layer exists for; new code should use this.. Other template changes visible in the compatibility notes:

  • t-portal is renamed t-custom-portal and t-model is renamed t-custom-model while running OWL 2 style code on top of OWL 3. Native OWL 3 has its own Portal component and t-model backed by signals.
  • t-esc still renders, but logs a deprecation warning: "t-esc has been deprecated in favor of t-out". Use t-out everywhere. In the Odoo 20 web addon t-out appears in 176 files and t-esc in 2.

docs.title: Services become plugins
docs.text:
OWL 3 introduces Plugin, usePlugin, providePlugins and Resource. The Odoo 20 core is mid-way through turning its services into plugins:

// notification_container.js (Odoo 20, simplified)
import { Component, usePlugin } from "@odoo/owl";
import { NotificationPlugin } from "./notification_plugin";

export class NotificationContainer extends Component {
    notificationPlugin = usePlugin(NotificationPlugin);
    ...
}

// registering a global plugin
import { Plugin } from "@odoo/owl";
import { services } from "@web/core/services";

export class LoanStatsPlugin extends Plugin {
    setup() { /* runs when the plugin starts */ }
}
services.add(LoanStatsPlugin);

services in @web/core/services is an OWL Resource that accepts Plugin subclasses (the validation is t.constructor(Plugin)). Everything added to it is started by the framework.

The old registry.category("services") still exists and still starts services in dependency order. The file core/legacy_service_starter.js is headed "temporary - to remove when all service are converted", and its schema validation still reads { start, dependencies?, async? }. The ORM is the clearest example: the real implementation is the ORM plugin class in core/orm_plugin.js, and a small legacy entry keeps useService("orm") working:

// end of orm_plugin.js
services.add(ORM);
registry.category("services").add("orm", {
    async: ["call", "create", "read", "searchRead", "unlink", "write", ...],
    start() { return Object.create(usePlugin(ORM)); },
});

What this means for module authors, for the source checked:

  • Existing useService("orm"), useService("action"), useService("notification") code keeps working through the bridge. You do not have to port a module's service usage on day one.
  • A service you write with registry.category("services") still works. Write new shared state as a Plugin if you target 20 only; keep the registry form if the module must also run on 18.
  • Both worlds are expected to converge on plugins, so do not build large new code on the bridge.

useService itself still exists in @web/core/utils/hooks and wraps methods so that a call pending at component destruction is dropped, as before.

docs.title: The compatibility layer
docs.text:
addons/web/static/src/owl2/owl3_compatibility_layer.js patches OWL 3 so OWL 2 style code can run during migration. Its own header spells out the steps, and they double as a porting checklist:

  1. Rename t-portal to t-custom-portal and t-model to t-custom-model in templates.
  2. Load the layer immediately after OWL 3.
  3. Replace useEffect with useLayoutEffect.
  4. After the app builds, remove the shims one by one: portals, models, effects.

The layer also provides OWL 2 names on top of OWL 3: useEnv, useSubEnv (via a plugin that holds the environment), onWillRender, useComponent, status (returns "new", "mounted" or "destroyed"), and the aliases owl.config, owl.plugin and owl.props. A helper module @web/owl2/utils re-exports useLayoutEffect, useEnv and useSubEnv and a deprecated render(component, deep).

Treat the layer as scaffolding for Odoo's own migration. For a module you write today, port to the OWL 3 idioms and import from @odoo/owl directly.

docs.title: Porting a component: before and after
docs.text:
The BookSearch component of the previous chapter, ported.

Before (Odoo 18):

export class BookSearch extends Component {
    static template = "library.BookSearch";
    static props = { "*": true };

    setup() {
        this.orm = useService("orm");
        this.state = useState({ q: "", rows: [], busy: false });
        this.search = useDebounced(this.runSearch, 300);
        this.input = useRef("q");
        onMounted(() => this.input.el.focus());
        onWillStart(() => this.runSearch());
    }
    // ...
}

After (Odoo 20):

import { Component, onMounted, onWillStart, proxy, signal, t, useProps } from "@odoo/owl";
import { useService } from "@web/core/utils/hooks";
import { useDebounced } from "@web/core/utils/timing";

export class BookSearch extends Component {
    static template = "library.BookSearch";
    props = useProps({});

    input = signal.ref();

    setup() {
        this.orm = useService("orm");
        this.state = proxy({ q: "", rows: [], busy: false });
        this.search = useDebounced(this.runSearch, 300);
        onMounted(() => this.input().focus());
        onWillStart(() => this.runSearch());
    }
    // runSearch unchanged
}

<t t-name="library.BookSearch">
    <div class="o_action p-3">
        <input class="form-control mb-3" t-ref="this.input"
               t-model="this.state.q" t-on-input="this.onInput"/>
        <div t-if="this.state.busy" class="text-muted">Searching...</div>
        <a t-foreach="this.state.rows" t-as="row" t-key="row.id" href="#"
           t-on-click.prevent="() => this.open(row.id)" t-out="row.name"/>
    </div>
</t>

A porting procedure that works in practice:

  1. Replace static props/defaultProps with props = useProps({...}), moving defaults into .optional(default).
  2. Replace useState with proxy.
  3. Replace useRef("name") with a signal.ref() field, ref.el with ref(), and t-ref="name" with t-ref="this.field".
  4. Prefix template members with this..
  5. Change t-esc to t-out.
  6. Load in a browser with debug on and read every console warning. A wrong prop schema and a leftover static props both name the component.

docs.title: Writing for 18 and 20 at the same time
docs.text:
If one module must run on both versions, you cannot share component code: static props throws on 20 and useProps does not exist on 18. Options, in order of preference (a manifest is a literal dictionary, not executable code, so it cannot choose files by version):

  1. Two branches of the module, one per major version, as Odoo itself maintains them. Cleanest.
  2. Write only logic that is independent of OWL (plain functions, rpc calls) in shared files and keep components per version.

What you should not do is feature-detect inside one component class; the base class constructor of Odoo 20 refuses static props outright.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Leaving static props on a 20 component. The constructor throws at first mount. Search for it with grep -rn "static props\|static defaultProps" static/src before running.
  • Importing useState, useRef, useExternalListener or useComponent from @odoo/owl on 20. They are absent from the library exports. useComponent and useEnv exist only through the compatibility layer, so importing them from @odoo/owl works at runtime only while the layer is loaded.
  • Forgetting to call a signal. this.input.focus() on a signal.ref() fails because this.input is the signal, not the element. Call it: this.input().focus().
  • Mixing this.-less templates with new components. It works under the compatibility layer, not as a convention. Pick one style per file.
  • Building on the bridge. The registry.category("services") path and useService("orm") are marked temporary in the source.
  • Copy-pasting from 18 documentation. Tutorials, forum answers and older versions of this book describe the OWL 2 API. When something fails on 20, the first suspect is the props and state primitives.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. In an Odoo 20 checkout, run grep -rn "static props" addons/web/static/src | head and grep -rn "useProps(" addons/web/static/src | head. Read what remains, and why.
  2. Port the systray LoanCounter of the overview chapter to 20. Run it and read the console.
  3. Add static props = {} to your ported component and find the exact error text.
Solution notes
  1. The checked tree has no static props left in web/static/src; components declare props = useProps(...), and Dialog keeps a propsSchema constant with a comment calling it temporary.
  2. The port is props = useProps({}), this.state = proxy({ open: 0 }), and this. prefixes in the template. useService("orm") and useService("action") continue to work.
  3. Component "LoanCounter" defines a static "props" or "defaultProps", which Owl 3 ignores. Declare the props schema through "useProps" instead, e.g. "props = useProps({ someProp: t.string().optional(defaultValue) })".

docs.title: Patching standard code
docs.text:
patch(obj, extension) from @web/core/utils/patch overrides properties of a class prototype or an object in place and returns a function that undoes the patch. It is the JavaScript counterpart of _inherit with a method override, with one difference that matters: a Python _inherit extends a model for every caller by design, while a JavaScript patch also changes every instance and every subclass of the target that does not override the patched method itself. That reach is why this chapter spends as much time on when not to patch as on how.

Verified against addons/web/static/src/core/utils/patch.js of Odoo 18 (identical in Odoo 20), and against the 16 and 17 branches for the signature change.

The Odoo 20 source tree ships its own web guidelines (skills/odoo-web-guidelines/guidelines/javascript.md). They say that patching is "strongly discouraged inside Odoo itself" and fine outside of it, because a patch makes the code harder to reason about and drifts from its target, and that a proper extension point is usually the better answer. For a module author this reads as a license with a condition: patching your database's behaviour from your own module is normal, but each patch should be small, guarded, and a candidate for replacement by a registry entry or a subclass.

docs.title: The mechanics
docs.text:
/** @odoo-module **/
import { patch } from "@web/core/utils/patch";
import { useService } from "@web/core/utils/hooks";
import { FormController } from "@web/views/form/form_controller";

patch(FormController.prototype, {
    setup() {
        super.setup(...arguments);
        this.libraryFlag = true;
        this.libraryNotification = useService("notification");
    },

    async onWillSaveRecord(record) {
        const ok = await super.onWillSaveRecord(...arguments);
        if (ok === false) {
            return false;
        }
        // custom check; returning false cancels the save
        if (record.resModel === "library.loan" && !record.data.book_id) {
            this.libraryNotification.add("Pick a book first", { type: "danger" });
            return false;
        }
    },
});

What happens inside patch:

  1. For each own property of the extension object it reads the current property descriptor on the target and keeps it.
  2. It defines the new property on the target. On a class prototype it is made non-enumerable, like a normal method.
  3. It rewires the extension object's prototype so that super.method(...) inside the extension reaches the previous implementation. That is how native super works in an object literal.
  4. If you give only a getter or only a setter, the other half is taken from the ancestor so the property does not lose its pair.
  5. It returns an unpatch function. Calling it restores the originals and re-applies any other patches that were stacked on the same target.

Consequences you can rely on:

  • Patches stack. Two modules patching the same method both run, in module load order, each calling super for the one before it. If one forgets super, every earlier patch (and the original) is skipped.
  • super works for methods, getters and setters, and for static members when you patch the class itself.
  • A patch is global and immediate: it takes effect when the patching module loads, for existing and future instances.

docs.title: What to patch: prototype versus class
docs.text:
patch(ListController.prototype, { ... });   // instance methods: what you want 95% of the time
patch(ListController, { ... });             // static members: props, components, template

For statics:

import { patch } from "@web/core/utils/patch";
import { FormStatusIndicator } from "@web/views/form/form_status_indicator/form_status_indicator";

patch(FormStatusIndicator, {
    props: {
        ...FormStatusIndicator.props,
        libraryHint: { type: String, optional: true },
    },
});

In Odoo 18, static props of core components is an object (a map from prop name to type description), so you spread it and add keys. Passing a prop that the class does not declare is a validation error in debug mode, which is why adding a prop to a patched component needs this step.

Do not write props: [...X.props, "name?"]. That is the array form of older OWL code. In Odoo 18 core components use the object form, and mixing the two breaks validation.

docs.title: Where to find the thing to patch
docs.text:
1. Open the screen with ?debug=assets. In the Sources tab find the class (@web/views/form/form_controller).
  2. Read the methods that look like hooks: onWillSaveRecord, beforeLeave, beforeExecuteActionButton, afterExecuteActionButton, onRecordSaved, onWillLoadRoot. Core developers add hook methods where they expect customisation. Patch a hook before you patch a private method.
  3. Confirm the method is looked up on the instance, not captured. Some code does this.props.onSave = this.save.bind(this) at setup; patching save later does nothing for those captures.

For example, the form controller of Odoo 18 documents onWillSaveRecord in a comment: "a callBack that will be executed before the record save if the record is valid. If it returns false, it will prevent the save." That is an invitation to patch (or, better, to subclass for one view).

docs.title: Always call super
docs.text:
patch(FormController.prototype, {
    async deleteRecord() {
        // 1. do your pre-work
        const result = await super.deleteRecord(...arguments);
        // 2. do your post-work
        return result;
    },
});

Return what the original returns. Callers that await the result expect it, and some check for false.

docs.title: Patch setup to add state or hooks
docs.text:
import { useState } from "@odoo/owl";
import { useService } from "@web/core/utils/hooks";

patch(FormController.prototype, {
    setup() {
        super.setup(...arguments);
        this.libraryState = useState({ checked: false });
        this.libraryOrm = useService("orm");
    },
});

A patched setup must call super.setup(...arguments) first or the base class never registers its own hooks, and then everything on the screen breaks in confusing ways. Hooks called here run inside the original setup window, so they work. Follow the same rules as in any setup: synchronous, no await before a hook.

docs.title: Guard by condition, not by absence
docs.text:
A patch applies to every form in the database. Restrict it to your model:

patch(FormController.prototype, {
    async beforeExecuteActionButton(clickParams) {
        if (this.props.resModel === "library.loan" && clickParams.name === "action_return") {
            const confirmed = await this.libraryConfirm(); // a method you define, e.g. opening a ConfirmationDialog
            if (!confirmed) {
                return false;
            }
        }
        return super.beforeExecuteActionButton(...arguments);
    },
});

Test the model, the view, or a context key first and fall through to super otherwise. A patch that changes behaviour for every model is almost always a bug waiting for another module to trip over.

docs.title: Patch a registry entry's value
docs.text:
Registry entries are often plain objects. Patch the value to change a widget definition in place:

import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";
import { patch } from "@web/core/utils/patch";

const charField = registry.category("fields").get("char");
patch(charField, {
    displayName: "Text (library)",
});

Keep this for small tweaks. If you need a different component, register a new entry and select it with widget="...", see the field widgets chapter.

docs.title: Patching templates
docs.text:
Markup changes use template inheritance, not patch. In an XML file in the same bundle as the JavaScript:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<templates xml:space="preserve">
    <t t-inherit="web.FormStatusIndicator" t-inherit-mode="extension">
        <xpath expr="//div[hasclass('o_form_status_indicator_buttons')]" position="after">
            <span t-if="props.libraryHint" class="text-muted ms-2" t-out="props.libraryHint"/>
        </xpath>
    </t>
</templates>
  • t-inherit names the template to extend, t-inherit-mode="extension" modifies it in place (every user of that template sees the change). The other mode, primary, creates a new template under a new t-name that inherits from the first and leaves the original alone; the core uses it for variants such as web.CheckboxItem built from web.DropdownItem.
  • xpath takes expr and position: inside (default), after, before, replace, attributes, move. hasclass('a', 'b') is supported as in Python views. Elements can also be matched with attribute selectors such as //button[@title='Full composer'], as portal does when it removes the full-composer button from message composers.
  • Inside an attributes position, children are <attribute name="class" add="..." remove="..."/> style entries, like in server views (check the existing core file you are patching for the exact form).
  • The extended template must exist when the bundle loads, so list your XML after the target's addon (it follows from depends).

Templates are global names. An xpath that matches nothing raises an error at template compilation, which makes version drift visible. A rename of the target element in the next release is the usual cause.

docs.title: Replacing instead of patching: subclass and register
docs.text:
When the target is looked up in a registry, you do not need a patch at all. A subclass registered under a new key, selected only by the views that ask for it, changes one screen and nothing else:

import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";
import { useService } from "@web/core/utils/hooks";
import { formView } from "@web/views/form/form_view";
import { FormController } from "@web/views/form/form_controller";

class LoanFormController extends FormController {
    setup() {
        super.setup(...arguments);
        this.notification = useService("notification");
    }

    async onWillSaveRecord(record) {
        if (!record.data.book_id) {
            this.notification.add("Pick a book first", { type: "danger" });
            return false;
        }
        return super.onWillSaveRecord(...arguments);
    }
}

registry.category("views").add("library_loan_form", {
    ...formView,
    Controller: LoanFormController,
});

<form js_class="library_loan_form">...</form>

The class is subject to the usual caveats about internals, but the blast radius is one view. The customising views chapter works this out fully. Rule of thumb: if the thing you want to change is reached through js_class, widget or an action tag, subclass. If it is not reached through any registry, patch.

docs.title: When patching is the right tool
docs.text:
• The behaviour is hard-wired in a core class with no registry in front of it (the navbar, the control panel, the list renderer's cell logic when you need it for all lists).
  • You are fixing a bug in a standard component for your database until the fix lands upstream.
  • You are extending a class from another module that defines no registry (many mail models in the Discuss code).

In each case keep the patch in its own file named after what it does (patch_form_controller.js), small, guarded by condition, and commented with the reason and the version it was written for.

docs.title: Testing a patch
docs.text: Patches are global, so tests must be able to remove them. The test helper patchWithCleanup(obj, patchValue) (in @web/../tests/web_test_helpers in Odoo 18) applies a patch for one test and restores it afterwards; use it when a test needs different behaviour of a core class. Your own production patch is tested by running the screen it touches, either in a unit test or in a tour (see the tests chapter).

docs.title: Version drift: why patches break
docs.text:
Patching internals ties you to the internals of that release. A concrete example from the two trees checked, FormController and ListController:

Method Odoo 18 Odoo 20 FormController.beforeLeave async beforeLeave() async beforeLeave({ forceLeave } = {}) ListController.openRecord async openRecord(record, force = false) async openRecord(record, { force, newWindow } = { force: false }) ListController.onDeleteSelectedRecords async onDeleteSelectedRecords() onDeleteSelectedRecords() (no longer async)

A patch of openRecord that does super.openRecord(record, true) works on 18 and silently passes the wrong argument shape on 20, where the second parameter is an options object. Patches that forward ...arguments are tolerant to such changes; patches that rebuild the argument list are not.

Defensive habits:

  • Forward ...arguments unless you must change an argument.
  • Do not rely on private names (_foo, onXInternal) or on the order of calls inside a method.
  • After every upgrade, grep your patch( calls and diff the target methods against the new branch. The migration chapter has a checklist.
  • Keep a short comment per patch: target, why, version. It saves an afternoon later.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Patching runs when its module loads. The module must be in a bundle that loads the patched module first, and it must import the target; the import is what guarantees order.

  • Patching an arrow-function property. Fields assigned in the constructor or in setup (this.handler = () => {...}) live on the instance, so a prototype patch does not see them. Patch the method that creates them, or the code that calls them.
  • A method captured by bind at setup time. Already-bound copies keep the old function for components created before the patch loaded; for new ones it is fine.
  • Forgetting super in setup. The base hooks never register. The screen renders empty or throws on first use.
  • Not returning the value of super. Callers waiting on a result get undefined.
  • Two modules patching the same method, one omitting super. Order-dependent bugs that appear only when both modules are installed.
  • A patch for everyone. Without a model or view guard it changes unrelated screens.
  • Patching a static props with the array form. Core components in 18 use the object form.
  • Patch name argument from 16. patch(obj, "name", {...}) throws in 17 and later. See Versions.
  • this._super(...) from 16. There is no _super in 17 and later: use super.
  • Patching to avoid registering an entry. If the target is looked up in a registry, register a subclass.
  • Patching what you can configure. Many behaviours are controlled by a context key, an arch attribute (options, class, js_class) or a field option. Look before you patch.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
16: the signature is patch(obj, patchName, patchValue, options). The name must be a string and must be unique for that object, otherwise it throws. Calling the original is done with this._super(...), because the patch is not an object with a prototype chain.

17 and 18: patch(objToPatch, extension). Passing a string as the second argument throws Patch "<name>": Second argument is not the patch name anymore, it should be the object containing the patched properties. Call the original with super.method(...).

20: same patch implementation and semantics. Patch targets themselves moved: signatures differ (table above), and components use props = useProps(...) instead of static props, so patching a component's props schema has to follow the OWL 3 form described in the previous chapter.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Patch FormController.prototype.setup to console.log("form", this.props.resModel), reload with ?debug=assets, open a form, and confirm the log. Remove the patch afterwards.
  2. Patch onWillSaveRecord so a library.loan cannot be saved without a book. Confirm other models still save.
  3. Add a second patch in another file that also overrides onWillSaveRecord but forgets super. Install both and see which behaviour wins and why.
  4. Extend the web.FormStatusIndicator template with a hint after the buttons, using hasclass.
Solution notes
  1. The log shows the model for every form you open, which also shows how global the patch is. Delete the file or keep the unpatch function in a variable if you want to remove it at runtime.
  2. The model guard (record.resModel === "library.loan") keeps other models unaffected, and returning false from onWillSaveRecord cancels the save.
  3. The patch that loads last wins when it does not call super: the earlier patch and the original are never reached. Load order follows manifest and module dependency order, which is why a forgotten super makes behaviour depend on which modules are installed.
  4. The xpath //div[hasclass('o_form_status_indicator_buttons')] with position="after" inserts the span right after the buttons container. If the class were renamed in a later version, template compilation would fail loudly.

docs.title: Registries and services
docs.text:
A registry is an ordered key-value store, and nearly every extension point of the web client is one. A service is a long-lived singleton started with the client, registered in the services registry. Together they are the reason you can add a field widget, a view, a menu entry or a global behaviour without touching Odoo's files.

Odoo 20 is mid-way through replacing services with OWL 3 plugins. The service API described here still works there through a bridge; the last section says what changed.

docs.title: The registry API
docs.text:
import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";

const systray = registry.category("systray");

systray.add("library.counter", { Component: LoanCounter }, { sequence: 25 });
systray.get("library.counter");            // the value, or throws KeyNotFoundError
systray.get("library.counter", null);      // default instead of throwing
systray.contains("library.counter");       // boolean
systray.getAll();                          // values, ordered by sequence
systray.getEntries();                      // [key, value] pairs, ordered by sequence
systray.remove("library.counter");

Behaviour that matters, from addons/web/static/src/core/registry.js:

  • add(key, value, { force, sequence }) returns the registry, so calls chain. If the key already exists and force is not true it throws Cannot add "key" in this registry: it already exists. With force: true it replaces the value.
  • The default sequence is 50. When you replace with force and give no sequence, the previous sequence is kept.
  • getAll() and getEntries() sort by sequence (ascending). Equal sequences keep insertion order, which is module load order.
  • get(key) without a second argument throws if missing; with a second argument (even undefined) it returns that instead.
  • category("a") creates the sub-registry on first use, and registry.category("a").category("b") nests. Categories are plain strings with no declared list, so a typo creates a new, empty category and your entry is never read. Copy names from existing code.
  • A registry is an event bus. Adding or removing triggers an UPDATE event with { operation, key, value }, which the service starter listens to. You can too, with addEventListener("UPDATE", ...).
  • addValidation(schema) installs a schema for entries (in 18 an OWL 2 validate schema, checked in debug mode). Odoo uses it for services so that a malformed service fails with a message naming the key.

Register at module top level, never inside setup() or a function that can run twice. Registration is idempotent only if the key is unique; the second run throws.

docs.title: Keys and sequences
docs.text:
Key naming, because keys are global across all installed modules:

  • Prefix with your module: library.counter, library.book_search. Core keys have no prefix and are short (many2one, list, orm), which is exactly why yours must not look like them.
  • Do not overwrite another module's key with force. You may hide their entry and break the module. Register your own key and subclass the original (see the patching chapter for when replacement is justified).
  • Use sequence to place yourself relative to others: lower comes first. Systray items from the core use 0, 1, 10 and so on (burger_menu is 0, SwitchCompanyMenu is 1).

docs.title: The categories and the shape of their entries
docs.text:
Registries do not validate the shape of an entry unless a schema is installed. The shape is whatever the code that reads the registry expects. The most useful categories in 18, with the shapes verified in the source:

Category Entry Read by systray { Component, props? } the navbar main_components { Component, props? } MainComponentsContainer, mounted once for the session actions an OWL component class, or a function (env, action) => ... the action service, for ir.actions.client with a matching tag views a view definition object (type, Controller, Renderer, Model, ArchParser, ...) the view service fields a field definition { component, supportedTypes, ... } views view_widgets { component, ... } <widget name="..."/> in view arch user_menuitems a function (env) => item the user menu error_handlers a function (env, error, originalError) => boolean the error service error_dialogs a dialog component keyed by Python exception name RPC error handler error_notifications { title?, message?, type?, sticky? } keyed by exception name RPC error handler command_provider provider object for the command palette command service debug functions that add items to the developer menu debug menu lazy_components component classes, loaded after their bundle LazyComponent public_components components mounted on website pages public root

Examples of the less obvious ones.

A user menu entry. Note it is a function that receives the environment and returns the item:

import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";

function libraryHelpItem(env) {
    return {
        type: "item",
        id: "library_help",
        description: "Library handbook",
        callback: () => window.open("https://example.com/library-handbook", "_blank"),
        sequence: 35,
    };
}
registry.category("user_menuitems").add("library_help", libraryHelpItem);

A mapping from a Python exception to a friendly notification. The error handler looks at the exceptionName of the server error, which is the dotted Python class name:

# library/models/library_loan.py
class LoanLimitError(UserError):
    pass

registry.category("error_notifications").add("odoo.addons.library.models.library_loan.LoanLimitError", {
    title: "Loan limit reached",
    type: "warning",
    sticky: false,
});

If the server error has an exceptionName found in error_notifications, the client shows a notification instead of the error dialog, using notif.message or the server message. If it is found in error_dialogs, that dialog component is used. For ordinary UserError messages you do not need this, the default dialog already shows them.

An error handler of your own, for a client-side failure. Return true if you handled it, false to let the next handler try:

registry.category("error_handlers").add("library.quietAbort", (env, error, originalError) => {
    if (originalError?.name === "AbortError") {
        return true;       // swallow: no dialog
    }
    return false;
}, { sequence: 5 });

docs.title: Writing a service
docs.text:
A service is a plain object with a start function and optional dependencies and async:

import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";

export const bookService = {
    dependencies: ["orm", "notification"],
    async: ["titleOf"],
    start(env, { orm, notification }) {
        const cache = new Map();

        async function titleOf(id) {
            if (!cache.has(id)) {
                const [rec] = await orm.read("library.book", [id], ["name"]);
                cache.set(id, rec.name);
            }
            return cache.get(id);
        }

        function forget(id) {
            cache.delete(id);
        }

        return { titleOf, forget };
    },
};

registry.category("services").add("library.book", bookService);

Use it in a component with useService("library.book"), or outside components through env.services["library.book"].

How the starter works (addons/web/static/src/env.js, startServices):

  • It collects every entry of the services registry that is not started yet, then repeatedly starts those whose dependencies are all started. Services without dependencies start first and everything else follows in dependency order.
  • A dependency name that is not registered (typo, module not installed) means the service never starts. The starter throws Some services could not be started: <names>. Missing dependencies: <names> and the web client does not come up. Read the console first.
  • start(env, deps) may return a promise. The client waits for it before starting dependants and before mounting. A slow start delays the entire web client: no network calls in start unless they are essential.
  • The value returned by start becomes env.services[name]. If you return nothing, the stored value is null.
  • A service registered after startup is started on the UPDATE event once its dependencies exist, so lazy modules can add services.
  • You cannot unregister: remove on the services registry is ignored by the starter.

docs.title: What async really does
docs.text:
The async list names methods that return promises and might outlive the component that called them. useService wraps only the listed methods:

const service = useService("library.book");
await service.titleOf(3);          // listed in async: protected
service.forget(3);                 // not listed: called as is

A protected call checks the component state. If the component is destroyed by the time the promise resolves, the returned promise never settles, so the code after await simply does not run. This stops a closed dialog from updating a component that no longer exists, and the price is that you must not rely on finally blocks for cleanup in components. If the component is already destroyed when you call, the call is not made.

Rules of thumb:

  • List every method that returns a promise.
  • A service method that must run to completion regardless of the caller (saving data) should not rely on the component calling it surviving. Use it from the service itself, or call env.services[name] directly rather than useService.
  • Methods not listed are never wrapped, so an unlisted async method does not get the destruction protection.

docs.title: State in services
docs.text:
A service is a singleton shared by every component. Keep per-component state in the component. Use a service for things that outlive a screen: a cache, a connection, a counter other components subscribe to.

To let components react to service changes, use a reactive object or an EventBus:

import { EventBus, reactive } from "@odoo/owl";

start(env) {
    const state = reactive({ unread: 0 });
    const bus = new EventBus();
    return {
        state,
        bus,
        bump() { state.unread++; bus.trigger("CHANGED"); },
    };
}

// component
this.stats = useState(useService("library.stats").state);   // re-render on change
useBus(useService("library.stats").bus, "CHANGED", () => this.refresh());

useBus(bus, eventName, callback) removes the listener when the component is destroyed.

docs.title: The built-in services you will use
orm
docs.text:
Calls model methods over RPC. All methods return promises and are async-protected. Signatures from orm_service.js (18):

const orm = useService("orm");

await orm.call("library.book", "action_archive", [[id]]);            // call(model, method, args, kwargs)
await orm.create("library.book", [{ name: "Dune" }]);                // returns the new ids
await orm.read("library.book", [id], ["name", "isbn"]);              // read(model, ids, fields)
await orm.search("library.book", [["state", "=", "available"]], { limit: 5 });  // ids
await orm.searchRead("library.book", domain, ["name"], { limit: 20, order: "name" });
await orm.searchCount("library.book", domain);
await orm.write("library.book", [id], { name: "Dune (2nd ed.)" });
await orm.unlink("library.book", [id]);
await orm.readGroup("library.book", domain, ["pages:sum"], ["author_id"]);
await orm.webSearchRead("library.book", domain, { specification: { name: {} }, limit: 20 });
await orm.webSave("library.book", [id], { name: "x" }, { specification: { name: {} } });
  • Contexts are added for you from the user's context. Pass { context: {...} } in kwargs to extend.
  • orm.silent.read(...) makes the same call without triggering the global error dialog; use it for background refreshes where you handle errors yourself.
  • x2ManyCommands in the same file builds one2many and many2many command tuples (create, update, delete, unlink, link, clear, set) for write and create values.
  • Record rules and access rights apply to the calling user, as always. The ORM service cannot do sudo.

Prefer one call that returns what the screen needs over several small ones. A controller route (below) returning prepared data is often better than three searchRead calls.

docs.title: rpc
docs.text:
For your own controllers, import the function:

import { rpc } from "@web/core/network/rpc";

const data = await rpc("/library/dashboard", { limit: 10 });

It posts JSON to the route and returns the parsed result. A server-side exception arrives as a rejected promise with an RPCError that carries data.message, data.name and exceptionName; connection loss gives ConnectionLostError. Use the orm service when you are calling model methods, and rpc for routes.

In 18, rpc is a module function and not a service (in 16 and 17 it is a service, useService("rpc"), which you will still see in older code).

docs.title: action
docs.text:
const action = useService("action");

await action.doAction("library.action_loan");                 // xml id
await action.doAction(42);                                     // database id
await action.doAction({                                        // action dictionary
    type: "ir.actions.act_window",
    res_model: "library.loan",
    views: [[false, "list"], [false, "form"]],
    domain: [["state", "=", "open"]],
    context: { search_default_overdue: 1 },
    name: "Open loans",
});

Options (ActionOptions in the source): additionalContext, clearBreadcrumbs, onClose (callback when the action closes, for dialogs), props (extra props for client actions), viewType, stackPosition ("replaceCurrentAction" or "replacePreviousAction"), index. A target: "new" in the action opens it as a dialog. { type: "ir.actions.act_window_close" } closes the current dialog.
