Other methods: switchView(viewType, props), restore(jsId) for breadcrumbs, and doActionButton(params) which handles <button type="action">.

docs.title: notification
docs.text:
const notification = useService("notification");
const close = notification.add("Book returned", { type: "success" });
notification.add("Could not reach the server", {
    title: "Warning",
    type: "danger",
    sticky: true,
    autocloseDelay: 8000,
    buttons: [{ name: "Retry", primary: true, onClick: () => this.retry() }],
});

Types are warning (default), danger, success, info. A non-sticky notification closes after autocloseDelay (default 4000 ms). add returns a function that closes it.

docs.title: dialog
docs.text:
import { ConfirmationDialog } from "@web/core/confirmation_dialog/confirmation_dialog";

const dialog = useService("dialog");
dialog.add(ConfirmationDialog, {
    title: "Return all books?",
    body: "This cannot be undone.",
    confirm: () => this.returnAll(),
    cancel: () => {},
});

dialog.add(Component, props, options) mounts the component in a dialog and returns a function that closes it. The component receives a close prop it can call. Dialogs opened this way share the lifetime of the dialog stack, not of the opening component. For a dialog tied to a component, use the useOwnedDialogs hook from @web/core/utils/hooks, which closes them when the component is destroyed.

docs.title: user
docs.text:
In 18, user is a module export, not a registry service:

import { user } from "@web/core/user";

user.userId;            // numeric id
user.name;
user.isAdmin;           // boolean
user.isInternalUser;    // boolean
user.partnerId;
user.lang;              // JS locale, e.g. "en-US"
user.tz;
user.context;           // copy of the user context, with uid
await user.hasGroup("library.group_librarian");
await user.checkAccessRight("library.book", "write", [id]);

hasGroup and checkAccessRight call the server once per distinct argument and cache the answer. checkAccessRight(model, operation, ids) takes an operation such as "read" or "write" and calls has_access on the model. Hiding a button for users without a group is a convenience; the server must still enforce it.

In 16 and 17 user is a service (useService("user")) backed by session and user_context. The property names also differ (for example the id is userId here, uid in session).

docs.title: Others
docs.text:
• ui: ui.block() and ui.unblock() to freeze the screen during a long call, ui.isSmall for mobile layouts, ui.bus for resize events.
  • hotkey: hotkey.add("alt+shift+l", callback, options) returns a remove function. In components prefer the useHotkey hook in @web/core/hotkeys/hotkey_hook.
  • title, menu, command, effect (rainbow man), popover, field, name (display names for many2one values), http, localization, company, currency, view. When in doubt, read the file named <service>_service.js in addons/web/static/src/core or webclient. Each is short.

docs.title: Putting it together: a service, a component and a client action
docs.text:
A "recent books" service that caches the last five opened books, plus a systray dropdown that shows them.

/** @odoo-module **/
import { Component, useState } from "@odoo/owl";
import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";
import { useService } from "@web/core/utils/hooks";
import { reactive } from "@odoo/owl";

export const recentBooksService = {
    dependencies: ["orm"],
    async: ["touch"],
    start(env, { orm }) {
        const state = reactive({ ids: [], names: {} });
        return {
            state,
            async touch(id) {
                if (!(id in state.names)) {
                    const [rec] = await orm.read("library.book", [id], ["name"]);
                    state.names[id] = rec.name;
                }
                state.ids = [id, ...state.ids.filter((i) => i !== id)].slice(0, 5);
            },
        };
    },
};
registry.category("services").add("library.recent_books", recentBooksService);

export class RecentBooks extends Component {
    static template = "library.RecentBooks";
    static props = {};
    setup() {
        this.recent = useState(useService("library.recent_books").state);
        this.action = useService("action");
    }
    open(id) {
        this.action.doAction({
            type: "ir.actions.act_window", res_model: "library.book",
            res_id: id, views: [[false, "form"]],
        });
    }
}
registry.category("systray").add("library.RecentBooks", { Component: RecentBooks }, { sequence: 30 });

<t t-name="library.RecentBooks">
  <div class="o_nav_entry">
    <span t-foreach="recent.ids" t-as="id" t-key="id" class="me-2">
      <a href="#" t-on-click.prevent="() => this.open(id)" t-out="recent.names[id]"/>
    </span>
  </div>
</t>

Anything that opens a book calls useService("library.recent_books").touch(id), and every systray instance updates because they read the same reactive state.

docs.title: Odoo 20: services and plugins
docs.text:
In the Odoo 20 source the web client moves services to OWL 3 plugins, but keeps the registry as a bridge. Verified in the tree available at the time of writing:

  • registry.category("services") still exists. Its validation schema is now written with OWL 3 types, but still expects { start, dependencies?, async? }. The file core/legacy_service_starter.js is marked "temporary - to remove when all service are converted".
  • Global plugins register through services.add(PluginClass) from @web/core/services, where services is an OWL Resource accepting Plugin subclasses.
  • The ORM is now class ORM extends Plugin in core/orm_plugin.js, and useService("orm") keeps working through a registry entry that returns usePlugin(ORM). A comment in the source says that entry is temporary.
  • useService still exists, and in 20 returns a proxy of the service when it is not already reactive.
  • Hook argument names differ in places (useAutofocus({ ref }), useBus(target, type, listener)). Check the signature before copying a 18 call.

So: service code you write for 18 keeps working on 20 for now, but the documented direction is plugins, and the next major version may drop the bridge. The OWL 3 chapter shows the plugin form.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• A dependency on a service that does not exist. Startup stops with a message naming it. Check spelling and that the providing module is in your depends.
  • Per-screen state in a service. It is a singleton and every component sees it.
  • A slow or failing start. The whole client waits for it; avoid network calls, or guard them.
  • registry.add on an existing key without force. Throws on load, and the module (and everything depending on it) never starts.
  • force: true on a core key to "replace" behaviour. You remove the original for everyone; subclass and register under your own key where the consumer allows it.
  • Wrong category name. No error, no effect.
  • Forgetting async. Calls from a destroyed component are not blocked, and their results land on dead state.
  • Relying on finally after a protected call. If the component is destroyed the promise never resolves and the block never runs.
  • Treating hasGroup as security. It hides UI; the server enforces access.
  • Importing rpc as a service on 18. It is a function: import { rpc } from "@web/core/network/rpc".
  • Copying useService("user") from 16. In 18 import user from @web/core/user.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
16: legacy and OWL registries coexist. rpc_service.js and user_service.js exist, so useService("rpc") and useService("user") work. Services and the registry API are otherwise as described.

17: the legacy layer is gone from the backend. rpc is still a service (core/network/rpc_service.js exists in 17.0) and so is user (core/user_service.js).

18: rpc is imported from @web/core/network/rpc and user from @web/core/user. The service list of this chapter is the 18 list.

20: services are being replaced by plugins. useService and the services registry keep working through a bridge.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. In the console, list services: odoo.loader.modules.get("@web/core/registry").registry.category("services").getEntries().map(([k]) => k).
  2. Add the library.recent_books service and the systray component above. Open two books and watch the systray update.
  3. Rename the dependency "orm" to "ormm" and read the startup error.
  4. In the systray component, call useService("library.recent_books") without listing touch in async, open a dialog that calls it, close the dialog quickly, and compare with the async version.
Solution notes
  1. The list contains orm, action, dialog, notification, hotkey, ui and the rest of the 18 services; user is absent because it is a module.
  2. Both items read the same reactive state, so they re-render together.
  3. The client fails to start, with Some services could not be started: library.book. Missing dependencies: ormm in the console.
  4. With async: ["touch"] the call from a destroyed component never resolves, so there is no write to dead state. Without the entry the promise resolves normally and code after await runs, even though the component is gone.

docs.title: Tours and frontend tests
docs.text:
Frontend code fails in ways Python tests never see: a bundle that does not load, a selector that matches nothing, a widget that works in forms and crashes in lists. Two kinds of test cover this. A tour drives a real headless browser through a scenario against a real database. A hoot unit test mounts a component or a view against a mocked server in milliseconds.

Verified against the Odoo 18 source (addons/web_tour, addons/web/static/tests, addons/web/tests/test_js.py, odoo/tests/common.py).

docs.title: Which test for which question
docs.text:
Question Tool Does the whole flow work through the real UI, server and database? tour Does my component render and react correctly in isolation? hoot unit test Does a field widget work in a form, a list, in readonly and edit mode? hoot view test with mountView Is my pure JavaScript logic right (an ISBN check digit)? hoot unit test without any mount Is the server rule enforced regardless of the UI? Python test, not a JavaScript one

Prefer many small unit tests and a handful of tours for the critical paths. Tours are slow (they start a browser and a server) and the first thing to become flaky.

docs.title: Anatomy
docs.text:
A tour is an entry in the web_tour.tours registry: a name, a starting URL, and a function returning the steps. Put it in the web.assets_tests bundle so it is only loaded when tests run.

/** @odoo-module **/
import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";
import { stepUtils } from "@web_tour/tour_service/tour_utils";

registry.category("web_tour.tours").add("library_loan_tour", {
    url: "/odoo",
    steps: () => [
        ...stepUtils.goToAppSteps("library.menu_root", "Open the Library app"),
        {
            content: "Create a loan",
            trigger: ".o_list_button_add",
            run: "click",
        },
        {
            content: "Pick a book",
            trigger: ".o_field_widget[name=book_id] input",
            run: "edit Dune",
        },
        {
            content: "Choose it in the dropdown",
            trigger: ".o-autocomplete--dropdown-item > a:contains('Dune')",
            run: "click",
        },
        {
            content: "Save",
            trigger: ".o_form_button_save",
            run: "click",
        },
        {
            content: "The loan is saved and open",
            trigger: ".o_field_widget[name=state]:contains('Open')",
        },
    ],
});

Registry validation in tour_service.js defines the shape: a tour has steps (a function), and optionally name, url and wait_for. A step has trigger (mandatory string) and optional content, run, isActive, timeout, tooltipPosition, expectUnloadPage, id, debugHelp, and in debug mode pause and break.

docs.title: How a step runs
docs.text:
For each step the engine:

  1. waits until trigger matches a visible, enabled element (default timeout 10000 ms; the schema accepts 0 to 60000 through timeout). It re-checks on DOM mutations;
  2. then performs run on that element;
  3. moves to the next step.

A step without run only waits for the trigger: it is an assertion that the element exists. In the 18 source an action is performed only when run is a string or a function. Do not write run: "click" on assertion steps, and do not omit it on steps that must click.

Triggers are CSS selectors extended by the hoot query engine, so you can use :contains(text), :visible, :hidden, :has(...), :not(:has(...)) and :iframe among others. A selector ending in :hidden or :visible overrides the default "must be visible".

docs.title: The run vocabulary
docs.text:
run is a string, a chain joined with &&, or a function.

String Effect click click the element dblclick double click edit text focus and type text (replaces content) fill text set the value of an input and fire events clear empty the input check, uncheck toggle a checkbox select value, selectByIndex n, selectByLabel text choose in a <select> press Enter key press hover hover range n set a range input editor text type into an HTML editor goToUrl /path navigate

Examples: run: "edit 42", run: "click && edit hello". The engine splits on && and parses each part as action argument. A function receives the helpers object and runs with this.anchor bound to the element:

{
    trigger: ".o_field_widget[name=due_date] input",
    run: function (helpers) {
        helpers.edit("2030-01-01");
    },
},

The helper methods are check, clear, click, dblclick, edit, editor, fill, hover, range, press, select, selectByIndex, selectByLabel, uncheck and goToUrl, as defined in tour_helpers.js.

docs.title: Reusable steps
docs.text:
@web_tour/tour_service/tour_utils exports stepUtils with ready-made steps: goToAppSteps(menuXmlid, description) opens an app from the home menu, saveForm() and discardForm(), statusbarButtonsSteps(text, description, trigger), autoExpandMoreButtons(), waitIframeIsReady(), goToUrl(url). Use them. They handle the community and enterprise differences (isActive: ["community"] and ["enterprise"]) that you would otherwise copy wrongly.

Make your own helpers the same way, as functions returning arrays of steps, and spread them:

function createLoan(bookName) {
    return [
        { trigger: ".o_list_button_add", run: "click" },
        { trigger: ".o_field_widget[name=book_id] input", run: `edit ${bookName}` },
        { trigger: `.o-autocomplete--dropdown-item > a:contains('${bookName}')`, run: "click" },
        stepUtils.saveForm(),
    ];
}

docs.title: Conditional steps
docs.text:
isActive skips a step when its condition is false. It accepts keywords ("community", "enterprise", "mobile", "desktop") and arrays of selectors that must all match. A skipped step is simply passed over:

{
    isActive: [".o_dialog .modal-footer"],
    trigger: ".modal-footer .btn-primary",
    run: "click",
},

Use it for optional UI (a confirmation dialog that appears only sometimes) instead of sleeps.

docs.title: Writing robust triggers
docs.text:
• Anchor on stable hooks: name="..." attributes (.o_field_widget[name=book_id]), data-menu-xmlid, data-hotkey, t-ref-based class names you control. Avoid positional selectors (:nth-child) and text that is translated.
  • Make steps wait for the result of the previous action. After saving, add a step that waits for something that appears only once the save completed. Never rely on time.
  • One action per step, with a content that says what and why. It becomes the failure message and, in manual mode, the tooltip.
  • Tours run with demo or test data of your module. Create what the tour needs in setUp of the Python test or in the tour's initial steps, never rely on whatever exists in the database.

docs.title: Running a tour from Python
docs.text:
The tour is launched by a Python HttpCase:

# library/tests/test_tours.py
from odoo.tests import HttpCase, tagged


@tagged("post_install", "-at_install")
class TestLibraryTours(HttpCase):

    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        super().setUpClass()
        cls.env["library.book"].create({"name": "Dune", "isbn": "9780306406157"})

    def test_loan_tour(self):
        self.start_tour("/odoo", "library_loan_tour", login="admin")

start_tour(url_path, tour_name, step_delay=None, **kwargs) is implemented in odoo/tests/common.py: it builds odoo.startTour(tour_name, options), waits for odoo.isTourReady(tour_name), and runs browser_js with the success signal tour succeeded and a default timeout of 60 seconds. Useful keyword arguments:

Argument Meaning login="admin" authenticate as that user before loading the page step_delay=500 milliseconds between steps, for watching watch=True show the browser window (needs a local Chrome, not headless) debug=True open the browser debugger timeout=120 override the 60 s limit for long tours

Tags matter:

  • post_install runs the test after all modules are installed, so the web client with all its bundles exists. -at_install prevents it from also running right after your module installs, when the full UI is not ready.
  • Select the tour from the command line with a test tag:
./odoo-bin -d test_library -i library --test-enable --test-tags /library:TestLibraryTours --stop-after-init

Tag syntax is [-][tag][/module][:class][.method], so /library:TestLibraryTours.test_loan_tour selects one test. The -i/-u run needs a database where demo data exists if your tour uses it; create the data in the test itself to avoid the dependency.

docs.title: Debugging a failing tour
docs.text:
1. Read the failure message: it names the step content and the trigger that was never found, and prints the DOM at that point.
  2. Reproduce interactively. Log in, open the starting URL with ?debug=tests (it adds the test bundle) and start the tour from the console with odoo.startTour("library_loan_tour", { mode: "manual" }), (the tests debug mode makes the web.assets_tests bundle load: the bootstrap template checks 'tests' in debug). In manual mode the tour shows a pointer and tooltips and waits for you to do each step.
  3. Run with watch=True, step_delay=500 locally to see it happen.
  4. Check whether the selector matches at all in the browser console: document.querySelector(".o_field_widget[name=book_id] input").
  5. If a step passes locally and fails in CI, the cause is usually timing (the previous action had not finished) or data (the record does not exist). Add a waiting step, create the data in setUp.

The engine also has a check for non-deterministic steps, enabled with the environment variable ODOO_TOUR_DELAY_TO_CHECK_UNDETERMINISMS (seconds). With it set above zero, start_tour adds that many seconds to the timeout and runs the tour in a mode that checks for non-deterministic steps (the web_tour tests include check_undeterminisms.test.js). Use it on tours that fail intermittently.

docs.title: Tours for the website and portal
docs.text:
The same registry is used on public pages. The bundle is the same (web.assets_tests), the URL is a public or portal path, and the test passes the login:

self.start_tour("/my/loans", "library_portal_tour", login="portal_user")

registry.category("web_tour.tours").add("library_portal_tour", {
    url: "/my/loans",
    steps: () => [
        { trigger: "a:contains('Dune')", run: "click" },
        { trigger: ".o_library_extend", run: "click" },
        { trigger: "p:contains('Due on')" },
    ],
});

docs.title: Hoot unit tests
docs.text: Hoot is Odoo's own test framework for JavaScript, living in addons/web/static/lib/hoot and hoot-dom. Tests are files ending in .test.js; each declares test("name", async () => {...}) and uses expect from @odoo/hoot. They run in a browser against a mock server, so no database is needed.

docs.title: Where files go and how they are picked up
docs.text:
The runner bundle is web.assets_unit_tests. It includes the framework (web.assets_unit_tests_setup, which itself includes web.assets_backend and web.assets_backend_lazy, so your module's production code is already loaded) and then the test files you list:

"assets": {
    "web.assets_backend": [
        "library/static/src/**/*",
        ("remove", "library/static/src/**/*.test.js"),
    ],
    "web.assets_unit_tests": [
        "library/static/src/**/*.test.js",
        "library/static/tests/**/*.test.js",
    ],
},

The remove line is important if tests live under static/src: without it they ship in the production bundle. The core addons keep tests in static/tests and list them in web.assets_unit_tests, as mail and web_tour do.

docs.title: Running them
docs.text:
In the browser: open /web/tests on a running server (you need to be logged in). The page lists suites and runs them. Add ?debug=assets to read the source, filter with the search box or ?id=<hash> URLs, and use ?headless to run without the UI. From the command line the Python class WebSuite.test_unit_desktop in addons/web/tests/test_js.py opens /web/tests?headless&loglevel=2&preset=desktop... in headless Chrome and waits for [HOOT] Test suite succeeded:

./odoo-bin -d test_library -i web,library --test-enable --test-tags /web:WebSuite.test_unit_desktop --stop-after-init

That runs every unit test of every installed module. Use the browser while developing; use the command line in CI.

docs.title: A pure-logic test
docs.text:
The ISBN functions of the widgets chapter, tested with no DOM. library/static/tests/isbn.test.js:

import { describe, expect, test } from "@odoo/hoot";
import { formatIsbn, isValidIsbn, normalizeIsbn } from "@library/fields/isbn";

describe("isbn helpers", () => {
    test("accepts valid ISBN-13 and ISBN-10", () => {
        expect(isValidIsbn("9780306406157")).toBe(true);
        expect(isValidIsbn("0-306-40615-2")).toBe(true);
        expect(isValidIsbn("080442957X")).toBe(true);
    });

    test("rejects wrong check digits and garbage", () => {
        expect(isValidIsbn("9780306406158")).toBe(false);
        expect(isValidIsbn("0306406153")).toBe(false);
        expect(isValidIsbn("abc")).toBe(false);
        expect(isValidIsbn("")).toBe(false);
    });

    test("normalises and formats", () => {
        expect(normalizeIsbn(" 978-0-306 40615-7 ")).toBe("9780306406157");
        expect(formatIsbn("9780306406157")).toBe("978-0-30640-615-7");
    });
});

The module path @library/fields/isbn follows the rule from the overview chapter: @addon/path under static/src, without extension. The same assertions were run in plain Node against the function bodies while writing this book, with the results noted in the widgets chapter.

docs.title: A field view test
docs.text:
This mirrors how the core tests its own widgets (views/fields/char_field.test.js): declare a model class for the mock server, register it, mount a view, interact, assert.

import { expect, test } from "@odoo/hoot";
import {
    clickSave,
    defineModels,
    fields,
    fieldInput,
    models,
    mountView,
} from "@web/../tests/web_test_helpers";

class LibraryBook extends models.Model {
    _name = "library.book";

    name = fields.Char();
    isbn = fields.Char();

    _records = [{ id: 1, name: "Dune", isbn: "9780306406157" }];
    _views = {
        form: /* xml */ `
            <form>
                <field name="name"/>
                <field name="isbn" widget="library_isbn"/>
            </form>
        `,
    };
}

defineModels([LibraryBook]);

test("isbn widget shows the formatted value", async () => {
    await mountView({ type: "form", resModel: "library.book", resId: 1 });
    expect(".o_field_widget[name=isbn] input").toHaveValue("978-0-30640-615-7");
});

test("an invalid ISBN marks the field invalid", async () => {
    await mountView({ type: "form", resModel: "library.book", resId: 1 });
    await fieldInput("isbn").edit("9780306406158");
    expect(".o_field_widget[name=isbn]").toHaveClass("o_field_invalid");
});

test("a valid ISBN is stored without hyphens", async () => {
    await mountView({ type: "form", resModel: "library.book", resId: 1 });
    await fieldInput("isbn").edit("0-306-40615-2");
    await clickSave();
    expect(LibraryBook._records[0].isbn).toBe("0306406152");
});

What the helpers do, from web_test_helpers.js and _framework:

  • models.Model plus fields.* declare a model the mock server serves. _records are the rows, _views the arch for each view type the test mounts.
  • defineModels([...]) registers the classes for the tests of the file (it uses before hooks, so call it at top level).
  • mountView({ type, resModel, resId?, arch? }) mounts a real view with the real controller, renderer and widgets against the mock server, and returns when it is ready.
  • fieldInput(name) gives access to the input of a field (.edit(value), .clear()), clickSave() clicks the save button, contains(selector) finds elements and offers actions, onRpc(route|method, handler) intercepts server calls, patchWithCleanup(obj, patch) applies a patch that is removed after the test.
  • expect(selector) returns assertions with DOM-aware matchers: toHaveCount, toHaveValue, toHaveText, toHaveClass, toHaveAttribute, toBeEnabled, and the usual toBe, toEqual.

The test file imports your widget module indirectly: web.assets_unit_tests_setup includes web.assets_backend, which lists your static/src/**/*, so library_isbn is registered when the test runs.

docs.title: Testing a component directly
docs.text:
For a component that is not a view, mount it with mountWithCleanup:

import { expect, test } from "@odoo/hoot";
import { click } from "@odoo/hoot-dom";
import { mountWithCleanup } from "@web/../tests/web_test_helpers";
import { LoanCounter } from "@library/systray/loan_counter";

test("shows the open loans count", async () => {
    await mountWithCleanup(LoanCounter);
    expect("button").toHaveText(/Loans:/);
});

Declare library.loan with defineModels and some _records before mounting a component that calls the ORM, since the mock server only knows the models you define. A component that calls a custom controller route needs onRpc("/library/dashboard", () => ({ ... })) registered first.

docs.title: Mocking and time
docs.text:
• onRpc handlers receive { args, kwargs, model, method, route } and return the response. The core uses the form onRpc("web_save", ({ args }) => { expect(args[1].name).toBe(false); }) to assert what the client sends.
  • Hoot controls time. Use its mocked clock helpers from @odoo/hoot-mock (animationFrame, runAllTimers, Deferred) instead of real setTimeout waits, so tests run instantly and deterministically.
  • Reset global state between tests with patchWithCleanup; avoid mutating registries or services directly. If you must register something, do it inside the test and rely on cleanup.

docs.title: Old QUnit tests
docs.text: Odoo 17 and the legacy folders of 18 contain QUnit tests (/web/tests/legacy, web.qunit_suite_tests). In 18 the QUnit suites are being ported to hoot, and the manifest comments say the legacy paths are to be removed "when all legacy tests are ported". Write new tests in hoot. If you maintain a 16 or 17 module, its tests are QUnit with QUnit.test and the legacy helpers; the shape differs, the ideas do not.

docs.title: Continuous integration checklist
docs.text:
1. Python tests, with post_install tours: ./odoo-bin -d ci -i library --test-enable --test-tags /library --stop-after-init.
  2. The web suite when you change shared code: --test-tags /web:WebSuite.test_unit_desktop (long) or /library hoot tests through your own tagged Python class.
  3. A tour must create its own data, must wait on results rather than time, and must pass three times in a row before you merge it.
  4. Fail the build on JavaScript console errors: the browser runner already treats an uncaught error as a failure, so do not silence it.
  5. Keep screenshots and logs. On failure the runner prints the console log and a DOM snapshot; keep those artefacts.

A Python class that runs only your module's hoot tests is a good idea. The core's HOOTCommon base class in addons/web/tests/test_js.py shows the pattern: tagged post_install, -at_install, calling browser_js on /web/tests?... with a filter and waiting for the [HOOT] Test suite succeeded log line.

docs.title: Odoo 20
docs.text:
The tour registry and start_tour carry over. Two cautions for 20:

  • The tours and tests use the same step and run vocabulary, but the component code under test changes (props with useProps, signal.ref(), this. in templates). Tests that mount your components do not change, selectors in tours rarely do. Tests that patch internals (patchWithCleanup(FormController.prototype, ...)) must follow the method signatures of 20.
  • Route type jsonrpc replaces json in controllers called by tours, and onRpc handlers still intercept by route or method.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Tours that depend on database contents you did not create are the most common cause of "works on my machine". Create what you need, in the test.

  • Sleeping. A fixed delay is either too short (flaky) or too long (slow). Wait for a trigger.
  • Triggers on translated text break when the test user's language changes. Prefer name, data-* and class hooks.
  • Missing post_install. The tour starts before the UI bundles exist and fails with obscure errors.
  • Test files in the production bundle. Add the remove entry and list them in web.assets_unit_tests.
  • Forgetting login=. The tour runs as an anonymous user and stops at the login page.
  • run: "click" on an assertion step. It clicks something you only meant to check.
  • Missing run on an action step. In 18 nothing happens: the step passes as soon as the element exists.
  • Duplicated tour names. The registry throws at load, and every later tour disappears.
  • Mounting a component without declaring the models it queries. The mock server raises an error; declare models and records.
  • Leaving only or debug calls in tests. The core has a check (test_check_suite) that fails the build when only() or debug() is left in a loaded test file.
  • Asserting right after an action without awaiting it. Hoot helpers are async; await them.
  • UI tests as the only protection for a business rule. Add a Python test for the rule too.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
16: tours live in the web_tour addon with an older step vocabulary, tests are QUnit. A tour or test written here needs rewriting for 17 and 18.

17: web_tour has the tour_service directory and steps use functional run: (actions) => ... forms; QUnit remains the main unit test runner. Check the vocabulary of your branch before copying 18 steps.

18: the engine and vocabulary of this chapter (run strings, isActive, stepUtils); hoot is the test framework for new unit tests, QUnit remains for legacy code. start_tour(url_path, tour_name, step_delay=None, **kwargs).

20: same tour API; route type="jsonrpc"; components under test use OWL 3 idioms.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Add the loan tour above, write the Python test, and run it with the --test-tags line. Make it fail on purpose by changing a trigger and read the message.
  2. Write the three ISBN hoot tests, run /web/tests in the browser and filter on isbn.
  3. Add the widget view tests. Watch the invalid class test fail if you remove the throw from parse.
  4. Run the tour with watch=True, step_delay=500 on a machine with Chrome.
Solution notes
  1. The failure message names the step's content and the trigger; with a wrong trigger the tour waits up to the step timeout (default 10 s) and then fails.
  2. The three tests appear under the @library module in the runner list and pass; the same assertions were run in Node on the function bodies.
  3. Without the throw, parse returns a value for the invalid ISBN, the field is not marked invalid, and the second test fails because o_field_invalid is absent.
  4. A visible Chrome window opens and each step runs 500 ms apart. If the tour starts but nothing is displayed, Chrome is not installed or headless mode is forced.

docs.title: Website and portal
docs.text:
The backend web client is not what visitors and portal users see. Their pages are rendered by a controller with QWeb, served with web.assets_frontend, and brought to life by a different set of JavaScript tools.

Everything was read from the Odoo 18 portal and web addons and the Odoo 20 tree. The teaching module library gives its members a page listing their loans.

docs.title: What runs where
docs.text:
Concern Odoo 17 and 18 Odoo 20 Page markup QWeb templates (portal.portal_layout, website.layout) same Page logic controller extending CustomerPortal same Behaviour on a page publicWidget.Widget subclasses registered in publicWidget.registry Interaction subclasses registered in public.interactions OWL on a public page <owl-component name="..."> plus public_components registry same element, mounted by an interaction JSON calls rpc from @web/core/network/rpc, route type="json" same rpc, route type="jsonrpc" Bundle web.assets_frontend web.assets_frontend

Public code has no env.services.orm guarantee for anonymous users and no web client. Anything it needs from the server goes through a controller route, which is where access control belongs.

docs.title: The portal in one page
docs.text:
The portal is the set of pages under /my that a logged-in portal user sees. CustomerPortal in addons/portal/controllers/portal.py is the controller to extend. Its relevant members in 18:

  • _prepare_home_portal_values(self, counters): returns the values for the home page cards. counters is the list of badges to compute; the base returns {}.
  • /my/counters (a JSON route) calls the same method for the lazily loaded badges, and caches the booleans in the session.
  • home() renders portal.portal_my_home.
  • _document_check_access(model_name, document_id, access_token=None): loads a record the user may see, either through normal access or through a valid access token. It returns the record sudoed and raises MissingError or AccessError.
  • _get_page_view_values(...): adds chatter and pager values for a detail page.
  • pager(url, total, page=1, step=30, scope=5, url_args=None): module-level function producing the dict for the pager template.

docs.title: Step 1: access rights first
docs.text:
Portal users are in base.group_portal. Without an access rule and a record rule they see nothing, and the page raises AccessError. Write the security before the page.

library/security/ir.model.access.csv (one line more):

access_library_loan_portal,library.loan portal,model_library_loan,base.group_portal,1,0,0,0

library/security/library_security.xml:

<record id="library_loan_rule_portal" model="ir.rule">
    <field name="name">Loan: portal users see their own</field>
    <field name="model_id" ref="model_library_loan"/>
    <field name="domain_force">[('member_id.partner_id', '=', user.partner_id.id)]</field>
    <field name="groups" eval="[(4, ref('base.group_portal'))]"/>
</record>

Read access only, and only the member's own loans. Everything the controller does with request.env then goes through this rule. Do not reach for sudo() to make the page work; fix the rule.

docs.title: Step 2: the controller
docs.text:
# library/controllers/portal.py
from odoo import http
from odoo.exceptions import AccessError, MissingError
from odoo.http import request

from odoo.addons.portal.controllers.portal import CustomerPortal, pager as portal_pager


class LibraryPortal(CustomerPortal):

    def _prepare_home_portal_values(self, counters):
        values = super()._prepare_home_portal_values(counters)
        if "loan_count" in counters:
            Loan = request.env["library.loan"]
            values["loan_count"] = (
                Loan.search_count([]) if Loan.has_access("read") else 0
            )
        return values

    @http.route(
        ["/my/loans", "/my/loans/page/<int:page>"],
        type="http", auth="user", website=True,
    )
    def portal_my_loans(self, page=1, **kw):
        Loan = request.env["library.loan"]
        total = Loan.search_count([])
        pager = portal_pager(
            url="/my/loans", total=total, page=page, step=self._items_per_page,
        )
        loans = Loan.search(
            [], order="due_date desc", limit=self._items_per_page, offset=pager["offset"],
        )
        values = self._prepare_portal_layout_values()
        values.update({
            "loans": loans,
            "page_name": "loans",
            "pager": pager,
            "default_url": "/my/loans",
        })
        return request.render("library.portal_my_loans", values)

    @http.route("/my/loans/<int:loan_id>", type="http", auth="user", website=True)
    def portal_my_loan(self, loan_id, access_token=None, **kw):
        try:
            loan_sudo = self._document_check_access("library.loan", loan_id, access_token)
        except (AccessError, MissingError):
            return request.redirect("/my")
        values = {"loan": loan_sudo, "page_name": "loan"}
        return request.render("library.portal_my_loan", values)

Points to check in this code:

  • Loan.search_count([]) is not unsafe: the record rule above narrows the result to the user's own loans, because the call runs as the portal user. That is why the controller uses the plain environment.
  • has_access("read") returns a boolean in 18. In 17 the equivalent is check_access_rights("read", raise_exception=False). Counting without the check would raise for users who lack the ACL.
  • _items_per_page is an attribute of CustomerPortal (80 in the 18 source); use it so your page matches the others, or define your own step.
  • portal_pager(...) returns a dict with an offset key, ready for search(offset=...).
  • _document_check_access returns the record sudoed, so everything you render from loan_sudo bypasses record rules after the check. Render only fields you mean to show, and never pass loan_sudo to code that writes.
  • auth="user" redirects anonymous visitors to the login page. Do not use auth="public" for private data.

Register the file in controllers/__init__.py (from . import portal) and in library/__init__.py (from . import controllers).

docs.title: Step 3: the templates
docs.text:
<odoo>
    <!-- 1. A card on /my -->
    <template id="portal_my_home_library" name="Library: loans card"
              inherit_id="portal.portal_my_home" customize_show="True" priority="30">
        <xpath expr="//div[hasclass('o_portal_docs')]" position="inside">
            <t t-call="portal.portal_docs_entry">
                <t t-set="title">Loans</t>
                <t t-set="url" t-value="'/my/loans'"/>
                <t t-set="text">Books you have borrowed</t>
                <t t-set="placeholder_count" t-value="'loan_count'"/>
            </t>
        </xpath>
    </template>

    <!-- 2. Breadcrumb entries -->
    <template id="portal_breadcrumbs_library" name="Library: breadcrumbs"
              inherit_id="portal.portal_breadcrumbs">
        <xpath expr="//ol[hasclass('o_portal_submenu')]" position="inside">
            <li t-if="page_name == 'loans'" class="breadcrumb-item active">Loans</li>
            <li t-if="page_name == 'loan'" class="breadcrumb-item">
                <a href="/my/loans">Loans</a>
            </li>
            <li t-if="page_name == 'loan'" class="breadcrumb-item active">
                <t t-out="loan.display_name"/>
            </li>
        </xpath>
    </template>

    <!-- 3. The list page -->
    <template id="portal_my_loans" name="Library: my loans">
        <t t-call="portal.portal_layout">
            <t t-set="breadcrumbs_searchbar" t-value="False"/>
            <t t-if="not loans">
                <p class="alert alert-info">You have no loans.</p>
            </t>
            <t t-else="">
                <t t-call="portal.portal_table">
                    <thead>
                        <tr>
                            <th>Book</th>
                            <th>Due</th>
                            <th class="text-end">State</th>
                        </tr>
                    </thead>
                    <tbody>
                        <tr t-foreach="loans" t-as="loan">
                            <td><a t-attf-href="/my/loans/#{loan.id}"><t t-out="loan.book_id.name"/></a></td>
                            <td><span t-field="loan.due_date"/></td>
                            <td class="text-end"><span t-field="loan.state"/></td>
                        </tr>
                    </tbody>
                </t>
            </t>
        </t>
    </template>

    <!-- 4. The detail page -->
    <template id="portal_my_loan" name="Library: my loan">
        <t t-call="portal.portal_layout">
            <div class="container pt-3 o_library_loan" t-att-data-loan-id="loan.id">
                <h2 t-out="loan.book_id.name"/>
                <p>Due on <span t-field="loan.due_date"/></p>
                <button t-if="loan.state == 'open'" type="button"
                        class="btn btn-primary o_library_extend">
                    Extend by 7 days
                </button>
            </div>
        </t>
    </template>
</odoo>

Details behind it:

  • portal.portal_docs_entry takes title, url, text, icon, placeholder_count, count, show_count and config_card (read from the template). A card with placeholder_count stays hidden until the lazily fetched /my/counters result says the count is non-zero, which is why _prepare_home_portal_values must answer to the key you pass.
  • portal.portal_table wraps whatever you put inside in a <table>, plus the pager when pager is in the values.
  • t-field renders a field with its formatting and widget rules (dates, selections), which is better than t-out for model values. It needs a record and a field.
  • page_name drives breadcrumbs and menu highlighting. Set it in the controller.
  • The home page template is inherited with customize_show="True" so an administrator can switch the card on and off from the website editor.
  • The xpath selectors reuse classes from the portal templates (o_portal_docs, o_portal_submenu). Check them in the branch you target; they are the part most likely to move.

docs.title: Step 4: put the files in the right bundles
docs.text:
Portal pages use web.assets_frontend for scripts and styles. Backend code does not belong there.

"assets": {
    "web.assets_frontend": [
        "library/static/src/portal/**/*",
    ],
},
"data": [
    "security/ir.model.access.csv",
    "security/library_security.xml",
    "views/portal_templates.xml",
],
"depends": ["portal", "library_base"],

docs.title: Behaviour on the page: public widgets (Odoo 17 and 18)
docs.text:
A publicWidget attaches to the elements matching its selector when the page loads, and gives you jQuery-style helpers (this.$el, events), a lifecycle, and automatic cleanup. This is the legacy-style API that portal and website still use in 18.

/** @odoo-module **/
import publicWidget from "@web/legacy/js/public/public_widget";
import { rpc } from "@web/core/network/rpc";

publicWidget.registry.LibraryLoanExtend = publicWidget.Widget.extend({
    selector: ".o_library_loan",
    events: {
        "click .o_library_extend": "_onExtendClick",
    },

    start() {
        this.loanId = parseInt(this.el.dataset.loanId, 10);
        return this._super(...arguments);
    },

    async _onExtendClick(ev) {
        const button = ev.currentTarget;
        button.disabled = true;
        try {
            const result = await rpc(`/my/loans/${this.loanId}/extend`, { days: 7 });
            this.el.querySelector("p").textContent = `Due on ${result.due_date}`;
        } catch (error) {
            button.disabled = false;
            throw error;
        }
    },
});

The pieces, from addons/web/static/src/legacy/js/public/public_widget.js:

  • selector is a CSS selector; one widget instance is created for each match.
  • events maps "event selector" to a method name, with jQuery-style delegation inside this.$el.
  • Lifecycle: init(parent, options) first, then willStart() (may return a promise, nothing is displayed before it resolves), then start() (the element is ready; return the parent's promise by calling this._super), and destroy() when the page unloads or the website editor takes over.
  • this._super(...arguments) calls the overridden method. It is required in start so the base class can finish.
  • Registered widgets are looked up through publicWidget.registry; the key is only a unique name.
  • Selectors are matched when the page loads. Elements injected later (a modal, an AJAX fragment) are not matched automatically, so prefer server-rendered pages.

The matching JSON route, with type="json" in 18. It needs from odoo import _, fields, http, and action_extend is a method of the teaching model library.loan (it adds the days to due_date):

@http.route("/my/loans/<int:loan_id>/extend", type="json", auth="user", website=True)
def portal_extend_loan(self, loan_id, days=7, **kw):
    try:
        loan_sudo = self._document_check_access("library.loan", loan_id)
    except (AccessError, MissingError):
        raise AccessError(_("You cannot extend this loan."))
    loan_sudo.action_extend(days=int(days))
    return {"due_date": fields.Date.to_string(loan_sudo.due_date)}

Do the check on the server every time. The button being hidden in the template is not a security measure.

docs.title: Behaviour on the page: interactions (Odoo 20)
docs.text:
Odoo 20 replaces publicWidget with Interaction classes (web/static/src/public/interaction.js), registered in public.interactions. The Odoo 20 core ports its portal pages to them (account/static/src/interactions/...). The same widget, as an interaction:

import { Interaction } from "@web/public/interaction";
import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";
import { rpc } from "@web/core/network/rpc";

export class LibraryLoanExtend extends Interaction {
    static selector = ".o_library_loan";
    dynamicContent = {
        ".o_library_extend": { "t-on-click": this.onExtendClick },
    };

    setup() {
        this.loanId = parseInt(this.el.dataset.loanId, 10);
    }

    async onExtendClick(ev) {
        const button = ev.currentTarget;
        button.disabled = true;
        try {
            const result = await this.waitFor(
                rpc(`/my/loans/${this.loanId}/extend`, { days: 7 })
            );
            this.el.querySelector("p").textContent = `Due on ${result.due_date}`;
        } catch (error) {
            button.disabled = false;
            throw error;
        }
    }
}

registry.category("public.interactions").add("library.loan_extend", LibraryLoanExtend);

What the base class documents in the source:

  • static selector picks the elements; selectorHas and selectorNotHas refine it. One instance per element, with this.el and this.env/this.services.
  • The constructor is not overridden; use setup() (sync initialisation), willStart() (async, awaited before dynamic content applies), start() (equivalent of OWL's mounted, handlers attached), and destroy() for cleanup. It is not necessary to call super in these unless you inherit from a concrete subclass.
  • dynamicContent is an object { selector: { directive: handler } } with directives t-on-* (with .prevent, .stop, .capture, .once, .noUpdate), t-att-*, t-out and t-component. Special selectors are _root, _body, _document, _window. The framework re-applies the dynamic content after each handler, so state-driven classes and attributes need no manual DOM code.
  • Helpers: waitFor(promise) (ignores a result that arrives after the interaction was destroyed), addListener, debounced, throttled, locked (one run at a time, optionally with a loading animation), setSafeInterval, waitForTimeout, insert, removeChildren, registerCleanup, mountComponent.
  • Interactions must clean up after themselves: they are destroyed when someone switches the website to edit mode.
  • The source states plainly that it "is not owl": the syntax resembles OWL templates but differs.

For a port from publicWidget: selector stays; events become entries of dynamicContent; start() becomes setup() or start(); this._super disappears; wrap asynchronous calls in this.waitFor.

docs.title: An OWL component on a public page
docs.text:
For richer UI on a public page, use OWL in a controlled way: register a component and place a custom element in the template.

/** @odoo-module **/
import { Component, useState } from "@odoo/owl";
import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";

class LoanCountdown extends Component {
    static template = "library.LoanCountdown";
    static props = { due: String };
    setup() {
        const ms = new Date(this.props.due) - Date.now();
        this.state = useState({ days: Math.ceil(ms / 86400000) });
    }
}

registry.category("public_components").add("library.loan_countdown", LoanCountdown);

<owl-component name="library.loan_countdown" t-att-props="json.dumps({'due': str(loan.due_date)})"/>

In 18 the public_component_service mounts each owl-component[name] element it finds, parsing the element's props attribute as JSON and creating a separate OWL app per element (addons/web/static/src/public/public_component_service.js). The component class comes from the public_components registry. In 20 a PublicComponentInteraction with selector owl-component[name] does the same through this.mountComponent.

The portal's own signature form uses exactly this shape: <owl-component name="portal.signature_form" t-att-props="json.dumps(signature_form_props)"/>. Build the dictionary in the controller and serialise it in the template as shown. A public OWL component gets the public environment: services like orm that need a session user are not safe to assume. Fetch data through your own routes.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text: Frontend styles go into web.assets_frontend as SCSS and can use Bootstrap utilities and the portal's CSS variables. Prefix your classes (o_library_...). To change colours globally for the portal, override variables in web._assets_primary_variables, as described in the assets chapter.

docs.title: Testing the portal
docs.text:
Python controller tests use HttpCase with self.authenticate("portal_user", "portal_user") and self.url_open("/my/loans"); they check status codes, redirects for anonymous users, and that a portal user cannot read another member's loan (/my/loans/<other id> redirects to /my). A tour (see the next chapter) drives the real page, including the widget click, with self.start_tour("/my/loans", "library_portal_tour", login="portal_user").

Write the access test first. It is the one that catches the expensive mistakes.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• No access rule for base.group_portal. The portal page raises AccessError or shows nothing. Write ACL and record rule first.
  • sudo() to "fix" a portal page. It exposes other members' records. Fix the rule instead.
  • Rendering a sudoed record into a writing code path. _document_check_access returns the record with elevated rights; keep it read-only.
  • auth="public" for private pages. Use auth="user".
  • A JSON route without server-side checks. The UI is not a boundary.
  • Backend code in web.assets_frontend, or the other way round. The module does not exist on that page.
  • Widget or interaction selector that matches nothing. Check the class in the rendered HTML (with ?debug=assets), not in the template source.
  • type="json" on 20. It is a deprecated alias of jsonrpc since 19; write jsonrpc when you target 20 only.
  • publicWidget on 20 for new code. Core is moving to interactions. Existing widgets may keep working for now; confirm in your build.
  • Assuming the orm service works for visitors. Public pages have no logged-in user; use routes.
  • Heavy JavaScript on every public page. web.assets_frontend is downloaded by every visitor. Use lazy bundles (loadBundle) for rarely needed code.
  • Hard-coded URLs. Use t-attf-href or url_for-style helpers so website and language prefixes keep working.
  • Counters without a matching key. A card with placeholder_count="loan_count" stays hidden if _prepare_home_portal_values does not return loan_count when asked.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
16: publicWidget is the only tool. The portal controller API and the rpc helper were not verified on 16 for this chapter; check _prepare_home_portal_values and the JSON call helper on your branch.

17: publicWidget; the portal helpers above exist. check_access_rights is the way to test access.

18: publicWidget, has_access, rpc import, type="json". Public OWL components via owl-component.

20: Interaction classes in public.interactions; routes use type="jsonrpc" (json is a deprecated alias with a warning).

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Create the ACL, rule, controller and templates above. Log in as a portal user whose partner owns two loans and check /my/loans.
  2. Log in as a second portal user and request the first user's loan id directly at /my/loans/<id>. What happens?
  3. Add the widget, open the loan page, click the button, and read the network tab.
  4. Write a HttpCase test that asserts step 2.
Solution notes
  1. The list shows only the user's loans, and the home card appears once /my/counters reports a non-zero loan_count.
  2. _document_check_access raises AccessError for a record the user cannot read without a token, and the controller redirects to /my. If you see the other user's data, the record rule is missing or has the wrong domain.
  3. One JSON request to /my/loans/<id>/extend; the date text updates without a page reload.
  4. self.authenticate("portal_b", "portal_b"), response = self.url_open("/my/loans/%d" % loan_a.id), then assert the final URL ends with /my (follow redirects) or the status is 302.

docs.title: Bidirectional synchronisation
docs.text: Two systems that both edit the same data need a sync that knows what changed, where it came from, and who wins a conflict. The failure mode is always the same: A writes to B, B's change hook writes back to A, and the two ping-pong forever. This chapter covers the mapping, the change detection, and the loop breakers.

docs.title: The mapping table
docs.text:
Do not scatter x_external_id fields over business models. One mapping model ties a local record to a remote id per system:

class LibrarySyncMap(models.Model):
    _name = "library.sync.map"
    _description = "Local to remote id mapping"

    model = fields.Char(required=True, index=True)
    res_id = fields.Many2oneReference(model_field="model", required=True)
    remote_system = fields.Char(required=True)
    remote_id = fields.Char(required=True)
    remote_hash = fields.Char()      # hash of the last synced payload
    remote_updated = fields.Datetime()
    last_sync = fields.Datetime()

    _sql_constraints = [
        ("remote_uniq", "unique(model, remote_system, remote_id)", "Already mapped."),
        ("local_uniq", "unique(model, res_id, remote_system)", "Already mapped."),
    ]

Both constraints matter. The first prevents two local records claiming one remote object; the second prevents one local record being pushed twice as two remote objects. Lookup is by index in both directions.

docs.title: Change detection
docs.text:
Never push or pull everything every time. Decide by comparing a fingerprint:

import hashlib, json

def _fingerprint(self, values):
    blob = json.dumps(values, sort_keys=True, default=str)
    return hashlib.sha256(blob.encode()).hexdigest()

Build values from the mapped fields only, in a canonical form (sorted keys, normalised whitespace and number formats). Compare with remote_hash stored at the last sync. If equal, skip. This also stops the loop: after you write the remote's data locally, the local fingerprint equals the stored one, so the write-back finds nothing to send.

When the remote offers a modification timestamp or cursor, use it to fetch only newer records (updated_since=last_sync), and still compare fingerprints, since timestamps lie around clock skew and bulk updates. Subtract a small overlap from the cursor and let the fingerprint discard the repeats.

docs.title: Breaking the loop
docs.text:
Combine two mechanisms.

A context flag for writes you make while applying remote data, so the push hooks on the local side stay quiet:

def write(self, vals):
    res = super().write(vals)
    if not self.env.context.get("library_sync_inbound"):
        self.env["library.export.job"]._enqueue(self)
    return res

def _apply_remote(self, record, values):
    record.with_context(library_sync_inbound=True).write(values)

The flag must be passed to every write the inbound path makes, including writes in overrides further down. Context propagates through with_context and through recordsets derived from the one you called it on, but not through a fresh self.env[...] built from another environment.

A write-origin marker for the other direction, where the remote echoes your own change back as an event. Store the id of the change you sent (or the version number the remote returned) in the map. When an inbound event carries a version equal to the one you just wrote, drop it. Many remotes return the new version in the response to your write, so record it immediately.

Use both: the flag protects against local hooks, the fingerprint and version protect against remote echoes. A flag alone fails across processes, since the echo arrives later in a different request where the context is gone.

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
Decide the policy per field, not per sync, and write it down:

  • One side is the master for a field (prices from the ERP, descriptions from the shop). The other side's edits are overwritten or rejected.
  • Last-writer-wins by timestamp, when both sides may edit. Compare remote updated with the local write_date and accept the newer. Needs reasonably synchronised clocks.
  • Field-level merge: compare against the last synced snapshot. A field changed only on one side since the snapshot is taken from that side; changed on both is a conflict to flag for a human.

Keep a snapshot (remote_hash is not enough for the merge; store the last synced values, for instance as JSON) if you need field-level merge.

docs.title: Deletes
docs.text: A missing record is ambiguous: deleted, or filtered out, or not yet visible. Prefer soft deletes (archive, active = False) mirrored as a status. If the remote only reports absence, delete locally only after a full, successful listing, never after a failed or paginated-out partial one.

docs.title: Ordering of creation
docs.text: Parents before children. Map a partner before the loan that references it. When the child arrives first, either create a placeholder parent and mark it incomplete, or park the event in the queue and retry after the parent syncs.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Loop breaker only in context. Echoes cross process boundaries; store a version or hash.
  • Hashing non-canonical data: float formatting, dict order, trailing spaces. A flapping hash looks like constant changes and defeats the whole mechanism.
  • write_date comparison across systems with different clock settings and time zones. Use UTC, and prefer remote versions where available.
  • Creating duplicates because the mapping row is written in a later transaction than the remote call. Commit the map as soon as the remote id is known, and rely on the unique constraint.
  • Syncing computed or related fields. Map stored, writable fields only.
  • Running initial load and live sync in the same code path with no guard, so the first run floods the queue. Throttle, and load in batches.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: Many2oneReference is available in 16, 17 and 18. _sql_constraints is the declaration style in all three.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Find mapping gaps, read-only:

SELECT b.id FROM library_book b
LEFT JOIN library_sync_map m
  ON m.model = 'library.book' AND m.res_id = b.id AND m.remote_system = 'catalogue'
WHERE m.id IS NULL;

docs.title: Business logic design
docs.text: A business rule is only a rule if it holds on every path: the form, an import, an RPC call, a cron and another module's code. This chapter is about deciding where each kind of rule lives, how to change standard flows without breaking others, and how to keep logic predictable when many modules overlap.

docs.title: Choose the right enforcement point
docs.text:
Kind of rule Where Value must be unique or non-null SQL constraint Condition across fields of a record @api.constrains Derived value @api.depends compute, stored if searched or grouped Default value field default or default_get Workflow step action method with a state guard (see State machines) UX hint while typing @api.onchange and view attributes only Access record rules and groups, not Python if

The common mistake is putting a real rule into an onchange or a view attribute. Both are skipped by RPC and imports.

docs.title: Keep rules in one place
docs.text: If a rule is needed in two places, there is a missing method. Extract it onto the model with a name that states the rule (_check_can_borrow, _get_due_date). Callers then agree by construction. Avoid copying a condition into a domain, a constraint and a button; derive the domain from the method or a stored flag.

docs.title: Change standard flows with care
docs.text:
Standard flows are chains of methods that dozens of modules extend. Three rules:

  1. Extend, do not replace. Override and call super(). Rewriting a method body copies a snapshot of the standard code that rots at the next upgrade and drops other modules' changes.
  2. Prefer the narrowest hook. A _prepare_*_vals method, a single compute, or a _get_* helper changes one thing. Overriding create or write of a core model changes everything and costs on every call.
  3. Trace before you touch. Before editing a flow, list its callers, overrides, dependent computes, constraints, automated actions and mail templates. Check what writing a field on this model triggers elsewhere. The cost of one grep is small against a regression discovered in accounting two weeks later.
# Narrow: one decision, one hook, composable with other modules
def _prepare_invoice_vals(self):
    vals = super()._prepare_invoice_vals()
    if self.library_account_id:
        vals['partner_bank_id'] = self.library_account_id.bank_id.id
    return vals

docs.title: Side effects deserve names and switches
docs.text: Side effects (emails, messages, record creation in other models, external calls) are where flows surprise people. Isolate them in methods, so they can be overridden or skipped, and honor the standard context keys for silencing them: tracking_disable, mail_notrack, mail_create_nolog, mail_auto_subscribe_no_notify. Imports and migrations then do not spam users.

docs.title: Design for recordsets and volume
docs.text: Code must not assume one record or small data. Write for the recordset, group queries, and precompute lookups outside the loop. Where you must loop, avoid searching or browsing inside it. Process large volumes in chunks and flush or invalidate between chunks (see Transactions in practice).

docs.title: Make logic idempotent
docs.text: A rule that runs twice should leave the same result as running once: recomputing a total, applying a transition only when the state allows it, creating a child only if absent. This is what lets crons resume, retries be safe and migrations be repeated. Where it cannot be pure (sending a message), record that it happened in a field or table and check it first.

docs.title: Configuration over code
docs.text: When a threshold or option varies by company, store it as a field on res.company or a res.config.settings parameter, not as a literal. Keep the literal out of the code and give it a default that matches the old behavior, so existing databases do not change on upgrade.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Onchange as validation. Silent on RPC. Add a constraint.
  • Overriding create with a loop over vals_list. Use @api.model_create_multi and handle the list; one-by-one defeats batching.
  • Calling sudo() to make an error disappear. An access error is information; fix the rule or narrow the elevation.
  • Hidden coupling through context. A context key that changes behavior three calls away is hard to find. Document it where it is read and where it is set.
  • Reimplementing standard computations. If a standard field has the number, use it.
  • Tests that only test the happy path of the form. Test the method with a recordset of mixed states, and through RPC.

Versions: @api.model_create_multi is standard from 12 onward. Attribute names for view conditions changed between 16 (attrs) and 17/18 (invisible, readonly expressions), but the rule of keeping real validation in the model is the same in all.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Before changing a standard method, list its overrides across all installed code:

grep -rn "def _prepare_invoice_vals" /path/to/odoo /path/to/custom-addons --include=*.py

Read each override and write down what it expects from super(). That list is your impact map.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text: Odoo runs several worker processes against one PostgreSQL database. Two requests will eventually touch the same record at the same moment, and code that is correct in a single thread will then lose updates, double-process records, or deadlock. This chapter covers the tools for that: the retry loop Odoo gives you for free, row locks, advisory locks, and idempotency keys.

docs.title: What Odoo already does for you
docs.text:
Each request runs in its own transaction with the default REPEATABLE READ isolation. When two transactions modify the same row, PostgreSQL aborts one with a serialization failure. In odoo/service/model.py, retrying() catches LockNotAvailable, SerializationFailure and DeadlockDetected, rolls back, and runs the request again, up to MAX_TRIES_ON_CONCURRENCY_FAILURE = 5 times, sleeping a random time of up to 2 ** tryno seconds between attempts.

This applies to RPC calls and to HTTP controllers dispatched through the normal request path. It has a direct consequence for your code: a request can run more than once. Anything with a side effect outside the database (an HTTP call, an email sent directly, a file written) is repeated if the transaction is retried.

# Wrong: the retry sends the request twice if the commit later fails
def action_confirm(self):
    self._push_to_remote()      # irreversible
    self.state = 'confirmed'    # may raise a serialization failure at commit

Do the database work first, and trigger the external effect after commit (see Transactions in practice).

Retries happen on a fresh cursor and a fresh environment. Do not keep records, caches or flags from the failed attempt. Do not catch psycopg2.errors.SerializationFailure yourself unless you re-raise it; swallowing it hides the failure from retrying() and leaves the transaction aborted.

docs.title: Never coordinate with time.sleep
docs.text: time.sleep() holds a worker, which is a scarce resource, and it proves nothing: the other transaction may take longer than your guess, or not have started yet. Coordination must come from the database. Use a lock, a unique constraint, or a state column changed atomically. If you need to wait for something external, schedule a later run with a cron or a queued job instead of blocking.

docs.title: Row locks: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
docs.text:
When you read a value, decide, and write it back, another transaction can change the value in between. Take a lock on the row before reading:

def _next_ticket_number(self):
    self.env.cr.execute(
        "SELECT id FROM library_book WHERE id = %s FOR UPDATE", [self.id]
    )
    # The row is locked until commit or rollback.
    self.invalidate_recordset()      # drop values read before the lock
    return self.last_ticket + 1

Two details matter. The ORM cache may hold values read before the lock, so invalidate after acquiring it. And pending ORM writes are not in the database yet; call self.env.flush_all() (or flush_model) before raw SQL that depends on them.

Use FOR UPDATE NOWAIT to fail immediately with LockNotAvailable (which retrying() handles) instead of queueing behind the other transaction.

docs.title: SKIP LOCKED for work queues
docs.text:
When several workers take items from a pool, you do not want them to wait for each other. Skip what is already taken:

def _claim_batch(self, limit=50):
    self.env.cr.execute("""
        SELECT id FROM library_loan
         WHERE state = 'to_notify'
         ORDER BY id
         LIMIT %s
           FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
    """, [limit])
    ids = [row[0] for row in self.env.cr.fetchall()]
    return self.browse(ids)

Each worker gets a disjoint set. Process and mark the records in the same transaction so the lock covers the whole unit of work. If a record fails, use a savepoint so one bad row does not discard the batch.

docs.title: Advisory locks
docs.text:
A row lock needs a row. When you need to serialize something that is not a record (an import of one file, a sync of one remote account, a cron that must never overlap with itself), use an advisory lock:

def _try_lock(self, key):
    self.env.cr.execute("SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(%s)", [key])
    return self.env.cr.fetchone()[0]

def sync_account(self):
    key = hash_key('library.sync', self.id)   # a stable 64-bit integer
    if not self._try_lock(key):
        return False                          # another worker has it, skip
    ... # do the work

The _xact_ variant releases the lock automatically at the end of the transaction. Prefer it: session-level advisory locks outlive the transaction, survive in pooled connections, and leak if you forget to unlock. Derive the integer with a stable function (not Python's hash(), which is randomized per process). A 64-bit value from a SHA-1 prefix is enough.

docs.title: Idempotency keys
docs.text:
Locks prevent simultaneous duplicates. They do not prevent a client retrying five minutes later. For anything that creates records on behalf of an external caller, store a key and enforce it with a unique constraint:

class LibraryLoan(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'library.loan'

    request_key = fields.Char(index=True, copy=False)

    _sql_constraints = [
        ('request_key_uniq', 'unique(request_key)', 'Duplicate request.'),
    ]

    @api.model
    def create_idempotent(self, key, vals):
        existing = self.search([('request_key', '=', key)], limit=1)
        if existing:
            return existing
        try:
            with self.env.cr.savepoint():
                return self.create({**vals, 'request_key': key})
        except psycopg2.errors.UniqueViolation:
            return self.search([('request_key', '=', key)], limit=1)

The search is the fast path; the constraint is the guarantee. The savepoint keeps the outer transaction usable after the violation.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Lock ordering. Two transactions locking the same rows in different order deadlock. Always lock in a fixed order (ORDER BY id).
  • Long transactions with locks. A lock held while you call a remote service blocks everyone else for the duration of the call. Lock late, release early.
  • Read, then write in Python. record.counter += 1 is a lost-update race. Use a locked read or UPDATE ... SET counter = counter + 1.
  • Searching for "does it exist" without a constraint. Two requests both see nothing and both create. Only a unique constraint closes the gap.
  • Locks across commits. A cron that commits in batches releases its transaction locks at each commit. Re-acquire for each batch.

Versions: the retry loop and the constants are the same in 16, 17 and 18. In 16 and 17 the code lives in odoo/service/model.py as retrying() under the same name; check MAX_TRIES_ON_CONCURRENCY_FAILURE in your installed copy before relying on the number.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Read-only: see who holds locks while you reproduce a race in two shells.

SELECT l.pid, l.locktype, l.mode, l.granted, a.query
  FROM pg_locks l JOIN pg_stat_activity a USING (pid)
 WHERE a.datname = current_database() AND l.locktype IN ('transactionid', 'advisory', 'tuple');

docs.title: Consuming external APIs
docs.text: Calling another system from Odoo fails in ways local code never does: the connection hangs, the server answers 502, the token expired an hour ago, the rate limit kicks in. This chapter is the client layer that survives those, built on requests, which Odoo already ships.

docs.title: One client class per remote system
docs.text:
Keep HTTP details out of business models. A small client owns the session, base URL, authentication, timeouts and error translation:

import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry

TIMEOUT = (3.05, 20)  # connect, read


class CatalogueError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, message, status=None, retryable=False):
        super().__init__(message)
        self.status = status
        self.retryable = retryable


class CatalogueClient:
    def __init__(self, base_url, token):
        self.base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")
        self.session = requests.Session()
        self.session.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {token}"
        retry = Retry(
            total=3, backoff_factor=0.5,
            status_forcelist=(429, 502, 503, 504),
            allowed_methods=frozenset({"GET", "PUT", "DELETE"}),
            respect_retry_after_header=True,
        )
        self.session.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))

    def request(self, method, path, **kwargs):
        try:
            resp = self.session.request(
                method, f"{self.base_url}{path}", timeout=TIMEOUT, **kwargs
            )
        except (requests.ConnectionError, requests.Timeout) as exc:
            raise CatalogueError(str(exc), retryable=True) from exc
        if resp.status_code >= 500 or resp.status_code == 429:
            raise CatalogueError(resp.text[:200], resp.status_code, retryable=True)
        if resp.status_code >= 400:
            raise CatalogueError(resp.text[:200], resp.status_code)
        return resp.json() if resp.content else None

docs.title: Timeouts are mandatory
docs.text: requests has no default timeout. A call without timeout= can block a worker indefinitely, and Odoo's own worker limits then kill the whole process mid-request. Always pass a tuple: a short connect timeout (a few seconds) and a read timeout sized to the slowest legitimate response. The timeout applies to each socket operation, not to the whole call, so a server that trickles bytes can still exceed it. Keep payloads small and paginate to bound total time.

docs.title: Retries: what is safe
docs.text:
Retry only what is idempotent. GET, PUT and DELETE are by definition; POST is not, unless the remote supports an idempotency key. Send one and POST becomes retryable:

headers = {"Idempotency-Key": f"library.loan-{loan.id}-{loan.write_date:%Y%m%d%H%M%S}"}

Two levels of retry coexist. The urllib3 Retry above handles brief network hiccups inside one call, with exponential backoff (backoff_factor * 2 ** n seconds). The queue handles long outages across cron runs (see Queues and background work). Do not stack long sleeps in the first level: a time.sleep inside a web request holds a worker.

docs.title: Classify errors
docs.text:
Decide per status code, once, in the client:

Outcome Action Network error, timeout, 429, 5xx retryable, back off 401 refresh the token once, retry, then fail 400, 404, 409, 422 permanent: record the message, no retry 2xx with an unexpected body treat as failure, log a body prefix

Callers branch on exc.retryable and never inspect status codes themselves.

docs.title: Credentials and configuration
docs.text:
Keep base URL and token in ir.config_parameter or a configuration record with restricted access, never in source or in a view everyone can read. Read them with sudo() inside a factory method and never log them. When a log line must show a request, log method, path and status, not headers or body.

def _get_client(self):
    icp = self.env["ir.config_parameter"].sudo()
    return CatalogueClient(
        icp.get_param("library_sync.base_url"),
        icp.get_param("library_sync.token"),
    )

docs.title: Outside the transaction
docs.text:
An HTTP call is not part of the database transaction. If the remote call succeeds and your transaction rolls back, the remote keeps the change. If you write locally and the remote call fails, the local record says something false. Two rules follow:

  1. Write locally first, enqueue the remote call, and perform it after commit (in a cron, or through self.env.cr.postcommit.add(func)).
  2. Store the remote id and sync state on the local record as soon as the call returns, in the same commit.

docs.title: Pagination and volume
docs.text: Never fetch "all". Follow the remote's cursor or page parameter, process each page, and commit between pages. Keep the cursor in a record (a last_synced timestamp or a page token) so a crashed run resumes instead of restarting.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Missing timeout. The most common cause of workers stuck for minutes.
  • verify=False to silence a certificate error. Fix the chain or supply a CA bundle.
  • Retrying a non-idempotent POST and creating duplicates on the remote.
  • Logging whole response bodies. Truncate.
  • Catching Exception around the client call and turning programming errors into "network errors". Catch the requests exceptions you expect.
  • Calling the API from a compute method. Computes run on reads, exports and onchanges, many times over.
  • Tests that reach the real network. Patch requests.Session.request or inject a client double.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: The installed urllib3 varies by distribution. allowed_methods replaced method_whitelist in urllib3 1.26, so check the version on your build. cr.postcommit is available in 16, 17 and 18.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Measure the remote from the server before wiring it in:

curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'connect=%{time_connect}s total=%{time_total}s code=%{http_code}\n' https://api.example.test/health

docs.title: HTTP controllers
docs.text: Controllers expose HTTP endpoints for the website, for portals, for webhooks and for custom JSON APIs. They are the least protected entry point of the system, because the caller is not always a logged-in user. Keep them short, explicit about who may call them, and delegate to models (see Thin controllers, fat models).

docs.title: A minimal controller
docs.text:
from odoo import http
from odoo.http import request

class LibraryController(http.Controller):

    @http.route('/library/books', type='http', auth='user', methods=['GET'])
    def books(self, **kw):
        books = request.env['library.book'].search([], limit=50)
        return request.render('library.book_list', {'books': books})

    @http.route('/library/api/borrow', type='json', auth='user', methods=['POST'])
    def borrow(self, book_id):
        book = request.env['library.book'].browse(int(book_id)).exists()
        if not book:
            raise request.not_found()
        return {'loan': book.borrow(request.env.user.partner_id).id}

The class must be imported from the module's controllers/__init__.py, which the module __init__.py imports. A controller that is not imported does not exist.

docs.title: Authentication types
docs.text:
auth= Who runs it Use for user Logged-in user, their access rights Backend and portal actions public The website's public user if not logged in Public pages and forms none No user, no database selected automatically Database-agnostic endpoints, health checks
