Under public you are running as an anonymous user with minimal rights. When you need more, use sudo() on the smallest possible call and validate everything the caller sent. Under auth='none', request.env has no usable user; pick the database and user explicitly if you need them.

docs.title: type=http versus type=json
docs.text: type='http' receives form or query parameters and returns any response. type='json' expects a JSON-RPC request body and wraps your return value in a JSON-RPC envelope. Errors raised in a json route are serialized into the envelope with an HTTP 200, which surprises clients that watch status codes. For third-party callers that expect plain REST semantics, use type='http', read request.httprequest.get_json() (or request.get_json_data()) yourself and build the response with request.make_json_response(data, status=...).

docs.title: CSRF, methods and CORS
docs.text:
• State-changing type='http' routes with auth='user' or 'public' are CSRF-protected by default; the form must carry the token. Disable with csrf=False only for endpoints with their own authentication such as a signed webhook.
  • Restrict methods=[...]; the default accepts everything.
  • cors='*' opens the route to other origins. Do not combine it with cookie authentication.

docs.title: Validate every input
docs.text:
Parameters arrive as strings and are fully attacker-controlled. Cast, check ranges, and re-check ownership:

loan = request.env['library.loan'].browse(int(loan_id)).exists()
if not loan or loan.partner_id != request.env.user.partner_id:
    raise request.not_found()

Do not use sudo() before the ownership check. Return the same response for "does not exist" and "not yours", so ids cannot be probed. Never build SQL or domains by string concatenation; pass parameters.

docs.title: Transactions and retries
docs.text: Each request is one transaction, committed after the controller returns. As described in Concurrency, the dispatcher can run the request again after a serialization failure. Keep non-idempotent external calls out of the controller body: write a job record, commit, process later. For endpoints that clients may retry, accept an idempotency key and store it with a unique constraint.

docs.title: Errors and responses
docs.text: Raise UserError, AccessError, ValidationError or werkzeug.exceptions.NotFound; do not catch broadly and return a 200 with an error text. Log with enough context to find the request, without logging tokens or personal data.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Controllers that do the work. A 120 line route handler with business rules cannot be called from a cron or a test.
  • auth='public' plus sudo() as a default. This is an unauthenticated write path to your data. Review each such route as if it were an open API.
  • Trusting request.env.user under auth='none'. It is not the logged-in user.
  • Large responses built in memory. Stream exports or generate them as attachments.
  • Route path collisions. Two modules defining the same route: the last loaded wins. Prefix your routes with the module name.
  • Overriding a standard controller without calling super(). You silently drop the behavior other modules added.

Versions: Odoo 16 uses type='json' and type='http' with request.jsonrequest for the body. In 17 and 18 the JSON body is read through the parameters of your method and request.get_json_data(), and request.jsonrequest is gone. Check the exact request helpers in odoo/http.py of your version before copying code between them. In 18, type='json' is the JSON-RPC route type; plain JSON routes are served by type='http'.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
List the routes your database actually serves (read-only):

grep -rn "@http.route" /path/to/custom-addons --include=*.py | grep -v "auth='user'"

Every line it prints is a route that is public or unauthenticated. Read each one.

docs.title: Importing and exporting data
docs.text: Moving data in and out of Odoo is mostly the import engine, a single method that does name resolution, validation and create-or-update. Use it from code instead of writing your own loader, and learn its quirks once.

docs.title: The engine: load()
docs.text:
Model.load(fields, data) takes a list of column names and a matrix of string values and returns {"ids": [...], "messages": [...]}. It is what the web import screen calls (verified in odoo/models.py: "Attempts to load the data matrix, and returns a list of ids ... and a list of messages").

fields_ = ["id", "title", "isbn", "author_id", "tag_ids"]
rows = [
    ["__import__.book_1", "Dune", "9780000000001", "Herbert", "Fiction,Classic"],
    ["__import__.book_2", "Emma", "9780000000002", "Austen", "Classic"],
]
result = self.env["library.book"].load(fields_, rows)
if result["messages"]:
    for m in result["messages"]:
        _logger.warning("row %s: %s", m.get("rows"), m["message"])

What it gives you over create:

  • External ids. The id column is an XML id. If it exists, the record is updated; if not, created. This makes imports repeatable. Without id you always create.
  • Name resolution. Many2one columns take a display name (author_id) or an external id (author_id/id), many2many take comma-separated names. Selection fields accept the label as well as the key.
  • Per-row messages. Errors carry row numbers and field names instead of aborting on the first exception. Rows are processed inside savepoints, and if any row has an error with ids set to False, nothing is saved.
  • Onchange and defaults are applied as for the UI.

Use id columns with your own module prefix, so reruns update instead of duplicating. Never invent ids that look like base. or another module's namespace.

docs.title: The pitfalls of name lookup
docs.text: Name resolution uses name_search. A duplicate name makes the import fail with an ambiguity message, a missing one fails with "no matching record". For big imports use external ids for relations (author_id/id) and import in dependency order: authors, then books, then loans. Do not rely on a name being unique just because it is today.

docs.title: CSV and Excel
docs.text:
Python's csv module and openpyxl (shipped with Odoo, since it reads xlsx for the UI) cover input:

import base64, csv, io

def _rows_from_csv(self, content_b64):
    text = base64.b64decode(content_b64).decode("utf-8-sig")
    reader = csv.reader(io.StringIO(text), delimiter=";")
    header = next(reader)
    return header, list(reader)

Details that bite:

  • Encoding. Excel writes CSV in a legacy code page unless told otherwise. utf-8-sig removes a BOM; fall back or ask for UTF-8 explicitly.
  • Delimiter and decimals. Locales that use a comma decimal use a semicolon delimiter. Detect with csv.Sniffer or make it a wizard option; do not guess silently.
  • Leading zeros and long numbers. A spreadsheet turns 00123 into 123 and 9780000000001 into scientific notation. Read cells as text or tell users to format the column as text.
  • Dates. Pass ISO YYYY-MM-DD. Ambiguous 03/04/2025 is parsed by the user's language settings in the UI import, but your code must pick a format.
  • Excel files. openpyxl.load_workbook(io.BytesIO(data), read_only=True, data_only=True) streams rows and reads cached formula values. Convert every cell to string, empty cells to "", before load().

docs.title: Batches and progress
docs.text:
load() on 100,000 rows in one call holds one transaction and a lot of memory. Split:

for start in range(0, len(rows), 500):
    result = Model.load(header, rows[start:start + 500])
    if not result["ids"]:
        errors.extend(result["messages"])
    self.env.cr.commit()   # only in a cron or script, not in a user request

For large imports, upload the file as an attachment, create a job, and let a cron process chunks (see Queues and background work). The user gets a status record with error counts and downloadable rejects.

Mail tracking dominates import time on mail-thread models. Import with with_context(tracking_disable=True, mail_notrack=True, mail_create_nolog=True) when notifications are not wanted.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
For code, export_data mirrors the UI export:

data = books.export_data(["id", "title", "author_id/name"])["datas"]

The UI export (/web/export) uses the same mechanism. Field paths with a slash traverse relations, id gives the external id (created on demand for records without one). For simple dumps, read or search_read plus csv.writer is clearer and faster:

out = io.StringIO()
w = csv.writer(out, delimiter=",", quoting=csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL)
w.writerow(["title", "isbn"])
for b in books.read(["title", "isbn"]):
    w.writerow([b["title"], b["isbn"]])

Prefer streaming and chunks for large sets, and mind CSV injection: a cell starting with =, +, - or @ runs as a formula when opened in a spreadsheet. Prefix such text values with an apostrophe or a space when the data comes from outside.

docs.title: Idempotent imports
docs.text: Design so a rerun is safe: stable external ids, load() for upserts, a natural-key uniqueness constraint behind it. When data has no stable key, create one from the source (file name plus row hash) and store it, rather than matching on a name.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Importing without external ids, then importing again and doubling everything.
  • Matching by name where names repeat.
  • Committing inside load() callers reachable from the UI.
  • Ignoring messages and trusting ids: a partial failure leaves ids False and the data unsaved.
  • Mail tracking left on: each row sends notifications.
  • Spreadsheets silently altering codes, dates and long numbers.
  • Importing as superuser for convenience, bypassing access rules the real user should hit.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: load(fields, data) has the same signature in 16, 17 and 18 (verified in 18). In 18 the helpers live in odoo/models.py (_load_records, _load_records_create, _load_records_write). Context keys and message structure have changed between releases, so inspect result["messages"] on your build rather than parsing text.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Dry-run an import in a test database and read what the engine says before committing:

res = env["library.book"].load(["id", "title"], [["__import__.t1", "Test"]])
print(res)
env.cr.rollback()

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Slow Odoo code is slow for a small number of reasons, and guessing which one costs more than measuring. This chapter is the measuring habit first, then the three causes behind most slowness: queries in loops, missing indexes, and work done per record that could be done per batch.

docs.title: Measure before changing anything
docs.text:
Find out where the time goes. Three tools cover most cases:

  • Query count and time. Run with --log-level=debug_sql on a test database, or watch pg_stat_statements on a busy one. Count the queries for one operation. A hundred identical queries differing by id is the signature of an N+1.
  • Python profile. Odoo ships a profiler: enable it from the developer menu, or in code:
from odoo.tools import profiler

with profiler.Profiler(db=self.env.cr.dbname):
    records.action_heavy()

The recorded sessions show Python time and SQL per call stack. * EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the slow query, to see sequential scans, row estimates that are off by orders of magnitude, and sorts that spill.

Change one thing, measure again, keep the number. If you cannot show a before and after, you do not know whether you fixed it.

docs.title: N+1 queries
docs.text:
The classic form:

for loan in loans:
    loan.book_id.title        # fine: prefetched
    self.env["library.book"].search([("id", "=", loan.book_id.id)])  # one query per loop

Field reads on records of the same recordset are prefetched: reading loan.book_id for one record loads it for the whole recordset in one query, up to PREFETCH_MAX (1000 in odoo/models.py) records at a time. The ORM protects you as long as you stay in the recordset. You lose it by calling search, browse on single ids, read or create inside the loop.

Fix by moving the query out and grouping:

books = self.env["library.book"].search([("id", "in", loans.book_id.ids)])
by_id = {b.id: b for b in books}

Or let the database aggregate:

groups = self.env["library.loan"]._read_group(
    [("state", "=", "open")], ["book_id"], ["__count"]
)

_read_group (the public read_group is for the web client) returns tuples of group values and aggregates, computed in SQL, with no records instantiated.

docs.title: Prefetch, and when it hurts
docs.text:
Prefetch loads every stored field of the model for the whole batch on first access, except large binaries and, by default, fields in other groups the user cannot read. For a wide model and a loop that needs one field, that loads far more than needed. Use read with explicit fields, or mapped/_read_group for a single column:

titles = books.mapped("title")                        # one query
rows = books.read(["title", "isbn"])                  # explicit columns

Opposite problem: a recordset rebuilt inside the loop breaks the prefetch group. self.browse(rec.id) inside a loop makes a one-record prefetch set every time. Keep the original recordset; pass with_prefetch() only if you deliberately construct new ones.

docs.title: Write and create in bulk
docs.text:
Loan.create([{"book_id": b, "member_id": m} for b, m in pairs])   # one call, list of dicts
records.write({"state": "done"})                                  # one write for all

create with a list batches inserts and computes once. Per-record write in a loop triggers recomputes and constraints each time. Group records by the value they receive and write once per group.

docs.title: Computed fields
docs.text:
A stored compute on a field read often, with correct @api.depends, is cheap. A non-stored compute that does a search per record is the usual culprit; compute for the whole recordset instead:

@api.depends("loan_ids.state")
def _compute_open_loans(self):
    data = dict(self.env["library.loan"]._read_group(
        [("book_id", "in", self.ids), ("state", "=", "open")],
        ["book_id"], ["__count"],
    ))
    for book in self:
        book.open_loans = data.get(book, 0)

Over-broad @api.depends (depending on a whole one2many, or on fields that change constantly) causes mass recomputes on unrelated writes. Depend on the narrowest path.

docs.title: Indexes
docs.text:
An index helps filters, joins and orderings you actually run. Declare index=True on fields used in search domains over large tables (state, foreign keys you filter by, external ids). Every index costs write time and disk, so do not index everything. Many2one fields get a foreign key index for ondelete handling only in some cases; check with \d table rather than assuming.

Confirm with EXPLAIN that the planner uses it. Low-selectivity columns (a boolean split 50/50) rarely benefit.

docs.title: Batching long work
docs.text:
Process large sets in chunks, with flush and a cache clear so memory stays flat:

for chunk in tools.split_every(500, ids):
    records = self.browse(chunk)
    records._do_work()
    self.env.flush_all()
    self.env.invalidate_all()

Commit between chunks only in cron or script contexts (see Queues and background work).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Optimising from intuition. Profile first; the slow line is rarely the one you suspect.
  • search followed by len(). Use search_count.
  • sudo() or with_context inside the loop, creating a new environment and cache each time.
  • Reading related fields through long chains (a.b.c.d) per record without prefetch benefit.
  • ORDER BY on a non-stored computed field, forcing Python sorting of everything.
  • Testing performance on a ten-record dev database. Test with realistic volume.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: _read_group with the ["__count"] aggregate style and tuple results is the 17 and 18 API. In 16 _read_group returns dicts and uses groupby/fields arguments differently, so verify the signature in your build. invalidate_all and flush_all exist from 16. PREFETCH_MAX is 1000 in 18.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
See the heaviest statements on a database you may read:

SELECT calls, round(total_exec_time) AS ms, left(query, 100)
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;

docs.title: Queues and background work
docs.text: A request has a few seconds to answer. Anything slower, flakier or larger than that belongs in a queue: a table of work items and a cron that drains it. Odoo has no job-queue framework in core, and for most integrations you do not need one. A model, a state field and ir.cron cover it.

docs.title: The shape of a queue
docs.text:
Make the work item a record. The record is the queue, the retry counter and the audit trail at once.

from odoo import api, fields, models


class LibraryExportJob(models.Model):
    _name = "library.export.job"
    _description = "Pending export to an external catalogue"
    _order = "id"

    book_id = fields.Many2one("library.book", required=True, ondelete="cascade")
    state = fields.Selection(
        [("pending", "Pending"), ("done", "Done"), ("failed", "Failed")],
        default="pending", required=True, index=True,
    )
    attempts = fields.Integer(default=0)
    last_error = fields.Text()
    not_before = fields.Datetime(index=True)

Producers insert rows and return. They never call the remote system themselves:

def action_publish(self):
    jobs = self.env["library.export.job"].create(
        [{"book_id": b.id} for b in self]
    )
    self.env.ref("library_sync.cron_export_jobs")._trigger()
    return jobs

_trigger() asks the cron worker to run that cron at the next opportunity instead of waiting for nextcall. It creates a row in ir.cron.trigger and notifies the cron worker. Pass at= a datetime (or a list of them) to schedule a delayed run; precision is about a minute. The cron must exist and be active. The trigger does not bypass the cron's own active flag.

docs.title: Batch and commit
docs.text:
The consumer takes a bounded slice, processes each item, and commits after each one so a failure at item 40 does not undo items 1 to 39.

@api.model
def _cron_process_jobs(self, batch_size=100):
    jobs = self.search(
        [("state", "=", "pending"),
         "|", ("not_before", "=", False), ("not_before", "<=", fields.Datetime.now())],
        limit=batch_size,
    )
    done = 0
    for job in jobs:
        try:
            with self.env.cr.savepoint():
                job._send()
            job.write({"state": "done", "last_error": False})
        except Exception as exc:
            job.write({
                "attempts": job.attempts + 1,
                "last_error": str(exc),
                "state": "failed" if job.attempts + 1 >= 5 else "pending",
            })
        self.env.cr.commit()
        done += 1
    remaining = self.search_count([("state", "=", "pending")])
    self.env.ref("library_sync.cron_export_jobs")._notify_progress(
        done=done, remaining=remaining
    )
    if remaining:
        self.env.ref("library_sync.cron_export_jobs")._trigger()

Three details matter here.

The savepoint isolates the ORM changes of _send(), so a half-written failure rolls back while the bookkeeping write of the failed attempt survives. Without it you are left with either a poisoned transaction or a lost error message.

The commit after each item makes progress durable. In a cron it is allowed, and in Odoo 18 the cron runner is designed around it (see Versions). Never commit inside code that can also be called from a user request: the caller loses its atomicity.

_notify_progress(done=, remaining=) tells the runner how much is done. If the cron is killed by its time limit, the runner uses this to decide whether to run it again straight away. The loop re-triggers itself when there is more to do, which is how you drain a large backlog without one giant run.

The Odoo 18 runner calls a cron job in a loop of at most MAX_BATCH_PER_CRON_JOB (10) runs while progress is reported. After CONSECUTIVE_TIMEOUT_FOR_FAILURE (3) consecutive timeouts the job is marked as failed and deactivated. Both constants are in odoo/addons/base/models/ir_cron.py.

docs.title: Choosing the batch size
docs.text:
Pick it from the time budget, not from the row count. If the remote call takes 300 ms and the cron limit is a few minutes, 100 items per run is comfortable. Make the size a system parameter or a cron argument so operations can change it without a deploy.

Order by id (or by not_before) so old work is not starved by new work. Add an index on state; a queue table grows with history, and an unindexed search on state gets slower every month. Delete or archive done rows on a schedule.

docs.title: Concurrent runs
docs.text:
Two cron workers do not run the same cron simultaneously, since the runner locks the cron row. But a manual "Run now" from the UI, or a second cron that touches the same table, can overlap. Claim rows explicitly when that matters:

self.env.cr.execute("""
    SELECT id FROM library_export_job
     WHERE state = 'pending'
     ORDER BY id
     LIMIT %s
       FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
""", (batch_size,))
ids = [r[0] for r in self.env.cr.fetchall()]
jobs = self.browse(ids)

SKIP LOCKED lets each runner take rows nobody else holds. Note that the lock lives until commit, so a commit inside the loop releases the rest of your claimed rows. Claim one batch, process it fully, commit once, or mark rows running first in a short transaction.

docs.title: Retries and backoff
docs.text:
Count attempts and compute not_before from the attempt number:

delay = min(60 * 2 ** job.attempts, 6 * 3600)  # seconds, capped
job.not_before = fields.Datetime.now() + timedelta(seconds=delay)

Stop after a fixed number of attempts and leave the row in failed with last_error. A failed state that someone can see and requeue by hand is worth more than an endless silent retry.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Calling the remote API inside the user's request "just this once". The first time the remote is slow, your workers all block on it.
  • Committing in the middle of a method that a test, a wizard or an import also calls. Keep commits in the cron entry point only.
  • Passing recordsets or lambdas through the queue. Store ids and plain values; the consumer rereads the current state, which also makes stale jobs harmless.
  • A job that fails before its bookkeeping write, for instance on a unique-constraint error in the same transaction. Hence the savepoint.
  • A cron with numbercall-style assumptions copied from old tutorials. In 18 the field is gone; control repetition by the interval and by _trigger.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: 16 and 17 have no _notify_progress and no automatic re-run loop; the cron body runs once per tick, so keep batches small and use _trigger or a short interval to drain. _trigger exists since 16. In 18 the runner commits progress between runs. Check ir_cron.py of your exact build before relying on the batch loop.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Read-only, to see what is waiting and what is scheduled:

SELECT state, count(*) FROM library_export_job GROUP BY state;
SELECT cron_id, call_at FROM ir_cron_trigger ORDER BY call_at;

docs.title: State machines
docs.text: Most business documents (a loan, an order, a request) move through a fixed set of states. A state machine makes that explicit: a selection field, a table of allowed transitions, and one method per transition. Done well, nobody can reach an invalid state by clicking, by RPC, or by import.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text:
class LibraryLoan(models.Model):
    _name = 'library.loan'
    _description = 'Book loan'

    state = fields.Selection([
        ('draft', 'Draft'),
        ('active', 'Active'),
        ('returned', 'Returned'),
        ('cancelled', 'Cancelled'),
    ], default='draft', required=True, readonly=True, copy=False, tracking=True, index=True)

    _TRANSITIONS = {
        'draft': {'active', 'cancelled'},
        'active': {'returned', 'cancelled'},
        'returned': set(),
        'cancelled': {'draft'},
    }

    def _transition(self, new_state):
        for rec in self:
            if new_state not in self._TRANSITIONS[rec.state]:
                raise UserError(_("A loan cannot go from %(a)s to %(b)s.",
                                  a=rec.state, b=new_state))
        self.write({'state': new_state})

readonly=True on the field hides editing in the form, but does not stop write() from RPC. The guard lives in the model.

docs.title: One method per transition
docs.text:
def action_confirm(self):
    self._transition('active')
    self._reserve_copy()

def action_return(self):
    self._transition('returned')

Buttons call these methods. Business effects (reserving, notifying, accounting) go in the action method, after the state check, so they run only for a valid transition. Name them action_* for user-triggered and _do_* for internal ones.

docs.title: Batch safety
docs.text:
self is a recordset. Validate every record before changing any, as _transition does: raising halfway through a loop is fine inside one transaction, but validating first gives one clear error and avoids partial side effects such as an email already queued for the first three records.

def action_confirm(self):
    to_confirm = self.filtered(lambda l: l.state == 'draft')   # skip silently, or raise: decide
    to_confirm._transition('active')

Decide deliberately between "skip records not in the right state" and "refuse the whole batch". Skipping suits server actions on lists; refusing suits API calls where the caller needs to know.

docs.title: Guarding writes outside the actions
docs.text:
Someone will write state directly: a server action, an import, another module. To enforce transitions regardless of the entry point, check in write:

def write(self, vals):
    if 'state' in vals:
        for rec in self:
            if vals['state'] != rec.state and vals['state'] not in self._TRANSITIONS[rec.state]:
                raise UserError(_("Invalid transition."))
    return super().write(vals)

This is stricter, and it also blocks legitimate data fixes by administrators. Keep a context key (self.with_context(force_state=True)) as an escape hatch that is documented, logged, and used only in migrations.

docs.title: Locks and fields that freeze
docs.text:
Once a document leaves draft, usually some fields must stop changing. Express it once:

LOCKED_FIELDS = {'book_id', 'partner_id'}

def write(self, vals):
    if LOCKED_FIELDS & vals.keys() and any(r.state != 'draft' for r in self):
        raise UserError(_("These fields can only change in draft."))
    return super().write(vals)

In views use invisible/readonly with state conditions for the user experience, and keep the model check as the real rule.

docs.title: Concurrency on transitions
docs.text: Two users pressing Confirm on the same record: both read draft, both pass the check. The second write usually fails with a serialization error and is retried by the framework, and the retry then sees active and raises a clean error. When the transition has side effects outside the record (stock, sequences), lock the row first with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (see Concurrency).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Transitions scattered across the code. If three modules write state freely, the table above is fiction. Centralize in one _transition.
  • Computed or related state. A state derived from other fields cannot be set; keep a stored selection for workflow, and compute flags beside it.
  • Cancel that destroys history. Cancel to a state, do not unlink, if anything referenced the record. Provide a reset to draft only if the business really allows it.
  • Inheriting and adding states. Use selection_add with ondelete={'new_state': 'set default'} (required, or uninstalling the module breaks existing rows).
  • Business logic in the view. Attrs that hide a button are not security.

Versions: in 17 and 18, attrs and states on view elements are replaced by direct invisible, readonly and required expressions. In 16 you still write attrs="{'invisible': [('state', '!=', 'draft')]}". selection_add with ondelete behaves the same in 16 to 18.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Read-only: count records per state to find impossible ones before adding a guard.

SELECT state, count(*) FROM library_loan GROUP BY state ORDER BY 2 DESC;

docs.title: Thin controllers, fat models
docs.text: Business rules live in models. Controllers, wizards, cron entries and server actions only translate an input into a model call. The reason is reuse and testability: a rule in a model works from the UI, from RPC, from a cron, from an import and from a test with one call. A rule in a controller works from one URL.

docs.title: What goes where
docs.text: Layer Responsibility Controller Parse request, authenticate, call one model method, shape the response Wizard (TransientModel) Collect user input, call the model method on the active records Cron / server action Select records, call the model method Model Validate, compute, change state, enforce invariants, create side effects

docs.title: An example
docs.text:
Thick controller, which is hard to test and impossible to reuse:

@http.route('/library/borrow', type='json', auth='user')
def borrow(self, book_id, days):
    book = request.env['library.book'].browse(book_id)
    if book.available_copies < 1:
        return {'error': 'no copies'}
    loan = request.env['library.loan'].create({
        'book_id': book.id, 'due_date': date.today() + timedelta(days=days)})
    book.available_copies -= 1
    return {'loan': loan.id}

The same rule in the model:

class LibraryBook(models.Model):
    _inherit = 'library.book'

    def borrow(self, partner, days=14):
        self.ensure_one()
        if self.available_copies < 1:
            raise UserError(_("No copies available."))
        loan = self.env['library.loan'].create({
            'book_id': self.id,
            'partner_id': partner.id,
            'due_date': fields.Date.today() + timedelta(days=days),
        })
        return loan

and the controller shrinks to authentication, a call and a response:

@http.route('/library/borrow', type='json', auth='user')
def borrow(self, book_id, days=14):
    book = request.env['library.book'].browse(book_id)
    loan = book.borrow(request.env.user.partner_id, days)
    return {'loan': loan.id}

UserError becomes a proper error response, so the controller does not need its own error encoding.

docs.title: Respect existing hooks
docs.text: Standard models already have extension points: create, write, _compute_*, _onchange_*, _prepare_*_vals, _action_*, _post. Prefer them over new parallel paths. If standard code builds values through _prepare_invoice_vals(), override that and your change applies on every route into the flow. If you instead write a new method that creates the invoice directly, you bypass every other module that extended the hook.

docs.title: Trace the impact before changing a standard flow
docs.text:
A change that looks local often is not. Before overriding or bypassing a standard method:

  1. Find all callers: grep -rn "_action_confirm" addons/ odoo/addons/ in the source of every installed module, including enterprise and your own.
  2. Find all overrides of the method and read their order. With super() chains, your code runs inside theirs and the reverse.
  3. Check which stored computes and constraints depend on the fields you write. A write to one field can trigger a recomputation chain across models.
  4. Check which automated actions, mail templates, followers and server actions are bound to the model. They fire on your write too.
  5. Run the standard test tags for the affected apps (--test-tags), not only your own.

This is the butterfly effect: a one-line change in write of a core model runs for every record of every flow. Narrow your override with a condition on vals and on the context so unrelated paths are not slowed or altered.

docs.title: Batch-safe code
docs.text:
Methods get recordsets. Write for self of any size, not for one record:

# Wrong: N queries, and breaks on empty or multi recordsets
def _compute_overdue(self):
    for loan in self:
        loan.overdue = self.env['library.fine'].search_count([('loan_id', '=', loan.id)]) > 0

# Right: one grouped query
def _compute_overdue(self):
    groups = self.env['library.fine']._read_group(
        [('loan_id', 'in', self.ids)], ['loan_id'], ['__count'])
    counts = {loan.id: count for loan, count in groups}
    for loan in self:
        loan.overdue = counts.get(loan.id, 0) > 0

Use ensure_one() only on methods that are single-record by nature, and say so in the name or docstring.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Logic in @api.onchange. It does not run on RPC or import. Rules go in create/write/constraints; onchange is only UX.
  • sudo() in controllers. It removes access rules for everything downstream. Call sudo() on the narrowest expression, and re-check rights by hand.
  • Helpers on the controller class. Anything another entry point might need belongs on a model.
  • God models. "Fat" means rules sit with their data, not that one model does everything. Split by responsibility with a helper model or mixin.

Versions: _read_group with ['__count'] aggregates and a list return is the 17 and 18 signature. In 16 use read_group or the older _read_group form with lazy and dict results.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Find every override of a standard method you plan to touch:

grep -rn "def _action_confirm" /path/to/odoo/addons /path/to/custom-addons --include=*.py

docs.title: Transactions in practice
docs.text: Every Odoo request is one database transaction. It commits when the request ends successfully and rolls back on an exception. Most bugs in this area come from code that works against that model: committing early, swallowing exceptions inside a transaction, or doing irreversible work before the outcome is known.

docs.title: The default: one request, one transaction
docs.text:
You do not call commit() in normal business code. If a method raises, everything it wrote disappears, including the writes of the methods that called it. That is the feature: a half-finished confirmation never exists.

def action_confirm(self):
    for loan in self:
        loan._reserve_copy()      # writes
        loan._compute_due_date()  # writes
        loan.state = 'active'     # if anything above raised, none of it persists

docs.title: Savepoints: partial failure inside a transaction
docs.text:
When one failing item must not cancel the rest, wrap it in a savepoint:

def action_send_reminders(self):
    failed = []
    for loan in self:
        try:
            with self.env.cr.savepoint():
                loan._send_reminder()
        except Exception as e:
            _logger.warning("Reminder failed for loan %s: %s", loan.id, e)
            failed.append(loan.id)
    return failed

On exception the savepoint rolls back to its start and the transaction continues. By default savepoint() flushes pending ORM writes first (flush=True), so the rollback boundary is exact, and it invalidates the cache on rollback so you do not read values from the discarded work.

Without the savepoint, a database error (a constraint violation, for example) leaves PostgreSQL in an aborted state: every later statement fails with current transaction is aborted. Catching the Python exception is not enough; the savepoint is what restores the transaction.

A savepoint only protects the database. In-memory state, files, and external calls made inside the block are not undone.

Catch narrow exceptions when you can. Catching Exception around a block that may raise a serialization failure hides it from the retry loop (see Concurrency); re-raise psycopg2.errors.SerializationFailure, LockNotAvailable and DeadlockDetected.

docs.title: Savepoints are cheap, but not free
docs.text:
Each savepoint is a round trip and PostgreSQL tracks subtransactions. A savepoint per record on a loop of 100,000 rows is slow. Use one savepoint per chunk and fall back to per-record only for a chunk that failed:

for chunk in split_every(500, self.ids):
    records = self.browse(chunk)
    try:
        with self.env.cr.savepoint():
            records._process()
    except Exception:
        for rec in records:
            try:
                with self.env.cr.savepoint():
                    rec._process()
            except Exception:
                _logger.exception("Record %s failed", rec.id)

docs.title: Committing manually
docs.text:
Sometimes you must commit: a cron that processes thousands of items and must keep progress, or a job that records an attempt before calling a remote service. Rules:

  1. Only in code that owns the transaction: crons, queue jobs, scripts. Never in a method a user can call from the UI, and never in code another module may call inside its own transaction. You would commit their half-finished work.
  2. Flush before, and expect the cache to be invalidated after.
  3. Commit per unit of work, and make each unit safe to repeat.
def _cron_process(self):
    todo = self.search([('state', '=', 'pending')], limit=200)
    for rec in todo:
        rec._process()
        rec.state = 'done'
        self.env.cr.commit()

In tests, cr.commit() is neutralized by the test cursor; code that relies on a commit being visible to another cursor needs care. Do not commit in a @api.constrains, create, write or compute.

docs.title: After-commit work
docs.text:
External side effects belong after the commit, so a rollback or retry does not repeat them. Use the cursor's postcommit hook:

def action_confirm(self):
    self.state = 'active'
    self.env.cr.postcommit.add(self._notify_remote)

In Odoo 18 cr.postcommit is a callback list run after a successful commit. Callbacks execute outside the transaction: they cannot write through the same cursor without opening a new one, and an exception in them cannot undo the commit. For anything that must not be lost, write a job row in the transaction and let a cron or queue process it; that survives a crash between commit and callback.

Versions: cr.savepoint() exists in 16, 17 and 18. cr.postcommit and cr.precommit are available in 16 and later as callback hooks; in 18 they are Callbacks objects, so register with .add(func) and pass data with .data. Check the signature in your installed odoo/sql_db.py before using the data dictionary.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• try/except without savepoint. After a SQL error the cursor is unusable. Always pair a catch of a database error with a savepoint.
  • Email or HTTP inside the transaction. If the commit later fails or the request is retried, the message goes out twice. Queue it, or send post-commit.
  • Commit inside a loop over self. After commit() the records in self still exist, but cached values are stale and locks are gone.
  • Assuming rollback undoes sequences. ir.sequence values drawn with nextval are not rolled back. Gaps are normal.
  • Mixing cursors. A second cursor opened with registry.cursor() does not see uncommitted data from the first, and can block waiting for a lock the first holds. This is a classic self-deadlock.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Read-only: watch transaction state from another shell while a long action runs.

SELECT pid, state, xact_start, now() - xact_start AS age, left(query, 80)
  FROM pg_stat_activity
 WHERE datname = current_database() AND state <> 'idle'
 ORDER BY xact_start;

Rows stuck in idle in transaction point to code that opened a transaction and then waited on something slow.

docs.title: Receiving webhooks
docs.text: A webhook is an HTTP request someone else sends to you when something happens. The sender expects a fast answer, retries when it does not get one, and may deliver the same event twice. A reliable receiver does three things: verifies the sender, acknowledges quickly, and processes each event exactly once.

docs.title: Verify the signature
docs.text:
Anyone can post to a public URL. Senders prove who they are by signing the raw body with a shared secret, typically HMAC-SHA256 in a header. Verify against the raw bytes, before parsing:

import hashlib
import hmac
import json

import psycopg2

from odoo import http
from odoo.http import request
from odoo.tools import consteq


class LibraryWebhook(http.Controller):

    @http.route("/library/webhook", type="http", auth="public",
                methods=["POST"], csrf=False)
    def receive(self):
        body = request.httprequest.get_data()  # raw bytes
        secret = request.env["ir.config_parameter"].sudo().get_param(
            "library_sync.webhook_secret", ""
        ).encode()
        sent = request.httprequest.headers.get("X-Signature", "")
        expected = hmac.new(secret, body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
        if not secret or not consteq(sent, expected):
            return request.make_response("", status=401)
        # ... store the event, see below

Points that matter:

  • Compare in constant time (odoo.tools.consteq, an alias of hmac.compare_digest) so response timing leaks nothing.
  • Sign the raw body. Re-serialising parsed JSON changes whitespace and key order, and the signature no longer matches.
  • Refuse when no secret is configured. With an empty secret anyone can compute a valid signature.
  • If the sender signs a timestamp, reject events older than a few minutes to stop replay.
  • type="http" with csrf=False is right here: the caller is a server, not a browser, and the HMAC replaces the CSRF token. type="json" expects a JSON-RPC envelope that third parties do not send.

docs.title: Acknowledge fast, work later
docs.text:
Senders time out after a few seconds and then resend. Do not process inside the request. Store the event, answer 200, and let a cron do the work:

        payload = json.loads(body)
        Event = request.env["library.webhook.event"].sudo()
        try:
            with request.env.cr.savepoint():
                Event.create({
                    "external_id": payload["id"],
                    "kind": payload["type"],
                    "payload": body.decode(),
                })
        except psycopg2.errors.UniqueViolation:
            pass  # duplicate delivery, already stored
        request.env.ref("library_sync.cron_webhook_events").sudo()._trigger()
        return request.make_response("ok", status=200)

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text:
Delivery is at least once. The same event arrives twice after a timeout, a retry or a manual replay. Make that harmless with a unique constraint on the sender's event id:

class LibraryWebhookEvent(models.Model):
    _name = "library.webhook.event"
    _description = "Inbound webhook event"

    external_id = fields.Char(required=True, index=True)
    kind = fields.Char(required=True)
    payload = fields.Text()
    state = fields.Selection(
        [("new", "New"), ("done", "Done"), ("error", "Error")], default="new"
    )

    _sql_constraints = [
        ("external_id_uniq", "unique(external_id)", "Duplicate event."),
    ]

The constraint, not a prior search, is the guard: two simultaneous deliveries both pass a search and both insert. The database decides. The savepoint keeps the unique violation from poisoning the request's transaction.

Processing must be idempotent too. "Set the loan to returned" is safe to repeat; "add one to the stock counter" is not. Prefer handlers that set state from the event over handlers that apply deltas, and check current state first.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text: Events can arrive out of order. If order matters, carry a version or timestamp in the payload and ignore anything older than what you have stored. Never rely on arrival order.

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text: 401 for a bad signature, 400 for an unparseable body, 200 for anything stored. Do not answer 5xx for business-processing problems: the event is safely stored, and a 5xx only makes the sender retry something you already have. Keep the error on the event record (state = "error") for a human.

docs.title: Outbound webhooks
docs.text: Sending mirrors this: sign the body, send with a timeout from a queue, retry with backoff, include a unique event id so the receiver can deduplicate. See External APIs for the client side.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Verifying a signature over parsed params instead of the raw body.
  • Comparing signatures with ==.
  • Processing inline, so the sender gives up and retries, creating the duplicate you then have to handle.
  • auth="public" and no sudo(): the public user cannot write. Use sudo() narrowly, on the event model only.
  • Leaking the secret in logs or views.
  • No unique constraint, then finding duplicate orders in production.
  • Trusting the payload for amounts or permissions. Treat it as a hint and refetch from the API when it matters.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: odoo.tools.consteq exists in 16, 17 and 18 (verified in 18). _sql_constraints is the declaration style in all three; check your build if you migrate to a later release.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Compute a signature locally and call your endpoint:

BODY='{"id":"evt_1","type":"loan.returned"}'
SIG=$(printf '%s' "$BODY" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$SECRET" | sed 's/^.* //')
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8069/library/webhook -H "X-Signature: $SIG" -d "$BODY"

Send it twice. The second call must also return 200 and create no new row.

docs.title: Coding standards
docs.text: Consistency is what lets a second developer open your module and find things. Odoo publishes its own guidelines; this chapter is the working subset, with the reasons and the review checklist we apply.

docs.title: Module layout
docs.text:
library/
  __init__.py
  __manifest__.py
  models/        # one file per model: library_book.py
  views/         # library_book_views.xml, library_menus.xml
  security/      # library_security.xml, ir.model.access.csv
  data/          # reference data, sequences, cron: noupdate where appropriate
  demo/          # demo data only
  wizard/        # transient models and their views
  controllers/
  report/
  static/        # src/js, src/xml, src/scss, description/icon.png
  tests/         # test_*.py, imported in tests/__init__.py
  i18n/          # .pot and translations

One model per file, named after the model with dots replaced by underscores. Add the import in models/__init__.py. Views for a model go in <model>_views.xml. Manifest data order: security first, then data, then views, then menus, then reports.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
• Model names: lowercase, dot-separated, module prefix: library.book. Table names follow by replacing dots.
  • Python classes: CamelCase of the model, LibraryBook; inherit classes: ResPartner.
  • Fields: snake_case. Many2one ends with _id, x2many with _ids. Booleans read as states: is_overdue, active. Avoid abbreviations.
  • Methods: _compute_<field>, _inverse_<field>, _search_<field>, _onchange_<field>, _check_<constraint> (decorated with @api.constrains), action_<verb> for button handlers, _default_<field>.
  • XML IDs: <model>_view_<type> (library_book_view_form), <model>_action, menu_library_<name>, <model>_rule_<what>, group_library_<role>. IDs are module-local, so no module prefix inside the module.
  • Never name a custom field with an x_ prefix in a module: that prefix is for fields created in the UI.

docs.title: Python style
docs.text:
• Follow PEP 8 with a line length of 120 (Odoo's linter settings); use ruff or flake8 plus pylint-odoo.
  • Import order: stdlib, third-party, odoo, odoo.addons.*, local. In this order, separated by blank lines.
  • Recordset loops should not call search or browse for each row; prefetch, mapped, filtered and read_group (named _read_group in 17 and later) exist for this.
  • Compute methods always assign the field on every record, including a default branch, or Odoo raises ValueError: Compute method failed to assign.
  • @api.depends lists every field the compute reads, including dotted paths. A missing dependency is a stale-value bug that survives code review for months.
  • Prefer _sql_constraints or database constraints for uniqueness, @api.constrains for logic that needs Python.
  • Use _() around user-visible messages, with %s placeholders and lazy formatting: _("Loan %s is overdue", loan.name).
  • Don't catch Exception broadly; an ORM error in a transaction aborts it, and swallowing it hides the failure until a later query. Wrap risky blocks in with self.env.cr.savepoint():.

Versions: _sql_constraints still works in 16 to 18; models.Constraint declarations replace it from 19, which is out of scope here. Likewise read_group is _read_group (private, tuple-returning) from 17 and public read_group remains for UI use.

docs.title: XML style
docs.text:
• Two-space indent, one attribute per line only when the line gets long.
  • Always name the record id and set string or name on views.
  • Use <field name="arch" type="xml"> with <list> in 18 (the tag <tree> was renamed in 18 and the old name is deprecated). Inherit with xpath on //field[@name='x'] and position, not on absolute positions.
  • Don't use attribute attrs and states in 17 and later; they were removed in 17 in favour of invisible, readonly, required as Python-like expressions.

docs.title: JavaScript
docs.text: Use ES modules (import/export) with /** @odoo-module **/ in 16 and 17; 18 treats files under static/src as modules by default and the header is no longer needed. Components are OWL. Follow the Prettier config of the repository.

docs.title: Review checklist
docs.text:
1. Does the module install on an empty database and upgrade cleanly on a copy of production?
  2. Does every new model have an ACL line, and a record rule where data is per company or per owner?
  3. Are there raw SQL or sudo() calls? Is each one justified in a comment?
  4. Do computes list full dependencies? Are expensive computes stored or indexed on purpose?
  5. Are loops free of per-record queries?
  6. Are user-visible strings translatable?
  7. Are there tests for the new behaviour, including one run as a non-admin user?
  8. Do views work for a user without every group? Are groups set on buttons and menus?
  9. Did the change touch data in data/ that needs noupdate or a migration script?
  10. Is the manifest version, depends and license correct, and are all new files listed?

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Reformatting unrelated code in a feature commit. It hides the real change and creates merge conflicts. Format on its own commit.
  • Business logic in views or controllers. Put it on the model so that RPC, cron, imports and tests share it.
  • Overriding create without @api.model_create_multi. The method receives a list of dicts since 14; ignoring that breaks batch creation.
  • Calling super() conditionally. Skipping it silently disables other modules' overrides.
  • Copy-pasting standard views. Inherit instead; a copy does not receive upstream fixes.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Add the linters to a copy of your module and see the baseline:

pip install ruff pylint-odoo
ruff check library/
pylint --load-plugins=pylint_odoo -d all -e odoolint library/

docs.title: Documenting your modules
docs.text: The person who maintains your module in two years has the code, the database and whatever you left next to them. Good documentation answers the questions the code cannot: what is this for, what are the non-obvious decisions, and how do I know it works. Keep it short, keep it in the repository, and keep it where it will be updated with the code.

docs.title: The manifest is documentation
docs.text:
{
    'name': 'Library',
    'summary': 'Book catalogue and loans',
    'description': """
Lets staff register books and lend them to members.
Overdue loans are flagged by a daily cron.
""",
    'category': 'Services/Library',
    'version': '18.0.1.0.0',
    'depends': ['base', 'mail'],
    'data': [...],
    'license': 'LGPL-3',
    'application': True,
}

summary is one line and shows in the Apps list. description in the manifest is legacy; Odoo prefers static/description/index.html for the Apps page, but a manifest description still works and is fine for internal modules. depends is documentation of coupling: keep it minimal and honest.

docs.title: README
docs.text:
One README.md (or README.rst, which the OCA tooling uses) at the module root, with these sections and no others unless needed:

  1. Purpose. Two or three sentences: the business problem, who uses it.
  2. Configuration. Settings, groups to assign, system parameters (ir.config_parameter keys), cron jobs and their schedule.
  3. Behaviour. The rules that are not obvious from the UI: what makes a loan overdue, who can extend it, what happens on archive.
  4. Technical notes. Models added or extended, hooks, known limitations, performance notes (stored computes, indexes).
  5. Upgrade notes. What each version changed that an operator must know.

Write for a developer who has not seen the project. Put a model diagram in text if there are more than three models.

docs.title: Docstrings and comments
docs.text:
Docstrings on models describe the concept, not the code:

class LibraryLoan(models.Model):
    """A book lent to one member.

    A loan is open until ``return_date`` is set. A book has at most one open
    loan, enforced by ``_check_single_open_loan``.
    """
    _name = 'library.loan'
    _description = 'Loan'

_description is mandatory in practice: it becomes the model's label in the UI and removes a log warning. Add help= to fields that users see; it becomes the tooltip and appears in fields_get, so it is user documentation for free.

Comments explain why:

# Not an SQL constraint: archived loans must be allowed to overlap.
@api.constrains('book_id', 'return_date')
def _check_single_open_loan(self): ...

Do not comment what the next line plainly does. Do comment: workarounds (with a ticket or upstream issue reference), ordering requirements, odd performance choices, and security decisions such as why a sudo() is safe.

docs.title: In-app help
docs.text:
• Field help for tooltips.
  • Action help for the empty-list message, which is the first thing a new user sees:
<field name="help" type="html">
  <p class="o_view_nocontent_smiling_face">Register your first book</p>
  <p>Books can be lent to members from here.</p>
</field>
  • Menu names and view titles in the language of the user. Terms should match across menus, fields and messages.

docs.title: Data models and decisions
docs.text:
For modules over a few models, add a docs/ folder with:

  • models.md: the models, key fields, relations (a text diagram is enough).
  • decisions.md: a log of choices, each with date, context and consequence ("Loans are not company-dependent because the library is shared"). A decision log is worth more than any amount of prose about what the code does.
  • runbook.md: how to check health (a SQL query that shows stuck records), how to rerun a failed cron, how to restore a deleted record.

Link them from the README.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
A CHANGELOG.md per module, newest first, one entry per manifest version bump, listing user-visible changes and any manual steps. It pairs with the migration scripts: if a version has a script, its changelog entry says what the script does.

## 18.0.1.2.0
- Overdue flag is now computed in the user timezone.
- Migration: renames loan.due to loan.due_date.

docs.title: Translations
docs.text: User-facing strings use _() in Python and are extracted automatically from XML. Keep an i18n/<module>.pot up to date at release time (export from Settings, Translations with the module selected, or odoo-bin --i18n-export). Translators are readers of your documentation too: avoid concatenated sentences and strings that depend on context they cannot see.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• README written once. Docs that are not updated with the code lie. Make "docs updated" an item in the review checklist.
  • Documenting the obvious. A paragraph per field wastes space; document the exceptions.
  • Client names and real data in examples. Docs get shared and copied. Use neutral sample data.
  • Tooltips as essays. A help text longer than three lines is a missing help page.
  • Orphan system parameters. Every ir.config_parameter key your code reads must appear in the README with its default and effect.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
List the models in your module with no _description, which also generates the log warning:

grep -rn "_name = " library/models | while read l; do f=${l%%:*}; grep -L "_description" "$f"; done | sort -u

docs.title: Git workflow for modules
docs.text: A module repository has an unusual constraint: the code is only half of the deployed state. The database holds data loaded from your XML, and an upgrade script may have to transform it. A good workflow treats the branch, the version bump and the migration as one unit.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text:
Either one repository per module group (the usual choice for a customer project) or one monorepo with modules at the top level, added to addons_path. Keep third-party modules in separate repositories or submodules, pinned to a commit, never copied into yours.

repo/
  library/
  library_loan_extras/
  .gitignore         # *.pyc, __pycache__, .venv, *.po~ , filestore never
  .pre-commit-config.yaml
  README.md

Do not commit the database, the filestore, odoo.conf with secrets, or exported production data. Add them to .gitignore before the first commit, because removing them from history later is painful.

docs.title: Branches
docs.text:
Name the long-lived branches after the Odoo version when you maintain more than one: 16.0, 17.0, 18.0. Odoo.sh requires that anyway: the branch you push is built into its own environment. Short-lived feature branches come off the version branch and return via a pull request:

18.0
 └─ feature/loan-overdue-cron
 └─ fix/loan-due-date-timezone

Rules that pay for themselves:

  • One concern per branch and per pull request.
  • Rebase the feature branch on the version branch before merging if your team prefers linear history; otherwise merge commits. Pick one and stick to it.
  • Never force-push a branch other people use. On a private feature branch it is fine.
  • Forward-port fixes across version branches with git cherry-pick -x, so the commit message records where it came from.

docs.title: Commits
docs.text:
Use a short imperative subject with a module tag, as the Odoo project does:

[FIX] library: compute due date in the user timezone

The cron compared naive UTC datetimes with a date, so loans due
today were flagged overdue after 22:00 local time.

Common tags: [ADD], [IMP], [FIX], [REF], [REM], [MIG], [I18N]. The body explains why, not what; the diff already says what. Reference the ticket in the body or the footer.

Keep commits atomic enough to revert. A commit that changes a model, its view, its security and its tests together is fine; a commit that also reformats five other files is not.

docs.title: What a module change must carry
docs.text:
1. Version bump in __manifest__.py, following <odoo_version>.<major>.<minor>.<patch> (for example 18.0.1.2.0). Bump it whenever a migration script is needed.
  2. Migration script when you rename a field or model, change a stored computed value, or change data semantics: migrations/18.0.1.2.0/pre-migrate.py and post-migrate.py, each with def migrate(cr, version):. Pre scripts run before the ORM loads the new definitions (rename columns here); post scripts run after (recompute, backfill).
  3. Tests for the behaviour.
  4. Data files loaded by the manifest, with noupdate chosen deliberately.
  5. Translations if strings changed (.pot export can wait until release).
# migrations/18.0.1.2.0/pre-migrate.py
def migrate(cr, version):
    if not version:
        return
    cr.execute("ALTER TABLE library_loan RENAME COLUMN due TO due_date")

Guard with if not version because the script also runs on fresh installs in some tooling. Test the migration on a restored copy of production, not on an empty database.

Versions: migration folders and the pre-, post-, end- script names work the same in 16, 17 and 18. The upgrade only runs when the manifest version is higher than the installed one.

docs.title: Moving between environments
docs.text:
The path is feature branch, staging (a copy of production data), then production. On Odoo.sh: push the feature branch to get a development build, merge to the staging branch to build on a copy of production data, merge to production once staging passes.

Before every production deployment:

  1. Upgrade a restored copy of the production database with the exact merged code, using -u your_module --stop-after-init.
  2. Run the test suite for changed modules on that copy.
  3. Click through the changed screens as a normal user, not only as admin.
  4. Take a backup and note the commit hash you deploy.

Deploying is git pull plus -u module plus a service restart; on a multi-worker server, restart all workers so that none runs old code against a new schema. For rollbacks, you need the backup: Odoo upgrades are not reversible by checking out the old commit, because the schema and data have moved on.

docs.title: Pre-commit
docs.text: A small .pre-commit-config.yaml with ruff, pylint-odoo and a trailing-whitespace check removes style debates from review. Run it in CI as well, so a missing local install does not skip the checks.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Editing already-merged migration scripts. Environments that ran the old version will not rerun it. Add a new version with a new script instead.
  • Forgetting the version bump. The code is deployed, but -u sees the same version and your pre-migrate script never runs.
  • Secrets in the history. Rotate, then clean; a deleted file still lives in older commits.
  • Dev data committed as data/. Demo or test records in data/ land in production. Put them in demo/.
  • Long-running branches. Odoo modules touch the same models; a month-old branch produces painful conflicts in views. Merge small and often.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Show what would change in the manifest and migrations between your branch and the version branch, read-only:

git diff --stat 18.0...HEAD -- '*/__manifest__.py' '*/migrations/*'

docs.title: HTTP and tour tests
docs.text: HttpCase boots the real HTTP stack in the test process and, optionally, a headless Chrome. You use it to test controllers (status codes, redirects, access) and complete UI flows (tours). These tests are slower than model tests, so keep them for what the model layer cannot show.

docs.title: Testing controllers
docs.text:
from odoo.tests import HttpCase, tagged


@tagged('post_install', '-at_install')
class TestLibraryController(HttpCase):

    def test_loan_page_requires_login(self):
        res = self.url_open('/library/loan/1', allow_redirects=False)
        self.assertIn(res.status_code, (303, 401, 403, 404))

    def test_loan_page_as_user(self):
        self.authenticate('plain_emp', 'plain_emp')
        res = self.url_open('/library/loan/%d' % self.loan.id)
        self.assertEqual(res.status_code, 200)

url_open(url, data=None, headers=None, timeout=...) returns a requests response; if data is given it POSTs. authenticate(login, password) logs the test session in; password equals login for users you create with password set the same. The server runs in the same process and shares the test cursor, so records created in setUp are visible, and changes made by the request are visible to your assertions without committing.

For JSON routes, post with self.make_jsonrpc_request(route, params) where available, or url_open with a JSON body and header Content-Type: application/json.

Versions: HttpCase warns when not post_install (verified in 18 common.py). url_open and authenticate exist in 16, 17 and 18; make_jsonrpc_request was added in 17.

Always include negative tests: an anonymous user, a user of another company, a user without the group. A controller that works for admin and leaks to the public passes a happy-path test.

docs.title: Tours
docs.text:
A tour is a scripted UI scenario written in JavaScript, registered in the web_tour.tours registry and run by the browser. In 18 the format is:

import { registry } from "@web/core/registry";

registry.category("web_tour.tours").add("library_loan_tour", {
    url: "/odoo/action-library.action_library_loan",
    steps: () => [
        { trigger: ".o_list_button_add", run: "click" },
        { trigger: ".o_field_widget[name=book_id] input", run: "edit Test Book" },
        { trigger: ".dropdown-item:contains('Test Book')", run: "click" },
        { trigger: ".o_form_button_save", run: "click" },
        { trigger: ".o_form_saved" },
    ],
});

Declare the file in the manifest under assets with the bundle web.assets_tests, and run it from Python:

def test_loan_tour(self):
    self.start_tour('/odoo', 'library_loan_tour', login='plain_emp')

start_tour(url_path, tour_name, step_delay=None, **kwargs) opens the page in headless Chrome and waits for the tour to finish; extra kwargs include login. A tour fails when a step's trigger is not found within the timeout, and the log prints the step and the page state.

Versions: the URL scheme changed. 16 and 17 use /web#action=...; 18 uses /odoo/action-... and /odoo. Tour step syntax also changed: 16 tours use run: "click" and old helpers such as run: function (actions); 17 and 18 prefer string run actions. Tours written for 16 need review when ported.

docs.title: Writing stable tours
docs.text:
• Trigger on stable selectors: field names ([name=book_id]), data- attributes, and o_* classes that are part of the framework. Avoid CSS paths based on position.
  • Wait for the right thing. A step that clicks and then reads must have a trigger that is only present after the previous action completed (.o_form_saved, a notification, a breadcrumb).
  • Keep tours short: one flow, 10 to 25 steps. If it breaks you want to know which flow.
  • Prepare the data in Python, in setUp. The tour should drive the UI, not set up the world through it.
  • Remember demo vs no demo. Tours must pass without demo data.

docs.title: Debugging a tour
docs.text:
Run in a visible browser so that you can watch:

def test_loan_tour_debug(self):
    self.start_tour('/odoo', 'library_loan_tour', login='plain_emp', watch=True)

watch=True opens a real browser window (needs a local Chrome and a display). Also debug=True pauses at the end for inspection in devtools. Never commit either flag. Alternatively, run the tour manually: open the URL with ?debug=assets,tests (18) and use the tour menu in the debug toolbar to step through it.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Chrome not installed in CI. Tours are skipped or fail with "Chrome headless not found". Install Chrome or Chromium on the runner, and fail loudly instead of skipping.
  • Flaky waits. sleep in a tour is a smell. Replace it with a trigger on the state you await.
  • Tests leaking data across tours. A tour that creates a record in the UI commits to the test cursor; the rollback at the end handles it, but a second tour in the same class sees the data. Use separate test methods and unique names.
  • Slow suites. A HttpCase per page is expensive. Group steps into a single tour, test permissions with url_open instead.
  • Assets not rebuilt. If you change tour JS and the test does not notice, clear the asset bundles (ir.attachment entries with /web/assets/ URLs) or run with --dev=assets locally.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Run a single HTTP test class and show the browser console log:

odoo-bin -d scratch -u library --test-tags /library:TestLibraryController --stop-after-init --log-level=test

docs.title: Writing tests
docs.text: Odoo's test framework is unittest with a database-backed base class. Each test method runs inside a transaction that is rolled back, so tests are isolated and fast. This chapter covers the classes you will use, how to set up data, how to test as a specific user, and how to run only what you need.

docs.title: The base classes
docs.text:
All live in odoo/tests/common.py, re-exported from odoo.tests:

Class Use TransactionCase Default. One transaction per test method, rolled back afterwards. setUpClass data is shared and also rolled back at the end of the class. SingleTransactionCase One transaction for the whole class; tests depend on order. Rarely a good idea. HttpCase Adds url_open, authenticate, and browser tours. See the next chapter. BaseCase The parent of those; you do not subclass it directly.

docs.title: A first test
docs.text:
from odoo.tests import TransactionCase, tagged
from odoo.exceptions import AccessError, ValidationError


@tagged('post_install', '-at_install')
class TestLibraryLoan(TransactionCase):

    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        super().setUpClass()
        cls.book = cls.env['library.book'].create({'name': 'Test Book'})
        cls.member = cls.env['res.partner'].create({'name': 'Test Member'})

    def test_loan_sets_due_date(self):
        loan = self.env['library.loan'].create({
            'book_id': self.book.id,
            'borrower_id': self.member.id,
        })
        self.assertTrue(loan.due_date)

    def test_cannot_loan_twice(self):
        vals = {'book_id': self.book.id, 'borrower_id': self.member.id}
        self.env['library.loan'].create(vals)
        with self.assertRaises(ValidationError):
            self.env['library.loan'].create(vals)

Use setUpClass for data that tests only read. Anything a test mutates should be created inside the test, or the tests will depend on each other. Never forget super().setUpClass(): it sets up cls.env and the registry cleanup.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
@tagged selects when and under what label a test runs. By default, tests are standard and at_install: they run right after their module is installed, before other modules. For tests that need the whole registry (inherits from other modules, HTTP), use post_install and remove at_install:

@tagged('post_install', '-at_install')

You can add custom tags (@tagged('library_slow')) and select with --test-tags. The default set is standard, so untagged tests always run.

Versions: @tagged, post_install, at_install and the -tag exclusion syntax are the same in 16, 17 and 18. HttpCase logs a warning if it is not post_install (from common.py).

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
Run a module's tests on a throwaway database, never on production:

odoo-bin -d test_db -i library --test-enable --stop-after-init
odoo-bin -d test_db -u library --test-tags /library --stop-after-init
odoo-bin -d test_db --test-tags /library:TestLibraryLoan.test_cannot_loan_twice -u library --stop-after-init

The tag selector format is [-][tag][/module][:class][.method]. --test-enable is implied by --test-tags in recent versions; keeping it is harmless. Use --log-level=test for more test output. On Odoo.sh the test run happens in the build; read the build log's "Tests" section.

docs.title: Testing as a user
docs.text:
def test_employee_cannot_delete(self):
    employee = self.env['res.users'].create({
        'name': 'Plain Employee', 'login': 'plain_emp',
        'groups_id': [(6, 0, [self.env.ref('library.group_library_user').id])],
    })
    loan = self.env['library.loan'].create({...})
    with self.assertRaises(AccessError):
        loan.with_user(employee).unlink()

with_user accepts a user record or id; self.env['x'].with_user(self.env.ref('base.user_demo')) also works if demo data is loaded, but don't depend on demo. Create your users in setUpClass.

If you create users, use new_test_user from odoo.addons.mail.tests.common where mail is a dependency: it handles groups and avoids notification side effects. Otherwise, set no_reset_password=True in the context to prevent invitation mails.

docs.title: Assertions worth knowing
docs.text:
• assertRecordValues(records, [{'field': value}, ...]) compares recordsets against dicts and reports diffs clearly. Order matters unless you sort.
  • assertQueryCount(admin=3) fixes the SQL query count for a block, a cheap regression guard against N+1.
  • with self.assertRaises(...) is wrapped by Odoo to use a savepoint, so the transaction stays usable after the exception. Plain unittest doesn't do this.
  • Form(record) from odoo.tests simulates the form view: onchanges, defaults, required fields, readonly rules.
from odoo.tests import Form

with Form(self.env['library.loan']) as f:
    f.book_id = self.book
    f.borrower_id = self.member
loan = f.save()

Form fails if a field is not in the view or is readonly, which makes it useful for testing that the view is usable, not just the model.

docs.title: Time and mail
docs.text: Freeze time with freezegun when the dependency exists (from freezegun import freeze_time), or use the Odoo helpers in odoo.tests.common (freeze_time is re-exported in recent versions). Mail sent in tests is not delivered; the mail queue is mocked in the framework, and mail.mail records can be inspected. Crons are not run automatically: call self.env.ref('library.cron_overdue')._trigger() is not enough, call the method directly.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
A test that passes alone and fails in the suite is almost always shared state: a record created in setUpClass and mutated, a cached ir.config_parameter, or a registry-level change. Make tests independent first.

  • cr.commit() in code under test. In tests the cursor is wrapped, so the commit is a no-op; code that relies on committed data in a second cursor will behave differently.
  • Testing as admin only. The superuser skips ACLs and rules. A test that never switches user proves nothing about security.
  • Relying on demo data. The test database may be created without demo. Create what you need.
  • at_install tests that depend on other modules. They run before later modules install. Use post_install.
  • Too many assertions on dates. fields.Date.today() changes at midnight. Fix the date explicitly.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Run only one test class and see its SQL count on a scratch database:

odoo-bin -d scratch -u library --test-tags /library:TestLibraryLoan --stop-after-init --log-level=test

docs.title: Deprecations
docs.text: Odoo marks an API as deprecated, logs a warning for a release or two, then removes it. The cost of ignoring the warnings is paid at the next upgrade, all at once. Many deprecations in the source carry their version in the message (Since 20.0, use ..., deprecated since 18.0), so the source itself tells you how long you have.

docs.title: Surface the warnings
docs.text:
odoo-bin -d dev -u library --stop-after-init --log-level=warn 2>&1 | grep -iE "deprecat|since (1[6-9]|20)"

Run the test suite with warnings visible too: many deprecations are raised only when the code path executes. To turn them into failures in tests, run Python with -W error::DeprecationWarning.

docs.title: Replacement table
docs.text:
Old New Deprecated or removed Checked in attrs, states in views invisible, readonly, required expressions removed in 17.0 17.0 view validation name_get() display_name, _compute_display_name deprecated 17.0, removed 18.0 17.0 and 18.0 models.py _name_search (old signature) _search_display_name(operator, value) returning a domain 18.0 18.0 models.py <tree>, view_mode tree <list>, list 18.0 18.0 ir_ui_view.py, script 17.5-01-tree-to-list.py ir.property rows company-dependent jsonb column removed 18.0 18.0 has no ir_property.py check_access_rights, check_access_rule, _filter_access_rules check_access, has_access, _filtered_access deprecated 18.0, removed 20 18.0 and 20 models.py @route(type='json') @route(type='jsonrpc') deprecated alias since 19.0 20 routing_map.py, script 18.1-02 _sql_constraints = [...] _name = models.Constraint(...) 19.0 script 18.1-00-sql-constraint.py self._cr, self._uid, self._context self.env.cr, self.env.uid, self.env.context deprecated 19.0 20 models.py, script 18.5-00 request.cr, request.uid, request.context request.env.cr, .uid, .context deprecated 19.0 20 http/requestlib.py ir.model.access + ir.rule data ir.access 20 script 19.4-00-ir-access.py check_field_access_rights check_field_access(field, operation) 20 20 models.py registry.clear_cache transaction.invalidate_ormcache 20 script 19.4-00 from odoo.tools import ormcache from odoo.api import ormcache 20 20 tools/__init__.py type="base64" in XML data type="bytes" 20 20 tools/convert.py

A row marked "Checked in 20" was read in the Odoo 20 tree. Odoo 19 itself was not installed, so 19 entries rest on the deprecation messages and scripts.

docs.title: Let the scripts rewrite what they can
docs.text:
Odoo 18 and later include odoo-bin upgrade_code, which applies the scripts in odoo/upgrade_code/ to the Python, XML, JS, CSS and CSV files of every addon on the addons path:

# list what would change, rewrite nothing
odoo-bin upgrade_code --addons-path=./my_addons --from 17.5 --dry-run

# apply one script
odoo-bin upgrade_code --addons-path=./my_addons --script tree-to-list

# apply every script from a version up to the current one
odoo-bin upgrade_code --addons-path=./my_addons --from 17.5

The options are --script, --from, --to (default: the running server's version), --glob to restrict files, --dry-run and --addons-path. The command exits with status 1 when it changed files, which is useful in CI. Read the diff: the docstring of the command says the scripts are "best-effort" and "not silver bullets". Commit the result on its own so the mechanical change is reviewable.

docs.title: Replace in an order that can be reviewed
docs.text:
1. Scripted XML and Python rewrites in one commit.
  2. Hand-written API replacements in a second commit, with tests.
  3. JavaScript last. A change of framework version is a rewrite, not a port, so keep it out of the mechanical commits.

docs.title: Writing code that is deprecated later
docs.text:
• Use the public ORM (search, browse, write, _read_group) and stay away from private helpers whose names start with _ unless a chapter names them.
  • Prefer registry entries and subclasses to patch() in JavaScript.
  • Keep raw SQL in one method per model and build it with SQL.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Silencing warnings in odoo.conf to quiet a noisy log removes the early signal.
  • Overriding name_get on 18 or later does nothing, because the method no longer exists.
  • Assuming read_group and _read_group are the same API: the web client uses read_group, Python code should use _read_group.
  • Running upgrade_code without --dry-run on a dirty working tree mixes your edits with its rewrites.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Run odoo-bin upgrade_code --addons-path=... --from 17.5 --dry-run on a copy of a 17.0 module and read the list.
  2. Run it for real on a branch and diff.
  3. Grep the result for attrs=, states= and name_get and fix what the scripts could not.
Solution notes
  1. The dry run lists the files the scripts would rewrite, grouped by script.
  2. Expect <tree> to <list> changes in XML, view_mode values, and tree_view_ref context keys.
  3. attrs and states are not converted by a script in the 20 tree, so those are manual.

docs.title: Migration scripts
docs.text: When a module's version in the manifest goes up and the module is updated (-u), Odoo can run your Python scripts before the module's data is loaded, after it, and after all modules are updated. This is where you rename columns, backfill new fields and clean data that the ORM cannot convert by itself. The mechanism below is read from odoo/modules/migration.py (18.0; the 20 tree has the same logic).

docs.title: Where scripts live
docs.text:
library/
  __manifest__.py              # 'version': '18.0.1.2.0'
  migrations/
    1.1/
      pre-rename-isbn.py
      post-fill-shelf.py
